RECOMMENDATION
Conduct a public hearing and upon its conclusion:
  (1) Adopt a Resolution certifying the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry
      Project Environmental Impact Report (EIR) (SCH #2025040995) and adopt
      related California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) findings, a statement of
      overriding considerations, mitigation measures, and a mitigation monitoring and
      reporting program (Attachment 1), and
  (2) Adopt a Resolution Approving the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry
      Project and affirming, as modified to incorporate the CEQA findings and
      mitigation measures, the decision of the Zoning Adjustments Board to approve
      Use Permit #ZP2026-0014 to establish transportation via public ferry service as
      an allowable use at the Berkeley Pier (Attachment 2), with certain clarifying
      modifications.


SUMMARY
The Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project (Project) would replace a portion
of the Berkeley Municipal Pier (approximately 1,080 ft), which has been closed to the
public since 2015, with a new dual-purpose public pier and breakwater that support both
public recreation and zero-emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San
Francisco, operated by the San Francisco Bay Area Water Emergency Transportation
Authority (WETA). In addition to the pier, breakwater and ferry terminal infrastructure
(including dredging), the Project also includes a new public plaza with public amenities,
improvements to University Avenue and Seawall Drive (including a raised cycle track
and expanded AC Transit bus facilities), renovation of the Seawall Drive parking lot, a
segment of the planned Bay Trail Extension, and shoreline erosion repair.

As lead agency under CEQA, the City prepared an EIR to evaluate the potentially
significant environmental effects of the Project. The Draft EIR was circulated for a 60-
day public review period from February 27, 2026 to April 28, 2026, and the Final EIR,

which includes responses to all comments on environmental issues received, was
published on November 5, 2026. The EIR concludes that all of the Project's significant
environmental effects can be reduced to less-than-significant levels through mitigation,
except for construction noise associated with pile driving and the Project's contribution
to cumulative noise, and the land use and recreation impacts resulting from that noise,
which would remain significant and unavoidable.

The Berkeley Waterfront is zoned Unclassified (U); therefore, a Use Permit is required
to establish any new use. The Planning Commission reviewed the Use Permit
application on January 21, 2026 and adopted a resolution recommending approval (6-0-
0-3), and the Zoning Adjustments Board (ZAB) approved Use Permit #ZP2026-0014 on
February 26, 2026 (5-0-3). Under the Berkeley Municipal Code (BMC), the ZAB’s
decision is not effective until the City Council acts, and the Council may affirm, reverse,
or modify it. This is not an appeal; Council action is required for all Use Permits in U
districts. Staff recommend that the Council affirm the ZAB decision, modified to
incorporate the Final EIR, the CEQA Findings, and the mitigation measures, and to
make minor technical corrections (Attachment 2, Exhibit A).

This report asks the City Council to take two sequential actions with distinct legal
standards. First, the Council would consider whether to certify the Final EIR as a
complete and adequate environmental document and adopt the related CEQA Findings,
Statement of Overriding Considerations, mitigation measures, and Mitigation Monitoring
and Reporting Program (MMRP) (Attachment 1). Certification requires findings that the
EIR was completed in compliance with CEQA, was reviewed and considered by the
Council, and reflects the City’s independent judgment (CEQA Guidelines Section
15090). The CEQA Findings and Statement of Overriding Considerations address each
significant impact and state the reasons the Project may be approved notwithstanding
its significant and unavoidable impacts (CEQA Guidelines Sections 15091 and 15093).

Second, the Council would consider a resolution approving the Project and affirming, as
modified, the ZAB’s decision to approve the Use Permit (Attachment 2), in reliance on
the certified EIR and the CEQA Findings, Statement of Overriding Considerations, and
MMRP adopted in the first resolution. This sequence is consistent with the process
described in Sections 1.1.4 and 1.5 of the Draft EIR.

FISCAL IMPACTS OF RECOMMENDATION
None. Certification of the EIR, adoption of the CEQA Findings, Statement of Overriding
Considerations, mitigation measures, and MMRP, approval of the Project, affirmation of
the ZAB decision and issuance of the Use Permit would have no direct fiscal impact and
does not commit the City to expenditure of construction funds.

Project Description
The Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry EIR evaluates the following Project
components:
   •   Demolition of portions of the closed Berkeley Pier;
   •   A new 1,080-foot-long public pier at the location of the closed pier, with
       pedestrian access and recreational amenities including interpretive and
       educational signage, public seating, a shade canopy, and a fish cleaning station;
   •   A new breakwater perpendicular to and connected to the pier, providing a safe
       harbor for ferry berthing as well as pedestrian access and recreational amenities
       (400 feet in length in the proposed project as analyzed in the Draft EIR;
       approximately 300 feet in length under Alternative 2, as discussed below);
   •   Ferry infrastructure, including charging and boarding float(s), landing(s),
       gangway(s), and a security entrance. The EIR also evaluates a second ferry
       berth to provide CEQA coverage for future expansion; initial construction is
       anticipated to include a single berth, and any future second berth would be
       subject to City and other agency permitting;
   •   One-time dredging along the existing U.S. Army Corps of Engineers federal
       navigation channel that parallels the closed pier, as well as at a turning basin at
       the ferry landing(s);
   •   A new public plaza with a public restroom, seating, bicycle parking, landscaping,
       and stormwater treatment;
   •   University Avenue improvements between the Marina Boulevard roundabout and
       Seawall Drive, including repaving and restriping, a raised cycle track, new
       sidewalks, a passenger drop-off zone, relocation of an existing AC Transit bus
       stop, and new bus loading facilities;
   •   Seawall Drive realignment, repaving, and restriping, landscaping, picnic sites,
       stormwater treatment, and construction of a segment of the planned Bay Trail
       Extension;
   •   Renovation of the Seawall Drive parking lot, including new paving, striping,
       lighting, electric vehicle charging, stormwater treatment, and replacement of
       existing stormwater outfalls;
   •   Repair of approximately 300 feet of eroding shoreline on the eastern side of the
       Seawall peninsula with rock riprap slope protection;
   •   New landscaping, tree removal and replacement, wayfinding signage, lighting,
       and utility connections, including electrical infrastructure to charge ferry vessels;
       and




                                               Page 3

   •   Operation of zero-emission electric passenger ferry service between the
       Berkeley ferry terminal and San Francisco.
The EIR also evaluates solar panels on raised canopies over the renovated Seawall
Drive parking lot as an optional improvement.

Environmental Review

The EIR was made available for review on the City’s website and the Project website,
and at 2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704. The environmental review process for
the Project has included:
   •   April 18, 2025. A Notice of Preparation (NOP) of a Draft EIR was circulated to
       public agencies, organizations, and interested parties for a 31-day comment
       period ending May 19, 2025.
   •   May 5, 2025. The City held an EIR scoping meeting, at which 12 members of the
       public provided verbal comments. The City also received written scoping
       comments from 6 agencies, 3 Native American tribes, 7 organizations, and 17
       individuals.
   •   February 27, 2026. A Notice of Availability (NOA) and Notice of Completion
       (NOC) of the Draft EIR was distributed and the Draft EIR was published for a 45-
       day public review period.
   •   March 16, 2026. The City held an online public meeting on the Draft EIR, at
       which 23 individuals provided verbal comments.
   •   April 1, 2026. The City issued a revised NOA extending the public review period
       by 15 days.
   •   April 28, 2026. The public comment period closed, for a total public review
       period of 60 days. The City received 102 written comment letters and emails on
       the Draft EIR.
   •   November 5, 2026. The Final EIR, consisting of the Draft EIR, Responses to
       Comments, and revisions to the Draft EIR (Errata), was published. Proposed
       written responses were provided to public agencies that commented on the Draft
       EIR at least 10 days prior to certification.
City Council certification that the EIR was prepared in compliance with CEQA is
required to complete the environmental review of the Project.

Tribal Consultation (AB 52)

Pursuant to Assembly Bill 52 (Public Resources Code Section 21080.3.1), the City
notified California Native American tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated
with the Project area and conducted consultation with the tribes that requested it. The
goal of tribal consultation is to avoid significant effects on tribal cultural resources or to
develop mutually agreed upon mitigation measures. The mitigation measures identified
in the EIR for tribal cultural resources (Mitigation Measures TCR-1 through TCR-5),

Draft EIR

Potentially Significant Impacts Identified in the Draft EIR

All environmental impacts and mitigation measures are summarized in the CEQA
Findings and Statement of Overriding Considerations (Attachment 1, Exhibit B). Other
than the impacts discussed below, all of the environmental effects of the Project can be
reduced to less-than-significant levels through implementation of the mitigation
measures identified in the EIR.

The Draft EIR1 identified significant and unavoidable impacts related to noise at both the
project level and the cumulative level. At the project level, the impact is related to
construction noise. At the cumulative level, the impact is related to both construction
noise due to potential overlapping construction periods and operational noise due to
vehicle traffic. Although most project-related construction noise impacts (Impact NOI-1)
would be reduced to less-than-significant levels through implementation of a
Construction Noise Management Plan (Mitigation Measure NOI-1), noise from daytime
and nighttime pile installation and demolition would continue to exceed City noise
standards at Shorebird Park and at some live-aboard boats in the Marina. These same
construction noise levels would be inconsistent with the noise standards of the Berkeley
Municipal Code, and would result from construction of the Project’s recreational
facilities. For that reason, the Draft EIR also identified related significant and
unavoidable impacts to Land Use and Planning (Impact LU-2) and Recreation (Impact
REC-2). These land use and recreation impacts are not independent physical effects.
They result directly from the same underlying construction noise.

The Draft EIR also found that the Project would make a cumulatively considerable
contribution to significant and unavoidable cumulative impacts related to Noise, Land
Use and Planning, and Recreation. These cumulative impacts result from potentially
overlapping construction of other planned projects at the Berkeley Waterfront and
cumulative operational vehicle noise on portions of University Avenue. As with project-
level impacts, the cumulative land use and recreation impacts are directly attributable to
the underlying cumulative noise impacts. The Findings include a Statement of
Overriding Considerations that provides the reasons the Project may be approved
notwithstanding their project-level and cumulative significant and unavoidable impacts.

Alternatives
As required by the CEQA Guidelines, an EIR must examine a range of reasonable
alternatives to the proposed project that would feasibly attain most of the basic project
objectives and avoid or substantially lessen the project’s significant environmental
impacts. The Draft EIR evaluated the following alternatives (see Draft EIR Chapter 5,
including Table 5-2, which compares the impacts of each alternative to the proposed
project):
   •   Alternative 1: No Project Alternative. None of the Project improvements would
       occur. The deteriorated pier would remain closed, no ferry service would be
       established, and existing conditions would continue. This alternative would avoid
       construction impacts but would result in greater long-term impacts related to
       aesthetics, air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, land use, and transportation,
       and would not meet any of the Project objectives.
   •   Alternative 2: Shortened Breakwater Alternative. All Project components
       would be constructed as proposed, but with a breakwater of approximately 300
       feet rather than 400 feet. The Project’s coastal study found that a 300-foot
       breakwater would provide sufficient sheltering for ferry operations, with only
       marginal additional benefit from a 400-foot breakwater. This alternative would
       reduce construction intensity, Bay fill, and pile installation, and associated
       impacts to air quality, biological resources, hydrology and water quality, and
       noise, while meeting most Project objectives with slightly reduced public access.
   •   Alternative 3: Shortened Pier Alternative. The pier would be shortened from
       approximately 1,080 feet to approximately 675 feet and would terminate at the
       breakwater. This alternative would reduce construction impacts but would
       substantially reduce public access and recreational opportunities.
   •   Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative. The pier, breakwater,
       and ferry infrastructure would be constructed, but most landside improvements
       (the public plaza, cycle track, Bay Trail Extension, parking lot upgrades, electric
       vehicle charging, and bus facilities) would be eliminated. This alternative would
       reduce certain construction impacts but could increase long-term impacts related
       to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, land use, and transportation, and would
       meet the Project objectives to a much lesser extent.
None of the alternatives other than the No Project Alternative would avoid the Project’s
significant and unavoidable construction noise impacts, because pile driving would still
be required.

Environmentally Superior Alternative. CEQA requires identification of the
environmentally superior alternative among those studied. Because the No Project
Alternative would not meet any Project objectives, the EIR identifies Alternative 4 as the
environmentally superior alternative among the action alternatives, as it would reduce
the greatest number of construction-related impacts. However, Alternative 4 would
eliminate key Project elements and would achieve the Project objectives to a




                                               Page 6
                                          Page 7 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Environmental Impact      PUBLIC HEARING
Report, Project Approval, and Use Permit                                   November 17, 2026


substantially lesser extent than both the project as proposed in the Draft EIR and the
preferred alternative (Alternative 2).

Preferred Alternative. The CEQA Findings identify Alternative 2, the Shortened
Breakwater Alternative, as the preferred alternative and the proposed Project, because
it reduces construction-related environmental impacts associated with Bay fill, pile
installation, and construction intensity while continuing to achieve the Project objectives
to a greater extent than the other alternatives. The Findings find Alternatives 1, 3, and 4
infeasible for the specific social, economic, and environmental reasons described in
Attachment 1, Exhibit B. Approval of the Project will be considered by the City Council
as a separate resolution.

Final EIR
The Final EIR consists of the Draft EIR, Responses to Comments on the Draft EIR, and
revisions to the Draft EIR (Errata), all of which are attached. The City received written
and oral comments on the Draft EIR during the public comment period (February 27,
2026 through April 28, 2026). All written comments are reproduced in their entirety in
the Final EIR, and responses are provided to all comments on the Draft EIR that pertain
to environmental issues and include revisions to the Draft EIR text that correct errors or
omissions or clarify information presented in the Draft EIR. The Final EIR was made
available for review through the City’s website at https://berkeleyca.gov/your-
government/our-work/capital-projects/berkeley-pier-ferry-access-project and at the
Parks, Recreation & Waterfront Department at 2180 Milvia Street (3rd Floor).

In no case do the revisions in the Final EIR result in a new significant impact or a
substantial increase in the severity of an impact identified in the Draft EIR such that
recirculation of the Draft EIR would be required.

Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP)
The EIR identifies 20 mitigation measures that will be implemented to reduce the
Project’s impacts, addressing aesthetics, air quality, biological resources, cultural
resources, geology and soils (paleontological resources), hydrology and water quality,
noise, and tribal cultural resources. For public agency projects, mitigation measures are
adopted and incorporated into the project at the time of approval. CEQA requires the
lead agency to adopt a mitigation, monitoring and reporting program for monitoring and
reporting on compliance with the adopted mitigation measures. The MMRP (Attachment
1, Exhibit A) identifies, for each measure, the action required, the timing and frequency
for implementing the action, the entity responsible for implementing the action, and the
agency or department responsible for verifying compliance. The City of Berkeley and its
contractors will implement most measures; WETA is identified as a potential
implementing entity for measures associated with dredging.

CEQA Findings and Statement of Overriding Considerations
For each significant impact identified in an EIR, CEQA requires that the lead agency
make one or more of the following findings:
   1. Changes or alterations have been required in, or incorporated into, the project
      which avoid or substantially lessen the significant environmental effect;
   2. Such changes or alterations are within the responsibility and jurisdiction of
      another public agency and have been, or can and should be, adopted by that
      agency; or
   3. Specific economic, legal, social, technological, or other considerations make
      infeasible the mitigation measures or project alternatives identified in the EIR.
The CEQA Findings (Attachment 1, Exhibit B) find that implementation of the mitigation
measures identified in the MMRP will reduce all significant impacts of the Project to
less-than-significant levels, except for the noise impacts and related land use and
recreation impacts described above, for which no additional feasible mitigation has been
identified.

CEQA Guidelines Section 15093(b) provides that when a public agency’s decision
results in significant impacts that are not avoided or substantially lessened, the agency
must state in writing the reasons to support its action. The Statement of Overriding
Considerations is a formal statement by the City that, having balanced the economic,
legal, social, technological, and other benefits of the Project, including region-wide and
statewide environmental benefits, against its significant and unavoidable environmental
impacts, the benefits of the Project outweigh its unavoidable adverse effects. In this
balancing, the Statement considers that the significant and unavoidable project-level
impacts would be temporary, limited to waterside construction activities involving pile
driving (an estimated 80 to 90 days), while the Project would provide benefits over a
design life of at least 50 years. As relates to cumulative impacts, the Statement
considers the project contribution compared to the cumulative contribution, and that
finding is based on a conservative assumption of the maximum buildout scenario in a
draft, un-adopted Waterfront Specific Plan document. The Statement of Overriding
Considerations identifies the following benefits:
   •   Recreational benefits. The Project would restore public access to the Bay by
       replacing the pier that has been closed since 2015 due to disrepair with a new
       public pier, breakwater, and ADA-accessible public plaza, and would construct a
       segment of the Bay Trail at the Berkeley Waterfront, which MTC’s Bay Trail Gap
       Closure Implementation Plan designates as a Tier 1 (higher priority, lower cost)
       gap closure.
   •   Transportation benefits. The Project would provide new transbay public ferry
       service, improving regional connectivity and access to jobs and education for
       East Bay residents, including West Berkeley, an area with relatively limited
       regional transit access. The ferry terminal, including the portion of pier used to
       access the terminal, is designed as an essential facility to support WETA’s



                                               Page 8
                                          Page 9 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Environmental Impact     PUBLIC HEARING
Report, Project Approval, and Use Permit                                  November 17, 2026


       emergency water transportation mandate when other transportation systems are
       disrupted.
   •   Sustainability benefits. Operation of zero-emission electric ferries and
       multimodal access improvements would result in an annual net reduction of
       approximately 2,368 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (MTCO₂e) and a
       net reduction of approximately 22,435 MTCO₂e over 30 years after accounting
       for construction emissions compared to the status quo if the Project is not
       approved. The Project also incorporates sea level rise adaptation and shoreline
       protection.
   •   Social benefits. The Project would invest in safe bicycle and pedestrian
       infrastructure and accessible facilities and would generate economic benefits
       through increased Waterfront visitation and support for existing local businesses.
       Increased visitation also contributes to the improvement in the perception of and
       actual safety at the Waterfront.
Use Permit #ZP2026-0014

The Berkeley Waterfront is a single parcel (APN 60-2545-1) designated
Waterfront/Marina in the General Plan and zoned Unclassified (U). In the U district, all
uses not prohibited by law are permitted, but a Use Permit is required to establish any
use (BMC Section 23.208.020(B)). Existing uses at the Waterfront are authorized by
Use Permit #5567, issued in January 1965 in accordance with the Berkeley Marina
Master Plan. Repair and replacement of existing infrastructure serving existing uses,
including replacement of the existing Berkeley Pier, trails, streets, parking areas, and
public spaces, does not require a new Use Permit.

Use Permit #ZP2026-0014 establishes a new use, transportation, specifically public
zero-emission electric ferry service, at the Berkeley Pier. Notably, all existing uses, such
as recreation, fishing, and parking, would continue as previously authorized. The ferry
terminal facilities that accommodate this new use are in-water infrastructure: charging
and boarding float(s), ferry gate and landing, gangway(s), and a breakwater. These
facilities would be designed to essential facility standards so that the ferry can serve as
a disaster response and recovery resource following a significant seismic event. WETA
would operate the ferry service. Prior to initiation of service, the City and WETA would
execute a Memorandum of Understanding or similar agreement, subject to Council
approval, authorizing WETA’s use of portions of the Berkeley Pier for ferry operations,
maintenance, and capital improvements.

BMC Section 23.208.020(C) establishes the review process for Use Permits in the U
district:

      The application is first submitted to the Planning Commission, which makes a
       report to the ZAB;




                                               Page 9
                                         Page 10 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Environmental Impact     PUBLIC HEARING

      ZAB then acts to approve, conditionally approve, or deny the application. The
       ZAB’s decision is not effective until after action by the City Council, and ZAB
       decisions may not be appealed; and

      The City Council reviews and acts on the application, and may affirm, reverse, or
       modify the ZAB decision.

The development standards for a project in the U district are set forth in the Use Permit
itself (BMC Section 23.208.020(D)), and ZAB, Planning Commission, and City Council
must all make the findings for approval in BMC Section 23.406.030(F) (BMC Section
23.208.020(E)).

Planning Commission Review

On January 21, 2026, the Planning Commission reviewed the Use Permit application
and recommended that the ZAB and City Council approve the Use Permit, including
findings pursuant to BMC Section 23.208.020(E) (Ayes: Marthinsen, Vincent, Oatfield,
Twu, Hauser, and Wang; Noes: None; Abstain: None; Absent: Owens, Kahn, and
Merker (6-0-0-3)). Commissioners discussed, among other topics, the Commission’s
role in the Use Permit approval, future transportation needs of the area, other uses on
the Pier and in the Marina, the importance of the ferry as an emergency transportation
option, connections to San Francisco to support tourism and Berkeley businesses,
connections with BART and AC Transit, and reinvigoration of the Waterfront and
Marina. Five members of the public commented (Attachment 4).

Zoning Adjustments Board Action

Following a notice posted on February 11, 2026 pursuant to BMC Section 23.404.050
and emailed to a broad stakeholder list (there are no private properties within the 0.5-
mile notice radius), the ZAB held a public hearing on February 26, 2026 and approved
Use Permit #ZP2026-0014 pursuant to the findings for approval and subject to Standard
and Project-Specific Conditions of Approval, by a vote of 5-0-3 (Attachment 5). The
Project-Specific Conditions require City Council approval, require the City to obtain
permits from all other agencies with jurisdiction prior to construction, and provide that
the mitigation measures in the Council-adopted MMRP are Conditions of Approval. Staff
determined that design review of the ferry terminal facilities will occur at the staff level
pursuant to BMC Section 23.406.070(D). Because the ZAB acted before the Draft EIR
was published, the ZAB added the following condition: “The ZAB’s decision to approve
the use permit was made prior to the publishing of the Draft Environmental Impact
Report (EIR) and the associated Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program
(MMRP).”

Findings for Approval

The Planning Commission and the ZAB each found that the proposed use would not be
detrimental to the health, safety, peace, morals, comfort, or general welfare of persons
residing or working in the area, and would not be detrimental or injurious to property and



                                               Page 10
                                         Page 11 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Environmental Impact    PUBLIC HEARING
Report, Project Approval, and Use Permit                                 November 17, 2026


improvements of adjacent properties, the surrounding area, or the general welfare of the
City. Staff recommends that the Council make the same findings (Attachment 2, Exhibit
A), for the following reasons:

      The Berkeley Waterfront is a single City-owned property, and the nearest
       residential zoning district is more than one mile from the ferry terminal. The
       nearest neighbors within 0.1 mile are a restaurant, a park, boats docked at the
       Marina (including some live-aboard boats), and a public parking lot;

      The use would establish a new transportation option for commuting, recreational,
       and personal travel to San Francisco, benefiting persons working, residing, or
       visiting in the area, including Marina live-aboard and floating home residents;

      Water transit facilities are expressly contemplated by the General Plan
       Waterfront/Marina designation, and the use is consistent with General Plan
       Policies T-2 (Public Transportation Improvements), T-9 (Ferry Service), and S-12
       (Utility and Transportation Systems), and with the Public Trust Doctrine’s
       requirement that public tidelands be devoted to water-dependent uses such as
       navigation;

      Ferry service is identified as a High Priority Action in the City’s Local Hazard
       Mitigation Plan and as a goal of the City’s Climate Action Plan, and is included in
       Plan Bay Area 2050+ and the WETA 2050 Service Vision;

      The City’s Parking and Transportation Demand Management Plan demonstrates
       that ferry rider parking can be accommodated in under-utilized Waterfront
       parking areas without impacting recreation parking; and

      The mitigation measures in the MMRP are Conditions of Approval, and the
       Project would result in a net reduction in vehicle miles traveled and greenhouse
       gas emissions.

Senate Bill 149 Status

On September 16, 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom certified the Berkeley
Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project as a transportation project qualifying for judicial
streamlining under SB 149. SB 149 requires the City to make certain public notices
within 10 days of the certification (Public Resources Code Section 21189.87). This
notification was fully completed by September 26, 2026 with the required notice posted
in the newspaper of record and emails sent to all agencies, organizations and
individuals who have commented on the project. The notice was also posted on the
City’s Project website. Consistent with SB 149, the City will certify the record of
proceedings within 5 days of approval of the Project.

Project Cost

The current design and environmental phase of the Project is funded through a
combination of City, WETA, and grant funding, including $2,960,900 from the State
Coastal Conservancy (Resolution No. 70,629-N.S.), $5,139,000 from the Alameda
County Transportation Commission (Resolution No. 70,950-N.S.), and WETA
contributions under the City-WETA Memorandum of Understanding (Resolution No.
71,325-N.S.).

The current total construction phase cost estimate for the Project is $139 million. This
estimate for the construction phase escalates the construction cost estimate provided
by design engineers in 2026 based on the 60% design to Spring 2028, and includes
additional estimated costs for contingency, design adjustments, construction
management, project management, and special inspections. This estimate does not
include the cost of electric vessels. Construction funding has not yet been identified.
The City anticipates that construction will be funded primarily through future grant
awards from regional, state, and federal sources, and that the Project may be
constructed in phases as funding becomes available. The City will not award
construction contracts until construction funding has been secured, and future actions to



                                               Page 12
                                         Page 13 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Environmental Impact      PUBLIC HEARING
Report, Project Approval, and Use Permit                                   November 17, 2026


accept grant funds and award construction contracts will be brought to the City Council
for consideration. The cost of implementing the mitigation measures in the MMRP are
incorporated into the Project’s construction costs.

BACKGROUND
The Berkeley Municipal Pier was originally constructed in 1926 by the Golden Gate
Ferry Company as an automobile causeway to a ferry terminal, and was acquired by the
City and operated as a recreational pier after ferry service ended in 1937. In July 2015,
the pier was closed indefinitely due to structural safety issues. A structural assessment
completed in 2021 identified options to repair the pier; since that time, the pier has
continued to degrade, and the Project’s structural engineers have concluded that repair
is no longer feasible.

WETA has identified ferry service in Berkeley as a system priority for more than 20
years. Berkeley ferry service is included in Plan Bay Area 2050 and the Plan Bay Area
2050+ Final Transportation Project List, and WETA published its Berkeley Ferry Service
Business Plan in 2022. In March 2019, the City Council authorized a Memorandum of
Understanding (MOU) with WETA to jointly fund a feasibility study for rebuilding the pier
for ferry service and recreational access (Resolution No. 68,782-N.S.). The findings of
the feasibility study and a preferred concept, developed with community input, were
presented to the City Council at a work session on December 7, 2021. In May 2024, the
City and WETA amended the MOU to cover the current design and environmental
phase (Resolution No. 71,325-N.S.).

The design and environmental phase began in 2023, is currently ongoing, and includes
detailed engineering, environmental analysis and documentation under CEQA and the
National Environmental Policy Act, public outreach, permitting, and preparation of bid-
ready plans and specifications. The Project will require permits and/or approvals from
agencies with jurisdiction over portions of the Project, including the California State
Lands Commission, the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development
Commission, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the National Marine Fisheries Service,
the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, CDFW, and the San Francisco Bay Regional Water
Quality Control Board. Certification of the EIR is necessary for these agencies to rely on
it in issuing their permits.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
The environmental effects of the Project, including greenhouse gas emissions and
energy, air quality, transportation, and hydrology and water quality, are disclosed and
analyzed in the EIR (Attachment 3). The Project would provide zero-emission electric
ferry service and multimodal access improvements, including a raised cycle track on
University Avenue, Bay Trail improvements, secure bicycle parking, improved bus
facilities, and electric vehicle charging, that would shift transbay trips away from single-
occupancy vehicles and result in a net reduction in vehicle miles traveled. As described
above, the Project would result in an annual net reduction of approximately 2,368 metric



                                               Page 13
                                         Page 14 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Environmental Impact    PUBLIC HEARING
Report, Project Approval, and Use Permit                                 November 17, 2026



tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (MTCO₂e) and a reduction of approximately 19,000
miles driven per day. The pier and plaza are designed to accommodate projected sea
level rise through the 2075 planning horizon, consistent with the 2024 California Ocean
Protection Council Sea Level Rise Guidance. The Project advances the goals of the
City’s Climate Action Plan and Climate Emergency declaration.

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
The EIR has been prepared in compliance with CEQA Guidelines and reflects the
independent judgment and analysis of the City. Certification of the EIR and adoption of
the CEQA Findings, Statement of Overriding Considerations, mitigation measures, and
MMRP are required before the City Council may consider approval of the Project.
Certification will also allow the City to complete permitting with state and federal
agencies and position the Project to compete for construction grant funding, which
typically requires completed environmental review.

The Project site is in the Unclassified (U) zoning district. In this district, BMC Section
23.208.020(C) requires City Council action on all Use Permits. The Planning
Commission reviewed the Use Permit application on January 21, 2026 and
recommended approval. The ZAB then approved Use Permit #ZP2026-0014 on
February 26, 2026. The ZAB’s decision was made before the Draft EIR and associated
MMRP were published. The recommended modifications to the Findings and Conditions
of Approval conform the Use Permit to the Final EIR and MMRP. Affirming the ZAB
decision as modified and approving the Project as Alternative 2 (Shortened Breakwater
Alternative) completes the City’s local land use approval for the Project.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
The City Council could decline to certify the EIR, or could direct staff to conduct
additional environmental analysis. In that case, the City Council could not consider
approval of the Project, and depending on the nature of any additional analysis, the EIR
could require revision and recirculation for public review. This would delay Project
permitting and the City’s ability to pursue construction funding, and could affect the
Project’s existing grant funding timelines.

Pursuant to BMC Section 23.208.020(C)(5), the City Council may affirm, reverse, or
modify the ZAB’s decision on Use Permit #ZP2026-0014. The Council could also certify
the EIR but decline to approve the Project, approve a different alternative analyzed in
the EIR, or continue its consideration of the Project and Use Permit to a future meeting.
Any of these actions would delay the Project.

Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program
CEQA requires that a reporting or monitoring program be adopted when mitigation measures are required
to mitigate or avoid significant effects on the environment and are adopted and incorporated into the
project (Public Resources Code 21081.6). This mitigation monitoring and reporting program (MMRP) is
intended to track and ensure compliance with adopted mitigation measures during project
implementation. To ensure that the mitigation measures are properly implemented, this MMRP identifies
the timing and responsibility for implementing and monitoring implementation of each mitigation
measure. Accordingly, for each mitigation measure, this MMRP identifies the action required, the timing
and frequency for implementing the action, the entity that will implement the action, and the agency or
department responsible for verifying compliance.

 Depending on survey results, the report will also include observations of burrowing owl or                                                                   of avoidance and minimization
 potential burrows, and the location and habitat description of the observations. If                                                                          measures.
 burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign (i.e., tracks or pellets) are not observed in the
 project site, no additional measures related to impact avoidance and minimization of the
 absent species are recommended. If burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign are
 observed within the project site, CDFW will be notified and the following measures will be
 implemented:
 • A qualified biological monitor will be present during landside construction on the project
   site to document burrowing owl observations, burrow statuses, and require that
   construction activities do not negatively affect burrowing owl. The duration and
   frequency of monitoring will be determined at the discretion of the qualified biologist and
   a monitoring report detailing monitoring results will be submitted to the City within 30
   days of the completion of project activities or breeding season (February 1 to August
   31), if applicable.
 • The biological monitor will visually inspect any pipes, debris piles, culverts, or similar
   structures for burrowing owl before the material is moved, buried, or capped. Open holes
   and trenches within the project site will be inspected at the beginning and end of each
   landside construction workday and immediately prior to backfilling. At the end of each
   such workday, trenches and holes will be ramped so that any animals that may have
   become trapped in the trench or hole can climb out. The ramp may be constructed of dirt
   fill or wood planking or other suitable material at an angle no greater than 30-45 degrees.
   If a burrowing owl is trapped in a trench or hole, work will stop and the qualified biologist
   will be notified immediately. The burrowing owl will be allowed to escape unimpeded.
 • If active burrows are observed on the project site, a non-disturbance buffer will be
   established restricting all ground-disturbing activities from occurring within the buffer
   and a qualified biological monitor will be present at the initiation of project activities. The
   buffer will be established by a qualified biologist and range from 330 ft. to 1,500 ft.
   depending on project activity, line of sight, and local topography during the breeding
   season. During the non-breeding season (September 1 to January 31), the buffer will
   range from 165 ft. to 330 ft. The buffer will be demarcated using brightly colored
   flagging and may only be reduced at the discretion of a qualified biologist based on the
   factors listed above and potential use of sound and visual barriers (i.e., hay bales).
   Removal of the buffer will only occur if a qualified biologist determines burrowing owl
   are not present in the vicinity and any potential burrows are inactive.
 • If active burrow avoidance is infeasible during the non-breeding season or during the
   breeding season, where resident owls have not yet begun egg laying or incubation, or
   where the juveniles are foraging independently and capable of independent survival, the
   City in coordination with a qualified biologist will consult with CDFW to prepare,
   authorize, and implement a passive relocation program consistent with Appendix E of
   the 2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation.
 • A habitat mitigation plan will be developed in coordination with the City and CDFW for
   loss of active burrowing owl burrow sites if implementation of a passive relocation plan
   is necessary and/or burrowing owl are documented to nest on site or within 500 feet of

    Nesting Birds
    Project construction activities, including but not limited to vegetation removal and ground
    disturbance that result in noise or disturbance affecting potential nesting bird habitat,
    should commence outside of the nesting season (February 1 through September 15), if
    feasible. If construction begins outside the nesting season, a nesting bird survey is not
    required.
    If ground disturbing project activities begin within the nesting season (February 1 through
    September 15), then no more than seven days prior to the initiation of project activities, a
    nesting bird pre-construction survey shall be conducted by a City-approved qualified
    biologist within the disturbance footprint, plus a 300-foot buffer for passerines and a
    1,000-foot buffer for raptors. During construction within the nesting season, an additional
    focused survey shall be conducted prior to tree removal to identify active nests with the
    subject tree(s). If no active nests are observed, no further action would be required.
    Ground-disturbing project activities that are initiated outside of the nesting season may
    continue into the nesting season without requiring new nesting bird surveys.
    Pre-construction nesting bird surveys shall be conducted by a qualified biologist during the
    time of day when birds are most active and should be of sufficient duration to reliably
    conclude presence or absence of nesting birds on the project site and within the
    designated buffer. A report of the nesting bird surveys results shall be submitted to the
    City for review and approval prior to clearance for mobilizing equipment. If nests are found,
    their locations shall be flagged (if possible) and recorded with the use of a GPS unit.
    Avoidance buffers shall be established around active nests. Depending upon the species,
    suitable minimum buffers may be 50 feet for non-raptor species and 300 feet for raptor
    species, or as determined by the qualified biologist in consultation with CDFW based on
    species sensitivity, construction activities, and other factors.
    If active nests are present, all project work shall be conducted outside the established
    avoidance buffer zone from the nest until it is no longer active. No staging of large
    equipment shall occur within the avoidance buffer until the qualified biologist confirms
    that breeding/nesting is complete and all the young have fledged. If buffer zones are
    determined to be infeasible, a City-approved qualified biological monitor shall be on site to
    monitor project activities within the avoidance buffer zones to ensure active nests and
    nesting birds are not impacted. Nesting bird surveys are not required for project activities
    that occur between September 16 and January 31. A report of all survey results and any
    proposed avoidance buffers shall be submitted to the City for review and approval.
    This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable
    regulatory agencies.

 cushion block methods shall also be employed as feasible to minimize impacts.
 If the intensity of the pile-driving activity needs to be increased or a marine mammal is
 within the safe zone buffer for the activity, pile driving shall be “ramped-up”, which is a
 slow increase in the intensity of pile-driving. At the start of pile-driving for each pile at all
 locations, the pile shall be struck once with the hammer and the second pile strike delayed
 long enough to permit adequate time for any marine mammals within the safe zone to
 leave the area prior to the start of sustained pile-driving activities.
 This measure, including the technique and the size of the safe zone, may be modified or
 supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory agencies.

   biologist shall document all marine-mammal observations, note behavioral responses,
   and immediately alert project personnel if a whale enters the modeled harassment
   distance or comes within 300 feet, or if any other marine mammal enters the modeled
   harassment distance or comes within 150 feet, whichever is greater. Upon such an
   observation, the contractor shall implement the appropriate delay or shutdown
   procedures identified in the MMMP.
 • Adaptive Management and Coordination: The MMMP shall outline communication and
   reporting protocols, including stop-work notification procedures and coordination with
   NMFS Protected Species Division. Results from daily monitoring will be used to assess
   the effectiveness of the protection zones and adjust them, if needed, in consultation with
   NMFS.
 • Nighttime Pile Driving: Nighttime pile driving shall be limited to situations where safety
   concerns or significant schedule delays require that pile driving started during daytime
   hours extend beyond typical work hours. For instances where nighttime pile driving is
   required, the MMMP shall include non-visual monitoring protocols, such as passive
   acoustic monitoring, thermal/infrared cameras, and night vision optics, as well as larger
   nighttime exclusion/shutdown zones, extended soft start procedures, and the most
   effective feasible hydroacoustic attenuation.

 SWPPP and implemented during pier demolition:                                                                                                         requirements.
 • Site washout areas shall be located at least 100 feet from a storm drain, open ditch or
   surface water and ensure that runoff flows from such activities do not enter receiving
   water bodies, unless otherwise approved by the RWQCB.
 • All re-fueling, cleaning, and maintenance of equipment shall occur at least 100 feet from
   storm drain, open ditch or surface water and/or within secondary containment, unless
   otherwise approved by the RWQCB.
 • Particular care shall be exercised to prevent foreign materials (e.g., construction scraps,
   wood preservatives, other chemicals and debris, etc.) from entering the San Francisco
   Bay during pier demolition.
 • If wood preservatives must be applied to cut-wood surfaces, the materials, whenever
   feasible, shall be treated at an onshore location to preclude the possibility of spills into
   State waters.
 • A containment boom shall be placed around all active portions of a construction site
   where wood scraps or other floatable debris could enter the water.
 • The containment boom and net shall be cleared daily or as often as necessary to prevent
   accumulation of debris.
 • Tarps and basins shall be used above deck to contain debris and materials.
 • Dipnets shall be on-site and can be used to retrieve debris if it accidentally falls into the
   water.
 • A 50-foot-long spill containment boom as well as absorbent pads shall be kept on-site
   and shall be deployed in the event that there is a release of fluids into the water.
 • Contractors shall make mandatory that work crews are carefully briefed on the
   importance of observing the appropriate precautions and reporting any accidental spills.

   construction site, or other conspicuous location, that includes a telephone number,
   website and email for project information, and a procedure in which a construction
   manager shall respond to and investigate noise complaints and take corrective action, if
   necessary, in a timely manner.
 • At least 21 days prior to the start of construction activities, businesses and residents
   (including occupied live-aboard boats) within 500 feet of the project site shall be notified
   of the planned construction activities. The notification shall include a brief description of
   the project, the activities that would occur, the hours when construction would occur, and
   the overall duration of the construction period. The notification shall include the
   telephone numbers and email addresses of the City’s and contractor’s authorized
   representatives that are assigned to respond in the event of a noise complaint.
 • If a construction noise complaint is registered and if City code enforcement is not
   available to make noise measurements, the City shall retain a City-approved noise
   consultant to conduct noise measurements at the properties that registered the
   complaint. The noise measurements shall be conducted for a minimum of one hour. The
   consultant shall prepare a letter report for code enforcement summarizing the
   measurements, calculation data used in determining impacts, and potential measures to
   reduce noise levels to the maximum extent feasible.
 • Prior to the start of and for the duration of construction, the contractor shall properly
   maintain and tune all construction equipment in accordance with the manufacturer’s
   recommendations to minimize noise emissions.
 • Prior to use of any construction equipment, the contractor shall fit all equipment with
   properly operating mufflers, air intake silencers, and engine shrouds no less effective
   than as originally equipped by the manufacturer.
 • Material hauling and deliveries shall be coordinated by the construction contractor to
   reduce the potential of trucks waiting to unload for protracted periods of time.
 • To the extent feasible, hydraulic equipment shall be used instead of pneumatic impact
   tools, and electric-powered equipment shall be used instead of diesel-powered
   equipment.

                       pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15091 and 15093 and

The Environmental Impact Report (EIR) prepared by the City of Berkeley (City) for the Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project (“the project”) consists of the February 2026 Draft EIR and the October 2026
Final EIR including Responses to Comments on the Draft EIR. The EIR identifies significant environmental
impacts that would result from implementation of the project. The City finds that the adoption of mitigation
measures identified in the EIR as part of project approval will reduce all but the following significant
environmental impacts to levels that are less than significant:
     • Project-level and cumulative temporary construction noise impacts and associated land use/ planning
       and recreation impacts related to construction noise.
     • Cumulatively considerable contribution to a significant cumulative operational roadway noise impact on
       University Avenue between Seawall Drive and Marina Boulevard, and associated land use/ planning
       and recreation impacts related to operational roadway noise.
No feasible mitigation measures have been identified to reduce these impacts to a less-than-significant level;
therefore, the impacts will remain significant and unavoidable impacts of the project. Construction noise levels
would exceed applicable thresholds even with implementation of identified feasible mitigation measures. For
those impacts, mitigation measures have been identified and will be adopted and incorporated into the project,
but will not reduce impacts to a less-than-significant level. Therefore, these impacts will remain significant and
unavoidable impacts of the project. These findings contain a statement of overriding considerations in Section
6, below, that explains why the benefits of the proposed project outweigh these temporary unavoidable
adverse environmental effects and are, therefore, acceptable.
As required by the California Environmental Quality Act, Public Resources Code Section 21000 et seq.
(CEQA) and the State CEQA Guidelines, California Code of Regulations, Title 14, Section 15000 et seq.
(CEQA Guidelines), the City, in addition to adopting these CEQA Findings and Statement of Overriding
Considerations, also adopts a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP) for the project. In
adopting the MMRP, the City finds that it meets the requirements of Public Resources Code Section 21081.6
by providing for the implementation and monitoring of measures intended to mitigate potentially significant
environmental effects of the project.
In accordance with CEQA and the CEQA Guidelines, the City adopts these findings as part of the project
approval. Pursuant to Public Resources Code Section 21082.1(c)(3), the City also finds that the Final EIR
reflects the City’s independent judgment as the lead agency for the project.

SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

Statutory Requirements for Findings

CEQA Guidelines § 15091 states that:
       (a) No public agency shall approve or carry out a project for which an EIR has been certified which
       identifies one or more significant environmental effects of the project unless the public agency makes one
       or more written findings for each of those significant effects, accompanied by a brief explanation of the
       rationale for each finding. The possible findings are:
       (1)    Changes or alterations have been required in, or incorporated into, the project which avoid or
              substantially lessen the significant environmental effect as identified in the final EIR.
       (2)    Such changes or alterations are within the responsibility and jurisdiction of another public agency
              and not the agency making the finding. Such changes have been adopted by such other agency or
              can and should be adopted by such other agency.
       (3)    Specific economic, legal, social, technological, or other considerations, including provision of
              employment opportunities for highly trained workers, make infeasible the mitigation measures or
              project alternatives identified in the final EIR.

In short, CEQA requires that the lead agency adopt mitigation measures or alternatives, where feasible, to
avoid or mitigate significant environmental effects (impacts) that will otherwise occur with implementation of the
project. Mitigation measures or project alternatives are not required, however, where they are infeasible or
where modifying the project or adopting mitigation is within the responsibility and jurisdiction of another
agency.1
For significant impacts that cannot be mitigated to a less-than-significant level, the public agency is required to
find that specific overriding economic, legal, social, technological, or other benefits of the project outweigh the
significant effects on the environment.2 CEQA Guidelines §15093(a) states that:
       If the specific economic, legal, social, technological, or other benefits, including region-wide or statewide
       environmental benefits, of a proposed project outweigh the unavoidable adverse environmental effects,
       the adverse environmental effects may be considered ‘acceptable.’”

SECTION 2: PROJECT DESCRIPTION: BERKELEY WATER TRANSPORTATION PIER
           FERRY PROJECT
This section provides a brief description of the project and lists the objectives of the proposed project.

2.1      Project Description

The Berkeley Pier was closed in July 2015 due to visually observed structural problems on the underside of the
concrete decking and pilings. The proposed project aims to revitalize the Berkeley Waterfront by developing a
new dual-purpose pier and ancillary uses that support both public recreation and zero-emission public ferry
service. Specifically, the project would include the following components:
       • Demolish portions of the closed pier;
       • Construct a new 1,080-foot-long public pier at the same location as the closed pier with pedestrian
         access and recreational amenities;
       • Construct a new 400-foot-long breakwater perpendicular to and connected to the new pier, providing
         pedestrian access and recreational amenities;



1 CEQA Guidelines Section 15091(a)(2) and (3).
2 Public Resources Code Section 21081(b).
                                                    Page 37 of 1541


                                                                                                             Page 2 of 41

      • Provide recreational amenities on the pier and breakwater for walking, sightseeing, and fishing,
          including interpretive and educational signs, benches, shade canopy, seats, and a fish cleaning
          station;
      •   Provide ferry infrastructure including but not limited to universal charging and boarding float(s),
          landing(s), gangway(s), and security entrance;
      •   One-time dredging along the existing 100-foot wide United States Army Corps of Engineers federal
          navigation channel that parallels the closed pier, as well as at a turning basin at the ferry landing(s);
      •   Construct a new public plaza with stormwater treatment and amenities such as a public restroom,
          public seating, bicycle lanes, public bicycle parking, and landscaping;
      •   Implement improvements to University Avenue, including repaving and restriping between the round-
          about intersection with Marina Boulevard and the intersection with Seawall Drive, stormwater
          treatment and a new raised bicycle track, passenger drop off zone, and public bus infrastructure,
          including the relocation of an existing AC Transit bus stop, installation of new bus passenger loading
          islands, and dedicated bus loading and unloading facilities; Implement improvements to Seawall Drive,
          including re-alignment, repaving, stormwater treatment, and restriping;
      •   Develop a portion of the planned Bay Trail Extension, south of the pier and along Seawall Drive;
      •   Renovate the parking lot off Seawall Drive with new pavement, surfacing, striping, lighting, stormwater
          treatment, and replacement of existing stormwater outfalls;
      •   Repair 300 feet of a stretch of shoreline located on the eastern side Seawall Peninsula, just north of
          the 199 Seawall Drive structure in the form of rock rip rap slope protection;
      •   Provide new landscaping as well as tree removal and replacement;
      •   Provide new way-finding signage and replacement lighting;
      •   Install new electric infrastructure to charge ferry vessels;
      •   Install new water connections for a restroom and hose bibs;
      •   Install new wastewater connections for a restroom; and
      •   Operate new zero-emission electric passenger ferry service, connecting the Berkeley ferry terminal to
          San Francisco.

In addition to the project components listed above, the City is considering adding solar panels to the renovated
parking lot as an optional improvement. The City is in the process of deciding whether this feature will be
incorporated into the project. The potential environmental impact from installing solar panels is analyzed in the
EIR. The EIR also analyzes alternatives to the project as described in SECTION 5:, below.

2.2       Project Objectives

Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15124(b), the EIR project description must include “[a] statement of
objectives sought by the proposed project… The statement of objectives should include the underlying purpose
of the project.” The Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project is intended to achieve the following
project objectives:
      • Enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront that:
          •     Develop or enhance public pier facilities at the City of Berkeley Waterfront.
              • Provide sufficient public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront that meet
                regional needs, consistent with BCDC Bay Plan Policies maximizing access to the Bay.
              • Minimize environmental impacts by considering existing infrastructure and sea level rise
                projections.
              • Encourage the use of public transit, bicycle, and other forms of active transportation and
                sustainable travel to access the site.
                                               Page 38 of 1541


                                                                                                        Page 3 of 41

     • Provide efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and
        San Francisco that:
        • Improves regional connectivity and resiliency with enhanced public transportation choices for East
          Bay residents, including for accessing jobs in San Francisco and other locations along the Bay for
          commerce and recreational purposes, and to address existing deficiencies in the Transbay
          transportation network.
        • Reduces the use of single-occupancy vehicles for Transbay trips, thereby reducing greenhouse gas
          and air quality emissions and decreasing congestion on the regional roadway system, consistent
          with regional and Statewide goals.
        • Provides travel times and costs that are competitive with other Transbay modes of travel.
        • Provides public transit facilities that are compatible with operations and recreational activities at the
          Berkeley Waterfront.
        • Provides navigable conditions for safe and efficient operation of ferry vessels.
        • Provides options for emergency response and transportation services in case of an emergency,
          such as natural or human-caused event that disables roads, other transit, bridges, and/or tunnels.

SECTION 3: ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW PROCESS
Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), lead agencies are required to consult with public
agencies having jurisdiction over a proposed project and to provide the general public with an opportunity to
comment on the Draft EIR.
On April 18, 2025, the City of Berkeley issued a Notice of Preparation (NOP) for a 31-day comment period until
May 19, 2025, to receive input on the scope and content of the EIR and help identify the types of impacts that
could result from the project as well as potential areas of controversy. The NOP was filed with the County
Clerk, published in a local newspaper, and mailed to public agencies (including the State Clearinghouse),
organizations, and individuals considered likely to be interested in the project and its potential impacts. The
City received written responses to the NOP regarding the scope and content of the EIR. The City also held an
EIR scoping meeting May 5, 2025, at which 12 members of the public provided verbal comments. In addition to
the verbal comments received during the EIR scoping meeting, the City received written scoping comment
letters from 6 agencies, 3 Native American Tribes, 7 organizations, and 17 individuals in response to the NOP
during the public review period.
The Draft EIR was made available for public review and comment on February 27, 2026. The Notice of
Availability of a Draft EIR was posted with the Alameda County Clerk, filed with the State Clearinghouse for
distribution to State agencies, published in a local newspaper, and mailed to local agencies and interested
organizations. A Notice of Completion was also filed with the State Clearinghouse. The Draft EIR and an
announcement of its availability were posted electronically on the City's website. The original public review and
comment period was established as a 45-day review period, ending on April 13, 2026. On April 1, 2026, the
City issued a revised Notice of Availability, notified the State Clearinghouse and project distribution list, and
extended the public review and comment period by an additional 15 days. As a result, the Draft EIR was
circulated for a total of 60 days, and the public comment period closed on April 28, 2026. The City received
102 written comment letters on the Draft EIR. The City also held a Draft EIR public meeting on March 16,
2026, to receive public comments on the environmental analysis during which 23 individual persons provided
verbal comments on the Draft EIR.

SECTION 4: FINDINGS
These findings summarize the environmental determinations of the EIR about project impacts before and after
mitigation, and do not attempt to repeat the full analysis of each environmental impact contained in the EIR.
Instead, these findings provide a summary description of and basis for impacts in the EIR, describe the
applicable mitigation measures identified in the EIR, and state the City’s findings and rationale regarding the
significance of impacts with the implementation of identified mitigation measures. A full explanation of these
                                                    Page 39 of 1541


                                                                                                               Page 4 of 41

environmental findings and conclusions can be found in the EIR, and these findings hereby incorporate by
reference the discussion and analysis in the EIR supporting the EIR’s determinations regarding mitigation
measures and the project’s impacts.

4.1      SIGNIFICANT EFFECTS THAT CANNOT BE MITIGATED TO A LESS-THAN-SIGNIFICANT
         LEVEL

The Draft EIR identifies the following significant and unavoidable adverse project-level impacts associated with
the approval of the project, some of which can be reduced, although not to a less-than-significant level, through
implementation of mitigation measures identified in the Final EIR (Public Resources Code § 21081(a)(1)). To
the extent that these mitigation measures will not mitigate or avoid all significant effects on the environment, it
is hereby determined that any remaining significant and unavoidable adverse impacts are acceptable for the
reasons specified in SECTION 6:, below (Public Resources Code § 21081(a)(3)). The findings in this section
are based on the Draft EIR, the discussion and analysis in which is hereby incorporated in full by this
reference.
The Draft EIR also identified significant and unavoidable cumulative impacts, which are addressed in Section
4.4.

4.1.1    Noise
Impact NOI-1: Operational Impacts: Mobile and stationary operational noise impacts would be less than
significant. Construction Impacts: Most project construction noise impacts would be less than significant with
mitigation; however, construction noise levels at Shorebird Park and some live-aboard boats, including for
demolition and daytime and nighttime pile installation, would still exceed City thresholds and, thus, overall
construction noise impacts would be significant and unavoidable.
        Mitigation Measure NOI-1: Prepare and Implement Construction Noise Management Plan Prior to
        and During Construction. Prior to the start of construction activities, a Construction Noise Management
        Plan shall be submitted to and approved by the City’s Public Works Department. The Construction Noise
        Management Plan shall include the following:
        • Prior to the initiation of construction activities at the project site, the contractor shall install temporary
          noise barriers/blankets between the construction boundary and nearby sensitive receptors. The
          temporary barriers/blankets shall have a minimum height of 12 feet to block the line of sight between
          operating construction equipment and adjacent sensitive receptors. Barriers shall be constructed with
          a solid material that has a density of at least one pound per square foot with no gaps from the ground
          to the top of the barrier and be lined on the construction side with acoustical blanket, curtain, or
          equivalent absorptive material rated STC 32 or higher. The temporary barriers/blankets shall be
          installed as follows:
           • For landside construction activities occurring near the pier entrance/public plaza, temporary noise
              barriers/blankets shall be installed around the construction boundaries between the construction
              work areas and the Skates on the Bay Restaurant and Horseshoe Park located to the north and
              Shorebird Park located to the east.
           • For construction activities occurring at/near the Seawall Drive parking lot, temporary noise
              barriers/blankets shall be installed between the construction boundary and Shorebird Park to the
              north.
           • For construction activities occurring along University Avenue, temporary noise barriers/blankets
              shall be installed between the construction work areas and the live-aboard boats in the Marina to
              the north and Shorebird Park and Adventure Playground to the south.
        • With approval of the project structural engineer, landside pile holes shall be pre-drilled to minimize the
          number of impacts necessary to seat the pile, where feasible.
        • Pile driving shall be scheduled to have the least impact on nearby live-aboards or houseboats.
                                             Page 40 of 1541


                                                                                                       Page 5 of 41

• Applicable pile driving noise control devices shall be integrated to the extent feasible to conduct both
    landside and in-water pile driving. These may include, but are not limited to, shrouding the pile
    hammer point of impact, by placing resilient padding directly on top of the pile cap, and/or by reducing
    exhaust noise with a sound-absorbing muffler.
•   Alternatives to impact hammers, such as oscillating or rotating pile installation systems, shall be used
    where possible for landside pile driving.
•   At least 10 days prior to the start of construction activities, a sign shall be posted at the construction
    site, or other conspicuous location, that includes a telephone number, website and email for project
    information, and a procedure in which a construction manager shall respond to and investigate noise
    complaints and take corrective action, if necessary, in a timely manner.
•   At least 21 days prior to the start of construction activities, businesses and residents (including
    occupied live-aboard boats) within 500 feet of the project site shall be notified of the planned
    construction activities. The notification shall include a brief description of the project, the activities that
    would occur, the hours when construction would occur, and the overall duration of the construction
    period. The notification shall include the telephone numbers and email addresses of the City’s and
    contractor’s authorized representatives that are assigned to respond in the event of a noise complaint.
•   If a construction noise complaint is registered and if City code enforcement is not available to make
    noise measurements, the City shall retain a City-approved noise consultant to conduct noise
    measurements at the properties that registered the complaint. The noise measurements shall be
    conducted for a minimum of one hour. The consultant shall prepare a letter report for code
    enforcement summarizing the measurements, calculation data used in determining impacts, and
    potential measures to reduce noise levels to the maximum extent feasible.
•   Prior to the start of and for the duration of construction, the contractor shall properly maintain and tune
    all construction equipment in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations to minimize noise
    emissions.
•   Prior to use of any construction equipment, the contractor shall fit all equipment with properly operating
    mufflers, air intake silencers, and engine shrouds no less effective than as originally equipped by the
    manufacturer.
•   Material hauling and deliveries shall be coordinated by the construction contractor to reduce the
    potential of trucks waiting to unload for protracted periods of time.
•   To the extent feasible, hydraulic equipment shall be used instead of pneumatic impact tools, and
    electric-powered equipment shall be used instead of diesel-powered equipment.
•   Stationary noise sources (e.g., generators) shall be located as far from sensitive receptors as
    practicable, and they shall be muffled and enclosed within temporary sheds, or insulation barriers with
    a minimum STC rating of 32.
•   The use of bells, whistles, alarms, and horns shall be restricted to safety warning purposes only.
•   Signs shall be posted at the job site entrance(s), within the on-site construction zones, and along
    queueing lanes (if any) to reinforce the prohibition of unnecessary engine idling. All other equipment
    shall be turned off if not in use for more than five minutes. The construction manager shall be
    responsible for enforcing this.

Finding: The City finds that implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1, which is hereby adopted and
incorporated into the project, would reduce construction noise impacts to the maximum extent feasible.
However, even with implementation of this mitigation measure, construction noise impacts would remain
significant and unavoidable. Specifically, daytime pile-driving activities and nighttime pile-driving activities
would continue to exceed applicable City noise standards at nearby sensitive receptors. No additional
feasible mitigation measures have been identified that would reduce these pile-driving impacts to a less-
than-significant level. The City further finds that although this impact would be significant and
unavoidable, the temporary impact is acceptable when weighed against the overriding social, economic,
and other considerations set forth in the Statement of Overriding Considerations (see SECTION 6: of this
document).

        Facts in Support of Finding: Implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1 would reduce construction
        noise levels through the use of temporary noise barriers, pile-driving noise attenuation measures,
