4.2      EFFECTS DETERMINED TO BE MITIGATED TO LESS-THAN-SIGNIFICANT LEVELS

The Draft EIR identified certain potentially significant effects that could result from the project. However, the
City finds for each of the significant or potentially significant impacts identified in this section (Section 4.2) that,
based upon substantial evidence in the record, changes or alterations have been required or incorporated into
the project which avoid or substantially lessen the significant effects as identified in the Final EIR (CEQA
Guidelines Section 15091) and, thus, that adoption of the mitigation measures set forth below will reduce these
significant or potentially significant effects to less-than-significant levels. These measures will be required of
the project as part of the City review and approval process where applicable.

4.2.1    Aesthetics
Impact AES-4. Construction lighting from the proposed project would affect nearby houseboat residents or
occupants. This impact would be less than significant with mitigation. Operation of the Proposed project would
result in sources of light and glare from overhead light fixtures and safety and wayfinding lighting. However,
operational levels of light and glare would be minor, similar to existing conditions, and all lighting associated
with the project would be designed with DarkSky approved fixtures, resulting in a less than significant impact
during operations.
        Mitigation Measure AES-1: Reduce Night Lighting During Construction of Facilities. Night lighting for
        construction activities, staging areas and other areas used for construction shall be the minimum
        necessary to ensure safety and security for nighttime activities and operations. As part of planning and
        project implementation, the City or its contractor(s) shall ensure nighttime lighting used for construction is
        shielded and oriented downwards toward the work area(s) to reduce off-site light spill during nighttime
        construction activities. Lighting at the project site shall consist of light-emitting diode lights in all areas
        where nighttime construction activities will occur and be either motion-activated or use timers to ensure
        safety and security and reduce the impact of nighttime light pollution. Furthermore, all lighting would be
        designed in compliance with Illuminating Engineering Society (IES) and DarkSky recommendations. The
        City of Berkeley shall verify that this mitigation measure is included in the project's final construction
        specifications prior to the initiation of construction activities.
        Finding: The City finds that implementation of Mitigation Measure AES-1, which is hereby adopted and
        incorporated into the project, would avoid or substantially reduce the significant environmental effect
        identified in the Final EIR to a less-than-significant level.

                                                                                                                                 Page 8 of 41

        Facts in Support of Finding: Implementation of Mitigation Measure AES-1 would require nighttime
        construction lighting to be limited to the minimum necessary for safety and security, shielded and directed
        downward and inward toward work areas, and designed consistent with IES and DarkSky
        recommendations. Therefore, impacts related to light and glare would be reduced to a less-than-
        significant level with implementation of Mitigation Measure AES-1.

4.2.2       Air Quality
Impact AQ-2. The project would result in a cumulatively considerable net increase of criteria pollutants
(specifically NOx) for which the project region is in non-attainment under an applicable federal or state air
quality standard, prior to mitigation. With implementation of Mitigation, NOx would be reduced to below
regulatory thresholds. Impacts would be less than significant with mitigation.
        Mitigation Measure AQ-1: Implement Construction Emissions Reduction Measures During
        Construction. Prior to issuance of grading and construction permits, the City or its contractor(s) shall
        include the following measures on all construction plans, and these measures shall be implemented
        during construction:
        • All mobile off-road equipment (wheeled or tracked) greater than 50 horsepower used during
          construction activities shall meet the USEPA Tier 4 final standards. Tier 4 certification can be for the
          original equipment or equipment that is retrofitted to meet the Tier 4 final standards.
        • Alternative Fuel (natural gas, propane, electric, etc.) construction equipment shall be incorporated
          where available. These requirements shall be incorporated into the contract agreement with the
          construction contractor. A copy of the equipment’s certification or model year specifications shall be
          available upon request for all equipment on-site.
        • Electricity shall be supplied to the site from the existing power grid to support the electric construction
          equipment. If connection to the grid is determined to be infeasible for portions of the project, a non-
          diesel fueled generator shall be used.
        • The project would comply with the CARB Air Toxics Control Measure that limits diesel powered
          equipment and vehicle idling to no more than five minutes at a location, and the CARB In-Use Off-
          Road Diesel Vehicle Regulation; compliance with these would minimize emissions of TACs during
          construction.
        In addition, the City shall require the proposed project to comply with the following current Bay Area Air
        District’s basic control measures for reducing construction emissions of PM103 :
        • All exposed surfaces (e.g., parking areas, staging areas, soil piles, graded areas, and unpaved access
            roads) shall be watered two times per day.
        •   All haul trucks transporting soil, sand, or other loose material off-site shall be covered.
        •   All visible mud or dirt track-out onto adjacent public roads shall be removed using wet power vacuum
            street sweepers at least once per day. The use of dry power sweeping is prohibited.
        •   All vehicle speeds on unpaved roads shall be limited to 15 mph.
        •   All roadways, driveways, and sidewalks to be paved shall be completed as soon as possible. Building
            pads shall be laid as soon as possible after grading unless seeding or soil binders are used.
        •   Idling times shall be minimized either by shutting equipment off when not in use or reducing the
            maximum idling time to 5 minutes (as required by the California airborne toxics control measure Title
            13, Section 2485 of California Code of Regulations [CCR]). Clear signage shall be provided for
            construction workers at all access points.
        •   All construction equipment shall be maintained and properly tuned in accordance with manufacturer’s
            specifications. All equipment shall be checked by a certified mechanic and determined to be running in
            proper condition prior to operation.

4.2.3    Biological Resources
Impact BIO-1: Construction of the project would result in direct or indirect impacts to special-status species or
their associated habitats including impacts to migratory bird nest sites. Impacts would be less than significant
with mitigation.
Crotch’s bumblebee has a low likelihood to be present in undeveloped portions of the project site. Based on
the low likelihood for this species to occur, the low quality of habitat in the project site, and the distance from
the known occurrence of this species, potential impacts to Crotch’s bumblebee are less than significant.
Nonetheless, the City would implement Mitigation Measure 1(f), as recommended by CDFW. Implementation
of this mitigation, however, does not change the conclusion that impacts to this species is less than significant
without mitigation.
        Mitigation Measure BIO-1(a): Implement Worker Environmental Awareness Program Prior to and
        During Construction. Prior to initiation of all construction activities (including staging and mobilization),
        all personnel associated with project construction shall attend a Worker Environmental Awareness

       CDFW immediately for guidance. Only a CDFW-approved biologist will capture and relocate wildlife.

       the capture and release sites (in UTM coordinates), the length of time between capture and release, and

       Mitigation Measure BIO-1(c): Conduct Burrowing Owl and Nesting Bird Survey and Avoidance Prior

       Burrowing Owl

       submitted to the City within 30 days of completion of the survey. The report will include the dates, times,
       weather conditions, and personnel involved in the survey. Depending on survey results, the report will
       also include observations of burrowing owl or potential burrows, and the location and habitat description
       of the observations. If burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign (i.e., tracks or pellets) are not observed
       in the project area, no additional measures related to impact avoidance and minimization of the absent

    31), the buffer will range from 165 ft. to 330 ft. The buffer will be demarcated using brightly colored

•   If active burrow avoidance is infeasible during the non-breeding season or during the breeding season,

    will consult with CDFW to prepare, authorize, and implement a passive relocation program consistent
    with Appendix E of the 2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation.
•   A habitat mitigation plan will be developed in coordination with the City and CDFW for loss of active
    burrowing owl burrow sites if implementation of a passive relocation plan is necessary and/or
    burrowing owl are documented to nest on site or within 500 feet of the project site. This would be
    based upon the portion of the project site that overlaps with the primary foraging area around the
    burrow site (approximately 500-foot buffer) to be replaced at a minimum 1:1 ratio.

Nesting Birds
Project construction activities, including but not limited to vegetation removal and ground disturbance that
result in noise or disturbance affecting potential nesting bird habitat, should commence outside of the
nesting season (February 1 through September 15), if feasible. If construction begins outside the nesting
season, a nesting bird survey is not required.
If ground disturbing project activities begin within the nesting season (February 1 through September 15),
then no more than seven days prior to the initiation of project activities, a nesting bird pre-construction
survey shall be conducted by a City-approved qualified biologist within the disturbance footprint, plus a
300-foot buffer for passerines and a 1,000-foot buffer for raptors. During construction within the nesting
season, an additional focused survey shall be conducted prior to tree removal to identify active nests with
the subject tree(s). If no active nests are observed, no further action would be required. Ground-
disturbing project activities that are initiated outside of the nesting season may continue into the nesting
season without requiring new nesting bird surveys.
                                             Page 47 of 1541


                                                                                                       Page 12 of 41

Pre-construction nesting bird surveys shall be conducted by a qualified biologist during the time of day
when birds are most active and should be of sufficient duration to reliably conclude presence or absence
of nesting birds on the project site and within the designated buffer. A report of the nesting bird surveys
results shall be submitted to the City for review and approval prior to clearance for mobilizing equipment.
If nests are found, their locations shall be flagged (if possible) and recorded with the use of a GPS unit.
Avoidance buffers shall be established around active nests. Depending upon the species, suitable
minimum buffers may be 50 feet for non-raptor species and 300 feet for raptor species, or as determined
by the qualified biologist in consultation with CDFW based on species sensitivity, construction activities,
and other factors.
If active nests are present, all project work shall be conducted outside the established avoidance buffer
zone from the nest until it is no longer active. No staging of large equipment shall occur within the
avoidance buffer until the qualified biologist confirms that breeding/nesting is complete and all the young
have fledged. If buffer zones are determined to be infeasible, a City-approved qualified biological monitor
shall be on site to monitor project activities within the avoidance buffer zones to ensure active nests and
nesting birds are not impacted. Nesting bird surveys are not required for project activities that occur
between September 16 and January 31. A report of all survey results and any proposed avoidance
buffers shall be submitted to the City for review and approval.
This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
agencies.
Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d): Conduct Pile Driving Impact Avoidance to Fish and Marine Mammals
Prior to and During Construction. In-water work, including pile driving and dredging, shall be limited to
the window of June 1 through November 30. The soft-start, ramp-up, exclusion-zone and sound
attenuation procedures described below apply to pile-driving and pile-extraction activities. A “soft start”
technique will be used to allow fish and marine mammals to vacate the area before the pile driver
reaches full power. For vibratory hammers, the contractor will initiate the driving for 15 seconds at
reduced energy, followed by a 1-minute waiting period when there has been downtime of 30 minutes or
more. This procedure shall be repeated two additional times before continuous driving is started. This
procedure would also apply to vibratory pile extraction. For impact driving, an initial set of three strikes
would be made by the hammer at 40 percent energy, followed by a 1-minute waiting period, then two
subsequent three-strike sets before initiating continuous driving. Pile-driving activity shall not begin at any
location if any marine mammal is observed within the applicable safe-zone distance for its hearing group,
as defined for the specific pile-driving method (e.g., pile diameter, vibratory or impact installation, and
number of piles installed per day). Safe-zone distances shall follow the most current NMFS-approved
guidance and the Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan prepared pursuant to Mitigation Measure BIO-1(E). In
all cases, a minimum exclusion distance of no less than 10 meters shall be maintained around the
pile-driving location. If a marine mammal moves within the safe zone after pile driving has begun, the
contractor shall implement the appropriate delay or shutdown as described in Mitigation Measure BIO-
1(E). A sound curtain, or bubble curtain, shall be employed during impact pile driving to break up sound
waves, as feasible. The sound curtain would consist of a perforated hose laid in a circle to release air
bubbles around the pile and diesel impact hammer. Jetting methods using pressurized water and/or
wood cushion block methods shall also be employed as feasible to minimize impacts.
If the intensity of the pile-driving activity needs to be increased or a marine mammal is within the safe
zone buffer for the activity, pile-driving shall be “ramped-up”, which is a slow increase in the intensity of
pile-driving. At the start of pile-driving for each pile at all locations, the pile shall be struck once with the
hammer and the second pile strike delayed long enough to permit adequate time for any marine
mammals within the safe zone to leave the area prior to the start of sustained pile-driving activities.
This measure, including the technique and the size of the safe zone, may be modified or supplemented
by permit conditions from applicable regulatory agencies.
Mitigation Measure BIO-1(e): Prepare Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan Prior to Construction and
Implement Recommendations During Construction. Prior to construction, the City shall prepare a
Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan (MMMP) to avoid and minimize potential adverse impacts on marine
                                                                Page 48 of 1541


                                                                                                                                          Page 13 of 41

       mammals during pile driving and tug operations. The MMMP shall implement general guidelines set forth
       in the MMPA and incorporate the hydroacoustic modeling results developed for the project to define site-
       specific protection zones and avoid exposure of marine mammals to underwater sound levels exceeding
       the most up to date Level A (injury) thresholds identified by NOAA Fisheries. The MMMP shall include the
       following:
       • Protection and Monitoring Zones: Using the hydroacoustic modeling results, the MMMP shall define
           shutdown and disturbance zones for each marine mammal hearing group. These zones will be tailored
           to the pile type, size, and driving method and will correspond to the Level A and Level B effect
           distances developed for the project. The plan will describe how these protection zones will be verified
           and monitored in the field, integrating them with the soft-start and observation procedures described in
           Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d).
       •   Vessel Operation Protocols: The MMMP shall include vessel-operation measures consistent with the
           MMPA. Construction vessels under power shall remain at least 300 feet from whales and 150 feet
           from dolphins, porpoises, seals, and sea lions. When marine mammals are encountered, vessel
           operators shall reduce speed to no-wake, shift to neutral, and allow the animals to pass safely before
           resuming operations.
       •   On-Site Monitoring and Response: A qualified biologist shall be present on site, either observing
           from the pier or aboard a vessel, during all pile-driving and tug operations. The biologist shall
           document all marine-mammal observations, note behavioral responses, and immediately alert project
           personnel if a whale enters the modeled harassment distance or comes within 300 feet, or if any other
           marine mammal enters the modeled harassment distance or comes within 150 feet, whichever is
           greater. Upon such an observation, the contractor shall implement the appropriate delay or shutdown
           procedures identified in the MMMP.
       •   Adaptive Management and Coordination: The MMMP shall outline communication and reporting
           protocols, including stop-work notification procedures and coordination with NMFS Protected Species
           Division. Results from daily monitoring will be used to assess the effectiveness of the protection zones
           and adjust them, if needed, in consultation with NMFS.
       •   Nighttime Pile Driving: Nighttime pile driving shall be limited to situations where safety concerns or
           significant schedule delays require that pile driving started during daytime hours extend beyond typical
           work hours. For instances where nighttime pile driving is required, the MMMP shall include non-visual
           monitoring protocols, such as passive acoustic monitoring, thermal/infrared cameras, and night vision
           optics, as well as larger nighttime exclusion/shutdown zones, extended soft start procedures, and the
           most effective feasible hydroacoustic attenuation.

       This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
       agencies.

       Mitigation Measure BIO-1(f): Implement CDFW-Requested Measure for Crotch’s Bumble Bee Prior
       to Construction.5 A formal habitat assessment of the project site landside project disturbance areas
       shall be performed by a qualified biologist prior to initiating ground disturbing activities to determine if
       suitable nesting or foraging habitat is present within the project site. The assessment shall include:
       • Review of occurrence record data
       • Analysis of foraging, nesting, and overwintering resources

Comments, and clarified in Chapter 3, Errata, of the Final EIR, impacts to Crotch's bumble bee were determined to be less than significant without

     • Documentation of plant species observed (including what is blooming at the time of the survey and

     The locations of nesting resources, including rodent burrows, cavities, thatched grasses, brush, rock
     piles, fallen logs, and manmade structures, shall be mapped during the assessment. Areas adjacent
     (within 50 feet) to the project site shall also be considered, if accessible, to determine if there is suitable
     nesting or foraging habitat.
     If suitable nesting and foraging resources are detected during the habitat assessment, they will be
     avoided by a minimum 50-foot buffer, where possible. If avoidance is not possible, protocol-surveys
     following the CDFW Survey Considerations for California Endangered Species Act (CESA) Candidate
     Bumble Bee Species (CDFW 2023) will be conducted to determine if Crotch’s bumble bee is present
     within the project site. A minimum of three visits will be conducted during the colony active season (April
     – August) and will be spaced 2-4 weeks apart. Surveys will be conducted each year that construction
     activities occur within suitable nesting habitat because bumble bees move their nests each year. If no
     Crotch’s bumble bees are detected on the project site, no further mitigation actions will be required. If
     Crotch’s bumble bees are detected, consultation with CDFW will be initiated to determine the most
     appropriate strategy to avoid impacts to bumble bees on the project site. If full take avoidance is not
     feasible, the City will apply to CDFW for take authorization under an Incidental Take Permit.

4.2.4    Cultural Resources
Impact CR-2: The proposed land and water disturbances during construction would adversely affect
unidentified archaeological resources. This impact would be less than significant with mitigation for potential
unknown archaeological resources.
        Mitigation Measure CR-1: Stop Work and Prepare and Implement a Data Recovery Plan if
        Unanticipated Archaeological Resources are Encountered During Construction. In the event that
        archaeological resources are unexpectedly encountered during ground-disturbing activities, work within
        100 feet of the find shall halt and an archaeologist meeting the Secretary of the Interior’s Professional
        Qualifications Standards for archaeology shall be contacted immediately to evaluate the resource.2 If the
        resource is determined by the qualified archaeologist to be precontact, then a Native American
        representative shall also be contacted to participate in the evaluation of the resource. If the resource is
        identified in the waterside improvements area, then a qualified marine archaeologist shall assist in the
                                                             Page 52 of 1541


                                                                                                                                   Page 17 of 41

        treatment and evaluation of the resource. Any waterside discoveries that are removed from their
        submerged environment shall be kept fully submerged in a container of freshwater for storage until the
        archaeologist can examine the find. If the qualified archaeologist and/or Native American representative
        determines it to be appropriate, archaeological testing for CRHR eligibility shall be completed. If the
        resource proves to be eligible for the CRHR and significant impacts to the resource cannot be avoided by
        means of changes in the design of the project, a qualified archaeologist shall prepare a data recovery
        plan tailored to the physical nature and characteristics of the resource, pursuant to the requirements of
        the California Code of Regulations, CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4(b)(3)(C). The data recovery plan
        shall identify data recovery excavation methods, measurable objectives, and data thresholds to reduce
        any significant impacts to cultural resources related to the resource. Pursuant to the data recovery plan,
        the qualified archaeologist and Native American representative, as appropriate, shall recover and
        document the scientifically consequential information that justifies the resource’s significance. The City
        shall review and approve the data recovery plan and archaeological testing as appropriate, and the
        resulting documentation shall be submitted to the regional repository of the California Historical
        Resources Information System, pursuant to California Code of Regulations, CEQA Guidelines Section
        15126.4(b)(3)(C).
        Finding: The City finds that implementation of Mitigation Measure CR-1, which is hereby adopted and
        incorporated into the project, would avoid or substantially reduce the significant environmental effect
        identified in the Final EIR to a less than significant level.
        Facts in Support of Finding: Implementation of Mitigation Measure CR-1 would require work stoppage if
        archaeological resources are discovered, evaluation by a qualified archaeologist, participation by a
        Native American representative and/or qualified marine archaeologist where appropriate, archaeological
        testing for CRHR eligibility when warranted, and preparation and implementation of a resource-specific
        data recovery plan if an eligible archaeological resource cannot be avoided. Therefore, impacts related to
        archaeological resources would be less than significant with mitigation.

4.2.5    Geology and Soils
Impact GEO-7: Construction activities such as dredging have the potential to impact paleontological
resources. Impacts would be less than significant with mitigation incorporated.
        Mitigation Measure GEO-1: Implement Paleontological Worker Environmental Awareness Program
        During Construction. Prior to the start of construction, a Qualified Professional Paleontologist, defined
        as a paleontologist who meets the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology standards, or his or her designee
        shall conduct a paleontological Worker Environmental Awareness Program training for all construction
        personnel participating in subsurface dredging regarding unanticipated discoveries and the procedures
        for notifying paleontological staff should fossils be discovered by construction staff. A training
        acknowledgment form shall be signed by all workers who receive the training, and a copy of the signed
        training acknowledgement form shall be retained by the project contractor and provided to the City.
        Mitigation Measure GEO-2: Stop Work Upon Unanticipated Discovery of Paleontological Resources
        and Implement Recommendations During Construction. The City shall require the following
        mitigation measure for dredging activities. If a potential fossil is discovered during dredging, construction
        activity within 50 feet of the find shall cease until the discovery is examined by a Qualified Professional
        Paleontologist as defined by the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology.6 If the find is determined to be
        scientifically significant, the Qualified Professional Paleontologist shall direct all mitigation measures
        related to paleontological resources consistent with the SVP (2010) standards, which shall include fossil
        salvage, laboratory preparation, curation in a paleontological repository, and a paleontological monitoring
        report. Additionally, the Qualified Professional Paleontologist and City shall decide if full- or part-time
        monitoring shall be instated for further project-related dredging. A Qualified Professional Paleontologist,
        is defined by the SVP (2010) as an individual with:


6
 Society of Vertebrate Paleontology. 2010. Standard Procedures for the Assessment and Mitigation of Adverse Impacts to Paleontological Resources.
Society of Vertebrate Paleontology Impact Mitigation Guidelines Revision Committee.
                                                  Page 53 of 1541


                                                                                                        Page 18 of 41

        • A graduate degree in paleontology or geology, and/or a publication record in peer reviewed journals;
            and demonstrated competence in field techniques, preparation, identification, curation, and reporting in
            the state or geologic province in which the project occurs. An advanced degree is less important than
            demonstrated competence and regional experience.
        •   At least two full years professional experience as assistant to a Project Paleontologist with
            administration and project management experience; supported by a list of projects and referral
            contacts.
        •   Proficiency in recognizing fossils in the field and determining their significance.
        •   Expertise in local geology, stratigraphy, and biostratigraphy.
        •   Experience collecting vertebrate fossils in the field.

        Finding: The City finds that implementation of Mitigation Measures GEO-1 and GEO-2, set forth above,
        which are hereby adopted and incorporated into the project, would avoid or substantially reduce the
        significant environmental effect identified in the Final EIR to a less-than-significant level.
        Facts in Support of Finding: Implementation of Mitigation Measure GEO-1 would ensure construction staff
        are trained to identify paleontological resources, and Mitigation Measure GEO-2 would ensure that
        construction work would stop if a paleontological resource is discovered and procedures are in place that
        would be followed to avoid destruction of paleontological resources. Therefore, impacts would be less
        than significant with mitigation.

4.2.6       Hydrology and Water Quality
Impact HYD-1: Due to the focused and limited construction elements and short duration of project
construction, the proposed project would not substantially degrade surface or groundwater quality, contribute
meaningfully to existing water quality impairments, or result in exceedances of applicable water quality
objectives or waste discharge requirements. Water quality impacts related to pier demolition would be less
than significant with mitigation.
        Mitigation Measure HYD-1: Include and Implement Additional Best Management Practices in the
        SWPPP Prior to and During Pier Demolition. In compliance with the requirements of the Construction
        Stormwater General Permit, prior to construction the construction contractor shall prepare a Stormwater
        Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) and implement the SWPPP during construction. The SWPPP shall
        be submitted to the Berkeley Public Works Department and the State Water Resources Control Board
        (via the Stormwater Multiple Application and Report Tracking System [SMARTS]) for review and approval
        at least 60 days prior to start of construction. In addition to standard Erosion Control, Sediment Control,
        and Good Housekeeping Best Management Practices, the following Best Management Practices shall be
        included in the SWPPP and implemented during pier demolition:
        • Site washout areas shall be located at least 100 feet from a storm drain, open ditch or surface water
            and ensure that runoff flows from such activities do not enter receiving water bodies, unless otherwise
            approved by the RWQCB.
        •   All re-fueling, cleaning, and maintenance of equipment shall occur at least 100 feet from storm drain,
            open ditch or surface water and/or within secondary containment, unless otherwise approved by the
            RWQCB.
        •   Particular care shall be exercised to prevent foreign materials (e.g., construction scraps, wood
            preservatives, other chemicals and debris, etc.) from entering the San Francisco Bay during pier
            demolition.
        •   If wood preservatives must be applied to cut-wood surfaces, the materials, whenever feasible, shall be
            treated at an onshore location to preclude the possibility of spills into State waters.
        •   A containment boom shall be placed around all active portions of a construction site where wood
            scraps or other floatable debris could enter the water.
        •   The containment boom and net shall be cleared daily or as often as necessary to prevent
            accumulation of debris.
                                                   Page 54 of 1541


                                                                                                           Page 19 of 41

        • Tarps and basins shall be used above deck to contain debris and materials.
        • Dipnets shall be on-site and can be used to retrieve debris if it accidentally falls into the water.
        • A 50-foot-long spill containment boom as well as absorbent pads shall be kept on-site and shall be
          deployed in the event that there is a release of fluids into the water.
        • Contractors shall make mandatory that work crews are carefully briefed on the importance of
          observing the appropriate precautions and reporting any accidental spills.

        This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
        agencies.
        Finding: The City finds that implementation of Mitigation Measure HYD-1, set forth above, which is
        hereby adopted and incorporated into the project, would avoid or substantially reduce the significant
        environmental effect identified in the Final EIR to a less than significant level.
        Facts in Support of Finding: Construction activities associated with dredging, pier demolition, pile
        installation, and other in-water work could temporarily affect water quality through sediment disturbance,
        turbidity, or the accidental release of debris and pollutants. Mitigation Measure HYD-1 would require
        preparation and implementation of a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan and additional project-specific
        best management practices in accordance with the SWRCB Stormwater Construction General Permit,
        including debris containment, spill prevention and response measures, equipment maintenance
        requirements, and protection of Bay waters during demolition activities. Project construction would also
        be required to comply with the conditions of a Regional Water Quality Control Board Section 401 Water
        Quality Certification for work within the San Francisco Bay, which would include water quality protection
        measures intended to help protect water quality during construction activities in surface waters and
        reduce the potential for construction to result in water quality exceedances or impair beneficial uses.
        Compliance with applicable permit requirements and implementation of Mitigation Measure HYD-1 would
        avoid or minimize water quality impacts and reduce impacts to a less-than-significant level.

4.2.9    Tribal Cultural Resources
Impact TCR-1: The proposed disturbances due to construction on the non-fill ground and seabed would
adversely affect Tribal Cultural Resources. With adherence to mitigation measures agreed upon through AB 52
consultation, impacts to tribal cultural resources would be less than significant with mitigation.
        Mitigation Measure TCR-1: Conduct Cultural Resources Sensitivity Training Prior to Construction.
        Prior to the start of any ground disturbing activities, including excavation on land and dredging in water,
        the City of Berkeley (City) or its contractor(s) shall provide all construction personnel conducting ground
        disturbing activities, with cultural resources sensitivity training. The training will be conducted in person,
        or via a video meeting, to be viewed by all construction personnel involved in ground disturbing activities
        prior to the start of construction. The training will be developed and conducted in coordination with locally
        affiliated California Native American Tribe(s) that have participated in consultation with the City for the
        project (referred to hereafter as “Consulting Tribes”). Cultural resources sensitivity training will include
        relevant information regarding sensitive tribal cultural resources, applicable regulations including
        consequences of violation, and protocols for unanticipated discoveries and avoidance. The training will
        emphasize the requirement of confidentiality and culturally appropriate treatment of any finds of
        significance to Native Americans.
        Mitigation Measure TCR-2: Provide Signage Acknowledging Native American History Prior to
        Operation. Prior to operation, the City shall provide signage at the project site that acknowledges Native
        American history and importance of the area. Language and design for the signage shall be developed in
        consultation with Consulting Tribes, including the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe. The location of the signage
        shall be thoughtfully integrated into the project design and shall be respectful of Native American culture
        and values. Photographs of human remains shall not be depicted on the signage. The City or its
        contractor(s) shall incorporate the location and content of the signage prior to Final Design. Consulting
        Tribes shall be given the opportunity to comment on the signage prior to the Final Design being approved
        by the City.
        Mitigation Measure TCR-3: Conduct Native American Monitoring During Construction. Prior to the
        start of any ground disturbing activities, including excavation and grading on land not previously covered
        by fill and any dredging in water, the City or its contractor(s) shall retain a Native American monitor(s)
        from a Consulting Tribe(s) for purposes of construction monitoring. If multiple Consulting Tribes request
        to monitor, the City will establish a rotating schedule to include all tribes requesting monitoring. The City
        shall provide monitors with at least 48 hours’ notice prior to the start of any ground disturbing activity that
        requires monitoring. Native American monitors shall observe project-related ground disturbing activities
        located in previously undisturbed areas (i.e., areas not consisting of fill) and provide daily monitoring logs
        to the City detailing construction observed and results at minimum (confidential information can be
        redacted at the monitor’s discretion). Monitors shall have the authority to temporarily halt work in the
        event of discovery or a potential Tribal Cultural Resource.
        If suspected Tribal Cultural Resources are encountered at any point during ground disturbing activities,
        work within a 100-foot radius shall halt and the find shall be evaluated for significance as required by
        Mitigation Measure TCR-4. The 100-foot radius may be reduced or expanded as appropriate by the
        monitor if conditions, such as expanded boundaries or increased sensitivity, warrant the reduction or
        expansion. Native American monitoring may be reduced to spot-checking or eliminated at the discretion
        of the monitor, in coordination with the City, as warranted by conditions such as encountering fill soils,
        bedrock, or negative findings during the first 60 percent of grading. If monitoring is reduced to spot-
        checking, spot-checking shall occur, at minimum, when ground-disturbance moves to a new location
        within the project site and when ground disturbance will extend to depths not previously reached (unless
        those depths are within bedrock). Ground disturbing activities shall not be contingent on the presence or
        availability of a Native American monitor, and ground disturbing may proceed regardless of whether or
        not a monitor is present on site.
                                               Page 58 of 1541


                                                                                                      Page 23 of 41

     Mitigation Measure TCR-4: Evaluate Discovered Tribal Cultural Resources and Implement Resulting
     Recommendations During Construction. If suspected Tribal Cultural Resources are encountered at
     any point during ground disturbing activities, work within a 100-foot radius shall halt and Consulting
     Tribes shall evaluate the suspected resource for significance as a Tribal Cultural Resource. If the find is
     archaeological in nature, then the City or its contractor(s) shall also retain a qualified archaeologist to
     respond and evaluate significance as required by Mitigation Measure CUL-1. The City shall review the
     significance evaluation of the Tribal Cultural Resource and determine whether the find meets the criteria
     in California PCR Section 21074. If a discovered Tribal Cultural Resource is determined by the City to
     meet the criteria in California PRC Section 21074, avoidance and preservation in place shall be the
     preferred method of mitigating impacts and the City shall first consider the measures in California PRC
     Section 21084.3(b) in consultation with Consulting Tribes. If significant impacts to the resource cannot be
     avoided via project redesign, then the City shall work with Consulting Tribes to develop other appropriate
     measures to mitigate impacts. This could include, but would not be limited to, data recovery, installation
     of a permanent plaque or mural to inform the public, interpretive and/or educational elements, and/or
     landscaping to include native plants. Work in the area may resume following the determination by the City
     and completion of any applicable measures mitigating impacts to the Tribal Cultural Resource, if any.
     Mitigation Measure TCR-5: Provide Respectful Treatment of Native American Human Remains
     Upon Unanticipated Discovery and Implement Recommendations During Construction. In addition
     to adherence to the California Health and Safety Code Sections 7050.5, should human remains be
     identified during construction, no photographs shall be taken without express permission from the on-site
     Native American Monitor, and no invasive scientific testing shall be completed without consultation with
     the NAHC appointed Most Likely Descendent. Any bone that cannot be identified as faunal shall be
     treated as human remains until positively identified as being non-human by the coroner and/or a qualified
     archaeologist, as appropriate. The Most Likely Descendant shall provide recommendations for reburial,
     and human remains and associated funerary items shall be reburied by Tribal representatives in a
     location agreed upon between the Tribe and the City. Any reburial location shall be accessible to Tribal
     members in perpetuity, not be subject to further disturbance, and kept confidential.
     Finding: The City finds that implementation of Mitigation Measures TCR-1 through TCR-5, set forth
     above, which are hereby adopted and incorporated into the project, would avoid or substantially reduce
     the significant environmental effect identified in the Final EIR to a less-than-significant level.
     Facts in Support of Finding: Mitigation Measures TCR-1 through TCR-5, developed through consultation
     conducted pursuant to Assembly Bill 52, would require cultural resources sensitivity training, Native
     American monitoring of construction activities in designated areas, evaluation and treatment of any
     discovered tribal cultural resources, interpretive signage acknowledging Native American history, and
     procedures for the respectful treatment of Native American human remains. Implementation of these
     measures would avoid or minimize impacts to tribal cultural resources and reduce impacts to a less-than-
     significant level.

4.4    CUMULATIVE IMPACTS

An EIR is required to discuss the cumulative impacts of a project when the project’s incremental effect is
cumulatively considerable. CEQA Guidelines §15130(a). “Cumulatively considerable” means that the
incremental effects of the project are significant when viewed in connection with the effects of past projects,
other current projects, and probable future projects. CEQA Guidelines § 15065(a)(3); Pub. Resources Code §
21083(b)(2). The cumulative impacts of the project, in combination with reasonably foreseeable probable future
projects, are analyzed throughout Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, of the Draft EIR. The findings in
this section are based on the Draft EIR, the discussion and analysis in which is hereby incorporated in full by
this reference.
The City finds that the proposed project would result in cumulatively considerable contributions to significant
cumulative impacts related to Noise, Land Use and Planning, and Recreation.
As discussed in Section 3.10, Noise, of the Draft EIR, construction of the proposed project would require
demolition of portions of the existing Berkeley Pier, dredging, pile installation, and construction of new
waterside and landside facilities. Construction activities, particularly waterside pile driving and limited nighttime
construction activities, would generate noise levels that exceed applicable City thresholds at nearby sensitive
receptors. Although Mitigation Measure NOI-1 would require implementation of a Construction Noise
Management Plan and a variety of feasible noise-reduction measures, some construction noise impacts would
remain significant and unavoidable. In addition, multiple cumulative projects are planned within the Berkeley
Waterfront area, several of which are located within 1,000 feet of the project site and could generate
                                                Page 64 of 1541


                                                                                                      Page 29 of 41

construction noise during overlapping construction periods. Concurrent construction of these projects could
increase noise levels experienced by nearby sensitive receptors, including live-aboard boats and recreational
users. The Draft EIR also concludes that cumulative operational mobile noise associated with increased
roadway vehicle volumes on portions of University Avenue could exceed applicable significance thresholds.
Accordingly, cumulative noise impacts would be significant and unavoidable, and the project's contribution
would be cumulatively considerable.
With respect to cumulative construction noise, Mitigation Measure NOI-1 has been adopted and incorporated
into the project and will substantially lessen the project's contribution to this cumulative impact, but will not
reduce it to a less-than-significant level. With respect to cumulative operational roadway noise, the City finds
that no feasible mitigation has been identified to reduce the project's contribution to a less-than-significant
level. Construction of a soundwall along this segment of University Avenue would introduce new environmental
impacts, change the character of adjacent parks, and conflict with General Plan Policy OS-12, which directs
that land adjacent to parks be sensitively developed so that safe access is maintained and views are not
significantly reduced. A soundwall is therefore infeasible. As discussed in Section 5, none of the alternatives
analyzed in the EIR would avoid this impact while meeting the basic project objectives. This significant and
unavoidable cumulative impact is acceptable for the reasons set forth in the Statement of Overriding
Considerations in Section 6.
As discussed in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, of the Draft EIR, the proposed project would generally be
consistent with the Berkeley General Plan, Berkeley Marina Master Plan, Plan Bay Area 2050, Bay Area Clean
Air Plan, Climate Action Plan, Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, Measure L, and the policies of the San
Francisco Bay Plan with implementation of mitigation measures. However, the Draft EIR concludes that
cumulative construction noise and cumulative operational mobile noise impacts would result in inconsistencies
with Berkeley Municipal Code noise standards adopted for the purpose of avoiding environmental effects.
Because cumulative noise impacts would remain significant and unavoidable, cumulative land use and
planning impacts would also remain significant and unavoidable, and the project's contribution would be
cumulatively considerable. Because these cumulative impacts result from the same underlying cumulative
noise impacts, no additional feasible mitigation is available beyond that described above, and the City's finding
with respect to cumulative noise applies equally to this impact.
As discussed in Section 3.11, Recreation, of the Draft EIR, the proposed project would provide substantial
recreational benefits through construction of a new public pier, breakwater, public plaza, Bay Trail
improvements, cycle track, and related public access amenities. The Draft EIR concludes that cumulative
growth would not create a deficiency in park acreage or require construction of additional recreational facilities
to maintain service standards. However, cumulative impacts associated with the construction and operation of
recreational facilities are addressed through the environmental analyses contained throughout the Draft EIR.
Because cumulative construction-related noise and cumulative operational mobile noise impacts would remain
significant and unavoidable, cumulative recreation impacts would also remain significant and unavoidable.
Accordingly, the project's contribution to cumulative recreation impacts would be cumulatively considerable.
Because these cumulative impacts result from the same underlying cumulative noise impacts, no additional
feasible mitigation is available beyond that described above, and the City's finding with respect to cumulative
noise applies equally to this impact.
The City finds that cumulative impacts related to Air Quality and Geology and Soils would be less than
significant with implementation of mitigation measures and compliance with applicable regulations. As
discussed in Sections 3.2, Air Quality; and 3.5, Geology and Soils, of the Draft EIR, the proposed project's
incremental contribution to cumulative impacts in these resource areas would not be cumulatively considerable
because identified mitigation measures and regulatory requirements would reduce impacts to a less-than-
significant level. Accordingly, cumulative impacts in these resource areas would be less than significant with
mitigation incorporated. The City further finds that cumulative impacts associated with all other environmental
resource topics analyzed in the Draft EIR would be less than significant or would not result in a cumulatively
considerable contribution to a significant cumulative impact. Accordingly, no significant unavoidable cumulative
impacts have been identified for those resource areas.

                                                                                                        Page 30 of 41

4.5    GROWTH INDUCING IMPACTS

An EIR is required to discuss growth inducing impacts, which consist of the ways in which the project could
foster economic or population growth, or the construction of additional housing, either directly or indirectly, in
the surrounding environment. CEQA Guidelines § 15126.2(e); Public Resources Code § 21100(b)(5). Direct
growth inducement would result, for example, if a project involves the construction of substantial new housing
that would support increased population in a community or establishes substantial new permanent employment
opportunities. This additional population could, in turn, increase demands for public utilities, public services,
roads, and other infrastructure. Indirect growth inducement would result if a project stimulates economic
activity that requires physical development or removes an obstacle to growth and development (e.g.,
increasing infrastructure capacity that would enable new or additional development). It must not be assumed
that growth in any area is necessarily beneficial, detrimental, or of little significance to the environment (CEQA
Guidelines § 15126.2(e)).
Section 4, Other CEQA Required Sections, of the Draft EIR analyzes the growth inducing impacts of the
project; the discussion and analysis in which is hereby incorporated in full by this reference.
The proposed project would replace the closed Berkeley Pier with a new publicly accessible pier, breakwater,
and ferry terminal that would support zero-emission ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco while
improving recreational access to the Berkeley Waterfront. The project would not include residential,
commercial, office, or industrial development and would not directly generate population growth or substantial
new employment opportunities. The project would also not alter the planned location, distribution, density, or
growth rate of population in Berkeley or the surrounding region. Rather, the project would provide a new
transportation option and recreational amenities that are consistent with regional and local planning
assumptions, including those reflected in Plan Bay Area 2050 and the City’s land use planning framework.
Accordingly, the project would not directly or indirectly induce substantial unplanned population or employment
growth.
Although certain transportation projects can indirectly induce growth by providing substantial new capacity that
removes constraints on future development, the proposed project is not capacity-enhancing. Rather, the
proposed ferry service, bicycle facilities, pedestrian improvements, and transit enhancements are intended to
serve existing transportation demand, improve regional connectivity, and provide an environmentally friendly
alternative to single-occupancy vehicle travel between the East Bay and San Francisco. The project would not
extend transportation or utility infrastructure into undeveloped areas, increase infrastructure capacity beyond
what is needed to serve the project, or otherwise enable new development that could not occur under existing
conditions. Future development in the Berkeley Waterfront area would continue to require separate
discretionary approvals from the City and would be governed by applicable planning documents, including the
Berkeley General Plan and future Waterfront planning efforts. Any growth that may occur in the vicinity of the
project site would therefore be planned, independently reviewed, and subject to its own environmental
analysis, rather than induced by the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project.
Therefore, the City finds that the project would not induce substantial unplanned population growth and would
not remove an obstacle to growth that could result in significant environmental effects beyond those analyzed
in the Draft EIR.

SECTION 5: FEASIBILITY OF PROJECT ALTERNATIVES
5.1    Project Alternatives

The Draft EIR analyzed four EIR alternatives, examining the environmental impacts and feasibility of each EIR
alternative, as well as the ability of the EIR alternatives to meet project objectives. The project objectives are
listed in Chapter 2, Project Description, of the Draft EIR; the potentially significant environmental effects of the
project, including feasible mitigation measures identified to avoid these impacts, are analyzed throughout
Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, of the Draft EIR; and the alternatives are described in detail in
Chapter 5, Alternatives, of the Draft EIR. Comparative information regarding the EIR alternatives, including
their distinguishing features and relative environmental impacts, is provided in Draft EIR Table 5-1, Alternatives
                                                Page 66 of 1541


                                                                                                        Page 31 of 41

Summary (Draft EIR page 5-3), and Table 5-2, Summary of Alternatives' Impacts and Comparison to Proposed
Project (Draft EIR page 5-29). Brief summaries of the alternatives are provided below. A brief discussion of the
Environmentally Superior Alternative follows the summaries of the alternatives. The findings in this section are
based on the Draft EIR, the discussion and analysis in which is hereby incorporated in full by this reference.
Based on the project objectives and anticipated environmental consequences, and pursuant to CEQA
Guidelines Section 15126.6, the following EIR alternatives were selected for environmental analysis:
     • Alternative 1: No Project Alternative. CEQA requires analysis of a No Project Alternative. CEQA
       Guidelines § 15126.6(e)(2). Under Alternative 1, none of the improvements associated with the
       proposed project would occur and the current uses would remain. The deteriorated pier would remain
       closed, no new ferry service from Berkeley would be established, vehicle trips across the Bay would
       continue at their current rate, no new public plaza would be installed, none of the improvements along
       University Avenue or Seawall Drive would be installed, and the Seawall Drive East Parking lot would
       remain in its current condition. Alternative 1 would result in avoided construction impacts compared to
       the proposed project but would generate greater long-term impacts to aesthetics due to the lack of
       improvements, as well as to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, transportation, and land use and
       planning due to the lack of circulation improvements and fewer reductions in criteria pollutants as a
       result of continued reliance on single-occupancy vehicle travel. In addition, Alternative 1 would not
       fulfill any of the project objectives.
     • Alternative 2: Shortened Breakwater Alternative. Alternative 2 would retain all components of the
       proposed project, with a reduced-length breakwater. Construction of a shortened breakwater would
       result in a decrease to construction-related impacts compared to the proposed project and would
       maintain similar operational impacts to that of the proposed project while fulfilling most project
       objectives, though with somewhat reduced public access.
     • Alternative 3: Shortened Pier Alternative. Alternative 3 would implement the proposed project as
       planned but would reduce the length of the pier such that it would not extend beyond the breakwater.
       A shortened pier would result in reductions to construction impacts compared to the proposed project
       while maintaining ferry service, and operational impacts would remain similar to the proposed project.
       However, public access and recreational opportunities would be limited, and therefore, Alternative 3
       would meet the project objectives to a lesser extent than the proposed project.
     • Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative. Alternative 4 would involve the construction
       of the full pier and breakwater but would eliminate landside improvements such as the public plaza,
       cycle track, Bay Trail Extension, parking lot upgrades, and bus facilities. Minimal landside construction
       would still be required under Alternative 4 to complete and ensure emergency access to the proposed
       Pier including the Pier Abutment itself (including deep soil mixing to create a seismically stable landing
       for the abutment) and retaining wall and fill in the area to create vehicle and accessible connections
       between the existing sidewalk/Seawall Drive and the new pier. Several construction-related impacts
       would be reduced compared to the proposed project as a result, however, impacts to air quality,
       greenhouse gas emissions, and transportation would increase long-term due to fewer multimodal
       access opportunities and continued reliance on single-occupancy vehicle travel to access the new
       pier. In addition, Alternative 4 would provide substantially fewer public access opportunities and
       recreational benefits and, therefore, would not fulfill all project objectives.

The City hereby concludes that the Final EIR sets forth a reasonable range of EIR alternatives to the Berkeley
Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project that address the significant environmental impacts of constructing and
operating the project, so as to foster informed public participation and informed decision making. The City finds
that the alternatives identified and described in the Final EIR were considered and further finds the No Project
Alternative (EIR Alternative 1), the Shortened Pier Alternative (EIR Alternative 3), and the Reduced Landside
Facilities Alternative (EIR Alternative 4) infeasible for the specific economic, social, or other considerations set
forth below pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21081(b). The City further finds that the Shortened
Breakwater Alternative EIR (Alternative 2) is feasible and would reduce certain construction-related
environmental impacts compared to the proposed project while still achieving most of the basic project
objectives, and is, therefore, adopted.

5.1.1   EIR Alternative 1 - No Project Alternative
Under the No Project Alternative (Alternative 1), none of the improvements associated with the Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project would be implemented. The existing Berkeley Pier would remain closed and
continue to deteriorate, no new ferry service would be established between Berkeley and San Francisco, no
public plaza, Bay Trail Extension, cycle track, bus improvements, or parking lot improvements would be
constructed. Existing transportation patterns, including transbay automobile travel, would continue under
existing conditions.
Findings: This alternative would result in reduced impacts with respect to biological resources, cultural
resources, geology and soils, hydrology and water quality, noise, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and
service systems because it would avoid construction-related environmental impacts. However, impacts relating
to aesthetics, air quality, greenhouse gas emissions and energy, land use and planning, and transportation
would be greater than under the selected project because Alternative 1 would not provide the long-term
benefits associated with zero-emission ferry service, reductions in vehicle miles traveled, improved multimodal
transportation infrastructure, or revitalization of the Berkeley Waterfront. In addition, Alternative 1 would not
eliminate the existing deterioration of the Berkeley Pier or provide the climate resilience, emergency response,
recreational, and regional connectivity benefits associated with the project. Specifically, Alternative 1 would not
replace the existing Berkeley Pier with a new seismically safe structure designed to meet Risk Category IV
(Essential Facility) standards, account for projected sea level rise and improve emergency response
capabilities. Nor would Alternative 1 repair an actively eroding section of shoreline or remove outdated
infrastructure that may contain hazardous materials such as creosote-treated pier piles. Furthermore,
Alternative 1 would not fulfill either of the project’s basic objectives because it would neither enhance public
access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront nor provide efficient and environmentally
friendly zero-emission ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco (see Section 5.5, No Project
Alternative, of the Draft EIR). Accordingly, Alternative 1 would also forego the economic benefits associated
with ferry service revenue, enhanced regional connectivity facilitating improved access to educational and
employment opportunities throughout the Bay Area, and increased opportunities for recreation and tourism at
the Waterfront.
The City finds that Alternative 1 is infeasible for social, economic, and environmental reasons. The No Project
Alternative would eliminate the environmental impacts associated with project construction, but would also
forego the substantial long-term public benefits associated with restoring public access to the Berkeley
Waterfront, providing zero-emission ferry service, improving multimodal transportation connections, enhancing
recreational opportunities, supporting regional mobility, increasing transportation resiliency, and reducing
reliance on single-occupancy vehicle travel. In addition, Alternative 1 would allow the Berkeley Pier to remain
closed and continue to deteriorate, thereby denying the public recreational, educational, transportation, and
access benefits that the project is intended to provide. Furthermore, because the No Project Alternative would
forego the project’s anticipated benefits related to regional mobility and increased Waterfront visitation, it would
also forego the associated economic benefits of improved access between Berkeley and San Francisco,
increased visitation to the Berkeley Waterfront and nearby businesses, and enhanced access to existing jobs,
commerce, and recreational destinations throughout the Bay Area. The City finds that these lost public benefits
would not be socially or economically acceptable and that Alternative 1 would not advance the environmental
benefits associated with reduced vehicle miles traveled, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, and expanded
sustainable transportation opportunities. Therefore, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15091(a)(3), the
City finds that specific social, economic, and environmental considerations make Alternative 1 infeasible.
Alternative 1 is hereby rejected because it would not meet the project objectives and, consistent with CEQA
Guidelines Section 15091(a)(3), specific social, economic, and environmental considerations make Alternative
1 infeasible.

5.1.2   EIR Alternative 2 – Shortened Breakwater Alternative
Alternative 2 would implement the project substantially as proposed, but with a shortened breakwater of
approximately 300 feet rather than the 400-foot breakwater evaluated as part of the proposed project. The
purpose of the breakwater is to provide a safe harbor for ferry operations while also providing public access
                                                             Page 68 of 1541


                                                                                                                        Page 33 of 41

and recreational opportunities. Under Alternative 2, all other major project components, including the ferry
service, public pier, public plaza, Bay Trail Extension, cycle track, parking lot improvements, and multimodal
transportation facilities, would be constructed as proposed.
Findings: This alternative would result in reduced impacts with respect to air quality, biological resources,
greenhouse gas emissions, hydrology and water quality, and noise because the shortened breakwater would
reduce construction intensity, Bay fill, and pile installation requirements. Impacts related to aesthetics, cultural
resources, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials, land use and planning, recreation,
transportation, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and service systems would generally remain similar to
those of the proposed project. However, Alternative 2 would not eliminate any of the significant and
unavoidable impacts identified for the project. Accordingly, significant and unavoidable impacts related to
construction noise, as well as related land use and planning and recreational impacts, would remain (refer to
Section 5.6, Alternative 2: Shortened Breakwater Alternative, of the Draft EIR).
The City finds that Alternative 2 is technologically feasible. The Coastal Study prepared for the project
evaluated 250-foot, 300-foot, and 400-foot breakwater configurations and concluded that a 300-foot
breakwater would provide sufficient sheltering for ferry operations, minimize wave exposure at the berths, and
achieve nearly the same reduction in operational downtime as the 400-foot configuration.7 The Coastal Study
specifically concludes that increasing the breakwater from 300 feet to 400 feet would provide only marginal
improvements in wave disturbance and operational downtime and supports the selection of the 300-foot
breakwater as the recommended design option (refer to Coastal Study, Executive Summary, pages 5 through
7).8 Additionally, the City finds that Alternative 2 is economically feasible because the reduction in breakwater
length would require less construction and accordingly fewer materials, less Bay fill, and fewer piles than the
proposed project, thereby reducing construction costs while still achieving the primary operational purpose of
the breakwater. As described above, Alternative 2 would also result in reduced construction-related impacts to
air quality, biological resources, greenhouse gas emissions, hydrology and water quality, and noise due to the
reduction in construction intensity and Bay fill. However, Alternative 2 would not eliminate any of the significant
and unavoidable impacts identified for the project, and accordingly, significant and unavoidable impacts for
construction noise, as well as related land use and planning and recreational impacts, would remain (refer to
Section 5.5, Alternative 2: Shortened Breakwater Alternative, of the Draft EIR). Nevertheless, the City finds that
Alternative 2 is environmentally feasible due to the reduction in construction-related and Bay fill impacts. The
City further finds that Alternative 2 is socially feasible. Although the shortened breakwater would slightly reduce
public access and recreational opportunities compared to the proposed project, the primary purpose of the
breakwater is to provide a safe harbor for ferry vessels, while improved public access is a secondary benefit
(refer to pages 5-9 and 5-10 of the Draft EIR). The evidence in the record demonstrates the social feasibility of
a reduction in the proposed breakwater length, because a 300-foot breakwater can achieve the safe harbor
function while still providing substantial public access and recreational opportunities. The City accordingly finds
that the modest reduction in public access associated with a shorter breakwater is acceptable considering the
reduction in environmental impacts, reduced construction intensity, and reduced cost associated with
Alternative 2.
Alternative 2 is hereby identified as the preferred alternative and the proposed Project, and the City further
finds that, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15091 (a)(1), changes or alterations have been made in
preferred Alternative 2 which substantially lessen significant construction-related environmental effects,
including those associated with air quality, biological resources, greenhouse gas emissions, hydrology and
water quality, and noise, as identified in the final EIR. Alternative 2 would meet the primary purpose and most
of the basic project objectives of the project by providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission
ferry service and enhanced public access and recreational opportunities. However, due to the shortened
