5.1.3   EIR Alternative 3 – Shortened Pier Alternative
Alternative 3 would implement the proposed project as planned, but would reduce the length of the pier from
approximately 1,080 feet to approximately 675 feet. Under this alternative, the pier would terminate at the point
where the pier and breakwater intersect and would not extend beyond the breakwater. Ferry service, the
breakwater, and landside improvements would remain substantially the same as under the approved project.
Findings: This alternative would result in reduced impacts with respect to air quality, biological resources,
greenhouse gas emissions and energy, hydrology and water quality, and noise due to the reduction in the
length of the pier and associated reduction in construction duration, Bay fill, and pile installation requirements.
Impacts related to aesthetics, cultural resources, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials, land
use and planning, recreation, transportation, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and service systems would
generally remain similar to those of the approved project. However, Alternative 3 would not eliminate any of the
significant and unavoidable impacts identified for the approved project. Significant and unavoidable impacts
related to construction noise, recreation, and land use and planning would remain because pile driving and
other construction activities would still occur under Alternative 3 (refer to Section 5.7, Alternative 3: Shortened
Pier Alternative, of the Draft EIR).
Although Alternative 3 would result in a slight reduction of construction-related impacts compared to the
proposed project, the City finds that Alternative 3 is socially infeasible. A primary purpose of the project is to
restore the Berkeley Pier as an important recreational and public access feature of the Berkeley Waterfront
(refer to Section 2.3, Project Objectives, of the Draft EIR). Unlike the breakwater, whose primary function is to
provide a safe harbor for ferry operations, the portion of the pier extending beyond the breakwater is intended
primarily to provide enhanced public access and recreational opportunities. As described in the Draft EIR,
reducing the length of the pier by approximately 405 feet would diminish public access to the Bay and reduce
the recreational benefits provided to the Berkeley community and the region (refer to page 5-19 of the Draft
EIR). Accordingly, Alternative 3 would fulfill most project objectives by providing ferry service and some
enhanced public access and recreational opportunities, however it would do so to a substantially lesser extent
compared to the proposed project and Alternative 2. Furthermore, while Alternative 3 would slightly reduce
certain temporary construction-related impacts, it would not eliminate any of the project's significant and
unavoidable impacts, and the limited reduction in temporary impacts does not justify the corresponding
reduction in the long-term public access and recreational benefits that a longer pier would provide. Therefore,
the City finds that the reduction in public access and recreational opportunity associated with Alternative 3
would not be socially beneficial when weighed against the limited environmental benefit provided by the
alternative.
Alternative 3 is hereby rejected because it would not eliminate any of the significant and unavoidable impacts
of the proposed project and, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15091(a)(3), specific social and
environmental considerations make Alternative 3 infeasible.

5.1.4   EIR Alternative 4 – Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative.
Alternative 4 would implement the waterside components of the project, including the pier, breakwater, and
ferry infrastructure, but would eliminate landside improvements such as the public plaza, cycle track, Bay Trail
Extension, parking lot upgrades, electric vehicle charging facilities, and bus facilities. Limited landside
construction would still occur to provide utility connections, emergency vehicle access, the pier abutment,
retaining walls, and other infrastructure necessary to support operation of the pier and ferry facilities.
Findings: This alternative would result in reduced impacts with respect to aesthetics, biological resources,
cultural resources, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials, hydrology and water quality, noise,
recreation, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and service systems due to the reduced landside footprint and
corresponding reduction in landside construction activities. However, Alternative 4 could result in greater
impacts related to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions and energy, land use and planning, and
                                                Page 70 of 1541


                                                                                                       Page 35 of 41

transportation because it would eliminate multimodal transportation improvements, electric vehicle charging
facilities, and active transportation amenities that support reductions in vehicle miles traveled and greenhouse
gas emissions. The Draft EIR concludes that significant and unavoidable impacts related to construction noise,
recreation, and land use and planning would remain under Alternative 4, because pile driving and other
waterside construction activities would still occur. Therefore, Alternative 4 would not eliminate any of the
project's significant and unavoidable impacts (refer to Section 5.8, Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities
Alternative, of the Draft EIR).
The City finds that Alternative 4 is infeasible for social and environmental reasons. Although Alternative 4
would reduce certain temporary construction-related impacts, it would do so by eliminating important public
recreational amenities and multimodal transportation improvements that are fundamental components of the
project. Specifically, Alternative 4 would eliminate the Bay Trail Extension, public plaza, cycle track, bus
facilities, parking lot improvements, and electric vehicle charging facilities that are intended to improve public
access, recreation, bicycle and pedestrian connectivity, transit access, and sustainable transportation
opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront. As described in the Draft EIR, these facilities are important
components of the project's objectives to enhance public access and recreational opportunities and to
encourage public transit, bicycle, and other active transportation modes. Alternative 4 would therefore fulfill the
project's objectives to a much lesser extent than the approved project (refer to page 5-25 of the Draft EIR).
Furthermore, the elimination of these facilities would not be consistent with broader City and regional
multimodal transportation goals described in Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, including policies
encouraging bicycle, pedestrian, and transit access to the Berkeley Waterfront. While Alternative 4 would
reduce certain temporary construction-related impacts, it would not eliminate any of the project's significant
and unavoidable impacts, and the limited reduction in temporary impacts does not justify the corresponding
loss of long-term transportation, recreation, sustainability, and public access benefits associated with the
approved project. Therefore, the City finds that the reduction in facilities and associated public benefits under
Alternative 4 would not be socially acceptable when weighed against the limited environmental benefits
provided by the alternative.
Alternative 4 is hereby rejected because it would not eliminate any of the significant and unavoidable impacts
of the proposed project and, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15091(a)(3), specific social and
environmental considerations make Alternative 3 infeasible.

5.2    Environmentally Superior Alternative

Section 15126.6(e)(2) of the CEQA Guidelines requires that an environmentally superior alternative be
identified from among the alternatives evaluated in the EIR. In accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section
15126.6(e)(2), if the environmentally superior alternative is the No Project alternative, the EIR shall also
identify an environmentally superior alternative from among the other alternatives.
The No Project Alternative would avoid most construction-related environmental impacts associated with the
project. However, the No Project Alternative would not achieve any of the project's basic objectives because it
would neither enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront nor provide
efficient and environmentally friendly zero-emission ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.
Therefore, the No Project Alternative is not identified as the environmentally superior alternative.
Among the action alternatives evaluated in the Draft EIR, Alternative 4, the Reduced Landside Facilities
Alternative, is identified as the environmentally superior alternative. As discussed in Section 5.10.2,
Identification of Environmentally Superior Alternative, of the Draft EIR, Alternative 4 would reduce a greater
number of construction-related impacts than the proposed project and the other action alternatives, including
impacts related to aesthetics, biological resources, cultural resources, geology and soils, hazards and
hazardous materials, hydrology and water quality, noise, recreation, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and
service systems due to the reduced extent of landside construction. However, Alternative 4 would achieve the
project's objectives to a substantially lesser extent than Alternative 2 because it would eliminate key project
elements, including the public plaza, cycle track, Bay Trail Extension, bus facilities, parking lot improvements,
and electric vehicle charging facilities. The Draft EIR concludes that Alternative 4 could also result in greater
long-term impacts related to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, land use and planning, and transportation
                                                Page 71 of 1541


                                                                                                      Page 36 of 41

due to reduced multimodal access opportunities and a potential reduction in the use of ferry service. In
addition, Alternative 4 would not eliminate any of the significant and unavoidable impacts identified for the
project (refer to pages 5-29 through 5-31 of the Draft EIR).
Although EIR Alternative 4 is identified as the environmentally superior alternative, the City finds that EIR
Alternative 2, the Shortened Breakwater Alternative, is the preferred alternative and the proposed project (see
Section 5.1.2, above), because it reduces construction-related environmental impacts associated with Bay fill,
pile installation, and construction intensity while continuing to achieve the project's objectives to a greater
extent than the other analyzed alternatives. Specifically, EIR Alternative 2 would provide substantially greater
public access, recreational, multimodal transportation, sustainability, and public benefit improvements than EIR
Alternative 4 while still reducing environmental impacts relative to the proposed project. Accordingly, while
Alternative 4 is identified as the environmentally superior alternative, the City finds that EIR Alternative 2
represents the superior balance of environmental protection and achievement of project objectives and is,
therefore, the preferred alternative and the proposed Project.

SECTION 6: STATEMENT OF OVERRIDING CONSIDERATIONS
CEQA requires the decision-making agency to balance the benefits of a project against its significant
unavoidable impacts when determining whether to approve a project. If the benefits of the project outweigh its
unavoidable adverse environmental effects, those effects may be considered acceptable. CEQA requires the
agency to state in writing the specific reasons for considering a project’s significant and unavoidable impacts to
be acceptable. Those reasons must be based on substantial evidence in the Final EIR or elsewhere in the
administrative record. CEQA Guidelines §15093(b); see also Public Resources Code Section 21081(b).
As set forth above, the City has found that the proposed project will result in project-level and cumulative
significant adverse environmental impacts related primarily to construction noise associated with waterside pile
driving and nighttime construction activities, and a cumulatively considerable contribution to a significant
cumulative operational roadway noise impact on University Avenue between Seawall Drive and Marina
Boulevard. As discussed in Draft EIR Sections 3.9, Land Use and Planning, 3.10, Noise, 3.11, Recreation, and
4.1, Significant Environmental Effects that Cannot Be Avoided, the project's significant and unavoidable Land
Use and Planning and Recreation impacts are not independent physical environmental effects, but instead
result from the same underlying significant and unavoidable construction noise impacts (refer to Impact LU-2,
Impact REC-2, and Draft EIR page 4-1). Similarly, the cumulative Land Use and Planning and Recreation
impacts are attributable to the project’s cumulatively considerable contribution to cumulative construction and
operational noise impacts. These significant impacts cannot be avoided following adoption, incorporation into
the project, and implementation of mitigation measures described in the EIR. The City has also considered the
range of alternatives analyzed in Draft EIR Chapter 5. As discussed in SECTION 5: of this document, the City
has identified the Shortened Breakwater Alternative (EIR Alternative 2) as the preferred alternative and the
proposed Project, because it would reduce certain environmental impacts related to Bay fill and the intensity of
construction activities, while still being technologically and socially feasible. However, significant and
unavoidable project-level and cumulative impacts related to construction noise and by extension land use and
planning and recreation would remain.
As required by CEQA Guidelines §15093(b) and Public Resources Code Section 21081(b), the City has
balanced the economic, legal, social, technological or other benefits of the proposed project, including region-
wide or Statewide environmental benefits, against its significant and unavoidable environmental impacts, the
finds that the benefits of the proposed project outweigh its unavoidable adverse environmental effects, and that
the adverse environmental effects are therefore acceptable.
In its balancing of the benefits associated with the project against its significant and unavoidable environmental
impacts, the City considered the duration of benefits and certain impacts. Specifically, the City considered that
the significant and unavoidable impacts associated with project construction would be temporary (up to an
estimated 80 to 90 days), would cease after construction of the project is completed, and would be limited to
                                                 Page 72 of 1541


                                                                                                          Page 37 of 41

only some project construction activities (i.e., waterside construction activities involving pile driving, including
the demolition and pile-installation phases).
In addition, for the significant and unavoidable cumulative impact related to operational noise from increased
roadway vehicles, the City considered the severity of the impact. The EIR found that when roadway vehicle
volumes from the proposed project and another cumulative project (the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan) are
combined, there is an increase in noise levels of 5.5 dBA Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL) (without
consideration of proposed project Transportation Demand Management [TDM]) and 5.4 dBA CNEL (when
accounting for proposed project TDM) along the stretch of University Avenue between Seawall Drive and
Marina Boulevard. This noise level would be greater than the threshold of 5 dBA CNEL (page 3.10-18 of the
Draft EIR, subheading Mobile Operational Noise identifies the applicability of this threshold). In making its
decision, the City considered that the cumulative impact is only 0.4 dBA CNEL above the threshold. The City
also considered the contribution of noise from the proposed project, compared to the contribution of noise from
the Waterfront Specific Plan. The increase in noise without the project [i.e., considering only the Waterfront
Specific Plan contribution] is estimated to be 4.5 dBA CNEL, whereas the increase in noise due to only the
proposed project is estimated to be 0.9 to 1.0 dBA CNEL. Furthermore, the City also considered the
conservative nature of the analysis presented in the EIR. The analysis presented in the EIR represents the
conservative scenario of implementing the maximum development potential of the Draft Waterfront Specific
Plan. There is the potential that the cumulative development scenario may be lower as the Draft Waterfront
Specific Plan proposed details are refined. The Draft Waterfront Specific Plan has not been adopted by the
Berkeley City Council, and the associated development scenario that is adopted by the Berkeley City Council
may be lower than what is presented in the EIR.
The City also considered that the benefits associated with the project would provide long-term benefits (i.e., the
lifetime of pier and ferry service is estimated at a minimum of 50 years) that would far exceed the duration of
construction activities that could result in significant and unavoidable impacts.
The following statement identifies the reasons why, in the City’s judgment, specific benefits of the project
outweigh the significant and unavoidable effects. The substantial evidence supporting the benefits of the
project can be found in the preceding sections of these Findings, in the project itself, and in the record of
proceedings as defined in SECTION 9:, below. The City further finds that each of the project benefits
discussed below is a separate and independent basis for these findings. The reasons set forth below are
based on the Final EIR and other information in the administrative record.
The City further finds that these significant and unavoidable impacts are outweighed by the benefits of the
project, each of which, independently of the others, constitutes overriding consideration warranting approval of
the project. Those benefits, and additional considerations related to this finding, are as follows:
      • Recreational Benefits
         • The project will restore public recreational access to the Berkeley Waterfront and San Francisco
           Bay by replacing the deteriorated Berkeley Municipal Pier, which has been closed to the public
           since 2015, with a new publicly accessible pier and breakwater that will provide opportunities for
           walking, sightseeing, fishing, environmental education, and shoreline access for current and future
           generations. The project has a design life of 50 years, meaning that the City of Berkeley would
           benefit from this important recreational amenity for at least 50 years.
         • The project will substantially enhance recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront through
           construction of a new pier, breakwater, public plaza, Bay Trail extension, bicycle facilities,
           interpretive signage, seating areas, fish-cleaning stations, landscaping, and accompanying public
           amenities that expand access to and support enjoyment of the Bay.
         • The project will implement a portion of the planned Bay Trail Extension along Seawall Drive and
           directly support the recreational goals of the San Francisco Bay Trail and the MTC Bay Trail Gap
                                                              Page 73 of 1541


                                                                                                                                  Page 38 of 41

             Closure Implementation Plan.9 The Draft EIR identifies the Berkeley Waterfront gap as Segment ID
             4151, which is designated as a Tier 1 (Higher Priority and Lower Cost) project and ranked third
             among Tier 1 Bay Trail gap-closure segments10 (refer to Draft EIR Page 3.11-11). By constructing a
             portion of this planned trail segment and improving bicycle and pedestrian access to the Waterfront,
             the project will help advance the long-term regional goal of completing a continuous shoreline trail
             around San Francisco Bay and improving public access to the Bay.
           • The project will replace the existing deteriorated pier entrance area with a new ADA-accessible
             public recreational plaza containing seating, landscaping, bicycle facilities, interpretive signage, and
             a public restroom. The plaza is intended to function as a new, publicly accessible recreational
             space and may accommodate future public events, educational programming, recreational
             activities, and other community gatherings and public uses that promote community engagement
             and improve public enjoyment of the Berkeley Waterfront (refer to Draft EIR Section 2.5.2,
             Landside).
           • The project will advance longstanding City and regional recreational goals and policies relating to
             waterfront access, recreation, multimodal transportation, and enhancement of the Berkeley
             Waterfront area as established by the adopted plans and policies such as the BCDC Bay Plan,
             ABAG/MTC Plan Bay Area 2050, the Berkeley General Plan, the Berkeley Waterfront Master Plan,
             the Berkeley Marina Master Plan (refer to Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, Impact
             LU-2).
       • Transportation Benefits

            • The project will provide new ferry service connecting Berkeley with San Francisco, improving
              regional transportation connectivity and resilience for East Bay residents, workers, students, and
              visitors. The Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) Berkeley Ferry Service Business
              Plan identifies the Berkeley ferry service as a long-planned component of the regional ferry network
              which will provide approximately 1,910 average weekday ferry trips during the first year of service
              and approximately 2,110 weekday trips by 2040, and concludes that the proposed ferry service
              would expand regional mobility options, support existing and future activities at the Berkeley
              Waterfront, and provide a meaningful new transbay transportation connection (refer to Section 1 of
              the Business Plan).11
            • The project will improve transportation access to existing employment, education, housing,
              services, and recreational opportunities throughout the Bay Area by providing a reliable and
              accessible transbay transit option that strengthens regional mobility and will facilitate access
              between East Bay communities and major employment centers, including higher-paying job centers
              located in San Francisco. As described in the WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, West
              Berkeley is an area with relatively limited regional transit access and reduced accessibility to jobs
              compared to other areas within Berkeley and the broader region. Within the region, areas such as
              San Francisco and San Mateo Counties have a greater number of jobs which provide average
              salaries approximately 21 percent higher than comparable jobs in Alameda County. Implementation
              of the proposed ferry service would provide East Bay residents with a new connection to higher-
              paying job centers across the Bay while also improving access to jobs, educational opportunities,
              and destinations within Berkeley, and would therefore expand access to economic opportunities for
              West Berkeley residents as well as the broader region (refer to Section 6 of the WETA Business
              Plan).12

              • The project will help reduce reliance on single-occupancy vehicle travel by providing a high-quality
               public transit transportation alternative to automobile transbay travel, thereby reducing regional
               vehicle miles traveled (VMT), roadway congestion, and associated environmental impacts. As
               discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation, the project would provide new ferry connection
               between Berkeley and San Francisco that would replace longer automobile commute trips with
               shorter trips to the Berkeley Waterfront. The project would also implement multimodal access
               improvements, including a raised cycle track along University Avenue, Bay Trail improvements,
               bicycle lockers and racks, improved bus facilities, pedestrian improvements, electric vehicle
               charging stations, and transportation demand management measures designed to encourage the
               use of transit and active transportation rather than single-occupancy vehicles. By reducing
               automobile travel demand and supporting shifts to other travel modes through implementation of
               these proposed project components, the project would result in a net decrease in VMT and
               associated environmental impacts (refer to Impact GHG-1, Impact TRA-1, and Impact TRA-2). For
               further discussion of VMT and associated environmental impacts, refer to the discussion below
               regarding Sustainability Benefits.
             • The project will enhance regional emergency transportation preparedness and resilience.
               WETA has a legislative mandate to operate and coordinate emergency water transit when
               regional transportation systems are disrupted due to disaster or other events.13 The new pier is
               designed as an essential facility to support emergency water transportation services in the
               event that natural disasters or other emergencies disrupt existing transportation infrastructure,
               thereby expanding WETA’s ability to provide emergency transportation for first responders,
               disaster service workers, and the general public (refer to Draft EIR Section 2.8, Emergency
               Operation Options).
          • Sustainability (Including region-wide or Statewide environmental benefits)
             • The project will advance State, regional, and local sustainability goals through operation of zero-
               emission electric ferry vessels, installation of ferry charging infrastructure, provision of electric
               vehicle charging facilities for Waterfront visitors, and implementation of multimodal transportation
               improvements that encourage transit use and bicycle and pedestrian travel.
             • The project will result in long-term greenhouse gas emissions reductions, including an annual net
               reduction of 2,368 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions, and support California’s
               transition to a low-carbon, sustainable transportation system through mode shift from automobile
               travel to electric ferry service. The Greenhouse Gas Analysis Memorandum prepared for the
               project’s SB 149 Infrastructure Project Application14 further concludes that the project would remain
               net-negative for greenhouse gas emissions even after accounting for all construction and
               operational emissions, resulting in a net reduction of approximately 22,435 metric tons of carbon
               dioxide equivalent emissions over the evaluated 30-year analysis period and thereby providing a
               long-term regional climate benefit consistent with the goals and policies of adopted greenhouse gas
               reduction plans (refer to Draft EIR Section 3.6, Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy, and Draft
               EIR Appendix B, Air Quality and Greenhouse Gas Emissions Information).
             • The project incorporates substantial climate adaptation and coastal resilience measures, including
               design features that account for and protect against projected sea level rise, physical shoreline
               protection improvements, resilient infrastructure, adaptable water transportation facilities, and long-
               term protection of public access to the waterfront.
          • Social Benefits
             • The project incorporates social investments in bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure, including a new
                 raised cycle track along University Avenue, Bay Trail improvements, bicycle parking facilities, and
                 enhanced pedestrian areas and transit connections, accompanied by ADA-accessible facilities,

On balance, the City finds that there are specific economic, legal, social, technological, or other benefits of the
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project that serve to override and outweigh the significant
unavoidable effects of the project. Therefore, pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15093(b), the City finds
that these significant adverse environmental effects are considered acceptable.

SECTION 7: INCORPORATION BY REFERENCE
These findings incorporate the text of the Final Environmental Impact Report for the Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project by reference and in its entirety. Without limitation, this incorporation is
intended to elaborate on the scope and nature of mitigation measures, the basis for determining the
significance of impacts, the comparative analysis of alternatives, the determination of the environmentally
superior alternative, and the reasons for approving the project in spite of the potential for associated significant
and unavoidable adverse impacts.
The City also incorporates by reference the Final Program Environmental Impact Report for the Expansion of
Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area (State Clearinghouse No. 2001112048), certified by the
WETA Board of Directors in June 2003. The WETA Program EIR evaluated expansion of ferry service
throughout the San Francisco Bay Area, including ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco, and
analyzed environmental topics including dredging, navigation, wake effects, water resources, biological
resources, air quality, land use, aesthetics, cultural resources, geology, noise, transportation, energy, and
growth-inducing impacts. The environmental setting information, environmental analyses, and mitigation
measures contained in the WETA Program EIR, including mitigation measures adopted by WETA for ferry
operations and ferry service expansion, are incorporated by reference into these findings to the extent relevant
to the proposed project. As described in Section 1.1.3 of the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project
EIR, the relevant portions of the WETA Program EIR are summarized and incorporated into the environmental
analysis contained in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, and Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials,
and are part of the evidentiary basis supporting these findings.

SECTION 8: RECIRCULATION NOT REQUIRED
No significant new information was added to the Draft EIR or the Final EIR as a result of the public review and
comment process. The Final EIR responds to comments, and clarifies, amplifies, and makes insignificant
modifications to the Draft EIR. It does not identify any new significant effects on the environment or a
substantial increase in the severity of an environmental impact requiring major revisions to the Draft EIR.
Similarly, the revised project would not result in new or substantially more severe significant impacts than
disclosed previously in the Draft EIR. Therefore, recirculation of the EIR is not required.

SECTION 9: RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Various documents and other materials related to the project constitute the record of proceedings upon which
the City bases its findings and decisions contained herein. The record of proceedings is available for public
review online on the following website: https://berkeleypierferryproject.com/.

SECTION 10: SUMMARY
A. Based on the foregoing Findings and the information contained in the record, the City has made one or
   more of the following Findings with respect to each of the significant effects of the project:
   1. Changes or alterations have been required in, or incorporated into, the project that avoid or
      substantially lessen the significant environmental effects identified in the EIR.
   2. Those changes or alterations are within the responsibility and jurisdiction of another public agency and
      have been, or can and should be, adopted by that other public agency.
   3. Specific economic, legal, social, technological, or other considerations, make infeasible the mitigation
      measures or alternatives identified in the EIR that would otherwise avoid or substantially lessen the
      identified significant environmental effects of the project.
B. Based on the foregoing Findings and the information contained in the record, the City determines that:
   1. Significant effects on the environment that would occur due to the approval of the project have been
      eliminated or substantially lessened where feasible.
   2. Remaining significant effects on the environment found to be unavoidable are acceptable due to the
      factors described in the Statement of Overriding Considerations in SECTION 6:, above.

WHEREAS, on January 12, 2026, the City of Berkeley Parks, Recreation & Waterfront
Department filed an application for Use Permit #ZP2026-0014 to establish transportation
via public ferry service as an allowable use at the Berkeley Pier (“Use Permit”), with
project plans received January 13, 2026; and

WHEREAS, on January 21, 2026, pursuant to Berkeley Municipal Code (“BMC”) Section
23.208.020(C)(1), the Planning Commission reviewed the Use Permit application and
recommended that the Zoning Adjustments Board (“ZAB”) and City Council approve the
Use Permit, and making the findings required by BMC Section 23.208.020(E); and

WHEREAS, on February 11, 2026, notice of the ZAB public hearing was posted pursuant
to BMC Section 23.404.050 and emailed to a broad stakeholder list, there being no private
properties within the 0.5-mile notice radius; and

WHEREAS, on February 26, 2026, the ZAB held a public hearing and, pursuant to BMC
Section 23.208.020(C)(2), approved the Use Permit by a vote of 5-0-3, subject to findings
and conditions, and an added condition noting that its decision was made prior to
publication of the Draft Environmental Impact Report; and

WHEREAS, pursuant to BMC Section 23.208.020(C)(2) and (C)(5), the ZAB’s decision is
not effective until after action by the City Council, and the City Council may affirm, reverse,
or modify the ZAB’s decision; and

WHEREAS, pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code
Section 21000 et seq.) (“CEQA”), the City, as lead agency, prepared an Environmental
Impact Report (SCH No. 2025040995) (“EIR”) for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier-
Ferry Project (“Project”), which includes the ferry use and ferry terminal facilities
authorized by the Use Permit; and

WHEREAS, on November 5, 2026, notice of the City Council public hearing was
published and posted; and

WHEREAS, on November 17, 2026, prior to consideration of this Resolution, the City
Council adopted Resolution No. ##,###-N.S. certifying the Final EIR and adopting CEQA
Findings and a Statement of Overriding Considerations, mitigation measures, and a
Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program for the Project, which CEQA Findings
identify the Shortened Breakwater Alternative (EIR Alternative 2) as the preferred
alternative and the proposed Project; and
                                      Page 78 of 1541




WHEREAS, the City Council desires to modify the ZAB decision to incorporate the
certified Final EIR, the CEQA Findings, and the mitigation measures, and to make minor
technical corrections; and

WHEREAS, on November 17, 2026, the City Council held a public hearing to consider
the ZAB’s decision, and, in the opinion of this Council, the facts stated in, or ascertainable
from the public record, including comments made at the public hearing, warrant approving
the Project and affirming the ZAB’s decision, as modified.

#ZP2026-0014.

FINDINGS FOR APPROVAL
As required by BMC Section 23.406.040 (E) (1-4) “Findings for Approval,” the following
findings shall be made:

1. To approve a Use Permit, the ZAB shall find that the proposed project or use:
       (a) Will not be detrimental to the health, safety, peace, morals, comfort, or general
           welfare of persons residing or visiting in the area or neighborhood of the proposed
           use; and

       Evidence: The project will not be detrimental to the health, safety, peace, morals,
       comfort or general welfare of persons residing or visiting in the area because the
       proposed use will establish a new transportation option for commuting, recreational
       or personal travel to San Francsico, which is a benefit to persons working, residing or
       visiting the area. The project will not be detrimental to the general welfare of persons
       who use the Berkeley Waterfront because the City has conducted an analysis of
       parking that demonstrates that there is sufficient parking available to accommodate
       this use.

       (b) Will not be detrimental or injurious to property and improvements of the adjacent
           properties, the surrounding area or neighborhood, or to the general welfare of the
           City.

       Evidence: The project will not be detrimental or injurious to property and
       improvements of the adjacent properties because the Berkeley Waterfront is a single
       property, owned and managed by the City of Berkeley and because the use of a public
       ferry is a water-related use consistent with the Public Trust Doctrine governing
       Berkeley waterfront land use. The project will not be detrimental to the general
       welfare of the City because establishing ferry service in Berkeley has been identified
       as a goal in multiple City and regional planning documents to improve the general
       welfare of the City by reducing greenhouse gases, improving transportation access
       and providing emergency response and disaster recovery. In addition, the findings for
       required discretionary permits are satisfied per the Evidence in 2 and 3 below.

                                 STANDARD CONDITIONS OF APPROVAL
                                          APPLICABILITY

Use Permits approved through the City of Berkeley are subject to Standard Conditions of Approval (Standard
COAs). The City of Berkeley has established Standard COAs that identify requirements for the construction
and operation of the approved project or use. This includes general administrative conditions, permitting
requirements, project construction and the regulation of on-going, on-site uses. Compliance requirements
with the Berkeley Municipal Code, building permit review and issuance process, construction, final
inspection requirements, certificate of occupancy, and on-going operations of the approved use are
included in this document.

The Standard COAs may vary based on site size, location, environmental settings, topography, historic
alteration or approved uses. Variations in the application of the Standard COAs may occur based on the
project scope and site-specific characteristics including but not limited to parcel size, location, topography,
and use.

         Avoid Disturbance of Nesting Birds. Initial site disturbance activities, including vegetation and
                                                                                                                       State of California     Demolition/Construction
         concrete removal, shall be prohibited during the general avian nesting season (February 1 to
         August 30), if feasible. If nesting season avoidance is not feasible, the applicant shall retain a
         qualified biologist to conduct a preconstruction nesting bird survey to determine the
         presence/absence, location, and activity status of any active nests on or adjacent to the Project
         site. The extent of the survey buffer area surrounding the site shall be established by the qualified
         biologist to ensure that direct and indirect effects to nesting birds are avoided. To avoid the
         destruction of active nests and to protect the reproductive success of birds protected by the
         Migratory Bird Treaty Act and the California Fish & Game Code, nesting bird surveys shall be
         performed not more than 14 days prior to scheduled vegetation and concrete removal. In the event
         that active nests are discovered, a suitable buffer (typically a minimum buffer of 50 feet for
         passerines and a minimum buffer of 250 feet for raptors) shall be established around such active
         nests and no construction shall be allowed inside the buffer areas until a qualified biologist has
         determined that the nest is no longer active (e.g., the nestlings have fledged and are no longer

                                                                                                  Introduction




1           Introduction

In accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15088, the City of
Berkeley has evaluated the comments received on the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Draft
Environmental Impact Report (EIR). The responses to the comments and errata, which are included in this
document—together with the Draft EIR and appendices as well as the Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting
Program (MMRP)—form the Final EIR for use by the City of Berkeley in its review, consideration, and
decision-making.
This document is organized into three chapters:
• Chapter 1 – Introduction. Discusses the purpose and organization of this document and summarizes
  the environmental review process for the project.
• Chapter 2 – Responses to Comments. Provides a list of the agencies, organizations, and persons who
  provided Draft EIR written comments as well as verbal comments during the March 16, 2026, Draft EIR
  public meeting. Copies of all Draft EIR comment letters received as well as the Draft EIR public meeting
  transcript are included and bracketed/labeled. Corresponding responses to these comments are also
  included in this section.
• Chapter 3 – Errata. Lists refinements to and clarifications to Draft EIR text, tables, and figures.

The Final EIR includes the following contents:
• Final EIR introduction (Chapter 1 of this document)
• Draft EIR comments received and responses to comments (Chapter 2 of this document)
• Errata (Chapter 3 of this document)
• Draft EIR and appendices (provided under separate cover)
• MMRP (provided under separate cover)


1.1         Environmental Review Process
Pursuant to CEQA, lead agencies are required to consult with public agencies having jurisdiction over a
proposed project and to provide the general public with an opportunity to comment on the Draft EIR.
The City of Berkeley distributed a Notice of Preparation (NOP) of the EIR for a 31-day agency and public

2.2.1       Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability
For clarification, the City notes that the State Clearinghouse number for the 2003 WETA EIR was omitted
from Draft EIR Section 1.1.3, Incorporation by Reference. Accordingly, the following clarification text
change has been made to Draft EIR Section 1.1.3, Incorporation by Reference (page 1-2):
    This EIR hereby incorporates by reference the Final Program EIR for the Expansion of Ferry Transit
    Service in the San Francisco Bay Area (State Clearinghouse Number 2001112048; WETA Program
    EIR).

This revision is clarifying in nature and does not alter the analysis, conclusions, or reliance on the 2003
WETA EIR as described in the Draft EIR.
CEQA Guidelines Section 15150 allows for an EIR to “incorporate by reference all or portions of another
document”, allowing for such incorporated language to be considered part of an EIR, thereby reducing
duplication and focusing analysis on what is new or relevant. As stated on Draft EIR Section 1.1.3,
Incorporation by Reference (page 1-2), the 2003 WETA EIR is incorporated into the proposed project Draft
EIR. The 2003 WETA EIR specifically analyzed dredging; navigation; wake analysis; water resources;
biology; air quality; land use and community issues; aesthetics; cultural resources; geology; noise;
transportation; energy; and growth inducing impacts. As stated on Page 1-2, the Draft EIR incorporates by
reference the analyses of all potential environmental impact topics, including background information
regarding the environmental setting and adopted mitigation measures. The 2003 WETA EIR is
incorporated by reference into the Draft EIR, but it does not tier from the 2003 WETA EIR. Tiering, as
defined in CEQA Guidelines Section 15152, refers to using information or analysis from a broader EIR to
concentrate the focus of a future project-level EIR. The 2003 WETA EIR is a programmatic analysis of
ferry service expansion in the San Francisco Bay Area, while the 2026 proposed project Draft EIR is a
project-level analysis for a specific and separate Berkeley pier ferry project not tiered from the 2003
WETA EIR.
Though the Draft EIR does incorporate select information from the older 2003 WETA EIR, the project-level
Draft EIR prepared for the proposed project provides new and current background setting information and
analyses based on the latest information available at the time of EIR Notice of Preparation. This approach
allows information from the 2003 WETA EIR to complement the information contained in the Draft EIR.
The mitigation measures outlined in the 2003 WETA EIR are implemented by WETA on all applicable
projects, including the proposed project, and are considered a part of the regulatory baseline for this Draft
EIR.
While the Draft EIR independently analyzes all the potential impacts of the project, it relies on some
information from the 2003 WETA EIR. Specifically, it incorporates by reference mitigation measures that
are now part of the regulatory context (as well as relevant underlying analysis) with respect to whale
strikes, hazards, accidental spills, and water quality, because these potential impacts are consistent with
and attributable to the expansion of ferry service Bay-wide. With respect to site-specific impacts such as
dredging, nearshore conditions, and terminal construction and operation, the Draft EIR provides
independent project-level analysis and does not rely on any part of the 2003 WETA EIR.
The Draft EIR independently analyzes site-specific dredging impacts and does not rely on the 2003 WETA
EIR. Instead, dredging associated with the project is fully evaluated in Section 3.3, Biological Resources;
Section 3.4, Cultural Resources; Section 3.5, Geology and Soils; Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous
Materials; Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality; Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning; Section 3.10,
Noise; Section 3.13, Tribal Cultural Resources; and Section 3.14, Utilities and Service Systems. Similarly, the
2003 WETA EIR evaluated general ferry routes between San Francisco and the East Bay, including
Berkeley. However, the Draft EIR does not rely on the 2003 WETA EIR for terminal siting or nearshore
route conditions. The specific Berkeley pier terminal location and approach routes were determined
through project feasibility and design analyses and are accordingly evaluated independently in the Draft
EIR.

Draft EIR Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, Section 3.7.3, Regulatory Framework states that
the analysis of potential impacts on water resources from accidental spills due to ferry operation, as well
as mitigation measures intended to minimize the potential for accidental spills and impacted water
quality from ferry operations found in the 2003 WETA EIR are incorporated by reference and have been
and would continue to be implemented by WETA as part of service expansions, including for the
proposed project (Page 3.7-19). As discussed, under Draft EIR Impact HAZ-1 (pages 3.7-24 through 3.7-
30) incorporation and implementation of 2003 WETA EIR Mitigation Measures W-3.1 through W-3.3 as
part of the proposed project will require implementation of spill prevention planning, contingency
planning, and operational controls, including training and response preparedness, to minimize the
potential for accidental discharges and related water quality impacts from ferry operations. As described
in the Draft EIR, potential operational discharges would be limited to minor onboard sources such as
lubricants, hydraulic fluids, or sewage, and WETA continues to implement these safety and contingency
planning measures across its ferry system (refer to Draft EIR Page 3.7-29). Accordingly, implementation
of 2003 WETA EIR Mitigation Measures W-3.1 through W-3.3, which is an existing regulatory baseline
condition, would minimize the potential for operational spill hazards resulting in a less-than-significant
impact with regard to potential operational spill hazards and potential related water quality impacts. The
Draft EIR independently evaluates construction-related spill risk in Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water
Quality, and incorporates project-specific mitigation, which requires the incorporation of BMPs in the
Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan prior to and during construction (refer to Impact HYD-1, pages 3.8-
27 through 3.8-35).
Concerning whale strikes, the Draft EIR incorporates by reference mitigation measures from the 2003
WETA EIR (see Section 3.3.3) but further analyzes the potential for whale strikes with updated
information. Refer to Section 2.2.28, Topical Response: Whale Strike, for a discussion specific to potential
whale strikes. As discussed, under Draft EIR Impact BIO-1 (pages 3.3-42 through 3.3-56), implementation
of 2003 WETA EIR Mitigation Measures B-15.1 and B-15.2, which are existing adopted WETA
requirements would require implementation of a whale sighting awareness and reporting program,
including crew training and real-time communication of whale locations among ferry operators and
coordination with U.S. Coast Guard sighting reports, and use of onboard whale detection technologies to
identify marine mammals and avoid vessel strikes, resulting in a less-than-significant impact with regard
to potential operational whale strike impacts (refer to Draft EIR page 3.3-53).
As discussed, under Draft EIR Impact BIO-1 (pages 3.3-42 through 3.3-56) the Draft EIR incorporates by
reference WETA Mitigation Measure NOI-4.1 from the 2003 WETA EIR, which requires coordination with
federal and state resource agencies regarding ferry routes and site-specific evaluation of potential
impacts to sensitive marine mammal haul-out areas to address potential impacts from operational noise.
However, because the proposed project is a site-specific project with defined terminal location and
approach routes and uses an electric rather than a diesel ferry, the Draft EIR does not rely on the 2003
WETA EIR for mitigation of in-water noise impacts. Instead, the Draft EIR provides updated project-level
analysis and mitigation tailored to the project setting. Specifically, Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d) requires
implementation of sound attenuation measures during pile driving, and Mitigation Measure BIO-1(e)
requires preparation and implementation of a Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan, including establishment
of shutdown zones, vessel operation protocols, and real-time monitoring by qualified biologists. These
project-specific measures, which are consistent with 2003 WETA EIR findings and reflect current NOAA
Fisheries guidance and NMFS-approved marine mammal protection practices, would result in a less-than-
significant impact with regard to aquatic resources impacts associated with operational in-water noise.
refer to Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry, for further discussion regarding the 2003 WETA
EIR and impacts to aquatic species from operational ferry noise. Section 3.3, Biological Resources,
evaluates potential operational impacts, including underwater noise and vessel interactions with aquatic
species (pages 3.3-39 through 3.3-66), while Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, considers in-water
infrastructure components and the reduced potential for fuel-related spill risks associated with
electrification (pages 3.8-25 through 3.8-42). Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, evaluates
safety considerations related to battery storage systems and electrical infrastructure (pages 3.7-22

2.2.2       Topical Response: Alternatives
Alternative Assumptions or Requirements
Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(a) and 15126.6(f), an EIR must evaluate a reasonable
range of potentially feasible alternatives that would attain most of the project objectives and permit a
meaningful comparison of environmental impacts. Consistent with CEQA Guidelines Sections 15125,
15126.6(d), and 15151, analysis may rely on reasonable assumptions, supported by available data and
professional evaluation, to describe baseline conditions, future conditions, and the comparative
environmental effects of the proposed project and alternatives.
Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, Sections 5.3 through 5.6 (pages 5-3 through 5-24) describe the project
objectives, screening criteria, and definitions of the alternatives analyzed, including Alternative 1 (No
Project Alternative), Alternative 2 (Shortened Breakwater Alternative), Alternative 3 (Shortened Pier
Alternative), and Alternative 4 (Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative). These sections identify the
assumptions used to define each alternative, including construction methods, operational characteristics,
and physical design characteristics such as pier length, breakwater extent, and recreational amenities.
The Draft EIR relies on a combination of engineering and environmental analyses to establish consistent
assumptions across alternatives, including engineering design inputs prepared by project engineers to
estimate construction duration, dredging quantities, pile driving activity, and footprints for each
alternative; environmental resource-specific quantitative and qualitative analyses, including
transportation and operational assumptions, which apply consistent methodologies to facilitate
comparison between the proposed project and all analyzed alternatives. As described in Draft EIR
Chapter 5, key differences between analyzed alternatives include reductions in Bay fill, differences in pier
and breakwater extent, provision of recreational amenities, and variations in construction intensity and
duration. These physical differences form the basis for quantitative comparisons across alternatives
(refer to Table 5-2, page 5-31).
These assumptions are necessary to ensure that the alternatives analysis provides a logical and
comparative framework for evaluating environmental impacts. CEQA recognizes that analysis of future
conditions necessarily involves forecasts and does not require absolute certainty, provided that
assumptions are reasonable and supported by substantial evidence in the record (CEQA Guidelines
Section 15144). The Draft EIR applies appropriate and consistent assumptions based on available data
and professional judgement throughout the analysis, including in defining and evaluating alternatives,
consistent with CEQA requirements for establishing an environmental baseline and reasonably
foreseeable future conditions (CEQA Guidelines Sections 15125 and 15126.6(e)). Accordingly, the
assumptions and requirements used to develop and evaluate alternatives, including baseline conditions,
No Project conditions, and design parameters, are appropriate and consistent with CEQA. Environmental
impacts associated with the proposed project and evaluated alternatives are addressed throughout the
Draft EIR using a consistent framework, and mitigation measures are identified as appropriate.
With respect to the No Project Alternative, the Draft EIR evaluates reasonably foreseeable future
conditions in the absence of the project, consistent with CEQA Guidelines 15126.6(e)(2). This includes
consideration of planned and expected changes in travel patterns, population, and regional growth that
would occur regardless of project approval. As described in the Draft EIR (refer to Section 3.12,
Transportation; Chapter 5, Alternatives; and Appendix F, Transportation Impact Analysis), these conditions
include continued reliance on existing travel modes, which are expected to result in greater regional
vehicle travel compared to conditions with the proposed project in place. The analysis is based on
available regional and project-specific data, including observed travel behavior and ridership



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                          2- 8
                                                    Page 113 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                                        Response to Comments

assumptions, and reflects a reasonable projection of future conditions rather than a speculative or
outcome-driven scenario. As a result, the No Project Alternative reflects a reasonable forecast of future
environmental conditions, including transportation patterns, in the absence of the project. The
comparative analysis appropriately uses this scenario to evaluate differences in environmental impacts,
including vehicle miles traveled and associated effects (refer to Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, Table 5-
2 on page 5-31).
In conclusion, the Draft EIR alternatives analysis and associated assumptions are adequate under CEQA.
Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR alternatives-related analyses or conclusions are necessary in
response to these comments.

Project Objectives
CEQA requires evaluation of a reasonable range of alternatives capable of feasibly attaining most of the
basic project objectives but avoiding or substantially lessening any of the significant impacts of the
project (CEQA Guidelines §15126.6(a)), and does not require consideration of alternatives that are
infeasible or that do not meet most of those objectives (CEQA Guidelines §15126.6(c)). Consistent with
these requirements, Chapter 5, Alternatives, evaluates options that could feasibly attain most of the
project's objectives while avoiding or reducing significant environmental effects associated with the
project.
The project objectives “should include the underlying purpose of the project and may discuss project
benefits.” CEQA Guidelines § 15124(b). The specific formulation of project objectives is a policy decision
of the lead agency. Lead agencies have discretion to define project objectives and to eliminate from
detailed consideration alternatives that do not reasonably achieve those objectives. Accordingly,
alternatives that would not meet most of the project’s fundamental purposes may be appropriately
screened from detailed analysis.
The City clearly defines the basic project objectives in Section 5.3 of the Draft EIR as follows: “(1)
enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and (2) provide efficient
and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.” The
City’s choice to include ferry service as part of its basic project objectives is not an overly narrow
definition of the project objectives and rather reflects a long-standing and well-documented interagency
effort to establish ferry service at the Berkeley Waterfront. As documented on the City’s project website 1,
the City has been coordinating with WETA since 2018 to evaluate and advance a dual-purpose pier that
would support both public access and ferry service, including execution of a Memorandum of
Understanding to fund and complete feasibility studies, followed by subsequent amendments and
funding agreements to advance design, environmental review, and permitting. These efforts build upon
WETA’s 2016 Strategic Plan identifying Berkeley as a priority location for expanded ferry service and
reflect a multi-year planning and funding partnership between the City and WETA. 2 Accordingly,
establishing ferry service at the Berkeley Waterfront is a fundamental and longstanding objective of the
project.
The basic project objectives used by the City have not precluded the analysis of a reasonable range of
alternatives, as evidenced by the analyses of four alternatives (including the No Project Alternative).
Furthermore, several of the alternatives that were considered but rejected were rejected because they
were infeasible, not because they did not meet the basic project objectives. For example, several off-site
alternatives, as well as alternatives involving increasing BART capacity were rejected for being infeasible,

avoiding or substantially lessening any of the significant effects of the project. This demonstrates that
the project objectives did not constrain the analysis of reasonable alternatives.
The City identified fundamentally different approaches in the Draft EIR, such as different locations,
different scales, and different transit projects, but ultimately rejected them, consistent with CEQA
Guidelines § 15126.6(c) because they either were infeasible, did not avoid or substantially lessen a
significant environmental effect, or did not attain most of the basic project objectives (refer to Section 5.9
of the Draft EIR). CEQA requires the EIR “set forth only those alternatives necessary to permit a reasoned
choice” and informed decision-making. CEQA Guidelines § 15126.6(f). Here, the City provided three
different action alternatives, in addition to the No Project Alternative, to provide a meaningful comparison
to the proposed project. The three EIR Alternatives provided sufficient variation to allow for meaningful
decision-making. Two of the alternatives included in the Draft EIR include a reduction in Bay fill (from a
shortened pier and a shortened breakwater), while reducing public access to the Bay. These alternatives
allow decision makers to weigh the environmental benefits of reduced fill with the consequence of
reduced public access to the Bay. One of the alternatives included in the Draft EIR reduces the amenities
associated with the proposed project. Specifically, it eliminates the cycle track; renovations to University
Avenue and Seawall Drive; bus facilities; public plaza; Bay Trail Extension; and renovated parking lot off
Seawall Drive, including no installation of EV charging for parking stalls. This alternative offers a very
different and reduced design compared to the proposed project. This alternative allows decision makers
to weigh the environmental benefits of reduced construction with the consequence of reduced facilities
for public use.
The Draft EIR provides sufficient and appropriate objectives to support the environmental review process,
including an adequate evaluation of a reasonable range of alternatives consistent with project objectives
and, thus, is consistent with CEQA requirements. Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR project objectives
or the project- or alternatives-related analyses and conclusions are necessary in response to these
comments.

Alternatives Dismissed
Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(a), an EIR is required to consider and analyze a range of
reasonable project alternatives that would feasibly attain most of the basic objectives but would avoid or
substantially lessen significant impacts of the project. Whether or not alternative sites should be included
as potential alternatives depends on the particular facts of the case, with the question focusing on
whether the range of analyzed alternatives is reasonable. Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, contains a
comparative impact assessment of four alternatives to the proposed project, a discussion of alternatives
considered but rejected, and a determination of the environmentally superior alternative. Therefore, Draft
EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, adequately evaluates alternatives that could feasibly attain most of the project
objectives while avoiding or reducing significant environmental effects associated with the project.
CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(c) states that an EIR should identify any alternatives that were rejected
during the scoping process and explain why they were rejected. The reasons for rejection may include
failure to meet project objectives, infeasibility, or the inability to avoid significant environmental impacts.
As discussed in Draft EIR Section 5.9, Alternatives Considered but Rejected, (pages 5-25 through 5-28), the
City considered 11 alternatives, some with several variations, that were ultimately rejected. Specific
reasons for rejection include increased environmental impact; no reduction in environmental impacts
when compared to the project; infeasibility, including jurisdiction issues; and failure to meet most of the
basic objectives of the project.
In this case, the EIR considered a range of alternatives and rejected those that were unreasonable or
infeasible including off-site alternatives. The EIR is not required to select an offsite alternative for
analysis. Alternatives located entirely outside of the City’s jurisdiction, such as the Golden Gate Fields and

Emeryville Marina locations identified by comments, are infeasible for the City to construct or approve, as

Several of the specific alternative locations considered in the 2008 EIS/EIR and referenced by comments
were similarly evaluated and rejected. An alternative near the Berkeley Fishing Pier was not considered
further because it was substantially similar in concept to the proposed project. An alternative off Gilman
Street was rejected because it would increase, rather than decrease, environmental impacts (page 5-26).
Given the geography of the shoreline, no alternative location near the foot of Gilman Street would avoid
siting the alternative within Eastshore State Park, an area more ecologically sensitive than the proposed
project site. Locating a ferry terminal within an established state park also presents a feasibility concern
independent of environmental impacts: the project is expected to be funded in part by federal Department
of Transportation funds, which would trigger Section 4(f) requirements under the US Department of
Transportation Act. Under Section 4(f), agencies must select an alternative that completely avoids the
use of protected public parks, historic sites, or wildlife refuges unless that alternative is deemed
infeasible or imprudent. Because other alternative sites have been found to be feasible and prudent (i.e.,
the proposed project site), an alternative off Gilman Street is not expected to be feasible, pursuant to
Section 4(f) requirements. More generally, the purpose of Draft EIR Section 5.9 is to identify the principal
reasons certain alternatives were not carried forward for detailed analysis, not to provide a project-level
environmental impact analysis of each conceptual alternative considered during early planning. The Draft
EIR therefore provides an adequate description of the alternatives screening process and the basis for
the City's determinations.
The City considered the alternatives identified by the comments in Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, but
ultimately determined that they were either infeasible, would not attain the basic objectives of the
proposed project, or would not provide reduced significant environmental impacts. Accordingly, the EIR
satisfies the CEQA requirement to evaluate a reasonable range of alternatives.
Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or analysis are necessary in response to these
comments.

BCDC Planning Consistency and Permit Compliance
Consistency with applicable Bay Plan policies, including those related to circulation, public access, and
parking for recreational users, are addressed in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, Impact LU-2 (pages
3.12 through 3.9-36), which evaluates whether the project would conflict with plans and policies adopted
to avoid or mitigate environmental effects. Project consistency with Bay Plan policies is specifically
addressed in pages 3.9-12 through 3.9-23 (including Table 3.9-1). As shown in Table 3.9-1, the project
incorporates specific design features and operational strategies for consistency with Bay Plan policies
related to circulation, public access, and parking. With respect to public access (Public Access Policies 9
and 11), the project restores and expands shoreline access through provision of a publicly accessible
pier, Bay Trail Extension, and new shoreline amenities, which enhance both physical and visual access to
the Bay and provide for safe and convenient movement along the shoreline.
With respect to circulation (Transportation Policy 4 and Public Access Policy 11), the project includes
multimodal circulation improvements such as the raised cycle track, improved transit stops, Bay Trail
connections, and defined pedestrian pathways that maintain safe, efficient, and clearly organized
circulation for all user groups and improve access to and along the shoreline.
Circulation conflicts among user groups are primarily a social consideration rather than a physical
environmental impact under CEQA and therefore is not analyzed in this EIR; however, the topic is
addressed through the City’s compliance with the BCDC Bay Plan, including Transportation Policy 4 and
Public Access Policy 11, which require that transportation and shoreline improvements maintain and
enhance safe, physical access to and along the Bay shoreline for all users. To that end, the City has
designed the project to reduce potential conflicts between ferry commuters and recreational users.
Mapping circulation routes under different time-based scenarios is not necessary to identify or address
these conflicts. The project incorporates dedicated infrastructure designed to safely accommodate both
user groups, including a new Class IV cycle track on University Avenue, raised table-top (i.e., flat top) style
crosswalks, a widened sidewalk connecting the AC Trans bus stop to the proposed plaza, wayfinding
signage for pedestrians, bicyclists and vehicles and improved shoreline pathways. Therefore, at any point
in time and under any plausible scenario, all user groups will be accommodated.
With respect to parking (Recreation Policy 9), Table 3.9‑1 explains that the City would implement a
parking strategy to balance shared-use parking for ferry patrons and recreational users, thereby
minimizing the shoreline area dedicated to parking while maintaining access for existing recreational
users and avoiding displacement of park and marina parking. The analysis therein concludes that the
project would not conflict with the Bay Plan policies related to parking. For further discussion of
compliance with Recreation Policy 9 refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking.
The City presented its circulation, parking and public access approach to the BCDC Design Review Board
(DRB), an advisory body composed of design and planning professionals that advises the BCDC
Commission on the adequacy of public access proposed as part of projects within BCDC’s jurisdiction,
including the project’s effects on circulation, access, and use by different user groups. At its May 11,
2026 meeting, the DRB reviewed the project’s trail network, circulation, and parking design, including the
balance between recreational and ferry-commuter use of the site, and did not identify a need for further
modification to the circulation approach presented. The DRB concluded that the project would not need
to return for further DRB review. 4 Although the Draft EIR concludes that the project would not conflict with
Bay Plan policies, BCDC independently evaluates consistency as part of its discretionary permit review
process. Accordingly, final determination of consistency with Bay Plan policies, including policies related

2.2.4         Topical Response: Biological/Underwater Noise
The Draft EIR's conclusion that operational underwater noise impacts on marine mammals would be less
than significant is supported by substantial evidence and remains valid.
As explained in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4, Impact BIO-1 (page 3.3-52), underwater noise measurements of
comparable hybrid-electric and conventional diesel ferry vessels demonstrate that electric propulsion
generates less underwater noise than diesel propulsion. Specifically, a report by the Swedish
Environmental Research Institute, directly compared a ferry retrofitted with electric motors, generators,
and batteries (Tellus) to its conventionally diesel-powered sister vessel (Neptunus) - vessels of identical
hull and propeller design, and similar in size to anticipated WETA electric ferry vessels - and found that
the electric vessel radiated up to 10 dB less underwater noise, a difference the report characterizes as
equivalent to a halving of noise. 5 This finding provides direct, vessel-comparable evidence that
electrification reduces, rather than increases or maintains, underwater noise output relative to
conventional diesel vessels.
Several comments cite two additional studies for the proposition that electric propulsion may generate
underwater noise levels of concern: Smith et al. (2026) 6 and Gaggero et al. (2024). 7 Neither study
undermines the Draft EIR's conclusion.
Smith et al. (2026) found that high-frequency tonal noise from electric propulsion "arise[s] from the pulse
width modulation (PWM) used to control the motor," but also found that such noise can be minimized
through "optimi[z]ed PWM switching frequencies that minimi[z]e harmonics in sensitive frequency
ranges" and "electromagnetic interference filters in the drive circuits." This finding directly supports the
Draft EIR's conclusion: it confirms that high-frequency tonal noise is a design-dependent characteristic of
electric propulsion, not an inherent or unavoidable one, and identifies the specific engineering measures
that address it. Since publication of the Draft EIR, WETA has advanced the design-build contract for the
project's electric ferry vessels, which incorporates measures consistent with those identified in Smith et
al.: propulsion motors mounted inboard in enclosed Propulsion Rooms with water-cooled, resilient-
mounted configurations, acoustic insulation and sound-damping coatings on propulsion equipment
spaces, and third-party acoustic measurement and verification during construction. These design
specifications reflect current WETA engineering commitments and constitute substantial evidence that
the noise-reduction findings in Smith et al. are applicable to, and consistent with, the vessels that will be
deployed for this project.
Smith et al. (2026) separately measured underwater noise from matched electric and conventionally
powered vessels across a speed range of 4 to 20 knots, finding that while the electric vessel remained

5 Silent@Sea. 2024. Noise from ships powered by LNG or electricity and its effects: a cross-domain investigation Final report of the
Silent@Sea project. Swedish Environmental Research Institute.
6 Smith, Findlay, Grech La Rosa & Wu (2026), "A comparative study of underwater radiated noise from electric and conventional
boats," J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 159(3): 2388–2397.
7 Gaggero, T., Armelloni, E., Codarin, A., & Borghini, D. (2024). Electric boat underwater radiated noise and its potential impact on
