Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

quieter than the conventional vessel throughout, the magnitude of the difference narrowed as speed
increased (from a 43 dB difference at 4 knots to a 10 dB difference at 20 knots) as propeller cavitation,
rather than motor or PWM noise, became the dominant noise source for both vessel types. This finding
does not undermine the Draft EIR's conclusion. Because cavitation-driven noise increases similarly for
electric and conventional vessels at higher speeds, this finding confirms that the project's electric ferry
vessels would not generate greater underwater noise than the conventional diesel vessels they replace,
consistent with the Draft EIR's determination.
Gaggero et al. (2024) measured underwater noise from a small 8-meter recreational electric vessel with
outboard motors, finding that while the vessel generated less broadband noise than a comparable
gasoline outboard boat, its motor controller produced a high-frequency tonal component exceeding 130
dB re 1 μPa m that could affect species with sensitive high-frequency hearing, such as bottlenose
dolphins. This finding does not translate to the project's ferry vessels. Smith et al. (2026), evaluating a
similarly configured electric outboard vessel, measured comparable tonal noise at only 83 dB re 1 μPa m
(roughly 50 dB lower than reported by Gaggero et al.) and attributed this difference to motor placement
and propulsion architecture: the vessel in Gaggero et al. used a motor mounted within the propeller hub,
whereas the vessel in Smith et al. used an above-waterline motor connected by an L-drive, a configuration
that further isolates the motor from the water. WETA's electric ferry vessels use an even more isolated
configuration, with motors mounted inboard within enclosed Propulsion Rooms, well removed from the
hull and waterline. Given that propulsion architecture and motor placement are established drivers of
high-frequency tonal noise output, Gaggero et al.'s findings, based on a hub-mounted motor configuration
not used in the project's vessels, do not indicate that the project's ferries would generate comparable
high-frequency tonal noise.
For these reasons, the studies cited in comments do not undermine the Draft EIR's finding, based on
direct ferry-to-ferry underwater noise measurements, that this project's electric ferry vessels will generate
less underwater noise than conventional diesel vessels. For further clarification, Draft EIR Section 3.3,
Biological Resources, page 3.3-52 has been revised as follows:
    While the electric ferry vessels would introduce a new noise source, they would generate significantly
    less noise, especially at lower frequency sounds, than traditional diesel engines. Underwater noise
    measurements made of various hybrid electric and conventional ferry vessels indicate that a ship
    retrofitted with electric motors, generators, and batteries (Tellus) radiated less underwater noise than
    a ship with a conventional diesel propulsion system (Neptunus). A report from 2024 prepared by
    Silent@Sea notes the following: "according to our measurements, Tellus radiates less underwater
    noise than Neptunus, with up to 10 dB [difference].” A 10dB difference is a halving of noise, as if a
    wall or barrier has been put in place. The report states: “This is an indication that retrofitting ships
    with modern hybrid propulsion is a potential way to reduce their noise radiation.”94 Additionally, recent
    research evaluating underwater noise generated by electric vessels indicates that while certain
    electric vessel configurations may generate high-frequency tonal noise associated with electric
    propulsion components, underwater noise characteristics vary substantially depending on vessel
    design, propulsion architecture, and motor installation. In particular, Smith et al. (2026) found that
    electric vessels remained quieter than a comparable conventionally powered vessel across the full
    range of operating speeds evaluated and found that such tonal noise can be reduced through
    engineering measures including optimization of motor controller switching frequencies and
    electromagnetic interference filtering.95 Similarly, Gaggero et al. (2024) found that although electric
    vessels may generate high-frequency tonal noise, propulsion architecture and motor placement are
    important factors influencing underwater noise generation.96 Accordingly, following publication of the
    Draft EIR, WETA has advanced the design-build contract for the proposed electric ferry vessels to
    incorporate features consistent with those identified in the recent literature, including propulsion
    motors mounted inboard in enclosed Propulsion Rooms with water-cooled, resilient-mounted
    configurations, acoustic insulation and sound-damping coatings on propulsion equipment spaces,
    and third-party acoustic measurement and verification during construction. These design features
    would minimize the potential for the proposed electric ferry vessels to generate underwater noise

2.2.5       Topical Response: CEQA Adequacy
Draft EIR Section 1.3.2, Content Adequacy, (page 1-13) discusses the adequacy of the content of the EIR
by explaining the standards for adequacy of an EIR identified in CEQA Guidelines Section 15151, and
states that the analysis in EIRs “need not be exhaustive, but the sufficiency of an EIR is to be reviewed in
light of what is reasonably feasible.” EIRs must provide substantial evidence, reasoned explanations of
environmental impacts, and disclose areas of disagreement among experts consistent with CEQA
requirements. Taken as a whole, the Draft EIR contains sufficient detail and analysis to support informed
decision-making and meaningful public participation, consistent with standards for adequacy in CEQA
Guidelines Section 15151. The Draft EIR conclusions are supported by substantial evidence, which is
defined in CEQA Guidelines Section 15384 as “facts, reasonable assumptions predicated upon facts, and
expert opinion supported by facts.” Accordingly, the Draft EIR provides sufficient information to fulfill the
CEQA core purposes of disclosing potential environmental impacts of the proposed project and informing
both decision makers and the public, in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Sections 15003 and 15151.
The City has reviewed the public comments received on the Draft EIR and has confirmed that the
conclusions in the Draft EIR are supported by substantial evidence and that the EIR meets the regulatory
standards of adequacy. For responses to specific issues raised by comments related to the adequacy of
the EIR please refer to those individual responses. No changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or analysis
are necessary in response to these comments.

2.2.6       Topical Response: CEQA Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users
With respect to City’s analysis on baseline recreation users, the Draft EIR assesses the thresholds in
CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, Sections XV and XVI, which provide that there is the potential for a
significant impact if: (1) a project would increase the use of existing facilities such that substantial
physical impacts would occur; (2) a project would include recreational facilities or require the expansion
of existing facilities resulting in a physical effect on the environment; or (3) a project would result in new
or altered parks to maintain acceptable service ratios for parks, the construction of which would cause
significant physical or environmental impacts.
To assess these factors, the Draft EIR (in Section 3.11, Recreation) describes the existing recreational
sites and facilities within and adjacent to the project site, including both publicly administered
recreational facilities and other shoreline- and water-oriented recreational activities occurring throughout
the Berkeley Waterfront. The Draft EIR also describes recreational use at the Berkeley Waterfront by
identifying the existing range of user groups and activities, as well as their primary locations. These
groups or activities include pedestrians, bicyclists, shoreline visitors, boaters, anglers, and passive
recreation users, as well as water-oriented uses such as sailing, kayaking, swimming, wind sports, and



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                          2- 17
                                             Page 122 of 1541

other marina-related activities occurring throughout the Berkeley Waterfront area. The Draft EIR also
identifies the specific locations where these activities occur, including the Bay Trail, Marina Basin, Marina
Mall, Horseshoe Park, the formerly named César E. Chávez Park, McLaughlin Eastshore State Park, South
Sailing Basin, un-improved shoreline access, San Francisco Bay, and additional nearby facilities (refer to
Pages 3.11-1 through 3.11-7).
In response to the comments, Page 3.11-6 of the Draft EIR (Section 3.11.2, Environmental Setting) has
been revised to incorporate the following clarifying text:
    The San Francisco Bay is a tidal estuary that provides a variety of natural resource and open space
    opportunities (refer to Figure 3.11-2). According to the BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, the San
    Francisco Bay is the most important open space in the Bay region, and it provides a variety of unique
    recreational opportunities. Primary recreation activities occurring throughout the San Francisco Bay
    include sailing, kayaking, paddle-boarding, swimming, windsurfing, kitesurfing, canoeing and dragon
    boat canoeing. Additional recreation activities on the Bay include wildlife viewing, fishing and boating
    via public ferry, private and charter boats. These water-based recreational activities often involve
    specialized equipment and access points to the shoreline and marina facilities, and are an integral
    component of the recreational setting at the Berkeley Waterfront.

This clarifying text emphasizes that water-based recreational activities, including those requiring
equipment and direct water access, are explicitly recognized as part of the existing recreational baseline
evaluated in the Draft EIR.
As described in the Draft EIR, the total area of parks and open space within the City is approximately
4,430 acres, which results in a park acres-to-persons ratio of approximately 34.5 acres per 1,000 people.
This ratio provides relevant context for evaluating recreational service capacity citywide, as discussed
further below and in Impact REC-1. In addition, there are several park and recreational areas proximate to
the project site that would remain accessible during project construction, such as the South Sailing docks
and Marina basin (refer to Draft EIR Page 3.11-17). With respect to changes in recreational demand, the
Draft EIR evaluates reasonably foreseeable conditions associated with project operation, including
increased visitation associated with ferry riders accessing the terminal and new recreation use of the pier
for activities such as walking, fishing and sightseeing (refer to Draft EIR Page 3.11-9, Proposed
Recreational Amenities). Impact REC-1 analyzes the impact of increased visitation, finding that the
project would increase the number of visitors to the Berkeley Waterfront area in a manner that may
increase the use of on-site and nearby recreational facilities (Draft EIR page 3.11-16). However, because
the project concurrently creates a net increase in recreational facilities and opportunities (a restored pier,
new Bay Trail and new dedicated cycle track), the Draft EIR concludes that resulting impacts related to
physical deterioration of existing recreational facilities, and the need for new or altered parks to maintain
acceptable service ratios, would be less than significant (refer to Impact REC-1, Draft EIR Pages 3.11-16
through 3.11-20). This conclusion is based on the project's new contribution of new recreational capacity
commensurate with the increased visitation it would generate, not on an assumption that visitation would
remain unchanged. Therefore, no quantified or more detailed baseline usage data is necessary to
determine whether the project would physically degrade recreational resources or require construction of
new facilities. Accordingly, the Draft EIR sufficiently describes the baseline for recreational uses and
describes the project’s changes due to increased recreational use based on substantial evidence.
Further, inclusion of additional quantitative visitation data or estimates of displaced users would not alter
the impact analysis or significance conclusions, which are based primarily on physical capacity, access,
and facility conditions. With respect to access and parking during operation, refer to Section 2.2.20,
Topical Response: Parking. With respect to recreational access during operation, the project would be
expected to improve recreational opportunities by providing new and improved amenities.
In summary, the Draft EIR fully described the baseline consisting of existing recreational uses, their
locations, and user groups at the Berkeley Waterfront; evaluates reasonably foreseeable changes
associated with ferry operations; and demonstrates that construction and operation of the project would
not result in physical degradation of or the need for expanded recreational facilities (Impact REC-1).

Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or mitigation measures are necessary in response to
these comments.

2.2.7       Topical Response: CEQA Process
After reviewing comments received on the Draft EIR, the City has concluded that recirculation of the Draft
EIR, per CEQA Guidelines Section 15088.5, is not warranted. Under CEQA Guidelines Section 15088.5,
recirculation is required only when significant new information is added that reveals a new significant
impact, substantially increases the severity of an identified impact, or otherwise deprives the public of a
meaningful opportunity to comment. The information provided by the comments do not identify a new
significant impact or an increase in the severity of any previously disclosed impact. In response to other
comments, certain specific clarifying edits have been made to the EIR to provide additional context
related to the existing conditions, methodology, and/or impact analysis. However, none of these clarifying
changes affect the impact conclusions or mitigation measures identified in the Draft EIR in a substantive
manner. Accordingly, recirculation of the Draft EIR is not required.

2.2.8       Topical Response: Construction & Operation Noise at Nearby Parks
The Draft EIR impact analysis with respect to noise did not analyze impacts at the formerly named César
E. Chávez Park, Horseshoe Park, Marina Mall, Adventure Playground, or the Bay Trail corridor because
they are located further away than the closest sensitive receptor park (i.e., Shorebird Park) (refer to Draft
EIR Section 3.10, Noise, page 3.10-5), which is the closest park to the primary construction area where the
noisiest activity associated with construction (pile driving) would occur. For Shorebird Park, the impact
analysis generally represents a worst-case scenario and was modeled and analyzed with respect to
project-related noise (refer to Impact NOI-1 on pages 3.10-19 to 3.10-32 of the Draft EIR). Noise levels at
other parks that are located further away would generally be less than these worst-case estimates for
Shorebird Park.
Nonetheless, in response to these comments and for information purposes, Draft EIR Section 3.10, Noise,
Table 3.10-14 (page 3.10-23), has been revised to present both unmitigated and mitigated construction
noise levels at nearby parks during all phases of landside construction, and Table 3.10-16 (page 3.10-26),
has been revised to present both unmitigated and mitigated construction noise levels at nearby parks
during all phases of waterside construction. Revisions to both tables are shown in underlined text below.

2.2.9         Topical Response: Cumulative Impacts
As discussed in Draft EIR Chapter 3.0, Environmental Impact Analysis, the Draft EIR includes a cumulative
impact analysis consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15130, which requires evaluation of the
incremental effects of the proposed project when combined with past, present, and reasonably
foreseeable probable future projects. The Draft EIR cumulative analysis identifies geographic scopes
(e.g., the radius area where other projects could interact with resource area impacts) appropriate to each
resource topic and analyzes a combination of past, present, and probable future projects listed in Draft
EIR Table 3-1 (pages 3-9 to 3-10). Table 3-1 includes 25 projects considered as cumulative projects. As
documented in the sources cited in Table 3-1, the list of cumulative projects was compiled based on
publicly available information published by the City of Berkeley, East Bay Regional Parks District, and the
Metropolitan Transportation Commission/Association of Bay Area Governments. The analysis evaluates
whether the proposed project’s incremental contribution to each identified cumulative impact would be
considerable. Where significant cumulative impacts were identified, the Draft EIR discloses whether the
proposed project would make a cumulatively considerable contribution and, where applicable, identifies
mitigation measures to reduce the project’s incremental contribution. In some cases, even with
mitigation, cumulative impacts may remain significant and unavoidable due to broader regional
conditions or factors beyond the control of the project (e.g., cumulative waterside construction noise
associated with pile driving and nighttime construction and cumulative operational mobile [i.e., roadway
vehicle] noise).
Several comments identify the reopening of a restaurant at 199 Seawall Drive (formerly Hs. Lordship
Restaurant) 8 as a cumulative project. This cumulative project is already included in the Draft EIR. Refer to
Draft EIR Chapter 3, Footnote 1 and Table 3-1, which includes the description of the Berkeley Draft
Waterfront Specific Plan (listed as Project 1 in Table 3-1), and explicitly states that the re-opening of the
restaurant at 199 Seawall Drive is included in the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan.
Several comments also discuss the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan. The Draft Waterfront Specific Plan is
discussed in the Draft EIR cumulative analysis (refer to Draft EIR Chapter 3 Table 3-1), which explains that
the proposed project and the Waterfront Specific Plan are separate projects that are not interdependent.
(See Relationship with Draft Waterfront Specific Plan Section of Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis.)
First, the Waterfront Specific Plan is a long-range planning document, while the proposed project is an
infrastructure project. Next, while the Waterfront Specific Plan would change the zoning designations at
the Waterfront, the Pier-Ferry project can obtain permits pursuant to the existing zoning designations –
the proposed project is in no way reliant on the passage of the Waterfront Specific Plan and would be
pursued regardless. Similarly, the Waterfront Specific Plan, which is still being developed at the staff level,
would proceed regardless of whether or not the proposed project is approved. As discussed further in the
Draft EIR, because the proposed project and the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan are not interdependent,
environmental review of each can proceed independently.
Several comments also refer to a cumulative scenario with 26 ferry terminals in the Bay. 9 This
information cited in comments regarding the establishment of 26 ferry terminals in the region is not an

“This memo details the technical analyses completed to evaluate three new network concepts to expand

The memorandum does include a concept titled “Coverage Network” with 26 ferry terminals but as
described in the Introduction of the memorandum, this is a network concept for consideration. After the
memo was prepared (April 12, 2023), the WETA Board adopted a 2050 Service Vision and Expansion

in WETA’s adopted Service Vision, 4 new tier 1 ferry projects are included (Mission Bay and Treasure

adopted as part of WETA’s vision; therefore, a scenario that includes 26 ferry terminals is not reasonably
foreseeable and the City’s decision not to analyze it is supported by substantial evidence. Page 3-6 of the
Draft EIR identifies what would constitute a cumulative project, and is included here for context:
“Reasonably foreseeable projects are future projects (including those currently proposed) that are likely
or probable, rather than those that are merely possible. Generally, projects are reasonably foreseeable if
they meet any one or more of the following conditions:
• The project is a foreseeable future phase of an existing project.
• Applications for project entitlements or construction are pending with a government agency (these
  projects may have been analyzed in a recent environmental document).
• The project is included in regional transportation plans; regional transportation improvement programs;
  local long-range transportation plans; local land use, general, and specific plans; or an agency’s budget
  or capital improvement program.”

The network concept of 26 ferry terminals does not meet this criteria. Therefore, it is not considered a
reasonably foreseeable cumulative project.
The 2003 WETA EIR evaluates ferry service expansion at a regional, programmatic scale, including
analysis of vessel operations over defined routes throughout the Bay and their potential effects on
biological resources and hydrology and water quality under a systemwide operational scenario. In
contrast, the Draft EIR for the proposed project evaluates project-specific and proximate environmental
effects associated with ferry operations at the Berkeley Waterfront using representative operational
assumptions (refer to Chapter 2, Section 2.7). These analyses focus on nearshore and localized
conditions, including terminal approach and docking, vessel presence within the project viewshed, and
project-related contributions to vessel traffic in the immediate vicinity. As described in Section 3.3,
Biological Resources, and 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, the Draft EIR concludes that operational
impacts associated with ferries, including vessel traffic, underwater noise, wake, and water quality effects
would be less than significant or less than significant with mitigation (refer to Sections 3.3.4 and 3.3.5),
and that the project would not result in a cumulatively considerable contribution to regional Bay-wide
impacts previously evaluated at the programmatic level in the 2003 WETA EIR (refer to Sections 3.3.5 and

2.2.10 Topical Response: Electric Ferry
As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, (pages 2-4, 2-10, and 2-11) the proposed project
assumes operation of electric ferry service consistent with WETA plans as well as regional and State
efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through actions such as increasing access to sustainable
transportation modes. The use of electric ferry vessels is explicitly included in the project description.
Neither the City nor WETA are planning to operate diesel ferry vessels as part of the proposed project,
and the only kind of ferry vessels being environmentally reviewed and cleared as part of the EIR are
electric ferry vessels. Under CEQA, an EIR must evaluate reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts
based on available data and reasonable assumptions supported by substantial evidence. CEQA does not
require that all project components be fully finalized at the time of analysis, nor does it require evaluation
of speculative or hypothetical alternatives, such as analysis of alternative fuel technologies or the use of
diesel vessels, that are not part of the proposed project or reasonably foreseeable conditions.
Regarding questions about the infrastructure for electric ferry vessels, Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project
Description, includes a description of the infrastructure required for electric ferry vessels, including the
Universal Charging Floats or UCFs (refer to Section 2.5.1, Proposed Ferry Vessel Infrastructure Subsection,
pages 2-10 through 2-11), as well as the electrical distribution utilities that would be required for the
proposed project (refer to Section 2.5.4, Electrical Distribution subsection, pages 2-23 through 2-24). As
described therein, the UCF system includes electrical infrastructure such as switchgear, transformers,
converters, and battery storage to support charging of zero-emission ferry vessels and is designed with
redundancy and safety features to address reliability and operational needs.
Environmental impacts associated with the installation and operation of electrical infrastructure required
to support electric ferry service are evaluated in the Draft EIR. As described in Section 3.14, Utilities and
Service Systems, implementation of the project would require electrical connections and infrastructure,
and the environmental effects of constructing these improvements are analyzed under Impact UTIL-1.
The Draft EIR concludes that construction-related impacts would be less than significant with mitigation,
and that operation would not require new or expanded electrical facilities beyond those described in
Chapter 2, Project Description (refer to Section 3.14, pages 3.14-26 through 3.14-30). In addition to the
utilities analysis, the Draft EIR evaluates the environmental effects of electric ferry infrastructure using
discipline-specific methodologies across all relevant resource areas. Section 3.2, Air Quality, and
Section 3.6, Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy, analyze emissions and energy demand associated
with electric ferry operations and charging systems (pages 3.2-21 through 3.2-35 and pages 3.6-30
through 3.6-47). Section 3.3, Biological Resources, evaluates potential operational impacts, including
underwater noise and vessel interactions with aquatic species (pages 3.3-39 through 3.3-66), while
Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, considers in-water infrastructure components and the reduced
potential for fuel-related spill risks associated with electrification (pages 3.8-25 through 3.8-42).
Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, evaluates safety considerations related to battery storage
systems and electrical infrastructure (pages 3.7-22 through 3.7-37), and Section 3.10, Noise, addresses
construction and operational noise generated by ferry vessels and associated electrical equipment
(pages 3.10-12 through 3.10-34).

addresses emergency conditions under which ferry service may be used. As described in Section 2.8,

associated analysis and conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid, and no changes to the EIR
are necessary in response to these comments.

2.2.11 Topical Response: Ferry Operations
As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, the proposed project includes representative
operational assumptions developed by WETA sufficient to support environmental review. These
assumptions include anticipated service frequency, general routing, and operational characteristics.
Specifically, the Draft EIR evaluates a representative weekday and weekend service scenario that includes
regular commute-period service and off-peak service, with ferry trips operating along established WETA
routes. While exact schedules may vary, this scenario reflects the maximum reasonably foreseeable level
of service for purposes of impact analysis (refer to Chapter 2, Project Description, Section 2.7, pages 2-30
through 2-33). Vessel speeds are not specified as fixed values in the Draft EIR; however, vessels are
assumed to operate at a maximum of 29 to 41 mph, consistent with the typical speeds for existing WETA
ferry service within San Francisco Bay and, consistent with current routes and navigation practices. 12,13
Speed during terminal approach and docking would be reduced (refer to Chapter 2, Project Description,
page 2-31) to provide safe maneuvering and compliance with applicable navigation practices. Given the
need for the ferry vessel to execute a multi-point turn in order to dock for passenger loading, the need to
reduce speeds during terminal approach is not an operational choice but a physical constraint.
Pursuant to the CEQA Guidelines, an EIR must evaluate reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts
based on available data and reasonable assumptions. However, CEQA does not require that all
operational details, such as final service schedules, vessel speeds under all conditions, or exact trip
frequencies, be fully finalized at the time of analysis (CEQA Guidelines Sections 15124 and 15144).
Rather, the analysis is appropriately based on representative operating conditions and planning-level
assumptions that allow for meaningful evaluation of potential environmental effects. Consistent with the
CEQA Guidelines Sections 15124 and 15144, Chapter 2, Project Description of the Draft EIR provides
sufficient information regarding ferry operations, including projected ridership, service frequency, and
general operational characteristics to evaluate environmental impacts (refer to Section 2.7, pages 2-30
through 2-33, including Table 2-4. As described in EIR Section 1.1.3, Incorporation by Reference, the
analysis also incorporates by reference the certified 2003 WETA EIR, which evaluated ferry system

2.2.12 Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative
CEQA Standard for Alternatives Analysis
Under CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6, an EIR is required to evaluate a reasonable range of alternatives
that could feasibly attain most of the basic project objectives while avoiding or substantially reducing
significant environmental effects. An EIR need not consider every conceivable alternative, and
alternatives that fail to meet most of the basic project objectives are infeasible, or would not reduce
significant environmental effects may properly be rejected from detailed analysis. The Draft EIR at
Section 5.9 identifies and explains the reasons for rejecting the Berkeley Marina Basin alternative from
detailed analysis. This response supplements that explanation with additional technical analysis
supporting the same conclusion.

The Alternative Does Not Meet Any Basic Project Objectives
As set forth in the Draft EIR at Section 5.3, the two basic project objectives are: (1) enhance public access
and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront; and (2) provide efficient and environmentally
friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco. An alternative must meet
both objectives to qualify for detailed analysis. The In-Marina Alternative fails to meet both.
With respect to the first objective, siting the ferry terminal inside the marina would leave the Berkeley Pier
closed and continuing to deteriorate. The new pier, public plaza, Bay Trail Extension, cycle track, and
associated waterfront improvements, which are the primary mechanisms by which the project enhances
public access and recreational opportunities are all tied to the pier location. While these improvements
would not be precluded by an In-Marina ferry terminal, none of them would be part of the In-Marina ferry
terminal project alternative because the need to implement multi-mode TDM measures along University



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                         2- 29
                                             Page 134 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

Avenue and Seawall Drive would not exist. Furthermore, as noted in the Draft EIR at Section 5.9,
construction of a new ferry terminal inside the marina would require removal of existing marina docks (at
least 8 slips would be lost per the 2008 Berkeley/Albany Ferry Terminal Study Draft EIR/EIR prepared by
URS), thereby directly reducing rather than enhancing recreational opportunities at the Berkeley
Waterfront.
With respect to the second objective, siting the ferry terminal inside the marina would impose
considerable operational constraints on ferry service safety, efficiency and reliability. As documented in
the Draft EIR at Section 5.9, based on communications with WETA's Project Manager, ferry vessels
operating inside the marina would face additional maneuvering constraints, increased docking and
departure times, wake and safety concerns and operational conflicts with recreational users. Passenger
access would also be constrained, potentially creating queuing conflicts. These factors would extend
overall travel times by an estimated 5-10 minutes, reduce service reliability and on-time performance, and
diminish the competitiveness of the Berkeley–San Francisco ferry route compared to other Transbay
modes of travel. An In-Marina terminal is not considered operationally feasible by WETA.

The Alternative Provides No Environmental Benefit
The In-Marina alternative would not reduce environmental impacts and would not avoid any significant
environmental impacts. With respect to in-Bay fill: the proposed project is designed to achieve no net
increase in Bay fill through removal of existing pier piles and decking at a minimum 1:1 ratio for the net
increase in fill and cover, per Mitigation Measure BIO-3. Under an In-Marina terminal alternative, there
would be no project-driven rationale to remove the deteriorated pier. Portions of the old pier are being
removed under the proposed project because the new pier replaces it. Without a new pier at that location,
the old pier piles would remain as existing in-Bay fill, and new fill would be added for the marina terminal
infrastructure. Prior to mitigation the In-Marina alternative would therefore result in a net increase in Bay
fill compared to the proposed project, not a reduction. If mitigation required removal of the derelict pier at
a 1:1 ratio, there would be the same no net fill as the proposed project.
With respect to dredging: the proposed project requires dredging of the approach channel and turning
basin to provide safe navigable depths for ferry vessels. An In-Marina terminal alternative would not
eliminate this dredging requirement. Ferry vessels require a navigable approach channel regardless of
terminal location. The area dredged for a turning basin would still be required in similar location and scale
to allow WETA vessels to safely navigate around marina traffic at the constrained entrance to the marina.
This would take the form of a widened maneuvering area outside the marina breakwater near the
narrower marina entrance channel. Therefore, the dredging requirement under the In-Marina alternative is
not significantly changed from the proposed project.
With respect to impacts on existing marina users: under the proposed project, ferry vessels travel and
dock in open Bay waters north of the pier, entirely outside the marina entrance. As described in the Draft
EIR at Section 3.11, Recreation, boats entering or exiting the marina would continue to navigate around
ferry infrastructure in a manner similar to how they currently navigate the existing pier and other Bay
vessels. An In-Marina terminal would require ferry vessels to travel through the marina entrance channel
and operate within the marina interior, introducing a large commercial vessel operating on a regular
schedule into a confined water body shared by recreational boaters, liveaboards, and commercial
operators. This would create new and notable operational conflicts with existing marina users that do not
exist under the proposed project. Finally, as noted in the Draft EIR the construction of a ferry terminal in
the marina would result in the loss of berths (at least 8 slips would be lost per the 2008 Berkeley/Albany
Ferry Terminal Study Draft EIR/EIR prepared by URS). Under CEQA, the displacement of recreational boat
berths would constitute a direct adverse impact on recreational resources. The Berkeley Marina Basin is
the largest public recreational marina in northern California, with approximately 1,000 berths; the loss of
even a small number of those berths diminishes the supply of recreational boating opportunities that the
Waterfront currently provides to the public, which would run counter to the project's core objective of
enhancing, rather than reducing, recreational access at the Berkeley Waterfront.




Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                         2- 30
                                             Page 135 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                        Response to Comments

The loss of eight or more berths would not only reduce public recreation opportunities but also indirectly
negatively impact public recreation opportunities in the City of Berkeley. The City relies on slip fees as its
primary source of revenue to operate and maintain the Berkeley Marina and its approximately 1,000
recreational berths; each berth removed represents a permanent reduction in the Marina's revenue base,
revenue that funds dock maintenance, dredging, harbormaster operations, and other public recreational
amenities across the entire Waterfront.

Summary
As described in Section 5.9 of the Draft EIR (see pages 5.9-25 to 5.9-26), the in-marina terminal
alternative: (1) fails to meet either of the two basic project objectives; (2) provides no environmental
benefit with respect to in-Bay fill; (3) provides no environmental benefit with respect to dredging
requirements; and (4) creates new and notable conflicts with existing marina users, including the
displacement of recreational berths (at least 8 slips would be lost per the 2008 Berkeley/Albany Ferry
Terminal Study Draft EIR/EIR prepared by URS), that do not exist under the proposed project. The Draft
EIR's rejection of this alternative from detailed analysis is fully supported by CEQA Guidelines
Section 15126.6, which requires only that a range of potentially feasible alternatives be evaluated, not
every alternative suggested in comments. Because the In-Marina option does not meet any of the basic
project objectives nor provides any meaningful avoidance or reduction of environmental effects the City's
alternatives analysis is adequate and no revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

2.2.13 Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency
Consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15125(d), which requires an EIR to disclose inconsistencies
between a proposed project and applicable land use plans and policies, Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use
and Planning, Impact LU-2 and respective Tables 3.9-1 through 3.9-4 (pages 3.9-12 through 3.9-35)
summarize local and regional policies applicable to the project and evaluates the project’s consistency
with those plans. Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15064, 15360, and 15382, CEQA defines an
environmental impact as a physical change in the environment. CEQA Guidelines Section 15382 defines a
significant effect related to the environment as “a substantial, or potentially substantial, adverse change
in any of the physical conditions within the area affected by the project,” and further states that “[a]n
economic or social change by itself shall not be considered a physical effect on the environment.” CEQA
Guidelines Section 15360 similarly defines the “environment” as the physical conditions that exist within
the area affected by a project. Consistent with these provisions, a conflict with an applicable land use
plan, policy, or regulation does not, in itself, constitute a significant environmental impact. This
framework is reflected in CEQA Guidelines Appendix G Land Use/Planning Significance Criterion b, which
asks whether a project would “cause a significant environmental impact due to a conflict with any land
use plan, policy, or regulation adopted for the purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect.”
Specifically, the Draft EIR analyzed land use consistency impacts with respect to the physical
environment for the following plans and policies: BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, ABAG/MTC Plan Bay
Area 2050, Bay Area Clean Air Plan, Berkeley Climate Action Plan, Berkeley General Plan, Berkeley
Municipal Code, Berkeley Waterfront Master Plan, Berkeley Marina Master Plan, Berkeley Local Hazard
Mitigation Plan, and Berkeley Measure L.
As concluded in Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, Impact LU-2 (pages 3.9-12 through 3.9-35),
the proposed project would be generally consistent with the goals and policies identified in applicable
plans; however, because the project would generate noise that even after mitigated would exceed
thresholds established in the Berkeley Municipal Code, impacts would be significant and unavoidable
(due to noise impacts).
Furthermore, to the extent that an inconsistency with a land use plan or policy would result in a physical
environmental effect, such effects are evaluated throughout the Draft EIR, and mitigation measures are
identified as appropriate. Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or mitigation measures are
necessary in response to these comments.

2.2.14 Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control
The proposed project has been designed to incorporate standard marine safety features, operational
protocols, and emergency response procedures consistent with applicable regulatory requirements and
industry practices. Specifically, the Draft EIR includes the following:
• Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description describes vessel approach, berthing conditions, and associated
  ferry infrastructure (see Section 2.5, pages 2-6 through 2-11); and
• Section 3.12, Transportation evaluates ferry navigation and vessel maneuverability (see Impact TRA-3,
  pages 3.12-23 and 3.12-24).

Potential risks associated with vessel operation, including low-probability incident scenarios such as loss
of control during approach or docking, are addressed through design features, vessel specifications, and
operational procedures implemented by WETA and subject to oversight by applicable regulatory agencies,
including the U.S. Coast Guard and other maritime safety authorities [see Draft EIR Section 2.9,
Discretionary Actions and Required Approvals (refer to page 2-33)]. Consistent with CEQA Guidelines, the
Draft EIR evaluates reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts and relies on compliance with
applicable safety regulations, engineering standards, and operational protocols to address potential
accident scenarios. Specifically, Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation, addresses vessel navigation,
maneuverability, and safety considerations and concludes that the operation of ferry vessels would not
increase transportation safety hazards, as the vessels would be designed with multiple layers of
redundancy to prevent loss of propulsion risk, crew training to respond to loss of propulsion scenarios,
and monitoring of U.S. Coast Guard advisories (refer to Impact TRA-3, pages 3.12-23 and 3.12-24).
Speculative accident scenarios that are not supported by substantial evidence are not required to be
analyzed in an EIR under CEQA, which focuses on reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts.
Notwithstanding that conclusion, since publication of the Draft EIR, the project design has been further
refined to include installation of fender piles 14 near the Skates on the Bay Restaurant and donut fenders 15
near the breakwater and floats. These project components would provide an additional passive safety
measure by helping to absorb or deflect vessel movement in the unlikely event of a loss of control during
approach or docking. This project design feature is consistent with standard marine engineering
practices to enhance docking safety and does not introduce new or more severe construction- or
operational-related environmental impacts beyond those already analyzed in the Draft EIR.
The following text changes have been made to Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, page 2-10:
     The proposed ferry vessel infrastructure would include up to two 120-foot-long and 10-foot-wide
     gangways89 that would bring passengers from the pier to the two proposed boarding floats910, which
     would measure approximately 135 feet in length and 42 feet in width. Each float would include 4 to 6
     steel guide piles to moor the floats in place. In addition, there would be a total of 6 donut fenders (2
     at the end of each float and 2 near the breakwater), each of which would be 6-feet in diameter and
     would require a 3-foot pile. Since publication of the Draft EIR, the project design has been refined to
     include additional fender piles and donut fenders (steel protection piles, 36-inches in diameter)
     located adjacent to the ferry berthing area and around portions of the breakwater and turning basin.
     These protection piles would function as passive marine safety features and would supplement the
     guide piles and donut fender system associated with the proposed ferry facilities. The protection
     piles are intended to provide additional protection for waterside infrastructure during vessel approach
     and docking operations, including in the unlikely event of a vessel loss-of-control incident (see
     Section 3.12, Transportation).

2.2.15 Topical Response: Maintenance Dredging
Page 2-36 of Section 2.6.1, Construction Details, within Chapter 2, Project Description, of the Draft EIR
describes the extent, location, and volume of dredging required for the project. As later described on
Page 3.3-14 in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, of the Draft EIR, dredging activities at the project site are
subject to oversight and permitting by USACE, with additional coordination with agencies such as the
Regional Water Quality Control Board and the Dredged Material Management Office. The City of Berkeley
or WETA would be responsible for implementing project-related dredging, subject to these regulatory
approvals. Future maintenance dredging within the navigation channel or turning basin would be required
to obtain applicable environmental clearances and regulatory permits and approvals.
In response to these comments, the following clarification text changes have been made to Draft EIR
Section 2.6.1, Construction Activities and Equipment, page 2-28 as follows:
    Dredged materials and demolition debris would all be transported via barge that have a capacity of
    between 3,000 and 6,000 cubic yards. The location for disposal of dredged materials would depend


Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                          2- 37

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                                       Response to Comments

     on the sampling results of the dredged materials, as well as permitting requirements. However, based
     on the recently completed Berkeley Marina Dredging Project of 2024 to 2025, it is expected that
     disposal would occur at Montezuma Wetland Restoration Project (Beneficial Reuse), Alcatraz
     Disposal Site, or another disposal site in the San Francisco Bay. The dredging described above
     represents one-time, project-specific dredging required to establish navigable depths for ferry
     operations. This dredging would be conducted on behalf of the City of Berkeley and/or WETA, subject
     to all applicable permits and approvals from the United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE),
     Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB), San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development
     Commission (BCDC), and the Dredged Material Management Office (DMMO). Although dredging
     would occur within the alignment of an existing USACE-designated federal navigation channel, this
     portion of the channel has not been maintained by USACE in recent decades and is not currently
     included in an active federal maintenance dredging program. Accordingly, dredging at this location
     would constitute new work dredging, and the proposed project does not assume that USACE would
     conduct or be responsible for this initial dredging.

The above clarifications do not change the project description as analyzed throughout the Draft EIR. The
environmental analysis conservatively evaluates the maximum dredging extent and all impacts
associated with project-related dredging were assessed assuming project implementation by the City
under applicable regulatory oversight.
Regarding maintenance dredging, the need for, timing of, and extent of future maintenance dredging
cannot be determined with certainty at this time. Refer to the 2025 Coastal Study prepared for the
project.16 As discussed therein, a hydrodynamic and sediment transport model was developed to
evaluate sediment deposition within the proposed dredged areas and estimate long-term maintenance
requirements. The study concluded that average annual sedimentation rates are approximately 0.20 feet
per year within the approach channel and approximately 0.09 feet per year within the berth pockets.
Based on these modeled sedimentation rates, the study estimated that maintenance dredging may not be
required for approximately 10 to 15 years within the approach channel and approximately 22 to 33 years
within the berth pockets, depending on the operational depths ultimately maintained. The study also
notes that these estimates are subject to uncertainty and are based on modeling assumptions, available
calibration data, and future conditions that may change over time (refer to Coastal Study, Executive
Summary, pages 7-8; and Sections 6-7, pages 64-67). Accordingly, there is currently no project-specific
maintenance dredging program, schedule, dredging volume, disposal plan, or operational commitment
that can be analyzed. Whether maintenance dredging will ultimately occur, when it may occur, the amount
of material that may require removal, the technologies available at that time, applicable regulatory
requirements, and environmental conditions present when such dredging may become necessary are
presently unknown.
CEQA does not require the analysis of impacts that are too speculative for meaningful evaluation. CEQA
Guidelines Section 15145 provides that where a lead agency determines, after thorough investigation,
that a particular impact is too speculative for evaluation, the agency may conclude its discussion of that
impact. Given that potential maintenance dredging, if needed, is not anticipated for at least 10 years and
potentially more than 30 years depending on location and operating conditions, and because the timing,
extent, methods, and environmental setting associated with any future maintenance dredging are
presently unknown, detailed environmental analysis of future maintenance dredging would be
speculative. Should maintenance dredging be proposed in the future, such activities would be subject to
applicable permitting requirements and any environmental review required under then-applicable federal,
state, and local regulations.

2.2.16 Topical Response: Measure L
Measure L was passed by City of Berkeley residents through a citywide vote in the November 1986
election. The initiative was placed on the ballot to ensure public oversight and protection of the city's
parks and open spaces. As stated in the Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning (See 3.9-33) of the Draft EIR,
Measure L provides that:
    "No public parks or public open space owned or controlled or leased by the City or agency thereof,
    shall be used for any other purpose than public parks and open space, without the Berkeley City
    Council first having submitted such use to the citizens for approval by a majority of registered
    Berkeley voters voting at the next general election; except that such voter approval is not required for
    temporary use of public parks or public open space for other purposes, if a state of emergency has
    been declared..."
    (BMC Section 6.42.010)

"Public parks" are defined as City of Berkeley parks, public school playgrounds, or lands held in trust by a
public entity that have been formally dedicated to permanent recreational use by the City of Berkeley and
funded for recreational use by City of Berkeley public funds. "Public open space" is defined as all City of
Berkeley parks, public school playgrounds, and vacant public land, whether formally dedicated to park use
or being used de facto as open space with recreational use or potential use on or after January 1, 1985
(BMC Section 6.42.030).
As discussed in the Draft EIR, the proposed project is consistent with Measure L. The analysis proceeds
component by component.




Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                        2- 39
                                             Page 144 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                      Response to Comments


Landside Improvements
None of the proposed landside improvements would take place within a public park, with the limited
exception of the installation of a new wayfinding sign in Shorebird Park. The installation of this sign
would not change the purpose or alter the use of Shorebird Park but rather is consistent with its park use.
The remaining landside improvements do not implicate Measure L because they are not occurring in a
public park. Even if Measure L applied, the improvements are consistent with Measure L as described
below.
• The parking lot improvements consist of renovation of an existing parking lot. This renovation would
  include removing a landscaped strip bordered on one side by Seawall Drive and the Parking Lot on
  another side. This median is not accessible to the public (there are no cross-walks or paths leading to it
  or amenities connected to it). Therefore, the Project would not result in a change of use.
• The public plaza improvements consist of enhancements to an existing paved plaza area, adding
  amenities such as seating, a public restroom, and bicycle parking. These amenities do not amount to a
  change in use. Rather, these improvements are intended to promote the space as a public gathering
  space, which is consistent with and supportive of the existing recreational use.
• The Bay Trail Extension and cycle track would be constructed in an area currently occupied by parking
  stalls and a dilapidated pathway. The use of this area is moving from parking to landscaped green
  space and multi-use trail for recreational use by bicyclists and pedestrians.
• The cycle track improvements and bus facilities would be built in the public right-of-way, which is not
  parkland or open space subject to Measure L. In any event, they do not change the character of the
  area, but rather facilitate use of the space for recreational purposes, consistent with Measure L.

Pier Improvements
The waterside improvements include building a new pier in the same location as the existing, deteriorated
pier. The pier would not be built in a public park or in public open space as defined by Measure L. Even if
the areas upon which the pier is built were subject to Measure L, these improvements are Measure L
compliant, because the new pier would not change the purpose or alter the use of these areas - it
replaces the existing pier and maintains the recreational use of the area. In fact, the new pier expands
recreational use because the current pier has been inaccessible to the public since its closure in 2015.

Ferry Terminal, Charging Infrastructure, and Breakwater
The ferry facility, ferry charging infrastructure, and breakwater would be installed in open Bay waters.
Open Bay waters are navigable waters of the State, subject to the public trust doctrine and the regulatory
jurisdiction of the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission and the State Lands
Commission, not “public parks” or “public open space”. Therefore, Measure L is not triggered.
For these reasons, as stated in the Draft EIR, the proposed project would not conflict with Measure L. No
revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

2.2.17 Topical Response: Mitigation Measure Requirements
CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4 requires that an EIR identify feasible mitigation measures for
potentially significant impacts and provides that the development of mitigation measures shall not be
deferred to a future time but also states that specific details of a mitigation measure may be developed
after project approval, where it is impractical to finalize those details during environmental review. CEQA
Guidelines Section 15126.4(a)(1)(B) states:
“Where several measures are available to mitigate an impact, each should be discussed and the basis for
selecting a particular measure should be identified. Formulation of mitigation measures shall not be
deferred until some future time. The specific details of a mitigation measure, however, may be developed
after project approval when it is impractical or infeasible to include those details during the project’s



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                       2- 40
                                             Page 145 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                      Response to Comments

environmental review provided that the agency (1) commits itself to the mitigation, (2) adopts specific
performance standards the mitigation will achieve, and (3) identifies the type(s) of potential action(s) that
can feasibly achieve that performance standard and that will considered, analyzed, and potentially
incorporated in the mitigation measure. Compliance with a regulatory permit or other similar process may
be identified as mitigation if compliance would result in implementation of measures that would be
reasonably expected, based on substantial evidence in the record, to reduce the significant impact to the
specified performance standards.”
The comments identified three mitigation measures that the comments refer to as deferred. Each is
addressed below.
First, Draft EIR Mitigation Measure BIO-3 (which requires removal of additional portions of the existing
pier) does not constitute deferred mitigation. Mitigation for impacts to waters of the United States and
waters of the State is typically determined through the regulatory permitting process, in coordination with
the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and Regional Water Quality Control Board. As part of this process,
project impacts must first be avoided, then minimized to the maximum extent practicable, after which the
permitting agencies establish the appropriate type, location, and amount of mitigation based on site-
specific conditions, resource functions and values, and applicable regulatory standards. The final
mitigation requirements, including mitigation ratios, performance standards, and monitoring
requirements, are formalized through permit conditions (e.g., Section 404 and Section 401
authorizations). Mitigation Measure BIO-3 commits the project to providing mitigation consistent with
these regulatory requirements and ensures that impacts to jurisdictional waters will be fully offset in
accordance with federal and state standards.
Consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4, the Draft EIR commits to the mitigation measures
identified throughout the document and will further commit to these measures by adopting and
implementing a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP). In addition, the mitigation
measure establishes performance standards that the measure must achieve (i.e., 1:1 mitigation ratio)
and identifies the types of actions that will be implemented to meet those standards (i.e., the removal of
existing pier piles and decking). To the extent that negotiations with regulatory agencies may result in a
higher mitigation ratio than the 1:1 minimum specified in Mitigation Measure BIO-3, the City states that
Mitigation Measure BIO-3 expressly establishes a floor, not a ceiling, and provides that the measure “may
be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory agencies.” Therefore,
adoption and incorporation into the project of Mitigation Measure BIO-3 will commit the City to mitigation
that includes specific performance standards and identifies the types of potential activities to achieve
these standards, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4(a)(1)(B). Accordingly, Mitigation
Measure BIO-3 is not deferred mitigation, but rather is structured in a manner which allows the City to
finalize implementation details, including removal ratio, at a later stage so long as enforceable standards
and commitments are met. Because the Draft EIR discloses the mitigation framework, performance
criteria, and anticipated methods of compliance, the public has been provided with a meaningful
opportunity to review and comment on the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed mitigation
measures. Therefore, the Draft EIR complies with CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.4 and does not
impermissibly defer mitigation.
Second, the City has not deferred mitigation by not providing a parking management plan. Parking supply
is not an impact under CEQA so no mitigation measure was identified to prepare a parking management
plan. Refer to the Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for more information on this topic.
Third, the implementation of mitigation from the 2003 WETA EIR is not deferred mitigation. As identified
in Section 2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability, the 2003 WETA EIR is not relied upon for
the discussion of land use impacts or recreational access amenities. For a discussion of recreational
access amenities, refer to Section 2.5 Proposed Project Components, Chapter 2 Project Description,
pages 2-6 through 2-22 which describes the recreational amenities on the waterside and landside for the
proposed project along with figures and plan views of the key components of the project that are
intended to provide an enhanced recreational amenity throughout the waterfront area. For the proposed
project land use impacts, please refer to Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning of the Draft EIR.

    Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces9
    The BCDC Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces (BCDC 2005) provides guidelines
    for shoreline design. Guidelines related to visual resources are listed below.
    • Taking advantage of existing site characteristics and opportunities, such as fishing, viewing,
      picnicking, swimming or boating.
    • Locating buildings, structures, parking lots and landscaping of new shoreline projects such that
      they enhance and dramatize views of the Bay and the shoreline from public thoroughfares and
      other public spaces.
    • Organizing shoreline development to allow Bay views and access between buildings.
    • In hilly areas, designing and locating shoreline buildings to allow for upland views down to the Bay
      and to Bay access areas.
    • In hilly areas, employing split-level roads to increase viewing and landscaping potential.
    • Designing towers, bridges or other structures as landmarks that suggest the location of the
      waterfront, even when the Bay itself is not visible.
    • Providing visual interest and architectural variety in massing and height to new buildings along the
      shoreline.
    • Using building footprints to create a diversity of public spaces along the Bay.
    • Articulating shoreline building facades with human-scale elements.
    • Using forms, materials, colors and textures that are compatible with the Bay and adjacent
      development.
    • Locating service areas, such as garbage facilities and loading docks, away from the shoreline or
      screen them with suitable fencing or landscaping.
    • Utilizing the shoreline for Bay-related land uses as much as possible; uses that do not complement
      the Bay should be set back from and not impact the shoreline.
    • Orienting the development to Bay views and providing physical connections to the Bay at every
      opportunity.
    • Orienting public access areas and improvements to take advantage of views of opposite shores,
      landmarks (such as islands and bridges) and adjacent maritime activities such as boat launching,
      gas docks, ferry landings or other marine-related uses.
    • Utilizing the shoreline for Bay-related uses. Uses that do not orient to the Bay should be set well
      back from the Bay and be sited, designed and managed so as to not impact the shoreline.
    • Provide buffers between roadways and public access areas, such as planting, low berms or
      roadside parking, and maintain views to the Bay.
    • Provide parking for shoreline access areas where appropriate, but keep parking areas reasonably
      sized, away from the Bay and adequately screened.
    • Provide small bayside parking areas or pull-offs for limited in-car Bay viewing, where compatible
      with existing roads and adjacent uses.
    • Provide elevated places for viewing the Bay.
    • Use site furnishings, such as benches, trash containers and lighting, to provide visual cues that the
      shoreline space is available for public use.

2.2.19 Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities)
The Marina Boundary
BMC Chapter 6.20 governs the Berkeley Marina. As defined in BMC Section 6.20.010(A), the "Berkeley
Marina" is the area owned or controlled by the City, including the municipal fishing pier, the breakwater,
the sea walls and the extensions thereof, located on the Berkeley waterfront, bounded on the west by a
north-south line through the end of the Municipal Fishing Pier. The pier footprint and adjacent Bay waters
fall within the defined boundaries of the Berkeley Marina as established by BMC 6.20.010(A). BMC
Chapter 6.20, including its prohibited activities provisions, therefore applies to the project's waterside
area.

Section 6.20.180(A): Swimming, Bathing, Wading, and Windsurfing.
Section 6.20.180(A) states that it is unlawful for any person to swim, bathe, wade, or windsurf in any
portion of the marina except at Shorebird Park and in the South Sailing Basin. As established by the
Marina boundary definition above, this prohibition applies within the project site. The Draft EIR correctly
states that swimming, bathing, windsurfing, and wading are prohibited within City jurisdictional waters in
the Marina except at the South Sailing Basin (including Shorebird Park Beach and the sailing docks). This
is an accurate statement of existing law. The project does not create this prohibition which predates the
project and reflects the existing regulatory baseline.

Section 6.20.180(B): Personal Watercraft
Section 6.20.180(B) is a separate and distinct provision from Section 6.20.180(A). Section B prohibits the
operation of jet skis and personal watercraft within 1,500 feet of the Berkeley shoreline or Berkeley
Fishing Pier, except within a designated access corridor.
"Personal watercraft" as defined in BMC Section 6.20.010(H) means vessels propelled by a water-jet
pump or other machinery as their primary source of motor propulsion - in common parlance, jet skis.
Windsurfing boards, kiteboarding equipment, kayaks, paddleboards, and similar wind- or human-powered
craft do not fall within this definition. The City agrees that the 1,500-foot personal watercraft restriction in
Section 6.20.180(B) does not apply to wind- or human-powered watercraft. However, the activities at
issue (swimming, windsurfing, wading, and bathing) are addressed not by Section B but by Section A,
which applies Marina-wide. The comments' focus on the legislative history of Section B is, therefore, not
relevant to the applicability of Section A.
The following clarifications are added to pages 3.11-18 and 3.11-19 of the Draft EIR:
    For construction occurring in the water, swimming, bathing, wading, and wind surfing, sailing, and
    kayaking are prohibited at the existing and new pier areas, pursuant to Berkeley Municipal Code

The Project Does Not Create or Expand the Prohibition
The proposed project does not impose any new restrictions on water-based recreation. The prohibitions
in BMC Section 6.20.180 are existing law applicable to the project site regardless of whether this project
is built. The project does not propose new enforcement of those restrictions, nor does it physically
preclude access to areas that are currently available for wind- or human-powered watercraft. As
described in the Draft EIR at Section 3.11, the primary launch points for swimmers, windsurfers, kayakers,
and paddleboarders at the Berkeley Waterfront (the South Sailing Basin docks and Shorebird Beach) are
located outside of the project site and would not be affected by the project. The un-improved rocky
shoreline at the southernmost point of the 199 Seawall peninsula, used by some water recreators, is
likewise south of the project site and not permanently impacted by the project; refer to Section 2.2.21,
Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access.

CEQA Baseline
Several comments state that the DEIR improperly uses BMC 6.20.180 to define the CEQA baseline.
However, under CEQA Guidelines Section 15125, an EIR must describe the physical environmental
conditions and existing regulatory environment at the time the NOP is published. Impacts to recreational
uses, including those activities that may occur informally in the project site, are also analyzed in
Section 3.11, Recreation, of the Draft EIR.
For these reasons, the Draft EIR's description of BMC Section 6.20 is correct and no revision to the Draft
EIR is warranted.

2.2.20 Topical Response: Parking
Parking Is Not an Environmental Impact Under CEQA
Issues related to parking are addressed in Draft EIR Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis (refer to
page 3-11). As explained therein, the Draft EIR evaluates potential secondary environmental effects
associated with parking conditions through the relevant environmental resource topics. To the extent
comments concern the allocation, management, or availability of parking, such comments do not raise
significant environmental issues requiring further response pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15088.

The Project is Consistent with Bay Plan Recreation Policy 9
Bay Plan Recreation Policy 9 requires that parking facilities not be usurped by ferry patrons and that
shared parking arrangements be provided to minimize the shoreline area needed for parking.
Even assuming inconsistency with the Bay Plan constituted an environmental impact, the DEIR
demonstrates that the proposed project is consistent with the Bay Plan, including Recreation Policy 9, and
would not usurp recreational parking. As the Draft EIR at Section 3.9 makes clear, the project’s Parking
and Transportation Demand Management (TDM) Plan demonstrates the Berkeley Waterfront's capacity
to accommodate both ferry patrons and recreational users while ensuring meaningful parking access for
each. Therefore, the proposed project is consistent with Recreation Policy 9 and there is no conflict with
the Bay Plan.
While some comments provided their own estimates of parking demand and availability and concerns
regarding the methodology used in the Parking and TDM plan, CEQA does not require the City to adopt or
respond point-by-point to such lay calculations or critiques where, as here, the City’s analysis is grounded
in empirical data and professional methodology prepared by qualified traffic and transportation
engineers. The City’s conclusions regarding parking sufficiency are based on the Parking and TDM Plan,
prepared by Kittelson & Associates, which constitutes substantial evidence supporting the Draft EIR’s
analysis. Furthermore, the project will require a permit from BCDC, which will independently assess and
confirm the project’s consistency with its laws and policies including the Bay Plan. During the permitting



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                        2- 47
                                             Page 152 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                     Response to Comments

process, BCDC may impose special conditions or project changes as necessary to ensure consistency
with its laws or policies.

The Project Includes a Robust Parking and TDM Strategy
The City has prepared a Parking and Transportation Demand Management (TDM) Plan for the project.
The Parking and TDM Plan establishes parking availability at various parking lots in the project vicinity,
estimates ferry-rider parking demand, identifies TDM measures that have been incorporated into the
project or could be implemented in the future, and provides recommendations related to shared parking
management and allocation. A subsequent Parking Management Implementation Plan will set forth the
operational strategies for shared parking, consistent with the recommendations of the Parking and TDM
Plan. The Parking and TDM Plan demonstrates that the Berkeley Waterfront has the capacity to
accommodate both ferry patrons and recreational users while ensuring meaningful, shared parking
access for each, consistent with BCDC Bay Plan Recreation Policy 9.

The Project Ensures Adequate Parking Supply
The existing Seawall Drive parking lot includes approximately 320 parking spaces, and the parking area
west of Seawall Drive adjacent to the Bay includes approximately 84 parking spaces, for a total of
approximately 404 existing parking spaces across the project site. The proposed project would replace all
existing parking spaces with 400 to 450 new parking spaces (pending final design), including ADA-
accessible and EV parking spaces. The project therefore maintains approximately the same overall
number of parking spaces at the project site and may result in a net increase in parking spaces. The
reconfiguration of parking is designed to support shared use consistent with BCDC Bay Plan Recreation
Policy 9, which requires that parking facilities not be usurped by ferry patrons and that shared parking
arrangements be provided to minimize the shoreline area needed for parking. Further, as discussed
above, the Parking and TDM Plan analyzes parking demand based on observed usage patterns at the
Berkeley Waterfront and WETA ridership projections and demonstrates that with implementation of
Parking and TDM strategies such as well-designed and convenient loading zones for family drop-off and
rideshare vehicles, enhanced bicycle and pedestrian access and improved secure bike parking, the
Waterfront will have sufficient spaces to accommodate all users.

Parking Availability Does Not Create Secondary Environmental Impacts
CEQA does require analysis of secondary physical impacts if a parking deficiency causes them. This
includes increased vehicle travel (including vehicle miles traveled [VMT]) or safety impacts from
degraded circulation. The Draft EIR evaluates parking and circulation to determine whether changes in
parking supply or management could result in such secondary environmental effects, consistent with
CEQA Guidelines Section 15064.3.
As documented in Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation, and Appendix F, Transportation Impact
Assessment, the project would generate vehicle trips that can be accommodated within the existing
transportation network without creating unsafe conditions or substantially degrading circulation (refer to
Section 3.12.4, Impact Analysis, on Pages 3.12-15 through 3.12-25). The analysis concludes that project-
related traffic would result in minor increases in delay and queuing and would not introduce a new
circulation deficiency or substantially worsen existing conditions (refer to Section 3.12.4, Impact TRA-1,
on pages 3.12-17 through 3.12-19; Appendix F, Operational Analysis sections).
With respect to secondary effects related to parking, including potential spillover, increased circulation
from drivers searching for parking, or increases in VMT, the Draft EIR and the supporting Parking and
TDM Plan demonstrate that the Berkeley Waterfront parking supply is sufficient to accommodate project
ferry parking demand without requiring drivers to circulate between lots or generate additional vehicle
travel. Where sufficient parking supply exists to meet demand, the conditions that would trigger
secondary circulation and VMT effects (namely, drivers unable to find parking) do not arise. Accordingly,

Some comments raise concerns that changes to parking, including the introduction of parking fees,

2.2.21 Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational
       Water Access
Existing Conditions Are Adequately Discussed in the EIR
As described in the Draft EIR at Section 3.11, Recreation, the Berkeley Waterfront provides multiple launch
points for water-based recreation. The public docks in the South Sailing Basin and Shorebird Beach are
the primary launch locations for swimmers, windsurfers, kayakers, and paddleboarders. The Draft EIR
acknowledges that the un-improved rocky shoreline at the southernmost point of the 199 Seawall
peninsula is used by water recreators, including when low tides make launching from the South Sailing
docks undesirable due to shallow water and exposed mudflats. This existing use is reflected in the
baseline conditions described in the EIR. Refer to 3.11.2, Environmental Setting, San Francisco Bay in

    Windsurfers, wingers, swimmers, paddleboarders, and kayakers launch from the South Sailing docks
    or Shorebird Beach for access throughout the South Sailing Cove and beyond. An un-improved rocky
    shoreline at the southernmost point of the 199 Seawall peninsula is used by some swimmers and
    windsurfers/wingers, primarily when low tides make launching from the South Cove undesirable due
    to shallow water and exposed mudflats.

BMC Section 6.20.180 Clarifies the Permitted Launch Points, Which Are Separate
from the Area Where Ferries Will Operate
The 199 Seawall launch point is considered by the City to be within the South Sailing Basin / South Cove
area. Launching from this area is permitted because users can travel south and/or east directly into the
South Cove, consistent with the provisions of BMC Section 6.20.180, refer to Section 2.2.19, Topical
Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities). While some users may navigate into the Marina
waters as defined by BMC Section 6.20.010(A), these users rarely travel north of the pier. When they do,
they must navigate around the extensive boat traffic that characterizes the Berkeley Marina as well as
any other watercraft in the San Francisco Bay. The ferry terminal and ferry operations are located north of
the pier, in an area geographically and operationally separate from the recreational uses at the 199
Seawall launch point and the South Sailing Basin.
