The Project Does Not Eliminate the 199 Seawall Launch Point, It Improves It
The proposed project does not include any construction or physical alteration at the 199 Seawall launch
point itself. The shoreline repair work included in the project is located on the eastern side of the Seawall
Peninsula, north and east of the 199 Seawall Drive structure, not at the informal launch area on the Bay-
facing south-western tip of the peninsula. Furthermore, the proposed project includes new amenities on
the shoreline in the vicinity of the 199 Seawall launch point, including seating, a small laydown area,
picnic tables, and rinse stations, specifically to support existing land and water based recreational uses at
this location. The project therefore not only preserves access to the 199 Seawall launch point but actively
enhances the recreational experience there.
Further, the project does not change low-tide access conditions at that location. To the extent that low-
tide access to Bay waters for informal water recreators is a concern, that concern exists independently of
this project and is not caused or worsened by project implementation.

Parking and Access
As discussed in the Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation, and as further addressed in Section 2.2.20,
Topical Response: Parking, access to parking for recreational use is a social impact rather than an
environmental impact under CEQA. Scarcity of parking is considered a potential secondary CEQA impact
only where it results in a physical impact on the environment, such as a significant increase in VMT. As
the Draft EIR concludes, and as further addressed in Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, the project
results in an overall net reduction in VMT, and any VMT increases attributable to parking scarcity are
expected to be nominal. Therefore, no secondary VMT impact results from parking conditions associated
with the project.

Bay Plan Policy 15 and Marina Master Plan
Bay Plan Map No. 4 Policy 15 calls for preserving "windsurfing access" at the Berkeley Waterfront. As
discussed in the Draft EIR at Section 3.9, Land Use Planning (Table 3.9-1), the project is consistent with
Bay Plan Map No. 4 Policy 15 because it does not affect existing windsurfing access at the South Sailing
Basin or at the 199 Seawall launch point, both of which are preserved and the latter of which is enhanced
by the project. The Marina Master Plan similarly identifies windsurfing access as a recreational value to
be preserved and enhanced at the waterfront. While this project does not propose implementing the
specific improvement conceptualized in the Marina Master Plan for enhancing windsurfer activity at this
location, the project's proposed amenities (seating, a laydown area, picnic tables, and rinse stations) are
supportive of and consistent with that goal. Furthermore, this project does not preclude the City from
implementing improvements proposed in the Marina Master Plan in the future.

Conclusion
The Draft EIR's recreation analysis at Section 3.11 addresses potential impacts to recreational uses from
both project construction and operation. The project does not physically alter the 199 Seawall launch
point, adds amenities to support its continued recreational use, and operates ferry service entirely north
of the pier in an area geographically separate from the recreational uses at issue. The EIR's treatment of
recreational impacts in this regard is adequate and no revision is warranted.
For these reasons, the Draft EIR adequately identifies and analyzes potential impacts to water-based
recreational access at the Berkeley Waterfront and no revision to the Draft EIR is warranted.

2.2.23 Topical Response: Sea Level Rise
Several comments discuss the project's sea level rise analysis, stating: (1) the project was designed only
for the Intermediate sea level rise scenario (1.6 feet by 2075) and does not adequately address more
severe scenarios including the High scenario (6.6 to 7 feet by 2100); (2) the EIR fails to address
operational adaptation for sea level rise beyond the project's 50-year design life; and (3) the project's sea
level rise analysis should conform to California Coastal Commission Sea Level Rise Policy Guidance. As
an initial matter, these comments address the adequacy of the project design in response to future
environmental conditions - that is, the impact of the environment on the project, rather than the impact of
the project on the environment. CEQA requires analysis of a project's effects on the environment, not an
assessment of whether the project itself is adequately designed to withstand future environmental
conditions. Nonetheless, the City provides the following response to address the substance of these
comments.

Design Basis and Updated SLR Scenario
The project's coastal engineering analysis was conducted by COWI North America, licensed professional
coastal engineers, and is documented in the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project Coastal
Study (COWI, December 2025) ("Coastal Study"). The Coastal Study established design parameters for
water levels, wave conditions, wind, and currents specific to the Berkeley Ferry Terminal site, using NOAA
tidal datums, AECOM's 2016 updated extreme tide elevations for San Francisco Bay, and the 2024
California Sea Level Rise Guidance.
The initial Coastal Study adopted the Intermediate sea level rise scenario with a 50-year project design
life, resulting in a sea level rise allowance of 1.6 feet and a design still water level of 11.9 feet (Berkeley
MLLW). However, as part of the BCDC Engineering Criteria Review Board (ECRB) review process
described below, the project team has formally updated the governing design condition from the
Intermediate scenario to the Intermediate-High scenario, resulting in a sea level rise allowance of 3.0 feet
and a design still water level of 13.3 feet (Berkeley MLLW). This update was confirmed in the COWI
response to ECRB questions dated April 10, 2026. To clarify how SLR was considered in the project
design process within the Draft EIR, Section 2.5.1, Proposed Project Components (Waterside, page 2-10)
has been revised as follows:
Draft EIR Page 2-10:
    In accordance with standards as set by the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE), the proposed
    pier would comply with ASCE Risk Category IV requirements and base design loads. The project
    design takes into account projected sea level rise incorporates sea level rise adaptation
    considerations through the design of the pier, breakwater, ferry infrastructure, and related facilities.7
    Design elevations and structural elements were developed to account for projected increases in
    surface water levels and coastal flood conditions over the life of the project, while floating ferry
    facilities and gangway connections have been designed to accommodate a range of future tidal and
    water surface elevations. Refer to Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, for an evaluation of the
    project with respect to future flooding and sea level rise. The City prepared a Coastal Study, including
    a project-specific sea level rise risk assessment, consistent with applicable BCDC permit
    requirements.8

This revision is clarifying in nature and does not alter the impact analysis, significance determinations, or

Intermediate scenario is, therefore, addressed by this update.

SLR Vulnerability Assessment
A Sea Level rise vulnerability assessment was conducted by the coastal engineers, following the
requirements of the updated 2024 California Sea Level Rise Guidance. The assessment confirms that all
project structures maintain full functionality and public safety under Intermediate-High conditions
through 2100, with only minor overtopping and splash impacts. All components retain structural integrity
under all evaluated scenarios, including the High scenario referenced in comments, and the breakwater
continues to provide substantial coastal protection even under the most extreme conditions evaluated.

Adaptation
Adaptation options for future sea level rise conditions are documented in the COWI SLR Risk Assessment
(Appendix to the Coastal Study, December 2025) and include conversion of the pier and breakwater
perimeter handrails to solid barriers to prevent wave overtopping from reaching the deck surface. The
pier and breakwater have been purposely designed in concrete specifically to be resilient to future wave
overtopping, should it occur. These design decisions reflect a forward-looking approach to long-term
resilience within the physical constraints of the site.

California Coastal Commission Sea Level Rise Policy Guidance
The California Coastal Commission does not have jurisdiction over the Berkeley Waterfront or the
proposed project; therefore, its Sea Level Rise Policy Guidance is not the applicable standard for the
project. The California Coastal Act expressly excludes San Francisco Bay from the California Coastal
Commission's jurisdiction. BCDC is the state agency with planning and regulatory authority over San
Francisco Bay, the Bay's shoreline band, and the Suisun Marsh. The project is subject to BCDC's
permitting jurisdiction under the McAteer-Petris Act and the San Francisco Bay Plan, not to the California
Coastal Act or California Coastal Commission policy guidance. The California Coastal Commission's Sea
Level Rise Policy Guidance, while a useful reference document for projects under CCC jurisdiction, does
not apply to this project.

BCDC ECRB Review
Although not part of the CEQA analysis, the structural and coastal engineering aspects of the project,
including the SLR analysis, have been subject to rigorous independent engineering criteria review by the
BCDC Engineering Criteria Review Board (ECRB), an advisory board composed of eminent structural,
coastal, and geotechnical engineers that assists BCDC in evaluating the engineering aspects of projects
requiring BCDC permits. The project has been presented to the ECRB on two occasions. The first meeting,
held February 25, 2026, generated detailed technical questions on datums, seismic codes, wave climate
methodology, wave loadings, SLR scenarios, elevation constraints, and structural details. The COWI
response to those questions, dated April 10, 2026, addressed each item in full, including the formal
upgrade to the Intermediate-High SLR scenario. Following the second ECRB meeting, the ECRB
determined that a further return presentation is not required, with outstanding technical items to be
resolved through the ongoing BCDC permitting process. The adequacy of the project's SLR and coastal

2.2.24 Topical Response: Seawall Drive/View Access
These comments are related to accessing scenic Bay views from in-car viewing locations at the Seawall
Drive parking area (i.e., policy and recreational opportunity aspects), not aesthetics impacts related to the
public view from the shoreline itself, which would not be significantly impacted by the proposed project.
Access to Bay views are policy issues, which are addressed in Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and
Planning, Table 3.9-1 (refer to Appearance, Design, and Scenic Views Policy 4). While impacts to views,
such as scenic vistas (e.g., blocking a scenic view) is considered a physical impact on the environment
and is subject to CEQA, access to those views from a parked vehicle would be considered a social
impact, not a physical impact on the environment, and would not be subject to CEQA. Refer to Draft EIR
Section 3.1.4, Aesthetics Impacts Analysis, Impact AES-1 (pages 3.1-20 through 3.1-27) for a discussion
of impacts on scenic vistas. Thus, the comments do not relate to nor necessitate changes to Draft EIR
conclusions or mitigation measures. Nonetheless, the City has provided the following response that
indicates how access to views of the Bay would be maintained and enhanced by the proposed project.
As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, and shown in Figures 2-11, 2-12 and 2-13, the
proposed project would include the reconfiguration of Bayside parking along the length of Seawall Drive
south of University Avenue and the parking lot at its terminus in order to accommodate between 400 and
450 total vehicles. Approximately 20 pull-in stalls and 13 parallel stalls would be retained for in-car Bay
viewing. In addition, the proposed project expands access to Bay views to additional non-vehicular viewer
groups in the vicinity, such as bicyclists, pedestrians, and other recreational users by providing
infrastructure (i.e., pathways, benches, picnic tables), while maintaining the availability of in-car viewing.
As reflected in Draft EIR Chapter 3.11, Recreation, with these improvements, the proposed project would
add new recreational facilities that currently do not exist, thereby creating a net increase in recreational
facilities. By expanding availability of public Bay views to a wider range of viewer groups, the proposed
project would support the goals, policies, and regulations of the Berkeley General Plan, Berkeley Marina
Master Plan, Berkeley Municipal Code, and the San Francisco Bay Plan related to maintaining and
enhancing public viewer access to scenic views of the Bay and expanding shoreline recreational
opportunities and resources.

2.2.25 Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate
Comments on this topic fall into three general categories: (1) sedimentation and siltation resulting from
dredging and the installation of the new breakwater; (2) changes to wave energy, wave fields, and
sediment transport patterns resulting from the breakwater; and (3) adequacy of bathymetric and
sedimentation data. The City addresses each category below.

Sedimentation Analysis -Technical Basis
The Draft EIR's sedimentation analysis is supported by the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry
Project Coastal Study (COWI, December 2025) ("Coastal Study"), prepared by licensed professional
coastal engineers at COWI North America. As part of the project design process, COWI carried out
hydrodynamic and sedimentation modeling using a two-dimensional hydrodynamic and sediment
transport model to assess currents, wave-driven transport, and long-term sediment deposition within the
dredged areas. The model was calibrated against historical survey data from the Berkeley Marina. The
modeling effort accounts for wind conditions, tidal forcing, regional hydrodynamic conditions, and site-
specific bathymetry.




Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                         2- 53
                                             Page 158 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments


Existing Sedimentation Rates and Bathymetric Data
As documented in the Coastal Study and reflected in the Draft EIR at Section 3.9 (Table 3.9-1, Bay Plan
Policy 5 consistency), sedimentation rates at the project site are currently low. Survey data from the
2020–2023 period indicate sedimentation of less than 0.05 feet over that period. Long-term historical
rates in the Berkeley Marina Channel average approximately 0.07 feet per year, consistent with historical
USACE surveys of the channel, as documented in the COWI Sediment Transport Study (Appendix D to the
Coastal Study, December 2025).
A site-specific bathymetric survey was conducted by eTrac in July 2024, covering the project site, and
was used as the basis for the hydrodynamic and sedimentation modeling. This survey was supplemented
by United States Geological Survey regional bathymetric data. The Coastal Study's model bathymetry was
developed from these datasets at a 2-meter grid resolution, providing a detailed and accurate
representation of existing Bay floor conditions within the project site.

Post-Project Sedimentation Rates and Maintenance Dredging
The Coastal Study's six-year simulation modeled sedimentation within the dredged areas under post-
project conditions with the breakwater installed and the channel and turning basin dredged to -12 feet
(Berkeley MLLW). Results show that sedimentation is highest in the first year following dredging (0.32
feet overall across the full dredged area) and then stabilizes over subsequent years. The average annual
sedimentation rate across the full dredged area is 0.15 feet per year, with the approach channel
experiencing a higher average rate of 0.20 feet per year and the turning basin a lower rate of 0.09 feet per
year. The lower turning basin sedimentation rate reflects the sheltering effect of the breakwater, which
reduces wave-driven sediment transport into the more protected turning basin area.
These modeled rates are consistent with post-dredge survey data collected at the Berkeley Marina in
December 2024 and June 2025 (six months after dredging operations were completed) which recorded
mean sediment accumulation of approximately 0.3 feet during that initial post-dredge period, closely
aligning with the model's first-year prediction for the BWTPF channel. This real-world validation provides
confidence in the modeling results.
Based on these rates, the Coastal Study estimates maintenance dredging of the approach channel would
be required approximately every 10 to 15 years depending on the to-be-determined vessel operational
depth, and maintenance dredging of the turning basin every 22 to 33 years. These dredging intervals are
consistent with typical maintenance dredging cycles for similar Bay ferry terminals. The assumptions
regarding future maintenance dredging are further clarified in Section 2.2.15, Topical Response:
Maintenance Dredging, which explains that maintenance dredging would be subject to separate permitting
and regulatory review, and is not included as part of the proposed project.
The sediment transport analysis was carried out for a 400-foot breakwater configuration. As documented
in the Coastal Study, the 100-foot reduction in breakwater length does not meaningfully change
sedimentation patterns in the navigation channel, and modeled sedimentation within the turning basin
remains minimal.
As described in the Draft EIR Section 3.3, Biological Resources, the project includes removal of existing
pier piles and decking to offset new net fill and cover. Mitigation Measure BIO-3 requires mitigation for
impacts on tidal waters of San Francisco Bay to achieve no net increase in Bay fill, provided at a minimum
1:1 ratio by square foot of impact through removal of existing pier piles and decking for net increase in fill
and cover, to be approved by the regulatory agencies. Some comments have requested that a higher
mitigation ratio (such as 3:1) be required. The EIR commits to no net increase in fill as a minimum
standard. Whether a higher ratio is appropriate is a matter to be negotiated with the relevant permitting
agencies, including BCDC and USACE, through the project permitting process. The EIR does not preclude
a higher ratio being required through permitting. Pile removal is not characterized in the EIR as mitigation
for dredging-related sedimentation impacts; it is mitigation for biological resources impacts associated
with in-Bay fill.

Wave Climate and Breakwater Effects
The Coastal Study's wave diffraction modeling assessed the wave climate effects of the breakwater.
COWI used a wave diffraction model to simulate wave transformation processes (including diffraction,
partial reflection, and nonlinear wave interactions) within the terminal area for multiple breakwater
configurations (250-foot, 300-foot, and 400-foot lengths) and multiple wave directions and periods. Wave
disturbance coefficients were calculated at key locations including the ferry berths, pier, and plaza. This
analysis was specifically designed to quantify how the breakwater reduces wave agitation at the ferry
berths and shoreline.
The modeling results confirm that a minimum 300-foot breakwater configuration provides sufficient
sheltering for both ferry berths, minimizes wave exposure, and achieves nearly the same reduction in
wave-induced downtime as the longer 400-foot alternative. Without a breakwater, the terminal would
experience notable wave-induced operational downtime, particularly during late spring and summer
months when southwesterly winds generate higher wave activity. With the 300-foot breakwater, monthly
average downtime remains below 2 percent for all months throughout the year, including the most
energetic wave periods.
With respect to effects on wave conditions beyond the project site, including the South Sailing Basin to
the south and nearby parks and shoreline areas, the wave disturbance coefficient maps presented in
Appendix C of the Coastal Study confirm that the breakwater's sheltering influence is confined to the
immediate project site. Wave disturbance coefficients at the outer limits of the geographic area evaluated
in the wave diffraction analysis approach 1.0, indicate that ambient wave conditions are unaffected by
the breakwater at those locations. The South Sailing Basin is located approximately 1,500 feet east of the
project, separated by the Seawall peninsula and well beyond any meaningful influence of the breakwater.
Likewise, the formerly named César E. Chávez Park is located 1,900 feet north of the project site,
McLaughlin Eastshore State Park State Seashore is located 3,900 feet east of the project site, Emeryville
Crescent is located more than 8,000 feet south of the project site, and Albany Mudflats is located more
than 9,000 feet north of the project site, well beyond any meaningful influence of the breakwater. There is
no technical basis to conclude that the breakwater would measurably alter wave conditions or sediment
transport patterns in the South Sailing Basin or other coastal or water areas of the Bay.

2.2.27 Topical Response: VMT
Several comments include questions about mode shift assumptions, potential diversion from other
transit services, and the basis for concluding that ferry service would reduce vehicle trips across the Bay.
Note that this response is specifically related to the project effect on regional travel patterns (i.e.,
between East Bay and San Francisco). For a discussion of local traffic circulation as relates to parking,
please refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking.
Pursuant to California SB 743, transportation impacts in CEQA documents are evaluated using vehicle
miles traveled (VMT) rather than roadway congestion measures such as Level of Service (LOS). The
project is expected to increase traffic volumes on certain roadways leading to the terminal because
additional users would travel to the Waterfront to access the ferry. However, existing roadway segments,
including University Avenue between Frontage Road and Marina Boulevard, would continue to operate
within acceptable capacity conditions (LOS A). At the same time, many ferry users would replace longer
automobile trips with ferry travel. As a result, the overall amount of driving per person is reduced, leading
to a decrease in VMT on a per capita basis.
Section 3.12, Transportation, of the Draft EIR evaluates transportation impacts using VMT consistent with
CEQA Guidelines Section 15064.3 (refer to Section 3.12.4, Impact TRA-2, on Pages 3.12-20 and 3.12-21).
Although the project is estimated to generate 1,127 daily vehicle trips, most of these trips represent the
redistribution of existing travel demand rather than the creation of new trips. As described on Page 3.12-
20 of the Draft EIR, many of these trips are expected to substitute for longer-distance travel that would
otherwise occur by automobile across the Bay Bridge or access to regional transit services. Because
transbay commute trips are relatively long-distance compared to local access trips to a ferry terminal,
this substitution results in a net reduction in VMT even where some riders access the terminal by
automobile.
The conclusion that ferry service would capture trips that might otherwise occur on the Bay Bridge or
other transbay corridors is supported by regional travel patterns and empirical data from existing ferry
operations. WETA most recently conducted onboard surveys in 2025, which indicate that a substantial
share of riders choose ferry service to avoid roadway congestion, and approximately two-thirds of riders
reported that they would otherwise use an automobile-based mode if the ferry were not available,
including a substantial portion who would drive alone. 18 While some respondents indicated that they
would otherwise use public transit, a greater share identified automobile travel as their alternative, and a
portion of riders reported having no viable alternative. This pattern indicates that ferry service primarily
captures trips that would otherwise be made by automobile and thereby reduces demand on regional

roadway facilities. Consistent with the VMT framework under CEQA, replacing longer-distance automobile
trips with shorter local access trips results in a net reduction in VMT.
With respect to proposed project trips potential diversion from BART or other transit services, the Draft
EIR, page 3.12-20, acknowledges that some of the ferry ridership will include people switching from
existing transit services. Even if only a relatively small share of travelers who currently drive choose to
switch to the ferry, each of those trips contributes to a measurable reduction in VMT. Because every
diverted automobile trip removes vehicle travel from the roadway system, the cumulative effect of even
modest mode shift from driving to ferry service will reduce overall VMT. The project site serves the West
Berkeley area, encompassing 9,000 jobs and 10,000 residents, an area less directly served by high-quality
transit than other parts of the East Bay 19, further supporting the conclusion that a substantial portion of

With regard to mode split assumptions, the analysis in Section 3.12, Transportation, and Appendix F,

that while a portion of riders access ferry terminals by automobile, these trips are short and local in
nature and are offset by the elimination of longer regional automobile trips. In addition, a substantial
share of riders access the ferry by walking, bicycling, or transit, particularly at urban terminals. 20 The
assumptions applied in the Draft EIR are therefore consistent with observed behavior and are
conservative, as they do not fully account for reductions associated with Transportation Demand

encourage alternative modes of access.

Localized increases in traffic volumes associated with terminal access do not correspond to an increase
in VMT, which is the applicable CEQA metric. As a regional transit improvement in a constrained corridor,
the project would provide an alternative to automobile travel and reduce reliance on longer-distance
vehicle trips, resulting in a net reduction in VMT, consistent with State guidance on transit projects.
The comments have not provided substantial evidence demonstrating that the methodology or
assumptions are inconsistent with CEQA Guidelines or State guidance. Because the project would reduce
VMT even under conservative assumptions, it would not result in a transportation impact under CEQA.
Accordingly, the analysis and conclusions in Section 3.12 of the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no
further response is required,

• Ferry operators taking proactive steps to avoid whales, such as cutting engines after spotting a gray

2.2.29 Topical Response: Wind
Several comments state that the proposed project might impact wind conditions at the Berkeley
Waterfront, focusing on two distinct issues: (1) whether removal of the vegetated berm and trees along
the Seawall Drive peninsula would change wind shelter conditions in the South Sailing Basin and South
Cove, particularly for beginner sailors and windsurfers using the Cal Sailing Club instructional area; and




Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                         2- 59
                                             Page 164 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                      Response to Comments

(2) whether the breakwater design adequately accounts for wind and wave conditions, including winter
gale-force northwest wind events. The City addresses each issue in turn.

CEQA Considerations
Consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15126, CEQA requires evaluation of a project’s physical
environmental effects within select resource areas. Wind conditions are not covered under any existing
CEQA Appendix G topic or threshold and are not typically analyzed unless they would result in a
secondary physical impact (e.g., exacerbating air quality emissions, soil erosion, or hazards from
structural failure). With respect to recreation, Appendix G asks whether a project would result in
accelerated substantial physical deterioration of a recreational facility or require the construction of
expansion of recreational facilities. The potential for localized changes in wind exposure affecting
recreational conditions does not constitute a direct or indirect physical impact under CEQA.
Tree removal is addressed in the aesthetics, biological resources and land use and planning sections:
Impact AES-1, pages 3.1-27; AES-3, pages 3.1-31 through 3.1-32; Mitigation Measure BIO-1(c), pages 3.3-
55 through 3.3-56, Impact BIO-5, pages 3.3-65 through 3.3-66, Cumulative Impacts, pages 3.3-69; and in
Impact LU-2, pages 3.9-12 and following with regard to the BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, Berkeley
General Plan, Berkeley Municipal Code, and Berkeley Marina Master Plan). The speculative possibility that
removal of some trees could alter localized wind patterns does not trigger CEQA review.
Additionally, the project does not include features that would create or exacerbate unsafe wind conditions
such as introduction of large structures or topographic alterations. Therefore, the EIR does not include a
specific analysis of wind exposure or related mitigation measures.

Wind Shelter Effects of Tree and Berm Removal
As described in the EIR at Section 2.5.3, Project Description, the proposed project includes removal of the
existing vegetated berm and approximately 39 trees across the project site (see Chapter 3, Errata of the
Final EIR), the majority of which are in poor health. The berm to be removed is on average four feet tall.
Species to be removed include Monterey Cypress, Monterey Pine, Italian Stone Pine, Japanese Black Pine,
and others. The project includes replacement planting of between 50 and 70 new trees as 24-inch box
trees throughout the project site, including California Buckeye, Monterey Cypress, Primrose Tree,
Drooping Melaleuca, and Torrey Pine. The trees proposed for removal are located primarily on the
western side of the Seawall Drive corridor and in the interior of the parking lot area; the majority of trees
on the eastern side of the peninsula are not proposed for removal and would remain in place. Cars in the
parking lot will generally be taller than the 4-foot tall berm being removed.
In addition, as a potential project component, a solar canopy structure ranging from approximately 14 to
20 feet in height supported by vertical steel posts approximately 16 feet in height would be installed over
the Seawall Drive parking lot. While the phasing and final determination of whether the solar canopy will
be constructed is not yet confirmed, if implemented it would provide a continuous horizontal structural
element along the parking lot that could act as a windbreak in the vicinity of the South Cove.
Comments request that the Final EIR specifically analyze whether removal of the berm and trees would
materially affect wind conditions and identify mitigation measures.
The question for purposes of CEQA is not whether any change in wind conditions would occur, but
whether such a change would constitute a significant environmental impact. As set forth in the Draft EIR
at Section 3.11, Recreation, the applicable significance thresholds for recreational impacts are whether
the project would: (1) increase the use of existing recreational facilities such that substantial physical
deterioration would occur; (2) result in a reduced recreational facilities per capita ratio requiring new
facilities; or (3) result in substantial adverse physical impacts associated with new or physically altered
recreational facilities.
A potential change in wind exposure conditions in the South Sailing Basin does not meet any of these
thresholds. The South Sailing Basin is not being physically altered, reduced in size, nor is access



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                       2- 60
                                             Page 165 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

restricted by the proposed project. The Cal Sailing Club's instructional area, the public sailing docks, and
the South Cove waters remain fully intact and available for their existing recreational uses. A change in
wind conditions that may affect the experience of beginner sailors does not constitute physical
deterioration of a recreational facility under CEQA - the recreational resource itself is preserved and
accessible. Regardless, based on over 25-years of professional experience, the Coastal Engineering
Design lead for the Project does not anticipate material changes to the wind conditions within the South
Sailing Basin due to the proposed project.
Even if wind conditions experienced by users were to change at the South Cove this would not constitute
a significant physical impact under CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Appendix G. Wind conditions are
one of many factors, including tides, wave conditions, weather, and personal preference, that influence
where recreational users choose to launch and sail on any given day. A potential modest change in wind
exposure at the South Cove does not physically degrade the facility, does not reduce its capacity, and
does not modify access to it. The South Cove and South Sailing Basin would remain fully available for
their existing recreational uses. Furthermore, the magnitude and direction of any wind change resulting
from berm and tree removal is speculative. Wind conditions in the South Cove are affected by a complex
range of factors including regional wind patterns, tidal conditions, shoreline geometry, and surrounding
landforms and structures, including the topography of Shorebird Park which is nearer to the area in
question and is not changed by the Project. Whether the removal of the berm and some existing trees and
replanting of new trees would change experienced wind conditions in the South Cove beyond the
localized area immediately adjacent to the changed vegetation is not established by the comments.
For these reasons, a potential change in wind shelter conditions in the South Sailing Basin does not
constitute a potentially significant or significant environmental impact under CEQA, and no revision to the
Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

Breakwater Design, Wave Climate, and Ferry Operations
Several comments state that the wind and wave data used in the breakwater design is inadequate,
including that winter gale-force northwest wind events are not adequately accounted for and that the
proposed breakwater would leave the ferry float unprotected in such conditions. One comment questions
whether ferries will be able to dock reliably during high wind events.
As an initial matter, these comments address the adequacy of the project design in response to
environmental conditions - that is, the impact of the environment on the project, rather than the impact of
the project on the environment. CEQA requires analysis of a project's effects on the environment, not an
assessment of whether the project itself is adequately designed to withstand environmental conditions.
The project's coastal engineering analysis was conducted by licensed professional coastal engineers
from COWI North America and is documented in the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project
Coastal Study (COWI, December 2025) ("Coastal Study"). The Coastal Study established design
parameters for water levels, wave conditions, wind, and currents specific to the Berkeley Ferry Terminal
site. The structural and coastal engineering aspects of the project, including the breakwater design and
wind and wave climate analysis, have been subject to rigorous independent engineering criteria review.
The BCDC Engineering Criteria Review Board (ECRB) is an advisory board composed of eminent
structural, coastal, and geotechnical engineers that assists BCDC in evaluating the engineering aspects of
projects requiring BCDC permits. The project has been presented to the ECRB on two occasions.
Following the second review, the ECRB determined that a third presentation was not required.
Outstanding technical questions, including those related to wind and wave conditions, will be resolved
through the ongoing BCDC permitting process, which includes continued ECRB coordination.
Ferry service reliability in high wind conditions is an operational matter governed by WETA safety
protocols, which establish the conditions under which ferry service operates and may be suspended.
WETA, as the ferry service operator, is responsible for establishing and enforcing those protocols. No
revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

appreciates the opportunity to review the Draft Environmental Impact Report for the
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project (DEIR). The DEIR evaluates the
potential environmental impacts associated with implementing the Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project (Project).

The project site is located at the Berkeley Waterfront along the San Francisco Bay (Bay)
in the City of Berkeley, Alameda County. The project site encompasses the closed
Berkeley Pier, including the entry area for the Berkeley Pier; the San Francisco Bay
waters surrounding a portion of the closed Berkeley Pier; the existing parking lot off                                        A1-2
Seawall Drive; the Skates on the Bay parking lot and parking lot M (for construction
staging); roadways with landscaping (University Avenue and Seawall Drive); and
various pathways and sidewalks.

The Berkeley Pier was closed in July 2015 due to visually observed structural problems
on the underside of the concrete decking and pilings. The proposed project aims to
revitalize the Berkeley Waterfront by developing new dual-purpose pier and ancillary
uses that support both public recreation and zero-emission public ferry service. The
project would include the following components: demolition of portions of the closed
pier, new public pier, new breakwater that provides pedestrian access and recreational
amenities, recreational amenities, ferry infrastructure, dredging, new public plaza,
improvements to University Avenue and Seawall Drive, a portion of the planned Bay

Comment 1. In Section 3.3.3, Regulatory Framework, the discussion of the extent
of Water Board jurisdiction on page 3.3-31 does not correctly identify the extent
of Water Board jurisdiction at the Project site.
Text on page 3.3-2 states that, “in many cases, the RWQCBs interpret the limits of                       A1-7
waters of the State to be bounded by the OHWM, unless isolated conditions or
ephemeral waters are present”. Along creeks and rivers, the Water Board has
consistently asserted jurisdiction up to at least the top of bank. Along the Bay shoreline,
the Water Board considers areas of the bank below the epochal high tide line to be
regulated as waters of the State.

Comment 2. To address potential impacts to aquatic species, the City should
consult with NOAA Fisheries, the USFWS, and CDFW during the permitting
process.
In Section 3.3.4, Impact Analysis, the discussion of impacts to fish during pile driving on
page 3.3-45 states that the City would consult with NOAA fisheries and CDFW during                       A1-8
the permitting process. Some of the aquatic species that may be impacted by pile
driving and other construction-related activities are managed by the U.S. Fish and
Wildlife Service (USFWS). In the Bay, USFWS consultation is necessary for potential
impacts to longfin smelt and foraging least terns. Also, since the beneficial uses of the
Bay in the Water Board’s Basin Plan include wildlife habitat and the preservation of rare
and endangered species, consultation with the Water Board is also necessary.

Comment 3. Biologists that monitor work at the Project site must be approved by
NMFS and CDFW.
In the discussion of Mitigation Measure BIO-1(A) on page 3.3-53, the text states that the
worker awareness program must be conducted by a City-approved qualified biologist.                       A1-9
The biologist must also be approved by NMFS and CDFW. If USFWS determines that
project work may impact species managed by USFWS, the biologist must also be
approved by USFWS.



                                                                                             2- 65
                                     Page 170 of 1541

City of Berkeley                            - 3 - Berkeley Water Transportation Ferry Project DEIR



Comment 4. Mitigation Measure BIO-3, Provide Compensatory Mitigation for Loss
of Jurisdictional Waters Prior to Operation, defers the preparation of an actual
compensatory mitigation plan to the permitting of the Project.
Text on page 3.3-61 states that the City will submit a proposed mitigation plan to the               A1-10
resource agencies for review and approval during permitting. The mitigation plan should
be provided in the DEIR so that the agencies can assess if the proposed compensatory
mitigation will be sufficient to mitigate the Project’s impacts to jurisdictional waters to a
less than significant level.

In a CEQA document, a project’s potential impacts and proposed mitigation measures
should be presented in sufficient detail for readers of the CEQA document to evaluate
the likelihood that the proposed remedy will actually reduce impacts to a less than
significant level. CEQA requires that mitigation measures for each significant
environmental effect be adequate, timely, and resolved by the lead agency. In an
                                                                                                     A1-11
adequate CEQA document, mitigation measures must be feasible and fully enforceable
through permit conditions, agreements, or other legally binding instruments (CEQA
Guidelines Section 15126.4). Mitigation measures to be identified at some future time
are not acceptable. It has been determined by court ruling that such mitigation
measures would be improperly exempted from the process of public and governmental
scrutiny which is required under the California Environmental Quality Act. Therefore, the
DEIR lacks an adequate discussion of proposed mitigation measures for the Project’s                  A1-12
impacts to waters of the State.

Comment 5. Mitigation Measures BIO-1(D) and BIO-1(E), do not address the
Project’s impacts to aquatic species associated with the proposed nighttime work
for pile driving in the Bay.
Text in Section 2.6.2, Construction Schedule, states that the Project may require up to
50 days in which nighttime work will be used for pile driving. However, Mitigation
Measure BIO-1(D), Conduct Pile Driving Impact Avoidance to Fish and Marine
Mammals Prior to and During Construction, and Mitigation Measure BIO-1(E), Prepare                   A1-13
Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan Prior to Construction and Implement
Recommendations During Construction, do not address impacts associated with the
proposed nighttime pile driving. Both of these mitigation measures included responses
to visual observations of fish or marine mammals. But such observations are not be
feasible after dark.

We prefer that pile driving and other construction activities be implemented during
daylight hours, when it is easier to observe any discharges of construction materials to
Bay water and it is easier to observe marine mammals, water birds, and fish in the                   A1-14
vicinity of the construction site. Please revise the Project description to remove the
proposed nighttime pile driving.

                                    Page 171 of 1541

City of Berkeley                           - 4 - Berkeley Water Transportation Ferry Project DEIR

Comment 6. Constituents detected in sediment at the Project site should be
compared to ecological screening levels.
On page 3.8-7, the discussion of chemicals detected in sediments at the Project site
states that the measured concentrations did not exceed State for Federal hazardous
waste criteria. Hazardous waste criteria are not the appropriate criteria to use in
screening sediments for potential impacts to wildlife. Constituent concentrations that are          A1-15
lower than hazardous waste criteria may negatively impact wildlife. Please compare the
chemical concentrations in the sediments with the surface layer screening levels in the
Master Quality Assurance Project Plan for the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay
National Wildlife Refuge (QAPP) (USFWS and H.T. Harvey, December 13, 2024). The
screening levels in the QAPP were developed to be protective of aquatic species in
marine environments.

Comment 7. The DEIR does not propose treatment for stormwater runoff from the
new pier and ferry dock.                                                                            A1-16
The DEIR must be revised to describe how runoff from the new pier and ferry dock’s
impervious surfaces will be treated prior to discharge to the Bay.

Comment 8. The proposed use of pervious pavement to treat stormwater runoff at
the Marina may not be appropriate.
The DEIR proposes to treat runoff from land side post-construction impervious surfaces
using permeable pavement and bioretention areas. Permeable pavement passes water
through the pavement and allows the runoff to infiltrate into the soil below the
permeable pavement. However, permeable pavement may not be appropriate at the
Berkeley Marina, which was built over landfilled waste materials. Water infiltrating into           A1-17
buried waste may mobilize contaminants that will then be conveyed to the Bay via the
movement of groundwater. Permeable pavement is only recommended when the
bottom of the gravel infiltration reservoir below the permeable pavement is at least 5
feet above the local groundwater. According to text on page 3.8-35, depth to
groundwater at the Project site is approximately 5 to 13.4 feet below the surface.

Prior to constructing areas of permeable pavement at the project site, the depth to
groundwater below the areas of proposed permeable surfaces should be determined
and the potential presence of waste materials in the subsurface should be assessed.

Response to Comment A1-7
For the purposes of CEQA, because the limits of State Water Board jurisdiction are not defined by Porter-
Cologne and there is no current written regulatory definition that specifies the limits of waters of the State
in tidal areas, no changes are warranted related to the Draft EIR analysis, conclusions or mitigation. Refer
to Draft EIR pages 3.3-31 and 3.3-32 for a discussion of how regulations for field determinations have not
been established for waters of the State. In response to this comment, the following clarification text
revisions have been made to the Draft EIR:
Section 3.3.3 page 3.3-32:
    The SWRCB and RWQCBs have not currently established regulations for field determinations of
    waters of the State except for wetlands. In many cases, the RWQCBs interpret the limits of waters of
    the State to be bounded by the OHWM unless isolated conditions or ephemeral waters are present.
    However, in the absence of statewide guidance, each RWQCB may interpret jurisdictional boundaries
    within their region, and the SWRCB has encouraged applicants to confirm jurisdictional limits with
    their RWQCB before submitting applications. As determined by the RWQCB, waters of the State may
    include riparian areas or other locations outside the OHWM, leading to a larger jurisdictional area over
    a given water body compared to USACE. The San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board has
    indicated that along creeks and rivers, they would assert jurisdiction up to at least the top of bank and
    along the Bay shoreline, they consider that areas of the bank below the epochal high tide line to be
    regulated waters of the State. For the purposes of this EIR, the one-year extreme high tide line was
    used to delineate the extent of jurisdictional waters, in line with USACE guidance, and assumed to
    encompass both waters of the U.S. and waters of the State. Further coordination with the SFRWQCB
    will be conducted during the permitting process.

consultation. Consultation with USFWS would also occur because the project has potential to affect
longfin smelt, a species managed by the USFWS. Refer to Response to Comment A2-35 to A2-38 for a
discussion of impacts to California least tern.

Response to Comment A1-10
Consistent with CEQA Guidelines §15126.4(a)(1)(B), when project‑specific details are not yet available,
mitigation measures may be formulated with performance standards that ensure the measure will be
effective once the missing information becomes available. CEQA expressly allows agencies to not
finalize all the details of mitigation if the agency commits to specific performance criteria and to a
process ensuring that the final mitigation will achieve the required outcomes, including finetuning that
could result from separate regulatory permitting processes. The Draft EIR includes a requirement that
existing pier structures be removed at a ratio of at least 1:1 for impacts to jurisdictional waters (refer to
Mitigation Measure BIO‑3 on page 3.3-61) to achieve a no-net increase in Bay fill, which is sufficient to
mitigate the impact on jurisdictional waters to a less-than-significant level under CEQA. Preparation of a
fully developed, site‑specific mitigation plan requires final design information and jurisdictional
determinations that are not yet available. Because the precise footprint, final pile and decking layouts,
and the results of a formal jurisdictional delineation will be established during final design and agency
permitting, it is not possible to calculate exact impact quantities or to prepare a fully developed mitigation
plan at this time. The final mitigation plan required to secure permits from USACE, SFBRWQCB, and BCDC
will be determined in coordination with these regulatory agencies, consistent with the performance
standards in Mitigation Measure BIO-3.
Refer to Section 2.2.17, Topical Response: Mitigation Measure Requirements, for further discussion about
how Mitigation Measure BIO-3 is not deferred mitigation under CEQA. In addition, refer to the errata in
Chapter 3 of the Final EIR for changes to the wording of Mitigation Measure BIO-3, and which clarifies
that implementation of Mitigation Measure BIO-3 would require no net increase in Bay fill, rather than
compensatory mitigation.

Response to Comment A1-12
The mitigation disclosed in an EIR must be adequate, enforceable, and sufficiently specific so that the
public and agencies can evaluate its likely effectiveness. The Draft EIR provides a clear, enforceable,
minimum mitigation requirement that avoids the net loss of jurisdictional waters due to project
implementation (refer to Mitigation Measure BIO‑3 on page 3.3-61 and as revised in the errata in
Chapter 3 of the Final EIR). A fully engineered mitigation plan is not typically completed at the Draft EIR
stage, and mitigation details are also further finalized during the separate regulatory permitting process.
At the end of Mitigation Measure BIO-3 in the Draft EIR (refer to page 3.3-66), it is stated that “This
measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory agencies.”
Refer also to Section 2.2.17, Topical Response: Mitigation Measure Requirements, for further discussion
about how Mitigation Measure BIO-3 is not deferred mitigation under CEQA. Draft EIR Table 3.3-4 in
Section 3.3.4 Impacts Analysis, Impact BIO-3, page 3.3-60, includes the estimated net change in square
feet of fill within waters of the State.

Response to Comment A1-13
Draft EIR Mitigation Measures BIO‑1(d) is related to time of year of in-water construction and requires a
soft startup of construction equipment in water to allow fish and marine mammals to vacate the area
before a pile driver reaches full power. Note that the starting up of construction equipment would not
happen during the nighttime but only during the daytime when construction commences. This allows for
visual observation during the start-up period to ensure that fish or marine mammals leave the vicinity of
the construction site. Once they vacate the area, it is not anticipated that fish or marine mammals would
revisit the construction site until after the construction ceases. Further, as described below, nighttime
pile-driving will be limited and additional non-visual monitoring protocols will be used. In response to this
comment, the text of Draft EIR Section 3.3, Biological Resources, has been clarified as follows:
Section 3.3.4 page 3.3-45:
    However, Mitigation Measure BIO-1(a) and BIO-1(d) would be required. Mitigation Measure BIO-1(a),
    which requires a Worker Environmental Awareness Program (in part to support implementation of
    Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d)), and Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d), which dictates seasonal work
    windows, soft-start and ramp-up procedures, exclusion zones, and sound attenuation measures
    during pile driving, would reduce impacts related to special-status fish to less than significant with
    mitigation. Soft-start procedures would occur when pile driving and pile-extraction activities
    commence during daytime hours, allowing marine mammals to leave the vicinity of the construction
    site before pile driving reaches full power. Nighttime pile driving, if required, would only occur as a
    continuation of work initiated during the daytime after implementation of the daytime soft-start
    procedures. In addition, the City would consult with NOAA Fisheries and CDFW during the permitting
    process.

Section 3.3.4 page 3.3-48:
    However, Mitigation Measure BIO-1(a) and BIO-1(d) would be required. Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d)
    requires implementation of soft-start and ramp-up procedures, monitoring, and exclusion zones
    based on the most current NMFS-approved guidance to avoid and minimize marine mammal
    exposure to pile-driving noise. Soft-start procedures would occur when pile driving and pile-extraction
    activities commence during daytime hours, allowing marine mammals to leave the vicinity of the
    construction site before pile driving reaches full power. Nighttime pile driving, if required, would only

    occur as a continuation of work initiated during the daytime after implementation of the daytime soft-
    start procedures. Implementation of these measures would reduce construction related, pile-driving

Section 3.3.4 page 3.3-50:
    In addition to the Worker Environmental Awareness Program required under Mitigation Measures

safety require extended hours and after construction activity has already begun earlier during the day.
Nonetheless, in response to this comment, the text of the Draft EIR Mitigation Measure BIO-1(e) has been
clarified to provide more specifics related to potential nighttime pile driving as follows:
Section 3.3.4 page 3.3-56:

    Mitigation Measure BIO-1(e): Prepare Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan Prior to Construction
    and Implement Recommendations During Construction
    Prior to construction, the City shall prepare a Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan (MMMP) to avoid and
    minimize potential adverse impacts on marine mammals during pile driving and tug operations. The
    MMMP shall implement general guidelines set forth in the MMPA and incorporate the hydroacoustic
    modeling results developed for the project to define site-specific protection zones and avoid
    exposure of marine mammals to underwater sound levels exceeding the most up to date Level A
    (injury) thresholds identified by NOAA Fisheries. The MMMP shall include the following:
    • Protection and Monitoring Zones: Using the hydroacoustic modeling results, the MMMP shall
      define shutdown and disturbance zones for each marine mammal hearing group. These zones will
      be tailored to the pile type, size, and driving method and will correspond to the Level A and Level B
      effect distances developed for the project. The plan will describe how these protection zones will
      be verified and monitored in the field, integrating them with the soft-start and observation
      procedures described in Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d).
    • Vessel Operation Protocols: The MMMP shall include vessel-operation measures consistent with
      the MMPA. Construction vessels under power shall remain at least 300 feet from whales and 150
      feet from dolphins, porpoises, seals, and sea lions. When marine mammals are encountered,
      vessel operators shall reduce speed to no-wake, shift to neutral, and allow the animals to pass
      safely before resuming operations.
    • On-Site Monitoring and Response: A qualified biologist shall be present on site, either observing
      from the pier or aboard a vessel, during all pile-driving and tug operations. The biologist shall
      document all marine-mammal observations, note behavioral responses, and immediately alert
      project personnel if a whale enters the modeled harassment distance or comes within 300 feet, or



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                      2- 72
                                                     Page 177 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                                          Response to Comments

        if any other marine mammal enters the modeled harassment distance or comes within 150 feet,
        whichever is greater. Upon such an observation, the contractor shall implement the appropriate
        delay or shutdown procedures identified in the MMMP.
     • Adaptive Management and Coordination: The MMMP shall outline communication and reporting
       protocols, including stop-work notification procedures and coordination with NMFS Protected
       Species Division. Results from daily monitoring will be used to assess the effectiveness of the
       protection zones and adjust them, if needed, in consultation with NMFS.
     • Nighttime Pile Driving: Nighttime pile driving shall be limited to situations where safety concerns
       or significant schedule delays require that pile driving started during daytime hours extend beyond
       typical work hours. For instances where nighttime pile driving is required, the MMMP shall include
       non-visual monitoring protocols, such as passive acoustic monitoring, thermal/infrared cameras,
       and night‑vision optics, as well as larger nighttime exclusion/shutdown zones, extended soft‑start
       procedures, and the most effective feasible hydroacoustic attenuation.

     This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
     agencies.

Response to Comment A1-14
As discussed in Response to Comment A1-13, construction work would be conducted primarily during the
daytime, and nighttime pile driving would only occur when absolutely necessary. No changes to the Draft
EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment A1-15
Impact HAZ-1 in Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials of the Draft EIR (page 3.7-27) discusses
the results of a 2025 sediment sampling analysis conducted within the five dredge units within the
project vicinity, which included evaluation of the sediments for placement at disposal sites in San
Francisco Bay, specifically the Cullinan Ranch Restoration Project (CRRP) and the Montezuma Wetlands
Restoration Project (MWRP) beneficial reuse sites. 22 Based on the findings of the sampling and analysis,
which included comparison of sediment chemistry to San Francisco Bay sediment background
concentrations and site-specific screening criteria for CRRP and MWRP, the sediments sampled are
suitable for reuse at San Francisco Bay, CRRP, and/or MWRP beneficial reuse sites. The sediment
screening levels requested for comparison by the commenter were established specifically for the Don
Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge, which is a different beneficial reuse site than those
evaluated in the 2025 sediment sampling analysis. Page 2-28 in Chapter 2, Project Description of the Draft
EIR indicates that the location for disposal of dredged materials would depend on the sampling results of
the dredged materials, as well as permitting requirements. Based on the results of the 2025 sediment
sampling analysis, it is expected that MWRP or another disposal site in the San Francisco Bay would be
used. The Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge is not identified in the Draft EIR as a
potential disposal site for dredged materials as part of the proposed project; therefore, comparison of the
2025 sediment samples to the site-specific screening levels for the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay
National Wildlife Refuge is not applicable to the proposed project.
The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact HAZ-1 in Section 3.7, Hazards and
Hazardous Materials, of the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No further revisions to the EIR are
necessary.

Response to Comment A1-16
The Draft EIR's analysis of stormwater runoff focuses on operational impacts from impervious surfaces
that generate contaminated runoff such as parking areas and roadways with vehicular activity (see Draft
EIR Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality). Because the new pier surface will not support vehicle
operations or fuel-related contamination sources, the runoff from the pier surface itself consists of
uncontaminated precipitation and does not meet the thresholds for a significant environmental impact
under CEQA. In addition, there is already an existing pier at the project site and stormwater runoff from
the existing pier represents the existing baseline conditions. When the proposed project is compared to
existing baseline conditions, the amount and quality of runoff from the proposed new pier is not expected
to change. This analysis is consistent with the Draft EIR's findings that project-related water quality
impacts would be less than significant, as documented in Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality and
the associated mitigation measure.
However, the City acknowledges that SFRWQCB regulatory requirements mandate stormwater treatment
standards for all new impervious surfaces, including the pier, regardless of CEQA significance. The
specific treatment approach and compliance mechanism will be established through the City's permit
application process and subject to SFRWQCB review and approval. This regulatory and design-level
analysis occurs outside CEQA scope and does not require revision to the Draft EIR.
No revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

Response to Comment A1-17
As described on page 2-18 of the Draft EIR, the proposed project includes permeable pavement for the
majority of the proposed parking. The proposed permeable pavement does not provide stormwater
treatment or rely on infiltration. As described in Draft EIR Section 2.5.2, the permeable pavement conveys
stormwater via an under-drain to new bioretention areas designed for stormwater treatment in
compliance with the City's NPDES permit and applicable stormwater quality standards. The detailed
design of the stormwater treatment system will be reviewed and permitted by the City and SFRWQCB to
ensure compliance with applicable regulatory requirements. The Draft EIR appropriately addresses
potential water quality impacts in Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality; detailed design and regulatory
compliance occur through separate permitting processes. Accordingly, no revisions to the Draft EIR are
required.

Response to Comment A1-18
As this comment does not raise any significant environmental issues, no further response is required.

Dear Liza McNulty:

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) received a Draft Environmental Impact Report
(DEIR) from the City of Berkeley for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry (Project) pursuant
to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and CEQA Guidelines.1

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments and recommendations regarding those activities                         A2-2
involved in the Project that may affect California fish and wildlife. Likewise, we appreciate the
opportunity to provide comments regarding those aspects of the Project that CDFW, by law, may be
required to carry out or approve through the exercise of its own regulatory authority under the Fish
and Game Code.

CDFW ROLE

CDFW is California’s Trustee Agency for fish and wildlife resources and holds those resources in trust
by statute for all the people of the state. (Fish & G. Code, § 711.7, subd. (a) & 1802; Pub. Resources
Code, § 21070; CEQA Guidelines §15386, subd. (a).) CDFW, in its trustee capacity, has jurisdiction
over the conservation, protection, and management of fish, wildlife, native plants, and habitat
necessary for biologically sustainable populations of those species. (Id., § 1802.) Similarly for                        A2-3
purposes of CEQA, CDFW is charged by law to provide, as available, biological expertise during
public agency environmental review efforts, focusing specifically on projects and related activities that
have the potential to adversely affect fish and wildlife resources. Additionally, CDFW is responsible
for marine biodiversity protection under the Marine Life Protection Act in coastal marine waters of
California, and ensuring fisheries are sustainably managed under the Marine Life Management Act.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION SUMMARY

Proponent: City of Berkeley

Objective: The objective of the Project is to replace the Berkley Pier with a new publicly accessible
pier, breakwater, and ferry terminal. The proposed project would include construction of a new 1,080-
foot pier, a 400-foot breakwater, and ferry boarding infrastructure. There would be development of a
new public plaza at the pier entrance; improvements along University Avenue and Seawall Drive
including a raised cycle track, new pedestrian amenities, and upgraded transit facilities. The project
also included renovation of existing parking areas with permeable pavement and potential solar
canopies, as well as installation of new utility connections, shoreline repair, and dredging to support
ferry operations. Primary Project activities include removal of the old Pier structures, installation of
new concrete piles, and the installation of a breakwater. On land, the project will consist of utility     A2-6
trenching, demolition of hardscapes, and repaving roads and parking areas.

Location: The Project is located within the City of Berkeley at the waterfront near the Berkeley Pier
and includes the adjacent land along Seawall Drive and University Avenue (37°51'40.3"N,
122°19'00.3"W).

Timeline: April 2027 to December 2028.

Lake and Streambed Alteration

CDFW requires a Lake or Streambed Alteration (LSA) Notification, pursuant to Fish and Game Code
section 1600 et seq., for Project activities affecting river, lakes or streams and associated riparian
habitat. Notification is required for any activity that may substantially divert or obstruct the natural
flow; change or use material from the bed, channel, or bank (including associated riparian or wetland
resources); or deposit or dispose of material where it may pass into a river, lake, or stream. Work
within ephemeral streams, drainage ditches, washes, watercourses with a subsurface flow, and               A2-8
floodplains is generally subject to notification requirements. In addition, infrastructure installed
beneath such aquatic features, such as through hydraulic directional drilling, is also generally subject
to notification requirements. Therefore, any impact to the mainstems, tributaries, or floodplains or
associated riparian habitat caused by the proposed Project will likely require an LSA Notification.
CDFW may not execute a final LSA Agreement until it has considered the final EIR and complied with
its responsibilities as a responsible agency under CEQA.

Migratory Birds and Raptors

CDFW has authority over actions that may result in the disturbance or destruction of active bird nest
sites or the unauthorized take of birds. Fish and Game Code sections protecting birds, their eggs, and
nests include section 3503 (regarding unlawful take, possession, or needless destruction of the nests A2-9
or eggs of any bird), section 3503.5 (regarding the take, possession, or destruction of any birds-of-
prey or their nests or eggs), and section 3513 (regarding unlawful take of any migratory nongame
bird). Migratory birds are also protected under the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

Fully Protected Species

Fully Protected Species (Fish & G. Code § 3511 and 4700) have the potential to occur within or
adjacent to the Project area, including, but not limited to: white-tailed kite (Elanus leucurus), and   A2-10
California least tern (Sternula antillarum browni) (LETE).

Project activities described in the DEIR should be designed to completely avoid any fully protected
species that have the potential to be present within or adjacent to the Project area. Fully protected
species may not be taken or possessed at any time and no licenses or permits may be issued for
their take except as follows:
   • Take is for necessary scientific research
   • Efforts to recover a fully protected, endangered, or threatened species, live capture and
        relocation of a bird species for the protection of livestock                                    A2-11
   • They are a covered species whose conservation and management is provided for in a Natural
        Community Conservation Plan (Fish & G. Code, §§ 3511, 4700, 5050, & 5515).

Specified types of infrastructure projects may be eligible for an Incidental Take Permit (ITP) for
unavoidable impacts to fully protected species if certain conditions are met (Fish & G. Code
§2081.15).

CDFW also recommends the DEIR analyze potential adverse impacts to fully protected species due
to habitat modification, loss of foraging habitat, and/or interruption of migratory and breeding
behaviors. CDFW recommends that the Lead Agency include in the analysis how appropriate                 A2-12
avoidance, minimization and mitigation measures will reduce indirect impacts to fully protected
species. Project proponents should consult with CDFW early in the Project planning process.

MARINE BIOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE

The San Francisco Bay-Delta is the second largest estuary in the United States and supports
numerous aquatic habitats and biological communities. It encompasses 479 square miles, including       A2-13
shallow mudflats. This ecologically significant ecosystem supports both state and federally threatened
and endangered species and sustains important commercial and recreational fisheries.

COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

CDFW offers the comments and recommendations below to assist the City of Berkeley in adequately
identifying and/or mitigating the Project’s significant, or potentially significant, direct, and indirect   A2-14
impacts on fish and wildlife (biological) resources. Editorial comments or other suggestions may also
be included to improve the clarity of the document.

I. Project Level Impacts and Other Considerations

Mitigation Measures BIO-1 and BIO-3

   Comment: The proposed Project includes using both a vibratory driving and impact hammer to
   drive up to 416 piles that range from concrete sheet piles to 24”-36” diameter steel and concrete
   piles. Mitigation Measure BIO-1 is broken up into multiple sections with measures to avoid and or        A2-15
   minimize impacts to aquatic species from pile driving, including through implementation of worker
   education, special status species surveys, work windows, and hydroacoustic attenuation.
   However, Mitigation Measure BIO-1 does not address potential compensatory mitigation to offset
   hydroacoustic impacts to aquatic species from pile driving.

   Additionally, the proposed Project would have an estimated net increase in cover area of 17,050
   square feet, or approximately 0.39 acres. The proposed Mitigation Measure BIO-3 proposes to
   offset this increase of cover by removing additional existing decking and piles from the defunct
   wharf at a 1:1 ratio. However, this ratio may not be sufficient to offset the potential impacts to state
   listed species based on the impacts of the proposed Project.                                             A2-16

   The increase in fill and cover from the proposed pier and ferry dock, in addition to the impacts
   from increased underwater sound during construction and new work dredging may require an
   increased ratio to appropriately offset the impacts to state listed species that will be considered
   under CDFW’s authorization of the Project.

   Recommendation: CDFW recommends adding a section to Mitigation Measure BIO-1 to address
   compensatory mitigation to offset impacts from pile driving, particularly hydroacoustic impacts to
   species. CDFW also recommends that the final EIR consider a total mitigation ratio of 3:1, if fill A2-17
   removal is chosen to mitigate for the Project’s impacts, to offset loss of species habitat and
   impacts from underwater sound. Additionally, mitigation credits, from a CDFW approved mitigation
   bank, may serve as an appropriate alternative mitigation option.

Crotch’s Bumble Bee

   Comment: The DEIR states that Crotch’s bumble bee (Bombus crotchii) have the potential to
   occur on the Project site but it does not state avoidance and minimization measures to reduce
   potential impacts to less-than-significant.

   The Project location is within the Crotch’s bumble bee range
   (https://wildlife.ca.gov/Conservation/CESA) and grassland adjacent to the Project site may contain
   potential habitat for Crotch’s bumble bee. As a candidate species, unauthorized take of this       A2-21
   species pursuant to CESA is a violation of California Fish and Game Code section 2080 et seq.

   The Project activities may result in the loss of nesting and foraging habitat for Crotch’s bumble
   bee, and potentially the loss of individuals in nests due to crushing by construction personnel or
   equipment, excavation, and placement of soil stockpiles. Additionally, Project activities may result
   in direct mortality through crushing or filling of active bee colonies and hibernating bee cavities,
   reduced reproductive success, loss of suitable breeding and foraging habitats, loss of native
   vegetation that may support essential foraging habitat.

   Recommended Mitigation Measure Habitat Assessment: A habitat assessment shall be
   conducted by a qualified entomologist knowledgeable with the life history and ecological
   requirements of Crotch’s bumble bee. The habitat assessment shall include all suitable nesting,
   overwintering, and foraging habitats within the Project area and surrounding areas. Potential nest
   habitat (February through October) could include that of other Bombus species such as bare
   ground, thatched grasses, abandoned rodent burrows or bird nests, brush piles, rock piles, and       A2-22
   fallen logs. Overwintering habitat (November through January) could include that of other Bombus
   species such as soft and disturbed soil or under leaf litter or other debris. The habitat assessment
   shall be conducted during peak bloom period for floral resources on which Crotch’s bumble bee
   feed. Further guidance on habitat surveys can be found within Survey Considerations for
   California Endangered Species Act (CESA) Candidate Bumble Bee Species
   (https://wildlife.ca.gov/Conservation/CESA).

   Recommended Mitigation Measure Survey Plan: If Crotch’s bumble bee habitat is present
