Burrowing Owl

   Comment: The DEIR states that burrowing owls (Athene cunicularia) are unlikely to be affected
   by the project due to the low potential to occur on the project site. However, a 2025 occurrence of
   burrowing owl is noted 0.7 miles north of the Project area in CNDDB.

   The burrowing owl is currently a candidate species under CESA and is afforded the same           A2-28
   protection as a CESA-listed species (CEQA Guidelines, §15380, subds. (b)). Unauthorized take of
   this species pursuant to CESA is a violation of Fish and Game Code section 2080 et seq. The
   mitigation measures in BIO-1(c) may not be sufficient to avoid impacts to burrowing owls as they
   do not address the potential for occurrence.

   Recommended Mitigation Measure: The DEIR should modify BIO-1 to state that if burrowing
   owls are detected during surveys within or near the Project area, a protective buffer will be
   established to ensure construction activities will not impact the burrowing owl or their habitat.
   Appropriate buffers typically have a 150 to 1,500-foot radius and vary depending on the level of
   disturbance and timing of construction. If the burrowing owl show signs of distress (e.g., defensive
   vocalizations and/or flying away from the nest), the buffer distance should be increased. The
   Designated Biologist shall submit the results of the surveys, including a Burrow Complex Map to
   CDFW for approval prior to beginning Covered Activities. If changes in burrowing owl presence
   are detected (e.g., burrowing owl have moved onsite or changed burrow use), the Designated
   Biologist shall contact the CDFW Regional Representative by phone or email within 24 hours of
   the observation to consult on appropriate measures to avoid or minimize impacts of the Project. If
                                                                                                        A2-29
   a lapse in Project-related work of 14 calendar days or longer occurs, the Lead Agency shall
   contact the CDFW Regional Representative by phone or email and may be required to conduct
   additional surveys before work may be reinitiated.

   The Designated Biologist shall visually inspect any pipes, debris piles, culverts, pallet stacks,
   burrow exclusion installations, or similar structures for burrowing owl before the material is moved,
   buried, or capped. The Designated Biologist shall inspect all open holes and trenches within the
   Project Area at a minimum of twice a day and immediately prior to backfilling. At the end of each
   workday, the Lead Agency shall place an escape ramp at each end of trenches or holes to allow
   any animals that may have become trapped in the trench or hole to climb out overnight. The ramp
   may be constructed of either dirt fill or wood planking or other suitable material that is placed at an
   angle no greater than 30-45 degrees. If any worker discovers that burrowing owls have become
   trapped, they shall halt Covered Activities and notify the Designated Biologist immediately. Project
   workers and the Designated Biologist shall allow the burrowing owl to escape unimpeded.

   Recommended Mitigation Measure Burrowing Owl Monitoring: The Designated Biologist(s)
   shall be present during construction activities to monitor the behavior of any burrowing owl. The     A2-30
   Designated Biologist(s) shall have the authority to order stop work if burrowing owl exhibit distress
   and/or abnormal behavior for (e.g., excessive vocalizations, defensive flights at intruders, flushing

   Designated Biologist(s), shall determine whether to increase the size of the no-disturbance buffer.

   Comment: The surveys and avoidance buffers proposed by mitigation measure BIO-1(c) may not A2-32
   be sufficient to reduce impacts to nesting birds to less-than-significant levels.

   Project activities, including grading, ground disturbance, operation of heavy machinery, increased

   turn result in nest abandonment, reduced reproductive success, loss, or reduced health or vigor of
   eggs or young. Grading, tree removal, and vegetation removal may also result in direct take of
   nesting birds.

California Least Tern

   Comment: The DEIR states that LETE are not expected to occur within the project site. However,
   LETE has been recorded adjacent to the project site according to CNDDB unprocessed data.
   Despite the existence of suitable nesting habitat and potential for LETE to nest or forage adjacent A2-35
   to Project and staging areas, the DEIR does not include analysis on the potential for the Project to
   significantly impact LETE, nor does it include measures to avoid, minimize or mitigate potentially
   significant impacts to LETE.

   LETE are CESA and federal Endangered Species Act (ESA) endangered and state fully protected
   species. Populations of LETE nest along the West coast of North America from Baja California
   north to the San Francisco Bay and establish nesting colonies on sandy soils with little vegetation
   along Pacific Ocean beaches, lagoons and bays (USFWS 1980). LETE were once widespread
   and abundant, but increasing human disturbance to sandy beaches, hunting for the millinery
   trade, and increasing predator populations caused the population to undergo a major decline in
                                                                                                         A2-36
   the early 1900s (USFWS 2006). LETE nesting occurs between April 15 and late September, and
   successful development and growth of chicks requires habitat free of human disturbance,
   protection from avian and mammal predators, and proximity to aquatic foraging habitat. LETE
   have high site fidelity and return to nesting areas year after year. This species is highly sensitive
   to human disturbance and will readily abandon nesting areas if disturbed.

   Project activities could impact LETE in the short term due to generation of noise from construction
   equipment, groundwork, and operation and movement of equipment and workers that would have
   the potential to disturb LETE foraging, roosting, and nesting. Direct mortality of LETE could occur A2-37
   through nest abandonment, resulting in reduced reproductive success (loss or reduced health or
   vigor of eggs or young).

   Recommended Mitigation Measure: A CDFW-approved biologist, in coordination with CDFW,
   shall conduct breeding and occupancy surveys for LETE in all suitable habitats within and
                                                                                                          A2-38
   adjacent to the Project area during the LETE nesting season (April 15- September 15) prior to
   each year of construction to determine whether LETE are present.




                                                                                             2- 85
                                            Page 190 of 1541

City of Berkeley
April 23, 2026
Page 11


   If LETE are found in suitable habitat near the Project site, appropriate buffers shall be
   incorporated to avoid and minimize impacts to LETE. A 700-foot no-work buffer shall be
   implemented between construction activities and any current-year breeding LETE detections.
   Noise-reducing modifications to equipment as well as portable acoustic barriers/blankets placed
   near noise sources may be appropriate to reduce auditory and visual impacts to breeding
   shorebirds. A qualified avian biologist shall advise and support buffer establishment in
   consultation with CDFW. Fully protected species such as LETE may not be taken or possessed at
   any time. The qualified biologist shall also be on-site during all Project activities to ensure that fully
   protected species impacts are avoided by all Project activities.

Section 3.3.2, page 3.3-22:

    Chinook Salmon - Central Valley Spring-Run ESU
    The Chinook salmon - Central Valley spring-run ESU is federally threatened. Chinook salmon is an
    anadromous fish spending most of its life in coastal waters. This population of chinook salmon
    spawns in the Sacramento River and its tributaries. Juveniles are reared in the San Joaquin Delta and
    migrate to the ocean between December, January, and February, and adult immigration through the
    delta and into the lower Sacramento River occurs from late January to early February.67 Therefore,
    there is a moderate potential for individuals to migrate, forage, and transit within the project site.

    Chinook Salmon – Central Valley fall/late-fall-run ESU
    The Chinook salmon - Central Valley fall/late-fall-run ESU includes both fall-run and late-fall-run
    Chinook salmon; however, only the fall-run is a CDFW SSC. Chinook salmon are anadromous,
    spending the majority of their life cycle in marine waters before returning to freshwater systems to
    spawn. Fall-run Chinook salmon migrate upstream through the San Joaquin Delta from July through
    December and spawn from early October through late December, with the timing of runs varying by
    stream.68 Late fall-run Chinook salmon migrate through the San Joaquin Delta from mid-October
    through December and spawn from January through mid-April. Following emergence, most juvenile
    fall-run and late-fall-run Chinook salmon rear in freshwater for approximately one to seven months
    before emigrating to the ocean, while a smaller proportion remain in freshwater and migrate as
    yearlings. Among the Central Valley Chinook salmon populations, the fall-run is the most abundant
    and exhibits a life history strategy characterized by a relatively short freshwater residence period. The
    fall-run population emigrates to the ocean during the spring, prior to the onset of elevated summer
    water temperatures, allowing juveniles to utilize lower-elevation reaches of Central Valley rivers
    during outmigration. This life history strategy, combined with the population's relative abundance, has
    resulted in fall-run Chinook salmon being the primary stock propagated at the five major Central
    Valley hatcheries.69 Based on the species' migration ecology, habitat use, and the location of the
    project site within a potential migratory corridor, there is moderate potential for Central Valley fall-
    run/late-fall-run Chinook salmon to occur within the project site and vicinity during migration or
    dispersal periods. Individuals may use aquatic habitats within or adjacent to the project site for
    passage and transient foraging; however, the project site does not provide suitable spawning or long-
    term rearing habitat.

Response to Comment A2-13 to A2-14
These comments do not pertain to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR.

Response to Comment A2-15
Impact BIO-1 (refer to pages 3.3-45 through 3.3-46 and 3.3-48 through 3.3-51) concludes less-than-
significant-with-mitigation impacts with regard to construction-related hydroacoustic (pile-driving)
impacts to aquatic species. The Draft EIR concludes that construction-related hydroacoustic impacts to
special-status aquatic species would be less-than-significant-with-mitigation (refer to Mitigation
Measures BIO-1(a) and BIO-1(d)). CEQA does not require compensation for temporary physiological or
behavioral disturbance. Therefore, compensatory mitigation is not appropriate for hydroacoustic impacts,
because such effects are acute, short‑term, and best addressed by avoidance, engineering controls,
timing, and monitoring as discussed in the Draft EIR. Additional mitigation measures, with regard to
potential impacts to aquatic species from pile driving required to secure permits from USFWS, NMFS,
CDFW, and SFBRWQCB will be determined in coordination with these regulatory agencies. No Draft EIR
changes are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comments A2-16 and A2-17
The 1:1 replacement ratio described in the Draft EIR is a minimum baseline commitment to ensure no net
loss of jurisdictional waters by the lead agency, City of Berkeley, under CEQA, and is not a fixed or final
future permitting‑stage outcome. This ratio is substantiated by the in-kind, in-place nature of the
proposed mitigation: removal of existing pier piles and decking offsets new net fill and cover within the
same water body and habitat type, avoiding the establishment risk, time lag, and functional uncertainty
typically associated with off-site or out-of-kind mitigation approaches that warrant higher ratios. The
actual mitigation ratio and specifics will be determined during agency permitting based on the final
design, the results of a formal jurisdictional and functional assessment, and regulatory agency review.
The analysis presented in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impacts BIO-1 and BIO-3, (pages 3.3-45 through
3.3-51 and 3.3-60 through 3.3-61, respectively) conclude that impacts to special-status aquatic species
regarding project cover area would be less-than-significant-with-mitigation (refer to Mitigation Measures
BIO-1(a), BIO-1(d), BIO-1(e), BIO-3, and HYD-1), and is, thus, adequate under CEQA. Refer also to Section
2.2.17, Topical Response: Mitigation Measure Requirements. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in
response to these comments.

Response to Comments A2-21 to A2-25
Based on the informal habitat assessment for Crotch’s Bumble Bee (CBB) done during a project site
reconnaissance survey on September 19, 2024, as noted in Draft EIR Section 3.3.1 (page 3.3-2), suitable
habitat for this species within the project site is present but marginal due to high levels of disturbance
and limited floral resources. Thus, the species has low potential to occur and, in the absence of new
information on potential species presence, that determination has not changed. Project activities would
not involve herbicide use and mowing activities during construction. Operational maintenance herbicide
use and mowing at the project site would be conducted in accordance with Berkeley Department of
Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront policies and would be similar to existing practices.
While impacts to CBB remain less than significant in the absence of mitigation, in response to this
request by CDFW and in acknowledgement that there is low potential for CBB to occur, the following
mitigation measure requiring a habitat assessment and pre-construction surveys has been added to Draft
EIR Section 3.3 Biological Resources:
Section 3.3.4, page 3.3-55:

    Mitigation Measure BIO-1(f): Implement CDFW-Requested Measure for Crotch’s Bumble Bee
    Prior to Construction
    A formal habitat assessment of the project site landside project disturbance areas shall be
    performed by a qualified biologist prior to initiating ground disturbing activities to determine if
    suitable nesting or foraging habitat is present within the project site. The assessment shall include:
    • Review of occurrence record data
    • Analysis of foraging, nesting, and overwintering resources
    • Documentation of plant species observed (including what is blooming at the time of the survey and
      percent cover)

    The locations of nesting resources, including rodent burrows, cavities, thatched grasses, brush, rock
    piles, fallen logs, and manmade structures, shall be mapped during the assessment. Areas adjacent
    (within 50 feet) to the project site shall also be considered, if accessible, to determine if there is
    suitable nesting or foraging habitat.
    If suitable nesting and foraging resources are detected during the habitat assessment, they will be
    avoided by a minimum 50-foot buffer, where possible. If avoidance is not possible, protocol-surveys
    following the CDFW Survey Considerations for California Endangered Species Act (CESA) Candidate
    Bumble Bee Species (CDFW 2023) will be conducted to determine if Crotch’s bumble bee is present
    within the project site. A minimum of three visits will be conducted during the colony active season
    (April – August) and will be spaced 2-4 weeks apart. Surveys will be conducted each year that
    construction activities occur within suitable nesting habitat, because bumble bees move their nests
    each year. If no Crotch’s bumble bees are detected on the project site, no further mitigation actions
    will be required. If Crotch’s bumble bees are detected, consultation with CDFW will be initiated to
    determine the most appropriate strategy to avoid impacts to bumble bees on the project site. If full
    take avoidance is not feasible, the City will apply to CDFW for take authorization under an Incidental
    Take Permit.

    Crotch’s Bumble Bee
    Crotch’s bumble bee occupies open, dry habitats such as coastal scrub, grasslands, chaparral
    margins, and sparsely vegetated alluvial terraces that support abundant spring and early summer
    blooming plants. The species relies on diverse nectar and pollen resources. Nesting typically occurs
    in abandoned rodent burrows or concealed upland cavities with sufficient thatch or loose soil, while
    overwintering queens select undisturbed, well drained areas.
    Crotch’s bumble bee has only one known occurrence recorded within five miles of the project site.
    Suitable habitat on the project site is of low quality because most terrestrial areas of the project site
    are paved or landscaped with sparse floral resources for foraging. Although small mammal burrows
    on the project site may provide suitable nesting habitat and floral resources for foraging occur
    adjacent to the site, the highly developed character of the project site and associated anthropogenic
    disturbance reduce the availability and connectivity of habitat needed to support the species.
    Therefore, there is low potential for this species to occur within the project site.

Response to Comments A2-28 to A2-31
There is low potential for burrowing owl to occur at the project site, as described in Draft EIR Appendix C

Section 3.3.4, page 3.3-55 and 3.3-56:

    Mitigation Measure BIO-1(c): Conduct Burrowing Owl and Nesting Bird Survey and
    Avoidance Prior to Construction

    Burrowing Owl
    Prior to project construction, a qualified biologist will conduct a habitat assessment to determine if
    potential habitat for burrowing owl is present in or near the project site. If potential habitat is present
    in or within 500 feet of the project site, a qualified biologist will conduct a pre-construction survey of
    the project site (plus a 500-foot buffer as access allows) for the presence of burrowing owl. The
    survey will be conducted no more than 14 days prior to ground disturbing activities and will conform
    to CDFW guidelines for burrowing owl Take Avoidance Surveys as described in Appendix D of the
    2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation.100 A report of pre-construction survey efforts
    and results will be submitted to the City within 30 days of completion of the survey. The report will
    include the dates, times, weather conditions, and personnel involved in the survey. Depending on
    survey results, the report will also include observations of burrowing owl or potential burrows, and the
    location and habitat description of the observations. If burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign
    (i.e., tracks or pellets) are not observed in the project site, no additional measures related to impact
    avoidance and minimization of the absent species are recommended. If burrowing owl, active
    burrows, or their sign are observed within the project site, CDFW will be notified and the following
    measures will be implemented:
    • A qualified biological monitor will be present during landside construction on the project site to
      document burrowing owl observations, burrow statuses, and require that construction activities do
      not negatively affect burrowing owl. The duration and frequency of monitoring will be determined
      at the discretion of the qualified biologist and a monitoring report detailing monitoring results will
      be submitted to the City within 30 days of the completion of project activities or breeding season
      (February 1 to August 31), if applicable.
    • The biological monitor will visually inspect any pipes, debris piles, culverts, or similar structures for
      burrowing owl before the material is moved, buried, or capped. Open holes and trenches within the
      project site will be inspected at the beginning and end of each landside construction workday and
      immediately prior to backfilling. At the end of each such workday, trenches and holes will be
      ramped so that any animals that may have become trapped in the trench or hole can climb out.
      The ramp may be constructed of dirt fill or wood planking or other suitable material at an angle no
      greater than 30-45 degrees. If a burrowing owl is trapped in a trench or hole, work will stop and the
      qualified biologist will be notified immediately. The burrowing owl will be allowed to escape
      unimpeded.
    • If active burrows are observed on the project site, a non-disturbance buffer will be established
      restricting all ground-disturbing activities from occurring within the buffer and a qualified
      biological monitor will be present at the initiation of project activities. The buffer will be
      established by a qualified biologist and range from 330 ft. to 1,500 ft. depending on project
      activity, line of sight, and local topography during the breeding season. During the non-breeding
      season (September 1 to January 31), the buffer will range from 165 ft. to 330 ft. The buffer will be
      demarcated using brightly colored flagging and may only be reduced at the discretion of a
      qualified biologist based on the factors listed above and potential use of sound and visual barriers
      (i.e., hay bales). Removal of the buffer will only occur if a qualified biologist determines burrowing
      owl are not present in the vicinity and any potential burrows are inactive.
    • If active burrow avoidance is infeasible during the non-breeding season or during the breeding
      season, where resident owls have not yet begun egg laying or incubation, or where the juveniles
      are foraging independently and capable of independent survival, the City in coordination with a
      qualified biologist will consult with CDFW to prepare, authorize, and implement a passive

                                             Page 202 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                      Response to Comments

           relocation program consistent with Appendix E of the 2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl
           Mitigation.
    • A habitat mitigation plan will be developed in coordination with the City and CDFW for loss of
      active burrowing owl burrow sites if implementation of a passive relocation plan is necessary
      and/or burrowing owl are documented to nest on site or within 500 feet of the project site. This
      would be based upon the portion of the project site that overlaps with the primary foraging area
      around the burrow site (approximately 500-foot buffer) to be replaced at a minimum 1:1 ratio.

    Nesting Birds
    Project construction activities, including but not limited to vegetation removal and ground
    disturbance that result in noise or disturbance affecting potential nesting bird habitat, should
    commence outside of the nesting season (February 1 through September 15), if feasible. If
    construction begins outside the nesting season, a nesting bird survey is not required.
    If ground disturbing project activities begin within the nesting season (February 1 through August 31
    September 15), then no more than seven days prior to the initiation of project activities, a nesting bird
    pre-construction survey shall be conducted by a City-approved qualified biologist within the
    disturbance footprint, plus a 300-foot buffer for passerines and a 1,000-foot buffer for raptors. During
    construction within the nesting season, an additional focused survey shall be conducted prior to tree
    removal to identify active nests with the subject tree(s). If no active nests are observed, no further
    action would be required. Ground-disturbing project activities that are initiated outside of the nesting
    season may continue into the nesting season without requiring new nesting bird surveys.
    Pre-construction nesting bird surveys shall be conducted by a qualified biologist during the time of
    day when birds are most active and should be of sufficient duration to reliably conclude presence or
    absence of nesting birds on the project site and within the designated buffer. A report of the nesting
    bird surveys results shall be submitted to the City for review and approval prior to clearance for
    mobilizing equipment. If nests are found, their locations shall be flagged (if possible) and recorded
    with the use of a GPS unit. Avoidance buffers shall be established around active nests. Depending
    upon the species, suitable minimum buffers may be 50 feet for non-raptor species and 300 feet for
    raptor species, or as determined by the qualified biologist in consultation with CDFW based on
    species sensitivity, construction activities, and other factors.
    If active nests are present, all project work shall be conducted outside the established avoidance
    buffer zone from the nest until it is no longer active. No staging of large equipment shall occur within
    the avoidance buffer until the qualified biologist confirms that breeding/nesting is complete and all
    the young have fledged. If buffer zones are determined to be infeasible, a City-approved qualified
    biological monitor shall be on site to monitor project activities within the avoidance buffer zones to
    ensure active nests and nesting birds are not impacted. Nesting bird surveys are not required for
    project activities that occur between September 16 and January 31. A report of all survey results and
    any proposed avoidance buffers shall be submitted to the City for review and approval.
    This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
    agencies.

    Burrowing Owl
    Burrowing owl occupy open, dry habitats such as grasslands, coastal dunes, salt marsh edges, and
    sparsely vegetated disturbed sites that support abundant small mammal and insect prey. The
    species relies on a mix of invertebrates and small vertebrates for foraging, with peak activity at dawn
    and dusk. Nesting and roosting typically occur in underground burrows—often those excavated by
    ground squirrels, pocket gophers, or other fossorial mammals—or in artificial burrows and cavities
    with loose soil for excavation, while nonbreeding individuals favor undisturbed, low‑vegetation areas
    for shelter and foraging.
    Although one occurrence has been documented within five miles of the project site and burrowing
    owls are known to overwinter at César Chávez Park, the project site itself does not provide the habitat
    conditions required for overwintering. The site lacks open, low-stature annual grassland and
    protected foraging areas with sufficient insect prey, which are essential for sustaining overwintering
    individuals.
    Adjacent areas, including fragmented grasslands in Shorebird Park and along University Avenue,
    contain limited open space but do not provide suitable overwintering habitat. While some ground
    squirrel burrows are present, these grassland areas are routinely mowed for park use and subject to
    heavy recreational use and frequent human disturbance, which reduces prey availability and limits
    habitat suitability. In addition, the grassland areas along University Avenue are narrow and linear, lack
    refuge from disturbance due to regular trail use, recreation, and the presence of dogs, and are
    exposed to numerous tall perching structures that support hawks and other avian predators.
    A migrating or displaced individual could briefly land on the project site or within nearby areas during
    movement; therefore, this species has a low potential to occur.

Section 3.3.2, page 3.3-19:

    Least Tern
    California least tern is a small tern with a distinctive black-capped head and is federally endangered,
    State endangered, and a State fully protected species. This species nests along the California coast
    and breeds colonially on bare or sparsely vegetated areas.62 The California least tern nests during
    summer from Baja California north to the San Francisco Bay. Least terns are migratory and spend
    winter months in coastal areas of Mexico and Central America. Least terns forage primarily on
    silversides (e.g., topsmelt), northern anchovies, Pacific herring, and surfperches.63 This species nests
    in colonies on bare or sparsely vegetated flat substrates, including beaches, alkali flats, or paved
    areas.
    California least terns have a low potential to forage over open water within and adjacent to the
    project site. This species has no potential to nest within the project site despite the presence of bare
    or sparsely vegetated areas due to the heavy recreational use and disturbed nature of the project site.
    62.

    https://www.allaboutbirds.org/. Accessed June 2026.
    63.
       Burton and Terrill. 2012. Least Tern Literature Review and Study Plan Development prepared for
    U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
    https://www.spn.usace.army.mil/Portals/68/docs/Dredging/LMTS/S%20and%20S/11%20-
    %20Least%20Tern%20Lit%20Rev%20Study%20Plan%20Report%20Final.pdf (accessed September

SUBJECT: Comments on the Draft Environmental Impact Report for the Berkeley Water

Dear Liza:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIR) for              A3-2
the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project (project).

The San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC) is providing the
following comments as a responsible agency under the California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) with discretionary approval power over aspects of the project within BCDC’s jurisdiction,
as described below. BCDC will rely on the Final EIR when considering the permit application for
the project, and we appreciate this opportunity to comment on the information and analyses                A3-3
presented in the DEIR. The Commission itself has not reviewed the DEIR; the following
comments are based on BCDC staff review of the DEIR, considered in relation to BCDC’s
governing authorities under the McAteer-Petris Act (Title 7.2 of the California Government
Code), and the San Francisco Bay Plan (Bay Plan).

San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission
BCDC is a State planning and regulatory agency with permitting authority over San Francisco
Bay, the Bay shoreline, and Suisun Marsh, as established in the McAteer-Petris Act and the
Suisun Marsh Preservation Act, respectively. Per the McAteer-Petris Act, BCDC is responsible for
granting or denying permits for any proposed fill; extraction of materials; or substantial changes        A3-4
in use of any water, land, or structure within the Commission’s jurisdiction (Government Code
Section 66632). Additionally, BCDC establishes land use policies for the Bay as a resource and
for development of the Bay and shoreline in the Bay Plan, which policies provide the basis for
the Commission’s review and actions on proposed projects.

Project Description
Based on the DEIR, the majority of the project would be located within at least two areas of                  A3-5
BCDC’s permitting jurisdiction:

                                       Page 209 of 1541
Liza McNu lt y, Cit y of Berkeley                                                         Page 2
Berkeley W at er T ransp ort at io n Pier F erry Pro j ect DEI R Comment s         April 28, 20 26




   •   In the San Francisco Bay, being all areas subject to tidal action, including the marshlands
       lying between mean high tide and five feet above mean sea level; tidelands (land lying
       between mean high tide and mean low tide); and submerged lands (Government Code
       Section 66610(a)). Areas of Bay jurisdiction include any filled areas where filling               A3-5
       commenced after September 17, 1965.

   •   In the shoreline band, consisting of all territory located between the shoreline of the
       Bay, as defined above, and 100 feet landward of and parallel with the shoreline
       (Government Code Section 66610(b)).

In addition, portions of the project are located within Bay Plan-designated “Waterfront Park,
Beach” priority use areas. Within the Commission’s jurisdiction, projects proposed within these          A3-6
priority use areas must be consistent with the Bay Plan’s Recreation policies and any relevant
policies specified in Bay Plan Map 4 (which is inclusive of the area where the project is
proposed).

BCDC requests that the City of Berkeley include mapping of BCDC’s jurisdiction in the Final EIR          A3-7
and pay particular attention to potential project impacts that may occur in these areas as they
relate to the Commission’s policies. The Final EIR project description should also clearly detail        A3-8
where each component of the project would take place relative to the Commission’s
jurisdiction. BCDC staff is available to review any mapping or draft language to ensure that our
agency’s jurisdiction is accurately depicted and described. BCDC provides data and mapping
tools on our website at https://www.bcdc.ca.gov/resources/maps-and-data/. Copies of our
planning documents are available at https://www.bcdc.ca.gov/resources/plans/. BCDC’s laws                A3-9
and regulations can be referenced at https://www.bcdc.ca.gov/resources/laws-and-
regulations/.

Our understanding is that project areas in the Bay jurisdiction include the proposed pier and
breakwater, ferry vessel infrastructure, dredging, and Seawall Drive Parking Lot. Project areas in
                                                                                                         A3-10
the shoreline band jurisdiction include the plaza, the proposed public restroom, Seawall Drive,
the Bay Trail extension at Seawall Drive, and a small section of University Avenue as it connects
with the plaza, encompassing portions of the proposed expanded AC Transit bus stop facilities,
new cycle track, and University Avenue roadway improvements.

BCDC staff recently reached an agreement with the City of Berkeley regarding the depiction of
BCDC jurisdiction at the project site. This depiction can be found in the project exhibits for the       A3-11
May 11, 2026, BCDC Design Review Board meeting, which are posted on BCDC’s website and
can be requested from staff.

       structure;

       throughout the project site;

       throughout the project site;

Environmental Analyses
Below are BCDC staff’s remaining questions and comments on the DEIR, organized by
environmental topic. Language from CEQA Appendix G: Environmental Checklist Form has been
included for reference. Addressing these questions and comments in the Final EIR and                    A3-13
addressing any related impacts with mitigation measures will support staff in efficiently and
expeditiously developing relevant conditions and necessary findings to include in the permit
application staff recommendation when the project comes before BCDC for consideration.

AESTHETICS
Would the project: c) In non-urbanized areas, substantially degrade the existing visual character
or quality of public views of the site and its surroundings? (Public views are those that are           A3-14
experienced from a publicly accessible vantage point). If the proposed project is in an urbanized
area, would the plan conflict with applicable zoning and other regulations governing scenic
quality?
                                                                                                •
                                                                                           11,      2-107
                                        Page 212 of 1541
Liza McNu lt y, Cit y of Berkeley                                                           Page 5
Berkeley W at er T ransp ort at io n Pier F erry Pro j ect DEI R Comment s           April 28, 20 26




Impact AES-3 discusses the potential impact of the solar canopy at the Seawall Drive Parking Lot
on visual character and the quality of public views. On page 3.1-32, the DEIR states, “The solar
shade structures introduce new linear elements and repetitive architectural forms, replacing
previously organic shapes and softened skyline with geometric forms and engineered materials.
The proposed redevelopment of this area introduces more distinct built elements that would
contrast with the existing naturalized features,” and concludes that the impact would be less
than significant because “while the proposed project would result in visual changes to this area,
the proposed updates to the Seawall Drive parking lot would be compatible with existing uses,
would enhance the site’s functionality while incorporating clean energy solutions, and would be                 A3-14
designed and implemented in adherence to the City’s goals, policies, and development review
criteria related to the maintenance and enhancement of visual character, while also aligning
with the City’s renewable energy goals.” This significance finding reads more like a statement of
overriding considerations than a finding of the degree to which an impact could occur. Please
revisit this conclusion and instead provide a more detailed explanation of how the project
would be designed and implemented in adherence to the applicable zoning and other
regulations regarding scenic quality, including BCDC’s policies regarding visual resources. Note
that as part of the significance finding, other considerations such as clean energy solutions
(while desirable) may not be relevant.

BIOLOGICAL RESOURCES
For the Regulatory Framework in Section 3.1.3, please note that in addition to the McAteer-
Petris Act, the Bay Plan includes policies regarding native and special-status species and                      A3-15
habitats. Please review the policies in the Bay Plan sections pertaining to Fish, Other Aquatic
Organisms and Wildlife; Subtidal Areas; and Mitigation, and ensure that the EIR appropriately
considers any relevant policies.

Would the project: a) Have a substantial adverse effect, either directly or through habitat
modifications, on any native or species identified as a candidate, sensitive, or special status
species in local or regional plans, policies, or regulations, or by the California Department of Fish
and Game, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, or NOAA’s National Marine Fisheries Service?
                                                                                                            A3-16
   1. Page 3.3-41 identifies the California least tern (Sternula antillarum browni) as a “species
      mentioned in public comments that are not expected to occur within the project site,
      nest, in the vicinity, or to be affected by the project.” According to page C-10 of the DEIR
      Appendices, there are no known occurrences of California least tern “within five miles,
      suitable colonial breeding sites are not present, and the project site is largely developed
      and disturbed by recreational use.” BCDC staff is aware of dredging restrictions from
      U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife that                A3-17
      prohibit dredging from the Berkeley Waterfront to San Leandro Bay to protect foraging
      California least tern during their breeding season. Please provide the reference data to
      substantiate the finding that California least tern are not expected to be impacted by                A3-18
      project activities.



                                                                                            11,         2-108
                                       Page 213 of 1541
Liza McNu lt y, Cit y of Berkeley                                                         Page 6
Berkeley W at er T ransp ort at io n Pier F erry Pro j ect DEI R Comment s         April 28, 20 26




   2. The Subtidal Nearshore Marine subsection on page 3.3-10 calls out benthic organisms
      associated with soft-sediment habitat. However, the habitat types for subtidal areas are
      not delineated or mapped in the DEIR as terrestrial habitats are. Therefore, the impacts            A3-19
      of the project on the marine and estuarine environment and associated organisms
      cannot be adequately assessed. Please map the distribution of specific habitat types in
      the submarine environment to effectively evaluate the potential for environmental
      impacts.

   3. Ferry operations have the potential to change flow dynamics within the water column,
      which may alter sediment deposition and erosion patterns and impact marine life,                    A3-20
      including fish, seabirds, and waterfowl. Please include an analysis of how the project
      may affect flow dynamics and evaluate associated environmental impacts. As requested
      above, the delineation of aquatic habitats and their tolerance levels to currents and
      turbulence is essential to understanding the actual expected resilience of biological               A3-21
      resources to the increased hydrological disturbance from both the introduced energy of
      ferry operations and dredging.

   4. The DEIR defines Oceanic Conditions on page 3.3-8 to include “parameters such as
      salinity, temperature, depth, turbidity, tidal range, and current velocity, as well as
      circulation patterns, wave energy, and sediment dynamics.” However, the subsequent                  A3-22
      sections are missing a discussion of salinity, turbidity, tidal range, current velocity,
      circulation patterns, wave energy, and sediment dynamics. Please include these
      parameters in the evaluation of marine and estuarine conditions.

   5. The DEIR does not appear to address operational light impacts on native and special
      status species and habitats from new lighting proposed at the Seawall Drive Parking Lot,
      on the pier, breakwater, gangways, and floats, and at the public plaza. Please include a            A3-23
      discussion of the potential for operational impacts of new lighting on biological
      resources as a result of the project.

Would the project: c) Have a substantial adverse effect on State or federally protected wetlands
(including but not limited to marsh, vernal pool, coastal, etc.) through direct removal, filling,
hydrological interruption, or other means?

   1. In permitting this project, BCDC may require compensatory mitigation for adverse
      environmental impacts associated with new Bay fill. The DEIR anticipates this with
      Mitigation Measure BIO-3: Provide Compensatory Mitigation for Loss of Jurisdictional
      Waters Prior to Operation, which requires the removal of additional portions of the                     A3-24
      existing pier as compensatory mitigation for new fill. On page 3.3-61, mitigation for fill is
      proposed to be provided at a minimum of 1:1 ratio and to occur prior to or concurrently
      with construction, as approved by regulatory agencies. The DEIR notes that the City
      plans to develop a mitigation plan detailing the required additional demolition, which
      may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory

                                                                                                              A3-24
       agencies. To the extent possible, please demonstrate the feasibility of fill removal for
                                                                                                      +-
       compensatory mitigation and evaluate potential environmental impacts anticipated with
       this method of compensatory mitigation in this EIR. The details provided should be                     A3-25
       sufficient to weigh the additional impacts to species and water quality against the
       benefit of fill removal. (Reference 14 CCR § 15126.4(a)(1)(D) [an EIR should discuss any
       adverse environmental impacts of a mitigation measure].)

   2. Page 2-28 indicates that the project proposes to dredge a 100-foot-wide, federally
      authorized U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) channel adjacent to the dilapidated
      pier and the turning basin to allow ferry vessels to turn and dock at the two boarding                  A3-26
      floats. It is important to note that this channel is not included in the USACE’s dredging
      program. The USACE has not dredged this channel in the past 25 years (or more), and
      dredging in this area would be considered new work dredging. Please include
      information regarding the new work and maintenance dredging volume and proposed                      A3-27
      frequency, as well as information on plans for proposed beneficial reuse or disposal. Per
      BCDC’s Bay Plan policies pertaining to Fish, Other Aquatic Organisms, and Wildlife;
      Subtidal Areas; Mitigation; and Dredging, dredging should be the minimum necessary
      for the project, and adverse impacts should be avoided and minimized. When impacts
      cannot be avoided, mitigation may be required. Please provide an analysis of the                     A3-28
      impacts to habitat and species from the expansion of the dredge footprint. Please also
      include avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures to address both the new
      work and maintenance dredging proposed by the project.

GEOLOGY AND SOILS
Would the project: a) Directly or indirectly cause potential substantial adverse effects, including
the risk of loss, injury, or death involving: iii) seismic-related ground failure, including
liquefaction or landslides?
                                                                                                           A3-29
As stated on page 2.5-28, “project construction would be required to comply with the American
Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) Seismic Design of Piers and Wharves (61-14) guidelines.” We
recognize that the updated ASCE 61-26 has not yet been adopted; however, this code update is
out for review, and its adoption is anticipated to occur this year. Please update the discussion in
this section to include the 2026 code changes and evaluate the project design against the
updated ASCE 61-26 guidelines.

Would the project: b) Result in substantial soil erosion or the loss of topsoil?

Page 3.5-31 states: “In addition, the shoreline around the project site is made of armored rip
rap; therefore, there is no soil that could be eroded.” BCDC staff believe that this conclusion          A3-30
may be oversimplified, especially in light of the project proposing shoreline repair along "a
stretch of the shoreline that is actively eroding" (page 2-22). Please a) provide more detail
justifying this statement or providing context on shoreline change over time at the project site,
and b) consider the impact of riprap placement on erosion rates in the surrounding areas, as

Would the project: c) Be located on a geologic unit or soil that is unstable, or that would become
unstable as a result of the project, and potentially result in on- or off-site landslide, lateral
spreading, subsidence, liquefaction, or collapse?
                                                                                                          A3-31
   1. Page 3.5-30 states that the groundwater table elevation at the project site is 5
      feet. Please provide a datum for this height and confirm that all other elevations have an
      associated datum.

   2. The potential for groundwater rise over the 50-year project life is not accounted for in
                                                                                                          A3-32
      the analysis. Please include and reassess the project area’s potential to experience
      liquefaction over the project’s estimated lifetime.

   3. Page 3.5-30 states: “Implementation of geotechnical recommendations, such as the use
      of deep soil mix, retaining wall recommendations, and continued geotechnical engineer
      oversight would reduce potential impacts related to liquefaction and lateral spreading.”            A3-33
      Please discuss the overall suitability of the underlying geologic unit/soils for the project,
      disclose the potential for failure as a result of seismic activity or ground failure, and
      describe how the mitigation measures above will avoid or mitigate such failure.

HAZARDS AND HAZARDOUS MATERIALS
Would the project: a) Create a significant hazard to the public or the environment through the
routine transport, use, or disposal of hazardous materials? or b) Create a significant hazard to
the public or the environment through reasonably foreseeable upset and accident conditions
involving the release of hazardous materials into the environment?

Impact HAZ-1 acknowledges that the pier pilings for the existing pier may have been treated
                                                                                                          A3-34
with chemicals that have the potential to lead to toxicity in the surrounding water and
sediment. On page 3.7-28, the DEIR concludes that impacts related to the disturbance of the
piles would be less than significant due to California Health and Safety Code and California Code
of Regulations requirements regarding Treated Wood Waste (TWW). However, it is not clear
whether the measures required by the code are to be implemented by default, or whether they
would only be implemented if the pier pilings are confirmed to be treated wood and, if so, how
that confirmation would be made. Please include a description of whether and when testing
would occur to confirm the composition of the piles and what would trigger implementation of
the TWW requirements. Please also ensure that the discussion in this section is consistent with           A3-35
the discussion of pile removal in the Hydrology and Water Quality section and vice versa (page
3.8-30). If necessary, please include a mitigation measure that includes an assessment of the             A3-36
pilings that could trigger the State code requirements.

HYDROLOGY AND WATER QUALITY
For the Regulatory Framework in Section 3.8.3, please note that BCDC’s governing legislation
has the status of State law, and the Bay Plan is effectively comprised of State regulations
                                                                                                       A3-37
subject to approval by the California Office of Administrative Law. While both BCDC’s laws and
policies have a regional focus, in terms of their legal effect, they are not regional or local
regulations. Additionally, please note that there are a number of Bay Plan policies that are
relevant to the Hydrology and Water Quality analysis, including those in the Water Surface Area
and Volume, Subtidal Areas, Climate Change, Shoreline Protection, and Dredging. Please review          A3-38
these sections of the Bay Plan and ensure the relevant policies are considered appropriately.

Would the project: a) Violate any water quality standards or waste discharge requirements or
otherwise substantially degrade surface or ground water quality?
                                                                                                       A3-39
   1. The project would result in a significant increase in vessel traffic within the turning
      basin. The area just outside of the turning basin is impaired for multiple pollutants,
      including PCBs. Please include an analysis of the impacts to water quality from increased
      traffic and provide BMPs that will be deployed to prevent further impairment. Please
      also consider potential impacts from increased traffic with respect to the possibility of        A3-40
      propeller wash causing scouring in the area and making the channel deeper.

   2. Proposed new amenities at the new pier include a fish cleaning station located at the
      western terminus of the pier. Please identify potential impacts to water quality related
      to the fish cleaning station and identify mitigation measures as appropriate to ensure
      water quality protection. Please clarify if the intent is for fish cleaning waste to be          A3-41
      disposed of in trash cans, thrown into the Bay, or disposed of by another means. Please
      indicate if/how instructional signage would be included to provide direction on the
      necessary waste disposal practices.

   3. Mitigation Measure HYD-1: Include and Implement Additional Best Management
      Practices in the SWPPP Prior to and During Pier Demolition, as described on page 3.8-34,
      requires that, prior to construction, the construction contractor shall prepare a
      Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) and implement the SWPPP during
      construction. The SWPPP shall be submitted to the Berkeley Public Works Department
      and the State Water Resources Control Board (via the Stormwater Multiple Application            A3-42
      and Report Tracking System [SMARTS]) for review and approval at least 60 days prior to
      start of construction. Page 3.3-46 references Section 3.8, indicating that the project will
      comply with the SWPPP and maintain appropriate turbidity levels using best
      management practices (BMPs). Please indicate specific BMPs that would be used to
      reduce turbidity for this project and state the turbidity limits to be used as triggers
      for additional actions.

   4. As described on page 3.8-35, “the landside portion of the site is already predominantly         A3-43
      covered by impervious surfaces, and the proposed project would result in a net


                                                                                                    2-112

                                                                                                     ◄
          decrease of approximately 32,000 square feet of impervious area through the inclusion
          of permeable paving, bioretention facilities, and other LID features. These measures
          would enhance localized infiltration opportunities compared to existing conditions and          A3-43
          would not reduce the capacity for groundwater recharge.” The proposed use of pervious
          pavement may not be appropriate, as the site is situated atop Bay fill. Please include a

Would the project: c) Substantially alter the existing drainage pattern of the site or area,
including through the alteration of the course of a stream or river or through the addition of
impervious surfaces, in a manner which would:

   i.        result in substantial erosion or siltation on- or off-site;
   ii.       substantially increase the rate or amount of surface runoff in a manner which would
             result in flooding on- or off-site;
   iii.      create or contribute runoff water which would exceed the capacity of existing or
             planned stormwater drainage systems or provide substantial additional sources of
             polluted runoff; or
   iv.       impede or redirect flood flows?
                                                                                                         A3-44
   1. The DEIR primarily uses the medium risk level projections for sea level rise and provides
      little in the risk assessment for the end-of-century or medium-high level
      projections. Chapter 2.5.1 states that, “the project design takes into account projected
      sea level rise.” This sentence is not enough to adequately describe the sea level rise
      adaptation measures that the project is incorporating. Please expand this and
      specifically look at the end-of-century risks. Note that as part of the BCDC permit
      application for the project, the project proponents are expected to provide a sea level
      rise risk assessment prepared by a qualified engineer, per Bay Plan Climate Change
      Policy No. 2. The risk assessment will be expected to include mid- and end-of-century
      scenarios at the medium-high risk level, with the high emissions assumption, using the
      NAVD 88 datum.

   2. The datums referenced in the DEIR alternate between NAVD88 and the City of Berkeley
      Mean Lower-low Water (MLLW). Please include all elevations with both datums, for                   A3-45
      example: X feet NAVD88 (X feet MLLW). A table relating these two datums for key
      identified elevations would also be useful.

   5. The water elevations presented on page 3.8-7 appear to have confused some of the tidal
      elevations. The Highest Astronomical Tide (HAT) is noted to be +10.3 feet MLLW;
                                                                                                         A3-46
      however, HAT at this site is +8.4 feet MLLW, and +10.3 feet MLLW is the Extreme Water
      Level. A table with various tidal levels, that uses both NAVD88 and MLLW, could help
      reduce confusion.

Would the Project: c) Substantially increase hazards due to a geometric design feature (e.g.,
sharp curves or dangerous intersections) or incompatible use (e.g., farm equipment)?
                                                                                                         A3-60
Impact TRA-3 assesses whether the proposed project would substantially increase hazards due
to a geometric design feature or incompatible use. However, the analysis itself is light on details
and is too high-level and vague, particularly regarding University Avenue and Seawall Drive
(page 3.12-22). As part of the pre-application review of this project, BCDC staff has seen a
potential for user conflicts with the introduction of the new ferry infrastructure and parking
program at the waterfront. The project will include a new parking lot configuration at the              A3-61
Seawall Drive Parking Lot, new expectations for parking for ferry customers, and new circulation
patterns and behaviors associated with commuting, which differ from those associated with
recreation. This impact cannot adequately be assessed without mapping projected circulation
routes for different user groups under different scenarios (peak hour commute times on
weekdays and peak recreation times on weekends) to identify where conflicts could potentially
occur. Similarly, with more details on the types and locations of potential conflicts, the analysis     A3-62
should also provide more details on the impact reduction measures to be implemented and
how they specifically address particular potential safety concerns. Otherwise, it cannot be
concluded that these measures (such as crosswalks, wayfinding, etc.) will have the desired
effect of reducing the impact.

ALTERNATIVES ANALYSIS
During the May 12, 2025, BCDC Design Review Board briefing on the project, a number of
concerns were raised by members of the public that siting the ferry terminal in the proposed            A3-63
location would have a detrimental effect on water recreation such as swimming and board
sailing that could lead to impacts on other water access points regionally as individuals who
currently use the Berkeley Marina are displaced. In BCDC’s May 21, 2025 comment letter on the
Notice of Preparation (NOP), BCDC requested that at least one of the alternatives presented in          A3-64
the EIR’s alternatives analysis allows for the evaluation of an alternate location for the ferry
terminal on the waterfront, and evaluate whether an alternate location could reduce potential
impacts related to recreation, ferry wake, dredging, and impacts on biological resources, etc.

Section 5.9: Alternatives Considered but Rejected indicates that the City considered but
ultimately rejected several alternatives previously studied as part of a Draft EIS/EIR from 2008,
including alternatives that sited the ferry terminal in alternate locations on the waterfront.           A3-65
Based on that study, the DEIR rejected the three alternative locations within the City of
Berkeley. However, the discussion supporting the rejection of the alternative sites was not
adequately detailed, and did not consider different versions of the project at those locations
that could reasonably achieve the project objectives or avoid environmental impacts. For
example for the Berkeley Marina Basin location, the DEIR states that the alternative would not
meet project objectives to enhance public access and recreational opportunities or provide              A3-66
efficient and environmentally friendly public ferry service, but does not adequately explain why
it would not. It does not answer the question of what would prevent a project located at that

    Project Site
    The project site has a Berkeley General Plan land use designation of Waterfront/Marina.1 The General
    Plan describes the Waterfront/Marina as areas intended to maintain and preserve areas of Berkeley
    adjacent to the Bay for open space, recreational uses, waterfront-related commercial and visitor
    services, boating, and water transit facilities. The project site has a zoning designation of
    Unclassified (U). Development within Unclassified areas requires a Use Permit in compliance with
    Berkeley Municipal Code Section 23.208.020, which governs Use Permits in Unclassified zones. The
    project site is subject to the Berkeley Marina Use Permit (Permit No. 5567), issued in 1965, which
    authorizes existing uses and permits implementation of the Marina Master Plan. This permit governs

Response to Comment A3-14
The first discussion paragraph under Impact AES-3 of the Draft EIR refers to a number of specific policies
and regulations implemented by the Berkeley General Plan, Berkeley Marina Master Plan, Berkeley
Municipal Code, and the San Francisco Bay Plan pertaining to visual resources and scenic quality.
To respond to this comment, the following clarifying text in underline has been added under Impact AES-
3, Seawall Drive, first full paragraph on page 3.1-32:
    As shown in Figure 3.1-7, the existing shoreline is characterized by natural elements; specifically, the
    mature tree canopy provides a soft, variable tree line which largely dominates the view as it contrasts
    against the sky. The proposed solar panels over the parking area present a distinct, solid horizontal
    line against the sky that is generally only visible from KVP 4; all other viewpoints discussed herein
    lack prominent views of the proposed solar panels due to their location and angle of view. Distant
    structures and development across the Bay are vaguely visible through the series of vertical lines
    created by the solar support columns. The solar shade structures introduce new linear elements and
    repetitive architectural forms, replacing previously organic shapes and softened skyline with
    geometric forms and engineered materials. The proposed redevelopment of this area introduces
    more distinct built elements that would contrast with the existing naturalized features. While the
    proposed project would result in visual changes to this area, the proposed updates to the Seawall
    Drive parking lot would be compatible with existing uses, would enhance the site’s functionality while
    incorporating clean energy solutions, and would be designed and implemented in adherence to the
    BCDC Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces10 and the City’s goals, policies, and
    development review criteria related to the maintenance and enhancement of visual character, while
    also aligning with the City’s renewable energy goals. For these reasons, impacts would be less than
    significant.
    10.
       San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC). 2005. Public Access
    Design Guidelines for the San Francisco Bay: Shoreline Spaces. https://www.bcdc.ca.gov/wp-
    content/uploads/sites/354/2023/09/Public-Access-Design-Guidelines-Shoreline-Spaces-PDF.pdf
    (accessed July 2026).

Environmental impacts associated with visual character or quality of public views are addressed in
Impact AES-1, pages 3.1-28 through 3.1-38, and compliance with local regulations governing scenic
quality are evaluated in Impact LU-2, page 3.9-12, in Table 3.9-1, page 3.9-19 and 3.19-20, of the Draft EIR.
In particular, BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan Consistency is identified in Table 3.9-1. Such analyses are
based on the assumptions described therein, and mitigation measures are identified as appropriate.
Accordingly, the analysis of visual character, scenic quality, and compliance with local regulations
governing scenic quality is adequate and consistent with CEQA Guidelines. The analysis and conclusions
presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no further revisions to the EIR are necessary
beyond the clarifying text included above.

Response to Comment A3-22
Project site oceanographic characteristics related to temperature, sediment dynamics, depth, current
velocities, circulation patterns, and tidal range are discussed in the Draft EIR Section 3.8.2, Environmental
Setting, pages 3.8-4 to 3.8-7. Refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for a
discussion of wave dynamics and energy and further discussion regarding sedimentation. In response to
this comment, text additions of project site oceanographic characteristics related to salinity and turbidity
have been added to Draft EIR Section 3.3.2 Environmental Setting, page 3.3-8, as follows:
Section 3.3.2, page 3.3-8:
    Water temperature in San Francisco Bay ranges from 53 °F to 60 °F. According to 2022 U.S.
    Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) Waterbody Reports, water quality in the San Francisco Bay
    Estuaries watershed is considered a CWA Section 303d impaired waterbody. Salinity in the vicinity of
    the project site is estuarine and seasonally variable, influenced by tidal exchange and freshwater
    inflow from the Delta, and typically ranges between 10 to 20 ppt.38 Ambient levels of turbidity in the
    San Francisco Bay are naturally elevated and highly variable due to tides, wind, and vessel traffic;
    resuspension of fine bay mud is common. Water quality is monitored for physical, chemical, and
    biological factors. The assessment of the water quality is analyzed against USEPA-approved water
    standards or thresholds, and water quality can either be categorized as good or impaired. The water
    quality parameters evaluated along the San Francisco Bay shoreline included dioxins, mercury,
    polychlorinated biphenyls, pesticides, foreign plants and/or animals, and trash. Bathymetric data
    indicates maximum depth within the project site at the end of the pier is approximately ten feet at
    mean lower low water (MLLW), and less than five feet at MLLW within the South Sailing Basin
    (Figure 3.3 2).
    38.
       Schraga, T., and Cloern, J.E. 2017. Water quality measurements in San Francisco Bay by the U.S.
    Geological Survey, 1969–2015: Scientific Data, v. 4, Article 170098: 14 p.,
    https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2017.98 (accessed July 2026).

Response to Comment A3-24
Refer to Response to Comment A3-25 regarding CEQA requirements compared to permitting process. In

Response to Comment A3-25
The Draft EIR discusses the impacts of pile installation and removal in Section 3.3.4, Impacts Analysis, on
pages 3.3-45 through 3.3-51. Impacts due to pile removal for mitigation would be the same as impacts of
pile removal during construction of the pier itself, as discussed on page 3.3-61 and 3.3-62. At this stage
of project design, the precise location and quantity of fill‑removal mitigation cannot be fully defined
because it is subject to subsequent regulatory agency reviews. Consistent with CEQA Guidelines
§15126.4(a)(1)(B), when specific design‑level details are not yet available, the specific details of a
mitigation measure may be developed after project approval so long as the lead agency establishes clear
performance standards ensuring that the mitigation will be effective once final design information
becomes available. The 1:1 replacement ratio described in the Draft EIR is a minimum baseline
commitment to no net loss of jurisdictional waters by the lead agency, City of Berkeley, under CEQA, and
is not a fixed or final future permitting‑stage outcome. The actual mitigation ratio and specifics of exact
piles to be removed will be determined during agency permitting based on the final design and regulatory
agency review.
The analysis presented in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impacts BIO-1 and BIO-3, (pages 3.3-45 through
3.3-51 and 3.3-60 through 3.3-61, respectively) concludes that impacts to special-status aquatic species
regarding project cover area would be less-than-significant-with-mitigation (refer to Mitigation Measures
BIO-1[a], BIO-1[d], BIO-1[e], BIO-3, and HYD-1), and thus adequate under CEQA. No changes to the Draft
EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comments A3-26 and A3-27
Refer to Section 2.2.15, Topical Response: Maintenance Dredging, which provides clarification that the
dredging identified in the Draft EIR is new work dredging, as well as a discussion about future dredging
for maintenance of the dredged channel.
The Draft EIR includes information about the construction dredging volumes and plans for dredged
material disposal or beneficial reuse. Section 2.6.1, Construction Activities and Equipment (subsection
Dredging and Debris Disposal), on page 2-28 of the Draft EIR describes the extent and volume of dredging
required for the proposed project (up to approximately 400,000 cubic yards). As clarified in Section
2.2.15, Topical Response: Maintenance Dredging, the City is proposing a one-time dredging event.
Regarding plans for dredged material disposal or beneficial reuse, page 2-28 of the Draft EIR provides a

Response to Comment A3-29
The comment’s concern regarding evolving seismic design standards is noted. The Draft EIR already
identifies that the proposed pier and ferry infrastructure would be designed as a Risk Category IV
essential facility and would comply with applicable seismic design standards, including the currently
effective ASCE 61-14 and the California Building Code. As noted in the comment, ASCE 61-26 is an
unpublished guideline that has not been adopted. CEQA requires that an EIR’s analysis be based on the
regulatory standards and guidelines in effect at the time of the analysis; an unadopted guideline that is
subject to review and revision does not constitute an applicable regulatory requirement and is not an
appropriate standard against which to evaluate project design. Should ASCE 61-26 be formally adopted
prior to the submittal of permit applications, the project’s engineering team will incorporate applicable
updated requirements through the standard design and permitting process. No revisions to the Draft EIR
are required.

Response to Comment A3-30
As described in the Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, the proposed project includes in-kind repair of
an approximately 300-foot-long segment of shoreline that is currently experiencing localized erosion
along the eastern side of the Seawall Peninsula. The improvement would consist of restoration and
stabilization of existing shoreline protection using geotextile/geogrid fabric, bedding material, and rock
riprap designed to match surrounding shoreline conditions.
In response to this comment, Draft EIR Section 3.5, Geology and Soils, Impact GEO-4 (Operation, page 3.5-
31) has been revised to clarify the existing shoreline conditions, the nature of the localized erosion
identified in the Project Description, and the effect of the proposed shoreline repair on erosion in adjacent
shoreline areas as follows:
    In addition, the shoreline around the project site ferry approach area is made of armored rip rap,
    rather than exposed native soils or unconsolidated shoreline sediments.; therefore, there is no soil
    that could be eroded. As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, a localized section of shoreline
    along the eastern side of the Seawall Peninsula is currently experiencing deterioration of existing
    shoreline protection and exposure of underlying fill material. The proposed project would repair and
    stabilize this already-armored shoreline segment through in-kind replacement and reinforcement of
    existing shoreline protection features. Because the proposed shoreline repair would restore and
    maintain an existing hardened shoreline condition, rather than introduce new armoring into a
    previously natural shoreline, the project would not substantially alter shoreline geomorphology, wave
    reflection patterns, or erosion processes relative to existing conditions. Although shoreline armoring
    can influence localized erosion patterns in adjacent unarmored areas, the shoreline areas
    immediately adjacent to the proposed repair are similarly developed and protected with existing
    shoreline stabilization features. Therefore, the proposed shoreline repair would not substantially
    increase erosion rates in nearby shoreline areas beyond existing conditions. Finally, the ferry vessels
    approaching the project site would reduce speed to 8 knots or less when approaching the Berkeley
    pier boarding float, which would further minimize wake-related shoreline effects.68 For these reasons,
    operational impacts on erosion or loss of topsoil would be less than significant.
    68.
          8 knots is equal to approximately 9.2 miles per hour.

The clarification added in response to this comment provides additional information regarding existing
shoreline conditions, the localized erosion area identified in the Project Description, and the function of
the proposed shoreline repair. The clarification does not alter the impact analysis or significance
determination presented in the Draft EIR and does not result in any new or more severe impacts. The
analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact GEO-4 (Soil Erosion or Topsoil Loss),
remain valid as written. Accordingly, impacts related to erosion and shoreline stability would remain less
than significant. No further revisions to the Draft EIR are required in response to this comment.

    Waterside Construction Surface Water Quality
    Construction activities within surface waters have the greatest potential to affect water quality in the
    San Francisco Bay. Impacts to the San Francisco Bay would be primarily due to construction-related
    dredging, demolition of the existing pier, and construction of a new pier. In-water construction
    activities, such as dredging, existing pile removal and new pile installation, and pier deck demolition
    and construction, as well as any associated sediment disturbance, have the potential to directly
    affect San Francisco Bay water quality. Some of the existing pier piles, if wooden, could contain
    hazardous materials, such as creosote, that could be released during demolition and removal
    activities. Consistent with standard practice, existing wooden piles would be evaluated for the
    presence of wood preservatives and managed in accordance with applicable requirements, including
    requirements related to Treated Wood Waste, if applicable, as discussed further in Section 3.7,
    Hazards and Hazardous Materials. Dredging of debris, removal of existing pier infrastructure, and pier
    installation could resuspend bottom sediments, increasing turbidity in the immediate project vicinity.
    Elevated turbidity can reduce light penetration, affecting photosynthetic organisms and potentially
    adversely affecting water quality. Sediment resuspension may also release adsorbed contaminants
    such as metals, hydrocarbons, or legacy pollutants into the water column, where they can be
    transported by currents and dispersed to adjacent areas.

A related clarification has also been incorporated into Draft EIR page 3.8-30, as follows:
    The work surface on the barge deck will include a containment basin for creosote, piles, concrete,
    and any mud or sediment removed during pulling. Upon removal from substrate, the piles will be
    moved expeditiously from the water into the containment basin. Any sediment accumulated from the
    pile removal operations will be assumed to contain creosote and will be contained, managed, and
    disposed offsite in an appropriate landfill of in accordance with applicable federal, State, and local
    requirements, including any requirements associated with treated wood preservatives identified
    during pre-construction materials characterization (refer to Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous
    Materials).

With regard to vessel traffic and turbulence, page 3.8-3 of the Draft EIR acknowledges that the Bay is
subject to lots of turbulence with existing vessel traffic.
     The Central Bay is characterized by strong tidal exchange, persistent wind, and complex underwater
     currents that routinely mobilize fine sediments and contribute to naturally elevated and highly
     variable turbidity levels. The U.S. Geological Survey has a long-running water-quality monitoring
     program in San Francisco Bay that tracks turbidity and suspended-sediment concentrations and
     notes that tidal currents change direction four times daily and wind direction/intensity fluctuate on a
     daily cycle, contributing to spatial and temporal variability in turbidity throughout the Bay.4 External
     factors such as tidal currents, waves, and wind affect water quality alongside freshwater and marine
     influences. These dynamic hydrodynamic conditions result in frequent resuspension of bottom
     sediments from wind waves, vessel traffic, and tidal currents, such that background turbidity levels
     are already influenced by ongoing natural and anthropogenic processes.
     4.
       U.S. Geological Survey. 2022. Water quality of San Francisco Bay, California, water years 2020–21
     (Fact Sheet 2022–3087). U.S. Department of the Interior. Available:

Response to Comment A3-40
Refer to Response to Comment A3-39, which provides text from the Draft EIR about how the design of the
project would dissipate jet energy for scour protection. The primary effect of propeller wash is localized
seabed disturbance and scour in the immediate vicinity of the vessel. Within the navigation channel,
localized scour would not adversely affect navigation because it increases, rather than reduces, available
water depth. The sediment transport assessment identified sediment deposition and gradual infilling of
the dredged channel as the dominant long-term process (refer to Coastal Study, Section 6, Hydrodynamic
and sediment transport). 24 The propeller wash may locally offset a portion of the sediment accumulation
predicted within the channel. The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact HYD-1 in
Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, of the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No further revisions to
the EIR are necessary.
