    approximately +6.8 feet mean lower-low water (MLLW) during average higher-high tide conditions to
    about +10.3 8.4 feet MLLW under 100-year extreme tide events during Highest Astronomical Tide
    (HAT) conditions. Extreme Water Level conditions may reach approximately +10.3 feet MLLW during
    severe storm and coastal flooding events. The design still water level, which accounts for
    astronomical tides, storm surge, and projected sea level rise through 2075, is estimated at +11.9 feet
    MLLW.

Response to Comment A3-47
Draft EIR Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, evaluates flood hazards, tsunami hazards, sea level
rise, and risks associated with inundation, and includes that impacts would be less than significant (refer
to Figure 3.8-2, Impact HYD-3, and Impact HYD-4). As discussed therein and in Section 2.2.23, Topical
Response: Sea Level Rise, the project was designed using site-specific coastal engineering analyses that



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                                        2-133
                                             Page 238 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                        Response to Comments

evaluated future water levels, storm conditions, and sea level rise projections over the 50-year design life
of the project.
With respect to the relationship between the project’s design and extreme flood events, the 500-year
floodplain represents water levels associated with a 0.2 percent annual chance flood event, which
corresponds to a 1-in-500 chance of occurring in any given year. While portions of the proposed
waterside facilities would be exposed to elevated water levels during such an extreme event, the project
has been designed so that the pier, breakwater, piles, gangways, and associated structural components
would withstand the water levels and wave forces associated with these conditions. However, the City
notes that the operational availability of the ferry terminal during an extreme storm event differs from the
structural integrity of the facility. During a 500-year storm event, ferry operations would likely be
suspended due to the severe weather conditions, including high winds and elevated wave activity, which
would affect navigational safety. Similarly, public access to the pier may be temporarily restricted during
such an event. However, these operational interruptions would be temporary and would not indicate
structural failure or loss of the facilities, as the pier, breakwater, piles, and other structural components
would have sufficient reserve capacity to withstand the wave forces and water levels associated with a
500-year storm event.
It should also be noted that the peak water levels associated with a 500-year storm are expected to
persist for a relatively short duration, typically less than four hours. Following passage of the storm and
the return of safe operating conditions, the ferry terminal would be capable of resuming operations.
Therefore, even in the unlikely circumstance that emergency response activities requiring waterborne
access to Berkeley coincided with an extreme storm event, any interruption in service would be temporary
and would not represent a substantial long-term loss of emergency transportation capabilities. To provide
additional clarification within the Draft EIR, the following text has been added to Section 3.8.4, Impacts
Analysis (Impact HYD-4, page 3.8-40):
    The Universal Charging Float battery systems would be housed in smoke-tight, watertight
    compartments with real-time monitoring, automated shutoff systems, and multiple redundant fire
    suppression systems, substantially reducing the potential for pollutant release in the event of
    inundation. Additionally, as depicted in Figure 3.8-3, portions of the project site are located within
    FEMA-designated 500-year floodplains. However, the proposed ferry terminal includes infrastructure
    intended to remain structurally resilient during extreme coastal flood events. As described in
    Section 3.12, Transportation, WETA and its contracted operator proactively monitor weather forecasts
    and U.S. Coast Guard advisories. In the event of an approaching storm, senior staff coordinate with
    vessel crews to evaluate the safety of continuing ferry service on affected routes. Although ferry
    operations may be temporarily suspended during severe storm conditions such as a 500-year flood
    event due to navigational safety concerns, the pier, breakwater, piles, and associated structural
    elements have been designed to accommodate water levels and wave forces associated with
    extreme flood events, as the project’s coastal engineering analyses considered future sea level rise
    and coastal flooding conditions over the life of the project. Therefore, any operational interruption
    associated with extreme storm or flooding events would be temporary and would not be expected to
    result in a substantial long-term loss of emergency transportation or evacuation capabilities, nor
    would any operational interruption indicate structural failure of the proposed facilities.

For additional discussion regarding future sea level rise conditions, flood elevations, project resiliency,
and adaptation considerations, refer to Section 2.2.23, Topical Response: Sea Level Rise.
The above revision is clarifying in nature and does not alter the impact analysis, significance
determinations, or mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR. Therefore, the analysis and
significance conclusions presented under Impact HYD-4 in Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality,
remain valid as written. No further revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment A3-51
Refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for a discussion about wave action and
sediment transport patterns. Wave disturbance coefficients were calculated at key locations including the
ferry berths, pier, and plaza. This analysis was specifically designed to quantify how the breakwater
reduces wave agitation at the ferry berths and shoreline. The modeling results confirm that a minimum
300-foot breakwater configuration provides sufficient sheltering for both ferry berths, minimizes wave
exposure, and achieves nearly the same reduction in wave-induced downtime as the longer 400-foot
breakwater. Without a breakwater, the terminal would experience notable wave-induced operational
downtime, particularly during late spring and summer months when southwesterly winds generate higher
wave activity. With the 300-foot breakwater, monthly average downtime remains below 2 percent for all
months throughout the year, including the most energetic wave periods.

Response to Comment A3-52
In response to this comment, the following text has been added to Draft EIR Section 3.9.3, Regulatory
Framework, within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning (page 3.9-4):

    BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan
    In compliance with the McAteer-Petris Act, BCDC prepared the first San Francisco Bay Plan in 1968
    which was transmitted to the California Legislature and the Governor in 1969. BCDC amends the Bay
    Plan over time to address regional needs. The San Francisco Bay Plan includes policies to guide
    future uses of the Bay and the shoreline. The Plan aims to protect the Bay from unnecessary filling,
    promote public access, and ensure sustainable development. It designates priority use areas for
    water-oriented activities, such as ports and recreational facilities, and establishes environmental
    safeguards to preserve the Bay's natural resources. The Plan also includes specific policies for
    shoreline protection, habitat restoration, and climate resilience, ensuring that land use and planning
    decisions support ecological health and community needs. Pertinent policies are identified and
    addressed in detail under Impact LU-2 within this EIR section.
    Although BCDC laws and policies have a regional focus and are therefore included within the
    Regional and Local Regulations subsection of Section 3.9.3, Regulatory Framework, BCDC’s governing
    legislation, the McAteer-Petris Act, has the status of State law and is effectively comprised of State
    regulations subject to approval by the California Office of Administrative Law.

The above revision is clarifying in nature and does not alter the analysis or significance conclusions
presented in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, of the Draft EIR. The analysis, significance conclusions,
and mitigation measures presented therein remain valid as written, and no further revisions are

Response to Comment A3-55
For discussion concerning existing recreational demand and construction period impacts on recreation
access, refer to Section 2.2.6, Topical Response: CEQA Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users.
While public access is an important consideration for project planning and community use, temporary
access disruptions during construction are not an environmental impact under CEQA, unless they result in
a physical deterioration of a recreational resource. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation
(page 3.12-17), the City of Berkeley regulates encroachment on roadways through a permitting process
that considers potential effects on roadways and includes requirements for traffic control plans. Any
potential effects on the roadway system during construction would be minimized through implementation
of the construction-related traffic control plan. As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description,
Section 2.6.2 (pages 2-28 to 2-29), project construction is expected to occur in phases. A traffic control
plan would be implemented in any given phase to maintain recreational access to the maximum extent
feasible. In addition, the City of Berkeley maintains standards relating to pedestrian access during
construction projects, which would require safe and accessible paths of travel for pedestrians throughout
the construction period. Prior to the beginning of construction, the contractor will be required to
implement the traffic control plan. Adopted standards require that recreational and vehicular access be
maintained during construction to the maximum extent feasible. Accordingly, construction traffic control



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                       2-137
                                             Page 242 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

plans would maintain, to the maximum extent feasible: (1) vehicular and recreational access to the South
Cove area; (2) vehicular access along University Avenue to Seawall Drive; and (3) access to the Bay Trail
and adjacent recreational areas. Pedestrian access along Seawall Drive and the shoreline would be
maintained except when actual construction of the Bay Trail was occurring, and pedestrian detours would
be provided during those periods. These access provisions are a required component of construction
permitting and are not discretionary measures. While final construction staging and circulation routes will
be determined by the contractor in coordination with the City, the City’s permitting process and standards
for maintaining vehicular and pedestrian access to the maximum extent feasible during construction
would ensure that no permanent or substantial adverse physical effect on recreations resources would
occur. Accordingly, temporary access disruptions during construction would not constitute a significant
impact under CEQA.

    McAteer-Petris Act
    The McAteer-Petris Act, enacted in 1965, established the San Francisco Bay Conservation and
    Development Commission (BCDC) to address public concerns about the future of San Francisco Bay.
    The Act empowers BCDC to regulate development and fill within the Bay, requiring that changes
    promote public access and recreational opportunities. This provision mandates comprehensive
    planning through the San Francisco Bay Plan, which includes requirements for parks and recreational
    areas to enhance public enjoyment of the Bay. Additionally, the Act empowers BCDC to issue and
    deny permits for projects within its jurisdiction, balancing development projects with environmental
    preservation and public access. In addition, Chapter 7 of the McAteer-Petris Act describes the San
    Francisco Bay Area Water Trail, a non- linear, recreational trail of launching and landing sites for non-
    motorized small boaters that circumnavigates the San Francisco Bay. The South Sailing Basin and
    Marina are designated San Francisco Bay Water Trail sites.

Impact TRA-3 in Section 3.12, Transportation of the Draft EIR (page 3.12-22) states the following:

    University Avenue and Seawall Drive Design and Use Safety
    The project would include improvements along University Avenue and Seawall Drive. As described in
    further detail in Chapter 2, Project Description, these improvements would not change the overall
    circulation of these roadways but, rather, would improve the roadways compared to existing
    conditions. The proposed project includes new facilities for transit, bicycle, and pedestrian users. The
    proposed project includes features to separate pedestrians and bicyclists from vehicles, compared to
    existing conditions. In addition, the improvements to AC transit bus stops would follow similar
    existing configurations and would not create any new safety hazards. This would minimize geometric
    design hazards for all types of transit utilizing the project site. In addition, the roadway design would
    be subject to the City of Berkeley Roadway Design Standards.
    The proposed project would introduce a new use, compared to existing conditions. Bicyclists,
    pedestrians, transit users, and motorists would bike, walk, take the bus, and drive to the project site to
    access the ferry service. While this would be a new use compared to existing conditions, people
    already access the site via bus, bike, walking, or car. The proposed project would include safety
    features that would overall improve safety, including crosswalks, wayfinding signage, and
    bicycle/pedestrian facilities separated from roadways.

There are several reasons that no design conflicts were identified for this intersection. The design of the
AC Transit bus route in this area was developed in consultation with AC Transit to remove potential
conflicts with different user groups. It was determined that this layout of through lanes, stopping lanes
and bus loading lanes would provide for the most effective paths of travel for each user group. Figure 2-
10, University Avenue Improvements (4 of 4) of the Draft EIR (page 2-17) identifies a blue passenger drop
off zone, orange bus stop and loading area, and green cycle track and path of travel. In addition, this
would enhance an existing throughfare as AC Transit currently travels through this area; this upgrade to
the bus loading zone would accommodate a greater number of users, while also providing separated
paths of travel for vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians. The 15-mile per hour speed limit in this area would
continue and additional signage and wayfinding would be introduced to designate travel ways for each
user group. For these reasons, no impacts with regard to a geometric design feature or incompatible use
were identified. The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact TRA-3 in Section 3.12,
Transportation, of the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No further revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment A3-61
As discussed in Response to Comment A3-60, the City developed roadway design in collaboration with
AC Transit to address potential circulation conflicts among different user groups. Refer also to Section
2.2.3, Topical Response: BCDC Jurisdiction, Planning Consistency, and Permit Compliance, for a discussion
of how the City addresses circulation conflicts. BCDC will independently evaluate the project for
consistency with San Francisco Bay Plan policies related to circulation as part of its permit review
process. No changes are warranted related to the Draft EIR analysis, conclusions, or mitigation.

Response to Comment A3-62
The design of the Project incorporates projected circulation routes for different user groups under various
use scenarios and has been developed in consultation with AC Transit and Cyclists user groups, as well
as extensive public feedback. Refer also to Response to Comments A3-60 and A3-61. No changes are
warranted related to the Draft EIR analysis, conclusions, or mitigation.

Response to Comment A3-63
Refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access,
concerning the unimproved water access near 199 Seawall Drive and other water access points, which
are separate from the area where ferries will operate.

The proposed ferry terminal would be located on the north side of the existing Berkeley pier. This location

Response to Comment A3-64
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives, which describes the City’s process in conducting an
Alternatives analysis, consistent with CEQA and how it considered alternative locations.

Response to Comment A3-65
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives, and Section 2.2.12, Topical Response: In-Marina
Ferry Terminal Alternative.
The 2008 EIS/EIR considered an alternative next to the Berkeley Fishing Pier. Because this alternative was
substantially similar to the concept identified in the proposed project, it was not considered further.
The 2008 EIS/EIR considered an alternative off Gilman Street. Different versions of this alternative would
not change the conclusions made in the Draft EIR that this alternative would increase not decrease
environmental impacts (page 5-26). Given the geography of the shoreline, there is no alternative location
near the foot of Gilman Street that would avoid locating the alternative within Eastshore State Park, which
is an area that is more ecologically sensitive than the proposed project site. In addition, locating a ferry
terminal within an established park presents the potential for the project to be deemed infeasible if the
project is funded with federal Department of Transportation funds, which is expected in the future. Once
U.S. Department of Transportation funds are obtained, the project will be required to comply with
Section 4(f) requirements. Under Section 4(f) of the U.S. Department of Transportation Act, agencies
must select an alternative that completely avoids using protected public parks, historic sites, or wildlife
refuges unless that alternative is deemed infeasible or imprudent. Because other alternative sites have
been found to be feasible and prudent (i.e., the proposed project site), an alternative off Gilman Street is
not expected to be feasible, pursuant to Section 4(f) requirements.
The 2008 EIS/EIR considered an alternative near Buchanan Street. This alternative location is in Albany,
outside of the City’s jurisdiction. The basis for considering but rejecting it from further evaluation can be
found on page 5-26 to 5-27 of the Draft EIR, under the bullet “Locations outside of the City of Berkeley.”
Potential different versions of this alternative would not change the fact that it is outside of the City’s
jurisdiction and would not change the conclusions in the Draft EIR.
The purpose of Draft EIR Section 5.9, Alternatives Considered but Rejected, is to identify the principal
reasons certain alternatives were not carried forward, rather than provide a project-level impact analysis
of each conceptual alternative considered during planning. See CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(c),
which provides that an EIR need only “briefly describe the rationale for selecting the alternatives to be
discussed,” and “briefly explain the reasons underlying the lead agency’s determination.” The Draft EIR
provides those reasons for each alternative discussed in Section 5.9, including jurisdictional
considerations, consistency with project objectives, environmental constraints, and other feasibility
considerations. The Draft EIR therefore provides an adequate description of the alternatives screening
process and the basis for the City's determinations. Accordingly, the analysis and conclusions presented
in Chapter 5, Alternatives, remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response
to this comment.

Response to Comment A3-66
Refer to Section 2.2.12, Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative, for a discussion related to
why the City rejected the In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative from further evaluation.

Response to Comment A3-67
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives, which describes the City’s process in conducting an
Alternatives analysis, consistent with CEQA and how it considered alternative locations. The 199 Seawall
Drive location studied in the 2008 Berkeley/Albany Ferry Terminal Study Draft EIS/EIR and referenced in
this comment is located “in the cove behind Hs Lordships Restaurant” (Section 2.8, page 2-43).” This
‘cove’ is the South Cove Sailing Basin, and locating a ferry terminal in this location would not only
significantly increase the area and volume of dredging required due to the ferry vessel route (40,000 cubic
yards of bay mud within the cove itself) but would also introduce conflicts with the recreational uses of
the South Cove Sailing Basin. Since the 2008 Berkeley/Albany Ferry Terminal Study Draft EIS/EIR was
published, no dredging of the South Cove Sailing Basin has occurred. As such, the estimates for
additional dredging from that document are considered conservative for existing conditions, since
additional sedimentation within the South Cove Sailing Basin has occurred over the past 18 years.
Furthermore, the proximity to existing recreational resources, including existing water access would
present greater potential impacts to recreational access, which could be inconsistent with policies in the
Bay Plan.
As a whole, the 199 Seawall Drive alternative site, which is within the South Cove Sailing Basin, would
present more environmental impacts through increased dredging footprint and volume and greater
potential conflicts with recreational users. Because this alternative would not reduce significant
environmental impacts, it has been considered but rejected in the Draft EIR.
The analysis and conclusions presented in Chapter 5, Alternatives, remain valid as written. No revisions to
the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment A3-68
These comments are nonsubstantive in nature and do not raise a significant environmental issue. No
further response is required.

     DRAFT EIR Characterized by Inadequate and Misleading Transit Impact
                                                Analysis​


Summary:


The Draft EIR1 fails to adequately analyze the cumulative adverse impacts imposed                              O2-1
by the project on the region’s ailing public transportation infrastructure. The EIR        2


acknowledges (but does not estimate) the impacts of drawing commuters from                                     O2-2
BART, AC Transit and existing WETA service (Jack London to San Francisco).
Additionally, the document lacks clear evidence supporting the revenue and fare
recovery projections. Ridership estimates appear speculative and are not supported                             O2-3
by available data; in fact, the projections contradict existing evidence and
longstanding experience. Collectively, these omissions obscure the fact that 80% of
ferry operations may require public subsidies at the expense of existing transit                               O2-4

options.


Regional Public Transportation is Ailing:

1
    https://berkeleyca.gov/your-government/our-work/capital-projects/berkeley-pier-ferry-access-project
2
    According to the Legislature: "New methodologies under the California Environmental Quality Act [were]
     needed for evaluating transportation impacts that are better able to promote the state’s goals of         O2-1
     reducing greenhouse gas emissions and traffic-related air pollution, promoting the development of a
     multimodal transportation system, and providing clean, efficient access to destinations.”
     https://lci.ca.gov/ceqa/sb-743/faq.html


                                                                                                       2-152
                                           Page 257 of 1541


            WITHIN OUR MEANS
            BERKELEY




Between new infrastructure and capital costs for ferry services the initial project
expenditure are approximately $125 M. City of Berkeley infrastructure projects have
consistently experienced 20-50% cost overruns. The project would consume
financial resources that would otherwise be available to existing systems that are
under financial strain as evidenced by:
                                                                                                                 O2-5
    ●   A recent $590 M emergency loan to maintain existing public transportation
        operations;
    ●   BART incurring a $350-400 M deficit and projecting service cuts up to 70%;
    ●   AC Transit projecting a $74 M deficit in 2026-27;
    ●   High operating costs resulting in proposed fare increases for all ferry routes.

The addition of new overhead costs from the proposed project will create additional
a majority strain to the existing transportation infrastructure.

The high costs for this project will adversely impact existing public
transportation by consuming federal, state, regional and local resources                                         O2-6
that would otherwise be available to existing systems experiencing
operating deficits.


Failure to Document Impacts on Existing WETA Service, AC Transit and
BART:


The EIR acknowledges (but does not estimate) the impact of drawing commuters
from BART and AC Transit:


     It is anticipated that most of these trips are not new trips, and were originally
     headed to San Francisco by driving across the Bay Bridge. Some of these trips
     might have shifted from commuters previously taking BART and Transbay bus                                   O2-7

     services. [3.12-20 DRAFT EIR]


There is no evidence presented to suggest the project will substantially reduce
driving trips across the Bay Bridge. Anecdotally, there are a range of social
determinants that limit trip reduction potential. For example, comparatively limited




2 WOM Berkeley Comments on Draft Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Berkeley Pier-Ferry Project   2-153

           WITHIN OUR MEANS
           BERKELEY




“on the hour” ferry schedules may not provide the time flexibility many working
family members require.


A plausible scenario is that a majority ridership will result from existing WETA, AC
Transit and BART commuters switching services. Switching by existing commuters
                                                                                                                 O2-7
seems particularly probable for bicycle-carrying customers. Thus, one new heavily
subsidized service will be pulling critical operating revenue from existing subsidized
services. WETA routinely surveys its ridership and this “switching” hypothesis could
be tested utilizing existing survey platforms.


The EIR should provide more robust (including survey-based) estimates on
the financial impact to existing WETA (Jack London), AC Transit and BART                                         O2-8

revenues resulting from existing transit users switching services.




Farebox Revenue Assumptions Defy Operational Experience:


The draft cites the WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan which projects:


     Ridership forecasts and fare assumptions for new weekday and weekend
     ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco generates farebox
     revenue that covers approximately 52 percent of operating costs in the
     tenth year of service
     [WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan p40.]


No ferry route has achieved greater than 44% other than Vallejo to San Francisco.                                O2-9
Across all routes system wide farebox recovery in 2023-2025 was 24% of operating
expenses. [Monthly Budget Report FY 2024/25]


This 24% figure is not evenly distributed across the system. Rather ridership and
farebox recovery are dominated by the Vallejo Service. The comparative success of
this service is likely related to the fact that riders have more limited public
transportation options. Routes shared with BART and AC Transit do not exceed 23%
revenue recovery, and half are less than 10% fare recovery.

Response to Comment O3-1
This comment does not pertain to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR.
No further response is required.

Response to Comment O3-2
Refer to Section 2.2.22, Topical Response: Project Cost/Financial Feasibility, for a discussion related to
economic considerations.
Refer to Section 2.2.12, Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative, for a discussion related to
why the City rejected the Marina Basin Alternative from further evaluation.

Response to Comment O3-3
Refer to Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, for a discussion related to the reduction of Vehicle Miles
Traveled (VMT).
With regard to use of the 2003 WETA EIR, the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Draft EIR did not
rely on the VMT estimates provided in 2003 and instead conducted a VMT analysis for this project, refer
to Impact TRA-2 in Section 3.12, Transportation of the Draft EIR (pages 3.12-20 to 3.12-21).
The systemwide VMT figures cited in the comment are drawn from the 2003 WETA EIR, which evaluated
expansion of ferry service across the entire Bay Area transit system. For this project, VMT significance is
evaluated under Section 3.12, Transportation Impact TRA-2, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section
15064.3, which requires project-specific evaluation and considers net change in Total VMT attributable to
the project rather than a systemwide percentage metric. As explained in Section 2.2.27, Topical Response:
VMT, many project-generated trips substitute for longer-distance automobile travel across the Bay Bridge,
resulting in a net reduction in VMT even where some riders access the terminal by automobile.
The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact TRA-2 in Section 3.12, Transportation of
the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O3-4
The proposed project is implementation of new ferry service. The EIR does not have an obligation to
evaluate a different project of increasing other transit use in the region. The EIR evaluates VMT as
discussed under Impact TRA-2 in Section 3.12, Transportation of the Draft EIR. The analysis remains valid
as written. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O3-5
The estimate of 1600 departing riders referenced by the comment appears to be based on total
passenger trips rather than unique riders. As described in Draft EIR Section 2.7.1, Operational Scenario
and Ridership, the ridership projections presented in Table 2-4 represent total trips. For example, the
projected 1,910 weekday trips in the first year of service would represent approximately 955 unique
round-trip riders, assuming a rider travels from Berkeley and returns the same day (refer to Draft EIR page
2-31). Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, regarding adequate parking supply. No further
response is necessary.

Response to Comment O3-13
As discussed in Draft EIR Section 5.8, Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative (pages 5-19
through 5-24), Alternative 4 was developed to evaluate whether environmental impacts could be reduced
by eliminating several proposed landside improvements, including the public plaza, Bay Trail Extension,
cycle track, renovated Seawall Drive parking lot, electric vehicle charging infrastructure, and certain
transit-related improvements. As disclosed in the Draft EIR, these modifications would result in reduced
construction activity and reduced impacts in several resource areas relative to the proposed project.
The Draft EIR also evaluates the effects of Alternative 4 on attainment of project objectives. As described
in Section 5.8, Alternative 4 would not meet the project objective of enhancing public access and
recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront to the same degree as the proposed project
because it would eliminate or substantially reduce several public access, recreational, bicycle, pedestrian,
and visitor-serving improvements. Specifically, the Draft EIR states that Alternative 4 would not provide
the proposed Bay Trail Extension, cycle track, public plaza, or several other amenities intended to expand
recreational opportunities and public access to the waterfront. For further discussion regarding the
formulation of project objectives as they relate to the development of project alternatives, please refer to
Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives (Sub-Section Project Objectives). For additional discussion
regarding alternatives, including the criteria used to develop and evaluate alternatives and alternatives
considered but rejected from detailed analysis, such as the no-ferry-service pier alternative, please refer
to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives.
The comment’s preference for Alternative 4 is noted. CEQA does not require selection of the
environmentally superior alternative; rather, it requires disclosure and evaluation of the environmental
consequences of the proposed project and reasonable alternatives. The Draft EIR identifies and
compares the environmental impacts and objective attainment of all alternatives to inform decision-
makers. Refer to Draft EIR Sections 5.8, Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative, and 5.10,
Environmentally Superior Alternative. Nevertheless, this comment has been included in the Project record
provided to City decision makers for consideration. No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in
response to this comment.

RE: Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission — Formal Comments on the Draft

Formal Comments on the Draft EIR
The Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission submits the following formal comments on
the Draft EIR for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project. These comments are
                                                                                                  O4-1
organized by topic area and are intended for inclusion in the public record and response in the
Final EIR. The Commission requests written responses to each comment pursuant to Public
Resources Code Section 21104 and CEQA Guidelines Section 15088.

Section A: Project Delineation and Description

Comment A-1: Incomplete Project Description — Universal Charging Float
EIR Section 2.5.1 and Figure 2-4 (footnote 5) describe the proposed Universal Charging Float
(UCF) as a key piece of ferry infrastructure, noting it would feature a 1.351 MWh Echandia
battery weighing approximately 47,554 pounds. However, Figure 2-4 states that "the UCF has
not yet been designed" and that "UCF dimensions may differ from what is shown" in                 O4-2
renderings. The UCF is not included in the project renderings.
The EIR should disclose the UCF's size, configuration, placement, and operational
characteristics, analyze the associated environmental impacts, and identify appropriate
mitigation measures.

Comment A-2: Marina Master Plan Consistency Requires Clarification
The 2003 Berkeley Marina Master Plan governs permitted uses at the project site (EIR Section
3.9.2). The Plan restricts new development to replacing and remodeling existing commercial
and non-profit facilities, with limited expansion on a case-by-case basis. The Plan does not
                                                                                                  O4-3
identify a commercial ferry terminal as a permitted use. EIR Section 3.9.4 (Impact LU-2)
evaluates the project against individual Master Plan policies but does not analyze whether a
commercial ferry terminal is a permitted use under the Plan's development restrictions. The
EIR should provide that analysis.                                                        2-167
                                       Page 272 of 1541


Section B: Parks and Open Space Impacts

Comment B-1: Significant and Unavoidable Recreation Impacts Lack Recreation-
Specific Mitigation
EIR Section 3.11.4 (Impact REC-2) finds significant and unavoidable construction impacts on
the surrounding recreational environment. The mitigation measures listed for this impact are
drawn entirely from other chapters (noise, air quality, biology, etc.) and none specifically
addresses the loss of recreational access during construction. The EIR should identify               O4-4
construction-period mitigation measures that directly address recreational displacement,
including maintenance of access to adjacent parks, wayfinding for recreational users, and
scheduling protocols to reduce disruption during peak use periods.
Comment B-2: Impacts on Existing Recreational Fishing Are Inadequately Analyzed
EIR Section 3.11.4 (Impact REC-1) identifies the restoration of pier fishing as a project benefit
but does not analyze how fishing activities will coexist with the gated ferry boarding areas
                                                                                                     O4-5
described in Section 2.5.1. The EIR should demonstrate how the pier layout accommodates
recreational fishing alongside ferry operations and should address construction phasing to
minimize the period during which no pier fishing access is available.

Comment B-3: Construction Noise Mitigation Does Not Address Named Adjacent Parks
EIR Section 2.2 identifies the project site as immediately adjacent to several heavily used
parks and recreational facilities, including the waterfront park (referred to in the EIR as César
E. Chávez Park), Horseshoe Park, Shorebird Park, Marina Mall, Adventure Playground, and
portions of the Bay Trail Extension.
EIR Section 3.10.4 (Impact NOI-1) and Section 3.11.4 (Impact REC-2) confirm that
                                                                                                     O4-6
construction noise, particularly pile driving, would exceed applicable Berkeley Municipal Code
thresholds at sensitive receptors. Mitigation Measure NOI-1 requires a Construction Noise
Management Plan but does not reference any of the named adjacent parks or require park-
specific protections. NOI-1 should be revised to include park-specific protections for each
adjacent park.
The EIR should disclose the expected construction noise levels at each park with those
protections in place.

Section C: Environmental and Biological Impacts

Comment C-1: Eelgrass Survey Findings Must Be Disclosed and Mitigated
EIR Section 3.3 concludes that no eelgrass is currently present within the project site based on
baywide inventories from 2003, 2009, and 2014. However, Figure 3.3-2 identifies areas of
potential eelgrass habitat within the project footprint, and no site-specific eelgrass delineation   O4-7
survey has been conducted. Eelgrass beds in San Francisco Bay constitute Essential Fish
Habitat under the Magnuson-Stevens Act (EIR Section 3.3).


                                                                                            2-168
                                       Page 273 of 1541


The EIR should require a pre-construction eelgrass delineation survey, analyze potential
impacts, and identify mitigation measures addressing NOAA Essential Fish Habitat
consultation requirements.
                                                                                                    l   O4-7



Comment C-2: Ferry Wake and Vessel Disturbance Impacts on Waterbirds and
Shorebird Park

EIR Section 3.3 concludes that ferry wake would be "consistent with existing vessel
operations" and finds operational biological impacts less than significant. This conclusion is not
supported by any quantitative wake comparison, species-specific assessment, or analysis of
foraging disruption along the transit corridor. The vessel approach speed protocol referenced
in the analysis was designed for water quality and turbidity, not biological protection.                O4-8

The EIR should provide a quantitative operational biological impact analysis that addresses the
combined disturbance from vessel operations — including wake, noise, lighting, vehicle traffic,
and passenger activity — on foraging and roosting waterbird populations, special-status fish,
and marine mammals along the transit corridor.

Comment C-3: Jurisdictional Waters Compensatory Mitigation Baseline Needs
Clarification

EIR Section 3.3 (Mitigation Measure BIO-3) requires compensatory mitigation for impacts to
jurisdictional waters at a 1:1 ratio, to be achieved through demolition of portions of the existing
pier, but defers the supporting mitigation plan entirely to a post-approval process. CEQA
requires that mitigation measures be sufficiently defined to allow meaningful evaluation prior to
project approval.                                                                                       O4-9

The EIR should include a preliminary calculation comparing the footprint of new fill against
proposed demolition to demonstrate the 1:1 ratio is achievable, clarify whether the ratio applies
to piling area, deck area, or both, and specify whether the mitigation plan will be subject to
public review and agency approval prior to construction.

Comment C-4: Tree Removal Analysis Is Inadequate and Mitigation Is Undefined
EIR Section 3.3 (Impact BIO-5) discloses that approximately 39 of 61 trees on the project site
would be removed, but the analysis is limited to confirming that no coast live oaks are among
the trees to be removed and that a removal permit will be obtained. The EIR should provide a            O4-10
tree-by-tree inventory identifying each tree proposed for removal by species, diameter at
breast height (DBH), condition rating, or location in order to enable the public to evaluate
whether individual trees qualify for protection under Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 12.44.
The EIR does not address the functional recreational role of the trees proposed for removal.
The EIR should analyze whether removal of the Seawall Drive tree canopy would change wind               O4-11
exposure conditions at the South Sailing Basin and whether those changes would affect the
safety of recreational water users, and identify appropriate mitigation measures.
The EIR defers the Urban Forestry Unit’s replacement evaluation entirely to post-approval,
stating only that “it is expected that some replacement would be required” (EIR Section 3.3).
                                                                                            2-169
                                                                                                    i   O4-12
                                      Page 274 of 1541


Unlike other biological resource impacts addressed in this EIR, Impact BIO-5 includes no
standalone mitigation measure for tree removal. The proposed replacement list is identified in
                                                                                                   O4-12
the project description (EIR Section 2.5.3) but is not incorporated into any mitigation measure,
commitment, or condition of approval. The EIR should be revised to identify protected trees,
potential impacts from their removal and appropriate mitigation measures.

Section D: Operational Impacts on the Multi-Use Recreation Area

Comment D-1: Ferry Wake Impacts on Non-Motorized Watercraft and Open-Water
Swimmers Not Analyzed for Operations
EIR Section 3.11.4 notes that the Berkeley Marina serves kayaks, sea kayaks, sailboards,
paddleboards, and windsurfers, and that open-water swimmers use the waters around the
                                                                                                   O4-13
marina coves. EIR Section 3.11 does not identify open-water swimming in its baseline
characterization of existing recreational uses, a baseline adequacy issue under CEQA
Guidelines Section 15125.
EIR Section 3.11.4 concludes that ferry wake “would not be noticeable within the context of the
Berkeley Waterfront area and existing sailboat, motorized boats, and other recreational craft
use.” This conclusion is not supported by any quantitative wake height or wake energy
analysis at locations where swimmers and non-motorized watercraft users are present. The
vessel speed protocol referenced in Section 3.11.4 is analyzed in Section 3.8.4 for turbidity      O4-14
and sediment resuspension, not for physical safety effects on people in the water. This is a
permanent operational impact that will exist for the life of the project.
The EIR should provide quantitative wake analysis for all recreational use locations, including
locations used by open water swimmers. The EIR should also identify the physical effects of
ferry wake on water conditions at kayak launch areas and sailboard launch zones. Vessel            O4-15
speed protocols should be adopted as mitigation measures to protect the safety of each
recreational user group.

Comment D-2: Maritime Security Exclusion Zone Impacts on Recreational Access Are
Not Addressed

The EIR does not address operational access restrictions that may arise from Maritime
Transportation Security Act (MTSA) compliance. Under 33 CFR § 105.200, passenger vessel
facilities serving vessels of 150 gross tons or more are subject to security zone requirements
that can extend 25 to 100 meters into surrounding waters. The EIR does not identify the gross      O4-16
tonnage of the proposed ferry vessels and therefore cannot determine whether MTSA
requirements apply. The EIR should disclose the gross tonnage of the proposed vessels,
determine whether MTSA security zone requirements are triggered, and if so, analyze the
impact of those zones on recreational water access adjacent to the terminal.

Comment D-3: Operational Noise from Terminal Activities Is Not Adequately Analyzed
The parks proximate to the ferry terminal and approach roadways are sensitive uses. EIR
Section 3.10.4 analyzes operational noise and does not assess impacts on adjacent parks,           O4-17
including Shorebird Park and the Bay Trail corridor, as distinct noise-sensitive receptors.
                                                                                          2-170
                                             Page 275 of 1541


The EIR's construction noise analysis applies a residential threshold to Shorebird Park
pursuant to Berkeley General Plan Policy EM-47, acknowledging parks as noise-sensitive
receptors (Section 3.10.4, footnote 14). Tables 3.10-13 and 3.10-15 show Shorebird Park                          O4-18
closer to the project site than Skates on the Bay.
The EIR should provide a cumulative operational noise impact analysis for Shorebird Park and
the Bay Trail corridor applying appropriate outdoor recreational noise compatibility standards,
and identify appropriate mitigation measures.
Comment D-4: Terminal Lighting Impacts on Adjacent Parks and Nesting Wildlife Not
Analyzed
EIR Section 3.1.4 (Impact AES-4) finds light and glare impacts less than significant, citing
DarkSky-compliant fixtures, photocell controls, and timers. The project site is immediately
adjacent to Shorebird Park, which provides nesting and foraging habitat for sensitive shorebird                   O4-19
species. The EIR should analyze the impact of artificial light at night (ALAN) from terminal
operations on nesting shorebirds and identify ALAN as a separate operational impact category.

Comment D-5: Sea Level Rise Operational Adaptation Not Adequately Addressed
EIR Section 3.8.4 and the project’s coastal study (COWI, December 2025, cited in EIR
footnote 7) confirm that the pier, breakwater, and plaza are designed to accommodate
approximately 1.6 feet of sea level rise by 2075. The EIR classifies the pier as a Risk Category
IV Essential Facility with a design life of approximately 50 years (EIR Section 2.5.1). The
California Coastal Commission’s Sea Level Rise Policy Guidance (November 2024)
                                                                                                                 O4-20
recommends that critical infrastructure use a planning horizon of 100 years or greater, and the
2024 OPC Sea Level Rise Guidance recommends evaluating Intermediate, Intermediate-High,
and High Scenarios to assess a spectrum of potential impacts. By 2100, the 2024 OPC
Guidance projects statewide sea level rise between 1.6 and 3.1 feet under Intermediate to
Intermediate-High scenarios, with higher amounts under High scenarios.
The EIR should provide a 100-year analysis of impacts to the pier, breakwater and landside
infrastructure under the Intermediate-High and High SLR scenarios as recommended by the
2024 OPC Guidance, and identify appropriate mitigation measures.

Response to Comment O4-1
This comment does not pertain to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR.
No further response is required.

Response to Comment O4-2
This comment references a footnote to Figure 2-4. As a matter of clarification, this footnote is meant to
refer to the figure and not the entire Project Description. The Draft EIR describes the Universal Charging
Float (UCF) in several places. Pages 2-10 to 2-11 of the Draft EIR provide an overview of the UCF and
page 2-27 describes the piles associated with the UCF. Throughout the Draft EIR, the analysis considers
the potential impacts associated with the installation of the UCF. For example, Section 3.3, Biological
Resources considers the impacts from the installation of piles associated with installing the UCF and
Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials considers the potential impacts related to accidental
release of hazardous chemicals.
To clarify the level of detail and ensure consistency with the environmental analysis, the following text
change has been made to Section 2.5.1, page 2-11 of the Draft EIR:
    In addition, the UCF would include a fire suppression system for the batteries comprised of a primary
    fire suppression (direct foam injection system), secondary fire suppression (aerosol fire
    suppression), and tertiary fire suppression (freshwater deluge system). Although the final engineering
    design and dimensions of the UCF are not yet complete, this EIR evaluates a conservative maximum
    design envelope that includes all major structural, electrical, and safety components. The final UCF
    configuration, dimensions, and layout would be determined during final design and permitting but
    would not exceed the scope or introduce impacts beyond those analyzed in this EIR.

Additionally, in response to this comment, the following clarifying text change has been made to Figure 2-
4, Footnote 5, on page 2-8 of the Draft EIR:
    The project would include a Universal Charging Float or UCF featuring a 1.351 MWh Echandia battery
    weighing approximately 47,554 pounds. The UCF has not yet been designed and is not included in
    this rendering. UCF dimensions may differ from what is shown in this rendering; however, the
    environmental analysis in this EIR assumes a conservative maximum design envelope that
    encompasses potential variations in size, equipment, and operation.

The Draft EIR discloses the UCF’s function, anticipated components, placement, and operational
characteristics at a level sufficient to support a conservative environmental analysis under CEQA.
Accordingly, the analysis and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written,
and no additional mitigation measures are required. No further revisions to the EIR are necessary beyond
the clarifications provided above.

Response to Comment O4-3
The statement that the Berkeley Marina Master Plan establishes a list of permitted land uses at the
project site is not accurate. The Berkeley Marina Master Plan provides a long-term vision, guiding
principles, policies, and capital improvement strategies for the Berkeley Marina. To the extent that the
Marina Master Plan contains applicable goals, principles, and policies relevant to the proposed project,
Draft EIR Section 3.9.4, Impacts Analysis, evaluates the proposed project's consistency with those
provisions and concludes that the project would be consistent with the applicable principles and policies,

including those related to preservation and enhancement of public access, recreational opportunities,
pedestrian and bicycle facilities, infrastructure improvements, and water-oriented recreational uses (refer
to Impact LU-2, Table 3.9-4, pages 3.9-29 through 3.9-33).
Regarding the specific claim that the proposed ferry terminal is not a permitted use at the project site,
Draft EIR Section 3.9.2, Environmental Setting, explains that the project site has a Berkeley General Plan
land use designation of Waterfront/Marina and a zoning designation of Unclassified (U). The Draft EIR
further explains that development within the Unclassified District is governed by Berkeley Municipal Code
Section 23.208.020 and that the proposed project would be required to obtain a Use Permit for operation
of a public ferry (refer to page 3.9-2). Accordingly, while the Marina Master Plan provides guidance
regarding the future development and management of the Berkeley Marina, it is not the regulatory
mechanism that establishes which uses are permitted at the project site. Accordingly, the Draft EIR
adequately addresses applicable land use designations, zoning regulations, permitting requirements, and
consistency with the Berkeley Marina Master Plan. For further discussion of land use plan consistency as
it pertains to the proposed project, refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid
as written, and no revisions are required.

Response to Comment O4-7
The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) California Eelgrass Mitigation Policy (CEMP; 2014)
recommends no net loss of eelgrass habitat function but does not address impacts to potential eelgrass
habitat [emphasis added]. As identified in Section 3.3 Biological Resources, eelgrass is not within the
project site and would not be affected by implementation of the project.
Finally, 250 meters is the adopted threshold for potential impacts to eelgrass. 25 No documented
occurrences of eelgrass have been reported less than 1,000 feet from the project site. Therefore, the
proposed project is not expected to impact eelgrass habitat function. No revisions to the EIR are
necessary.

Response to Comment O4-8
The Draft EIR addresses operational impacts, including ferry operational noise and lighting, to special
status fish and marine mammals in Section 3.3.4, under Impact BIO-1, pages 3.3-52 through 3.3-54, Refer
to Response to Comment O7-17 for discussion of and Draft EIR clarification text changes addressing
ferry operations impacts on waterbirds. Impacts from ferry vessel operational wake are discussed under
Impact BIO-3, page 3.3-61. Impacts to aquatic species movement from operational noise are discussed
under Impact BIO-4, page 3.3-64. These various related ferry vessel operational impacts were determined
to be less than significant in the Draft EIR. In addition, refer to Section 2.2.11, Topical Response: Ferry
Operations, for further discussion of vessel interaction with aquatic species and Section 2.2.4, Topical
Response: Biological/Underwater Noise, and Section 2.2.28, Topical Response: Whale Strike, for discussion
of effects of vessel speed on aquatic species.
Revision of the EIR to add a full, quantitative operational analysis of every combined disturbance pathway
(wake, noise, lighting, vessel, and passenger activity) is not warranted under CEQA, because the project’s
incremental increase in ferry vessel operation is small relative to existing Bay vessel operational levels. In
addition, comment claims of population‑level effects are speculative without site‑specific exposure and
demographic data such as the frequency, duration, and spatial overlap of foraging areas with project
vessel wake envelopes under actual operating conditions and demographic data, including local
abundance, seasonal residency patterns, foraging success rates, and survival or reproductive metrics for
the affected species. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this comment, beyond the
clarifying revisions made in Response to Comment O7-17.

Response to Comment O4-9
Preparation of a fully developed, site‑specific mitigation plan requires final design information and
jurisdictional determinations that are not yet available. Refer to Section 2.2.17, Topical Response:
Mitigation Measure Requirements, as well as Response to Comment A1-10 for further discussion about
how Mitigation Measure BIO-3 is not deferred mitigation under CEQA. In addition, refer to the errata in
Chapter 3 of the Final EIR for changes to the wording of Mitigation Measure BIO-3.

Response to Comment O4-12
The Draft EIR addresses the proposed removal of trees and consistency with the Berkeley Municipal Code
in Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO-5, page 3.3-65 and concludes a less-than-significant impact. CEQA
requires the Draft EIR to disclose potential impacts and identify feasible mitigation, but it does not require
the document to duplicate other regulatory processes that already govern technical details like
tree‑replacement ratios. Under the Berkeley Municipal Code, the City Urban Forestry Unit, not the Draft
EIR, determines which trees are protected and what replacement is required. In addition, the list of trees
to be removed in the Draft EIR Project Description does not need to also be incorporated as mitigation in
the Draft EIR Biological Resources section, as potentially significant environmental impacts were not
identified with respect to the protection of trees and, thus, mitigation is not required. No changes to the
Draft EIR are necessary.

Section 3.11, Recreation of the Draft EIR identifies swimming as an existing recreational use within the

which describe swimming as a primary recreational activity occurring throughout the San Francisco Bay
and describes the South Sailing Basin, public docks located south of University Avenue and the sailing
club facilities, and the rocky shoreline at the southernmost point of the 199 Seawall peninsula as

the existing recreational use of swimming under Impact REC-1, and concludes that impacts would be less
than significant (refer to Draft EIR pages 3.11-16 through 3.11-20).

the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further revisions are required.

Response to Comment O4-14
Refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, regarding the Coastal Study analysis of
wave climate and potential changes near the proposed ferry terminal, including at the South Cove Sailing
Basin. As part of the project design process, the City’s Design Team (COWI) carried out hydrodynamic
and sedimentation modeling using a two-dimensional hydrodynamic and sediment transport model to
assess currents, wave-driven transport, and long-term sediment deposition within the dredged areas. The
model was calibrated against historical survey data from the Berkeley Marina. The modeling effort
accounts for wind conditions, tidal forcing, regional hydrodynamic conditions, and site-specific
bathymetry.

these topics are provided in Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, and Section
2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities).
The text changes presented under Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, and
Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities), are clarifying in nature,

Response to Comment O4-16
The comment’s discussion of Maritime Transportation Security Act (MTSA) requirements conflates
provisions that are not applicable to the proposed project. 33 CFR Part 105 (Maritime Security: Facilities)
applies to certain facilities, including those serving passenger vessels carrying more than 150
passengers, and establishes requirements related to Facility Security Plans, restricted access areas, and
operational security procedures. These regulations do not establish or require fixed “security zones”
extending 25 to 100 meters into surrounding waters, as stated in the comment.
The proposed Berkeley ferry terminal would be operated by the Water Emergency Transportation
Authority (WETA), which already complies with applicable MTSA and U.S. Coast Guard requirements at its
existing ferry facilities. These requirements involve operational and administrative security measures
(e.g., access control, screening, and coordination with vessel security plans) rather than establishment of
large, permanent exclusion areas in surrounding waters.
With respect to vessel characteristics, ferry vessels similar to those proposed for the project (e.g.,
Dorado-class electric ferries) have a gross tonnage of approximately 96, which is below the 150 gross
tonnage threshold referenced in the comment. Accordingly, the specific trigger cited by the comment is
not applicable to the project.
Section 3.11, Recreation of the Draft EIR (pages 3.11-14 through 3.11-24) evaluates potential impacts to
water-based recreational uses, including boating and shoreline access. The analysis considers the
physical footprint of the terminal, docking operations, and navigation safety requirements, and concludes
that the project would not substantially reduce recreational access or use of surrounding waters.
To the extent that operational safety buffers or standard navigational practices would be implemented
(as is typical for any ferry terminal), these would be limited in spatial extent and duration and would not
preclude continued recreational use of adjacent waters.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented under Impact REC-1 in Section 3.11, Recreation, and
throughout the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions are required.

EFFECTS OF FERRY TRAFFIC ON MIGRATORY WATERBIRDS IN THE SAN FRANCISCO BAY

Commuter ferry routes cross valuable subtidal and intertidal habitats in the San Francisco Bay estuary
that support a wealth of natural resources, including large numbers of migratory waterbirds during the
winter. When new routes were proposed for the region under a new transit authority in 1999, we initiated
studies to evaluate the ecological effects of commuter ferries on rafting waterbirds. The main objectives
were to: 1) conduct on-board ferry surveys to assess species-specific buffer distances; 2) examine
waterbird avoidance of watercraft in land-based surveys at selected areas; and 3) document distribution of
waterbirds along ferry routes with aerial surveys.

On-board ferry surveys were used to determine how waterbirds responded behaviorally to the passage of a
commuter ferry. Observers recorded the behavioral response (fly, dive, swim, alert posture) of waterbirds
and their distance from the ferry. Surf scoters (Melanitta perspicillata), lesser and greater scaup (Aythya
affinis and A. marila), and western and Clark’s grebes (Aechmophorus occidentalis and A. clarkii) were
the most abundant species found across all ferry routes, with diving ducks representing the most
abundant guild. Behavior response distances ranged from 50-500 m for grebes, 30-900 m for scoters, and
60-500 m for scaup. Most waterbirds showed a behavior response within 300 m, and we used that
distance to estimate the zone within which birds were affected. In addition, we used GPS tracking to          O5-49
determine that variation in the path of the ferries was usually 200 m. Thus, we calculated a total effect
area along a ferry route from their sum or a distance of 500 m. Affected areas ranged from 2.44 to 75.75
km2 and included 0.07-14.26 km2 of shoals preferred for foraging (<4 m deep).

We studied the duration of disturbance of a ferry transit from land-based surveys. At selected sites, we
recorded numbers and behavior of waterbirds before and after transit. Scaup densities declined after ferry
transit along the Vallejo and Alameda Harbor Bay route, and scoters decreased after passage of the
Larkspur ferry. However, patterns were not consistent, probably because birds were responding to several
factors such as time-of-day, weather, and other disturbances. When we compared weekday to weekend
surveys, we found more waterbirds along routes during the weekdays despite more frequent ferry traffic.

Aerial surveys indicated that diving ducks accounted for 85% of open water birds, dominated by scaup
and scoter (90%). Numbers were highest during Nov-Dec in the North Bay, consistent in the central Bay,
and lowest in the South Bay. While new commuter ferries may be beneficial at reducing vehicle traffic,
they will have an effect on waterbird populations. Although they do not eliminate open water habitats,
they may preclude use of it by waterbirds. Thus, our study indicated that effects on waterbirds should be
considered when planning new transit routes or increasing their frequency, especially in shoal areas used
for foraging.

Letter O5
Commenter:         John J. Bauters, Chair, Sierra Club San Francisco Bay Chapter

Response to Comments O5-1 to O5-3
Refer to subsequent Response to Comments for responses to the specific comments raised. This
comment does not pertain to the proposed project or the adequacy, significance conclusions, or
mitigation in the Draft EIR. No further response is required.

Response to Comment O5-4
Refer to Section 2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability, for discussion related to the use of
the 2003 WETA EIR in the Draft EIR. The 2003 WETA EIR is a programmatic analysis of ferry service
expansion in the San Francisco Bay Area, while the 2026 proposed project Draft EIR is a project-level
analysis for a specific and separate Berkeley pier ferry project not tiered from the 2003 WETA EIR. No
further response is required.

Response to Comment O5-5
Responses to subsequent comments are provided in Responses O5-6 through O5-49 as appropriate. No
further response is required.

Response to Comment O5-6
The comment states that the Draft EIR incorrectly concludes that the California least tern would not occur
within the project site or be affected by the project and requests that the EIR consider this species.
Refer to Response to Comment A2-35 to A2-38 for discussion of and Draft EIR clarification text changes
with regard to California least tern. Refer also to Section 2.2.11, Topical Response: Ferry Operations, for
discussion of ferry service impacts to biological resources. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in
response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-7
Refer to Response to Comment O7-17 for discussion of and Draft EIR clarification text changes with
regard to waterbirds. Refer to Section 2.2.11, Topical Response: Ferry Operations, for discussion of vessel
interaction with aquatic species. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-8
Refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for discussion of wave climate and
breakwater effects beyond the project site. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this
comment.

Response to Comment O5-9
A project objective stated in Draft EIR Section 2.3 is to: “Minimize environmental impacts by considering
existing infrastructure and sea level rise projections.” The Draft EIR further discusses sea level rise and
requirements of the Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan and Regional Shoreline Adaptation Plan
(Section 3.5.3 Regulatory Framework on page 3.5-22, and Section 3.8.3 Regulatory Framework on
page 3.8-21, respectively). Sea level rise concerns are addressed in Draft EIR Section 3.8.4 under Impact
HYD-4, page 3.8-40 and under Impact HYD-5, page 3.8-42, concluding that impacts related to sea level
rise on shorelines would be less than significant. Refer also to Section 2.2.23, Topical Response: Sea Level

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                                Response to Comments

Rise, for discussion of analysis done to inform project design as related to sea level rise and Section
2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for discussion of wave energy impacts within the project
site and beyond. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-10
Because CEQA focuses on and requires analysis of physical environmental impacts, ADA requirements
are not explicitly discussed in CEQA documents. The Draft EIR evaluates transportation, circulation, and
access-related physical environmental effects consistent with CEQA requirements. While these analyses
may overlap conceptually with accessibility considerations, the EIR’s purpose is not to determine
compliance with ADA standards. ADA requirements are addressed through project design.
Nonetheless, please refer to the 2024 Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project Basis of Design
Report, which was made available during the public review period of the Draft EIR. 26 As noted in this
report, the ferry landing’s passenger boarding system, including the gangway, float, ramps, and platform
will be designed and constructed to ADA codes and standards. The proposed fish cleaning station will
also have an ADA compliant stainless steel table and sink for public use.
This comment does not pertain to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR.
No further response is required.

Response to Comment O5-11
Refer to Response to Comment O5-10 for more information about this topic. No further discussion is
required.

Response to Comment O5-12
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion of how parking is addressed under
CEQA and equity concerns.

Response to Comment O5-13
While it is true that an increase in parking, relative to existing conditions, could result in a greater number
of vehicle trips, the Draft EIR concluded in Impact TRA-2 in Section 3.12, Transportation (pages 3.12-20 to
3.12-21) that VMT impacts would be less than significant. In fact, as explained in Impact TRA-2, the
project is expected to result in an overall reduction in regional VMT. While the proposed project would
increase the number of parking spaces, relative to existing conditions, the City has also identified TDM
measures, as part of its Parking and TDM Plan, that would help decrease the number of vehicle trips to
the Waterfront. The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact TRA-2 in Section 3.12,
Transportation, of the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O5-14
Refer to Response to Comment O5-13 for a discussion about how transportation impacts would remain
less than significant, even if the project would increase the number of parking spaces relative to existing
conditions.

Response to Comment O5-15
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives (subsection Alternatives Dismissed) for a
discussion related to how the City determined which Alternatives to consider in its analysis. As explained
in that Topical Response, the City need not consider alternatives that do not lessen a significant
environmental impact. As explained in Response to Comment O5-13, the proposed project would result in

Response to Comment O5-16
Refer to Response to Comment 05-15 for a discussion of the CEQA requirements to address alternatives.
The proposed project includes improvements to bus facilities that would serve AC Transit route 51B,
including improving facilities to allow for future expansion (see Chapter 2, Project Description page 2-12).
The project is implementation of ferry service, which would have a net benefit on transit service in the
region.
The analysis and significance conclusion presented in the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No revisions
to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O5-17
The City of Berkeley has the ability to establish parking fees independently of this project; the parking
pass referenced in this comment is not the subject of this EIR.
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking. Issues related to parking pricing (such as removing
existing annual passes or establishing new fee structures) are potential policy decisions that may be
implemented by the City as part of project operations or broader waterfront management. Such policies
are not part of the CEQA project description, are not environmental impacts under CEQA and further are
not required to ensure the Waterfront can accommodate all users. CEQA focuses on physical
environmental effects, and social or economic considerations such as user cost are not treated as
environmental impacts unless they result in a physical change in the environment. The analysis,
significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions are required.

Response to Comment O5-18
Refer to Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry, for a discussion of how the proposed project
includes, and the Draft EIR analyses assume, installation and operation of an electric ferry, and not a ferry
that would be propelled by any other means of fuel or energy source. GHG and energy impacts, including
the source of electricity were discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.6.4 Energy Sources.
In addition, refer to Response to Comment P36-115 for a full discussion of why the BTU-per-passenger
comparison is not necessary. The CEQA significance thresholds for GHG and energy consumption do not
have a BTU per passenger mile threshold nor do they require the comparison of project emissions to
alternative project options. Further, Draft EIR Alternatives (Section 5.9) discussed alternative projects
such as increasing Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) capacity and improving access to BART, both of which
were alternatives that were considered but rejected as they did not meet the project objective of provision
of zero emission ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco. The analysis in the Draft EIR
accurately analyzes GHG and energy emissions with respect to CEQA and Bay Area Air District
thresholds, demonstrates that electrical consumption would be from 100 percent renewable energy
sources from 2030 throughout the lifetime of the project, and incorporates the emissions from the two
years of non-100 percent renewable electricity consumption into the analysis (refer to methodology
discussion on Draft EIR page 6.3-31). Therefore, the Draft EIR GHG emissions and energy significance
conclusions remain the same, and no Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-19
Refer to Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry, for a discussion of how the proposed project
includes, and the Draft EIR analyses assume, installation and operation of an electric ferry, and not a ferry
that would be propelled by any other means of fuel or energy source.
WETA currently has 150-passenger and 400-passenger electric ferry projects currently funded and/or
under construction. The Draft EIR provides an analysis for a 250-passenger vehicle, which is consistent
with the assumptions in the WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan 1.0 prepared in March 2022 and
available https://sanfranciscobayferry.com/project/berkeley-ferry-project/. The fact that 250-passenger
ferries are not currently available does not mean that non-electric ferries would be operated as part of the
proposed project. WETA is under contract with several developers to build and implement electric ferries
to transition the San Francisco Bay ferry fleet to a 100 percent electrified fleet.
Therefore, additional air quality modeling and analysis is not required. The Draft EIR air quality
significance conclusions and mitigation measures remain the same, and no Draft EIR text changes are
necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-20
As described in the Draft EIR, the proposed project differs substantially from the 2003 project because it
would utilize battery-electric ferry vessels and shore-based charging infrastructure, which fundamentally
changes the project’s energy characteristics. While the Draft EIR incorporates portions of the 2003 WETA
EIR by reference pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15150 and 15152, it does not rely on that
document for project-specific analysis. The Draft EIR provides current, project-specific analysis of the
proposed electric ferry system, including energy use. As such, the diesel-based energy intensity
comparisons presented in the 2003 WETA EIR are not applicable to the proposed battery-electric ferry
operations evaluated in this Draft EIR. Section 2.7.2, Energy Source and Consumption (Page 2-31), of the
Draft EIR describes the project’s electrical demand, charging requirements, and operational profile, while
energy demand and related utility impacts are evaluated in Sections 3.6 (Greenhouse Gas Emissions and
Energy, Impact GHG-2) and 3.14 (Utilities and Service Systems, Impact UTIL-1). Unlike the diesel-based
ferries evaluated in 2003, the proposed vessels would operate using grid-supplied electricity stored in
onboard batteries and the Universal Charging Float (UCF). As a result, energy consumption is not directly
comparable to prior analyses based on fossil fuel use and BTUs per passenger-mile.
CEQA does not require an EIR to demonstrate that a proposed project is more energy-efficient than other
transportation modes or to replicate comparative metrics such as BTUs per passenger-mile. Rather,
CEQA requires analysis of a project’s energy demand and potential for wasteful, inefficient, or
unnecessary consumption of energy resources (CEQA Guidelines Appendix G). The Draft EIR provides
this analysis and evaluates the project’s electrical energy demand, infrastructure requirements, and
operational efficiency. Based on this analysis, the project would not result in wasteful or inefficient energy
use, particularly given its use of zero-emission electric propulsion and modern vessel technology (refer to
Impact GHG-2 and GHG-3 of the Draft EIR, pages 3.6-43 to 3.6-46).
The Draft EIR adequately evaluates the project’s energy demand and efficiency consistent with current
CEQA requirements. Comparisons to diesel-based ferry energy intensity metrics presented in the 2003
WETA EIR are not applicable to the proposed battery-electric ferry system. The analysis and significance
conclusion presented in the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No further revisions to the EIR are
necessary.
