Response to Comment O5-35
The Draft EIR evaluates construction impacts due to dredging on sensitive species, including longfin
smelt, chinook salmon, steelhead, marine mammals, and special-status birds in Section 3.3.4 under
Impact BIO-1 on pages 3.3-45 through 3.3-51, and concludes that impacts would be less than significant
with implementation of mitigation (refer to Mitigation Measures BIO-1[a], BIO-1[c], BIO-1[d], BIO-1[e], and
HYD-1). Delta smelt and western snowy plover are not expected to occur in the project site. Draft EIR
Appendix C Supporting Biological Resources provides reasoning for why western snowy plover is not
expected to occur. Delta smelt is not included in Appendix C because the species did not come up in
                                                                                                 27
database searches. Its range is currently limited to the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, although
historically could be found in the upper San Francisco Estuary, including western San Pablo Bay near
Napa and Sonoma counties. Recent population declines related to multiple factors, including drought,
reduced availability of freshwater inputs, and increases in water temperatures, among other factors, have
led to continued decline of this species. 28 Additionally, dredging would result in only short-term temporary
impacts to water quality and benthic infaunal communities. In addition, refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical
Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for a discussion of sedimentation and Section 2.2.15, Topical
Response: Maintenance Dredging, regarding maintenance dredging. No additional Draft EIR clarification
text changes are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-36
The Draft EIR addresses project-specific impacts to special-status species, whether directly or via habitat
change, due to dredging and in-water construction in Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO-1 (pages 3.3-45
through 3.3-51) and concludes that impacts would be less than significant with implementation of
mitigation (refer to Mitigation Measures BIO-1[a], BIO-1[c], BIO-1[d], BIO-1[e], and HYD-1). Additionally, the
Draft EIR discusses the natural high turbidity of waters in the San Francisco Bay in Section 3.8.4 under
Impact HYD-1, page 3.8-30, and concludes that given waters in the project site are subject to pronounced
fluctuations due to tidal action, wind-driven waves, and regional sediment transport. Project-related
turbidity would not be expected to measurably increase local or regional turbidity beyond existing
conditions and, thus, impacts would be less than significant. In addition, refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical
Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for a discussion of sedimentation and Section 2.2.15, Topical
Response: Maintenance Dredging, regarding maintenance dredging. Finally, Draft EIR analysis of project-
specific construction-related noise impacts on species is presented under Impact BIO-1 (page 3.3-45
through 3.3-51) and concludes less than significant with mitigation (refer to Mitigation Measures BIO-1[a]
and BIO-1[d]). No additional Draft EIR clarification text changes are necessary in response to this

Response to Comment O5-42
As discussed in Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, CEQA requires evaluation of a reasonable range of
project alternatives capable of attaining most of the project's basic objectives while potentially reducing
environmental impacts. CEQA does not require evaluation of every conceivable engineering design
variation. For additional discussion of the range of alternatives evaluated, their related assumptions, and
alternatives considered but dismissed from detailed analysis in the Draft EIR, please refer to Section
2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives.
To the extent that the comment specifically requests evaluation of helical piles, the City’s licensed
professional coastal engineers considered the feasibility of alternative foundation systems during project
design. However, helical piles are generally used in marine environments as anchoring systems for
floating facilities rather than as the primary vertical support system for large fixed pier structures. Due to
their relatively small cross section, helical piles have limited axial and lateral load capacity when
extending above the mudline to support substantial structures. As a result, helical piles would not provide
the axial capacity needed to support gravity loads associated with the proposed pier and breakwater, nor
would they provide the lateral capacity required to resist seismic, wave, wind, berthing, and other marine
loading conditions applicable to the project. 29 Because helical piles are not a feasible foundation system
for the proposed project, the City did not evaluate them as a separate project alternative. Instead, the
Draft EIR evaluates the environmental effects of the feasible pile-supported marine structures proposed
for the project and includes measures, including Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d), to avoid and minimize
biological impacts associated with pile installation activities (refer to Draft EIR page 3.3-55).
Accordingly, the analysis and conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions
to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O5-43
The analysis supporting this document is consistent with CEQA requirements and incorporates the
avoidance, minimization, and mitigation sequencing that aligns with BCDC’s policy framework. As

Save The Bay appreciates the opportunity to submit comments regarding the Draft
                                                                                                                 O6-1
Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project.
Save The Bay protects and restores San Francisco Bay for people and wildlife, as we have for 65   ~
years. To comply with state laws and regulations, this environmental review process must
include a comprehensive analysis of the project impacts and assess a reasonable range of                         O6-2
alternatives to inform the public and agency decision-making.

 The DEIR fails to analyze a project alternative that would place the ferry terminal within the




                                                                                                     ---- ----
existing marina basin that is already served by a dredged channel, which would not require
dredging approximately 400,000 cubic yards of material for a federal navigation channel and a
new turning basin. The DEIR includes insufficient justification for excluding analysis of that                   O6-3
marina alternative, so its designation of Alternative 4 as the environmentally superior option
cannot reasonably be supported. The final EIR should compare the impacts of dredging a new
channel with any dredging required to deepen or maintain the existing channel to the marina
basin.
Additionally, in its treatment of potential San Francisco Bay Trail extensions and upgrades to be
included in the final project, the Draft EIR prioritizes avoidance of temporary construction
impacts over the long-term environmental benefits of integrated public transit and public access
to the Bay. Completing the Bay Trail is a regional priority, and closing all gaps in the Bay Trail               O6-4
in this area would increase the environmental, transportation and recreational benefits of the
project, facilitating more bike-to-ferry connections and more users of this section of the trail.

To summarize, The EIR should analyze a Marina Basin Alternative and fully evaluate Bay Trail
improvements, as outlined below.

The Need for a True Analysis of the Marina Basin Alternative
                                                                                                                 O6-5

operational preferences rather than providing a thorough comparison of benefits and impacts.The

Evaluate the Long-Term Benefits of Bay Trail Improvements in Any Project Alternative

Response to Comment O6-4
The City acknowledges the importance of the San Francisco Bay Trail as a regional recreational and
transportation resource and agrees that enhancing public access and non-motorized connections is a key
benefit. With respect to the comment’s suggestion that additional Bay Trail extensions or upgrades
should be included as part of the project, CEQA requires an EIR to evaluate the environmental impacts of
the proposed project as defined by the lead agency and a reasonable range of alternatives (CEQA
Guidelines Section 15126.6). The Draft EIR includes Bay Trail improvements that are within the project’s
defined scope. Expanding the project to include additional Bay Trail segments is beyond the currently
defined scope and would constitute a different or expanded project. To the extent that additional Bay
Trail segments could be constructed in the future through separate projects, those improvements would
be subject to their own environmental review and permitting processes. This comment does not pertain
to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR. Nevertheless, this comment has
been included in the project record considered by City decision makers. No further response is required.

the In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative was rejected from further evaluation by the City.

and no revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O6-6
This comment reiterates regulatory agency permitting requirements and does not speak to the adequacy,
significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR. The Draft EIR acknowledges that the proposed
project is subject to the jurisdiction of the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development
Commission (BCDC), the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB), and other
responsible and permitting agencies. As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, and
throughout the relevant sections of Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, the City of Berkeley will
obtain all necessary permits and approvals from such agencies prior to commencement of construction
activities.
Compliance with agency-specific requirements will be confirmed through the separate respective
permitting processes. Such permits will include conditions that ensure the project meets applicable
regulatory standards before project construction begins. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response
to this comment.

Response to Comment O6-7
The Draft EIR acknowledges that different users of the Berkeley Waterfront may have different
preferences regarding existing conditions and future improvements. Consistent with CEQA, however, the
Draft EIR evaluates the recreational features proposed as part of the project against the environmental
baseline and analyzes the recreational effects of the proposed project and alternatives. As discussed in
Draft EIR Section 5.5, Alternative 1: No Project Alternative, the No Project Alternative would not include the
reconstructed pier, ferry-related public access improvements, public plaza, Bay Trail Extension, cycle
track, or other recreational amenities included in the proposed project (refer to Draft EIR pages 5-3
through 5-9).
The purpose of the alternatives analysis is to evaluate the environmental consequences and objective
attainment of reasonable alternatives, not to determine individual recreational preferences. The
recreational consequences within the CEQA context of each alternative are described in Draft EIR
Chapter 5, Alternatives, and the recreational benefits associated with the proposed project are evaluated
in Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, which acknowledges existing recreational uses and determines that
the proposed project would result in a net increase in recreational opportunities (refer to Impact REC-1).
Individual user or organizational preferences and concerns are matters for decision-makers to consider
when determine whether or not to approve the project.
Insofar the comment refers to existing water access at the project site at 199 Seawall Drive, refer to
Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access, which notes
that access to this site would be maintained under the proposed project.
The analysis and conclusions presented in Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, and Chapter 5,
Alternatives, remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this
comment.

Response to Comment O6-8
Draft EIR Section 5.8, Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative (pages 5-19 through 5-24),
expressly identifies the landside improvements that would be eliminated under Alternative 4, including the
Bay Trail Extension, public plaza, cycle track, bus facilities, improvements to University Avenue and
Seawall Drive, and associated parking lot enhancements. The Draft EIR further acknowledges that
Alternative 4 would provide fewer public access and recreational benefits than the proposed project and
would not meet the project objective of enhancing public access and recreational opportunities at the
Berkeley Waterfront to the same extent as the proposed project.
Section 5.10, Environmentally Superior Alternative, of the Draft EIR also evaluates environmental impacts
associated with Alternative 4 across all resource areas analyzed in Chapter 5, including air quality,
greenhouse gas emissions, transportation, recreation, and land use (refer to Draft EIR pages 5-28 through

Commentors:

CCCR, with a membership of 2,000, has an ongoing history of interest in wetlands protection,
wetlands restoration and wetlands acquisition. Our senior members were part of a group of
citizens who became alarmed at the degradation of the Bay and its wetlands. We joined
together, and with the support of Congressman Don Edwards, requested that Congress
establish the Nation’s first national wildlife refuge in an urban setting. The process took seven                      O7-7
long years and in 1972 legislation was passed to form the San Francisco Bay National Wildlife
Refuge (“Refuge”). We turned to Mr. Edwards again, and in 1988 (the first year he submitted it),
his legislation to double the size of the Refuge was signed into law. The Refuge now bears his
name in honor of his efforts.

CCCR has taken an active interest in the protection of the habitats and species that occur within San
Francisco Bay, and the local, regional, state and federal regulations and policies that protect the Bay.

status species occurring within San Francisco Bay that could be adversely impacted by the proposed

of ferry traffic to marine mammals and sea ducks. The DEIR fails to analyze or propose mitigation
measures to reduce the adverse impacts of ferry operations to sensitive/special-status species.

California Code of Regulations Title 14, § 15162 (a) requires that additional environmental review occurs
if:
        “(2) Substantial changes occur with respect to the circumstances under which the project is
        undertaken which will require major revisions of the previous EIR or negative declaration due to
        the involvement of new significant environmental effects or a substantial increase in the severity
        of previously identified significant effects;” [emphasis added]                                                        O7-8


Or:

        “(3) New information of substantial importance, which was not known and could not have been
known with the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time the previous EIR was certified as complete
or the negative declaration was adopted, shows any of the following:

                 (A) The project will have one or more significant effects not discussed in the previous EIR
                 or negative declaration;
                 (B) Significant effects previously examined will be substantially more severe than shown
                 in the previous EIR;” [emphasis added]

Berkeley to Larkspur Ferry Route Not Analyzed in the 2003 WTA EIR:
                                                                                                                               O7-9
The 2003 WTA EIR did not analyze a Berkeley to Larkspur ferry route. The direct, indirect, and
cumulative impacts to biological resources that might occur from operation of a ferry along this route
were not identified or analyzed and as such, mitigation measures were not proposed.

Impacts to Gray Whales Inadequately Analyzed:

The 2003 WTA EIR includes Impact B-15 High-speed ferries could potentially strike gray whales in San
Francisco Bay, and acknowledges the “increase in gray whale sightings in San Francisco Bay.” The 2003
WTA EIR attributes this increase to the fact that the “gray whale population in the Pacific has returned
to historic levels.” The 2003 WTA EIR states:

        “…Since there have been no recorded whale strikes, whales are likely not migrating
        perpendicularly to ferry routes but are probably feeding at preferred locations and likely are                         O7-10
        actively avoiding ferry vessel routes…As alluded to above, no documented collisions between
        gray whales and any type of vessel have occurred in San Francisco Bay (Cordero 2001).”
        [emphasis added]

A recent paper by Slaathaug et al 1 reports that the Eastern Northern Pacific population of gray whales
has declined by 52% since 2016, and suggests that increased gray whale sightings within San Francisco

The 2003 WTA EIR Mitigation B-14.1, mentions the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) minimum
distance guidance of 100 yards for whales, and notes that the guidance does not consider potential boat     O7-11
speeds. The mitigation measure does not explicitly require that the minimum distance for whales be
adhered to.

Mitigation B-15.1 from the 2003 WTA EIR requires that:

       “Ferry operators shall be aware of the potential for whales entering the Bay and should know
       how to spot whales at the surface. The USCG reports whale sightings and distance to vessels
       when they receive a report of a whale sighting. Ferry captains shall be made aware of these
       reports and exercise diligence when a whale sighting has been reported. The ferry system shall
       implement a program of informing ferry operators of whale sightings and locations. For example,
       if one captain sights a whale, it should be reported through a network to all other captains.        O7-12
       Operators should be informed or reminded during seasonal periods of heightened whale
       activities or presence. If whale sightings continue to increase in the Bay, having dedicated
       lookouts on board or other detection equipment could be warranted, especially during certain
       times of the year. Devices (such as sound-generating equipment) used to scare whales from the
       area may be considered intentional harassment by NMFS and would not likely
       be allowed.”

And Mitigation B-15.2 requires that “Ferries shall be equipped with a whale detection system such as
forward-looking sonar. Such a system is currently under development and being tested on a NOAA
vessel in Cape Cod Bay.”

The Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project Administrative Record
(https://berkeleypierferryproject.com/) includes a Memorandum dated February 18, 2026 from Tom
Hall, Director of Operations and Tim Hanners, Director of Project Delivery & Engineering San Francisco
Bay Ferry (WETA), to Liza McNulty, Capital Improvement Program Manager, City of Berkeley, “Marine
Mammal Protection & Whale Avoidance.” If the Operational Measures at #3 are proposed to be

        “The following operational measures shall be observed by all vessel operators: mandatory second bridge
        watch at speeds exceeding 30 knots; mandatory second bridge watch when exceeding 10 knots anywhere
                                                                                                                     O7-13
        in the Bay whales are known to be present via visual observation or regional information sharing; logging

Can a ferry traveling at speeds exceeding 30 knots effectively avoid a whale strike? This is an important
question, especially since gray whales like to cruise low in the water, only briefly coming to the surface. 22

The DEIR must identify, analyze and propose mitigation measures for significant direct, indirect and
cumulative impacts to gray whales resulting from ferry operation, not just impacts associated with the
construction of the proposed ferry terminal.

porpoise resulting from ferry operations. In addition, the DEIR must propose mitigation measures to

DEIR should include in its analysis of impacts, electric ferry noise impacts that may adversely affect
foraging efficacy of the harbor porpoise. Smith et al 5 report:                                                                   O7-14


         “The second component to consider is the potential for electric motors and power electronics to
         create significant levels of high-frequency tonal noise. These tones arise from the pulse width
         modulation (PWM) used to control the motor, and this was the source of the high-frequency
         tonal noise in the study of Gaggero et al. (2024). This high frequency tonal noise produced by
         electric outboards may therefore be of concern for high-frequency hearing specialists, such as
         harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena), which have best hearing in the range of approximately
         10 to 140kHz (Kastelein et al., 2017), and have been documented to elicit strong behavioral
         responses (Dyndo et al., 2015; Wisniewska et al., 2018) and be at an increased risk of auditory
         masking (Beedholm et al., 2025) during exposure to the high-frequency signals produced by a
         vessel.” [emphasis added]

Impacts to Waterbirds Inadequately Analyzed:


The potential for adverse impacts to waterbirds on the Bay from Project ferries must be analyzed in the
DEIR. Impact B-11 of the 2003 WTA EIR states, “Ferry traffic could disturb roosting, rafting, and foraging
waterfowl in the Bay,” and acknowledges that waterfowl are “sensitive to the noise level, speed, size,        O7-15
and visual effects of traveling vessels, and generally react to this disturbance by flushing (taking flight
away from the area of disturbance).” The EIR also acknowledged that:

       “The projected ferry routes for the Proposed Project would bisect shallow areas of the Bay that
       are used as foraging and roosting areas for diving birds, particularly surf scoter, canvasback,
       lesser and greater scaup, and ruddy duck,” and that “An increase in the frequency of flushing of
       waterfowl flocks would be considered potentially significant.”

Mitigation B-11.1 states, “Ferry routes shall be consolidated within common corridors, travel down
deeper channel areas as much as possible, and choose the shortest routes across shallow areas to
leave as much undisturbed shallow open-water habitat as possible.”

However, Mitigation B-11.2 defers development of additional specific mitigation measures to an
undisclosed later date, without providing any minimum standards, “Response of waterfowl to new ferry
routes in shallow North and South Bay roosting, rafting, and foraging habitat shall be evaluated.             O7-16
Evaluation could include observations of ferry operations and waterfowl responses by an authority such1
as the Point Reyes Bird Observatory (PRBO).” [emphasis added] Yet incomprehensibly concludes, “Impact
After Mitigation: This impact would be considered less than significant after implementation of
Mitigations B-11.1 and B-11.2.” The current DEIR cannot rely upon the 2003 WTA EIR to address the
impacts of ferry operations on waterbirds.

       bottom substrate (Dahl & Kofoed-Hansen 2003). Changes in substrate composition may in turn
       affect the benthic fauna on which sea ducks depend. Sailing, like many other human activities, is5
       a source of disturbance to birds. A boat passing through a sea-duck site will cause a temporary
       displacement of birds and a change in activity pattern within a corridor along the route travelled.
       Depending on the frequency of disturbance and the ability of birds to compensate for the
       resultant loss of feeding time, and the concomitant increase in energy expenditure, this may lead       O7-16
       to a loss of feeding habitat. Finally, high-speed ferries may pose a collision risk to sea ducks. The
       speed at which a high-speed ferry travels leaves limited reaction time for sea ducks located in the
       ferry’s immediate path, which might be especially critical during feeding bouts, when sea ducks
       spend much time underwater, or when visibility is reduced. Birds may collide with the ferry or,
       when attempting to escape by diving, become caught in the underwater turbulence.” [emphasis

These studies raise significant concerns regarding the potential negative impacts of the proposed ferry
service transiting the San Francisco Bay – questions that must be answered through the environmental
review:

   •   What are the potential long-term direct, indirect, and cumulative impacts to diving duck and            O7-17
       other waterbirds (i.e., Double-crested Cormorant) populations, and their use of foraging areas
       from disturbance caused by 28 daily trips of high-speed ferries between San Francisco Bay and
       Berkeley during the week and 14 daily trips on the weekend, and 12 daily trips of high-speed
       ferries between Berkeley and Larkspur on the weekends, plus an unspecified number of special
       event trips for each of the two routes?
   •   Could the repeated flushing response to ferry disturbance result in decreased body condition of
       diving ducks due to disruption of critical feeding and roosting behaviors. Repeated flushing in
       response to disturbance requires an expenditure of energy that may have negative impacts on             O7-18
       energy stores for migration or reproduction (i.e., will the birds have sufficient energy store to
       reach their breeding ground and once there, will they have sufficient energy to successfully
       reproduce?). Scoters have a low reproductive rate so any negative impacts on breeding success
       will have negative repercussions at the population level.
   •   Could the substrate disturbance of the high-speed ferry in adjacent shallower waters have
                                                                                                               O7-19
       negative impacts on benthic invertebrates – i.e. diving duck food supply?

Consideration of the Use of Helical Piles:

   •   The proposed project would install approximately 416 concrete or steel piles of various width
       and shape. The installation would require impact pile driving, resulting in potential significant
       adverse impacts to wildlife. For aquatic species there are numerous mitigation measures
       proposed that may or may not reduce the adverse impacts to a level that is less than significant,       O7-23
       including soft-start and ramp-up procedures, utilization of a sound/bubble curtain, etc. to
       address noise and vibratory impacts. In addition, there are turbidity concerns that could result in
       reduced visibility, impaired foraging ability, and clogged gills in fish. We urge the City to analyze
       the use of helical piles to assess whether the reduction in construction time, reduction in noise,
       vibration and turbidity offset the higher initial costs.

   Incomplete List of Species Within the Project Vicinity:

   •   The DEIR dismissed the occurrence of the state fully protected White-tailed Kite within the
       project vicinity despite the fact that there are numerous reports of the species occurring at
       Shorebird Park as recently as March 2026 on iNaturalist, YouTube videos of a White-tailed Kite          O7-24
       nest with adults feeding nestlings at Cesar Chavez Park in May 2020, and an eBird observation of,f
       an individual carrying nesting material within the project boundary in April 2026. White-tailed
       Kite should be added to the list of species with a high likelihood of occurring within the project
       vicinity.
   •   Similarly, the DEIR does not include the federally listed threatened California Least Tern,
                                                                                                               O7-25
       reported on eBird at Berkeley Marina-bayside in May of 2023.
   •   There are numerous reports of Brown Pelican from Berkeley Marina-bayside from April 26, 2026)
       and other adjacent locations, including April 13, 2026 at Shorebird Park, and February 2026 at          O7-26
       the Berkeley Pier.
   •   The longfin smelt is listed as having a high potential to occur within the project site. The EIR
       should give special consideration of mitigation measures necessary to adequately protect this           O7-27
       species, as well as green sturgeon, white sturgeon, and winter-run Chinook salmon given the
       significant declines in the population numbers for all of these species.

Specifications of Electric Ferries to be Used Should be Provided:

   •   Information regarding the speed at which the electric ferries can travel should be provided in EIR. I O7-28
   •   Analysis of the potential impacts of speed/different acoustic signatures on marine mammals anda
       rafting sea ducks should be provided, to assess whether additional mitigation measures should         O7-29
       be proposed to ensure the adverse impacts of electric ferry operations are less than significant
       for these suites of species.

Observation of the Conversion from Diesel Engines to Electric Ferries in the state of Washington:

   •   Several news articles have circulated regarding the delay in converting from diesel to electric
       engines due to rising costs. We recognize the Washington State ferries are much larger as they          O7-30
       transport cars and large vehicles. Is it certain that the ferry service proposed for the Berkeley
       Ferry Terminal will in fact be based on electric ferries? If not, additional analysis must be
       conducted to identify impacts of diesel engines on air quality, biological resources, water quality,
       hazardous materials, and energy consumption.

Conclusion:

Based upon our review of the information provided in the 2003 WTA EIR and the change in
circumstances for biological resources of the Bay, it is evident that the analysis of impacts of ferry
operations on biological resources of the Bay, and the mitigation measures that were (or were not)           O7-31
proposed to ensure those impacts were reduced to a level that is less than significant, are clearly
inadequate. We urge that this be rectified and that the public is provided the opportunity to review and:l
provide comments on any changes made before the Final EIR is released and certified.

opportunities for review and comment on this project.

These comments do not pertain to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR.

provides new and current background setting information and analyses based on the latest information

Response to Comment O7-4
Refer to Section 2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability, for a discussion about how the
2003 WETA EIR is used in the Draft EIR, and an explanation of how the Draft EIR, where appropriate,
provides new and current background setting information and analyses based on the latest information
available at the time of EIR Notice of Preparation. This Topical Response also clarifies that the Draft EIR
does not tier from the 2003 WETA EIR.
Regarding the Berkeley to Larkspur route, although WETA’s Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, Version
1.0 does identify weekend service to Larkspur, additional project planning would be needed to provide
this service. Specifically, while the range of proposed electric ferry vessels allow for service to San
Francisco, the range may not yet allow for service to Larkspur. In addition, additional infrastructure would
be necessary to dock electrical ferry vessels in Larkspur. For these reasons, the City has removed the
Berkeley to Larkspur service from the Project Description of the EIR. For these reasons, the Berkeley to
Larkspur route is not reasonably foreseeable, and would be subject to additional environmental review if
and when it were to be proposed for implementation.
Specifically, Draft EIR Section 2.7.1, Operational Scenario and Ridership (page 2-30), has been revised as
follows.

    captured described in future updates. The following ferry operation is proposed in the current
    Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, Version 1.0:

    3. At least three round-trip services would be completed during peak hours for the Berkeley/San

       and the San Francisco Ferry Terminal. The total one-way travel time would be 25 minutes, door-

Response to Comment O7-8
The Draft EIR is based on a comprehensive literature and database review and on project‑specific
technical studies. Specifically, the Draft EIR biological resources analysis in Section 3.3.2, Environmental
Setting, pages 3.3-3 through 3.3-24, relied on current agency databases and peer‑reviewed literature
(including State and federal species occurrence records, CNDDB/CDFW data, NOAA/USFWS records,
eBird and other observational databases, and the 2003 WETA EIR), together with recent field surveys.
That review informed the Draft EIR conclusions about species presence, habitat suitability, and the likely
magnitude of project‑level effects.
The Draft EIR evaluates impacts to marine mammals and special-status birds from project construction
and operation in Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO-1, pages 3.3-45 through 3.3-51, and Impact BIO-4, pages
3.3-63 through 3.3-62, and concludes that impacts would be less than significant or less than significant
with implementation of mitigation (refer to Mitigation Measures BIO-1[a], BIO-1[c], BIO-1[d], BIO-1[e], and
HYD-1). Cumulative impacts on biological resources are evaluated in Draft EIR Section 3.3.5, pages 3.3-67
through 3.3-69 and concluded to be less than significant. Refer to Response to Comment O4-8 for further
discussion of operational impacts on marine mammals. Refer to Response to Comment O7-17 for
discussion of and Draft EIR clarification text changes with regard to waterbirds. Refer to Section 2.2.11,
Topical Response: Ferry Operations, for discussion of vessel interaction with aquatic species. Refer to
Section 2.2.4, Topical Response: Biological/Underwater Noise, and Section 2.2.28, Topical Response: Whale
Strike, for discussion of effects of vessel speed on aquatic species. Finally, there are no new
circumstances or new, substantial information that affects the aforementioned significance conclusions
in the Draft EIR or triggers the need for additional environmental planning review. The analysis and
significance conclusions in the Draft EIR remain valid. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to
this comment.

Response to Comment O7-17
Most diving ducks and other waterbird species in San Francisco Bay are not considered special‑status
under CEQA, because they are common, widespread, and not listed as threatened, endangered, or
otherwise protected under federal or State endangered species acts or CDFW special‑status criteria.
Thus, such species are not evaluated individually as special‑status species in the Draft EIR. The Central
Bay already supports dense commercial, recreational, and ferry operational levels; the Draft EIR compares
the incremental ferry operations of the project to this existing baseline rather than to an undisturbed Bay.
Refer to Response to Comment O7-8 for further discussion of waterbirds in the Draft EIR. In response to
this comment the following discussion has been added to Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO-4, page 3.3-64:
Section 3.3.4, page 3.3-63:

    Marine
    Operation of ferry vessels would occur at the water surface level, with some incremental increase in
    ferry boat noise and lighting within the project area vicinity. The project proposes to operate two ferry
    vessels with regular service to San Francisco and weekend service to Larkspur, which are both is an
    active shipping ports with existing recreational and ferryboat use. Therefore, the project would
    represent an incremental increase in existing boat trips on the Bay.
    Temporary disturbance from ferry operations would be localized and intermittent, affecting only a
    small portion of the broad open‑water foraging and roosting areas used by migratory and wintering
    birds in San Francisco Bay. The project’s operational corridor represents a minor fraction of the
    available bay habitat, and similar foraging and roosting sites occur immediately north and south of
    the corridor. Because displacement events would be shorter and birds can move to adjacent habitat
    with comparable resources, the loss of usable foraging or roosting area is expected to be temporary
    and minimal.
    Special-status fish and marine mammals, specifically whales, are likely habituated to existing levels
    of boat trip levels and would avoid new ferry boat service….

This clarification text change does not change the significance conclusions in the Draft EIR. In addition,
refer to Section 2.2.11, Topical Response: Ferry Operations, for discussion of ferry vessel operational
impacts related to aquatic species. No additional Draft EIR clarification text changes are necessary in
response to this comment.

Response to Comment O7-26
The Draft EIR focuses its special‑status species evaluation on taxa that are currently listed or otherwise
designated as special‑status by federal, State, or recognized conservation lists, and on species for which
the project site provides suitable habitat. Special-status species are defined in Draft EIR Section 3.3.2,
Environmental Setting, page 3.3-17. Brown pelican was delisted under both the federal and California
Endangered Species Acts in 2009 because the populations were found to be recovered based on the best
scientific and commercial data. 31 Recovery means that the species is no longer in danger of extinction or
likely to become so within the foreseeable future. Following delisting, the brown pelican remained a fully

31 Removal of the Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) From the Federal List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife; Final Rule,

https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2009/11/17/E9-27402/endangered-and-threatened-wildlife-and-plants-removal-of-the-

protected species under California Fish and Game Code (CFGC) until 2023, when its fully protected
species status was also removed by State Bill 147. Species that have been formally delisted or that lack
current regulatory special‑status are not treated as special‑status species under CEQA. The decisions by
wildlife regulatory agencies to remove more stringent species protections were made specifically
because this species is no longer “rare.” Rare is defined under CCR 15380(b)(2) as existing in small
numbers throughout all or a significant portion of its range that it may become endangered if its
environment worsens or that the species is likely to become endangered within the foreseeable future
throughout all or a significant portion of its range and may be considered “threatened” as that term is
used in the federal Endangered Species Act. Brown pelican is rated as a species of low conservation
concern on the Continental Concern Score by Partners in Flight, further indicating that this species is no
longer rare, as defined by CCR 15380(b)(2). 32, 33 Brown pelican is still protected under CFGC Section 3503
and the MBTA, and any impacts to this species would be less than significant via implementation of
Mitigation Measures BIO-1(a) and BIO-1(c). No changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this
comment.

Re: Comments on the Draft Environmental Impact Report — Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project

Dear Ms. McNulty and the Project Team,
                                                                                                 O8-1
On behalf of the Cal Sailing Club (CSC) Board of Directors, we welcome the opportunity
to comment on the Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) for the Berkeley
Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project. CSC has long called the Berkeley waterfront
home, and we see exciting potential upsides in environmentally friendly developments
that make the Bay more accessible to Berkeley residents and visitors — including our
own members. We appreciate the City’s sustained effort to advance this project, and the
community engagement to shape it.
                                                                                                 O8-2
CSC’s membership holds a range of views on the project, and as a club we take no
position for or against it. We do, however, share a collective interest in ensuring that the
EIR provides a thorough analysis of potential impacts on the waterfront’s recreational
uses. The South Sailing Basin and its environs are the foundation of our educational
and recreational programs, and a number of physical and environmental questions
about the project’s effects on that area do not appear to be fully addressed in the Draft
EIR. We raise these as areas where we believe additional analysis would strengthen
the document and lead to better outcomes for everyone.

Requests for Additional Environmental Analysis
   1. Parking Access for Recreational Users
      CSC members, volunteers, and guests depend on nearby parking to participate
      in sailing, windsurfing, kayaking, and paddleboard programs. Many participants
      carry equipment that cannot easily be transported via transit. The Draft EIR
      acknowledges a net reduction in available parking spaces but does not appear to            O8-3
      fully assess the downstream effect on recreational users who rely on that
      capacity.
       Specifically, the Draft EIR’s analysis in Chapter 3, Environmental Impact
       Analysis, states that “parking scarcity alone does not constitute a significant
       impact on the environment” and that the EIR “has found no secondary
       environmental impacts related to parking” (see page 3-11 and Section 3.9, Land
       Use and Planning, Table 3.9-1, BCDC Bay Plan Consistency discussion).



                                                                                        2- 257
                                Page 362 of 1541




   However, the BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan policy on Recreation and Public
   Access states that “facilities provided for park and marina patrons, such as
   parking, should not be usurped by ferry patrons” and that “shared parking
   arrangements should be provided to minimize the amount of shoreline area
                                                                                                O8-4
   needed for parking.” While the Draft EIR references the City’s forthcoming
   Parking and TDM Plan (cited at footnotes 19 and 20 of Section 3.9), neither that
   plan nor the EIR itself appears to quantitatively evaluate whether the shared-use
   parking strategy will preserve adequate access for equipment-dependent
   recreational users such as CSC’s members.

   Section 3.11, Recreation, identifies CSC and Cal Adventures as users of the
   South Sailing Basin public docks (page 3.11-6) and lists construction staging at
   the Skates/N Lot and Parking Lot M as potentially reducing parking availability
   (Impact REC-1, page 3.11-16). However, the operational analysis does not                     O8-5
   address the long-term displacement of recreational parking by ferry commuter
   demand. It is important to recognize that even if there is a “net increase in
   recreational facilities that do not currently exist,” (Impact REC-1, page 3.11-16),
   the “impacts related to a substantial physical deterioration of existing recreational
   facilities,” are indeed very significant to users of those facilities.
   The Final EIR must explicitly evaluate impacts on recreational parking in
   compliance with the 2025 San Francisco Bay Plan, which calls for “conveniently
   located areas where vehicles can be parked for more than short periods of time”              O8-6
   at waterfront recreational facilities. If ferry ridership is projected to increase
   demand for parking beyond current capacity, the EIR should identify mitigation
   measures that preserve adequate access for recreational users.
2. Wind Shadow Effects from Peninsula and Berm Changes
   The South Sailing Basin benefits from wind shelter provided by the existing
   landforms along Seawall Drive. This sheltered area is essential to CSC’s                     O8-7
   instructional programs: it allows beginners to develop sailing and windsurfing
   skills in a protected environment before venturing into the more exposed and
   therefore challenging Bay. Any changes to the berm, tree height, or peninsula
   geometry could alter this wind shadow in ways that are difficult to reverse.
   The Project Description (Section 2.5.2, page 2-18) explains that the project would
   remove the existing vegetated berm at the Seawall Drive parking lot along with               O8-8
   approximately 40 trees, including Monterey Cypress, Monterey Pine, and other
   species (page 2-22). Replacement plantings of 50 to 70 new trees are proposed,
   but these would be 24-inch box trees that would take years to reach the canopy
   height of the mature trees being removed. Section 3.1, Aesthetics (page 3.1-31),
   acknowledges that the removal of these trees and berm would change the visual                O8-9
   character of the Seawall Drive corridor, replacing “organic shapes and softened
   skyline with geometric forms and engineered materials,” but the Draft EIR does
                                                                                            t   O8-10




                                                                                   2- 258
                                    Page 363 of 1541




      not evaluate the functional recreational impacts of these landform changes on
      wind exposure in the adjacent South Sailing Basin.
      The Final EIR should specifically evaluate whether proposed modifications to              O8-10
      these landforms would materially affect wind conditions in the South Sailing
      Basin, and if so, on what timescale vegetation or other mitigations might restore
      that shelter.
   3. Siltation and Sediment Transport
      Construction activities and alterations to the pier footprint, new breakwater, and
      adjacent shoreline have the potential to disturb sediment and affect siltation
      patterns in the South Sailing Basin. The Draft EIR does not appear to include a
      thorough analysis of sediment transport under the proposed project.
      The Draft EIR addresses dredging-related turbidity in Section 3.8, Hydrology and
      Water Quality (pages 2-28 and 3.8-30), noting that up to 400,000 cubic yards of
      material would be dredged and that turbidity from dredging “diminishes to
      background levels within a radius of approximately 600 feet within one tidal
      cycle.” However, this analysis focuses on water quality in the immediate dredging
      zone and does not evaluate longer-term sediment redistribution to the South               O8-11
      Sailing Basin. Similarly, Section 3.5, Geology and Soils (Impact GEO-4, page
      3.5-31) addresses ferry wake and erosion but concludes impacts are less than
      significant based on the armored rip-rap shoreline, without analyzing sediment
      deposition patterns in the South Sailing Basin. The new 400-foot breakwater
      could alter wave energy and current patterns in the project vicinity, which could
      redirect sediment transport toward or away from the basin’s shallow areas.
      We request that the Final EIR assess whether construction or long-term ferry
      operations could alter siltation or erosion rates in the South Sailing Basin, and if
      so, what mitigation measures would be employed. Siltation could affect the
      navigability of the basin’s shallow-water areas, which are used for beginner
      instruction and non-motorized watercraft.

We recognize that these questions may require additional technical study, and we offer
CSC’s institutional knowledge of the South Sailing Basin and its conditions as a
resource to the project team. We look forward to reviewing the responses to these
comments in the Final EIR and hope to see proposed changes that benefit the entire
                                                                                                O8-12
Berkeley waterfront community.

Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,


Cal Sailing Club Executive Committee
Cal Sailing Club

Response to Comment O8-1 and O8-2
These comments do not pertain to the proposed project or the adequacy, significance conclusions, or
mitigation in the Draft EIR. No further response is required.

Response to Comment O8-3
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, which discusses parking considerations under CEQA,
the evaluation of secondary physical effects related to parking, parking availability, and the City’s parking
management approach for managing both ferry patrons and recreational users. Refer also to Section
2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access, Section 2.2.6, Topical
Response: CEQA Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users, and Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance
(Prohibited Recreational Activities), regarding equipment-dependent recreational activities and access
needs.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in Sections 3.11, Recreation, 3.12, Transportation,
and related sections of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment O8-4
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion of how parking is addressed under
CEQA, as well as how the project would provide sufficient parking for all users.

Response to Comment O8-5
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion of how parking is addressed
consistent with CEQA.
To the extent the comment is concerned with construction staging, refer to Response to Comment A3-55,
which revises Section 3.11, Recreation, of the Draft EIR to clarify the analysis of temporary recreational
impacts on recreational access. The revision presented therein is clarifying in nature, and does not alter
the analysis or subsequent significance conclusion under Impact REC-1. The comment suggests that are
impacts related to a substantial physical deterioration of existing facilities but does not provide
information about what existing facilities they are referring to, nor any evidence to how existing facilities
would be degraded as a result of the project.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid
as written. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O8-6
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking. As discussed therein, parking availability and
convenience are not environmental impacts under CEQA in themselves. The Draft EIR evaluates potential
secondary physical impacts associated with parking and concludes that project implementation would
not result in significant adverse impacts related to recreational access.
To the extent the comment’s concerns relate to the BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, the Draft EIR evaluates
consistency with applicable Bay Plan policies in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, including policies
related to shoreline access, parking, and recreation. The analysis concludes that the project would
maintain and enhance public access to the waterfront through a combination of retained and
reconfigured parking, active transportation improvements, public transit access, and new recreational

RE: Comments on the Draft EIR for the Berkeley Pier with Ferry Access Project
Dear Liza McNulty,
Thank you for the opportunity to provide public comment on the Draft Environmental Impact Report
(DEIR) for the Berkeley Pier with Ferry Access Project, as required by the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA). Please see the detailed list of comments below. Our primary concern is the lack of              O9-1
study of wintering waterbirds, especially rafting and foraging terns, grebes, and ducks. The environmental
impacts of construction and ferry operation on those birds and their open-water habitat was not
sufficiently addressed in the DEIR.
Golden Gate Bird Alliance is a non-profit organization whose mission is to inspire people to protect Bay
Area birds and our shared natural environment. For over 100 years we have been a leader in bird                     O9-2
conservation and habitat protection. Our 7,000 members and supporters envision a world where birds,
wildlife, and all people flourish together.
Impacts to Wintering Waterbirds
The DEIR is deficient in outlining impacts and mitigation related to the offshore wintering habitat for
many bird species including state and federal Special Status Species as well as species experiencing
population declines in the Bay Area. A single land-based survey date in September is insufficient to
understand the ecology and species composition, let alone the environmental impacts to these
species from pier construction phases and later ferry operations. The Biological Resources table in
Appendix 2 is incomplete without consideration of overwintering presence. Disturbance from
construction or ferries is shown to flush waterbirds from their roosting and foraging grounds1. Local               O9-3
habitat changes at one location on a migratory flyway can have significant impacts to larger populations
of waterfowl2.


1

On Migratory Waterbirds In The San Francisco Bay. USGS Western Ecological Research Center, San Francisco Bay  .y
Estuary Field Station. john_takekawa@usgs.gov
2

California Least Terns (Sernula antillarum browni) are in fact present and foraging in and adjacent to the
project site, primarily in the months of May through August. While the DEIR is correct in that there is not
suitable nesting habitat for this species in the project site, there is very suitable habitat for foraging as
demonstrated by the birds currently using it according to eBird observations,3 likely commuting from the           O9-4
Alameda nesting colony. Without consideration of the impacts of both construction and ferry operations
on this sensitive state and federally listed Endangered species and its foraging patterns and habitat in the
Berkeley off-shore area, this project should not proceed.
Additionally, the following species are present in the project site throughout the winter and are listed by
US Fish and Wildlife Service or California Department of Fish and Wildlife4 as species of special
conservation concern: Ruddy Duck, Western Grebe, Clark’s Grebe, Elegant Tern, Caspian Tern, Osprey,
California Gull, California Brown Pelican, and Common Loon. While their designation is specific to their
                                                                                                                   O9-5
nesting habitat, these birds overwinter and forage in the open bay, in the project area. Their critical
overwintering habitat is key to their survival. The DEIR identifies thresholds of significance as impacts
that “result in direct take or habitat removal or alteration for candidate, sensitive, or special-status
species.” The pier construction and ongoing ferry operations would absolutely result in habitat removal
and alteration for California Least Tern as well as these special-status species.
In addition to these species with special designation, an analysis of Christmas Bird Count and eBird data
show dramatic declines in these species’ populations in the greater Bay Area over the last 50 years:
Greater Scaup, Lesser Scaup, Surf Scoter, Bufflehead, Common Goldeneye, and Western Sandpiper. All
are present in abundance in the project site during winter.
                                                                                                                   O9-6
The DEIR does outline mitigation strategies for protecting and surveying for nesting birds, including
avoiding terrestrial construction during the bird breeding season which we were happy to see. However,
breeding habitat is only one important part of a bird’s life cycle and overwintering habitat is also critical
for protecting migratory birds. This project should not proceed without further study of overwintering
offshore birds during construction and ferry operation, and outlining appropriate mitigation measures.
2003 PEIR Out of Date
The 2003 Programmatic EIR (PEIR) for Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay
Area, prepared for the Water Transit Authority, lacks alignment with current San Francisco Bay
ecological science. There have been substantial changes in the ecology of the Bay since 2003, including            O9-7
declines in multiple wintering and migratory bird populations as outlined above as well as increased
presence of multiple whale species. Increased Ferry use in the Bay, including an added ferry terminal in
Berkeley as part of this project, calls for a new PEIR based on the changing conditions in species presence
and the overall ecology of the San Francisco Bay. These changing conditions and species declines,

Lighting Impacts to Birds and Wildlife
Impact AES-4 in the DEIR outlines lighting impacts of the project and suggests using Dark Sky approved
lighting fixtures. We strongly encourage this mitigation measure and support the use of Dark Sky
approved lighting in all projects including this one. The impacts of artificial lighting at night are beyond
aesthetic for birds, nocturnal insects, and other wildlife. The cumulative light from urban environments,
skyglow, has shown to be a top predictor for bird migration stopover frequency6, putting the birds at risk                 O9-8
of collision7 and predation. Mitigation measure AES-1 should be adopted to prevent these impacts.
Based on the project design it seems there will be significantly more lighting fixtures than currently in
place, both on the land in the parking area and on the new pier. In addition to ensuring the fixtures are
Dark Sky approved, we also recommend following the Dark Skies principles for responsible outdoor
lighting8 which asks that lighting be only as bright as absolutely necessary, and only on when necessary.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Response to Comment O9-1
Refer to Responses to Comments O9-3 through O9-8 for a discussion of waterbirds and the evaluation of

Response to Comment O9-2
This comment does not pertain to the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR.
No further response is required.

Response to Comment O9-3
A reconnaissance‑level field survey, when combined with targeted database and literature review and the
application of standard CEQA avoidance/minimization measures, provides sufficient, project‑specific
information to map and evaluate potential species habitats and sensitive biological resources to support
CEQA impact analysis. CEQA requires enough information to evaluate environmental effects and to adopt
feasible mitigation; it does not require exhaustive scientific research or the generation of new baseline
science beyond what is necessary to make an informed determination. The “biological resources table in
Appendix 2” is in fact a table titled Special Status Animal Species in the Regional Vicinity of the Project Site
in Appendix C (pages C-7 through C-12) and evaluates the potential to occur of all special-status species
with known occurrence records in standard database searches described in Draft EIR Section 3.3.1,
Introduction, page 3.3-1. If overwintering birds did not meet the definition of a special-status species
under CEQA, as defined in Section 3.3.2, Environmental Setting, page 3.3-17, they were not included in the
table in Appendix C. Refer to Responses to Comment O7-17 and P46-4 for details of Draft EIR clarification
text changes related to waterbirds, including offshore wintering birds, and the Pacific Flyway,
respectively. No further revisions to the EIR are necessary. No changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in
response to this comment.

Response to Comment O9-4
Refer to Response to Comment A2-35 to A2-38 for details of the Draft EIR clarification text addition
changes related to California least tern. No additional changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in response
to this comment.

Response to Comment O9-5
Refer to Response to Comment A2-35 to A2-38 for details of the Draft EIR clarification text changes
related to California least tern. Ruddy duck, western grebe, Clark’s grebe, elegant tern, Caspian tern,
osprey, California gull, and California brown pelican, are not CDFW species of special concern. Common
loon is a species of special concern, and osprey and elegant tern are CDFW Watchlist species. These
species had no occurrence records in the standard nine USGS 7.5-minute quadrangle search of the
California Natural Diversity Database (CNDDB) including the project site and, thus, were not considered in
the Draft EIR. California is outside the breeding range for common loon, which is limited to northern North
America, from Alaska and much of Canada south into the northern United States, with clear, fish‑rich
lakes in boreal and near‑arctic regions. Elegant tern nests in large colonies on beaches, and there is no
suitable breeding habitat within the project site or its vicinity given the high anthropogenic disturbance in
the vicinity of the project site. Osprey are not known to nest at the Berkeley Marina according to the
Golden Gate Bird Alliance-run website SFBayOspreys.org, and prefer to build nests off the ground in
treetops, cliffs, or elevated human-built structures. There is low potential for common loon, osprey, and

Response to Comment O9-7
The comment discusses the 2003 WETA EIR and states that the Draft EIR does not provide an updated
analysis to account for changed circumstances, specifically concerning biological resources.
Refer to Section 2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability, for a discussion about how the
2003 WETA EIR is used in the Draft EIR, and an explanation of how the Draft EIR, where appropriate,
provides new and current background setting information and analyses based on the latest information
available at the time of EIR Notice of Preparation.

Response to Comment O9-8
Construction lighting impacts to terrestrial wildlife are discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impact
BIO-1, page 3.3-44, and were determined to be less than significant with implementation of Mitigation
Measure AES-1. Lighting impacts to terrestrial wildlife during project operation are discussed under
Impact BIO-1, page 3.3-51, which concludes that, because lighting added as part of the project would be
designed in accordance with City ordinance and would be similar to existing levels of lighting already
present on the project site, impacts would be less than significant. For further discussion of nighttime
lighting and its effects on the shoreline, refer to Section 2.2.18, Topical Response: Nighttime

Lighting/ALAN. In response to this comment the following clarification text change has been added to
Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO-1, page 3.3-51:
Section 3.3.4, page 3.3-51:

    Special-Status Wildlife
    […]
    Impacts on nesting birds, including double-crested cormorant, from operation would also be minimal.
    Any additional lighting added as part of the project, as discussed in Section 3.1, Aesthetics, under
    Impact AES-4, would be designed in accordance with City ordinance, and would be similar to existing
    levels of lighting present on the project site. The ferry would operate in open water, and the existing
    use of the project site for recreation would continue with similar levels of activity and disturbance.
    Wake generated by ferry operation would be consistent with existing vessel operations in the Bay and
    not result in disturbance to nesting or roosting habitats above the existing shoreline riprap armoring.
    Therefore, impacts on migratory and nesting birds due to operation would be less than significant.

This clarification text change does not result in changes to the Draft EIR significance conclusions.

Berkeley Waterfront Community Coalition (BWCC) is a nonprofit organization formed

          ---=-====--
under the auspices of Berkeley Partners for Parks, a 501(c)3 organization. Its founding
members seek to preserve and expand access for a diverse public to enjoy the
waterfront and share ideas for supporting this unique urban shoreline. BWCC’s mission
                                                                                                   O10-2

is to develop projects that raise awareness of the waterfront, enhance a sense of
community, and support the waterfront’s role in providing affordable public access to
blue- and greenspace amenities to the region and beyond. BWCC submitted scoping
comments in response to the City of Berkeley’s (COB) Notice of Preparation (NOP) in
May 2025 for the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry project (the “project”).
Below, we are pleased to submit comments to the City of Berkeley’s Draft Water                     O10-3
Transportation Berkeley Pier Ferry Environmental Impact Report, made available
Friday, February 27, 2026 (~3pm). We submit these comments to inform the city that
this Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIR) is inadequate under the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), Public Resources Code § 21000 et seq., and the
CEQA Guidelines, California Code of Regulations, title 14, §15000 et seq. (CEQA
Guidelines).

This letter is submitted along with the reports/linked attachments prepared by BWCC,
EBOWS, Placer.ai through COB’s license managed by Visit Berkeley tourist bureau,
and public comments on elements of the project. We also list references to studies
                                                                                                   O10-4
which bear on the health and equity benefits of bluespace - areas near bodies of water
like lakes, oceans and rivers - and the importance of those needs in California as they
relate to the waterfront area in the vicinity of the project. We respectfully refer the city to
those, both here and throughout these comments, for further detail on our comments.

We request that the city reply to each of the comments in this letter and prepare and             O10-5
recirculate a new and adequate DEIR.

I.     Overview of principal deficiencies

The DEIR, as prepared, contains fundamental deficiencies that undermine its
usefulness as an informational and decision-making document under CEQA. The                       O10-6
project setting, description, and baseline conditions are incomplete and, in key respects,
inaccurate. These shortcomings permeate the entire analysis and compromise the
evaluation of environmental impacts relative to baseline conditions. The DEIR fails to
incorporate readily available data necessary to characterize existing recreational use in         O10-7
and around the project area, and the impact analyses frequently ignore, misstate, or
omit relevant evidence available at the time of the Notice of Preparation, including any
meaningful cumulative impact assessment. Moreover, the DEIR provides no credible
evidentiary basis for its conclusion that the project would result in a net increase in
recreational activity along with less-than-significant impacts. On the contrary, available         O10-8
evidence indicates that the proposed ferry project would reduce public access to the
waterfront and increase the cost of bluespace recreation. None of these impacts, nor
the inconsistencies of the project, can be discerned from reading the DEIR.

The stated need for the project—beyond basic pier restoration—is not substantiated,               O10-9
calling into question the adequacy of the project objectives and the resulting range of
alternatives, which are either improperly rejected or insufficiently analyzed. Many
sections of the DEIR justify impacts or project as a whole based on obtaining a
recreational pier, with the Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) ferry                 O10-10
expansion plan for Berkeley as the only option, with the ferry service almost incidental,
for achieving this objective. The DEIR poses too narrow a framing for this objective.
Moreover, as this letter notes, the ferry component of the project as framed in the DEIR
and related documents not fully integrated into the DEIR introduces significant
environmental impacts. It has a potential for significant environmental impacts, if the
DEIR had included required CEQA information with analysis. Many of the project’s                  O10-11
recreational improvements as claimed by the DEIR will occur in the baseline scenario,
and feasible alternatives exist for pier replacement/restoration claimed by the project
based on historical patterns and recent documentation. The DEIR’s rationale for
rejection or noninclusion of these feasible alternatives is missing or cursory.

With regard to each of CEQA’s substantive requirements––a complete and stable
project description, a thorough analysis of significant impacts, identification of feasible
                                                                                                  O10-12
and enforceable mitigation measures, an analysis of a reasonable range of
alternatives––the DEIR falls short. As a result, the DEIR fails to meet CEQA’s


                                                                                              2
                                                                                          2-273
                                         Page 378 of 1541




fundamental purpose of providing disclosure to the public of the project’s environmental
effects.

Finally, as context for any consideration of overriding significant impacts, we present
                                                                                                             i   O10-12




evidence demonstrating a lack of substantial economic benefits and the presence of
adverse social impacts, further undermining any claim of overriding considerations.                              O10-13
Rather, the DEIR relies on unsubstantiated claims of increased economic and social
benefits for justification at several points.

II.     DEIR fails to provide adequate project description

An accurate, stable and finite project description is the sine qua non of an informative
and legally sufficient EIR.”1 On the other hand, “[a] curtailed, enigmatic or unstable
project description draws a red herring across the path of public input.”2 “[O]nly through
an accurate view of the project may the public and interested parties and public                                 O10-14
agencies balance the proposed project's benefits against its environmental cost,
consider appropriate mitigation measures, assess the advantages of terminating the
proposal and properly weigh other alternatives ... .”3

Further, “[t]he project description must contain (1) the precise location and boundaries
of the proposed project; (2) a statement of the objectives sought by the proposed
project, including the underlying purpose; (3) a general description of the project's
technical, economic, and environmental characteristics; and (4) a statement briefly
describing the intended uses of the EIR.”4

        A. Electric ferry - no vessel specifications

The cover photo of the DEIR shows a sailboat alongside the pier, a pier with
recreational extension, but no ferry. The project objective is to put in a zero-emission                         O10-15
ferry. The operational details in Section 2.7 call for a 250-passenger ferry. However, we
were not able to identify an electric ferry model of 250-passengers. WETA is building

three 150-seat electric ferries and two 400-passenger ferries5. BWCC members note
that the 150-passenger electrics would probably only have the range for Treasure Island            O10-15
to San Francisco, and the 400-passenger boats could possibly manage the entire route.
The diesel-powered Bay Breeze vessel class at 97’ length overall does carry 250
passengers.6

The DEIR does not identify which vessel WETA is planning to use at the Berkeley
marina. The project description cannot be based on hypothetical concepts that may
come to fruition in the future, but must be based on existing technology and                       O10-16
contractual plans at the time of the NOP scoping call. To properly understand the
environmental impact, the EIR must provide specifications of the electric vessel it plans
to use.

Further, it must provide specifications on infrastructure to serve an electric ferry vessel
in an emergency. Alternative transportation across the Bay in an emergency is in the
scope of the project and is one objective. It must specify electrification infrastructure to
withstand natural disasters. It should also specify whether and to what extent the                 O10-17
electric ferry service will be able to handle emergency vehicles and emergency
personnel. If the city cannot perform this request, then it must change references to
electric ferries as constituting only hypothetical scenarios not in the foreseeable
future, and omit any project outcomes that rely on electric ferries.

       B. Missing information on level of ferry service

City of Berkeley documents describe the project as a large-scale commuter ferry with
fourteen roundtrips or 28 crossings during weekdays (Large-Scale Ferry Feasibility
                                                                                                   O10-18
Study, City Council Work Session, Tuesday, December 7th, 2021) and thirteen
departures or 26 crossings to SF and Larkspur on weekends. This information is not
provided in the DEIR. Operational details give a generic WETA minimum systemwide
standard for peak weekday service: “At least three round-trip services must be
completed during peak hours for the Berkeley/San Francisco weekday service, per
WETA Board-adopted standards.” With three roundtrips in the morning and three in the
                                                                                                    O10-19
evening peak hours, this implies only 12 crossings during weekdays and none on the
weekends. The DEIR characterizes the ferry as recreational. However, the WETA
Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan Version 1, a CEQA and DEIR planning
document, (WETA Berkeley Ferry Service)

documents are provided.

       C. Project transportation demand management omitted

Transportation demand management (TDM) to accommodate ferry patron traffic to the
waterfront has been developed for the project and serves as a key design feature for
the landside elements of the project. The COB has hired various consultants to address
this project element. Both the latest draft of the Kittelson study and the Nelson-Nygaard
studies address parking needs for the ferry, with the Kittelson study (link includes both            O10-21
Berkeley WTPF Baseline Parking Conditions, February 28, 2025 and the Water
Transportation Pier-Ferry Project Parking and TDM Plan, March 7, 2025) as the most
recent document. The DEIR partially integrates aspects of the Kittelson study in
reference to mitigation measures, e.g. bicycle and bus facilities, but it does not include
in the project description the project elements that call for the mitigation measures. The
description should indicate clearly that across planning documents that the majority of
ferry patrons arrive by car versus all other transit options, even with mitigation
measures. The bulk of landside project features call for shifting land use from
recreational public access to ferry patron parking. The Kittelson study estimates 421
ferry patron parking spaces needed versus the 250 currently accommodated in the
project design. The needed 421 spaces reduces to 356-389 with the mitigation
measures and 42 more with paid parking, still exceeding allotted spaces. This
information bears on impact analysis throughout the document, such as for VMT
estimates, noise, emissions, land use planning, and recreation. The current DEIR does                O10-22
not make this apparent. The full details of the TDM should be included in the project
description and analysis along with descriptions of TDM enforcement and administration
methods.7

patterns. To provide context, the Task 2.1 Berkeley Marina Dredging Needs Technical
Memo by Moffat and Nichol written for the Berkeley Marina Specific Plan, April 21,
2021, states that: “The average rate of sediment accumulation in the Harbor Basin is
approximately 0.05’ per year and the rate at the harbor entrance is approximately 0.1’
per year. There are some locations at the harbor entrance which accumulate sediment
at a faster rate – closer to 0.2’ per year.” For this reason, the marina has been dredged
periodically. From this same report, we know Maintenance Dredging Permits issued to                                                                                                                              O10-29
the City of Berkeley for maintenance dredging of the marina are as follows:

       ●           02/1973 dredging 5,000 Cubic Yards (CY)
       ●           08/1991 dredging 73,000 CY apparently from the harbor entrance
       ●           02/2005 dredging < 500 CY Dock H-I apparently to repair revetment
       ●           04/2006 dredging < 8,750 CY Dock A-C associated with dock replacement

With the 2025 dredging, the range of maintenance dredging events is 14-19 years.

information for both construction and long-term dredging over the life of the project.
