          b. The project is inconsistent with State and regional eelgrass habitat
             conservation and restoration policies and goals.


             i. Inconsistent with SF Bay Subtidal Habitat Goals

The Ocean Protection Council seeks to protect the state’s 15,000 acres of eelgrass and
restore more. Worldwide, seagrass bed conservation could lead to avoided emissions of
0.65 Gt CO2 per year (Hoegh-Guldberg, p. 50 cited in Eelgrass restoration in San
Francisco Bay: an Interdisciplinary Stated Preference Classroom Experiment). The US
EPA (Program Priorities: Subtidal Habitat, Eelgrass and Oyster Reef Restoration | US
EPA) lists eelgrass restoration as a program priority for the San Francisco Bay Program
for subtidal ecosystems:

“Subtidal ecosystems are where many shellfish, invertebrates, fish, marine mammals,
diving ducks, and other wildlife feed, rest, hide, and reproduce. Native oysters can form
                                                                                                  O10-178
reefs that filter nutrients from the Bay water and are a food source for fish and birds.
Eelgrass in shallow areas depends on light filtration to grow and when present in large
acreages support a wide range of marine life and have the added benefit of stabilizing
shorelines by reducing wave energy and preventing erosion of sediments. Urbanization
of the shoreline and shipping channels areas have significantly reduced native eelgrass
beds and other beneficial underwater vegetation . EPA's San Francisco Bay Program
works closely with regional partners to achieve the subtidal restoration goals outlined in
the Subtidal Habitat Goals Report (pdf).”

Under Regional and Local regulations on page 3.3-37-8, for the San Francisco Bay
Subtidal Habitat Goal Report, A 50-Year Conservation Plan, SUBMERGED AQUATIC
VEGETATION GOALS include: protect existing eelgrass habitat …through no net loss to
existing beds, identify and protect areas ..for future eelgrass expansion, restoration and


                                                                                             63
                                                                                         2-334
                                    Page 439 of 1541




creation, increase eelgrass population where one of the priority areas are the Albany
and Berkeley shorelines.
                                                                                                    O10-178
The existing available eelgrass inventories and habitat models demonstrate a conflict
with these policies and significant impact and must be addressed as such.

On the same basis, the project is not consistent with BCDC Subtidal Area Policy 2
(see p. 451 of pdf).

              ii. Inconsistent with NOAA Fisheries California Eelgrass Mitigation
              Policy and Implementing Guidelines October 2014

NOAA Fisheries have a stated goal of no net loss of eelgrass habitat function in
California. Their policy states the following: Eelgrass warrants a strong protection
strategy because of the important biological, physical, and economic values it provides,
as well as its importance to managed species under the Magnuson Stevens Fishery
Conservation and Management Act (MSA).
                                                                                                    O10-179

Given the proximity to known and persistent eelgrass beds and the habit suitability and
likely presence of eelgrass in the project area, and the continued project-lifetime
dredging activity in the project area, the project conflicts with this goal and does not
adequately address mitigation measures.

See:

      c. Inaccurate framing of project activities
Overall, the mitigation measures only address construction. They do not address

      2. Fish habitat and marine ecosystem impact for operations and life of
      project not assessed

The Bay waters around the pier prior are known among sportfishing operators and
recreational fishers as fish spawning grounds. Fish populations are also migratory and
seasonal, and interact with other parts of the Bay ecosystem. A number of plan                     O10-183
elements were not discussed or mitigated in terms of their impact on fish species and
habitat and spawning:

   ● Ongoing maintenance dredging around the ferry terminal, breakwater and
     navigational channel running parallel to the existing pier for the project ferry
     route. Only construction activity seems to be addressed.
   ● The assumed ferry schedule of 28 ferry crossings per day and impact on the
     underlying marina ecosystem is not included for analysis. The DEIR concludes,
     in reference to water quality but also relevant here, that “[g]iven that Bay waters
     are naturally highly turbid and subject to pronounced fluctuations due to tidal
     action, wind-driven waves, and regional sediment transport, project-related
     turbidity would not be expected to measurably increase local or regional turbidity
     beyond baseline conditions and impacts would be less than significant.”
                                                                                                   O10-184
     (p. 3.8-30 and 423 of pdf). However, the resuspension of particulates and other
     turbulence caused by the WETA-assumed operational schedule, plus the
     cumulative impacts overall, are not analyzed for fish habitat.
   ● The original WETA plan called for a diesel ferry, while electric ferries were
     mentioned later in the process. Uncertainty remains whether an electric ferry
     would accommodate the natural conditions of the Berkeley pier, which                          O10-185
     experiences high winds and waves during much of the year. As no electric ferry
     model exists for the route and service as described, the analysis should be


                                                                                             65
                                                                                           2-336
                                         Page 441 of 1541




        reassessed on the assumption of a diesel ferry. Impacts cannot be assessed                              O10-185
        based on hypothetical conditions.

We also did not see any discussion of impact on recreational fishing, particularly in
regards to white sturgeons and halibut, which are historically popular species caught at
the Berkeley pier. A white sturgeon was recently caught from the shoreline by a night
fisherman and reported on social media for the Berkeley Bait shop. The DEIR needs to
reassess its impacts with a new project description and include analysis of all elements
of the project.

V. The DEIR fails to substantiate objectives and therefore a feasible
                                                                                                 O10-189
range of alternatives, falling short of CEQA intent


   A. EIR fails to substantiate the basic purpose or need for the ferry service as
      proposed, thereby artificially constraining the range of alternatives.                     O10-190

The DEIR has not demonstrated an underlying need for ferry service at the Berkeley
location. The Berkeley terminal is a part of several of WETA’s Network Concepts in the
Business Evaluation. However, this in and of itself does not establish a need for the
City of Berkeley, particularly when the project may not meet the narrowly defined project
objectives listed on page 5-3 of the DEIR and following.

According to the DEIR and the 2003 EIR, the project does not meet the objective of
reducing vehicle miles traveled as associated with reducing single-occupancy vehicles.
It converts recreational parking to commuter parking. There is no substantiated
                                                                                                 O10-191
evidence to say that the project is cost competitive or meets higher performance
standards than other transportation options, as noted in the Social and Economic
Benefits section of this comment document. Very little mitigation of transportation loads
is expected or demonstrable with the project. The WETA 2003 EIR shows minimal
percentage (0.07%) change in vehicle miles traveled as a consequence of ferry system
expansion systemwide, much less for new terminals, including the Berkeley terminal as
part of the overall plan. To the contrary, new terminals increase VMT (WETA 2003
EIR). This DEIR corroborates that the current project increases ADT because of
vehicles - many single-occupancy - driving to the ferry terminal located in a
                                                                                                 O10-192
low-density zone and nature-based recreational park not zoned for housing, away
from any transportation nexus, as discussed in the Recreation/Land Use impacts
section. It has not demonstrated that the project reduces VMT overall. The city’s
survey of Berkeleyans on the planned use of the ferry indicates that most will use the
ferry as an amenity, not for commuting.




                                                                                            67
                                                                                        2-338
                                     Page 443 of 1541




But the project as described in the DEIR appears to address a second objective of
restoring a recreational pier, a generally desired goal for the City of Berkeley. Since it
has not established that large-scale ferry service meets its project objectives,
                                                                                                      O10-193
alternatives under CEQA must consider alternative bluespace amenities that
legitimately increase recreation, including ferry service scaled as a recreational amenity
and recreational-only pier. These are feasible alternatives that fulfill project objectives as
well as those that fill some project objectives. By limiting the analysis to incremental
modifications of the commuter-scale ferry service for which there is unsubstantiated
need, the DEIR fails to provide a reasonable range of alternatives as required.

Here, DEIR objectives stated in Section 5 effectively predetermine the outcome of the
alternatives analysis by prioritizing a large-scale ferry-based solution that does not meet
its objectives. This approach improperly constrains the range of alternatives and
                                                                                                      O10-194
undermines CEQA’s core requirement that alternatives be capable of attaining most of
the project’s basic objectives while reducing environmental impacts. (CEQA Guidelines,
§15126.6(a).)

Cases to support these claims:

       ● City of Santee v. County of San Diego (1989) 214 Cal.App.3d 1438
       ● The court invalidated an EIR where the project objectives were framed so
       narrowly that they effectively precluded meaningful alternatives.
       ● Laurel Heights Improvement Assn. v. Regents (1988) 47 Cal.3d 376
       ● San Francisco Tomorrow v. City and County of San Francisco (2014) 229
       Cal.App.4th 498
       ● Bay-Delta Programmatic EIR (2008) 43 Cal.4th 1143
       ● Citizens of Goleta Valley v. Board of Supervisors (1990) 52 Cal.3d 553                       O10-195
       ● California Native Plant Society v. City of Santa Cruz (2009) 177 Cal.App.4th
       957 The court faulted the EIR for failing to adequately consider feasible
       alternatives raised in comments.
       ● Banning Ranch Conservancy v. City of Newport Beach (2017) 2 Cal.5th 918
       Reinforces that CEQA requires serious consideration of feasible alternatives,
       and dismissal must be supported by substantial evidence.

   B. DEIR alternatives analysis is biased towards the proposed project; it is
                                                                                                 O10-196
      unclear, unsubstantiated, shows minimal differentiation and is unrealistic.

          1. Alternative 1 “No Project” is presented in a misleading way and with
             a false baseline.

MISLEADING BASELINE. Alternative 1 No Project is inconsistent with CEQA
Guidelines §15126.6. CEQA Guidelines §15126.6(e)(2) requires that the “No Project”
Alternative be based on existing conditions and what would reasonably be expected
to occur in the foreseeable future if the project is not approved. For development               O10-197
projects, this requires analysis of the conditions under which the project does not
proceed, evaluated against a baseline grounded in existing conditions and
independently supported foreseeable changes. What is given in the DEIR is a
constrained or outcome-oriented scenario constructed to emphasize the benefits of the
proposed project. See the Baseline section of this document for exposition of existing
conditions not represented in the DEIR. Because the required CEQA No Project
Alternative is derived from the environmental baseline, any incompleteness or
distortion in the baseline necessarily carries through into the No Project analysis.
Where existing conditions are not fully and clearly established, the resulting No Project
Alternative lacks a stable evidentiary foundation for projecting reasonably foreseeable
future conditions and evaluating environmental change. These flaws undermine the
function of No Project as a reliable CEQA comparison scenario, as explained in the
Baseline section, and disqualifies the No-Project assessment.

The DEIR assumes, without substantial evidence, that environmental conditions would
worsen in the absence of the project, including increased VMT, higher emissions, and
stagnant recreational opportunities. These assumptions are speculative and do not                O10-198
meet the evidentiary standard under CEQA. (CEQA Guidelines, §15064(a).)

The DEIR also omits reasonably foreseeable improvements to the project area,
including ongoing redevelopment efforts. By artificially constraining the baseline, the
DEIR inflates the perceived benefits of the proposed project and undermines the validity         O10-199
of the alternatives comparison.

UNSUPPORTED ASSUMPTIONS. Beginning at page 5-3 of the DEIR, the analysis
assumes that the project’s absence will result in worsened environmental conditions,
including increased vehicle miles traveled, higher emissions, and static recreational
opportunities. These claims are speculative and do not meet the substantial evidence             O10-200
standard required under CEQA Guidelines §15064. Baseline conditions are such that
recreational opportunities in fact increase without the project, as explained in the
baseline section of this document. In contrast, many project elements decrease
recreation or have the potential to decrease recreation. See the Recreational and                O10-201


                                                                                            69
                                                                                        2-340
                                         Page 445 of 1541




Land Use Impact sections of this comment document. It is specious and incorrect to                              O10-201
say that no improvements would be made without the Project. As noted, there are
material precedents for such improvements. For example, the 199 Seawall site building
and parking lot is currently under an option agreement between the city and with TSA
Holdings, LLC (TSA) to renovate the building and repair the parking lot and Seawall
Drive and Bay Trail. Before its closure, Hs Lordships restaurant was heavily used as an
                                                                                                                O10-202
event space for large groups (e.g. school proms, Berkeley Public Schools Fund annual
fundraiser, family reunions, etc.). The No Project Alternative does not include any
demand forecast for this in-negotiation lease for activities developed for this location
within the project area.

This assumption is repeated across Alternatives 1–4. The No Project Alternative
therefore could maintain a lower VMT and ADT in comparison to the project and the                               O10-203
other stated alternatives, and should incorporate the 2003 EIR analysis.

EMISSIONS. The DEIR provides no mode-shift modeling, empirical substitution
analysis, or quantified travel demand data demonstrating that ferry users would                                 O10-204
otherwise drive alone across the Bay, as opposed to taking BART, for example,12 or that
ferry service is the determinative factor in regional emissions outcomes.

SPECULATIVE. Under CEQA Guidelines §15064, impact determinations must be
supported by facts, reasonable assumptions based on facts, or expert analysis
grounded in evidence. The DEIR’s reliance on speculative behavioral assumptions and
unsupported projections of future conditions fails to meet this standard. By presenting
                                                                                                                O10-205
a future No Project scenario that is not grounded in evidence, the DEIR inflates the
relative benefits of the proposed project and undermines the integrity of the alternatives
comparison required under CEQA Guidelines §15126.6.

           2. Alternatives 2–4 are not meaningfully distinct approaches.

An EIR may not limit its analysis to variations of a single project where other feasible
approaches exist. (Laurel Heights, supra, 47 Cal.3d at 400.) By failing to evaluate
fundamentally different approaches—such as alternative locations, reduced-scale
development, or non-ferry-based improvements—the DEIR does not provide the                                      O10-206
“reasonable range” required under CEQA.

SPURIOUS ALTERNATIVES. Alternatives 2, 3, and 4 do not represent meaningfully
distinct options, but instead consist of minor design variations of the same ferry-based
                                                                                                                O10-207
project. All retain the same core elements, including ferry service, project location, and

12
  Daily transbay BART passenger rides are estimated at around 60,000 to 83,000, with rush-hour use
increasing, translating to 30,000 - 41,500 roundtrips. Source: BART Ridership Reports. The WETA ferry           O10-204
project for Berkeley estimates 955 roundtrips for their base scenario used for the DEIR.

                                                                                                          70
                                                                                                        2-341
                                    Page 446 of 1541




operational assumptions, and differ only in limited features such as pier length,
breakwater configuration, or landside amenities. As a result, the DEIR does not                     010-207
evaluate alternative approaches such as eliminating ferry operations, relocating the
project, or pursuing non-ferry or recreation-focused improvements.

The descriptions are so limited that the alternatives collapse into vague variations that
are difficult to distinguish beyond the most general level. This lack of clarity prevents
meaningful evaluation and comparison, further undermining the purpose of the
                                                                                                    O10-208
alternatives analysis.

By embedding project benefits into the comparative framework and relying on
unsupported assumptions about future conditions, the DEIR effectively treats the
proposed project as the functional baseline for comparison, rather than evaluating                  O10-209
impacts relative to existing conditions and a properly defined No Project scenario.

While CEQA Guidelines §15126.6 of the California Environmental Quality Act
Guidelines Section 15126.6 does not require that alternatives be entirely different
projects, it does require a reasonable range of alternatives capable of fostering informed
decision-making and meaningful environmental comparison. Here, the alternatives
analysis fails to meet that standard because it does not evaluate fundamentally different
ways of achieving the project’s underlying objectives.                                              O10-210

By limiting the alternatives to minor variations of the same project, the DEIR constrains
the range of feasible alternatives and precludes a meaningful comparison of
environmental outcomes. This approach undermines CEQA’s purpose of ensuring that
decision-makers and the public are informed of a true range of options, rather than a
narrow set of variations that inherently favor the proposed Project.

We also note the potentially irresponsible mention of a shortened breakwater. As the
design is currently presented, the breakwater barely protects the docking platform from
south winds and has no protection from north winds. A shorter breakwater would cause                O10-211
unsafe situations. This is not a feasible alternative.

Alternative 3 envisions a ferry terminal without the pier extension. This would not
achieve the objective of recreational access. Instead, it would cede space to a WETA
ferry, to be compatible with standard WETA terminal design noted in the
Recreational/Land Use impact section of this comment document. By following this
option, Berkeley would sacrifice 100 years of pier access to the Bay for recreation                 O10-212
to support WETA business plans. Most project environmental impacts would remain
and recreation would decrease substantially from baseline, failing this project objective
for which there is a reasonably substantiated need.



                                                                                              71
                                                                                            2-342
                                    Page 447 of 1541




Therefore, Alternatives 2, 3, and 4 do not constitute a reasonable range of alternatives
capable of informing environmental decision-making under CEQA Guidelines §15126.6.
Instead, they function as incremental design variations of a predetermined project.
                                                                                                      O10-213
Accordingly, the DEIR fails to provide adequate alternatives analysis: it does not present
a meaningful spectrum of project options that could avoid or substantially reduce
environmental impacts.

       C. Reasonable alternatives rejected and no valid range of options

CEQA Guidelines §15126.6 requires an EIR to evaluate a reasonable range of feasible
alternatives that could achieve most of the project’s basic objectives while reducing
environmental impacts. §15126.6(c) requires that the EIR “identify any alternatives…
that were rejected as infeasible… and briefly explain the reasons.” The purpose of this
requirement is to ensure informed decision-making through meaningful comparison of                    O10-214
different project options. The DEIR does not satisfy this requirement. The DEIR fails to
articulate a need for the ferry commuter service. For waterfront access and recreation
as an objective, the DEIR purports to restore a recreational pier. Yet, the DEIR has
improperly screened out reasonable alternatives of a pier-only option and ignored other
ferry terminal options, contributing to its constrained alternatives analysis. In this
situation, public comments suggesting broader or different feasible alternatives become
especially important, and agencies must address them.

          1. DEIR does not adequately explore pier-no ferry alternative
Analogous to the ferry-only pier Alternative 3, the DEIR should include a pier-only
alternative consisting of a 500’ or longer public access pier without a ferry.

The DEIR provides no explanation for why a pier-only (without ferry) alternative was
excluded, even though funding needs for Berkeley would be much less. The DEIR does
not evaluate a pier-only alternative, and provides no explanation as to why it does not,
despite substantial evidence that such an alternative is feasible and would meet key
                                                                                                      O10-215
objectives related to public access and recreation while avoiding ferry-related impacts.

It would achieve the first project objective, i.e., repairing and extending the pier. By
ignoring a pier-only alternative as in fact feasible, meeting recreation and public access
objectives while reducing ferry-related impacts, the DEIR fails to provide a meaningful
comparison or rationale for rejecting alternatives, thereby limiting informed
decision-making and public participation.

A pier-without-ferry option was in fact funded by a state grant of $15 million for pier and
                                                                                                      O10-216
marina infrastructure. Funding was diverted to other uses; however, the fact remains
that potential funding options exist. The GHD engineering firm has already provided

                                                                                                72
                                                                                              2-343
                                   Page 448 of 1541




COB with a feasibility study of replacing the existing pier. COB (2021) states that
replacing the existing structure alone with a 2,000-foot pier would cost $26 million (and
to 3,000 feet, around $32-$44 million). City staff have indicated in public meetings that
                                                                                                 O10
COB’s share of the waterside costs alone for the pier/ferry project would be                       -
approximately $26 million. Therefore, a reopened pier up to 2,000’ at least, without a           216
ferry, is a feasible alternative. While WETA, COB and GHD estimates can be
updated, a recreational pier without ferry service is a feasible option for COB.

Research and reports indicate a large increase in public demand if the pier were
reopened and a basic functional facility maintained for fishing, walking, and cycling.
Data by Antinori et al. (2025) (provided to the city prior to NOP date) and peer-reviewed
in Antinori et al. (2026), predicted a restored pier alone would see a 96% increase in
annual average visitation among anglers. Breaking this into income categories, the               O10-
                                                                                                 217
predicted increases are 70%, 88% and 114% for low, medium and high-income anglers.
These increases are above baseline for the recreational pier-alone alternative. The
benefits of this option should be considered against the DEIR project and its
environmental impacts.

          2. Rejected in-marina alternatives
The Berkeley Waterfront Community Coalition (BWCC), in scoping comments, asked
city staff to analyze in-marina locations. They rejected the option based on the WETA
2008 Berkeley/Albany Ferry Terminal Study Draft EIS/EIR prepared by URS that
configured a terminal and new dock next to the Hornblower docks. The DEIR fails to
consider any other reasonable configurations or locations that reduce environmental              O10-
impacts. This version of the in-marina alternative from the 2008 WETA EIR functions              218
much like a “straw man” in the current analysis. Other options exist. Hornblower docks
next to the DoubleTree Hotel are one option. These docks are an underused space.
See image below. The DEIR dismissed this alternative without analysis. The image
below by Paul Kamen shows cost as well as impact comparisons.




                                                                                            73
                                                                                        2-344
                                   Page 449 of 1541




                                                                                                 O10-
                                                                                                 218




Another possibility is the K-dock slips used by the Genentech and Tidelines ferries. This
is a central location in the Marina and adds only two minutes’ travel time to San
Francisco, based on the Genentech ferry departures/arrivals, excluding docking
maneuver time. Tidelines was a private company operating under a public grant which              O10-
                                                                                                 219
ran twice in the morning and twice in the afternoon. The Genentech ferry ran a similar
schedule. Neither posed major interference with marina traffic. These ferries blended
into marina activity without costly investments. All that was lacking was regular parking
enforcement to restrict ferry patron parking to their designated Marina Boulevard
location.

BWCC scoping comments asked: “Data on current usage by Genentech ferry and
previous usage of Tidelines ferry ridership must be made available publicly for the
report for a feasibility comparison of a small commuter ferry service operating in
Berkeley.” This data was not provided, although it was requested prior to the DEIR               O10-
issuance. This data would assist in decision-making on the viability of in-marina                220
service.



                                                                                            74
                                                                                        2-345
                                   Page 450 of 1541




This alternative also meshes with WETA’s Tack-to-Wind business outlook, under which             O10-220
WETA focuses on recreational instead of weekday commuter use, reflecting most
Berkeleyans’ pattern of usage.

An in-marina terminal was in fact assumed for the first assessment of the Berkeley-SF
WETA ferry route in 2003. In Figure 5.1.1 and Table 5.1.5 of that 2003 EIR, it is
estimated that dredging for a Berkeley/Albany service would only require 13,260 cubic
yards of dredging, implying an in-marina terminal. Under these options, the in-marina
alternative still meets the objective of enhanced recreation with transportation options
for commuter service through a potentially modified weekday schedule. Reduced CEQA
and COB impacts include:                                                                        O10-221
       ● Reduced dredging and shared WETA/COB marina maintenance costs
       ● Lower project costs and potentially greater revenue generator for Berkeley
       ● Access to a ferry consistent with demand
       ● Reduced environmental impacts on water quality, acoustics, biological and
       aesthetic resources

VI. Social and economic benefits to Berkeley contextualized for
decisionmaking

   A. Social and economic context relevant to DEIR
                                                                                                O10-222
In response to BWCC scoping comments, the DEIR says that “Economic factors are not
an environmental impact of CEQA. This comment will be considered by the City
decision-makers as part of the project approval process.” In fact, the DEIR relies at
several points on economic or social benefits to deliver its analysis:
    ● P. 447 of pdf and 3.9-10 says there will be positive economic and social benefits
       to dismiss public comment.
    ● P. 452 of pdf to claim consistency with BCDC Climate Change Policy 7                      O10-223
    ● Address Berkeley Marina Master Plan Consistency Principle 5 to enhance
       access and use of the Marina, especially for elderly, economically disadvantaged
       or physically challenged persons (p. 469 of pdf).                                        O10-224

It is also worth noting social and economic impacts because of the lead agency’s
authority to override significant environmental impacts and mitigation measures based
on claims of economic and social benefits:

                                                                                                O10-225
   ● Page 1-15: Lead Agency Project Decision. The lead agency may a) disapprove
     of the proposed project because of its significant environmental effects; b)
     require changes to the proposed project to reduce or avoid significant
     environmental effects; or c) approve the proposed project despite its significant

                                                                                           75
                                                                                        2-346
                                   Page 451 of 1541




     environmental effects, if the proper findings and statement of overriding
     considerations are adopted (CEQA Guidelines Sections 15042 and 15043).
   ● Findings/Statement of Overriding Considerations. For each significant impact
     of the proposed project identified in the EIR, the lead agency must find, based on
     substantial evidence, that either: a) the proposed project has been changed to
     avoid or substantially reduce the magnitude of the impact; b) changes to the                 O10-225
     proposed project are within another agency’s jurisdiction and such changes have
     been or should be adopted; or c) specific economic, social, or other
     considerations make the mitigation measures or proposed project alternatives
     infeasible (CEQA Guidelines Section 15091). If an agency approves a project
     with unavoidable significant environmental effects, it must prepare a written
     Statement of Overriding Considerations that sets forth the specific social,
     economic, or other reasons supporting the agency’s decision.

In this section we review social and economic factors to provide context to the project
and better inform decisionmaking.
                                                                                                  O10-226
   B. Weak evidence of economic or social benefits to Berkeley

   1. WETA service economic and cumulative impacts
There is no evidence to support the claim of net positive economic and social benefits to
Berkeley, although there is evidence to support the opposite conclusion. From the
WETA Business Plan Evaluation, April 12, 2023, Summary of Network Concepts pages
2-6 of report, WETA lists the following visions for expansion:

   1. Existing Network: 10 terminals
   2. Plan Bay Area Network: 14 terminals
   3. Core Network: 18 terminals
   4. Coverage Network: 26 terminals

Plans 2-4 offer some form of Berkeley/Albany/Emeryville ferry service but the                     O10-227
cumulative impacts are considerable, and are not fully discussed in the DEIR, as noted
above. Compared to the existing 10-terminal network, the Coverage Network shows
worse cumulative environmental impact, worse financial capacity, and worse
productivity (Business Plan Evaluation, Table 8). The plan continues to outline four
business future outlooks for the year 2050 (Table 2), with two based on pre-pandemic
ridership levels (Steady as it Goes and Chart a New Course) and two with 30%
reduction in commuter travel (Throttle Back and Tack to the Wind). They have no
probabilities assigned to each scenario.




                                                                                            76
                                                                                          2-347
                                      Page 452 of 1541




Across all four of WETA’s 2050 ridership outlook scenarios, the existing network
remains the most productive, and operating costs per passenger-mile are highest under
Coverage Network in every scenario. It is clear that we are not on a "new course."
BART itself has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. Even under the "Throttle Back"
scenario, operating costs jump substantially over the existing system. If anything,
current outlooks appear to be most aligned with the “Tack-to-Wind” scenario that                   O10-227
envisions as follows for WETA: 30% reduction of commuter travel but in order “to
diversify its ridership base, WETA would expand its midday and off-peak and weekend
service offerings, align its fares with other regional operators, and substantially enhance
access to ferry terminals” (p.8 of 29), i.e. an amenity ferry.
The Berkeley terminal would require subsidies from general public and Berkeley funds
costing more than twice as much per passenger as the existing bus network. Kamen
calculated from WETA’s 2024–2025 budget that WETA annually delivers 2.57 million
one-way rides at an actual cost of $61.60 each, with fares recovering 8.9% of cost and
a public subsidy of $56.10 per ride. AC Transit, by contrast, delivers 34.6 million
one-way bus rides annually at a cost of $25.20 each, with farebox recovery of 3.4% and
a subsidy of $24.30 per ride.

                                                                                          2-348
                                    Page 453 of 1541




The economic costs to Berkeley should be kept in mind. WETA’s Berkeley ferry
business plan describes local funding as a source of capital and operating funds for
several currently existing routes as well as for the Berkeley route. The ferry project's
                                                                                                      O10-229
paid parking plans, currently being considered within the city, rely on recreational users
to defray the city's costs of maintaining the ferry project's infrastructure and operations
and will depress recreational visitation.

Historically, Berkeley ferries have failed. Tidelines commuter ferry service, which
operated from inside the Marina, has not returned after the pandemic. Genentech
closed its employee ferry to the Oyster Point campus as too expensive and replaced it                 O10-230
with buses. In planning meetings (e.g. BCDC’s DRB), staff have already discussed
reducing the project from two docks to one. Unlike the Richmond and Vallejo routes —
where ferry service saves commuters substantial time from the North and East Bay — a
Berkeley-to-San Francisco ferry would take about the same time as BART, with a
first-mile/last-mile problem BART does not have.

       2. Transportation Impact TRA-2 conclusion not substantiated
The DEIR (pdf p. 555), for justifying Impact TRA-2, asserts without substantiation that
West Berkeley residents, who have more limited public transit options, will experience
                                                                                                      O10-231
increased employment in higher-paying San Francisco and San Mateo county jobs
because of the ferry service. The justification is based on social and economic benefits.
As the basis for an impact finding, we would ask for more analysis. According to
Census data, West Berkeley (a SB535 community) on average is lower income than the
rest of Berkeley. The WETA 2022 Passenger Survey Report reports that ferry riders are
historically concentrated in higher income brackets, with large shares reporting
household incomes above $100,000. This has changed. In 2017, only 6% of riders
earned under $50,000 per year; pandemic-era fare reforms drastically reduced fares                    O10-232
and raised that share to roughly 19% by 2021, and WETA’s 2022 annual report
describes a “significantly increased percentage of low-income riders.” Even so,
higher-income riders remain overrepresented, and Seamless Bay Area continues to
characterize the rider base as “white-collar commuters paying a premium fare relative to
BART or bus.” Was 2017-2021 shift due only to low fares available during the pandemic
and does the WETA budget now include subsidies that will keep fares at pandemic-level
lows to maintain this distributional profile? On existing evidence and without further                O10-233
analysis, we would assume the Berkeley terminal would still disproportionately serve a
high-income profile for commuter needs. Finally, we note again that the city’s public
questionnaire on ferry service indicated higher usage of the ferry as an amenity rather
than as a commuter option. The questionnaire was made available to the public via the                 O10-234
local online newspaper Berkeleyside and councilmember newsletters. Berkeleyside
readership matches Berkeley’s demographic profile, according to its documents (see
Attachments).
For social and economic benefits, decisionmaking should also weigh a substantiated
impact under TRA-2 with the distribution of social and economic benefits. Visitors to the
southern Berkeley waterfront — the area the project most directly affects — are on


                                                                                                78
                                                                                                      l
                                                                                                      O10-235




                                                                                              2-349
                                   Page 454 of 1541




average lower-income than visitors to other waterfront areas and already value the
                                                                                                  O10-235
waterfront for its recreational value.

      3. Secondary benefits are aspirational
The Keyser Marston analysis commissioned by the City is the most substantive
statement of the project’s secondary economic benefits. It is cautious. The study
projects “very modest contributions to Marina Fund — perhaps may generate up to
10% of any revenues the city receives from food and beverage consumer spending”
(Keyser Marston, 2021, pp. 8–9). Its strongest forward-looking statement is the hope
that a large-scale ferry with weekend service might attract an additional hotel.                  O10-236

The experience of the existing WETA terminal at Jack London Square in Oakland
counsels against this hope. The surrounding commercial area has struggled with a
substantial vacancy rate despite the operating ferry, and the Waterfront Hotel — 145
rooms, a short walk from the terminal — closed in January 2025. The City’s own public
outreach in the 2021 community survey found that 60% of respondents would never
use the ferry to commute, and 56% would rarely/never use it for leisure or would use it
fewer than ten times per year.

      4. High business risk potential
A commuter ferry vessel operating approximately 28 daily crossings, designed against a
ridership estimate of >2000 (with Mission Bay service) and capacity to handle 4000 in
more extreme business scenarios, represents a substantial capital commitment against
uncertain demand. The risk of stranded assets is real, and would fall on both WETA and            O10-237
COB.
There is option value in waiting. WETA’s own planning allows it to expand where the fit
is better — where ferry service meaningfully reduces transbay commute times, the
environmental cost is lower, and rider base already exists. Berkeley is not that place
today, and the evidence suggests it may not be for some time.
If approved, the WETA terminal would be the only terminal in the WETA system located
within a pre-existing public park with long-established recreational use. Many families           O10-238
and seniors rely on this area for affordable recreation and access to the
water—activities widely recognized as contributing to physical and mental
well-being. Data indicate that visitors to the southern waterfront are, on average,
lower-income than visitors to other waterfront areas not affected by the ferry proposal,
which appears to serve a narrow ridership demographic. State grants for the marina
area and pier were awarded on the condition that they were to be used for
recreational purposes. Prior city planners advised comprehensive waterfront planning.             O10-239
In contrast, the current process divides the WETA pier-ferry project from all other
waterfront planning as represented in the stalled Waterfront Specific Plan.

The marina is already designated for transportation uses, as demonstrated by previous
                                                                                                  O10-240
ferry services operating there, including Prop SF, Tidelines and most recently,

                                                                                            79
                                                                                          2-350
                                    Page 455 of 1541




Genentech. Displacement of recreational uses is not necessary to accommodate
in-marina ferry service if Berkeley wants to support WETA’s ferry service plans outlined           O10-240
in the “Tack-to-Wind” post-pandemic scenario.

The Berkeley Waterfront Community Coalition therefore recommends that the City
rescind, reevaluate and reissue the DEIR and give careful analysis to the alternatives,            O10-241
including restoration of the recreational pier without ferry service, and to a feasible
range of project alternatives that do not impose adverse economic and social impacts
for the region nor impose CEQA impacts to subsidize a costly and underused commuter
transit mode.

VII. Conclusion

The project will have a number of potentially significant impacts on the environment,
including (but not limited to) impacts on special status biological resources, critical            O10-242
habitats, aesthetics, public access, land use and culturally significant resources. As the
project description, setting and baselines were improperly set, these impacts and others           O10-243
were not adequately analyzed and mitigated in the DEIR. Feasible alternatives with
lower environmental impacts were rejected. As a result, the DEIR fails to serve as an              O10-244
adequate informational document and its conclusions are not supported by substantial
evidence. For the foregoing reasons, BWCC urges the Council to delay further                       O10-245
consideration of the project unless and until the city prepares and recirculates a revised
DEIR that fully complies with CEQA and the CEQA Guidelines.

Respectfully,

Berkeley Waterfront Community Coalition

Visitation to south v. north areas of waterfront, by income
Consistent with the public’s general understanding and earlier city-led focus groups, we define the waterfront’s geographic areas as follows:

          • “South” refers to South Cove East and West lots, J&K, L&M, Skates/N, O lot, and Seawall Drive. Data points from the 199 Seawall next
            to the derelict HsL restaurant in the south part of the waterfront are currently not included as the lot’s gates are usually locked during
            the weekdays on which the respondents’ data was collected, indicating the data may be in error. We are seeking clarification from city
            staff and will update as we receive more information
          • “North” refers to D&E, the launch ramps, Spinnaker Way and Spinnaker Circle.
          • “Other” includes any response not in “north” or “south” above.

The barchart below indicates a tendency for the south area in aggregate to attract lower income visitors more than other parts of the waterfront.
While north and other have similar breakdowns of lower income (defined as <$75k) and higher income (defined as >=$75k), the south area has
more lower and less higher income as a percentage.

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in Section 3.11, Recreation,
and 3.12, Transportation, of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O10-9
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives, for a discussion of project objectives and its
alternatives analyses.

Response to Comment O10-10
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives (Project Objectives subsection), which clarifies that
the City’s inclusion of ferry service as a core objective is consistent with a long-standing and well-
documented interagency effort to establish ferry service at the Berkeley Waterfront and expand water
transit service in the Bay Area. Therefore, the objectives appropriately define the purpose of the project
consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15124.
The Draft EIR appropriately defines project objectives and evaluates environmental impacts
independently of those objectives, consistent with CEQA requirements. The analysis, significance
conclusions, and mitigation measures presented throughout the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no
revisions to the Draft EIR are required in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-11
The comment that the Draft EIR fails to adequately analyze the ferry component of the project or its
associated environmental impacts is not correct. The Draft EIR includes a comprehensive, project-level
evaluation of ferry operations and infrastructure across all relevant resource areas, consistent with CEQA
requirements. This analysis is based on the Project Description provided in Chapter 2 and evaluates both
construction and operational impacts in Chapter 3, supported by technical studies and substantial
evidence in the record.
With respect to comments about improvements being attributed to the project, the Draft EIR establishes
the environmental baseline in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15125 and evaluates the
project’s incremental contribution to recreational access and facilities. Refer to Response to Comments
O10-47 to O10-49 for a discussion of specific recreational improvements identified in the comment letter.
Regarding alternatives, Chapter 5, Alternatives, evaluates a reasonable range of feasible alternatives
consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6. The Draft EIR also includes a discussion of
alternatives considered but rejected, including the reasons for their dismissal based on feasibility,
environmental considerations, and the ability to meet project objectives. The comment’s suggested pier
restoration or replacement approaches are either encompassed within the alternatives screening process
or would not meet the fundamental objectives of the project, as described in Sections 5.3 and 5.9 (Pages
5-2 and 5-25 through 5-28 of the Draft EIR). CEQA does not require evaluation of every conceivable
alternative, but rather a reasonable range sufficient to inform decision makers. For additional information
about how alternatives were considered consistent with CEQA, refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response:
Alternatives.
The analysis, significance conclusions, mitigation measures, and discussion of alternatives presented in
the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no revisions to the Draft EIR are required in response to this
comment.

Response to Comment O10-12
As discussed in Section 2.2.5, Topical Response: CEQA Adequacy, the City has concluded that the Draft
EIR is sufficient from a CEQA perspective. No further response is required.
For responses to specific issues raised in the comment letter, please refer to the following Response to
Comments.

Response to Comment O10-13
The comment is referring to later specific comments which are responded to in subsequent Response to
Comments. Refer to Section 2.2.22, Topical Response: Project Cost/Financial Feasibility, for a discussion
related to economic considerations within CEQA documents.
This comment has been included in the project record considered by City decision makers. No further
response is required.

Response to Comment O10-14
CEQA Guidelines Section 15124 requires that an EIR include a project description containing sufficient
detail to allow evaluation of environmental impacts, including the project’s location, objectives, and
general characteristics. The Draft EIR includes these required elements in Chapter 2, Project Description,
including Section 2.1 (Project Location and Setting), Section 2.3 (Project Objectives), Section 2.5 (Proposed
Project Components), and Section 2.6 (Construction Details), as well as a description of operational
characteristics in Section 2.7.
The Draft EIR project description represents the current and reasonably foreseeable project design at the
time of preparation and provides a stable and comprehensive basis for environmental analysis. To the
extent that earlier project concepts were presented during the Notice of Preparation (NOP) and scoping
process at a more conceptual level, the refinement of project details reflected in the Draft EIR is a normal
and expected part of the CEQA process and does not indicate an unstable or shifting project description.
Rather, the Draft EIR provides a more fully developed and detailed description consistent with CEQA
Guidelines requirements.
Refer to subsequent response to comments for responses to specific issues raised in the comment
letter. The analysis, significance conclusions, mitigation measures, and discussion of alternatives
presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no revisions to the Draft EIR are required in
response to this comment.

Refer to Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry.

Response to Comment O10-17

sufficient details in the Project Description according to CEQA requirements, including a description of
electric ferry infrastructure and emergency operations.

Response to Comment O10-21
First as a matter of clarification, the comment incorrectly describes TDM Measures as mitigation. As
explained in Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, TDM Measures are not mitigation measures
because there are no environmental impacts under CEQA that would require mitigation in the form of
TDM.
Chapter 2, Project Description of the Draft EIR describes the physical improvements that could result on a
physical impact on the environment, including those physical improvements that provide TDM benefits
such as enhanced bicycle facilities and secure bike parking; improved bicycle and pedestrian access
including a two-way cycle track along University Avenue and Bay Trail improvements; designated pick-up
and drop-off zones; and wayfinding that would direct visitors to appropriate parking lots. All of these
features are described in Chapter 2, Project Description (refer to pages 2-11 to 2-22 of the Draft EIR).
Thus, the characterization that the Draft EIR has omitted information about TDM is incorrect. The
analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as
written, and no further revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment O10-37
The comment provides information regarding user opinions and preferences. Under CEQA, the purpose of
an EIR is to evaluate environmental effects on physical conditions, not user perceptions or preferences
(CEQA Guidelines §15382). As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, Subsection 2.3, Project
Objectives, enhancing public pier facilities and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront are
key objectives of the proposed project. Chapter 2 further states in Subsection 2.5.1, Waterside, that the
project would incorporate amenities that would directly support fishing at the Waterfront, including the
development of a new pier and breakwater with safety railings, a fish cleaning station, seating, shade
canopy, and security gates, which would remain open to the public, except in cases where public safety
requires closure (refer to Page 2-6). Accordingly, the analysis provides in Section 3.11, Recreation,
evaluates potential impacts to recreation and concludes that the project would provide a net increase in
recreational opportunities, including restored fishing access (refer to Impact REC-1, Pages 3.11-16
through 3.11-20). Additionally, Section 3.3, Biological Resources, Subsection 3.3.4, Impacts Analysis,
evaluates potential impacts on marine wildlife, including fish species. The analysis therein concludes that
impacts to fish species would be less than significant with mitigation incorporated (refer to Pages 3.3-39
through 3.3-66).
This comment does not provide supporting arguments, data, or analysis to substantiate concerns related
to impacts on fish behavior. Accordingly, no changes are warranted to the Draft EIR analysis, conclusions,
or mitigation, and no further response is required.

summary of the CEQA process. Prior to making a decision on the proposed project, the City must certify
that the Final EIR was presented to the Berkeley City Council and that they reviewed and considered the
information in the Final EIR prior to making a decision about approving the project, consistent with CEQA
Guidelines Section 15090. As discussed in CEQA Guidelines Section 15093, agencies must balance the
various benefits of a project, such as economic, legal, social, technological, and larger-scale
environmental benefits, with the potential environmental impacts associated with the project when
making their decision. No further response is required.

Response to Comment O10-44
As described in Response to Comment O10-43, the Draft EIR relies upon the best available information at
the time of the Notice of Preparation (April 18, 2025) to define baseline conditions. At the time of Notice
of Preparation, the referenced closure and repairs were ongoing and the project was identified as a
cumulative project because completion and reopening of the facility was reasonably foreseeable prior to
implementation of the proposed project (refer to Table 3-1, page 3-9 of the Draft EIR).
The City acknowledges that the South Cove East Dock reopened in September 2025 after publication of
the Notice of Preparation and prior to preparation of the Final EIR. Accordingly, in response to this
comment Draft EIR Table 3-1, Present and Reasonably Foreseeable Cumulative Projects List, has been
revised to update the project status. Please refer to Response to Comment O10-43, which includes this
revision as well as additional clarifying revisions in response to similar comments.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid
as written. Aside from the clarifying revision to Table 3-1, no further revisions to the Draft EIR are
necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-45
Refer to Section 2.2.9, Topical Response: Cumulative Impacts, and Section 2.2.20, Topical Response:
Parking, for discussions regarding the cumulative impact assessment methodology and parking
considerations as they relate to CEQA analysis.
The City acknowledges that, following publication of the Notice of Preparation, the Berkeley City Council
approved implementation of parking fees at the South Cove East, South Cove West, and J/K parking lots.
The fee program was scheduled to take effect beginning January 1, 2026, and would apply to more than
200 parking spaces within these lots. The program involves placement of parking fee collection
equipment and associated payment kiosks that would be placed on existing concrete surfaces. Public
Resource Code 21065 provides the following definition for a project: “ ’Project’ means an activity which
may cause either a direct physical change in the environment, or a reasonably foreseeable indirect
physical change in the environment…” The implementation of parking fees does not meet this definition
pursuant to CEQA; therefore, the fee program identified by the commenter does not meet the definition of
a cumulative project.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid.
No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-46
Page 3-6 of the Draft EIR defined reasonably foreseeable projects as follows: “Reasonably foreseeable
future projects are defined as those likely to occur during the same period of time as construction and
operation of the project and that could contribute to the cumulative impact on a particular environmental
resource. Reasonably foreseeable projects are future projects (including those currently proposed) that
are likely or probable, rather than those that are merely possible. Generally, projects are reasonably
foreseeable if they meet any one or more of the following conditions:
• The project is a foreseeable future phase of an existing project.
• Applications for project entitlements or construction are pending with a government agency (these
  projects may have been analyzed in a recent environmental document).
• The project is included in regional transportation plans; regional transportation improvement programs;
  local long-range transportation plans; local land use, general, and specific plans; or an agency’s budget
  or capital improvement program.”

Funding commitments alone do not constitute a reasonably foreseeable cumulative project. When it
comes to Measure FF, a cumulative project would need to be a specific project located near the project



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                     2- 383
                                                       Page 488 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                                           Response to Comments

site that is reasonably foreseeable and not just merely possible. The comment has not identified a
specific cumulative project that is funded through Measure FF that would constitute a cumulative project.
The City’s Measure FF webpage identifies two specific funded projects, including the Replacing Traffic
Barriers with Planter Boxes project and the Outdoor Warning System: Emergency Siren Network project. 34
The planter box project involves replacement of existing traffic barriers at locations including
Woolsey/Hillegass, Fulton/Ashby, and Harmon/California. 35 The emergency siren project involves
installation of warning sirens at various locations throughout Berkeley. 36 Neither project is located within
the project vicinity, involves bicycle recreation facilities, nor would contribute to recreation-related
cumulative impacts associated with the proposed project. In addition, neither project would provide the
type of bicycle facility improvements referenced in the comment. Accordingly, these Measure FF-funded
projects do not constitute cumulative projects relevant to the recreation analysis for the proposed
project.
The comment has not identified any specific bicycle improvement project funded through Measure FF.
The general existence of Measure FF funding itself does not provide evidence that a reasonably
foreseeable recreation or transportation project should be added to the cumulative projects list or
discussed as an alternative recreational facility within the EIR. For further discussion regarding the
identification of cumulative projects and cumulative analysis under CEQA, refer to Section 2.2.9, Topical

conditions and evaluates the project’s contribution to cumulative impacts consistent with CEQA
Guidelines. Accordingly, the analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the
Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this
comment.

    Open space is a broad term for undeveloped land that provides public access, while a park is a

    playgrounds, sports fields, and paved paths, whereas open spaces can be more natural and less
    developed areas like forests, farms, or grasslands. Both open space and parks can be publicly owned

    facility is a specific, human-made structure or area designed for a particular recreational activity and
    can include elements such as parks and picnic sites, pathways and trails, boating docks, community

Response to Comment O10-55
As identified on Page 3.11-1, Section 3.11, Recreation, of the Draft EIR, the park acreage ratio is 34.5 acres
per 1,000 residents. As described therein, the City has a total of 4,430 acres of public parks and open
space within City limits, spanning 52 parks (and associated buildings, parking lots, and play areas), 21 turf
medians, 75 developed paths, 40 undeveloped paths, the Berkeley Marina, and 310 acres of parklands, as
well as portions of the 1,833-acre McLaughlin Eastshore State Park, the 2,079-acre East Bay Regional
Park District Tilden Regional Park, and 209-Claremont Canyon Regional preserve. The acreage of these
parks and open space resources was obtained from publicly available information published by the
agencies that manage these facilities, including the City of Berkeley General Plan, the City of Berkeley
Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Department website, and the East Bay Regional Park District website.
These publicly available acreage figures represent the agencies’ characterization of the recreational
resources they manage and therefore provide a reasonable basis for evaluating existing park and
recreation resources, as well as calculating the park acreage ratio presented in the Draft EIR. The total of
4,430 acres of parks and open space and a population of 128,348 residents in 2025 equates to 0.0345
acres per person, or 34.5 acres per 1,000 residents when multiplied by a factor of 1,000 to achieve the
standard metric of acreage per 1,000 residents. which results in a total of 34.5 acres per 1,000 residents.
The calculation of park acreage per resident is consistent with the City’s methodology of identifying park
acreage per resident. In addition, the Draft EIR does not rely solely on the park acreage ratio to evaluate
impacts. As discussed within Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis, the Draft EIR evaluates whether the project
would increase the use of existing recreational facilities such that substantial deterioration would occur
or be accelerated (refer to Impact REC-1). Based on the information presented therein, the Draft EIR
identifies that the project would improve and expand recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront
through the construction of new public amenities, including Bay Trail improvements, waterfront access
enhancements, public open space features, viewing areas, seating areas, and related recreational
infrastructure. As such, the Draft EIR concludes that the project would add recreational resources and
improve public access rather than reducing recreational opportunities available to residents, and
accordingly concludes that impacts would be less than significant. No change to the Draft EIR or other
response is necessary.

Response to Comment O10-57
As discussed in Section 3.11, Recreation, the Draft EIR evaluates environmental impacts to recreational
resources consistent with CEQA Guidelines, which focus on physical environmental conditions and
effects. CEQA does not require characterization of user demographics unless such information is
necessary to evaluate whether a project would result in a physical environmental impact. Accordingly, the
recreational baseline focuses on the location, capacity, and function of recreational facilities and access,
which are the relevant factors for evaluating potential physical deterioration or the need for expanded
facilities (see Draft EIR Section 3.11.4).
While socioeconomic considerations such as environmental justice are not a resource requiring
evaluation under CEQA, the City continues to consider such issues through its broader planning and
policy efforts, including its General Plan Environmental Justice Element. The Environmental Justice
Technical Report describes how the City engaged with Environmental Justice communities in its
extensive public engagement efforts and how that input helped to inform project design.
As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description (see Section 2.5, Proposed Project Components),
and Section 3.11, Recreation (see Impact REC-1), the project would expand recreational opportunities and
improve public access to the waterfront through new and enhanced facilities, including shoreline access,
a restored pier, public open space, and multimodal connections. These improvements would benefit a
diverse range of users and increase overall accessibility.
The Draft EIR evaluates environmental impacts to physical recreational resources consistent with CEQA
Guidelines, which do not require demographic analysis unless tied to physical environmental impacts. For
additional discussion of baseline adequacy, refer to Section 2.2.6, Topical Response: CEQA
Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions are required.

SB 1000 (Government Code Section 65302(h)) requires local jurisdictions to address environmental
justice in their General Plans, including through the preparation of an Environmental Justice Element or
equivalent policies for disadvantaged communities. SB 1000 applies to the preparation or update of
General Plans and does not establish a separate CEQA significance threshold for individual development
projects. The proposed project is not a General Plan amendment or General Plan update, and therefore,
the requirements of SB 1000 do not apply to the proposed project. Nevertheless, environmental justice
considerations were incorporated into the planning process for the proposed project. As summarized in
Draft EIR Section 1.2.2, Public Outreach, the City conducted extensive public outreach in 2025, including
engagement with community organizations and groups representing historically underserved populations
(see Draft EIR pages 1-4 and 1-5). In addition, the City prepared the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier
Ferry Environmental Justice Existing Conditions and Constraints Technical Study, which was cited within
Draft EIR Section 1.2.2 and made publicly available as part of the environmental review process 37, to
evaluate environmental justice conditions in the project vicinity.
The Draft EIR evaluates the project’s consistency with applicable local and regional plans, including
policies related to public access and recreation, within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning (see Impact LU-
2), and evaluates potential physical environmental impacts that could affect surrounding communities,
throughout Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, and identifies mitigation measures as appropriate.
The analysis therein did not identify substantial evidence that the proposed project would result in

Response to Comment O10-59
SB 535 established a framework for identifying disadvantaged communities for purposes of directing
portions of State climate-investment funding to communities experiencing disproportionate
environmental burdens, with the goal of improving public health, quality of life, and economic
opportunities while reducing climate-related pollution. 38 However, SB 535 does not establish independent
CEQA significance thresholds, create environmental justice analysis requirements under CEQA, or
otherwise modify the standards used to determine the significance of environmental impacts under
CEQA.
Although SB 535 does not impose CEQA requirements, the proposed project would generally support
many of the policy objectives associated with State identification of and investment in disadvantaged
communities. As described throughout the Draft EIR, the proposed project would expand public access to
the Berkeley Waterfront through construction of a public pier and breakwater, improved bicycle and
pedestrian connections including a new cycle track and Bay Trail Extension, enhanced public transit
facilities, and new public amenities (refer to Draft EIR Section 2.5, Proposed Project Components). In
addition, the proposed project would provide a new zero-emission transportation option connecting
Berkeley to regional job centers while reducing greenhouse gas emissions and supporting multimodal
mobility. The project would provide public health benefits through reduced greenhouse gas emissions
and expanded opportunities for active transportation, including improved bicycle and pedestrian
infrastructure and supporting amenities that promote walking, bicycling, and transit use while improving
access to the Berkeley Waterfront. Furthermore, WETA has identified the surrounding community as
having comparatively limited transit access and a greater concentration of lower-income and historically
underserved populations. 39 Accordingly, the proposed zero-emission ferry service would improve
connectivity between the community and higher-paying regional job centers throughout the Bay Area
while advancing the goals of SB 535 to improve public health and economic opportunity in disadvantaged
communities.
However, the fact that nearby communities may be identified as disadvantaged communities under SB
535 does not create a separate CEQA impact category or significance threshold. Rather, potential
environmental impacts of the proposed project are evaluated in the Draft EIR using the significance
criteria established under CEQA. Consistent with that analysis, the project would not result in
disproportionately severe adverse physical environmental impacts on disadvantaged communities.
For further discussion of how the Draft EIR evaluates consistency with applicable plans and policies,
including those related to public access and recreation, refer to Response to Comment O10-58 and to
Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency. The analysis, significance conclusions, and
mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no revisions are required.

Response to Comment O10-62
Page 3.11-7, Section 3.11, Recreation (Section 3.11.3, Regulatory Framework), states that Section 4(f)
would only apply should project implementation involve federal funding. The comment is incorrect. CEQA
compliance often occurs independently of NEPA compliance. NEPA compliance is required if the project
has a federal nexus such as federal funding, requirement for a federal permit, or the use of federal land. In
this instance, the project has not yet received any federal funding. It is likely that the project will require
NEPA clearance when pursuing federal permits from National Marine Fisheries Service or U.S. Army
Corps of Engineers (USACE). At that time, the federal lead agency would determine the NEPA pathway for
environmental compliance. In summary, CEQA does not require an analysis of Section 4(f) impacts, and
no change to the Draft EIR or other response is necessary.

    evaluation.43 Additionally, the updated 2025 Berkeley Pier evaluation considered the Berkeley Pier
    within its broader historical context, including its relationship to the Berkeley Marina, and assessed
    local eligibility, which was not included in previous evaluations. The results of the 2025 updated
    evaluation indicate that the Berkeley Pier does not meet the criteria for listing in the NRHP, CRHR,
    Berkeley Register of Designated Landmarks BERD, or as a City of Berkeley historical resource.
    Accordingly, the updated evaluation confirms that no historical resources are present within or
    directly adjacent to the project site.

The above text change is clarifying in nature, as it provides additional information regarding the
evaluation outcome, but does not result in a change to the analysis or impact conclusions presented in
the Draft EIR. The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in Section 3.4,
Cultural Resources, of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further revisions are required.

Response to Comment O10-100
The threshold question for Impact AES-2, page 3.1-28, of the Draft EIR, is directly quoted from the
Appendix G of the CEQA Guidelines, “Would the project… Substantially damage scenic resources,
including, but not limited to, trees, rock outcroppings, and historic buildings within a state scenic
highway?” (Emphasis added.) Thus, since there are no State scenic highways within the project site, no
impact to these scenic resources would occur. Discussion and analysis of scenic resources within the
project vicinity, but outside a state scenic highway, are provided in Impact Evaluation, pages 3.1-20
through 3.1-36, Section 3.1, Aesthetics.

under Impact AES-2, page 3.1-28, of the Draft EIR. Such analyses are based on the assumptions
described therein, and mitigation measures are identified as appropriate. Accordingly, the analysis of
scenic resources within a state scenic highway is adequate and consistent with CEQA Guidelines. The
analysis and conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written.

Response to Comment O10-101
Impact AES-2 evaluates whether the project would damage scenic resources within a designated State
scenic highway, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Appendix G significance criteria. As explained in
Response to Comment O10-100, because no State scenic highway exists at or near the project site, traffic
volumes are not relevant to this threshold. To the extent the comment is concerned with the visual
presence of increased vehicle traffic on University Avenue or Seawall Drive as a change to the visual
character of the corridor, vehicle traffic is a transient condition rather than a permanent physical
alteration to the visual environment. Vehicles move through and clear the corridor continuously, and
University Avenue and Seawall Drive are existing paved roadways where vehicular use is already part of
the established visual and functional character of the area. An increase in the volume of an existing,
transient use does not constitute a permanent visual change to the physical environment.
Refer to Response to Comment O10-100 and refer to Section 2.2.18, Topical Response: Nighttime
Lighting/ALAN, for a discussion related to aesthetic traffic impacts. The analysis and conclusions
presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written.
