Response to Comment O10-129
As described in the Draft EIR, the proposed project would introduce new and enhanced recreational
features that do not currently exist, including a restored public pier, Bay Trail extension, and dedicated
cycle track (see Section 2.5.2 and Impact REC-1). These features would expand recreational access and
opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront. In addition, although the project may increase visitation, the
analysis concludes that this increased use would not result in substantial physical deterioration of
existing facilities because the project itself includes new recreational infrastructure that accommodates
additional demand (Impact REC-1).
Furthermore, the Draft EIR does not rely solely on a generalized “net increase” conclusion. Instead, it
evaluates existing recreational conditions at the project site and vicinity (Section 3.11.2), the specific
recreational components included in the project design (Section 2.5, Proposed Project Components), and
whether project-related increase in use would result in physical environmental effects (Impact REC-1).
Based on this analysis, the Draft EIR determines that the project would provide additional recreational
opportunities and would not cause adverse physical impacts requiring new facilities or resulting in
deterioration of existing ones. This conclusion is supported by substantial evidence and is consistent
with CEQA Guidelines Appendix G.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid
as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-135
Potential impacts to fish and marine habitat are evaluated in Draft EIR Section 3.3, Biological Resources,
including Impact BIO-1 (effects to special-status species and habitats) and Impact BIO-3 (effects to
jurisdictional aquatic habitat), while recreational fishing access is evaluated in Draft EIR Section 3.11,
Recreation (see Impact REC-1).
Within Section 3.3, Biological Resources, the Draft EIR evaluates both construction and operational effects
of the proposed project on aquatic habitats, including fish and Essential Fish Habitat, and concludes that
construction and operational impacts to fish habitat would be less than significant with the incorporation
of mitigation measures such as seasonal work windows, soft-start pile driving procedures, and
monitoring requirements to minimize disturbance to fish and marine species, as well as mitigation to
ensure no net increase in Bay fill or substantial loss of aquatic habitat (see Section 3.3.4, Impacts
Analysis, Impacts BIO-1 and BIO-3). CEQA requires evaluation of physical environmental impacts, such as
changes to aquatic habitat and species behavior. While recreational fishing depends in part on underlying
ecological conditions, CEQA does not require analysis of changes in fishing success, catch rates, or user
experience. Because the Draft EIR concludes that the project would not result in significant adverse
effects to fish habitat, no significant indirect impact to recreational fishing would occur under CEQA.
Recreational fishing access is evaluated in Section 3.11, Recreation, which considers both existing access
conditions and the addition of new publicly accessible facilities, including the restored pier and enhanced
shoreline access. As described therein, the project would maintain and expand opportunities for public
access to the waterfront and fishing locations, and impacts to recreational access are concluded to be
less than significant (see Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis, Impact REC-1).
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in the Draft EIR remain valid
as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

As described in Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, and Section 3.11, Recreation, the

(BCDC) and provides the statutory framework governing development and public access within San
Francisco Bay (see Section 3.9.2 and 3.11.2). Implementation of the Act’s policies occurs primarily
through BCDC’s administration of the San Francisco Bay Plan and permitting authority. Accordingly,
consistency with the McAteer-Petris Act is evaluated through analysis of project consistency with
applicable Bay Plan policies and BCDC regulations. The Draft EIR primarily addresses this framework in
Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, which evaluates the project’s consistency with applicable regional
plans and policies, including the San Francisco Bay Plan administered by BCDC and the Berkeley Marina
Master Plan (see Impact LU-2, Table 3.9-1 and Table 3.9-4). This analysis concludes that the project is
consistent with Bay Plan policies related to public access, recreation, and shoreline use, which are
intended to implement the goals of the McAteer-Petris Act, and that the project is consistent with the key
principles of the Berkeley Marina Master Plan, which similarly is intended to preserve marina access (see
Draft EIR pages 3.9-23 and 3.9-33).
The Draft EIR evaluates existing recreational uses and access conditions in Section 3.11, Recreation, and
analyzes whether the project would result in adverse physical effects on recreational resources or reduce
public access (see Impact REC-1). As described therein, although certain existing site conditions would
change, the project would restore public access to the Berkeley Pier, which has been closed since 2015;
provide new and enhanced recreational facilities, including improved Bay Trail connections and shoreline
access; and maintain public access to waterfront areas, including parking and viewing opportunities
along Seawall Drive and adjacent areas (see Section 3.1, Aesthetics, Impact AES-3 and Section 3.9, Table
3.9-1). The Draft EIR acknowledges that recreational use patterns may shift as a result of these changes.
However, CEQA requires evaluation of physical environmental effects, such as the availability and
condition of recreational facilities and access, not preservation of specific informal use patterns or user
preferences. Thus, the analysis in Draft EIR Section 3.11 appropriately concludes that the project would

Response to Comment O10-149
For a detailed discussion of land use plan consistency considerations related to the Draft EIR, refer to
Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency.
Impact LU-2 within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, of the Draft EIR (see Table 3.9-1, pages 3.9-12
through 3.9-23) evaluates the project's consistency with applicable Bay Plan policies, including
Transportation Policy 5. As discussed on Draft EIR page 3.9-17, the project is consistent with
Transportation Policy 5. The Draft EIR does not interpret Transportation Policy 5 as requiring that all ferry
terminals be located adjacent to higher-density, mixed-use development. Rather, the policy provides that
such locations should be used "wherever possible," recognizing that site-specific conditions may warrant
alternative locations. As described on Draft EIR page 3.9-17, the project site provides direct access to an
existing federal navigation channel, experiences minimal sedimentation, provides an opportunity for dual-
use recreation improvements and is served by existing AC Transit service. The proposed project would
further improve multimodal access to the ferry terminal through enhancements to AC Transit facilities
that would support expanded transit service, as well as new bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure. In
addition, BCDC Bay Plan Map No. 4 Policy 15 specifically identifies a ferry terminal as a potential use at
the Berkeley Waterfront, provided that the facility remains compatible with park and marina uses. As
discussed on Draft EIR page 3.9-22, the project is consistent with those requirements because it would
maintain compatibility with existing recreational and marina uses while expanding public access and
recreational amenities. For further explanation of the project’s consistency with the other elements of
Transportation Policy 5, refer to Response to Comment O10-117.
To the extent the comment expresses concern regarding the proposed ferry terminal site due to the
comment’s characterization of the site as a recreational area, the Draft EIR acknowledges and evaluates
the existing recreational uses of the Berkeley Waterfront within Section 3.11, Recreation. As discussed
therein, the proposed project has been designed as a dual-purpose facility that would both accommodate
ferry service and expand public recreational opportunities. The project would preserve existing marina,
shoreline, and recreational uses while providing new recreational infrastructure, including a publicly
accessible pier, Bay Trail improvements, public open space, and shoreline viewing opportunities. As a
result, the Draft EIR concludes that the project would result in a net increase in recreational opportunities
and facilities available to the public (see Impact REC-1).
Accordingly, Impact LU-2 concludes that the proposed project would be consistent with Transportation
Policy 5 and other applicable Bay Plan policies (refer to page 3.9-23). The Draft EIR therefore does not
conclude that the project's location within a recreational waterfront setting results in a conflict with
Transportation Policy 5.
The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact LU-2 in Section 3.9, Land Use and
Planning, remain valid as written in the Draft EIR. No revisions are required.

Response to Comment O10-152
The Draft EIR evaluates recreation impacts under two distinct CEQA thresholds in Section 3.11,
Recreation:
• Impact REC-1, which evaluates whether the project would increase use of existing recreational facilities
  such that substantial physical deterioration would occur or require construction of new or expanded
  facilities (pages 3.11-14 through 3.11-20); and
• Impact REC-2, which evaluates whether the project includes construction of recreational facilities or
  requires expansion of such facilities that could result in adverse environmental effects (pages 3.11-20
  through 3.11-24).

With respect to construction-related access, refer to Response to Comment A3-55. Under Impact REC-1,
the Draft EIR evaluates whether temporary construction-induced constraints would result in a substantial
physical deterioration of recreational resources. Given the availability of numerous other waterfront
areas, including the South Sailing Basin, Marina Basin, Bay Trail, and adjacent regional shoreline facilities,
the Draft EIR concludes that temporary displacement of recreational users would not result in physical
degradation of facilities or require construction of new recreational resources. This conclusion does not
assume recreational uses are fully interchangeable; rather, it reflects the CEQA standard, which focuses
on physical environmental effects, not temporary inconvenience or limitations at specific preferred
locations.
With respect to Impact REC-2, the Draft EIR concludes that the project would include construction of
recreational facilities (e.g., pier improvements, shoreline amenities, Bay Trail improvements), and that
construction of these facilities would result in significant and unavoidable environmental impacts due to
impacts disclosed in other sections of the Draft EIR related to other CEQA-defined resources, rather than
direct impacts to existing recreational uses(see Section 3.11.4, pages 3.11-20 through 3.11-24).
Accordingly, the Draft EIR does not conclude that all construction-related recreation impacts are less than
significant; rather, it recognizes significant impacts associated with facility construction, consistent with
CEQA requirements.
The commenter’s reference to the duration of construction does not alter the CEQA significance
determination under Impact REC-1. CEQA distinguishes between temporary construction-phase
disruptions and permanent physical impacts. As described in the Draft EIR, construction would be time-
limited and would not permanently remove or degrade recreational facilities or access. Seasonal variation
in recreational use does not change this conclusion, as access to the broader Berkeley Waterfront and
surrounding shoreline resources would remain available throughout the construction period. For further
discussion regarding the Draft EIR analysis of construction-related impacts to recreation, refer to
Response to Comment A3-55.
With respect to policies referenced by the commenter, consistency with the Berkeley Marina Plan and
BCDC Bay Plan policies is evaluated in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning (Impact LU-2, Table 3.9-1). As
described therein, the project would maintain and enhance long-term public access and recreational

                                             Page 516 of 1541

City of Berkeley

Response to Comment O10-156
As described in page 3.12-8 of the Draft EIR, prior rules treated automobile delay and congestion as an
environmental impact; however, the final update to CEQA Guidelines consistent with SB 743 recommends
using vehicle miles traveled (VMT) as the most appropriate metric of transportation impact to align local
environmental review under CEQA with California’s long-term greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals.
However, the EIR did evaluate project traffic with regard to queuing of vehicles and safety and found that
the traffic added from the project would not result in a worsening of traffic and result in safety hazards
(refer to Impact TRA-3 in Section 3.12, Transportation of the Draft EIR, page 3.12-22 through 3.12-24).
Refer to Section 2.2.3, Topical Response: BCDC Jurisdiction, Planning Consistency, and Permit Compliance,
regarding conflicts between commuter and recreational users. Circulation conflicts among user groups
are primarily a social consideration rather than a physical environmental impact under CEQA; however,
the topic is also addressed through the City’s compliance with the BCDC Bay Plan, including
Transportation Policy 4 and Public Access Policy 11, which require that transportation and shoreline
improvements maintain and enhance safe, physical access to and along the Bay shoreline for all users.
The project incorporates dedicated infrastructure designed to safely accommodate both user groups,
including a new Class IV cycle track on University Avenue, raised table-top style crosswalks, a widened
sidewalk connecting the AC Trans bus stop to the proposed plaza, wayfinding signage for pedestrians,
bicyclists and vehicles and improved shoreline pathways. The City presented exhibits illustrating
circulation routes and connections for land, water and ferry users groups at the DRB May 11, 2026
meeting. The DRB indicated it was satisfied that the design addressed their concerns.

CEQA Guidelines 15123(a) states that “An EIR shall contain a brief summary of the proposed actions and
its consequences. The language of the summary should be as clear and simple as reasonably practical.”
CEQA Guidelines 15123(b)(2) states that the summary shall identify “Areas of controversy known to the
Lead Agency including issues raised by agencies and the public.” The City has provided a “brief summary”
of areas of controversy, consistent with the CEQA Guidelines. Please also note that Table 1-1 in
Chapter 1, Introduction of the Draft EIR includes a more detailed list of comments raised by the public,
including areas of controversy, and Appendix A includes the full text of all scoping comments received,
including those expressing comments related to the controversy of the project.

Response to Comment O10-160
CEQA requires evaluation of physical environmental effects, and does not require analysis of social or
demographic equity impacts unless such effects would result in a physical change in the environment
(CEQA Guidelines §15064(e)). Accordingly, the Draft EIR appropriately focuses on physical conditions,
including the availability, capacity, and accessibility of recreational facilities, rather than demographic
characteristics of users. Consistent with CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, Section 3.11, Recreation, evaluates
whether the project would (1) increase use of existing recreational facilities such that substantial physical
deterioration would occur, or (2) require construction of new or expanded facilities that could result in
adverse physical environmental effects. The analysis concludes that the project would result in a net
increase in recreational opportunities, including a restored public pier, new Bay Trail connection, shoreline
access improvements, and additional amenities such as seating, shade structures, restrooms, and a fish-
cleaning station (Impact REC-1).
The comment’s concerns regarding potential effects of parking availability, congestion, or cost on
specific user groups represent socioeconomic and policy considerations. Under CEQA, such
considerations are not treated as environmental impacts unless they would cause a physical

Refer to Figure 15b of the 2004 Baywide Eelgrass Inventory that shows eelgrass distribution in Central
San Francisco Bay; the figure shows eelgrass was detected within the Southern Sailing Basin.
The commenter also states that Figure 7 and Figure 8b of the 2004 Baywide Eelgrass Inventory show
there is a high potential for eelgrass in the area surrounding the Project site. These figures show the
results of the Habitat Suitability Index (HSI), a pre-survey screening model. The discussion on page 36 of
the 2004 Baywide Eelgrass Inventory indicates that only 8.6% of the areas identified as potential eelgrass
habitat by the pre-survey screening model actually supported eelgrass during the surveys. In addition, the
discussion suggested that updated eelgrass distribution and more accurate bathymetry is needed to
allow for a more exact model. No eelgrass is currently documented to be present in the project site. No
further response is necessary and no revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O10-174
All iNaturalist observations in the vicinity of the project site show eelgrass wrack, or uprooted eelgrass
mixed with organic debris. In sheltered bays, tracking studies show that detached seagrass can drift over
3 miles depending on tide and wind shifts. 45 Therefore, the presence of eelgrass wrack is not indicative of
the presence of eelgrass beds in the immediate vicinity of the project site. This comment does not
change the significance conclusions or mitigation in the Draft EIR. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment O10-188
See Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, for a discussion of how the proposed project would result in a
net reduction in regional VMT. The mobile source emissions in the GHG analysis in the Draft EIR were
based on the Technical Memorandum for the project dated January 16, 2026, and included as Draft EIR
Appendix F. The Technical Memorandum states in Table 3 page 4, that there are 955 person trips, of
which 48 are transit, 153 are bike, 38 are pedestrian, and 96 are “other” (defined as including multiple
modes and private shuttles) along with 382 single passenger trips, 115 carpool trips, 76 passenger drop
off in personal vehicles, and 48 Taxi/transportation network (TNC) trips. The 1,127 daily vehicle trips
include only the drive alone, carpool, passenger drop off, and Taxi/TNC trips. The Memorandum states
the trip generation provided in Table 3 is conservative and doesn’t account for the parking and TDM
strategies. The Memorandum further states that “Factors such as limiting parking supply would constrain
the number of trips that could be supported to the project, so while the pier may attract some new
demand, overall trip levels at the Waterfront would be expected to self-regulate. Furthermore, the trips
associated with pier and recreational visitors would be expected to be higher during the weekends when
the ferry usage would be lower than weekdays. Hence, the estimated trip generation only shows
information from the proposed ferry which as mentioned earlier is considered conservative as it doesn’t
account for parking and TDM strategies.” Therefore, the 1,127 vehicle trips would more than account for
the recreational trips that could occur on the weekends and during the week when ferry usage is lower.
The mobile-related GHG emissions analysis in the EIR is accurate (see methodology approach discussion
on Draft EIR page 3.6-32), and no additional analysis is required. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in
response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-193
Refer to Response to Comment O10-189 for a discussion of project objectives. Furthermore, as a matter
of clarification, one of the basic project objectives is to “provide efficient and environmentally friendly
zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco” (see Section 5.3 in Chapter 5,
Alternatives of the Draft EIR, page 5-2). Large scale ferry service does meet this project objective.
The comment suggests that the Draft EIR should have evaluated ferry service as a recreational amenity
rather than as a transportation service. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 5.9, Alternatives Considered but
Rejected (page 5-27), the City considered a Smaller Scale Ferry Service Alternative during the alternatives
screening process. The Draft EIR explains that a smaller ferry service would still introduce ferry
operations and associated infrastructure but would not substantially reduce significant environmental
impacts relative to the proposed project. Accordingly, the City determined that further evaluation of this
alternative would not provide a meaningful environmental comparison. To provide further clarification,
Draft EIR Section 5.9, Alternatives Considered but Rejected (page 5-27) is revised as follows:
    Smaller scale ferry service. Under this potential alternative, smaller ferry vessels or a reduced ferry
    vessel schedule would be used. A smaller ferry or reduced ferry vessel schedule would still result in
    additional ferry vessels and would not reduce a significant environmental impact. Regarding
    biological resources, in general, fish and marine mammals potentially near the Berkeley waterfront
    are adapted to the high activity level of an active marina and would avoid ferry boats as they now
    avoid commercial and recreational boaters. An alternative that would introduce a smaller scale ferry
    service would still have the same potential impact. Therefore, this alternative would not reduce any
    environmental impacts. Similarly, the use of smaller vessels or smaller scale ferry service would also
    not avoid or substantially lessen significant environmental impacts associated with dredging.
    Regardless of vessel size or the schedule of ferry vessels, ferry operations would still require in-water
    improvements and construction activities within the San Francisco Bay to provide safe vessel access
    and passenger boarding facilities and therefore, although a smaller vessel could potentially reduce
    dredging requirements, there is no assurance that dredging would be avoided altogether. In addition,
    to the extent that a smaller scale ferry service or smaller ferry vessel could operate from within the
    Berkeley Marina using an existing berth or marina facilities, such an alternative would present similar
    operational and feasibility concerns as the Berkeley Marina Basin alternative (refer to Section 2.2.12,
    Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative, of the Final EIR). Similar to the Berkeley Marina
    Basin alternative, a smaller scale ferry service or smaller ferry vessel would result in operational
    inefficiencies and decreased reliability, as ferry operations within the marina would be subject to
    maneuvering constraints, increased docking and departure times, and potential conflicts with
    slipholders. Furthermore, a substantially smaller ferry service or smaller ferry vessel would not fully
    meet the project’s basic objective of providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero-emission
    public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco, as a smaller vessel or substantially reduced
    service schedule would lessen the project’s capacity to improve regional connectivity and reduce
    single-occupancy vehicle trips. Because this alternative would not reduce significant environmental
    impacts and would not meet the project’s basic objective of providing efficient ferry service, this
    alternative has been considered but rejected.

The comment also suggests that the Draft EIR should have evaluated a recreational-only pier alternative
without ferry service. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 5.9 (page 5-27), the City considered a No Ferry
Service with New Pier Alternative but did not carry it forward for detailed evaluation because it would not
meet one of the project's two basic objectives: providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero-
emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco. The Draft EIR also notes that funding

Response to Comment O10-199
Refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives, for a discussion of how the Draft EIR addresses the
No Project Alternative. The Draft EIR clearly identifies the assumptions underlying Alternative 1 and
applies those assumptions consistently throughout the alternatives analysis.
As described in Draft EIR Section 5.5, Alternative 1: No Project Alternative (pages 5-3 through 5-9),
Alternative 1 evaluates conditions under which the proposed project would not proceed. The purpose of
the No Project Alternative is to provide a basis for comparison with the proposed project, rather than to
speculate regarding every potential future improvement that could occur in the project vicinity.
Additionally, the Draft EIR does not overstate the benefits of the proposed project. Rather, it identifies the
project features and improvements proposed by the City in Chapter 2, Project Description (see Draft EIR
Section 2.5, Proposed Project Objectives), and evaluates the environmental effects of those features,
including their environmental benefits and impacts, in accordance with CEQA’s informational and
comparative analysis requirements.
The City has identified reasonably foreseeable projects in Table 3-1 of the Draft EIR, which include
recreational amenities. It is true that these projects may continue under the No Project Alternative;
however, the greatest influence of the No Project Alternatives analysis, for the purposes of a meaningful
comparative analysis, continues to be the elimination of project features associated with the proposed
project. For example, in terms of temporary construction impacts, while the implementation of these
future projects would require construction, these would also occur under proposed project conditions,
and the main difference to disclose is the reduced impacts from reduced construction associated with
the elimination of proposed project amenities. In terms of operational impacts, such as VMT, GHG, and
air quality impacts, the addition of future recreational projects will not measurably affect the VMT, GHG,
or air quality analysis for the No Project Alternative. This is because the proposed project results in VMT
reductions that could not be realized by any of the reasonably foreseeable projects identified in the Draft
EIR.
The comment's views regarding other potential future improvements and proposed project benefits are
noted. However, the comment does not identify information demonstrating that the Draft EIR's
alternatives analysis fails to provide the meaningful environmental comparison required by CEQA. The
analysis and conclusions in Chapter 5, Alternatives, remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR
are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-203
Refer to Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, which demonstrates that the project would result in
lowered VMT compared to the No Project Alternative. Under California SB 743, transportation impacts in
CEQA documents are evaluated using VMT rather than roadway congestion measures such as Level of
Service (LOS). Because the project would reduce VMT even under conservative assumptions, it would not
result in a transportation impact under CEQA. With respect to the No Project Alternative, the Draft EIR
evaluates reasonably foreseeable future conditions in the absence of the project, consistent with CEQA
guidelines 15126.6(e)(2). This includes consideration of planned and expected changes in travel patterns,
population, and regional growth that would occur regardless of project approval. As described in the Draft
EIR (refer to Section 3.12, Transportation; Chapter 5, Alternatives; and Appendix F, Transportation Impact
Analysis), these conditions include continued reliance on existing travel modes, which are expected to
result in greater regional vehicle travel compared to conditions with the proposed project in place.
Accordingly, the analysis and conclusions in Section 3.12,Transportation and Chapter 5, Alternatives of the
Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no further revisions are required.

Response to Comment O10-204

objectives. The analysis concludes that the No Project Alternative would not enhance public access and
recreational opportunities because the existing pier would remain closed and continue to deteriorate. The
analysis further concludes that Alternative 2 (Shortened Breakwater), Alternative 3 (Shortened Pier), and
Alternative 4 (Reduced Landside Facilities) would provide public access and recreational benefits, but to
a lesser extent than the proposed project because they would reduce recreational amenities or public
access opportunities. In addition, Draft EIR Chapter 5 concludes that the No Project Alternative would
generally result in greater impacts related to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, land use and
planning, and transportation because it would not provide the transportation and environmental benefits
associated with the proposed ferry service.

routes and terminals are shown on Figure 2.1. Further site-specific studies and design would be
necessary prior to IOP implementation to determine actual terminal sites and routes.” The suggestion
that the 2003 WETA EIR proposed a terminal within the marina is not accurate and the 2003 WETA EIR
specifically identifies that additional studies will be needed to determine the actual terminal site. This
Draft EIR provides that project-level analysis for a terminal site in the Berkeley Waterfront.
Refer to Section 2.2.12, Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative, for a discussion related to
why the City rejected the In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative from further evaluation.
The comment does not identify a deficiency in the Draft EIR's environmental analysis or alternatives

Response to Comment O10-222
This comment specifically refers to text on page 3.9-10 within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, of the

Response to Comment O10-223
This comment specifically refers to text on page 3.9-15 within Table 3.9-1, BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan

Response to Comment O10-225
It is correct that if a lead agency approves a project with significant and unavoidable impacts, that agency
must prepare a Statement of Overriding Considerations that describes the specific social, economic, or
other reasons supporting their decision. The purpose of the EIR is to disclose the environmental impacts
of a project, identify mitigation to avoid or reduce impacts, and consider alternatives to a project. The EIR
is used as an informational document for agencies and the public. The preparation of a Statement of
Overriding Considerations happens after the preparation of the Final EIR and is a part of the materials
used by the decision-making body to make a decision on the project. No revision to the Draft EIR is
required in response to this comment.

Response to Comment O10-231
The discussion of Impact TRA-2 in Section 3.12, Transportation, of the Draft EIR states that ferry service
between Berkeley and San Francisco would increase access to higher-paying jobs, which is substantiated
by the 2022 WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Plan. Ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco would
allow workers to live in the East Bay while working in San Francisco or other regional areas providing
higher-paying employment opportunities. Refer to Chapter 6, Equity Considerations, of the 2022 WETA
Berkeley Service Plan for more information. Rather than social or economic benefits, the discussion in
Impact TRA-2 is focused on how daily vehicle trips associated with the project may not necessarily be
new trips and could be shifted rides from other commuters; people in West Berkeley currently have
limited transit options. The expansion of ferry service would result in a new transit option for West
Berkeley residents, which could lead to a shift in rides across the region. No further response is required.

Response to Comment O10-235
Refer to Response to Comments O10-13 and O10-231. As discussed in Response to Comment O10-13,
economic merits or social considerations are not environmental issues subject to analysis under CEQA.
Nevertheless, this comment has been included in the project record considered by City decision makers.
To the extent the comment raises concerns about the distribution of costs and benefits among
waterfront users of different income levels, these are important policy considerations that the City
Council should weigh in its deliberations on the project. However, the distribution of costs and benefits
among different user groups does not constitute a physical environmental impact under CEQA. CEQA
Guidelines Section 15131 provides that economic and social effects of a project shall not be treated as
significant effects on the environment. Section 3.11, Recreation of the Draft EIR analyzes whether the
project would have physical impacts on recreational uses and access, and concludes that the project
enhances rather than diminishes recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront. The equity
implications of fee structures for marina and ferry infrastructure are policy matters appropriately
addressed through the City's public deliberative process, not through the CEQA environmental review of
the physical project. No revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

Response to Comment P3-1
The comment does not identify a deficiency in the environmental analysis presented in the Draft EIR.
Nevertheless, the City notes that sustainability concerns are incorporated throughout the project design.
As described in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, the project would support a transition to zero-
emission regional transportation options and would be served by all-electric ferry vessels operated by
WETA (see Section 2.3, Project Objectives, page 2-4). The project also includes multimodal access
improvements intended to reduce reliance on single-occupant vehicle trips, including bicycle and
pedestrian facilities, Bay Trail improvements, transit connections, bicycle parking, and transportation
demand management measures (see Section 2.5.2, pages 2-11 through 2-22). In addition, the project
would include electric vehicle charging infrastructure within the parking area and has been designed to
accommodate future solar photovoltaic installations over portions of the parking facilities. Refer to Draft
EIR Chapter 2, Project Description (Section 2.5.2, page 2-18).
The Draft EIR also evaluates greenhouse gas emissions in Section 3.7, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, which
concludes that the project would not conflict with applicable plans, policies, or regulations adopted to
reduce greenhouse gas emissions and would not generate significant greenhouse gas impacts (see
Impacts GHG-1 and GHG-2). The greenhouse gas analysis accounts for the project's transportation
characteristics, operational features, and consistency with regional and State climate objectives.
While the comment questions whether the terminal's location relative to residential areas affects project
sustainability, the comment does not identify specific sustainability concerns or provide evidence
demonstrating that the project's environmental analysis or greenhouse gas conclusions are inaccurate.
The analyses, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented throughout the Draft EIR
remain valid as written. No revisions are required.

Response to Comment P3-2
The ridership estimates presented in Table 2-4 of the Draft EIR (refer to page 2-31) were derived from the
WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, Version 1.0 (herein referred to as WETA Business Plan),
dated March 17, 2022. The Business Plan explains that the ridership projections are based on pre-
pandemic ridership assumptions and demand data but were adjusted to account for pandemic-related
changes in travel behavior, fare structures, and ferry service demand. Specifically, the Business Plan
states that it was prepared "amidst the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and in the context of emerging
recovery trends" and that the ridership projections are "based upon pre-COVID assumptions but have
been adjusted to reflect a 'pandemic recovery' fare structure and changing commuter travel pattern
trends and demand for weekend services," (see WETA Business Plan, page 1).
The WETA Business Plan further explains that the ridership projections were developed using updated
assumptions regarding post-pandemic travel patterns, including changes in peak-period travel demand
and increased demand for weekend ferry service, and that projections will continue to be refined as
additional information becomes available (see WETA Business Plan pages 1 and 13-18). Accordingly, the
ridership estimates presented in the Draft EIR were developed after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic
using a methodology that incorporated both pre-pandemic ridership data and post-pandemic recovery
assumptions.
Refer to Response to Comment O7-4, which revises Table 2-4, Daily Ridership Projections (trips), on Draft
EIR page 2-31 within Chapter 2, Project Description, to provide additional clarity regarding the ridership
assumptions associated with the proposed project. The revision presented in Response to Comment O7-

I was on the Berkeley Waterfront Commission when the restrictions on Jetski operation
was passed as a recommendation to Council. In fact I contributed to the proposed
wording, increasing the speed limit in the access corridor from 5 to 15 MPH for better
control in waves outside the harbor. Clearly this has no application to paddleboards,
kayaks, swimmers, etc. The wording "No jetski or personal watercraft of any kind..." is used
because "Jetski" is a registered trademark of Kawasaki, and a "Jetski" may actually be a
"Sea-Doo" (Bombardier) or a "Waverunner" (Yamaha). Hence the term "PWC" or Personal
Watercraft is used to accurately describe what is commonly recognized in the English
language as a "Jetski" from a builder other than Kawasaki. The wording "of any kind" is
there to make sure jetskis/PWCs from other manufacturers are covered. It's a "Scotch                                  P6-1
Tape" kind of thing. If you say "cellophane tape" to avoid the trademark, it's not interpreted
as packing tape, etc.

I've tried to use "jetski" in papers about jetski safety I've written for the National Academy
of Forensic Engineers, but the peer reviewers have insisted that I stay clear of that word
and use PWC to describe the same thing.

Ask any AI server for the definition of a PWC: Perplexity gives me this one in the first cited
reference: "A Personal Watercraft (PWC) often known as a jet ski, is a compact
recreational waterfacft propelled by an inboard jet drive system..."

Point is, you can't extend the ordinance to apply Berkeley Municipal Code Section 6.20.180
to anything other than what is commonly known as a "jet ski." This based on both                                      P6-2
widespread modern usage of the terms "PWC" or "Personal Watercraft," and on legislative
intent, of which I have personal knowledge.
--

The EIR is deficient in that it does not address the effect of various TDM (Transportation
Demand Management) strategies on the environment. More specifically, it does not                                      P7-1
provide the detail required to asses where ferry passengers will park when demand
exceeds the dedicated lot for ferry passengers. Also, the EIR does not include the
environmental effects of using fast ferries to partially compensate for excessive time                                P7-2
required to find a parking space.

Of particular interest to boat berthers (who provide about 2/3 of Marina Fund revenue) is
how guests, crew and family will be differentiated from ferry passengers who have strong
incentives to use the lots intended for boat berthers. We assume that boat berthers will be
issued parking permits in some for that will exempt them from time-of-day or elapsed time
restrictions. But boats are rarely used by the owner alone. My 25 ft sailboat, for example,
usually sails with a total crew of five, so four additional parking spaces are needed in the                          P7-3
O-Dock lot. None of my crew live near a direct bus line, and they all bring a heavy sea bag
and personal safety gear. That, and distance make bike access infeasible. Crew and
guests have the same time-of-day requirements as ferry passengers: Early arrival and all-
day, and sometimes overnight, use of the parking space. Larger boats may sail with ten
crew or more. Boats that go fishing for the day have similar requirements for guest parking.

How will this be handled? Will all crew or guests have to stop by the marina office to get a
temporary pass? Does the economic forecast allow for keeping the marina office open on
Sunday mornings? Adding cost, whether monetary or tranactional (e.g.time wasted)
reduces the marketability of berths on the south side of the harbor and will reduce berther
revenue.

There will be unintended consequences. For example, a ferry commuter might buy an
inexpensive (or even a semi-derelict) boat for the sole purpose of obtaining a parking pass.
Note that some of the berther parking lots are closer to the proposed ferry terminal than
                                                                                                                      P7-4
the designated ferry passenger log. At $300/month (typical for a 25 ft berth) this is only
$10/day, a bargain for a reliable and convenient space. This use would be a clear violation
of tideland public trust (see 1913 tideland grant and 1962 amendments...) It's a non-


                                                                                                             2- 450
                                     Page 555 of 1541




maritime and non-recreational use.

A related but often ignored environmental effect of insufficient parking: When passengers
                                                                                                 I
have to spend time finding a legal parking space, it increasing the required speed and               P7-5
carbon footprint of the ferries in order to meet a door-to-door transit time.

Various studies have shown that when missing a boat, train or carpool has serious
consequences, e.g. being very late for work, most commuters will allow two standard
deviations of time margin. Example: If parking is adequate and easy to find (see Richmond
ferry terminal) the process of parking and walking back to the boarding gangway only takes
about two minutes with a standard deviation of about one minute at most. So arriving five
minutes before scheduled departure is a reliable strategy. But what if it takes 15 minutes to        P7-6
find a more distant parking space, searching in several lots or cruising for the closest on-
street parking possibility, then at least five minutes to walk back to the ferry. Standard
deviation perhaps 5 minutes. The average commuter will allow the 20 (15+5) minutes
average delay, plus two sigma or ten minutes (2x5) margin to be sure not to miss the boat.
This adds 25 minutes to the door-to-door commute time, compared to a scenario with
ample parking.

For our short route to SF, the ferry has to very much faster to provide the same commute
time, door-to-door. Remember that required power is proportional to speed cubed -- so                P7-7
the environmental impact of the ferry system is much reduced if sufficient parking is part of
the system. It's cheaper and greener to provide the parking and slow down the boats.

Successful ski resorts offer a variety of difficulty levels: There's a bunny slope, some
intermediate runs, and the expert slopes. A ski resort needs all three.

Windsurfing and beginner sailing in the South Cove have the same requirements: A popular
                                                                                                                      P8-1
site needs to provide conditions for a wide range of skill levels.

One of the features that make the South Cove so desirable and popular for small boat
sailing and windsurfing (and related wind-powered activities) is that it offers wind and
waves at all levels of skill.

The "inner sailing area," with wind moderated by the land mass and the trees on Hs.
Lordships peninsula, is of particular importance for the novice area. There are about 40
trees slated to be removed in order to increase the capacity of the Hs. Lordships parking
lot from approx. 250 to 400. This will likely change the wind environment of the inner South                          P8-2
Cove. More wind, more difficulty for novice sailors, more demands on the rescue skiff for
both Cal Sailing Club and Cal Adventures. And less continued use by the more skilled
sailors, if they had to go elsewhere to learn.

The South Cove site is unique among windsurfing sites for its skill level variety. Removing
wind-attenuating trees will cause an environmental impact not mentioned in the EIR that                               P8-3
will be difficult to undo. It will compromise access and safety. This needs to be analyzed in
detail.

allow them to park in the South Cove West parking lot instead of waiting through the

Ouch!

$100 cket, and be on me for the ferry and for work.

To the Berkeley City Council and relevant planning authorities,



Preserving the South Peninsula and maintaining public access to the seawall for future generations must        P19-1
remain a priority. Retiring this area to accommodate ferry-terminal logistics is not what the public has asked
for. Community comments have been consistent and unequivocal: people come to this stretch of shoreline to P19-2
experience nature, watch birds, enjoy the Bay and the sunset, or simply take a quiet, romantic walk.

This area also supports constant, year-round recreational use. Anglers rely on it daily. Those of us who                               P19-3
windsurf, kayak, foil, or swim depend on the beachhead at the point for safe water access. There is no
alternative access at low tide—or even at mid-ebb, depending on equipment. Attempting to reach the
waterline from any of the docks along the South Sailing Basin requires slogging through hundreds of feet of
                                                                                                                                       P19-4
deep, slippery mud, which is unsafe and effectively unusable. There is a reason the Cal Sailing Club cannot
operate when water depth at the docks drops below two feet, which occurs roughly 40 percent of the time.



                                                                 1                                                   2- 479
                                               Page 584 of 1541

The small cove at the foot of the former Hs. Lordships Restaurant is, quite literally, the only reliable low-tide
                                                                                                                    P19-4
access point for aquatic recreation in Berkeley, especially for anyone carrying gear such as boards or kayaks.

For these reasons, I urge you not to remove the already limited parking on the South Peninsula. Eliminating         P19-5
access—whether by restricting shoreline space or by removing the parking that makes it reachable—would
                                                                                                                    P19-6
effectively shut down one of Berkeley’s most valued and irreplaceable public waterfront areas.

Response to Comment P19-6
With respect to restricting shoreline access, refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts
on Existing Recreational Water Access, which provides further clarification on how the project would
preserve water-based recreation access and Section 2.2.24, Topical Response: Seawall Drive/View Access,
regarding parking on Seawall Drive. With respect to removing parking, refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical
Response: Parking.
In response to this comment, page 3.11-20 of the Draft EIR (Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis), has been
revised to include the following clarifying text confirming that the project would not remove or restrict
shoreline access for water-based recreation:
    Operation of the ferry would not hinder existing and new physical access to recreational resources on
    the project site or adjacent areas. The project would not restrict shoreline areas used for water-based
    recreation within the South Sailing Basin, and existing access points to these areas would be
    maintained.
    While certain access points, circulation patterns, and parking configurations within the project vicinity
    would be modified, overall access to recreational resources would be maintained and enhanced. The
    proposed new pier and breakwater, Bay Trail Extension, and green space next to the Bay Trail
    Extension would be publicly accessible and access to such project-related recreational uses would
    not be hindered by ferry operation or riders commuting to and from the Berkeley Waterfront area to
    utilize ferry services. Furthermore, the proposed project would include amenities such as fish
    cleaning stations, seating, and public restrooms, which would enhance the experience of people
    visiting the pier and breakwater for recreation.

The Draft EIR demonstrates that the project would maintain and expand public access to recreational
resources, and would not result in the loss of recreational facilities or shoreline access under CEQA
thresholds.
The revision above is clarifying in nature and does not alter the analysis or conclusions of Impact REC-1.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further
revisions are required.

To Whom It May Concern: I am submitting this comment in response to the WETA Ferry                                    P25-1
Terminal Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIR). The DEIR’s dismissal of recreational
impacts—particularly those affecting wind-powered water sports such as windsurfing,
winging, kiteboarding, and paddling—is based on a misinterpretation of Berkeley Municipal
Code § 6.20.180, a misunderstanding of the ordinance’s legislative history, and a disregard
                                                                                                                      P25-2
for decades of established public use of the Berkeley waterfront. The code clearly prohibits
swimming and windsurfing only within the marina, and explicitly allows windsurfing in the
South Sailing Basin; it does not regulate the open waters of the Bay west of the Berkeley
Pier. The City’s attempt to extend this prohibition by reinterpreting the term “personal
watercraft” to include windsurfing, kiteboarding, kayaking, stand-up paddling, foiling, and
winging is legally indefensible. The 1,500-foot “personal watercraft” provision was adopted
in 2001 to address jet-ski use following litigation over municipal jet-ski bans, not to                               P25-3
regulate human-powered or wind-powered recreation. At the time, foiling and winging did
not exist, stand-up paddling was not mainstream, and windsurfing had already been
occurring in these waters for decades. Under basic principles of statutory construction,
different terms in an ordinance must be given different meanings; because the ordinance                               P25-4
explicitly names windsurfing in one subsection, the City cannot credibly claim that
“personal watercraft” was intended to include it. The City’s reinterpretation contradicts
more than forty years of continuous, well-documented public use of the open Bay for
wind-powered sports, and appears designed to avoid CEQA’s requirement to analyze the                                  P25-5
impacts of the proposed breakwater and marina basin expansion on existing recreational
resources. CEQA does not permit agencies to redefine existing conditions to avoid
acknowledging impacts. Furthermore, Article X, Section 4 of the California Constitution
guarantees public access to navigable waters and prohibits exclusion of the public from
                                                                                                                      P25-6
such waters when needed for public purposes. The City’s interpretation would create a de
facto exclusion zone in navigable state waters, undermining constitutionally protected
access rights. For these reasons, the DEIR must correct its misinterpretation of the Marina
Code, acknowledge the long-standing recreational use of the open Bay by wind-powered                                  P25-7
and human-powered water sports, and fully analyze the impacts of the proposed
structures on these activities as CEQA requires. Wind-powered water sports are a defining
and legally protected component of the Berkeley waterfront, and the environmental review                              P25-8
must reflect that reality. Respectfully submitted, Jeffrey Finn

Response to Comment P25-6
The comment reflects a misunderstanding of the Draft EIR’s analysis. The Draft EIR does not propose or
assume the creation of new restrictions on water-based recreation. Rather, it describes existing
regulatory conditions, including provisions of the Berkeley Municipal Code (BMC), as part of the
environmental baseline used for analysis under CEQA.
As explained in Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, and Section 3.12, Transportation, the discussion of
compatibility between ferry operations and water-based recreation reflects the fact that certain activities
are already regulated or restricted in specific areas of the Berkeley Marina for safety and navigation
purposes. These conditions are part of the existing baseline, consistent with CEQA Guidelines
Section 15125. The project does not expand the geographic extent of these restrictions or introduce new
prohibitions on recreational uses. Please refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on
Existing Recreational Water Access, and Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited
Recreational Activities), which provide additional detail regarding recreational water access and the scope
and application of BMC Section 6.20.180. As described therein, the ordinance establishes localized safety
regulations applicable to specific areas of the marina (e.g., near the pier and navigation areas) and does
not prohibit public access to navigable waters more broadly. The Draft EIR appropriately considers these
existing conditions in evaluating whether the project would result in a physical conflict with water-based
recreation.
Under CEQA, the relevant question is whether the project would result in a physical environmental impact,
such as the loss or substantial impairment of recreational resources. As analyzed in Impact REC-1, the
project would maintain and enhance recreational access, and would not result in a substantial adverse
effect on water-based recreation. The commenter’s statements regarding constitutional interpretation
and public access rights raise legal and policy considerations outside the scope of CEQA environmental
impact analysis.
In response to this comment, the City notes that page 3.11-19 of the Draft EIR (Section 3.11.4, Impacts
Analysis), has been revised to clarify the discussion of ferry operations, existing recreational uses, and the
applicability of Berkeley Municipal Code Section 6.20.180. The text revision addressing these topics is
provided in Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control.
The revision presented under Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational
Activities), ensures that the Draft EIR clearly distinguishes between existing regulatory conditions and
potential project effects, and confirms that the project does not introduce new restrictions on water-
based recreation or access to navigable waters.
The above revision is clarifying in nature and does not change the analysis or conclusions of Impact
REC-1. The analyses and significance conclusions presented in Section 3.11, Recreation, and related
sections of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further revisions are required.

Response to Comment P25-7
Refer to Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities), which discusses
this Berkeley Municipal Code provision and its role in relation to the project. Section 2.2.19, Topical
Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities), presents a revision to the Draft EIR that ensures
the analysis therein clearly distinguishes between existing regulatory conditions and potential project
effects, and confirms that the project does not introduce new restrictions on water-based recreation or
access to navigable waters. For discussion regarding potential project impacts on wind-powered
recreational uses, refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational
Water Access.
The revision referenced above is clarifying in nature and does not change the analysis or conclusions of
Impact REC-1. The analyses and significance conclusions presented in Section 3.11, Recreation, and
related sections of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further revisions are required.

Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, establishes that the activities identified by the commenter represent

support these uses within Section 3.11.2, Environmental Setting (pages 3.11-1 through 3.11-7). The Draft
EIR also describes the applicable regulatory context, including local policies and ordinances governing
waterfront uses such as BMC Section 6.20.180, in Section 3.11.3, Regulatory Framework (pages 3.11-7
through 3.11-14). Potential impacts to the recreational uses described in Draft EIR Section 3.11.2 are
evaluated in Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis (pages 3.11-14 through 3.11-24), which considers whether
the proposed project would result in a substantial physical deterioration of recreational resources or
restrict physical access to such resources, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Appendix G. The analysis
concludes that the project would maintain and enhance recreational access and facilities, and would not

A PWC (Personal Watercraft) is a small, jet-propelled motorboat designed for                                          P27-4

individuals to sit, stand, or kneel on rather than inside, such as jet skis or wet bikes. It is
primarily used for recreation, fishing, or watersports.

                                                                                                       P27-4

      Key Features: Operated on the water, inboard engine, usually under 16 feet, restricted

                                           know the content is safe.
To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this comment in response to the WETA Ferry Terminal Draft Environmental                               P29-1
Impact Report (DEIR). The DEIR’s dismissal of recreational impacts—particularly those
affecting wind-powered water sports such as windsurfing, winging, kiteboarding, and
paddling—is based on a misinterpretation of Berkeley Municipal Code § 6.20.180, a                                     P29-2
misunderstanding of the ordinance’s legislative history, and a disregard for decades of
established public use of the Berkeley waterfront. I have personally been using these
waters for windsurfing and winging for over 40 years. The San Francisco bay is one of the                             P29-3
premier locations for these sports in the world and it is imperative that public access is
maintained for these sports.

The code clearly prohibits swimming and windsurfing only within the marina, and explicitly
allows windsurfing in the South Sailing Basin; it does not regulate the open waters of the                            P29-4
Bay west of the Berkeley Pier. The City’s attempt to extend this prohibition by reinterpreting
the term “personal watercraft” to include windsurfing, kiteboarding, kayaking, stand-up
paddling, foiling, and winging is legally indefensible. The 1,500-foot “personal watercraft”
provision was adopted in 2001 to address jet-ski use following litigation over municipal
                                                                                                                      P29-5
jet-ski bans, not to regulate human-powered or wind-powered recreation. At the time,
foiling and winging did not exist, stand-up paddling was not mainstream, and windsurfing
had already been occurring in these waters for decades. Under basic principles of
statutory construction, different terms in an ordinance must be given different meanings;                             P29-6
because the ordinance explicitly names windsurfing in one subsection, the City cannot
credibly claim that “personal watercraft” was intended to include it. The City’s
reinterpretation contradicts more than forty years of continuous, well-documented public
use of the open Bay for wind-powered sports, and appears designed to avoid CEQA’s                                     P29-7
requirement to analyze the impacts of the proposed breakwater and marina basin
expansion on existing recreational resources. CEQA does not permit agencies to redefine
existing conditions to avoid acknowledging impacts. Furthermore, Article X, Section 4 of
the California Constitution guarantees public access to navigable waters and prohibits
exclusion of the public from such waters when needed for public purposes. The City’s                                  P29-8
interpretation would create a de facto exclusion zone in navigable state waters,
undermining constitutionally protected access rights. For these reasons, the DEIR must
correct its misinterpretation of the Marina Code, acknowledge the long-standing
                                                                                                                      P29-9
recreational use of the open Bay by wind-powered and human-powered water sports, and
fully analyze the impacts of the proposed structures on these activities as CEQA requires.




                                                                                                             2- 508
                                   Page 613 of 1541




Wind-powered water sports are a defining and legally protected component of the Berkeley    P29-10
waterfront, and the environmental review must reflect that reality.

Respectfully submitted,

John Bosche

The City responded directly to this commenter and indicated that a transcript of the public meeting will be
published with the Final EIR, to which the commenter replied that it would be too late if published in the
Final EIR. CEQA requires that a lead agency provides public notice and an opportunity for public review
and comment on a Draft EIR (per CEQA Guidelines Sections 15087 and 15105). Public meetings or
hearings may be held to facilitate public participation; however, CEQA does not require that a public
meeting be held or that transcripts of such meetings be published in advance of a Final EIR. Consistent
with CEQA, the lead agency has provided a copy of all timely submitted comments and a response to
each in this Final EIR. To the extent oral comments were provided at public meetings, those comments
have been considered in the preparation of responses. No further response is required.

Hello thanks for the opportunity to provide feedback on the Berkeley ferry plan.                                    P35-2
As a Berkeley resident and wind-sports practitioner I am concerned about the following:
1. The ferry commuter parking will cause parking problems for long-standing recreation
                                                                                                                    P35-3
uses of the marina area.
2. We will spend a great deal of money subsidizing a ferry based on estimated usage when
other similar projects got much lower ridership than anticipated. Here's a sobering story:
When the BART connector to the airport was first conceived it replaced a very efficient
shuttle bus--and probably saved about ten minutes. It was forecast to carry 10,000
passengers as the boosters believed traffic at the Airport would increase from 12 million                           P35-4
annual passengers to 20 million annual passengers. It cost $500 million to build, costs
about $6 million a year to maintain (not including opportunity cost or capital
accumulation for replacement) and serves in the low hundreds of passengers. The
most recent annual air traffic through OAK was 9.3 million passengers.
I agree that the backup/redundancy of a ferry is a good idea, as we saw after the 1989
earthquake, but there are other important bay transportation options that are overdue
                                                                                                                    P35-5
including a bike lane across the entire bridge and a second BART tube.

3. Please clarify in the Final EIR where the wind-sports, kayaks, and other small craft will
be permitted to go. The area off of His Lordships is an excellent launch and a very popular
spot during the summer windy season. Proficient sailors fly several miles west towards                              P35-6
Treasure Island and surf swells back towards Berkeley. Your Draft EIR has big red boxes
around the proposed Ferry Terminal pier and the southern box west of His Lordships
overlaps with the prime wind sports area.

4. Finally, in consulting with a friend in the Coast Guard he writes: it is already against the
regulations for a vessel less than 20 Meters (wing sport vessels) to impede the passage of a                        P35-7
vessel that can only navigate safely within a channel or fairway (Nav Rules, Rule 9). There is
no need for a localized "buffer." USCG Nav Rules protects the ferry in many situations.

Other ferry terminals around the Bay such as Richmond (near the Rosie the Riveter
museum) do not have a specific closure adjacent the ferry despite being right next to an
extremely popular sailing spot at Marina Bay. Wind users just stay out of the way of the                             P35-8
ferry so there is no need for the city to add additional prohibitions.

If we're to invest in a ferry at this point my vote is to put the ferry inside the marina where
other craft already moor and not interfere with existing uses.
Thank you
