Subject: Comments on Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project draft EIR

Dear Ms. McNulty:

INTRODUCTION

On January 20, 1967, the Bay Conservation and Development Commission issued a permit
to the City of Berkeley to dredge 40,000 cubic yards of material to ﬁll 4.6 acres of open Bay
in order to create land for a marina, a restaurant, a public beach, a park area, a relocated
University of California sailing facility, and the parking to support those uses. That permit                             P36-1
was approved in a public hearing on January 5, 1967, with support from Sylvia McLaughlin
because it would implement the city’s plan and its commitment that “..Berkeley’s portion of
the shoreline of the Bay should be reserved exclusively for public recreation and related
public use.”

Now the City of Berkeley proposes to break that commitment to public recreation and
eliminate most of the existing public parking spaces and devote the land in question to a
                                                                                                                          P36-2
ferry terminal for commuters. We are expected to accept on faith that a ferry terminal that
can easily accommodate 1600 passengers will work ﬁne with 399 parking spaces—and
look the other way when those parking spaces are made unavailable to those who now use
them. But we have seen how Berkeley has artiﬁcially restricted recreational parking by                                t   P36-3



                                                                                                             2- 532
                                     Page 637 of 1541




locking the Seawall lot without a BCDC permit, by approving small ferry operations without
coordinating with BCDC or considering Bay Plan policies, and by relocating the Parking
                                                                                                       P36-3
Bureau, a non-trust use, into the marina. Those policies restricted the amount of parking
so that recreational users were turned away, and the city failed to enforce the parking
management promises they made to BCDC. This EIR does not evaluate whether there will
be enough parking for a new ferry terminal, or what the impact would be on recreational
uses. Instead, the city argues that despite this history and the promises the city made, and
Bay Plan policies that protect recreational access, CEQA does not require them to address              P36-4
parking. With such analysis not available in the EIR, the city then blithely concludes that
any impact on recreation would not be signiﬁcant. The rationale and analysis behind that
conclusion is inadequate, as I will explain in detail in the following comments.


CONFLICTS WITH ADOPTED PLAN POLICIES

Consistency with adopted plans is discussed in EIR Section 3.9, Land Use Planning

Under the California Environmental Quality Act, an EIR is required to discuss any
inconsistencies between the proposed project and the applicable plans of regional
agencies. (Section 15125(d) of the CEQA Guidelines.) Where a local or regional policy of
general applicability, such as an ordinance, is adopted in order to avoid or mitigate
environmental e ects, a conﬂict with that policy indicates a potentially signiﬁcant impact
on the environment. (Pocket Protectors v. Sacramento (2005) 124 Cal.App.4th 903.) Any
inconsistencies between a proposed project and applicable plans must be discussed in an                P36-5
EIR. (14 CCR § 15125(d); City of Long Beach v. Los Angeles Unif. School Dist. (2009) 176
Cal. App. 4th 889, 918; Friends of the Eel River v. Sonoma County Water Agency (2003) 108
Cal. App. 4th 859, 874 (EIR inadequate when Lead Agency failed to identify relationship of
project to relevant local plans).) A Project’s inconsistencies with local plans and policies
constitute signiﬁcant impacts under CEQA. (Endangered Habitats League, Inc. v. County of
Orange (2005) 131 Cal.App.4th 777, 783-4, 32 Cal.Rptr.3d 177). Particular emphasis in the
Guidelines is given to agencies—like BCDC—that are responsible for protection of
San Francisco Bay and access to and along the Bay.


The draft EIR cherry-picks policies within BCDC’s Bay Plan, as well as policies in the City’s
own “Berkeley Marina Master Plan” (June 1, 2003), eliding any policy in those plans that
does not support their view of the project. Instead of discussing the inconsistencies, the
                                                                                                       P36-6
EIR ignores them, and without discussion or analysis concludes that there are no such
inconsistencies. This approach is inadequate and requires a revised Draft EIR to disclose
all inconsistencies between the proposed project and applicable plans and policies.

       RELEVANT BERKELEY PLANS, LAND USE DESIGNATIONS, AND POLICIES
                                                                                                   t   P36-7



                                                                                          2- 533
                                     Page 638 of 1541




There are two directly applicable Berkeley plans, the Marina Master Plan cited above, and
Measure L, passed as a citizen initiative in 1986. Rather than enumerate and analyze
                                                                                                  t    P36-7


speciﬁc policies within those plans that appear to conﬂict with the proposed project, the
EIR pivots to very general language in the city’s General Plan. But that plan does not
designate this site, or indeed any site in the marina for a ferry terminal, while the Marina
Master Plan designates this site for access improvements and open space. (Figures 2.0                 P36-8
and 12.0) Berkeley has stalled its e orts to complete a revision to the Waterfront Planning
Documents. This leaves in place the Berkeley Marina Master Plan (BMMP), dated June 1,
2003.

In both adopted policies and in land use designations, there are fundamental conﬂicts
between the Berkeley Marina Master Plan (BMMP) and the project contemplated in the EIR.
Most of these can be seen by reviewing the adopted map, Figure 2.0. Those conﬂicts
include:                                                                                              P36-9

      The only ferry site considered in the plan is located within the marina, and the plan
       adopts policies to make that site seismically safe.
      The site now proposed for a ferry terminal and ferry parking is designated for other
       recreational uses, including enhanced windsurﬁng access. An illustration of that
       concept is provided in Figure 12, that shows head in parking for public viewing,
       improvements to the windsurﬁng launch and staging area, and open space at the                  P36-10
       water’s edge. The proposed project conﬂicts with this plan by eliminating much of
       the open space on the peninsula, not increasing it, eliminating the staging area for
       windsurﬁng, and eliminating most of the parking places that are currently used for
       ﬁshing access and viewing the Bay. The EIR does not discuss any of these conﬂicts.
       The project entails removal of much of the green area and landscaping that now
       exists, including 40 trees (or perhaps 39; both numbers are provided) and makes no             P36-11
       quantitative assessment of the impact on open space.

Among the other important BMMP policies elided from the EIR are:
                                                                                                      P36-12
      Enhance open space and recreational opportunities
      Enhance and protect wildlife habitat                                                       I P36-13
      Address the future viability of the Marina                                                 I P36-14
      Protect scenic view and view corridors                                                     I P36-15
      Increase green space                                                                       I P36-16
      Upgrade the Ferry Pier to comply with seismic regulations                                  I P36-17
      Enhance Windsurfer Activities at the point immediately to the west of H’s
       Lordships Restaurant. Includes a reference to staging areas                                I   P36-18


The EIR concludes that providing a much shorter recreational pier, bikeway and plaza will
enhance recreation. But this is simply provided as a conclusion, without any discussion of
                                                                                                  l   P36-19




                                                                                         2- 534
                                     Page 639 of 1541




how the project might impact existing recreation. As we point out repeatedly, currently
over 600,000 people visited this recreational area in the year that ended in May 2024. The
                                                                                                  t   P36-19

EIR lacks any quantitative discussion of changes in green space or impacts to that                    P36-20
recreation—while proposing to remove many of the scenic view parking spaces protected
in the BMMP. Since the BMMP included discussion of a ferry terminal site within the
                                                                                                      P36-21
marina, it cannot be said that this new location in the open Bay is consistent with that plan.

The EIR doesn’t merely ignore the need to address the ﬁscal viability of the marina, it avoids        P36-22
any discussion of the cost of the project or who would pay. Currently, the marina needs
more than $100 million in repairs just to address existing problems. Many of those are
within the commercial area of the marina, which provides about 2/3 of the revenue for the
marina fund. Cost information that I obtained only through Public Records Act requests                P36-23
shows that the proposed project would cost about $170 million. No ﬁrm sources of
revenue for those costs have been identiﬁed, but it appears that the city’s share would be
more than $30 million. Since there would be no direct revenue from the project, it is
impossible to understand how making this site into a commuter terminal would address
the future viability of the marina. It seems clear that it would divert funds, and land areas,        P36-24
that could be used to repair assets that generate the revenue needed to maintain the
marina.

As with the lack of discussion on the policies in the BMMP, the discussion of the 1986
Measure L is cursory and conclusory, without presenting the policy or discussing the
                                                                                                  P36-25
provisions. Measure L was adopted by Berkeley voters on November 3, 1986. It is included
in the city’s laws as ORDINANCE NO. 5785-N.S. and titled THE BERKELEY PUBLIC PARKS
AND OPEN SPACE PRESERVATION ORDINANCE. The speciﬁc provisions that are relevant
to consideration in this part of an EIR include:


       Section 1. VOTER AUTHORIZATION PROCEDURE.

       That no public parks (hereinafter deﬁned) or public open space (hereinafter
       deﬁned) owned or controlled or leased by the City of Berkeley or agency                        P36-26
       thereof, shall be used for any other purpose than public parks and open
       space, without The Berkeley City Council ﬁrst having submitted such use
       to the citizens for approval by a majority of registered Berkeley voters
       voting at the next general election.

       Section 2. FUNDING LEVELS TO ALLOW FULL USE
                                                                                                      P36-27
       2(a): That wherever public parks and open space currently exist in Berkeley,
       such use shall continue and be funded at least to allow the maintenance of
       the present condition and services. (b) That all undedicated or unimproved
       open space owned or controlled by the City of Berkeley (including land                         P36-28
       held by the City in trust) shall be retained and funded by the Berkeley


                                                                                         2- 535
                                      Page 640 of 1541



                                                                                                    P36-28
       City Council to enable public recreational use of those lands. (c) That
       those census tracts containing less that the Master Plan provision of two
       acres of parks and open space per 1,000 population shall be singled out as                   P36-29
       having a high priority for funding the acquisition, development and
       maintenance of parks and recreational facilities.

       Section 3. DEFINITIONS

       3(a): Public parks shall be deﬁned as City of Berkeley parks, public school                  P36-30
       playgrounds or lands held in trust by a public entity, which have been
       formally dedicated to permanent recreational use by the City of Berkeley, and
       funded for recreational use by City of Berkeley public funds.
       3(b): Public open space shall be deﬁned as all City of Berkeley parks,
       public school playgrounds, and vacant public land, whether dedicated                         P36-31
       formally to park use or being used de facto as open space with
       recreational use or potential use on or after January 1, 1985.

This area clearly meets the deﬁnition of open space as it has been used for various                 P36-32
recreational purposes since it was ﬁlled in about 1970. The EIR does not discuss the
Measure in any detail or provide any quantitative analysis or discussion. Instead, the EIR
claims that this area, designated a shoreline park in BCDC’s Bay Plan and including
landscaped areas of open space, is not open space. The EIR leaps to this conclusion:
                                                                                                    P36-33
       Even if the improvements were located on public parks or open space as
       deﬁned by Measure L, they would be Measure L compliant because they do
       not change the use or purpose of these areas but rather maintain their
       recreational nature and in fact enhance recreational opportunities there.

The EIR is for a project that will regrade this area, ﬁlled to create a recreational area,
eliminating trees, berms, and public parking spaces where people access the Bay and                 P36-34
enjoy the view, to create additional space that will then be privatized for ferry or restaurant
use. This will reduce open space and eliminate the parking now used for recreational
access to the Bay and access to Shorebird Park. The EIR in essence argues that despite
city policies which protect these uses, parking lies outside the scope of CEQA. A cursory           P36-35
discussion of city policies that argue that obvious open space is not really open space is
fundamentally inadequate.

Pursuant to Section 1 of Measure L, the project must be presented to the voters for the city
to comply with Measure L. Obviously, a city must comply with its own regulations. (Paciﬁca
Corp. v. City of Camarillo (1983) 149 Cal.App.3d 168, 180-181.) Also, the city may not
approve the project due to its conﬂict with Measure L. Under CEQA a city may not approve            P36-36
a project with signiﬁcant unavoidable imposed unless it is “otherwise permissible under
applicable laws and regulations.” (CEQA §21002.1(c).) Since the project conﬂicts with
Measure L, the city may not approve the project pursuant to CEQA.


                                                                                           2- 536
                                      Page 641 of 1541




       RELEVANT BCDC POLICIES

As I pointed out in my scoping comments of May 16, 2025, Section 15125(d) of the CEQA
                                                                                                   P36-37
Guidelines requires discussion of inconsistencies between a proposed project and
regional plans. There are multiple Bay Plan policies that govern any proposal to alter the
peninsula of land ﬁlled in about 1967. Those policies establish protection for recreational        P36-38
uses, and a standard for consideration of a project like a ferry terminal. This site is unique;
it was approved in the early days of the BCDC program to create a permanent recreational
area, including parking to support those recreational uses. BCDC continues to have permit          P36-39
authority over the area, and its policies have more weight than normal EIR considerations
of consistency with agency plans. The approach in the EIR cherry picks among BCDC’s                P36-40
policies. For recreational access, which is protected by Bay Plan Policies, the EIR only
considers policies 7 and 9, and limits analysis with a claim that an EIR need not consider         P36-41
parking, even if Local Plans require protection of recreational parking as an essential
resource. The relevant Bay Plan policies include:

Plan Map 4 includes the following guidance:

       Berkeley Waterfront - Cesar Chavez Park - Preserve marina, beach, small                     P36-42
       boat launch, windsurﬁng access, ﬁshing pier, interpretive center and multi-

       marina use… (emphasis added)

       THE CITY HAS REFUSED TO DOCUMENT EXISTING RECREATIONAL USES OR
       CONSIDER FUTURE RECREATIONAL NEEDS

Stakeholders representing the existing recreational users have documented current
recreational uses. Speciﬁcally, we obtained a report from Placer AI using cell phone data       P36-49
to document visitation to the marina for the period from June 1, 2024, through May 31,
2025. Excluding the commercial areas, that report showed more than 600,000 annual
visits—more than 1800 a day. It further showed a peak use of more than 4,000 visitors
during summer months. A copy of a page of data from that report is attached.

BCDC echoed our scoping comments that the planning e ort needed to document existing
recreational uses with this comment:
                                                                                                P36-50
       The EIR should document the recreational uses of the Bay and shoreline in
       and around the Project site, identify the service area and service population
       for the recreational facilities serving those uses…




                                                                                       2- 538
                                     Page 643 of 1541




Despite that comment, Berkeley has made no e ort to document the current recreational
uses and incorporate them into a baseline that could be used to evaluate the project’s           P36-51
impacts. Existing uses are protected; therefore, a baseline of existing recreational use is
essential to analyze consistency with the relevant Bay Plan policies.

Every CEQA document must start from a “baseline” assumption. The CEQA “baseline” is
the set of environmental conditions against which to compare a project’s anticipated
impacts. (Communities for a Better Environment v. So Coast Air Qual. Mgmnt. Dist. (2010)
48 Cal. 4th 310, 321.) Section 15125(a) of the CEQA Guidelines (14 C.C.R., § 15125(a))
states in pertinent part that a lead agency’s environmental review under CEQA:

       “…must include a description of the physical environmental conditions in the
       vicinity of the project, as they exist at the time [environmental analysis] is
       commenced, from both a local and regional perspective. This environmental setting
       will normally constitute the baseline physical conditions by which a Lead Agency          P36-52
       determines whether an impact is signiﬁcant.”

(See, Save Our Peninsula Committee v. County of Monterey (2001) 87 Cal.App.4th 99, 124-
125.) As the court of appeal has explained, “the impacts of the project must be measured
against the ‘real conditions on the ground,’” and not against hypothetical permitted levels.
(Save Our Peninsula, 87 Cal.App.4th 99, 121-123.) As the court has explained, using such a
skewed baseline “mislead(s) the public” and “draws a red herring across the path of public
input.” (San Joaquin Raptor Rescue Center v. County of Merced (2007) 149 Cal.App.4th
645, 656; Woodward Park Homeowners v. City of Fresno (2007) 150 Cal.App.4th 683, 708-
711.) The EIR fails entirely to analyze the recreational use baseline.

Berkeley also fails to consider future recreational needs and the guidance provided in the       P36-53
BCDC scoping comments. Two on-site uses are obvious; re-opening of the old H’s
Lordships Restaurant and opening a pier that would provide recreational access. On the
restaurant use—a protected commercial recreational use—the city has an exclusive
negotiating agreement for that facility that would reserve 150 of what are now public
                                                                                                 P36-54
parking spaces for that use. While the portion of the proposed pier suitable for ﬁshing is
much shorter than the closed section (580 feet compared to 3000 feet), the city has made
no attempt to account for these two future uses—which are protected under Bay Plan
Recreational Policy 9.

Instead of providing an adequate analysis of whether the project meets Bay Plan policies,
and provides for future regional recreational needs, as suggested in the BCDC scoping
comments, the EIR considers only the future recreational needs of Berkeley. The city             P36-55
contends on page 3.11-19 that there is no need for future park facilities. While this may
satisfy Berkeley’s requirement, it ignores the provisions in the Bay Plan, which must
consider regional needs for recreational access only available in a waterfront park.




                                                                                        2- 539
                                     Page 644 of 1541




The draft EIR is conclusory and fails to support its conclusions with analysis that links to
existing recreational use or the Bay plan—because the city has not established what the
protected uses are. Here is the limited information to be found on page 3.9-18 of the draft
EIR:
                                                                                                   P36-56
       Consistent. The proposed ferry facility is located within a waterfront park
       priority use area and would be located at the proposed pier that will also be
       used for ﬁshing, sight-seeing, and walking. The proposed ferry facility would
       not interfere with current or future park and recreational users. This project
       would actually enhance recreational use by providing a pier that can be used
       for recreation. Navigational safety would be assured through adherence to
       WETA safety protocols. The project would not disrupt shoreline access; in
       fact, the project would restore shoreline access that is not publicly available
       under existing conditions.

       Regarding parking facilities, the City would implement a parking strategy
       to balance shared-use parking for both future ferry patrons and
       recreational users. The exact strategies that would be implemented
       would follow the guidelines established in the project Parking and TDM
       Plan19,20 and may be subject to approval from BCDC via the Project                          P36-57
       permitting process. It should be noted that consistency with this policy
       related to parking would not be considered an environmental impact
       under CEQA. Please refer to Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, for a
       discussion about how parking is addressed in this EIR. This EIR has found no
       secondary environmental impacts related to parking.

In support of this position, the city cites, on page 3-11 in a footnote that impacts to
parking cannot be a signiﬁcant impact under CEQA, citing San Franciscans
Upholding the Downtown Plan v. City & County of San Francisco (2002) 102 Cal.App.
656 at 697, “The social inconvenience of having to hunt for scarce parking spaces is
not an environmental impact; the secondary e ect of scarce parking on tra ic and
air quality is. Under CEQA, a project's social impacts need not be treated as
signiﬁcant impacts on the environment. An EIR need only address the secondary
physical impacts that could be triggered by a social impact.”                                      P36-58


This is an erroneous conclusion for the current proposal. Here, under BCDC’s Bay
Plan, a ferry terminal can only be considered for a waterfront park if it does not
usurp recreational parking. This is not matter of parking becoming less convenient,
but instead it is an inconsistency with the adopted plan of a responsible agency that
has a mission to protect the recreational uses that it allowed Bay ﬁll to create.
CEQA continues to consider such inconsistencies signiﬁcant impacts—particularly
here where the Bay Plan policy is not merely an advisory land use policy where the
city could adopt a ﬁnding of overriding circumstances, but a regulatory standard.
Unlike here, the San Francisco case did not involve any plan inconsistency.


                                                                                          2- 540
                                     Page 645 of 1541




The second paragraph in the city’s document promises that the city would, outside
of this EIR, implement a parking strategy to protect recreational use. The language of
this proposal is too vague to be acceptable as a mitigation measure. Further, in
addressing the regulatory standard, the vague promise by the city is insu icient if it
has not prepared an analysis that allows the public to comment on the su iciency
and enforceability of that program. This is contrary to CEQA guidance, which
provides:                                                                                         P36-59

       Mitigation measures must be fully enforceable through permit
       conditions, agreements or other legally binding instruments. 14 CCR §
       15126.4(a)(2). See Woodward Park Homeowners Assn., Inc. v. City of
       Fresno (2007) 150 Cal. App. 4th 683, 730 (project proponent’s agreement to a
       mitigation by itself is insu icient; mitigation measure must be an enforceable
       requirement). (emphasis added)

CEQA disallows deferring the formulation of mitigation measures to post-approval
studies. (CEQA Guidelines § 15126.4(a)(1)(B); Sundstrom v. County of Mendocino
(1988) 202 Cal.App.3d 296, 308-309.) An agency may only defer the formulation of
mitigation measures when it possesses “‘meaningful information’ reasonably
justifying an expectation of compliance.” (Sundstrom at 308; see also,
Communities for a Better Environment v. City of Richmond (2010) 184 Cal.App.4th
                                                                                                   P36-60
70, 92.) A lead agency is precluded from making the required CEQA ﬁndings unless
the record shows that all uncertainties regarding the mitigation of impacts have
been resolved; an agency may not rely on mitigation measures of uncertain e icacy
or feasibility (Kings County Farm Bureau v. City of Hanford (1990) 221 Cal.App.3d
692, 727 (ﬁnding groundwater purchase agreement inadequate mitigation because
there was no evidence that replacement water was available).) This approach
helps “insure the integrity of the process of decisionmaking by precluding stubborn
problems or serious criticism from being swept under the rug.” (Concerned Citizens
of Costa Mesa, Inc. v. 32nd Dist. Agricultural Assn. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 929, 935.)

We have seen that happen when Berkeley approved charters to let Prop SF and
Tidelines start a private ferry service in December 2016. As the city’s ﬁrst
transportation consultant, Nelson\Nygaard pointed out in their September 11, 2018,
report, “Ferry customers continue to park in South Coast Eat, J&K, and L&M Lots
due to a lack of enforcement. Since re-opening, South Cove East Lot experiences
                                                                                                  P36-61
as much as 90% occupancy.” So even the much smaller ferries were usurping
recreational parking, and the city was not enforcing restrictions to prevent that. The
city acknowledged that in response to concerns from BCDC, stating in a letter dated
April 15, 2019, that “over 300 customers depart from K-dock in the early morning
hours, occupying the majority of the 400 total parking spaces…” Examination of the
ridership records show that a peak daily ridership by PropSF was 68 passengers per
day, while Tidelines only served a higher of 71 passengers for their highest month


                                                                                         2- 541
                                      Page 646 of 1541




during the period of March 2022 through October 2022. Even with thatlimited
number of passengers, recreational parking was usurped. While the city adopted
                                                                                                    P36-61
restrictions on such parking, and promised BCDC it would protect recreational
parking, they failed to enforce those restrictions.

       PARKING FEES WILL NOT PROTECT RECREATIONAL PARKING

What little detail is provided about the city’s intent to protect recreational parking
from usurpation convinces us that it will not only be ine ective, but end much of the                P36-62
recreation that currently occurs. The City Council has endorsed a sta plan to
initiate parking fees for the area south of University Avenue where BCDC has
continuing jurisdiction. No details of that plan or its e icacy are included in the EIR;
the EIR claims that CEQA allows them to experiment with parking in the marina
without oversight under CEQA. But the report to the City Council contemplates an
annual pass of $500 for parking. A regular ferry commuter could purchase such a
pass; it represents a cost of only about $2 a day—less than the recently established                 P36-63
parking fee in Alameda. With such a pass, a commuter who purchased a
recreational pass could park anywhere in the recreational lots, knowing that the
Seawall lot is likely to ﬁll up. Since there are only 729 parking spaces in close
proximity to the proposed terminal, and a capacity for 1600 departing passengers, it
can readily be seen that initiating a ferry service under such a program could result               P36-64
in every parking space being occupied by 10:00 a.m., e ectively displacing almost
all recreational users.

       THE CITY HAS NOT COLLECTED AN ADEQUATE BASELINE OF EXISTING USE
       FOR RECREATIONAL PARKING THAT SHOULD BE PROTECTED FROM
       USURPATION

There are many di erent types of recreation that occur at Berkeley waterfront. It is
not in dispute that the most heavily used parking lots are on the South side of
University Avenue. Data provided by the city’s consultant Kittelson & Associates in a                P36-65
March 7, 2025, report established that peak usage occurred at 2 pm on weekends
and weekdays. The Placer AI data, which tracked cell phone movement into the
marina has a similar peak. The peak season for use is summer after school ends for
the summer. Parking utilization by ferry patrons is most critical on weekdays
because ridership projections are highest on weekdays as a primarily commuter
service.

Kittelson had Quality Counts collect parking data on only two days that correspond
to summer weekdays—Thursday August 1, 2024, and Thursday August 22, 2024.
However, in their report they combined those counts with other remote areas and                     P36-66
thus avoided providing even two days of data about peak use of the recreational lots
where ferry riders might usurp recreational parking. This practice underestimates
the potential for impact by diluting the data and is an improper statistical approach


                                                                                           2- 542
                                     Page 647 of 1541



                                                                                                  P36-66
to time series analysis. Other lot-by-lot counts were not included in the March 7,
2025, report or in subsequent Kittelson & Associates reports. As Kittelson informed
the city in their May 7, 2025, report “The South Cove West Lot reaches peak
occupancy between 1 and 3 pm on both weekdays and weekends.” To be adequate,
a statistically robust data set must be developed for the individual lots, and                    P36-67
particularly those closest to the proposed terminal. I requested a copy of the
Quality Counts report—and received a series of GPS readings of latitude and
longitude that did not show the counts at the individual parking lots. The city has

reverse engineer data collection to obscure actual use or not, no conclusions can
be drawn about parking use at peak times from the information that the city has
made public.

This Kittelson & Associates approach uses 1,541 parking spaces as the total parking
inventory, the denominator if you will. However, there is a much smaller inventory of

and ﬁshing; Skates/N lot, 137 spaces supporting a restaurant and overﬂow parking

That is a total of 729 spaces, supporting most of the 600,000+ annual visitors. In
e ect, the approach by the City and Kittelson doubles the denominator and thus
cuts the actual inventory of use at these sites by at least 50%.

The city cites other parking counts to assert that there is plenty of parking. The city
has had contract employees collect parking data for several years to determine
whether there were cars or RV’s parked overnight in the marina. Those counts were
taken at 8:00 pm and 10:00 am and provide no useful information about recreational
parking demand. City sta increased the frequency of counts for a brief period from
July 23, 2024, through August 23, 2024. The parking area closest to the proposed                  P36-69
ferry terminal is along Seawall Drive, and the next closest are the two South Cove
lots. The Kittelson report noted that the peak use at the South Cove lots was earlier,
between 1 and 3 pm. For those two lots, the city collected parking counts on only
12 weekdays, with all data taken at 4:00 pm, after the peak period. Even then that
data showed the South Cove lots as much as 96% full. Only 8 days of use were
counted for parking along Seawall Drive, again at 4:00. Those parking spaces
support recreational access by swimmers, windsurfers, anglers, and people simply
enjoying the view, and are protected in the City’s Marina Plan. The city proposes,
under the revised Kittelson Memorandum dated May 7, 2025, to provide 83 ferry
parking spaces along Seawall Drive, where only 90 spaces are now present. It is not               P36-70
clear whether that would reduce the number of public parking to 7. The project

the EIR that shows some spaces still facing the water, no discussion or quantitative

This EIR uses 1160 departures as their projection for passengers leaving the

       THE CITY HAS RELIED ON ASSUMPTIONS RATHER THAN EXISTING PATTERNS
       TO UNDERESTIMATE THE MOST LIKELY CAR USE

Instead of using mode split information from similar terminals now in operation,
Berkeley has used assumptions that underestimate car use and overestimate use                      P36-72
by bicycles. WETA, or San Francisco Bay Ferry, published a summary report on
November 2022 based on on-board passenger surveys. For Richmond, an existing
terminal like Berkeley more than a mile from residential areas, 57% of passengers
drove alone and 11% of passengers rode bicycles. More passengers carpooled and
parked, but that number was combined with drop o s and transit. The 2021 and
2017 survey had Alameda with 57% and 58% of passengers driving alone.

Initial estimates on mode split for Berkeley were prepared by Nelson/Nygaard in a
report date April 2021. That report estimated that 54% of passengers would drive
alone. Another 9%, with an average of 2 passengers per vehicle, would carpool.
That means that 58.5% of passengers would arrive by car and need a parking space.                  P36-73
Berkeley hired a new parking consultant, and developed estimates based on
assumptions rather than investigating the mode split that was occurring in the
marina with the two small ferry operations. Without explanation or substantial
evidence to counter existing practices, Berkeley now assumes that most people will
not drive.

The court in the case Stanislaus Audobon Society, Inc. v. County of Stanislaus (1995)
33 Cal.App.4th 144 rejected a county’s argument that a revised initial study
prepared by the county which contradicted the ﬁndings of the ﬁrst initial study had
“relegated the ﬁrst initial study to oblivion.” (Id. at 154.) The court stated, “We                P36-74
analogize such an untenable position to the unringing of a bell. The ﬁrst initial study
is part of the record. The fact that a revised initial study was later prepared does not
make the ﬁrst initial study any less a record entry nor does it diminish its
signiﬁcance, particularly when the revised study does not conclude that the project


                                                                                           2-544
                                     Page 649 of 1541




would not be growth inducing but instead simply proceeds on the assumption that
evaluation of future housing can be deferred until such housing is proposed.” (Id. at           P36-74
154) Similarly here, the city cannot simply pretend that the Nelson/Nygaard study
does not exist and disregard its ﬁndings.

If the Nelson\Nygaard estimate is applied to 955 passengers, nearly 560 drivers
would be looking for parking with a supply of only 399 spaces. If the higher                    P36-75
estimates of 1018 (2035) and 1055 (2040) from the WETA business plan, that means
that 596 to 617 cars will arrive to encounter a supply of only 399 spaces. Clearly
usurpation of recreational parking is an issue. The actual capacity of the proposed
ferry system is even greater. WETA proposes to run 8 morning departures from
Berkeley in 250 passenger ferries. WETA uses 80% occupancy as a practical
                                                                                                P36-76
estimate of capacity, giving a departure capacity of 1600 passengers. Berkeley
cannot determine what equipment WETA uses on a new route, or restrict the
number of departures, so the analysis is based on unrealistically low departures.

To meet the needs of these departing passengers, Berkeley initially proposed
designating 250 of the existing 320 spaces in Seawall lot for ferry use instead of
public use. Earlier proposals by WETA in a 2008 draft EIR were for at least 400
spaces. In an addendum dated May 7, 2025, Kittelson lays out the current, and
revised proposal by the city and WETA. That proposal would provide 250 spaces in
Seawall Lot, 83 spaces along Seawall Drive, and 66 spaces in the Skate’s lot, for a
total of 399 spaces to serve 1160 departing passengers. Currently, Seawall lot has
only 320 spaces and the city proposes to reserve 150 spaces for a new restaurant                P36-77
lessee. To reach these numbers, it would be necessary to restripe Seawall lot,
eliminating most of the existing landscaping. At present, the 90 spaces along
Seawall Drive facing the Bay are used for access to the Bay and for viewing—uses
protected by policies like Recreation Policy 3. The Kittelson addendum noted that
peak use of those spaces (according to their limited counts) is 49 cars parked, while
parking counts mentioned above show 63% of the 90 spaces, or 57 spaces
occupied by recreational users so this proposal directly usurps existing recreational
parking.

       THE CITY HAS FAILED TO ENFORCE PARKING RESTRICTIONS AND HAS NOT

       PROTECTION OF RECREATIONAL USE CANNOT BE ACHIEVED BY ADOPTING
       POLICIES INTENDED TO REDUCE ACCESS TO THE MARINA BY AUTOMOBILE
       WHEN THE CITY’S OWN SURVEYS SHOW THAT 90% OF THE VISITORS TO                                P36-82
       THE MARINA DO SO BY AUTOMOBILE

Rather than address the obvious issues raised by planning for more than 1000
passengers in an area where most of the existing parking is needed for recreational


                                                                                         2-546
                                      Page 651 of 1541




use, the city pivoted to considering a transportation demand management
approach. In e ect, the city decided to charge recreational users enough money to
drive some out of the marina’s recreational area and make room for commuters.
Berkeley has long been considering ways to discourage recreational activities that
depend on car access—as about 90% of access presently does. As early as

charge recreational users of this public trust park land enough to drive many away
and make room for ferry parking.

FEASIBILITY AND ALTERNATIVES

It is certainly unusual to see a project proponent ignore the scoping comments of a
responsible agency. Yet in the cursory dismissal of alternatives and lack of
discussion of costs and feasibility, that is exactly what this document does. BCDC
provided scoping comments similar to those submitted by stakeholders and Save
Berkeley Pier. BCDC’s comments were clear and direct:                                           P36-83

       Therefore, the alternatives evaluated in the EIR should include at least one
       alternative that reduces or eliminates the amount of ﬁll proposed.

BCDC’s scoping letter identiﬁes the speciﬁc Bay Plan policies that compel
consideration of alternatives with less dredging and ﬁll. Similar policies are
included in the Clean Water Act, where Section 404(b) and its implementing
regulations require analysis of alternatives that would avoid ﬁll completely, further           P36-84
analysis of alternatives with less impact, and then mitigation only if there were no
practicable alternatives.

The EIR short circuits this process by insisting that there are no alternatives that
would meet the city’s objectives. In e ect, they argue the city’s objectives are
superior to the regulatory standards for considering marine impacts, which don’t
merit discussion. That position can be found in this assertion:
                                                                                                P36-85
       For the purposes of this alternatives analysis, the City considers the two top
       bullets as the basic project objectives. In other words, for an alternative to
       meet the basic project objectives, they would need to meet of the following
       basic objectives: (1) enhance public access and recreational opportunities at
       the Berkeley Waterfront and (2) provide e icient and environmentally friendly
       zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.


                                                                                        2-547
                                     Page 652 of 1541




The city cannot avoid considering alternatives by including some recreational
beneﬁts as mandatory elements of the city’s objectives. The objectives of improving
access and providing ferry service are independent objectives. Restoration of pier                P36-86
access and improvements to the Bay Trail are separate projects from establishment
of a ferry service—although the city has consistently argued otherwise. Both are
subject to feasibility and alternative tests.

CEQA requires that an EIR provide a discussion of project alternatives that allows
meaningful analysis. (Laurel Heights Improvement Assn. v. Regents of Univ. of
California (1988) 47 Cal. 3d 376, 403.) An overly narrow deﬁnition of project
objectives renders the alternatives analysis inadequate. To narrowly deﬁne the
primary "objective" of the proposed project itself constitutes a violation of CEQA                P36-87
since such a restrictive formulation would improperly foreclose consideration of
alternatives. (See, City of Santee v. County of San Diego (1989) 214 Cal.App.3d
1438) (holding that when project objectives are deﬁned too narrowly an EIR’s
treatment of analysis may also be inadequate). It is an abuse of discretion for an
agency to exclude a potentially feasible alternative that would substantially reduce
signiﬁcant impacts from analysis in the EIR simply because it does not meet all
project objectives. (Habitat & Watershed Caretakers v. City of Santa Cruz (2013) 213
Cal.App.4th 1277, 1304 [“limited-water alternative could not be eliminated from
consideration solely because it would impede to some extent the attainment of the                 P36-88
project’s objectives”]; Watsonville Pilots Assn. v. City of Watsonville (2010) 183 Cal.
App. 4th 1059, 1087 [agency’s refusal to analyze a reduced development alternative
because it failed to meet two of 12 project objectives was legal error].)

The EIR’s alternatives analysis is inadequate because it fails to consider a feasible
                                                                                                  P36-89
reduced ﬁll alternative suggested by BCDC, and it has deﬁned the project
alternatives so narrowly as to foreclose the consideration of environmentally                     P36-90
superior alternatives.

       RESTORATION OF BERKELEY PIER

Berkeley received a grant of $15 million that could have been used to restore
Berkeley Pier. The most recent cost estimates, obtained through a Public Records
Act request, estimate the total cost of 1080’ feet of pier, including demolition,
pilings, and a new deck, is about $14 million. I ﬁrst pitched the idea of State funding
for restoration of the pier to then Senator Nancy Skinner and then to newly elected
Council Member Terry Taplin. The city requested a grant and received $15 million. It              P36-91
was not limited to construction of a pier and a new ferry service; the grant made no
mention of a ferry service, the money was simply available for the pier and the
marina. Senator Skinner wrote eloquently about the importance of a pier as a way
to get people out onto the Bay without owning a boat—a sentiment I heartily
support. Restoring the pier has a much easier regulatory path than the proposed


                                                                                          2-548
                                     Page 653 of 1541




project. Demolition of the old pier would be in-kind mitigation for a new pier.
Construction of a new ﬁshing pier, even if only 1080 feet long, would not entail new
ﬁll for a terminal breakwater or 400,000 cubic yards of dredging that would deepen
                                                                                                  P36-91
the ﬂats that have supported a pier ﬁshery for decades. Even if not matched by the
city, the $15 million grant was su icient to restore a substantial recreational pier.
The city chose not to do so; that is a policy choice, not evidence that a pier is only
feasible in combination with a new, in-bay ferry terminal.

A revised EIR should consider the restoration alternative as a “no project”                       P36-92
alternative. It would clearly be environmentally superior to the proposed project.

       BUILDING A NEW PIER IN THE BAY REQUIRES CAREFUL ANALYSIS OF
       IMPACTS, ALTERNATIVES AND FEASIBILITY

Cost estimates obtained through a Public Records Act request, although not
included in the EIR, estimate the cost of the current project, not including new
ferries for operation, at $131,133,445. Previous estimates for the cost of ferries
were $38 million, bringing the total cost of the project close to $170 million. A copy            P36-93
of that estimate is attached and incorporated by evidence. In contrast, the
construction of a ferry terminal at Richmond, built inside the breakwater, was $20
million. As the City of Berkeley has admitted in their presentation to the Design
Review Board at BCDC, there are no identiﬁed funding sources for the project—
which undermines their argument that only the project and no cheaper alternatives
are feasible. The city has not provided an update of the city’s costs for construction
or for management and maintenance of the landside improvements, but those                        P36-94
costs appear to be in excess of $30 million just for the initial cost. That would fund
restoration of a much longer recreational pier, with better ﬁsheries resources, than
the current proposal. A feasibility analysis would allow consideration of the
considerable value of recreational access for ﬁshing and other uses.
Feasibility, and the related term practicability, pose regulatory hurdles beyond
simply ﬁnding $131 million. As noted above, the Bay Plan, the Clean Water Act, and
the Porter-Cologne Act all require rigorous analysis of alternatives before new ﬁll              P36-95
and 400,000 cubic yards of dredging can be permitted. Most of those hurdles
disappear with a location inside the marina.

Operation of the terminal would require ongoing costs and subsidies for direct
subsidy of the passengers, and for parking management. While WETA has not
updated its strategic vision document for 2050, a draft was prepared for the                 P36-96
WETA Board. Dated April 12, 2023, and contained in Table 14: Route Summary
Metrics, it estimates the annual operational subsidy required for a Berkeley service
at $9 to $12 million a year.

The EIR fails to adequately establish either the impacts of dredging or propose
adequate, in-kind mitigation measures for the dredging impacts, as requested in          i   P36-97



                                                                                         2-549

BCDC’s scoping comments. Those impacts need to be established to consider

                                                                                                 P36-98
       Because implementation of Mitigation Measures BIO-3 would result in no net
       loss of jurisdictional waters, impacts would be less than signiﬁcant with
       mitigation. (Page 3.3-59)

While replacement of an existing pier structure with a similar structure might be

management practices, the proposed project involves construction of a terminal                   P36-99
breakwater to shelter the proposed ferry berths, 400,000 cubic yards of dredging,

These impacts are neither captured in analysis nor adequately mitigated, despite

       The City shall develop a mitigation plan documenting the existing pier

       needed to meet the mitigation goal. This plan shall be developed by a

This falls far short of the comment in the BCDC scoping letter:

       Impacts to the subtidal habitat area should be discussed in the EIR analysis,         P36-101
       and it should also describe the mitigation that will be required for those
       impacts.

As CEQA litigation has long held, a proposal for a future plan for mitigation does not
provide for an e ective or legally binding mitigation measure and does not allow the
public to comment on those issues. Deferred mitigation is prohibited under CEQA.
                                                                                             P36-102
Mitigation measures must be set forth in the EIR so the public can assess the
adequacy of the measure. (Communities for a Better Environment v. City of
Richmond (2010) 184 Cal.App.4th 70, 92.)

       ALTERNATIVE PARKING ARRANGEMENTS SHOULD BE CONSIDERED

Currently, the City of Berkely’s parking division is located on public trust land just

period—and is only dealt with in the EIR by treating the shorter breakwater as an

“An accurate, stable and ﬁnite project description is the sine qua non of an

AIR QUALITY AND VMT

In my scoping letter I asked for an analysis of energy use normalized as British                   P36-115
Thermal Units, ( BTU’s) per passenger, and a comparison of e iciency to BART and
AC Transit as a carbon signature analysis. On page 3.2-21, Berkeley limits the EIR’s
consideration of air quality impacts to 4 factors, none of which consider carbon
emissions from the whole of the project. A lack of analysis does not prevent                       P36-116
Berkeley and the EIR from claiming, without providing enforceable implementation
measures, that the project will be a zero-emission project that will reduce VMT.
Such claims cannot be made without some substantial evidence and analysis that
bridges the analytical gap to support the claim. Paul Kamen has prepared an
analysis of energy use per passenger mile that shows the existing ferry ﬂeet                       P36-117
requiring 4 times as much energy (measured as BTU’s/passenger mile) as AC
Transit, and 40 times as much energy as BART. While that analysis may be subject
to change in an adequate EIR, the very low e iciency of the ferry system and the fact
that energy generation for charging batteries and for cars driving to the terminal still           P36-118
involves fossil fuel sources compels a more detailed analysis.

Berkeley does not control the source of emissions from ferries, or the purchase
practices of WETA. As I pointed out in my scoping comments, the Executive
Director of WETA has qualiﬁed any commitment to electric ferry propulsion with the
caveat of “if feasible.” While WETA has entered into contracts for purchase of some
electric ferries and retroﬁt of others, meeting agendas have made it clear that
                                                                                                   P36-119
continued electriﬁcation depends on sources that are not now available. None of
those ferries are intended for a new Berkeley route, and WETA Board reports make it
clear that continued electriﬁcation depends on funding which is not now available.
As such, electric ferries may not be feasible, and Berkeley cannot require their use if
a terminal is built


                                                                                           2-553
                                      Page 658 of 1541




Instead of analysis that shows certainty or feasibility, the EIR relies on
unsubstantiated claims. For example, on page 3.6-43 the document asserts,
without quantitative analysis, that the project would convert auto trips into ferry
trips. The EIR claims, without substantiation, that the project would reduce VMT.
That is an appropriate metric for consideration, the Bay Area Air Quality
Management has issued advisory CEQA guidelines that suggest that a project might                   P36-120
have a less than signiﬁcant impact if the project “will achieve a reduction in project-
generated vehicle miles traveled (VMT) below the regional average…” The air quality
section does not include any quantitative discussion of the project’s impact on VMT
to address this guideline. The potential impacts on VMT are brieﬂy discussed
beginning on page 3.12-20, but proceeds from an assumption:

        Operation Transit projects typically reduce VMT and are therefore presumed
       to have a less-than-signiﬁcant impact on transportation.

No origin and destination information is provided, either for the anticipated
passengers, or from analysis of other WETA terminals or on-board surveys. The                      P36-121
analysis is assumption driven and concludes that VMT will be reduced if passengers
on a ferry travel to the new ferry terminal instead of crossing the Bay Bridge.

However, the practices and fare structure of WETA in recent years suggests another
source for many passengers. In 2021, WETA reduced fares by 30% in order to
increase ridership in the wake of the pandemic. An account of that can be found in
an article in the Alameda Post dated March 7, 2023. Discussion at WETA Board
meetings and on-board surveys established that fares were set at a level intended to
compete with BART, and at least some of the increased ridership came from BART
passengers. If some combination of elimination of parking at the North Berkeley
and Ashby Bart stations, and cheaper fares or less crowded conditions on the ferry                 P36-122
induce people to drive further to the ferry, or drive to the ferry instead of walking to
BART or bus stops, VMT may increase. WETA has collected on-board surveys to
determine why new passengers are now riding the ferry. Many passengers cited the
lower fares as the reason they switched to the ferry and said they would return to
BART if the fares increased. As WETA Executive Director is quoted in the Alameda
Post, “San Francisco Bay Ferry is a premium option for travelers, but we can’t charge
premium prices if we want to rebuild ridership.” WETA clearly attracted passengers
away from BART with lower fares, on-board cocktails, and seats for all. The question
is how many. Information from on-board surveys, rather than assumptions, should                    P36-123
be used to determine whether a new ferry service in Berkeley will reduce VMT.

RECREATIONAL IMPACTS

In my scoping letter I pointed out that construction of a vertical breakwater in a
highly used recreational area—one designated as part of a waterfront park—would               t    P36-124

alter wind and wave patterns. Those might in turn a ect the safety of sailing near

                                                                                                    P36-125

The city dismisses scoping comments about recreational impacts being a ected by

that is recreational by citing Berkeley Municipal Code Section 6.20.180. The
interpretation of the city ignores the language of the code, the genesis of the
language, and decades of practice. The language of the code prohibits swimming                      P36-126
and windsurﬁng in the marina. The speciﬁc language makes that clear.

       It is unlawful for any person to swim, bathe, wade or windsurf in any portion

protective breakwaters and thus is arguing that the existing recreational use is illicit
and they are not required to consider it in this EIR. The city further argues that
neither windsurﬁng or similar activities can occur within 1500 feet of the Berkeley
Pier—open waters of the bay outside the marina and where the city’s jurisdiction is
limited. The genesis of this section of the Marina Code was as an outcome from
Berkeley’s e ort to ban jetskis that generated litigation. Berkeley and other cities
which adopted ordinances banning jetskis were sued successfully. The genesis of
the code is a result of this lawsuit, and its adoption in 2001, reﬂects this history. The
literal language is:                                                                                P36-128


       No jetski or personal watercraft of any kind may be operated within 1,500
       feet of the Berkeley shoreline or the Berkeley Fishing Pier except in the 200-

CUMULATIVE IMPACT

The city of Berkeley has issued a draft of the Waterfront Speciﬁc Plan, dated
November 8, 2024. The City Council authorized environmental work under CEQA for
that plan, which included a development scenario that would increase commercial
development on the waterfront from 380,000 square feet to 1.215 million square
feet. Yet a reviewer of this EIR would search in vain for any analysis of the
cumulative impact of the city’s development plans. Section 3.95, in land use,                   P36-134
avoids any mention of this land use plan. The EIR devotes a short paragraph on
page 1-5, section 1.2.3, that dismisses the need to consider their future plans,
reasoning “Because the draft WSP is currently a draft document and has not yet
been adopted by the City, policies in the Draft WSP would not apply to the proposed
project unless the City adopts the WSP prior to approval of the proposed project.”
With that sentence the city tips us o that they have piecemealed their
development plans to avoid providing any analysis of the cumulative impact of
those plans.



                                                                                        2-557
                                     Page 662 of 1541




The city also avoids any discussion of their plans for redevelopment of the former
H’s Lordships restaurant. The city has entered into an exclusive negotiating
agreement with a ﬁrm to market that site, including remodeling, CEQA clearance,              P36-135
and reserving 150 of the public parking spaces for that lease. This plan does not
make it into the EIR.

There is a fundamental problem with the city’s approach. There is no existing land
use plan for Berkeley that designates this site, and the adjacent parking lot, for a
ferry terminal for commuters. Section 1.2.3 acknowledges that adoption of the WSP
would provide such a designation, with the statement “As described in the Draft              P36-136
WSP, ferry access is a proposed allowable use in the Berkeley Waterfront.” Rather
than complete a land use planning process that is far advanced, the city has tabled
the WSP and thereby argues that they don’t have to consider cumulative impacts.
Or, as the comedienne used to say, “Never mind.” This approach is clearly
inconsistent with CEQA case law.

An EIR must discuss signiﬁcant cumulative impacts. (CEQA Guidelines section
15130(a).) This requirement ﬂows from CEQA section 21083, which requires a
ﬁnding that a project may have a signiﬁcant e ect on the environment if “the
possible e ects of a project are individually limited but cumulatively considerable. .
. . ‘Cumulatively considerable’ means that the incremental e ects of an individual
project are considerable when viewed in connection with the e ects of past
projects, the e ects of other current projects, and the e ects of probable future
projects.” “Cumulative impacts” are deﬁned as “two or more individual e ects
which, when considered together, are considerable or which compound or increase
other environmental impacts.” CEQA Guidelines section 15355(a). “[I]ndividual
e ects may be changes resulting from a single project or a number of separate
projects.” CEQA Guidelines section 15355(a).

“The cumulative impact from several projects is the change in the environment                P36-137
which results from the incremental impact of the project when added to other
closely related past, present, and reasonably foreseeable probable future projects.
Cumulative impacts can result from individually minor but collectively signiﬁcant
projects taking place over a period of time.” (Communities for a Better Environment
v. Cal. Resources Agency (“CBE v. CRA”), (2002) 103 Cal.App.4th 98, 117.) A legally
adequate cumulative impacts analysis views a particular project over time and in
conjunction with other related past, present, and reasonably foreseeable probable
future projects whose impacts might compound or interrelate with those of the
project at hand. “Cumulative impacts can result from individually minor but
collectively signiﬁcant projects taking place over a period of time.” (CEQA
Guidelines § 15355(b).)

The city clearly ignores reasonably foreseeable future projects in the area, and the
EIR therefore lacks an adequate cumulative impacts analysis.


                                                                                         2-558
                                  Page 663 of 1541

Letter P36
Commenter:         Jim McGrath
Date:              March 27, 2026

Response to Comment P36-1
As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, the objectives of the proposed project include enhancing
public access and recreational opportunities at the waterfront and providing efficient, environmentally
sustainable ferry service to support regional mobility and resiliency. Refer to Section 3.11.4, Impacts
Analysis, of the Draft EIR for detailed information regarding the level of impacts to recreation.
Refer to Section 2.2.3, Topical Response: BCDC Jurisdiction, Planning Consistency, and Permit Compliance,
regarding BCDC and its policies and processes. The City of Berkeley will obtain all necessary permits and
approvals from BCDC and other relevant agencies prior to commencement of construction activities.
Compliance with agency-specific requirements will be confirmed through the respective permitting
processes. These permits will include conditions that ensure the project meets all applicable regulatory
standards before construction begins. No revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment P36-2
The comment questions adequacy of parking relative to ferry capacity.
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion about parking adequacy. The analysis,
significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented within the Draft EIR remain valid as written.
No further response or revisions to the EIR are required.

Response to Comment P36-3
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, and Section 2.2.3, Topical Response: BCDC Jurisdiction,
Planning Consistency, and Permit Compliance. The City acknowledges the commenter’s discussion of
historical actions related to parking management at the Berkeley Waterfront. However, the environmental
review conducted under CEQA is focused on the potential physical environmental impacts of the
proposed project and the adequacy of the analysis presented in the Draft EIR. Prior actions, decisions, or
disputes regarding parking management do not, by themselves, constitute evidence that the Draft EIR’s
analysis of the proposed project is deficient. Rather, the relevant question under CEQA is whether the
proposed project would result in significant physical environmental impacts.
As discussed in the referenced topical responses, the Draft EIR evaluates parking-related secondary
effects, recreational access, and consistency with applicable Bay Plan policies and concludes that the
project would not result in significant parking-related environmental impacts. The commenter does not
identify a deficiency in that analysis or provide evidence demonstrating that the Draft EIR’s conclusions
are incorrect. Accordingly, the analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain
valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P36-4
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking. As discussed therein, the analysis of whether parking
changes could result in secondary physical environmental effects are addressed in Sections 3.2, Air
Quality, 3.10, Noise, and 3.12, Transportation. Additionally, the Draft EIR evaluates potential effects on
recreational access, recreational facility use, transportation, and plan consistency accordingly within
Sections 3.9, Land Use and Planning (Impact LU-2), 3.11, Recreation (Impact REC-1), and 3.12,
Transportation (Impact TRA-2), which conclude that project implementation would not result in physical
deterioration of recreational facilities, would maintain recreational access, and would not result in

significant parking-related environmental impacts. The analyses and significance conclusions presented
in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P36-5
The Draft EIR evaluates the project for consistency with all applicable land use plans and policies under
Impact LU-2 within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning. Therein, the Draft EIR identifies applicable plans
and policies and discloses any potential inconsistencies in accordance with CEQA Guidelines. This
includes a consistency analysis with the Bay Plan.
Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency, for a discussion related to how the
Draft EIR addresses inconsistencies with relevant land use plans and policies.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented under Impact LU-2 in Section 3.9, Land Use and
Planning, and throughout the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions are required.

Response to Comment P36-6
Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency, for a discussion related to how the
Draft EIR addresses inconsistencies with relevant land use plans and policies.
Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, of the Draft EIR includes a comprehensive evaluation of applicable
policies under Impact LU-2. Specifically, Table 3.9-1 (pages 3.9-12 through 3.9-23) evaluates consistency
with Bay Plan policies, and Table 3.9-4 (page 3.9-31) evaluates consistency with the Berkeley Marina
Master Plan. These analyses identify applicable policy topics and assess consistency based on project
design, including recreational access, shoreline access, and multimodal circulation improvements. Any
potential inconsistencies with Bay Plan and Marina Master Plan policies are disclosed therein in
accordance with CEQA Guidelines.
Regarding the statement that the Draft EIR selectively identifies policies, Section 3.9.4, Impacts Analysis,
Approach to Analysis discussion explains that although the subsequent analysis discusses the most
relevant policies from the applicable planning documents, the City’s overall consistency conclusions are
based upon the complete planning documents (see Draft EIR page 3.9-10). Additionally, some planning
documents or policies omitted from Section 3.9 are addressed in other Draft EIR sections within
Chapter 3, Environmental Impact Analysis, as summarized on Draft EIR page 3.9-10.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented under Impact LU-2 in Section 3.9, Land Use and
Planning, and throughout the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions are required.
Refer to subsequent Responses to Comments for specific responses to the policies raised in the
comments.

The Draft EIR evaluates the project for consistency with all applicable land use plans and policies under
Impact LU-2 within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning. This includes a consistency analysis with the
Berkeley Marina Master Plan (pages 3.9-29 to 3.9-33) and Measure L (page 3.9-33).
Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency, for a discussion related to how the

Refer to Section 2.2.16, Topical Response: Measure L, for a discussion related to how the project would
not conflict with Measure L.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented throughout the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions are required.

Response to Comment P36-8
This statement is not accurate. The Draft EIR includes a consistency analysis of relevant policies in the
Berkeley Marina Master Plan (see Table 3.9-3 in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning of the Draft EIR,
pages 3.9-31 to 3.9-33). For Measure L, the Draft EIR includes a robust discussion of why the project
would not conflict with Measure L (see Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning of the Draft EIR, page 3.9-33).
Refer also to Section 2.2.16, Topical Response: Measure L, for a discussion related to how the project
would not conflict with Measure L.
Regarding the references to Figures 2.0 and 12.0 in the Berkeley Marina Master Plan, refer to Response to
Comment P36-10.
The analysis and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further
revisions to the EIR are required.

Response to Comment P36-9
The Draft EIR evaluates the project for consistency with all applicable land use plans and policies under
Impact LU-2 within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning. This includes a consistency analysis with the
Berkeley Marina Master Plan (pages 3.9-29 to 3.9-33). Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land
Use/Plan Consistency, for a discussion related to how the Draft EIR addresses inconsistencies with
relevant land use plans and policies.
Regarding the statement that “the only ferry site considered in the plan is located within the marina, and
the plan adopts policies to make that site seismically safe”, the City has reviewed the Berkeley Marina
Master Plan, including Figure 2.0, which is referenced in this comment, and has found no mention of a
new ferry site. The Berkeley Marina Master Plan does reference an existing “ferry pier” when discussing
compliance with seismic regulations, under Principle 3. The first policy under Principle 3 is to “update the
ferry pier to comply with seismic regulations.” Page 3.9-32 of the Draft EIR analyses consistency with this
policy, and finds that the project would be consistent with this policy.
The comment does not provide evidence that “the only ferry site considered in the plan is located within
the marina, and the plan adopts policies to make that site seismically safe.” No changes are warranted
related to the Draft EIR analysis, conclusions, or mitigation. No further response is required.

Response to Comment P36-10
Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency, for a discussion related to how the
Draft EIR addresses inconsistencies with relevant land use plans and policies.
First, as a matter of clarification, the comment incorrectly characterizes the project. The project would not
eliminate much of the open space of the peninsula. As described in Chapter 2, Project Description of the
Draft EIR, the project features on land are primarily within existing roadways or parking areas. While the
project would eliminate a planter that consists of a raised berm with landscaped trees withing the
Seawall Parking Lot, this is not considered open space and the project would not eliminate open space. In
addition, as described in Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational
Water Access, the project would not eliminate the staging area for windsurfing, but rather the proposed
amenities for the project would be supportive and consistent with goals in the Berkeley Marina Master
Plan related to recreational activities and it would not preclude the development of future recreational
amenities identified in the Berkeley Marina Master Plan. Furthermore, the comment incorrectly states that
the project would eliminate most of the parking places that are currently used for fishing access and
viewing the Bay. Refer to Section 2.2.24, Topical Response: Seawall Drive/View Access, for a discussion of
the parking spaces off Seawall Drive and Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion
about how parking is addressed under CEQA.
The Draft EIR considered relevant policies in the Berkeley Marina Master Plan related to recreation (see
Impact LU-2 in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning of the Draft EIR, page 3.9-32). Nonetheless, in response

Response to Comment P36-11
As stated in Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description: Landside, page 2-23, the proposed project would
remove approximately 40 existing trees and would plant between 50 and 70 new trees. The Draft EIR
analysis presented under Impact BIO-5 in Section 3.3.4, page 3.3-65 concluded that impacts to protected
trees would be less than significant. In addition, see Response to Comment P36-10 for a discussion
regarding open space. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P36-12 to P36-18
The Draft EIR evaluates the project for consistency with all applicable land use plans and policies under
Impact LU-2 within Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning. This includes a consistency analysis with the
Berkeley Marina Master Plan (pages 3.9-29 to 3.9-33). Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land
Use/Plan Consistency, for a discussion related to how the Draft EIR addresses inconsistencies with
relevant land use plans and policies.
The comment provides a bulleted list of “policies”; however, these bullets appear to be the commenters
own interpretation of policies and not the actual policies in the Berkeley Marina Master Plan. The
consistency analysis in the Draft EIR (pages 3.9-29 to 3.9-33) includes the relevant policies from the
Berkeley Marina Master Plan verbatim and cover the summarized list identified in the comment. For a
discussion of windsurfer activities (comment P36-18), refer to Response to Comment P36-10.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented under Impact LU-2 within Section 3.9, Land Use and
Planning, and related sections remain valid as written in the Draft EIR. No revisions are required.

Refer to Section 2.2.6, Topical Response: CEQA Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users, regarding how existing
recreation would be affected by the project. The analysis and conclusions presented therein remain valid
as written, and no further clarifications are required.

Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users. For discussion of Seawall Drive in-car Bay viewing, refer to Section
2.2.24, Topical Response: Seawall Drive/View Access.
The Draft EIR appropriately characterizes existing recreational conditions, evaluates potential changes to
recreational space and access, and demonstrates that scenic-view parking and recreational opportunities
would be maintained. The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid

consistency analysis under Impact LU-2 focuses on plans and policies that are relevant to the proposed
project and the environmental issues evaluated in the Draft EIR, consistent with CEQA Guidelines
Section 15125(d), which requires discussion of inconsistencies with plans adopted for environmental
purposes. However, the City’s overall consistency conclusions are based upon the planning documents in
their entirety, rather than individual policies (see Draft EIR page 3.9-10). The Draft EIR further explains that
some applicable plans or policies are evaluated in other sections within Chapter 3, Environmental Impact
Analysis, where they are more directly related to the environmental topic being analyzed (see Draft EIR
page 3.9-10).
Consistent with this approach, Impact LU-2 evaluates the project's consistency with applicable BCDC Bay
Plan policies in Table 3.9-1 (pages 3.9-12 through 3.9-23). The table includes a broad range of Bay Plan
policies addressing topics such as environmental justice, public access, recreation, transportation,
climate change, shoreline protection, operational safety, water quality, marine resources, and special area
plans. In addition, where specific Bay Plan policies relate to resource areas evaluated elsewhere in the
Draft EIR, those issues are addressed in the corresponding environmental sections, including Section 3.3,
Biological Resources; Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality; Section 3.11, Recreation; and Section 3.12,
Transportation. The City also notes that BCDC, the agency responsible for administering and enforcing the
Bay Plan, reviewed the Draft EIR and provided extensive comments regarding project impacts, regulatory
considerations, and areas where additional analysis or clarification would be beneficial. BCDC did not
identify any Bay Plan policy that was improperly omitted from the Draft EIR's land use consistency
analysis under Impact LU-2. Rather, BCDC acknowledged the Draft EIR's Bay Plan consistency analysis
and noted that it would conduct its own independent review of project consistency with applicable Bay
Plan policies as part of its permit review process.
