Response to Comment P36-54
Under CEQA an EIR must evaluate a project’s impacts relative to existing environmental conditions, which
“normally constitute the baseline” for determining CEQA significance (CEQA Guidelines
Section 15125(a)). The Guidelines further specify that the baseline shall not include hypothetical
conditions that have not occurred, even if such uses could be allowed under existing plans or
agreements. Consistent with these requirements, the Draft EIR evaluates environmental impacts based
on existing conditions at the project site at the time of environmental review. The potential reopening of
the restaurant at 199 Seawall and other future uses referenced by the commenter are not part of the
proposed project and are not existing conditions; therefore, they are not treated as baseline conditions
under CEQA. However, CEQA does require consideration of reasonably foreseeable future projects and
development in a cumulative context. Accordingly, the Draft EIR evaluates the project’s incremental
contribution to cumulative impacts in each resource Chapter (Chapter 3), in combination with other past,
present, and reasonably foreseeable future projects, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15130.
This cumulative analysis captures the combined effects of the proposed project and other anticipated
development activities in the project vicinity.
With respect to the reopening of the 199 Seawall restaurant, refer to Response to Comment P36-108,
which explains that the City does consider a potential new restaurant at the 199 Seawall Drive site as a
cumulative project. Response to Comment P36-108 also includes a discussion of the City of Berkeley
lease agreement providing 150 parking stalls to the new restaurant.
With respect to “opening a pier that would provide recreational access”, this proposed project that has
been analyzed in the Draft EIR proposed to create a new pier that would provide recreational access.
The Draft EIR appropriately evaluates project impacts based on existing environmental conditions and
includes cumulative impact analysis that considers reasonably foreseeable future development.

Response to Comment P36-71
The comment does not identify an inadequacy in the environmental analysis. As described in the Draft
EIR (pages 2-30 to 2-31 of the Draft EIR), the ridership assumptions used for the project were based on
ridership forecasts developed through the WETA Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan. The Business Plan
includes ridership forecasts prepared by CDM Smith using accepted transportation planning and travel
demand modeling methodologies developed to evaluate proposed ferry services. The forecasts estimate
weekday, weekend, and special event ridership under multiple service scenarios and incorporate
assumptions regarding travel demand, service characteristics, and phased ridership growth over time.
The Business Plan also recognizes that new transit services typically experience a multi-year ridership
ramp-up period and incorporates a service adoption factor into its evaluation of future service
performance.
Under CEQA, an EIR must be supported by substantial evidence in the administrative record and may rely
on reasonable assumptions, expert opinion, and facts to support its analysis (Pub. Resources Code, §
21080, subd. (e); CEQA Guidelines, §§ 15144, 15145, 15151). CEQA Guidelines Section 15151 expressly
provides that “[d]isagreement among experts does not make an EIR inadequate,” and that an EIR should
be judged based on whether it reflects a good-faith effort at full disclosure rather than by a standard of
absolute perfection. The ridership projections relied upon in the Draft EIR were prepared by qualified
professionals using accepted transportation planning methodologies and constitute substantial evidence
supporting the environmental analysis. While the commenter has provided an alternative estimate of
future ridership, CEQA does not require the Lead Agency to adopt a commenter’s assumptions or
conclusions where the EIR relies on reasonable forecasting methodologies supported by substantial




Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                      2-581
                                             Page 686 of 1541

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

evidence in the administrative record. A difference of opinion regarding future ridership projections does
not demonstrate that the Draft EIR’s analysis is inadequate.
In addition, higher ridership in the future represents an environmental benefit, through the reduction of
VMT and GHG emissions. Insofar the comment is expressing concern about parking, refer to Section
2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion of parking supply adequacy.
Accordingly, the comment has been noted. The information provided by the commenter does not alter the
conclusions of the Draft EIR, and no revisions to the environmental analysis are required.

Response to Comment P36-73 to P36-76
This comment is inaccurate. The Parking and TDM Plan, as well as the Draft EIR directly address the
relationship between the prior and current mode share estimates. As documented in Section 3.0 of the
Parking and TDM Plan (page 5), the City’s Traffic Consultant (Kittelson and Associates) expressly
reviewed the Berkeley Marina Ferry Parking & Transportation Demand Management Strategy
(Nelson\Nygaard, October 2021) and the 2018 Short-Term Recommendations for Waterfront Parking
Management on which it was based. Appendix F (page 2) of the Draft EIR identifies the 54 percent
baseline as one of the sources used in developing the mode split. The City’s Traffic Consultant also
reviewed the WETA Business Service Plan (31 percent drive-alone) and updated WETA onboard survey
data from 2022 (44 percent drive-alone) and derived a recommended baseline of 40 percent drive-alone, a
figure that reflects more current observed travel behavior than the 2021 Feasibility Study estimate. This
methodology is explained in Section 3.4 of the Parking and TDM Plan (page 10) and constitutes
substantial evidence supporting the Draft EIR's analysis. The commenter's preferred 54 percent figure is
not ignored; it is one data point among several that the City’s Traffic Consultant weighed in arriving at a
more current and comprehensive estimate.
The commenter's parking demand calculations in P36-75 similarly rely on the 54 percent figure and a
parking supply figure of 399 spaces that does not reflect the full parking supply available to ferry riders
under the project. As discussed in Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, the City's analysis
demonstrates that sufficient parking capacity exists within the Berkeley Waterfront to accommodate
projected ferry demand. While some commenters offered their own demand calculations, the City's
conclusions are based on the Parking and TDM Plan prepared by the City’s Traffic Consultant using
empirical data and professional methodology. These mode split assumptions that have been
substantiated in the Parking and TDM Plan are also identified in the Draft EIR, as part of Appendix F
(subsection Mode Split Assumptions, page 2). Regarding potential ferry ridership, refer to Response to
Comment P36-71.
The commenter's reliance on Stanislaus Audubon Society, Inc. v. County of Stanislaus (1995) 33
Cal.App.4th 144 is misplaced. In Stanislaus, the question at issue was whether there was substantial
evidence in the record supporting a fair argument that the proposed project may have a significant
impact on the environment, thus necessitating an EIR. Here, the City has prepared an EIR. Accordingly, no
revision to the Draft EIR is warranted in response to these comments.

Response to Comment P36-78 and P36-79
First, as a matter of clarification, the Draft EIR uses a 16 percent mode split for bicycle use. Refer to
Page 2 of Appendix F of the Draft EIR.
The data referenced in the comment (5.9% percent bicycle use in Berkeley, per Data USA) is for the entire
city 48, 49 and not for the Berkeley Waterfront sub region. It is important to note that the data from the
Census or Data USA is only based commuting characteristics, i.e., home-to-work trips, and does not
include trips such as recreational trips or trips made for shopping and going to school. The data used for
the analysis in the Draft EIR is 16 percent for the sub region and specifically looks at the bicyclist using
ferry (see Table 2 in Appendix F of the Draft EIR). Other ferry terminals have documented over 10 percent
of the users bicycling to the ferry terminals. 50 The WETA Business Plan estimated that approximately 16
percent of ferry passengers would access the terminal by bicycle, based on observed travel patterns at
comparable WETA ferry terminals. The Berkeley Ferry Feasibility Study prepared by Nelson\Nygaard
estimated a similar bicycle mode share of 18 percent. All of these sources have been identified on page 2
of Appendix F of the Draft EIR.
To further validate these assumptions, Kittelson reviewed the most recent WETA onboard survey data,
including surveys conducted in 2022, and applied the methodology used in the WETA Business Plan.
Based on the updated survey data, Kittelson estimated that approximately 11 percent of ferry passengers
would access the terminal by bicycle.
The three estimates (11 percent, 16 percent, and 18 percent) were compared as part of the analysis. After
considering the methodologies, underlying datasets, and consistency with previous WETA planning
efforts, the 16 percent bicycle mode share from the WETA Business Plan was determined to be the most
reasonable and defensible assumption for this environmental analysis because it is based on observed
travel behavior at comparable ferry terminals and is consistent with WETA's planning assumptions.
The City concludes that the mode split assumptions used for the Draft EIR are supported by substantial
evidence and appropriate for CEQA analysis. The analysis and conclusions in the Draft EIR remain valid.
No further revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment P36-92
It is not accurate that restoration of the pier constitutes the No Project Alternative under CEQA. CEQA
Guidelines Section 15126.6(e) requires that an EIR evaluate a No Project Alternative that describes the
existing conditions and reasonably foreseeable future conditions if the proposed project is not approved.
Consistent with this requirement, the Draft EIR's No Project Alternative assumes that the proposed
project would not be implemented and that the existing pier would remain closed due to its deteriorated
structural condition. As discussed in Chapter 5, Alternatives, the No Project Alternative therefore reflects
continuation of existing conditions rather than implementation of a separate project involving repair or
reconstruction of the pier. There are no planning documents, funding, or other evidence to suggest that
the restoration of the pier, without ferry service, would be reasonably foreseeable.
Restoration or reconstruction of the pier would constitute a distinct project requiring discretionary
approvals, funding, design, and construction activities. Accordingly, it is more appropriately considered an
action alternative rather than a No Project Alternative. As discussed in Section 5.9, Alternatives
Considered but Rejected, alternatives involving restoration of the pier without ferry service were
considered but not carried forward because they would not attain most of the project's basic objectives,
including provision of zero-emission ferry service. For further discussion, please refer to Response to
Comment O10-215, as well as Section 2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives.
The comment’s preference for a restored pier without ferry service is noted; however, that preference
does not demonstrate that the Draft EIR's No Project Alternative is inconsistent with CEQA requirements.
This comment has been included in the project record considered by City decision makers. The analysis
and conclusions presented in Chapter 5 remain valid, and no revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in
response to this comment.

Response to Comment P36-108
Refer to Section 2.2.9, Topical Response: Cumulative Impacts, which explains that the City does consider a
potential new restaurant at the 199 Seawall Drive site as a cumulative project. The comment mentions
150 parking spaces, which is a reference to the City of Berkeley lease agreement providing 150 exclusive-
use parking stalls at the Seawall Lot for 45 years. 51 As described in Section 2.2.20, Topical Response:
Parking, parking scarcity alone does not constitute a significant impact on the environment. Rather,
projects must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis to determine whether secondary physical impacts -
such as increased VMT, roadway noise, or air quality impacts result from parking condition. The “Parking
Availability Does Not Create Secondary Environmental Impacts” subsection of Section 2.2.20, Topical
Response: Parking, explains that the Draft EIR and the supporting Parking and TDM Plan demonstrate that
the Berkeley Waterfront parking supply is sufficient to accommodate project ferry parking demand
without requiring drivers to circulate between parking lots or generate additional vehicle travel.
In addition, the future redevelopment of 199 Seawall Drive would be located within BCDC jurisdiction and
any future redevelopment proposal would be required to demonstrate consistency with applicable BCDC
policies during the BCDC permit review process. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and
Planning, the proposed project has been evaluated for consistency with applicable Bay Plan policies,
including Bay Plan Recreation Policy 9 which provides that ferry terminals may be located within
waterfront park priority use areas provided that facilities for park and marina patrons, such as parking, are
not usurped by ferry users and that shared parking arrangements are provided to minimize the amount of
shoreline area devoted to parking (refer to Impact LU-2, Table 3.9-1). The Bay Plan further provides that
terminal parking facilities should be set back from the shoreline to allow for public access and enjoyment
of the Bay, and that public access to and along the shoreline should be maintained. Likewise, any future
restaurant redevelopment and associated parking arrangements would be subject to independent review
by BCDC to demonstrate consistency with applicable Bay Plan policies concerning shared parking, public
access, and recreational use of the Berkeley Waterfront. In addition, as described in Draft EIR Section 3.9,
Land Use and Planning, the 199 Seawall Drive property is located within Berkeley’s Unclassified (U)
District, where establishment of a new use requires discretionary approval through a Use Permit process.
As part of that process, the City may establish project-specific development standards, including
standards related to off-street parking. Therefore, future redevelopment of 199 Seawall Drive and any
associated parking allocation or management program would be subject to independent review and
discretionary approval by both the City and BCDC, both of which would ensure development consistency

Response to Comment P36-109

Response to Comment P36-115
A BTU-per-passenger measurement would mean the amount of heat energy per passenger anticipated to
be consumed. The more BTUs consumed in general as well as per passenger could indicate a lower level
of energy efficiency.
Air quality impacts analyze energy emissions project from natural gas use and not electricity. This is
because use of natural gas results in criteria air pollutant emissions directly associated with onsite
project activities, whereas the use of electricity does not result in air quality impacts directly generated at
the project site. Specifically, for the proposed project, there would be no project-related natural gas use at
the project site and, therefore, energy use from an air quality perspective is zero, because air quality
emissions associated with electrical generation are assumed by the generating facility and are not part of
an individual project’s criteria pollutant emissions inventory.
From an energy and GHG standpoint, CEQA significance thresholds identified in the Draft EIR through
either the CEQA Checklist or the Bay Area Air District thresholds do not use a BTU-per-passenger mile
threshold nor do they require the comparison of project emissions to alternative modes of transportation
not proposed as part of a project. Further, the Draft EIR Alternatives Section (Section 5.9) discussed
alternative projects such as increasing Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) capacity and improving access to
BART, both of which were alternatives that were considered but rejected. The analysis in the Draft EIR
accurately analyzes energy impacts with respect to CEQA Guidelines Appendix G significance criteria,
specifically, would the proposed project result in a potentially significant environmental impact due to a
wasteful, inefficient, or unnecessary consumption of energy resources, during project construction or
operation; and would the proposed project conflict or obstruct a state or local plan for renewable energy
or energy efficiency. Thresholds are discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.6.4 on page 3.6-30. Since the Draft
EIR used CEQA Guidelines and Public Resource Code methodology to analyze impacts related to energy
efficiency and use, additional energy analysis is not required.
The Draft EIR under Impact GHG-2 (pages 3.6-43 through 3.6-44) concludes that the project would not
result in wasteful, inefficient, or unnecessary consumption of energy resources. And the Draft EIR under

obstruct a State or local plan for renewable energy or energy efficiency. Therefore, additional energy
analysis is not required.

Response to Comment P36-116
Carbon is not a criteria pollutant that is addressed under the federal or State Ambient Air Quality
Standards and is, therefore, not analyzed as part of the air quality analysis as it does not have a State or
federal threshold for which states or regions are required to comply with. The air quality analysis does
include an analysis of direct carbon monoxide emissions associated with the construction and operation
of the project. As discussed in Response to Comment P36-115, carbon monoxide emissions, along with
the other criteria pollutants, from electrical consumption are not analyzed under air quality impacts.
Carbon monoxide emissions from the mobile sources associated with the proposed project are included
in Draft EIR Tables 3.2-9 and 3.2-10 on page 3.2-28 and result in 26 lbs per day or 5 tons per year of
carbon monoxide emissions. There are no air district thresholds for carbon monoxide emissions at this
time and, therefore, carbon monoxide emissions are less than significant.
See Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry, for a discussion of how the proposed project includes
and the Draft EIR analyses assume installation and operation of an electric ferry, and not a ferry that
would be propelled by any other means of fuel or energy source. In addition, see Responses to Comments
O5-18 and 05-19 that discuss the project’s commitment to zero-emission ferry and 100 percent
renewable energy consumption past 2030. The reference to a zero-emissions project is specific to zero
GHG emissions associated with proposed all-electric ferry operation as well as ferry and recreational
amenities that would use 100 percent renewable energy-sourced electricity past 2030.
See Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, for a discussion of how the proposed project would result in a
net reduction in regional VMT. Draft EIR Section 3.12 Transportation page 3.12-21 details the VMT
analysis and how the project would reduce vehicle miles traveled from the current 1,127 trips traveling
into San Francisco at 25 miles to an 8 mile commute to the ferry terminal. The source of the information
for determining trip lengths is Transportation Research Board of the National Academies. Coffel, K.,
Parks, J., Semler, C., Ryus, P., Bose, D., Vandehey, M., Petritsch, T., Proulx, F., & Chang, J. (2012).
Guidelines for providing access to public transportation stations (TCRP Report 153) are available at
https://nacto.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/1-4_Coffell-et-al_Guidelines-for-Providing-Access-to-
Public-TransportationStations_TCRP-153_2012.pdf and the use of the information is summarized in Draft
EIR Section 3.12 Transportation. Together, this Draft EIR analysis, information source, and guidelines
document how the project would result in a net reduction in regional VMT. No changes to the Draft EIR
are necessary in response to this comment.

used for the determination of significance from a project’s GHG emissions. The discussion of the

trips to the project site, the existing commute results in 2,351 MT CO2e that would be removed from the
region with the implementation of the project. Therefore, the GHG analysis adequately analyzes and
substantiates the reduction in VMT below regional average, as there is a reduction in overall VMT in the
region with implementation of the project. No changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this
comment.

Response to Comment P36-121
The VMT analysis is based on the ridership projections identified in the WETA Business Plan. Page 13 of
the WETA Business Plan includes the discussion about the ferry ridership projections. The ridership has
been estimated using the Alameda Countywide Travel Demand Model which was developed for the Plan
Bay Area 2040. The forecasts were compared against the unconstrained capacity (4,250 daily boardings).
The ridership projections account for several factors such as headways, capacity, directional split,
parking availability. The mode split were estimated using the on-board surveys at the existing East and
North Bay Terminals.
Regarding origin and destinations, the business plan includes the information ferry catchment area which
is where most of the origin and destination will be in Berkeley. A trip between the Berkeley Waterfront and
San Francisco's Embarcadero is approximately 10 miles by car. When a traveler chooses the ferry instead
of driving, those approximately 10 vehicle miles are eliminated from the roadway network, resulting in a
direct reduction in VMT. Even if only a relatively small share of travelers who currently drive choose to
switch to the ferry, each of those trips contributes to a measurable reduction in VMT. Because every
diverted automobile trip removes vehicle travel from the roadway system, the cumulative effect of even
modest mode shift from driving to ferry service will reduce overall VMT.

BERKELEY FERRY PROJECT DRAFT EIR COMMENTS

THE BERKELEY FERRY PROJECT VIOLATES BERKELEY’S 1986 MEASURE ‘L’ –THE BERKELEY PUBLIC PARKS
AND OPEN SPACE PRESERVATION ORDINANCE

By pursuing the massive Berkeley Ferry Project, the City is clearly violating the 1986 Citizens’ Initiative
Measure ‘L’.

Measure ‘L’ - The Berkeley Parks and Open Space Preservation Ordinance, was adopted by Berkeley
voters in November 1986 by a vote of 21,946 to 18,854. It is codified in BMC Chapter 6.42.

Measure ‘L’ states, "Shall an ordinance be adopted to require voter approval of non-recreational uses of
parks or open space and require acquisition of open space controlled or leased by the City if acquisition
is the only means of preserving the open space?"

I was one of the signers of the ballot argument in favor of Measure ‘L’.
                                                                                                                 P42-1
Measure ‘L‘ is still in effect today.

Measure ‘L’ thus requires approval by Berkeley’s voters before any aspect of the Berkeley Ferry Project
can be built.

In 1996, the City of Berkeley wanted to place temporary buildings on Civic Center (Provo) Park for
various city bureaucratic functions while the Civic Center building on Milvia Street went through
extensive renovations and a seismic upgrade. Because of Measure ‘L’, the City had to put a measure on
the November 1996 ballot - Measure X - to get the public's approval.

The last of the “where as’s” at the start of the Full Text of Measure X” states,

“Where as Measure ‘L’, BMC Chapter 6.42 requires voter approval to use public parks for purposes
other than park or open space uses,”


                                                                                                        2- 613
                                            Page 718 of 1541




“Shall the MLK Jr. Civic Center Park be used for a period to expire no later than June 30, 2001 for the
purpose of temporarily housing City of Berkeley offices in portable buildings, as well as associated site
preparation and maintenance activities in order to allow the abatement of seismic hazards at the site of
the MLK Jr. Civic Center Building at 2180 Milvia Street if the Council finds after a public hearing that
there is no other feasible alternative to relocate City employees during such seismic work?”

Measure X failed 17,476 to 23,151. The City could not install temporary offices in Civic Center Park, and
thus leased commercial property around downtown instead.

Thus, Measure ‘L’ requires voter approval before any park or open space under the city’s control can be
used for other purposes.                                                                                          P42-1
Measure ‘L’ is still in effect, & covers all City parks & city owned or controlled open space.

Councilmember Terry Taplin has cited Measure ‘L’ in insisting that the City preserve the open space at
the former Lawn Bowling Club site.

Last year, Councilmember Cecilia Lunaparra cited Measure 'L' to insist that the City preserve the public
open space at the Dwight - Telegraph triangle.

And in recent years, former Councilmember Kate Harrison cited Measure ‘L’ to designate the open space
around old City Hall as a city park, so as to give it more protection.

THE FERRY PROJECT IS CLEARLY FOR TRANSPORTATION, NOT RECREATION

The Ferry Project would include a breakwater, a 1200 square foot gangway, 750 square foot gates and
landings, and a 5700 square foot ferry charging/boarding float.                                                   P42-2

The official description of the Project specifically states that it is for transportation, to take commuters
to and from San Francisco.

REMOVING THE EXISTING LANDMARKED PIER WOULD VIOLATE MEASURE ‘L’.

The landmarked and iconic Berkeley Pier was for many years used for open space and recreation. The
Project would replace it with a much smaller Pier that would not be conducive the recreation.

It’s not the public’s fault that the Pier has been deemed unsafe to use for the last eleven years. By
keeping the Pier closed and refusing to repair it for the last 11 years, the City has been violating
Measure ‘L’.                                                                                                      P42-3

Demolishing the existing pier and replacing it with a smaller and more officious pier should first require
approval of the voters as per Measure ‘L’.

All of the SF Bay that is within Berkeley’s City Limits is as much City of Berkeley recreational open space
as is the Aquatic Park Lagoon.




                                                                                                         2- 614
                                            Page 719 of 1541




Any development on the SF Bay that is within Berkeley’s City Limits is no less the destruction of
recreational open space for non-recreational uses than would the dredging of the Aquatic Park Lagoon             P42-3
and constructing office buildings where the Lagoon once was.

The proposed Ferry Complex’s gates, and landing, the gangway, and the ferry charging and boarding
float would all destroy the incomparable view of the SF Bay looking out toward the Golden Gate that              P42-4
generations of Berkeley residents have long enjoyed.

The San Francisco Bay within Berkeley’s City Limits is Berkeley public open space. It has been enjoyed by
tens of thousands of Berkeley residents for over 100 years as passive recreation, and by many other
people for recreational boating.

Transportation is not recreation. As the City’s own official description of the Ferry Project clearly states,
the purpose of the Project is Transportation.

Construction is construction, whether on land or water.

Measure ‘L’ should not be seen as an inconvenience, but as an opportunity to allow the public to vote
on proposed changes to existing city parks and open space.

In 1996, city officials were not dismissive of Measure ‘L’ even though it would slow down the seismic
upgrade of the 2180 Milvia Civic Center Building. They put approval of the temporary use of Civic Center         P42-5
Park for city offices on the ballot, because honoring the law and the will of the voters was the right thing
to do.

Today in 2026, city officials should not be dismissive of Measure ‘L’ just because its implementation
could delay construction of the Berkeley Ferry Project Complex.

Response to Comment P42-7
The City acknowledges the comment's support for restoration of public access to the pier. The proposed
project includes reconstruction of the existing deteriorated pier and would restore public access
opportunities that have been unavailable since the pier was closed. As discussed in Draft EIR Chapter 2,
Project Description, the proposed project would provide a new public-access pier and breakwater, along
with additional recreational amenities designed to enhance opportunities for walking, sightseeing, fishing,
bicycling, and enjoyment of Bay views (see Section 2.5, Proposed Project Components).
To the extent the comment is advocating for reconstruction of the pier without ferry service, please refer
to Response to Comment O10-215. As discussed therein, the City considered a "No Ferry Service with
New Pier Alternative" and explains in Draft EIR Section 5.9, Alternatives Considered but Rejected, why that
alternative was not carried forward for detailed analysis (refer to page 5-28). Specifically, while a pier-only
alternative would provide recreation and public access benefits, it would not meet one of the project's two
basic objectives: providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero-emission ferry service between
Berkeley and San Francisco. In addition, Chapter 5 evaluates the No Project Alternative and three action
alternatives and concludes that the No Project Alternative would not restore public access because the
existing pier would remain closed and continue to deteriorate, while alternatives with reduced project
features would provide fewer public access and recreational benefits than the proposed project. For
additional discussion regarding the assumptions, screening criteria, and requirements used in developing
and evaluating alternatives, and alternatives considered but rejected, refer to Section 2.2.2, Topical
Response: Alternatives.
Accordingly, the Draft EIR considered recreational and public-access objectives in formulating and
evaluating alternatives. The comment does not identify a deficiency in the Draft EIR's alternatives
analysis, and no revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P42-8
Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, evaluates the No Project Alternative (Alternative 1), as required by CEQA
Guidelines Section 15126.6(e), and compares its environmental impacts and ability to meet project
objectives relative to the proposed project and other alternatives. The Draft EIR concludes that, under the
No Project Alternative, the existing pier would remain closed and continue to deteriorate, no ferry service
would be established from Berkeley, and none of the proposed public access, recreational, bicycle,
pedestrian, or transportation improvements would occur. The Draft EIR further concludes that the No
Project Alternative would not meet either of the project's basic objectives and would generally result in
greater impacts related to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, land use and planning, and
transportation because it would not provide the transportation and environmental benefits associated
with the proposed ferry service.
To the extent the comment suggests providing ferry service from another location, please refer to Section
2.2.2, Topical Response: Alternatives. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 5.9, Alternatives Considered but
Rejected, the City considered alternative ferry terminal locations, including locations outside the Berkeley
Waterfront, and determined that such alternatives would either not be feasible, would not attain most of
the project's basic objectives, or were outside the City's jurisdiction. The project's objectives include both
enhancing public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and providing efficient
and environmentally friendly zero-emission ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.
Accordingly, the City concludes that the Draft EIR evaluates a reasonable range of feasible alternatives,
including the No Project Alternative, consistent with CEQA requirements. No revisions to the Draft EIR are
necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P42-9
Section 2.3, Project Objectives, (Pages 2-7 and 2-8 of the Draft EIR) and Section 1.2.1, Project Background,
(Page 1-3 and 1-4 of the Draft EIR) describe the objectives for the project, including enhancing public

access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and providing zero-emission ferry

Response to Comment P42-11
The environmental topics evaluated in the Draft EIR are based on CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, which
does not explicitly identify EMF radiation exposure as a topic for consideration. Electric and magnetic
fields are generally associated with power substations and utility facilities. For example, the California
Energy Commission regularly approves electrical facilities. These are dedicated region-serving battery
energy storage systems. In one such assessment, the CEC explicitly addressed EMF from the project's
electrical facilities: “The construction and operation of the project’s new collector feeders, gen[eration]-tie
line, on-site substation, and switchyard would not contribute to electromagnetic field (EMF) levels ...
beyond acceptable standards.52” Staff further concluded that worker and public exposure would be short
term and consistent with comparable PG&E facilities, and that grounding and field reduction measures
would minimize nuisance-shock potential. The same assessment concluded that transmission-line safety
and nuisance impacts, including EMF-related considerations, would be less than significant with
proposed conditions of certification. The proposed conditions are in compliance with CPUC General
Order 131-E. The project does not include components that require compliance with CPUC General Order
131-E. Consequently, an assessment of EMF effects was not provided. Accordingly, EMF is not included
in the Draft EIR. No revision to the Draft EIR is required in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P42-13
As discussed in Section 1.4.1, Lead Agency, of the Draft EIR, the City of Berkeley is the lead agency for the
project as defined by CEQA Guidelines Section 15367 because it holds the principal responsibility for
approving the proposed project. The City of Berkeley Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Department is
proposing the project. Section 1.1.4, Legal Authority, explains that the approval of the project cannot be
considered until the EIR has been certified by the Berkeley City Council. Consistent with CEQA Guidelines
Section 15084, the draft EIR reflects the independent judgement of the City as lead agency. It is common
for a government agency to propose a project and act as CEQA lead. Even in cases where the lead agency
is not a project’s applicant, the lead agency still must review the Draft EIR and take responsibility for its
contents. CEQA requires that led agencies exercise independent judgement and maintain objectivity in
CEQA documentation. No further response is required.

Response to Comment P42-14
Refer to Section 2.2.16, Topical Response: Measure L, for a discussion related to how the project would
not conflict with Measure L. The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented
within the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further response or revisions to the EIR are required.

Response to Comment P42-15
This is not correct. Under CEQA, the lead agency (in this case, the City of Berkeley) is the entity
responsible for preparing and certifying the EIR and for making the project approval decision. CEQA
Guidelines Section 15050 designates the lead agency as the public agency with the greatest
responsibility for carrying out or approving a project. The Berkeley City Council, as the lead agency's
decision-making body, is vested by law with the authority and responsibility to: (a) certify that the Final
EIR has been completed in compliance with CEQA; (b) consider the environmental information presented
in the Final EIR; and (c) decide whether to approve, modify, or reject the proposed project (CEQA
Guidelines Sections 15090–15096). There is no provision in CEQA or the CEQA Guidelines for delegation
of this decision-making authority to an impartial third party. No revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on
this basis.

Response to Comment P42-16
This comment does not pertain to the proposed project or the adequacy, significance conclusions, or
mitigation in the Draft EIR. Nevertheless, this comment has been included in the project record
considered by City decision makers. No further response is required.

Response to Comment P42-17
All comments on the Draft EIR have been responded to and are included in their respective responses to
comments. Refer to Section 2.2.7, Topical Response: CEQA Process, which describes that although
clarifying edits have been made to the Draft EIR in response to comments, none of the edits have
affected the impact conclusions or mitigation measures in a substantive manner. Recirculation of the
Draft EIR is not required.

Response to Comment P42-18
The City notes that this is precisely what CEQA requires, and the project's approval process is designed
accordingly. Section 1.1.4, Legal Authority in Chapter 1, Introduction of the Draft EIR (page 1-3) states the
following: "Adoption of the proposed project may not be considered until this EIR has first been
considered by the decision makers and certified by the approving body, in this case the Berkeley City
Council." Similarly, Section 1.5, Environmental Review Process in Chapter 1, Introduction of the Draft EIR
(page 1-15, bullet number 5) describes the Final EIR certification process as a prerequisite to any project



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                        2- 621
                                             Page 726 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                     Response to Comments

approval decision, consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15090, which requires the lead agency to
certify the Final EIR before approving the project.
The City Council will first consider whether to certify the Final EIR as a complete and adequate
environmental document, and only after certification may it consider whether to approve the project itself.
Though both actions could occur sequentially at the same meeting, these are distinct actions with
distinct legal standards. Certification requires findings that the EIR has been completed in compliance
with CEQA, was reviewed and considered by the decision-making body prior to project approval, and
reflects the lead agency’s independent judgment and analysis, pursuant to CEQA Guidelines
Section 15090. By contrast, project approval requires findings including that significant environmental
impacts have been avoided, mitigated, or are outweighed by project benefits, pursuant to CEQA
Guidelines Sections 15091 and 15093. The Draft EIR describes this sequence accurately, and the City's
approval process will follow it (see Section 1.5, Environmental Review Process in Chapter 1, Introduction of
the Draft EIR). No revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis.

future notices via email in accordance with CEQA and City procedures. No further response is required.

conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR. No further response is required.

BERKELEY FERRY PROJECT DRAFT EIR COMMENTS

THE BERKELEY FERRY PROJECT VIOLATES BERKELEY’S 1986 MEASURE ‘L’ –THE BERKELEY PUBLIC
PARKS AND OPEN SPACE PRESERVATION ORDINANCE

By pursuing the massive Berkeley Ferry Project, the City is clearly violating the 1986 Citizens’
Initiative Measure ‘L’.

Measure ‘L’ - The Berkeley Parks and Open Space Preservation Ordinance, was adopted by
Berkeley voters in November 1986 by a vote of 21,946 to 18,854. It is codified in BMC Chapter 6.42.

Measure ‘L’ states, "Shall an ordinance be adopted to require voter approval of
non-recreational uses of parks or open space and require acquisition of open space controlled or
leased by the City if acquisition is the only means of preserving the open space?"
                                                                                                            P43-1
I was one of the signers of the ballot argument in favor of Measure ‘L’.

Measure ‘L‘ is still in effect today.

Measure ‘L’ thus requires approval by Berkeley’s voters before any aspect of the Berkeley Ferry
Project can be built.

In 1996, the City of Berkeley wanted to place temporary buildings on Civic Center (Provo) Park for
various city bureaucratic functions while the Civic Center building on Milvia Street went through
extensive renovations and a seismic upgrade. Because of Measure ‘L’, the City had to put a
measure on the November 1996 ballot - Measure X - to get the public's approval.

The last of the “where as’s” at the start of the Full Text of Measure X” states,

“Where as Measure ‘L’, BMC Chapter 6.42 requires voter approval to use public parks for purposes
other than park or open space uses,”


                                                                                                   2- 623
                                           Page 728 of 1541




“Shall the MLK Jr. Civic Center Park be used for a period to expire no later than June 30, 2001 for the
purpose of temporarily housing City of Berkeley offices in portable buildings, as well as associated
site preparation and maintenance activities in order to allow the abatement of seismic hazards at
the site of the MLK Jr. Civic Center Building at 2180 Milvia Street if the Council finds after a public
hearing that there is no other feasible alternative to relocate City employees during such seismic
work?”

Measure X failed 17,476 to 23,151. The City could not install temporary offices in Civic Center Park,
and thus leased commercial property around downtown instead.

Thus, Measure ‘L’ requires voter approval before any park or open space under the city’s control
can be used for other purposes

Measure ‘L’ is still in effect, & covers all City parks & city owned or controlled open space.

Councilmember Terry Taplin has cited Measure ‘L’ in insisting that the City preserve the open
space at the former Lawn Bowling Club site.

Last year, Councilmember Cecilia Lunaparra cited Measure 'L' to insist that the City preserve the
public open space at the Dwight - Telegraph triangle.

And in recent years, former Councilmember Kate Harrison cited Measure ‘L’ to designate the open
space around old City Hall as a city park, so as to give it more protection.
                                                                                                              P43-1
THE FERRY PROJECT IS CLEARLY FOR TRANSPORTATION, NOT RECREATION

The Ferry Project would include a breakwater, a 1200 square foot gangway, 750 square foot gates
and landings, and a 5700 square foot ferry charging/boarding float.

The official description of the Project specifically states that it is for transportation, to take
commuters to and from San Francisco.

REMOVING THE EXISTING LANDMARKED PIER WOULD VIOLATE MEASURE ‘L’.

The landmarked and iconic Berkeley Pier was for many years used for open space and recreation.
The Project would replace it with a much smaller Pier that would not be conducive the recreation.

It’s not the public’s fault that the Pier has been deemed unsafe to use for the last eleven years. By
keeping the Pier closed and refusing to repair it for the last 11 years, the City has been violating
Measure ‘L’.

Demolishing the existing pier and replacing it with a smaller and more officious pier should first
require approval of the voters as per Measure ‘L’.

All of the SF Bay that is within Berkeley’s City Limits is as much City of Berkeley recreational open
space as is the Aquatic Park Lagoon.

Subject: Comments on Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project draft EIR

Dear Ms. McNulty:

The following are additional comments on the EIR which reﬂect my reading of the Final
                                                                                                                          P47-1
Program EIR by the Water Transit Authority “Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San
Francisco Bay Area.” That EIR was completed in June of 2003. While a programmatic FEIR
prepared twenty-three years ago may still be used for preparation of a draft EIR for one of                               P47-2
the projects contemplated in that document, it is essential to update the parts of that
document that may no longer be accurate. The subject EIR relies on that FEIR for its
consideration of environmental impacts, particularly operational impacts, but does not                                    P47-3
update the analysis to address the many signiﬁcant di erences between the project
described in that document and the current proposal. Where those changes may
constitute “changed circumstances” under the California Environmental Quality Act, or
increase cumulative impacts, the current EIR is required to analyze and disclose those
changes and impacts, and include feasible mitigation measures. Where there are conﬂicts                                   P47-4
between that adopted document and the current proposal, those conﬂicts may rise to the
level of signiﬁcant impacts. The current document fails to do that.

CHANGED PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The WTA Final EIR contemplates a very di erent project for expanding service to Berkeley,                             I   P47-5
and includes mitigation measures that the current document has ignored. In describing
the regional system, the Final EIR makes it clear that only limited dredging will be required,                        t   P47-6




                                                                                                             2- 636
                                     Page 741 of 1541

                                              2


and only for the Rodeo/Hercules service. The current proposal includes a proposal for up
to 400,000 cubic yards of dredging. The rationale behind the Final EIR proposal can be
found in this language from page 2-2:

       …only the Hercules/Rodeo terminal would require additional dredging for
       implementation. All other terminal sites proposed for expanded ferry
       service are within existing ports or marinas.


The FEIR clearly contemplated a terminal site in Berkeley that would not require dredging.
This language is included under Impact D-1: “Ferries have relatively low draft requirements
(approximately 7 feet) and would not be deeper than those at existing marinas and ports.”         P47-6
The associated mitigation measure D-21, ignored in the draft EIR states “Dredging shall be
minimized.” Additional information about the rationale for concluding that there would be
little or no dredging required for initiating Berkeley ferry service can be found on page 2-6,
where it indicates that the vessels that would be used would be “relatively shallow draft.”
Exhibits in the FEIR conﬁrm that the programmatic document did not contemplate an open
water site that would require massive dredging. Figure 5.1.1 and the related Table 5.1.5
conclude that a Berkeley marina terminal would only require 13,260 cubic yards of
construction dredging—not the 400,000 cubic yards in the current draft EIR.

This is particularly relevant to the current proposal, which is fundamentally di erent from
that contemplated in the 2003 FEIR, and that considered in the existing Berkeley Marina
Master Plan, dated June 1, 2003, which also contemplated ferry service only inside the
marina. That can be seen in Principle 3, which establishes a principle to “Upgrade the
Ferry Pier to comply with seismic regulations.” It is also relevant to the Bay Plan Recreation
Policy 9, adopted in September 2006. At that time—and still—the adopted plans for ferry
expansion and the adopted Marina Plan anticipated a ferry expansion staged out of the             P47-7
marina. As noted in my ﬁrst letter, the current proposal is inconsistent with those adopted
plans and clearly falls under the changed circumstances provisions of CEQA because it
entails a di erent location that would require extensive dredging. Yet no discussion of
those changes can be found in the draft EIR, and the discussion of the environmental
e ects of dredging is brief and conclusory. That issue will be discussed below.

It may be that the type of equipment currently contemplated for a new Berkeley service has
also changed and that a deeper channel and berthing areas are required for that di erent
equipment. But again, that would be a changed circumstance, limiting the degree to which          P47-8
the 2003 FEIR can be relied upon. The 2003 FEIR had an extensive discussion of ferry
wakes, or wake wash in Section 3.3. The current draft EIR does not revisit that discussion
and concludes that the analysis is still valid with the deeper draft vessels now proposed.

IMPACTS OF CONCERN WITH CHANGED CIRCUMSTANCES




                                                                                         2- 637
                                      Page 742 of 1541

                                               3


Since the adoption of the FEIR in 2003, there are changes in the sensitivity of the marine
environment that might be a ected by a new service and substantial dredging. The FEIR
concluded that whale strikes were unlikely but would be signiﬁcant if they occurred. But           P47-9
whale visits to San Francisco Bay have become much more frequent, with clear evidence
that whales are feeding in the Bay. No consideration of this as a changed circumstance is
included in the draft EIR.

The longﬁn smelt was listed as endangered by the State of California in 2009, and as of
August 29, 2024, is also listed under the Federal Endangered Species Act. Smelt can be             P47-10
entrained and killed in dredging operations. Both construction and operation of a ferry
terminal might a ect this species.

While the Green sturgeon was listed as endangered, and discussed in the program FEIR,
additional research has been completed and NOAA formally adopted “take” provision rules            P47-11
for the species. Dredging may reduce benthic habitat value and operations may have
greater impacts than previously disclosed in the program FEIR.

The increased presence of whales feeding in San Francisco Bay is yet another area where
the changed circumstances warrant discussion in the draft EIR. Biologists are well aware
of both whales feeding in the bay, and increasing deaths due to vessel strikes. Press media
has reported this concern, for example
                                                                                                   P47-12
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/13/climate/gray-whales-san-francisco-bay.html

and the April 15, 2026 San Francisco Chronicle. Whale strikes are identiﬁed as a signiﬁcant
impact in the 2023 FEIR, but considered rare—a conclusion no longer tenable. Yet the
current draft EIR makes no e ort to analyze the impacts.

RECREATIONAL IMPACTS

As noted in my initial letter, Berkeley dismisses recreational impacts, concluding without
providing substantial evidence that a ferry project would be beneﬁcial to recreation. In
doing so, the city ignores the concerns about impacts on parking, largely ignoring any             P47-13
quantitative e ort to demonstrate compliance with Bay Plan Recreational Policy 9. The
city’s claim that parking analysis is not required ﬂies in the face of impacts and mitigation
measures contained in the program FEIR that they are relying on. I would note that the
relocation of the ferry site from within the marina and the use of parts of the bay ﬁlled to       P47-14
create recreational uses and supporting parking make this impact much more signiﬁcant
than considered in 2003. The city also ignores the enactment of the Water Trail Act,
enacted in 2005:
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=200520060AB1296
That act establishes legislative policy that: “ Water-oriented recreational uses of the San        P47-15
Francisco Bay… are of great beneﬁt to the public welfare of the San Francisco Bay Area.”
Commuter ferries are not among the listed water-oriented uses. Berkeley has
obtained grants through the Water Trail program but fails to use the standards of



                                                                                          2- 638
                                     Page 743 of 1541

                                              4


that act for evaluation of recreational impacts. The FEIR recognizes the potential for            P47-15
recreational impacts and includes a mitigation provision to prevent signiﬁcant impacts.

The Final EIR lists Impact LU-4 on page 3.7-16, recognizing that adverse impacts to
shoreline access could occur. It establishes mitigation LU-4.1 that includes the phrase
that incorporating public access at the next stage of planning “…may include trails, parking
set aside for shoreline users, viewpoints, disabled access, etc.” That Final EIR also
establishes a very di erent mode split for access to the terminal, estimating that on an
                                                                                                  P47-16
average day 24 would walk, 1789 would drive, and 344 would take transit. (Table 3.12.12)
Table 3.12.13 forecasts a demand for at least 510 parking spaces to meet the estimated
ridership. The current EIR simply casts aside all previous analyses of mode split without
explanation, as well as the mitigation responsibilities established in the 2003 FEIR.

The draft EIR fails to follow up with a mitigation plan that implements the standard in the
FEIR in a manner that provides full disclosure and allows public review of the su iciency.        P47-17
Indeed, it is impossible to generate such a plan without developing an adequate baseline of
existing recreational use and considering latent use and regional population growth.

ENERGY EFFICIENCY AND VMT REDUCTION

The 2003 FEIR discusses energy e iciency, as required by Public Resources Code Section
21100(b)(3). The analysis in that document presents energy use by transit modes using a
metric of BTU’s per passenger mile. That analysis showed that ferries use nearly 10 times         P47-18
as much energy as buses, and about 90 times as much energy as BART. The draft EIR
includes no discussion of energy e iciency and assumes that all ferry passengers would be
drivers at present, rather than considering the number that might be diverted from current
bus and BART crossings. That despite the dedicated marketing e orts of WETA for exactly
that purpose. Energy is of su icient import to merit an appendix, F, in the CEQA
                                                                                                  P47-19
Guidelines. Despite those guidelines and my scoping comments on the need for to
update the e iciency analysis, the EIR fails to address this issue or include a CO2 emission
comparison. This analysis is clearly inadequate. Among the many policies elided from the
draft EIR is Policy T-9 Ferry Service from the General Plan:
                                                                                                  P47-20
       B. Prioritize transit, pedestrian, and bicycle public expenditures over expenditures
       of public funds for ferry service, and ensure that new ferry service will not result
       in a reduction in public subsidies for existing transit services.


FEASIBIILTY

Feasibility is an important term of art under CEQA, under BCDC’s requirements for
providing maximum feasible public access, and for consideration under the Clean Water             P47-21
Act. Yet a discussion of even the current cost of the project is absent from the current draft
EIR. In my previous letter, I attached a copy of the cost estimates prepared by city


                                                                                         2- 639
                                      Page 744 of 1541

                                              5


consultants, prepared on 7/11/2025, that showed the estimate for the project, not
including ferries, was $131,133,445. The previous cost estimate for ferries, not updated to        P47-21
include the current costs, was $38 million, leaving a total cost of about $170 million. It
appears that the City of Berkeley’s share of that costs would be about $32 million.

No sources for Berkeley’s funding have been identiﬁed. Signiﬁcantly, Berkeley’s marina
fund has struggled with a structural deﬁcit, in part because boating revenues instead of
Berkeley’s parks tax have been used to maintain the waterfront parks. The most recent
estimate of the deferred maintenance at the waterfront can be found in the recent Auditor’s
report. On page 15 of that report, the size of that problem was noted: “unfunded capital
infrastructure needs at the waterfront still exceed an estimated $163 million.”
                                                                                                   P47-22
Berkeley relies on WETA’s Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan in numerous places in the
draft EIR, but then avoids the discussion of local funding in that plan which concludes:

       One option would include a Transient Occupancy Tax surcharge on hotel
       night stays in the marina that would reinvest revenue in the Berkeley
       waterfront and support maintenance of the pier and shared parking facilities.

With revenues from the DoubleTree Hotel already reduced, and the hospitality industry
continuing to contract, with bankruptcy of yet another Berkeley hotel reported in the news         P47-23
on April 16, 2026, the sta who prepared this EIR hardly need to be reminded of the
infeasibility of such an approach.

The current approach, avoiding any discussion of feasibility or costs, is a departure from
the FEIR. That document included in Table 2.2 estimates of the capital cost per rider ($4)
and the annual operating subsidy per rider ($5) to compare the feasibility of reducing VMT
by improving ferry service as compared to rail and bus alternatives. WETA no longer reports        P47-24
either the capital cost or the operating subsidy per rider, and no discussion of feasibility of
any depth is included in the draft EIR. Yet current operational subsidies for are more than
$30 per passenger for a round trip and WETA documents have made it clear that the
available subsidies will be exhausted to support the existing system..

While many of the recreational activities that currently occur at the waterfront do not
generate revenue into the marina fund, they have substantial economic value. Boating
activities directly contribute about 2/3 of the funding for the marina fund. Other visitors
from outside Berkeley visit the waterfront as part of other activities such as dining that
indirectly generate revenue. If parking for those users is usurped by commuters, those
                                                                                                   P47-25
activities would be reduced. If Berkeley leases the Seawall lot to WETA but does not collect
revenue for that lease, there will be no opportunity to use that site for uses that might
generate revenue. Further, if managing parking costs more than parking fees generate, or
Berkeley agrees to devote some of the TOT funds from the marina to subsidies, a measure
proposed by their consultants, the structural deﬁcit in the marina fund will be increased.



                                                                                          2- 640
                                     Page 745 of 1541

                                             6


To put the cost of the proposed terminal into context, if there are an average of 955
occupied seats on the new service, the capital cost per seat is $178,000. At a 5%
discounting rate, that is $8900 a year, or $35.60 a day as an opportunity cost. Well above
the $4 in the programmatic document. The lower annual operating subsidy cost estimate
by WETA is $9 million a year. Again using 955 seats, that is about $9,425 per seat of subsidy    P47-26
required, or $37.70 per seat per day. This does not include the cost to manage parking in
an attempt to preserve some recreational use. Of course, if less than 955 passengers use
the service the impacts on recreation will go down, but the subsidy required will go up
proportionately. With the most recent East Bay terminal at Richmond constructed at a cost
of $20 million, the need for analysis of alternatives becomes compelling.

No sources for city capital costs, WETA capital costs, or annual operating subsidies are
identiﬁed—yet the EIR insists that only this project is feasible. Without analysis of the
economic value of recreational uses that might be lost and might be improved on the land
instead of a commuter terminal, this is a fatal ﬂaw. Conclusions in an EIR must be               P47-27
supported by substantial evidence, and by analysis that links the facts to the conclusion.
But in this EIR, feasibility does not warrant even a discussion. That is inadequate to
support consideration of alternatives or answer questions of maximum feasible public
access under BCDC’s law.

As described in Draft EIR Section 2.6, Construction Details (page 2‑28), 400,000 cubic yards of dredge
volume represents the maximum potential dredging extent and is a conservative upper bound that may
be reduced as final design progresses. The project would primarily occur within the existing
100‑foot‑wide USACE federal navigation channel that parallels the closed pier. Dredging impacts are
discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impacts BIO-1 and BIO-3 (pages 3.3-46 through 3.3-51 and
pages 3.3-60 through 3.3-61), respectively, and were determined to be less than significant with
implementation of mitigation (see Mitigation Measures BIO-1[a], BIO-1[d], BIO-1[e], BIO-3, and HYD-1). See
also Section 2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability, for discussion of how analysis of
project dredging impacts has been addressed independently in the Draft EIR. No changes to the Draft EIR
are necessary in response to this comment.

transit speeds. The Draft EIR discusses the impacts of ferry wake in Section 3.8.4. Impacts Analysis (on
page 3.8-33) and concludes that water-side operational impacts related to water quality would be less

Response to Comment P47-12
As described in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO‑1 (pages 3.3-52 to -54), the analysis

Response to Comment P47-13
With respect to the comment’s claim that the City fails to provide substantial evidence that the proposed
ferry would be beneficial to recreation, CEQA does not require an EIR to demonstrate that a project is
affirmatively beneficial to recreation. Rather, CEQA requires evaluation of whether a project would result
in significant adverse physical environmental impacts related to recreational facilities. Accordingly, Draft
EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, evaluates recreation based on the applicable CEQA Guidelines Appendix G
thresholds of significance, specifically analyzing whether the proposed project would (1) increase the use
of existing recreational facilities such that substantial physical deterioration of the facilities would occur
or be accelerated, or (2) require the construction or expansion of recreational facilities that might result in
adverse physical environmental effects (see Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis). Based on the analysis
therein, the Draft EIR concludes that the project would enhance recreational activities and would not
result in substantial physical deterioration of recreational facilities (see Impact REC-1). Regarding
concerns about parking, as it relates to consistency with Bay Plan Policy 9, refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical
Response: Parking, for a detailed discussion related to how parking is considered consistent with CEQA.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented within Section 3.9, Land Use
and Planning, and related sections in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No revisions are required.

Response to Comment P47-14
When referring to an increase in significant impacts, the comment is referring to the impacts compared to
what was provided in the 2003 WETA EIR. However, the 2003 WETA EIR is a programmatic document that
did not include a project-level analysis for a terminal at the Berkeley Waterfront. Page 2-2 of the WETA EIR
states the following: “While the IOP does not represent a precisely fixed set of routes and terminal sites,
the Proposed Project is based on the anticipated routes and terminals that would result from
implementation of the IOP. The routes, terminals, and frequency of service (headways) associated with
the Proposed Project are listed in Table 2.1. The routes and terminals are shown on Figure 2.1. Further
site-specific studies and design would be necessary prior to IOP implementation to determine actual
terminal sites and routes.” The suggestion that the 2003 WETA EIR proposed a terminal within the marina
is not accurate and the 2003 WETA EIR specifically identifies that additional studies will be needed to
determine the actual terminal site. This Draft EIR provides that project-level analysis for a terminal site in
the Berkeley Waterfront.

Response to Comment P47-18
With respect to the commenter's comparison of the energy efficiency of ferry service relative to buses
and BART as analyzed in the 2003 WETA EIR, the comment concerns the relative merits of different
transportation modes and the policy decision to provide ferry service in Berkeley. CEQA does not require
an EIR to determine whether the proposed project is the most energy-efficient transportation option
available. Rather, CEQA requires disclosure and evaluation of a project's environmental impacts. The City
acknowledges the commenter's opinion regarding the comparative efficiency of various transit modes
and has included the comment in the project record provided to City decision-makers for consideration.
The City also notes that the energy comparisons cited by the commenter were developed as part of the
2003 WETA EIR, which evaluated a substantially different ferry program and did not analyze the electric
ferry vessels proposed as part of the Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project. For additional
discussion regarding the proposed project’s electric ferry operations and the relationship between the
Draft EIR and the 2003 WETA EIR, please refer to Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry, and
Section 2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability.
The comment that the Draft EIR does not evaluate energy efficiency is not correct. Draft EIR Section 3.6,
Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy, evaluates energy consumption associated with both project

construction and operation and assesses the project's consistency with applicable energy conservation

Response to Comment P47-19
The CEQA significance thresholds for GHG emissions and energy consumption do not have a
requirement for comparing efficiencies from one form of transit to another. The project as proposed is
not anticipating replacing existing forms of transit but rather including an additional option to remove
passenger vehicles from the roadways. The current bus and BART operations would continue with or
without the project, and the implementation of the project would not require a reduction in trips of these
alternate modes of transit. Therefore, the GHG emissions and energy consumption from buses and BART
are assumed to continue consistent with what they are consuming today. The analysis of the project in
isolation of a GHG emissions and energy efficiency comparisons with other forms of transit is accurate.
Further, Draft EIR Alternatives (Section 5.9) discussed alternative projects such as increasing Bay Area
Rapid Transit (BART) capacity and improving access to BART, both of which were alternatives that were
considered but rejected as they did not meet the project objective of provision of all-electric ferry service
between Berkeley and San Francisco. The analysis in the Draft EIR accurately analyzes GHG emissions
and energy consumption with respect to CEQA and Bay Area Air District methodologies and thresholds.
Therefore, additional analysis is not required. No Draft EIR changes are necessary in response to this
comment.

Response to Comment P47-20
This statement is not accurate. The Draft EIR considered consistency with Policy T-9, including Action B,
as part of its analysis in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning (see Table 3.9-3 in Impact LU#2, page 3.9-26).
As stated in the EIR, page 3.9-26, the project would build infrastructure to facilitate regular ferry service
and would be supported by nearby AC Transit routes and bus stops, as well as existing and proposed
bicycle and pedestrian paths to encourage visitors to reduce vehicle miles travelled. The project includes
substantial transit improvements to AC Transit, and bicycle and pedestrian pathways including the Bay
Trail.
As concluded in Draft EIR Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, Impact LU-2 (pages 3.9-12 through 3.9-35),
the proposed project would be generally consistent with the goals and policies identified in applicable
plans; however, because the project would generate noise that even after mitigated would exceed
thresholds established in the Berkeley Municipal Code, impacts would be significant and unavoidable
(due to noise impacts).
Furthermore, to the extent that an inconsistency with a land use plan or policy would result in a physical
environmental effect, such effects are evaluated throughout the Draft EIR, and mitigation measures are
identified as appropriate. Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or mitigation measures are
necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P50-4
While transit ridership patterns have fluctuated in recent years, recent trends indicate that ridership on
regional transit systems, including BART, has been steadily recovering as travel demand increases, fuel
costs rise, and more employees return to in-person work. According to BART, average weekday ridership
has continued to grow and is trending toward pre-pandemic levels. 54
Transit infrastructure projects are planned and evaluated based on long-term transportation needs rather
than short-term ridership fluctuations. The proposed ferry service is intended to provide an additional
transportation option, improve regional mobility, provide emergency response and resiliency, and
accommodate future travel demand. As population and employment continue to grow in the region,
maintaining and expanding a diverse transit network helps ensure that residents and workers have
access to reliable transportation choices.
The analysis performed in the Draft EIR is based on the best available information at the time. Refer to
Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, for a discussion related to the information used to conduct the
VMT analysis.

maps in the BMMP repeatedly refer to this site, with language like “Enhance windsurfer

activity”, (Figure 2.0) and “Preserve the areas devoted to …recreational activities [and]

construction. Recreational policy 9 which provides that ferry terminal may only be allowed
if "development" does not interfere with current recreational uses. A project where              P53-3
development would terminate protected recreational uses for an indeterminate time is
inconsistent with that policy and thus has a signiﬁcant impact. Consideration of
alternatives and mitigation is therefore required.

physical reality of tides. Public meetings chaired by the city have repeatedly featured          P53-4

presented therein is clarifying in nature, and does not alter the analysis or subsequent significance
conclusion under Impact REC-1.
For additional discussion of shoreline and equipment-dependent access and how site-specific conditions
are considered in the analysis, refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing
Recreational Water Access. Refer to Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land Use/Plan Consistency,
regarding appropriate consideration of plans and policies.
Accordingly, the Draft EIR provides an appropriate evaluation of construction-related recreational impacts
consistent with CEQA requirements. The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact
REC-1 in Section 3.11, Recreation, and related sections of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further
revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P53-2
The comment that the Berkeley Marina Master Plan and Policy 9 of the Bay Plan are not referenced in the
EIR is not accurate. A consistency analysis with the Berkeley Marina Master Plan is discussed on pages
3.9-29 to 3.9-33 of the Draft EIR. Recreation Policy 9 of the Bay Plan is discussed on page 3.9-18 of the
Draft EIR.
The comment identifies two specific policies in the Berkeley Marina Master Plan. One is Figure 2.0, which
includes a label that says “Enhance Windsurfer Activity.” The second is Item C under Principle 4, which
states: “Enhance Windsurfer Activities at the point immediately west of H’s [sic] Lordships Restaurant.”
Refer to Response to Comment P36-10 for a discussion of the project’s consistency with these policies.

Response to Comment P53-3
Construction-related impacts to recreation are evaluated in Section 3.11, Recreation, which considers
temporary disruptions and concludes that impacts would be less than significant because construction
effects are temporary and the project would provide long-term increases in recreational facilities (refer to
Impact REC-1). While localized construction areas, staging areas, and temporary detours may affect
access within portions of the project vicinity during construction, recreational access to the broader
Berkeley Waterfront would remain available throughout the construction period.
As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, and Section 3.11, Recreation, construction would be
managed to maintain recreational access to the maximum extent feasible. Access routes may be
temporarily modified; however, the City would implement standard access management practices,
including maintaining access where feasible, providing temporary detours around active construction
areas, and installing temporary signage and wayfinding to direct recreational users to available waterfront
facilities. In addition, the Berkeley Waterfront encompasses a large recreational area with multiple access
points and numerous recreational resources that would remain available during construction. Under
CEQA, the relevant question is whether temporary construction activities would result in a substantial
adverse physical impact on recreational facilities or require the construction of new recreational facilities.
As discussed in Impact REC-1, temporary construction-related access limitations would not result in
substantial physical deterioration of recreational facilities, would not require construction of new

CEQA Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users.

inconsistency with Bay Plan Recreation Policy 9, refer to Response to Comment O10-116 regarding the
Draft EIR's consistency analysis for Recreation Policy 9 and Section 2.2.13, Topical Response: Land

Response to Comment P54-1
The City acknowledges the importance of Waterfront recreation accessibility for all residents. However,
parking scarcity, as well as social, economic, and affordability considerations related to parking fees are
not environmental impacts under CEQA. The Draft EIR accordingly evaluates the potential physical
environmental impacts associated with parking conditions. For further discussion of the Draft EIR
evaluation of parking considerations, please refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking.
While socioeconomic and affordability considerations are generally outside the scope of CEQA unless
they result in a physical environmental impact, the City recognizes the importance of equitable access to
public amenities and recreational resources. Accordingly, the City has undertaken separate efforts to
evaluate environmental justice and equity considerations, including preparation of an Environmental
Justice Technical Study 55 for the proposed project and ongoing development of the City's General Plan
Environmental Justice Element 56. These efforts provide additional opportunities for the City to consider
issues related to accessibility, equity, and community benefits beyond the environmental review required
under CEQA.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

"The FY 2024/25 operating budget is made up of two primary components: a $69.2 million

                                                                                                                      P55-2
From Table 2: Fares = $14.1M; Ridership (projected) = 2.6M

Operating cost per ride = $74.4M / 2.6M = $28.8 per ride
Fare revenue per ride $14.1M / 2.6M = $5.4 per ride
Subsidy per ride = operating cost per ride - revenue per ride = $28.8 - $5.4 = $23.4 per ride

But omitting the capital budget is not a valid estimate of actual subsidy level. Boats need to
be replaced, terminals need to be maintained, maintenance dredging is required. Capital
