Dear Ms. McNulty,

Herein I provide comments addressing the Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIR) for the
Proposed Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project.

Thank you very much for the extension of the comment. I note that prior personal comment
letters on the Specific Waterfront Plan and other City of Berkeley projects included a request
for preparation of an environmental impact report due to significant impacts. I found the                  P72-2
document deficient but am grateful that the effort was made.

I grew up in Berkeley and attended Berkeley High School. I visit the waterfront almost every
month for birdwatching, nature bathing, and walking. I have led approximately four Golden
Gate Bird Alliance field trips to the Berkeley waterfront/Eastshore State Park. The Berkeley
waterfront is important!

After much thought, I advocate adoption of Alternative 1: No Project Alternative.                          P72-3

I have not read all 660 pages of the Draft Environmental Impact Report (DEIR), but sections I              P72-4
studied are deficient in (a) scope, (b) wildlife and San Francisco Bay ecological health data, and         P72-5
(c) cumulative impact analysis. In lieu of Alternative 1, a Subsequent EIR is required. A                  P72-6
Supplemental EIR is generated when only minor additions are needed to revise the project EIR.
A Subsequent EIR is required when the first EIR is no longer sufficient due to changes in the
existing condition. There have been significant changes to San Francisco Bay baseline ecological           P72-7
health since the program EIR was written in 2003. See discussion below. A Subsequent EIR is
essential for the general public to make an informed decision about the impacts from the
project.

On general grounds, I am opposed to construction of the ferry. I believe it is overly expensive,
will do little to relieve congestion and will not reduce climate change. The ferry and pier as
currently planned would sanitize/sterilize waterfront character, make access elitist via fees              P72-8
garnered at parking lots, tarnish the wild and scenic nature of the current view shed, and
reduce both biodiversity and abundance of wildlife. Why do we have three BART stations and
need a ferry? Berkeley is becoming denser. We need our wild spaces.

Overview: DEIR’s/CEQA Definition of “Sufficient Degree of Analysis”.

       “An EIR should be prepared with a sufficient degree of analysis to provide decision-
       makers with information which enables them to make a decision which intelligently               i   P72-9




                                                                                              2- 745
                                       Page 850 of 1541




       takes account of environmental consequences. An evaluation of the environmental
       effects of the proposed project need not be exhaustive, but the sufficiency of an EIR is
       to be reviewed in light of what is reasonably feasible. Disagreement among experts does         P72-9
       not make an EIR inadequate, but the EIR should summarize the main points of
       disagreement among the experts. The courts have looked not for perfection, but for
       adequacy, completeness, and a good faith effort at full disclosure.” DEIR, 1.3.2.

DEIR relies on a 23-year-old document/Synopsis of Changes to SF Bay Ecological Health.

The DEIR is inadequate because it depends on a 23-year-old document, “Expansion of Ferry
Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area Program EIR” (2003 [please see DEIR for full
citation]). Since 2003, there have been intensive and escalating negative impacts to wildlife of
the San Francisco Bay. Wildlife has declined tremendously and sea surface rise has (already)
                                                                                                       P72-10
altered San Francisco Bay shorelines. The Bay has been hammered by outbreaks of
cyanobacteria causing fish kill. Shorebirds are in decline. Mercury and selenium continue to
threaten health of fish and birds. Decreased freshwater flows through San Francisco Bay impact
native fish and thus impacts many bird species (SFEI 2025). Not mentioned by SFEI, at least in
the sections I read, is the relatively recent increase in utilization of San Francisco Bay by gray
whales, recent devastating mortality of gray whales (likely by boat strike), and impacts to birds
and marine mammals from avian flu.

Baseline/DEIR Study Area Incomplete (DEIR, Fig. 3.3-1) (DEIR Section 3-1).

The Study Area “terrestrial polygon” is a narrow linear band running down University Avenue.
The “terrrstrial polygon” thus neglects indirect impacts to a suite of rare and sensitive bird         P72-11
species discussed in the avian section below. The Study Area’s similarly slender “aquatic
polygon” does not include consequences to waterbirds and shorebirds from the ferry itself, the
                                                                                                       P72-12
Ferry Wake 600’ death zone to waterbirds, and smothering of benthic invertebrates by
sediment.

The myopic Study Area does not address tree removal, increased lighting, and hardscape
changes from parking. The document implies it does not need to address parking because need
for parking is not part of CEQA:

       From DEIR (Section 3.1 – Baseline) regarding lack of inclusion of impacts from parking in
       the DEIR :“As part of the scoping process, the City received comments from the public
       requesting the use of a different baseline …. Lack of parking is not considered an              P72-13
       environmental impact under CEQA. Given the guidance from CEQA Guidelines Section
       15125 and that the main concern raised by the public requesting the use of a different
       baseline is for a non-CEQA topic, a baseline that differs from the existing condition at the
       time of the NOP publication is not used for this analysis.”

If I’m reading the document correctly, it denies the need to address parking reconfiguration and
expansion of trails. Inconsistently, however, the DEIR discussed tree removal in preparation for
parking! The DEIR explains that removal of trees at Seawall Drive (DEIR Figure 3.1.7) is
mitigated by planting of new trees. Removal of mature old gnarled conifers such as planned is
a habitat element that will not be available to birds within most of our lifetimes.
                                                                                                       P72-13

DEIR Inadequately Relies on One Day of Field Surveys.

The DEIR is inadequate because field surveys were restricted to one day (19 September 2024)
(DEIR, Appendix C, p. 37). This date avoids appropriate phenological windows for almost all of
                                                                                                       P72-14
the rare plants and animals mentioned in Appendix C. A further discussion of survey
requirements to obtain an adequate environmental baseline is provided below.

Ferry Wake.

The impact of the ferry wake creating a “dead zone” of 600’ width has been well-documented
by Takekawa (circa 2004). Background from USGS biologists:

       Waterbirds such as shorebirds, waders, and ducks depend on healthy and productive
       estuaries to “fuel up” for long distance migrations along the Pacific flyway. As the largest
       estuary on the Pacific Coast of North America, California’s San Francisco Bay-Delta is a
       critically important diving duck wintering area. Continentally, populations of Bay and sea      P72-15
       duck species such as Lesser Scaup and Surf Scoters have declined dramatically over the
       past three decades… Several hypothetical reasons for these declines are changes in
       habitat quality and quantity at wintering and spring stop-over sites” (USGS 2026:
       (Https://www.usgs.gov/centers/werc/science/avian-studies-san-francisco-bay).

Sediment.

The ferry wake, dredging to install new pier and ferry channel, redredging of ferry channel every
10 years or so, and pile driving will increase sedimentation. This could negatively affect eelgrass    P72-16
beds and reduce benthic prey critical to fish and birds.

Not fully acknowledged in the DEIR are wildlife unfriendly projects proposed by City of Berkeley
and Eastshore State Park including North Basin boat access and various projects proposed in the

"Berkeley Bulb". Also proposed are various climate resiliency projects that could include
                                                                                                           P72-17
massive changes to the waterfront area. See DEIR: Table 3-1 Present and Reasonably

What is “dead zone” wake from increased bike use?

Demolition of Portions of Closed Pier.

It was disappointing that 1280’of the old Berkeley fishing pier was slated for removal See DEIR,
Figure 2-2; Also Section 2.5.1. The old pilings support invertebrates (mussels, etc.) important for
foraging waterbirds. The tip of the old pier supports a large high tide shorebird roost. Prior to
the closure of the pier, it was common birdwatcher’s practice to walk the pier to westernmost
end of the pier at high tide, look through the wooden slats, and search for rare shorebirds that
                                                                                                           P72-18
might be present amongst the hundreds to low thousands of assembled waders. The data for
my high counts are buried in old notebooks. I am slowly going through the data and entering it
into EBird but did not have time to ferret it out. A photo in Anderson, Hart, and Rauzon 2021
illustrates the roost. Also see Rauzon’s comment letter on ferry impacts. High tide roosts for
shorebirds are a limiting factor in the central Bay (Gary Page, Pt Blue Cons. Science senior
biologist; personal communication).

What is the the relative densities of invertebrates on concrete versus old wooden piers? That
should be addressed in the Subsequent DEIR. I have seen discussions of recent San Francisco
Bay projects that create living shorelines using “slippery” hard substrate that encourages native
versus non-native invertebrates to colonize. I am in favor of encouragement of native species,             P72-19
but the reality is that waterbirds and San Francisco Bay have intermittently benefited from
massive invasions of non-native plants, etc. I believe I heard about this through a presentation
by Susan De La Cruz (USGS)(https://www.usgs.gov/centers/werc/science/avian-studies-san-
francisco-bay) at a State of the Estuary conference a few years ago.

Pigeon guillemot boxes as advocated by Mark Rauzon (see his comments on DEIR) should be                P72-20
installed (Anderson, Hart, and Rauzon 2021).

Impacts of the ferry wake to waterfowl, shorebird high tide roosts, and impacts to wildlife in

                                                                                                        P72-21

Incomplete assessment of Environmental Justice.

If parking lots were to require fees, it might challenge options for income-disadvantaged
hominids to enjoy the currently free sensational views of the bay on Seawall Drive. Seawall

for him. By the time he was ready to venture forth, bay conditions were windy and cold. Both of
us enjoyed watching the boats and the sensation of being close to the bay from the warm
shelter of the car. Similarly, many people fish from the Seawall Drive bay shore and watch their
rod tips from behind a windshield.

                                                                                                    t   P72-27

California Least Tern.

California Least Terns are state and federally endangered (CDFW 2026). Appendix C states
that “there are no known occurrences within 5 miles”. This is incorrect. I myself have seen
them foraging in North Basin and Cesar Chavez (“Farmworkers” Park). There are 75
observations of California least terns at Cesar Chavez Park (“Farmworkers” Park) documented in
EBird. See: https://ebird.org/species/leater1/L285281 {eBird 2026]). Least Terns “occurred
regularly” (Avocet 2007, Appendix D).

Surveys should be conducted for the species during the chick provisioning period to assess
habitat utilization within the ferry travel lanes as well as North Basin and habitat west of the
west end of the waterfront.

been recently documented just north of the proposed ferry route. There are probably many
other records in the waterfront area in EBird. Brant are a California State Species of Special
Concern (CDFW 2026). They do not nest in California. Brant staging and wintering habitat is            P72-30
protected. There are eelgrass beds in this locale. See comment letter by Mark Rauzon. Mark’s
letter includes an excellent photo of staging Brant taken in April 2026. This photo is an example
of staging habitat utilization. Staging refers to dense gatherings of waterfowl or shorebirds prior
to migrating north. The DEIR insufficiently addresses impacts to eelgrass beds. Appendix C
describes eelgrass surveys in 2009 and 2014 (DEIR, Appendix C, p. 3.3-11). In fact, the DEIR
maps that eelgrass beds (p. 3.3-9) as “historic” thus implying that the authors acknowledge that       P72-31
data should be updated. Eelgrass across central SF Bay should be re-surveyed by appropriate
eelgrass experts. Sedimentation and sea surface rise in recent years may have redistributed
eelgrass.

Snowy Plover.

Appendix C notes that this species would be “unexpected” and I would tentatively agree.
There is a record for Western Snowy Plover (North Basin [Avocet 2007]). Although unlikely,
                                                                                                       P72-32
Snowy Plovers might utilize mudflats at the Ferry/ Pier site at extreme low tide or the tip of
the old fishing pier at high tide. I did not search EBird for occurrences.

Osprey.

No mention of Osprey in Appendix C summary chart of sensitive species with potential to occur.
The species, however, is indeed mentioned on page 181 of DEIR where it is incorrectly classified
as a “seabird”. Osprey have been sighted frequently at the Berkeley Waterfront. Osprey are on
the California Department of Fish and Wildlife Watch List (CDFW 2026). They frequently nest in         P72-33
old piers around north/central San Francisco Bay (see publications by Tony Brake). I do not
personally know of a nest on the old fishing pier and, by the way, as EBird is current configured
it is difficult to query for nests. Surveys for nesting Osprey must be conducted.

White-Tailed Kite.

Appendix C list only “two known occurrences”. Construction along University Avenue
would likely reduce foraging habitat. Under CDFW regulations, only nesting trees are
protected but it is reasonable to complain that there may be some impact to foraging                   P72-34
habitat. See CDFW 2026.

Burrowing owl.

I thought authors of the DEIR had a good discussion in Appendix C. However, impacts from
massive parking planned for project might take out burrowing owl habitat. Burrowing owls              P72-35
often use riprap.

Bald Eagle. “No known occurrences”. Mining EBird data will no doubt show many                         P72-36
observations in the general area,

Bryant’s Savannah Sparrow.

No mention of Bryant’s Savannah Sparrow in Appendix C summary chart of sensitive species
with potential to occur. Bryant’s Savannah Sparrow, a subspecies of the Savannah Sparrow, is a
California State Species of Special Concern that potentially nests in the remnant unmowed
grassland patches at Cesar Chavez (“Farmworkers” Park). Bryant’s Savannah Sparrow are in              P72-37
decline because they are restricted to coastal grasslands which have been heavily developed
across its range. Identification of many Savannah Sparrow subspecies, including Bryant’s, is
difficult in the field. Cesar Chavez (“Farmworkers” Park) harbors Savannah Sparrows in its
grasslands that are likely nesting as they occupy territories (eg. sing) through spring and


                                                                                             2- 752
                                      Page 857 of 1541




summer (E. Strauss, pers. observation). These Passerculus were not identified to the subspecies
P. sandwichensis alaudinus. Appropriate nesting habitat is is present at the Berkeley                P72-37
waterfront. See: Bird Species of Special Concern (CDFW website accessed 2026) and scroll down
to Bryant’s Savannah Sparrow for further discussion of habitat requirements.

Willow thicket.

The willow thicket is in the southeast corner of the junction of University Avenue and Seawall
Drive. The willow thicket is one of the waterfront’s neotropical migrant patches. It has harbored
Macgillivray’s, Wilson’s and Yellow Warblers. Wildlife utilizing the willow thicket, even if it      P72-38
survives pier/ferry construction, would have a reduced foraging area due to removal of Seawall
Drive trees.




In closing, I do not believe the DEIR provides a sufficient discussion of the significant            P72-39
aspects of probable environmental consequences (paraphrase from DEIR 1.3.2). I support
adoption of Alternative 1: No Project Alternative. Berkeley does not need another expensive          P72-40
white elephant like the research labs that sit empty at Aquatic Park. If Berkeley continues to
pursue construction of the ferry/pier then a Subsequent EIR must be prepared.                        P72-41

Thank you for consideration of my views.

Guidelines Section 15161, which focuses on the specific environmental effects of the proposed Berkeley
Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project.

where appropriate provides new and current background setting information and analyses based on the
latest information available at the time of EIR Notice of Preparation.

document, and not an update to the 2003 WETA EIR, preparation of a subsequent or supplemental EIR is
not required. The Draft EIR’s analysis, significance determinations, and mitigation measures are based on
current conditions and substantial evidence in the record and remain valid as presented. Accordingly, no
revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P72-17
The Draft EIR includes a cumulative impacts analysis consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section 15130 and
identifies present and reasonably foreseeable projects in Table 3-1 (pages 3-9 through 3-10). The
cumulative analysis evaluates the project's incremental contribution to cumulative impacts for each
environmental resource topic.
The comment references North Basin boat access. The City notes that the Berkeley North Basin Project is
already included in the cumulative projects list in Draft EIR Table 3-1 as Project No. 15 (page 3-9). As
described therein, the project includes habitat improvements and public access improvements within the
North Basin area of McLaughlin Eastshore State Park. Accordingly, this project was considered as part of
the cumulative scenario evaluated in the Draft EIR. To the extent the comment references projects
proposed in the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan (WSP) and the potential for regional ferry expansion, refer
to Section 2.2.9, Topical Response: Cumulative Impacts, which explains that the Draft WSP is included in
the Draft EIR cumulative impacts analysis (see Draft EIR page 3-9 and 3-11) and provides further
clarification regarding the relationship between the Draft EIR cumulative analysis and the Draft WSP.
The comment also references creation of a large bicycle “freeway” around the exterior of the Berkeley
Bulb. However, the comment does not identify a specific project by that name or provide information
demonstrating that it is a separate reasonably foreseeable project not already captured within the Draft
WSP or other projects listed in Draft EIR Table 3-1. The City is not aware of a cumulative project identified


Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                       2- 757
                                             Page 862 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                        Response to Comments

as a bicycle freeway in the capital improvement projects lists reviewed during preparation of the Draft
EIR. To the extent the comment is referring to future bicycle improvements that may be implemented as
part of broader waterfront planning efforts, those efforts would either be encompassed within projects
already included in the cumulative projects list or would be evaluated separately if and when they become
reasonably foreseeable projects.
Additionally, the comment references climate resiliency projects that could result in changes to the
waterfront area, but does not identify specific projects. However, the cumulative projects list provided in
the Draft EIR (Table 3-1) includes several projects that could be responsive to this concern, including the
César E. Chávez Park Pathway Restoration Project, Marina Boulevard Shoreline Resiliency and Public
Access Improvements Project, Berkeley North Basin Project, and other shoreline restoration, habitat
enhancement, and public access improvement projects that were reasonably foreseeable at the time the
Draft EIR was prepared. These projects were considered in the cumulative impact analysis based on the
best available project information. With respect to the question regarding the projected paved footprint of
each cumulative project, CEQA does not require a cumulative analysis to quantify the paving area of every
cumulative project. Rather, CEQA requires evaluation of the environmental effects of past, present, and
reasonably foreseeable future projects. The Draft EIR relies on the available project descriptions and
planning documents associated with cumulative projects to evaluate cumulative environmental
conditions and determine whether the proposed project would make a cumulatively considerable
contribution to identified impacts. The comment also asks about a "dead zone wake" from increased
bicycle use. Increased bicycle use does not generate a wake and, by itself, is not a physical environmental
impact under CEQA. To the extent new bicycle facilities require physical improvements, any associated
environmental impacts would result from construction or operation of those facilities and would be
evaluated as part of the applicable project. Increased bicycle use itself is generally associated with
reduced reliance on motor vehicles and does not constitute a significant environmental impact.
Finally, the comment states that the Draft EIR does not address cumulative impacts associated with a
buildout of 26 ferry terminals across San Francisco Bay. As discussed in Section 2.2.9, Topical Response:
Cumulative Impacts, the 26-terminal scenario was a conceptual planning network considered during
development of WETA's long-range planning efforts but was not adopted as part of WETA's 2050 Service
Vision. Because the 26-terminal concept was not adopted and does not meet the Draft EIR's definition of
a reasonably foreseeable project, it was appropriately not included in the cumulative projects analysis.
The Draft EIR analyzes reasonably foreseeable ferry service expansion projects that meet the criteria
identified on Page 3-6 of the Draft EIR.
The Draft EIR adequately evaluates cumulative conditions and the project’s incremental contributions to
cumulative impacts consistent with CEQA requirements. Therefore, the analysis, impact determinations,
and mitigation measures remain valid as presented, and no revisions to the Draft EIR are required in
response to this comment.

Response to Comment P72-18
The historic Berkeley Pier extended almost 4 miles out from the shore, and pier pilings will remain in
place that will provide sufficient substrate for sessile invertebrate and roosting birds despite the pier
pilings that will be removed to ensure no-net loss of jurisdictional waters due to project construction. As
discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.3.2, Environmental Setting, page 3.3-10, invertebrate communities
present on pier pilings are also present on the rip rap shoreline within the project site, providing alternate
foraging opportunities for waterbirds. Removal of the pier pilings would be a temporary impact to
invertebrate communities, as the breakwater and new piles that are to be installed would provide hard
substrate that could be recolonized by these communities, as discussed in Section 3.3.4, Shading and
Soft Bottom Habitat Impacts, page 3.3-61. See Responses to Comment O7-17 and P46-4 for further
discussion of project impacts specific to foraging and roosting birds. No changes to the Draft EIR are
necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P72-19
The density of invertebrates on the existing pilings is beyond the scope of the Draft EIR, because CEQA
evaluates whether a project would cause a substantial, adverse change in biological resources or exceed
established significance thresholds, not the absolute abundance of organisms on individual structural
elements. A records review and the project reconnaissance found no evidence that the pilings support
special-status species or constitute a unique or irreplaceable benthic habitat; thus, quantifying
invertebrate density on pilings would not change the conclusion that impacts are unlikely to be
significant. See Response to Comment P72-18 for additional discussion of invertebrate communities on
pier pilings. No changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Op Ed by Paul Kamen, Naval Architect
March 7, 2023

Why is Berkeley Going Backwards on Climate Change?

Berkeley is poised to embrace one of the dirtiest, highest-carbon, globally-destructive forms of
transportation ever devised: Diesel Powered High Speed Commuter Ferries.

The numbers speak for themselves: A modern fast ferry is a carbon hog, using about 2300 BTU of
liquid fossil fuel energy per passenger mile. Compare to commuter buss at 130 BTU per passenger-
mile, lilght rail at 91, or BART at only 68. Even an older gasoline-powered car, 20 MPG in a four-
person carpool, leaves a lighter carbon footprint than the ferry at 1750 BTU/passenger-mile.

Modern battery-electric cars, single-occupancy, have an energy consumption range from 853 to about
1180 BTU equivalent per passenger-mile. Also consider that with private vehicles there’s no reverse
commute; with public transportation, a half-load in the reverse commute direction doubles the per-mile
carbon footprint. If our high speed diesel ferry averages 50% passenger load throughout the day
(probably optimistic), then the ferry’s actual carbon footprint per passenger-mile is doubled.

While it’s true that modern “Tier 4” emission controls can remove particulates and other pollutants
from diesel exhaust, they do nothing for carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas produced when
petroleum fuel is burned. The carbon footprint tracks closely with the energy content of the liquid fossil
fuel burned, so BTU per passenger-mile is a good measure of the carbon footprint of a diesel ferry.
                                                                                                             P75-3
(Electric vehicle energy is more commonly given as kilowatt-hours rather than British thermal units,
but the conversion is easy: 1 kWh = 3412 BTU.)

Now look at the latest purchase by our local ferry authority, WETA: Two diesel engines of 2557 HP
each, 36 knots at full load, 320 passengers. It works out to 2719 BTU per passenger-mile, assuming
every seat is occupied in both commute directions.

Meanwhile, California is aggressively pursuing full electrification of our transportation fleet. New cars
must be all electric by 2035. We are transitioning to zero-emission busses. Electric ferries are in the
works all over the world (Seattle, Vancouver, New York, Europe, and Asia). Norway is particularly
progressive: A new 27 knot, 150-passenger all-electric ferry is now operational, joining a fleet of 70
zero-emission ferries. It runs at a relatively efficient 927 BTU/passenger-mile. And their largest all-
electric ferry transports 360 passengers plus 120 vehicles at about 12 knots on a 4 mile route. If we
count each car as equivalent to four more passengers, carbon footprint is a very clean 305 BTU per
passenger-mile.

Thailand is planning no less than 27 250-passenger electric ferries to serve routes on the Chao Phraya
River in Bangkok. Other electrification projects are underway in Taiwan, New York and several
European routes.

Closer to home, BC Ferries is already operating two Island Class hybrid car ferries in Puget Sound –
capacity is 47 vehicles and up to 450 passengers.

Here in the U.S., the Federal Trade Commission recently awarded $97.6 million to fund the “Electric or
Low-Emitting Ferry Pilot Program” in 7 states. Washington State Ferries, the largest ferry operator in
the U.S., has initiated a $4B program to first hybridize and then electrify its fleet by 2040.

                                                                                                   2- 775
                                           Page 880 of 1541




Even the humble old Tiburon-Angel Island ferry will be electrified next year, moving 400 passengers at
only 256 BTU/passenger-mile. This is less than one-tenth of the per-passenger per-mile carbon
footprint of WETA’s newest diesel ferries.

The proposed Berkeley to San Francisco ferry service is well suited to electrification. It’s a short route
at only 6.5 miles, with a long enough dwell time at each end for useful recharge. (The SF-Jack London
Square route if even shorter, at 6.2 miles.)

Before proceeding with plans for a major ferry terminal at the Berkeley Marina, Berkeley needs a firm
contractual guarantee from WETA that ONLY electric ferries will operate from the new terminal. Yes,
WETA has made this promise, but their cost projections are still based on diesel power. We need an
enforceable agreement that we can hold them to. And we need to see realistic costs and revenue
projections based on electric boats.                                                                         P75-3

A ferry has a useful life of 30 to 40 years. In 2050 and beyond, do we really imagine that we will still
be supporting a diesel fleet for the short run from Berkeley to San Francisco? Diesel will cost more,
diesel will contribute to disastrous climate change, and adding more diesel exhaust is absolutely the
wrong legacy to leave to those who come after us.

It’s easy to see why the Berkeley City Council would love to take credit for bringing ferry service back
to Berkeley. But if large diesel-powered boats come to Berkeley, the legacy will be regressive climate
policy and an inexcusable disregard for the future.

Paul Kamen, Naval Architect

Response to Comment P78-1
Refer to Section 2.2.5, Topical Response: CEQA Adequacy, for more information on this topic. No further
response is required.

Response to Comment P78-2
Double crested cormorant (Nannopterum auritum) is on the CDFW Watch List for nesting colonies, but is
not a Species of Special Concern, and Clark's grebe (Aechmophorus clarkii) is currently listed as Least
Concern by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Sixteen (16) new ferry trips daily
(eight in the morning and eight in the afternoon) would not contribute significantly to existing levels of
vessel operational levels on the Bay. The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact
BIO-1 in Section 3.3.4, Impacts Analysis, Page 3.3-56 of the Draft EIR remains valid as written. The Draft
EIR discusses the impacts of ferry wake in Section 3.8.4. Impacts Analysis on page 3.8-33. No changes to
the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P78-3
Refer to Section 3.3.2, Environmental Setting, of the Draft EIR for information regarding eelgrass. There
are no documented occurrences of eelgrass within the project site. Therefore, the proposed project is not
expected to impact eelgrass habitat. No further revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment P78-4
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion of parking supply, demand, and
transportation demand management project elements that would maximize accessibility of the Berkeley
Waterfront for all users.
To the extent the comment raises concerns about the distribution of costs and benefits among
waterfront users of different income levels, these are important policy considerations that the City
Council should weigh in its deliberations on the project. However, the distribution of costs and benefits
among different user groups does not constitute a physical environmental impact under CEQA. CEQA
Guidelines Section 15131 provides that economic and social effects of a project shall not be treated as
significant effects on the environment. The Draft EIR at Section 3.11, Recreation, analyzes whether the
project would have physical impacts on recreational uses and access, and concludes that the project
enhances rather than diminishes recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront. The equity
implications of fee structures for marina and ferry infrastructure are policy matters appropriately
addressed through the City's public deliberative process, not through the CEQA environmental review of
the physical project. No revision to the Draft EIR is warranted on this basis. The project would provide a
range of public benefits, including expanded public access, improved recreational facilities, and enhanced
multimodal transportation options, which are intended to support continued public use of the waterfront.
The Draft EIR appropriately evaluates the physical environmental effects of all project features, including
potential impacts related to changes to parking configuration and supply, and concludes based on
substantial recorded evidence that impacts related to transportation and related impacts to recreational
access would be less than significant, as described in Section 3.11, Recreation (refer to Impact REC-1),
and Section 3.12, Transportation (refer to Impact TRA-1).
Accordingly, the analysis and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written,
and no revisions are necessary.

Response to Comment P78-5
Conditions along the Richmond shoreline are outside the project vicinity and do not reflect the design
approach of the proposed project at the Berkeley Waterfront. The Draft EIR evaluates pedestrian and
bicycle circulation in Section 3.12, Transportation, and identifies the Bay Trail as a key recreational and
circulation feature in Section 3.11, Recreation (see Section 3.11.2, Environmental Setting, pages 3.11-1
through 3.11-7).
As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, the proposed project has been specifically designed to
reduce conflicts between different user groups and improve safety and accessibility for all users,
including those with limited mobility. The project would incorporate a raised cycle track, which would
physically separate bicycle and micromobility traffic from pedestrian pathways and public spaces. In
addition, pedestrian routes, the public plaza, and shoreline access areas would be designed to be
ADA-accessible, with improved surfaces, grades, and circulation that enhance usability for individuals
with mobility constraints (see Section 2.5, Proposed Project Components). These features represent an
improvement over existing shared-use conditions by providing clear separation of travel modes and
upgraded accessible infrastructure, thereby addressing potential safety conflicts such as those described
by the comment. The Draft EIR concludes that access and circulation conditions for recreation and
transportation users would be maintained and enhanced (see Sections 3.11 and 3.12).
Accordingly, the comment’s concerns regarding conditions at other shoreline locations do not indicate a
deficiency in the Draft EIR’s analysis, and the proposed project includes design measures specifically
intended to improve safety for pedestrians, including disabled and elderly users.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in Sections 3.11, Recreation, and 3.12,
Transportation, remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P78-6
For comments about cost, refer to Section 2.2.22, Topical Response: Project Cost/Financial Feasibility, for
a discussion related to economic considerations.
For comments about traffic, pursuant to California SB 743, transportation impacts in CEQA documents
are evaluated using vehicle miles traveled (VMT) rather than roadway congestion measures such as Level
of Service (LOS). The project is expected to increase traffic volumes on certain roadways leading to the
terminal because additional users would travel to the Waterfront to access the ferry. However, existing
roadway segments, including University Avenue between Frontage Road and Marina Boulevard, would
continue to operate within acceptable capacity conditions (LOS A). At the same time, many ferry users
would replace longer automobile trips with ferry travel. As a result, the overall amount of driving per
person is reduced, leading to a decrease in VMT on a per capita basis.
Regarding the comment about mitigation, the Draft EIR has appropriately identified potentially significant
environmental impacts and feasible mitigation measures to reduce those impacts. Refer to page 4-1 of
the Draft EIR, which discloses the significant and unavoidable impacts from the project.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P78-7
The City acknowledges the comment's preference for a pier restoration project without ferry service. This
comment has been included in the project record considered by City decision makers.

Ferry Service with New Pier Alternative" but did not carry it forward for detailed analysis because it would
not meet one of the project's two basic objectives: providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero-
emission ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco. The Draft EIR further explains that funding
available through WETA is tied to implementation of ferry service.

 Date: April 28, 2026

Biological Resources:
Potential Impacts to Whales
In your document you analyzed potential impacts to whales but I believe this merits a more in-depth analysis and should not just rely on
the very dated WETA’s 23 year old programmatic EIR that determined the following:
“Given the existing setting of the Central Bay, and WETA’s ongoing implementation of best practices to reduce the potential for whale
strikes per the Mitigation Measures in the 2003 Program EIR, impacts would be less than significant.”
But yet according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association, 18% of gray whales that enter the SF Bay die there, with fast             P81-3
moving vessel traffic and resulting strikes being a primary cause. Just a few days ago another body of a gray whale, the 8th so far this
season, was spotted in the Bay. And while the EIR does cite the “WETA Marine Mammal Protection & Whale Avoidance
Memorandum” that document is not fully reproduced in the EIR. This makes WETA’s internal whale-protection guidance less than
transparent.
Since vessel speed is the major concern in avoiding striking whales, it is of great concern that this DEIR does not support imposing
mandatory ferry speed reductions, and simply relies on “personal communication regarding ferry speeds.” So the reduction of the speed            P81-4
is NOT regulated but simply dependent on “conditional” observations.

Outside of the SF Bay NOAA etc promotes a 10 knot slow zone in whale habitats, but there is no equivalent enforceable standard with
ferry operators. The DEIR asserts that “marine mammal activity, particularly for whales, is expected to be lower in the project vicinity         P81-5
than elsewhere in the Bay.” But a whale protection approach must analyze cumulative impacts of the ferry system, not just individually.
In reaching the conclusion that “No mitigation would be required” around this issue, the DEIR states that “Special-status fish and marine
mammals, specifically whales, are likely habituated to existing levels of boat trip levels and would avoid new ferry boat service.” This
certainly sounds more like “wishful” thinking than any in-depth analysis that this important matter merits. In fact many of the whales that
come into the Bay are new to the area, so don’t have any memory of it to acclimate to it. It is hoped that the deficiencies in the
                                                                                                                                                 P81-6
environmental review of valuable resources, such as protection of the whales, be further explored so that the public and policymakers can
make an informed judgment regarding the project.
DEIR Parking and Parking Fee Program
For more “wishful” thinking there is the DEIR’s analysis around providing parking for both ferry riders and to the many other users and
recreationists who visit the waterfront. I realize that you have already received many comments about the deficiencies of the DEIR’s plan
to provide sufficient parking for ferry riders, especially since it relies mostly on data collected from other terminals in non-park settings
in the Bay Area. So while I do not have much more to add to those comments except to provide a short recent history of how the city of
Berkeley, in anticipating the advent of a ferry, thought to impose paid parking on some of the most popular areas, for recreationists, in
the waterfront area.
On May 14, 2025, the idea of paid parking first came to the Parks, Recreation and Waterfront Commission, on which I served as vice
chair (for the previous 2 years I was its chair). At that time the idea of exploring added revenue generation was extremely important,           P81-7
partially due to the fact that the Doubletree hotel had not paid its lease payments for quite some time, so the PRW formed a
subcommittee to study this issue.
The commission had heard from a wide range of Waterfront users and stakeholders about how this proposed parking fee would have an
insurmountable impact on their and others’ ability to use the waterfront. This ran counter to one of the state goals of the Waterfront
Planning process (WSP) to attract a wider range of users. It was thought that a parking fee would do quite the opposite. According to the
Kittelson report parking data found that a third of visitors made less than $75K/yr. The commission requested that it be “fully integrated
into the City’s evaluation of any trial program of parking fees”, and also appointed me to speak for the commission at the June 24 city
council meeting regarding this issue.




                                                                                                                                      2- 793
                                                       Page 898 of 1541




At that meeting the PRW staff presented its quickly developed paid parking program, that was NOT included in the agenda packet for
public review, and with little time given to any further analysis, or acknowledgement of the concerns of the public (who had written
hundreds of letters on this issue), the council approved this paid parking plan. The PRW commission was not informed beforehand
either.                                                                                                                                      P81-7
Frankly it is hard to imagine that this parking fee program would not have happened if it hadn’t been to create a parking plan for this
DEIR that was thought to discourage ferry riders from using those lots that were most popular with recreationists. Although by offering a
$500/annual fee that would allow “free” daily parking, that in itself seems to be an attractive alternative to a higher income level ferry
rider than to those in the recreational community. (Because of the “behind closed doors” decision making from policymakers, I tendered
my resignation from the PRW commission. Equity and fairness were at the heart of my concerns.)
There should be more analysis of how the DEIR’s parking plan will affect current waterfront users (not just the patrons of the ferry) and
how programs that are designed to help implement this plan, like the paid parking one, will affect future usage of Berkeley’s waterfront.

In your document you analyzed potential impacts to whales but I believe this merits a more

EIR that determined the following:

“Given the existing setting of the Central Bay, and WETA’s ongoing implementation of best
practices to reduce the potential for whale strikes per the Mitigation Measures in the 2003             P81-9
Program EIR, impacts would be less than significant.”

But yet according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association, 18% of gray whales
that enter the SF Bay die there, with fast moving vessel traffic and resulting strikes being a
primary cause. Just a few days ago another body of a gray whale, the 8th so far this season, was
spotted in the Bay. And while the EIR does cite the “WETA Marine Mammal Protection &
Whale Avoidance Memorandum” that document is not fully reproduced in the EIR. This makes
WETA’s internal whale-protection guidance less than transparent.

Since vessel speed is the major concern in avoiding striking whales, it is of great concern that
this DEIR does not support imposing mandatory ferry speed reductions, and simply relies on
“personal communication regarding ferry speeds.” So the reduction of the speed is NOT
regulated but simply dependent on “conditional” observations.



                                                                                               2- 795
                                       Page 900 of 1541




Outside of the SF Bay NOAA etc promotes a 10 knot slow zone in whale habitats, but there is no
equivalent enforceable standard with ferry operators. The DEIR asserts that “marine mammal
activity, particularly for whales, is expected to be lower in the project vicinity than elsewhere in
the Bay.” But a whale protection approach must analyze cumulative impacts of the ferry system,
not just individually.

In reaching the conclusion that “No mitigation would be required” around this issue, the DEIR
states that “Special-status fish and marine mammals, specifically whales, are likely habituated to
existing levels of boat trip levels and would avoid new ferry boat service.” This certainly sounds
more like “wishful” thinking than any in-depth analysis that this important matter merits. In fact
many of the whales that come into the Bay are new to the area, so don’t have any memory of it to
acclimate to it. It is hoped that the deficiencies in the environmental review of valuable
resources, such as protection of the whales, be further explored so that the public and
policymakers can make an informed judgment regarding the project.

DEIR Parking and Parking Fee Program
For more “wishful” thinking there is the DEIR’s analysis around providing parking for both ferry
riders and to the many other users and recreationists who visit the waterfront. I realize that you
have already received many comments about the deficiencies of the DEIR’s plan to provide                P81-9
sufficient parking for ferry riders, especially since it relies mostly on data collected from other
terminals in non-park settings in the Bay Area. So while I do not have much more to add to those
comments except to provide a short recent history of how the city of Berkeley, in anticipating the
advent of a ferry, thought to impose paid parking on some of the most popular areas, for
recreationists, in the waterfront area.

On May 14, 2025, the idea of paid parking first came to the Parks, Recreation and Waterfront
Commission, on which I served as vice chair (for the previous 2 years I was its chair). At that
time the idea of exploring added revenue generation was extremely important, partially due to
the fact that the Doubletree hotel had not paid its lease payments for quite some time, so the
PRW formed a subcommittee to study this issue.

The commission had heard from a wide range of Waterfront users and stakeholders about how
this proposed parking fee would have an insurmountable impact on their and others’ ability to
use the waterfront. This ran counter to one of the state goals of the Waterfront Planning process
(WSP) to attract a wider range of users. It was thought that a parking fee would do quite the
opposite. According to the Kittelson report parking data found that a third of visitors made less
than $75K/yr. The commission requested that it be “fully integrated into the City’s evaluation of
any trial program of parking fees”, and also appointed me to speak for the commission at the
June 24 city council meeting regarding this issue.



                                                                                               2- 796
                                        Page 901 of 1541




At that meeting the PRW staff presented its quickly developed paid parking program, that was
NOT included in the agenda packet for public review, and with little time given to any further
analysis, or acknowledgement of the concerns of the public (who had written hundreds of letters
on this issue), the council approved this paid parking plan. The PRW commission was not
informed beforehand either.

Frankly it is hard to imagine that this parking fee program would not have happened if it hadn’t
been to create a parking plan for this DEIR that was thought to discourage ferry riders from
using those lots that were most popular with recreationists. Although by offering a $500/annual           P81-9
fee that would allow “free” daily parking, that in itself seems to be an attractive alternative to a
higher income level ferry rider than to those in the recreational community. (Because of the
“behind closed doors” decision making from policymakers, I tendered my resignation from the
PRW commission. Equity and fairness were at the heart of my concerns.)

There should be more analysis of how the DEIR’s parking plan will affect current waterfront
users (not just the patrons of the ferry) and how programs that are designed to help implement
this plan, like the paid parking one, will affect future usage of Berkeley’s waterfront.

The Draft EIR is seriously deficient in its estimation of the environmental effects of dredging and land fill. This is   P82-1
because the required size and extent of the breakwater is grossly underestimated.
The problem is not the methodology, it is the omission of complete wind and wave data, specifically the
occurrence of winter gale force north or north-west winds. These wind events produce waves that leave the                P82-2
ferry float entirely unprotected by the proposed breakwater design.

The same mistake was made in 1965 when the Berkeley Marina was designed.
The original design only included the rip-ra[ breakwater, which was insufficient protection. During winter
northerlies, the wave action INSIDE the marina was enough to repeatedly damage the docks on O-Dock that                  P82-3
were in the waves' path. One section of boat berths had to be abandoned.

In the early '70s, the required fix was to add the sheet pile breakwater to the north of the original rip-rap
breakwater, at great expense. The missing berths were replaced.

The problem then, as now, was that none of the wind measurement stations used for the wave analysis were
accurately recording these north or north-west wind events. When these conditions are considered in the wave             P82-4
analysis for the proposed ferry terminal, it will be found that the breakwater must be much longer. Siltation and
maintenance dredging requirements will increase beyond current estimates. With the longer breakwater
protecting the ferry float from the north, the location of the breakwater and the ferry floats may have to move          P82-5
farther west to allow sufficient maneuvering room for the ferry.

The analysis must include more extensive fill for a longer breakwater, a new assessment of landfill and
maintenance dredging and related costs and impacts, and possible upgrades to the ferry float design or                   P82-6
allowance for more frequent repairs after north wind events.

These costs should be considered as part of the feasibility assessment of the project as proposed, otherwise the
City, WETA, and other funding agencies will be responsible for another expensive retrofit, similar to what               P82-7
happened in the same location more than 50 years ago.

Response to Comment P83-1
The Draft EIR recognizes the Cal Sailing Club and similar community-serving recreational uses as
important components of the Berkeley Waterfront. Section 3.11.2, Environmental Setting (pages 3.11-1
through 3.11-7), identifies sailing, windsurfing, kayaking, and other water-based activities as key existing
uses, including those supported by nonprofit organizations that provide public access and educational
opportunities.
Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis (pages 3.11-14 through 3.11-24), evaluates whether the proposed project
would result in a physical loss of recreational resources or restrict access to these uses. As discussed
therein, the Draft EIR concludes that the project would maintain and enhance recreational opportunities
and access, including improved shoreline access, restoration of public access to the Berkeley Pier, and
the addition of new amenities (Impact REC-1). The project does not remove or preclude continued use of
facilities such as the Cal Sailing Club.
For additional discussion of shoreline and equipment-dependent access for activities such as sailing and
kayaking, refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water
Access, and Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities).
Accordingly, the Draft EIR does not support the statement that the project would adversely affect or
displace the recreational community referenced by the comment. The analyses and significance
conclusions presented in Section 3.11, Recreation, remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR
are required.

accessibility for recreational users. The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR

Response to Comment P83-5
Refer to Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, of the Draft EIR and Section 2.2.25, Topical Response:
Siltation/Wave Climate. As discussed therein, any increase in turbidity associated with dredging activities
would be temporary and limited to the construction period. Suspended sediments generated during
dredging would be expected to settle following completion of the work, and standard construction best
management practices would be implemented to minimize sediment dispersion beyond the immediate
work area. Sediment transport analyses prepared for the project indicate that the highest sedimentation
rates would occur within the dredged navigation channel, where natural sediment transport processes
would tend to gradually infill the dredged area over time.
Although the South Sailing Basin was not specifically evaluated as part of the sediment transport
modeling, the basin is shallower and more sheltered from wave action than the navigation channel,
resulting in different hydrodynamic and sediment transport conditions. Given the localized nature of
dredging activities and the expected settling of suspended sediments near the dredged area, the project
is not anticipated to result in a measurable increase in sediment deposition within the South Sailing Basin
or a reduction in access beyond existing tidal limitations.

Hydrology and Water Quality (page 3.8-30):
    Dredging activities have the potential to temporarily degrade water quality by resuspending bottom
    sediments into the water column. As described previously, in 2025, sediment sampling and analysis
    was conducted within five dredge units in the project vicinity and sediment samples were found to
    contain metals, organochlorine pesticides, polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, PCBs, and

Draft EIR statement: "The project would introduce battery-electric ferry vessels operating
on the project site. In the unlikely event of a loss of propulsion on an electric vessel,
multiple layers of redundancy would be in place to prevent a complete failure. The vessel
would be equipped with independent electric motors and multiple battery banks, each
with isolated controls and protection systems, ensuring that a single point of failure does
not disable the entire system.”

Response: See below, the diagram shows one battery per side (port and starboard) each
with an input and charging module and a DC Hub (output bus). Not quite per the rosy
description above— “Multiple battery banks” is actually only two battery assemblies, one
for port and one for starboard, and you probably only get limp-along capability with one
bank out. These will be new prototype designs with as yet no operational track record—
understand that the failure modes expected from a novel, very complex system will require
careful analysis, way beyond what a paragraph or two can do. We trust that Wartsila will
provide WETA with a very detailed failure mode and e ect analysis that will guide our
thinking.

At the end of the day, please don’t bet 400 lives on the assumption that the control system
will never fail—the system must have a backup, a foolproof way to stop the ferry if there is a
control failure that leaves the ferry adrift. The consequences of a ferry being blown onto
the Berkeley rocks or the Skates restaurant are much too serious to take risks with.                                                                                             P84-2

       Berkeley Ferry Dock Safety Comments, see draft EIR pages 3.12-23 to 3.12-24

Draft EIR statement: “Crew members are trained regularly to respond to such scenarios,
including loss of propulsion drills. In the rare case that all propulsion is lost, the crew would
deploy the vessel’s anchor to maintain position and initiate protocols to ensure passenger
safety.” Response: Such drills are indeed essential, and should be based on scenarios                P84-3
that include actual windy-day anchoring in response to surprise control failures. Drills
should also cover simulated evacuation of passengers. The drills should follow well
thought out protocols that are described in detail. A simulator, such as the one at the Cal
Poly Maritime Academy, could be very useful in developing protocols.

Draft EIR statement: “WETA and its contracted operator proactively monitor weather
forecasts. In the event of an approaching storm, senior sta coordinate with vessel crews
to evaluate the safety of continuing ferry service on a ected routes.” Response: Fair                P84-4
enough, but will WETA help getting stranded passengers to their jobs across the bay? Not a
trivial problem for passengers who ﬁnd themselves stranded at the Marina without transit
options. The EIR needs to consider what to do with weather-stranded passengers.

Draft EIR statement: “It should be noted that other marine vessels regularly operate near
the project site, given that the project site is next to an active Marina. Similar to other
vessels, ferry vessels would operate safely. For example, when approaching the ferry ﬂoats,
ferry vessels would slow down signiﬁcantly and adhere to speed limits and docking safety
procedures. For these reasons, the operation of ferry vessels would not increase
transportation safety use hazards due to the introduction of a new use on the project site
(i.e., operation of ferry vessels).” Response: There are indeed many ﬁshing charter boats            P84-5
that transit the area safely, but they do not brave wind and waves several times per day to
make the ferry’s amazing 180-degree turn and docking in the middle of a very windy high-
tra ic area. And these new ferries will be prototypes with as yet no operational track
record, so we should be prepared for some failures.

In the end, a large, 400-passenger ferry blown onto Skates or the shore would do much
more damage, and risk many more lives, than a grounding of any of the Berkeley ﬁshing
charter boats. We need to be very sure we can stop a ferry with any foreseeable control
failure.

Marine Exchange of the San Francisco Bay Region

Draft Minutes Harbor Safety Committee of the San Francisco Bay Region February 13, 2025
https://www.sfmx.org/wp-content/uploads/2025-02 HSCMinutes DRAFT.pdf
Total of 29 entries, the four below were LOP for passenger vessels
Loss of Propulsion {17DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced a Loss of Propulsion
on the port engine. Vessel moored safely at San Francisco Gate Band received permission for a
one-time transit from San Francisco to Larkspur for repairs. Coast Guard issued the vessel an
Operational Control, rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers {Code 701). On 07JAN2025, vessel
operator reported the root cause of the loss of propulsion as a failed fuel injector. On
21JAN2025, Coast Guard received a report that the vessel propulsion system operated as
intended following satisfactory sea trials. Deficiency Cleared. Case pends.

Loss of Propulsion {23DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced a reduction in
propulsion on the starboard engine due to a low fuel oil pressure alarm. Vessel received
permission from the Coast Guard for one time transit to Alameda facility to identify root cause,
provide tech report, and conduct sea trials. Coast Guard issued an Operational Control, rectify
Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). On 01JAN2025, Coast Guard received an email
outlining the root cause of the reduction in propulsion to be from an issue with the ECU                P84-6
connecting to the starboard main engine. Vessel replaced the ECU and completed
satisfactory sea trials. Operational Control Cleared. Case Pends.

Loss of Propulsion (27DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced an engine stall while
transiting in the San Francisco Bay. Vessel returned to Pier 3 in Alameda and determined the
engine stall occurred due to a leaky fuel fitting. Vessel crew also found a loose connection at a
fuel hardline which caused air intrusion into the fuel system. Coast Guard issued an operational
control, rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). Crew repaired the faulty connection
and engine reached full RPM during satisfactory sea trials. Operational Control Cleared. Case
Pends.

Operational Control (23DEC2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel received an operational control,
rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701). Vessel reported loss of throttle control to port
and starboard propulsion drives while mooring at Pier 41. On 26DEC2024, operator submitted a
tech report that no abnormalities were found, sea trials conducted satisfactorily, and all systems
operational. Operational Control Cleared. On 27DEC2024, during transit, the vessel experienced
loss of throttle control to the port and starboard propulsion drives. Vessel moored at Pier 41.
Coast Guard issued an operational control, rectify Prior to Carriage of Passengers (Code 701).
Vessel received authorization for one-time transit to Pier 9 for maintenance and repairs. On
10JAN2025, the vessel conducted sea trials. While underway the operator completed several
propulsion tests, including full ahead followed by full astern. On 14JAN2025, technicians
reported that the throttles were calibrated to disable themselves until RPMs reduced below 70
when going from ahead to astern. Vessel installed new throttle controls. Operational control
Cleared. Case Closed.

Loss of Propulsion (10NOV2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced a loss of propulsion
on their STBD engine due to loss of propeller while transiting to Richmond. The vessel returned
to the pier and offloaded all passengers. Coast Guard issued the vessel an operational control
(Code 60, Prior to Movement), with a one-time transit to Alameda for drydock. At drydock
damage was found to have occurred to the strut, shaft, rudder, and cutless (sic) bearing. On
17NOV2024, Coast Guard attended vessel for sea trials, sea trials conducted satisfactorily.
Operational Control Cleared. Case Closed.

Loss of Steering (22NOV2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel experienced a loss of steering; vessel       P84-6
operator reported issues with the STBD steering system while underway, with alternate jet
propulsion available. Vessel returned to the pier. Coast Guard issued an operational control
(Code 701, Prior to Carraige of Passengers). On 24NOV2024, vessel operator submitted tech
report attesting to satisfactory repairs. Vessel conducted satisfactory sea trial. Operational
Control Cleared. Case Pends.

Operational Control (02NOV2024): A U.S. flag passenger vessel was issued an Operational
Control (Code 70, Prior to Carraige of Passengers). While departing the pier, the vessel lost
power from one of two generators, reducing propulsion to approximately 66% power. Vessel
safely moored and was issued the operational control. On 03NOV2024, operator notified
Coast Guard that the issue had been resolved. Identified a failure of two electrical relays that
send the key switch signal to the control system. Both relays were replaced, and sea trials
conducted . Coast Guard received satisfactory tech report. Operational Control Cleared. Case
Closed.

On November 23, 2018 a Golden Gate Ferry rammed a dock at the San Francisco Ferry building,
check out the bow damage in the picture above and this video. Fortunately, there were no serious
injuries and damage was relatively minor. The cause of the accident appears to have been the
captain's unfamiliarity with a recently upgraded control system.




                                               1
                                                                                           2- 811
                                          Page 916 of 1541




Consider the possibility of a loss of control incident occurring in a ferry approaching the dock
proposed for the Berkeley WETA ferry (see below). An inbound ferry will normally arrive
downwind roughly along the "Ferry Approach" arrow, then make a 180° turn in the "Ferry
Turning Basin" so the ferry ends up pointed upwind when it arrives at the dock. The summer
afternoon winds are often well above 20 mph, the chop is significant, and most of the marina's
boat traffic leaves and arrives through this area. The 180° turn and docking will be demanding
even with perfectly functioning equipment.




                                                                                                                  P84-8




FINAL_Ferry Terminal Facility Feasibility Study - Berkeley Municipal Pier   See Page 34 (arrows added)

Zoomed-in image showing Dorado-sized (~300 passenger) ferry halfway through a 180° turn.




This is a very tight situation in which to suffer a control or propulsion loss. The inshore end of
the ferry's dock is only 200 feet upwind of the rocky shore, and a 20- or 25-mph wind would
soon push a disabled ferry downwind onto the rocks or the Skates restaurant. Skates is built on

                                                    2
                                                                                                         2- 812
                                       Page 917 of 1541




tall, slender pilings (see next page) and might not survive wind and waves pushing a 135-foot-
long ferry against and perhaps underneath it. Injuries and damage in such an accident would be         P84-8
very likely.

Information with some bearing on how likely a control loss event might be:

   1. The meeting minutes of the Harbor Safety Committee of the San Francisco Bay Region
      for January and February 2025 described seven instances of loss of propulsion or steering
      in passenger vessels on the Bay. (see Harbor Safety Committee Reports of Loss of
      Propulsion Jan and Feb 2025.pdf, attached with this document).
   2. Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis are recalling over 146,000 electric vehicles because a faulty
      part may cause them to lose power while driving. What will be the reliability of the new
      WETA electric ferries?
   3. After the Baltimore bridge collapse caused by a power loss in a big container ship, USA
      Today summarized US Coast Guard data showing that at least 6,000 times in the past 22
      years - an average of more than five times a week - crews on board large cargo ships, oil
      tankers, container barges and even cruise vessels have reported what befell the Dali, a
      loss of propulsion and/or steering.

Docking Maneuvers:

   •    The ferry battery will be at a low state of charge when the ferry arrives at Berkeley,
        which may exacerbate some system failure modes.
   •    To the extent that the docking maneuvers involve dramatic steering or propulsion inputs,
        they may stress the control system and cause an incipient control failure to manifest as a
        hard failure during the docking.
   •    The 180° tum requires the skipper to shift attention from starboard to port, which adds to
        the skipper's workload. A Dorado's beam is 34.5 feet.                                          P84-9
   •    If the final approach requires the ferry to drop backwards into position, the helmsman
        must look backwards to the dock, again adding to workload.
   •    Marina traffic needs to use the South entrance when the tide is low, and even if the ferry
        has the right of way, someone aboard will need to watch for approaching vessels. Boats
        leaving the marina will not be visible until they are close to the turning basin.
   •    If the loss of control occurs before the ferry slows for the 180° tum, the ferry's downwind
        speed will greatly reduce the available time to respond.

Anchoring:
The best response to a loss of control event would probably be to drop an anchor, though better
solutions might be found. An anchor would need to be dropped very quickly or the ferry will not
stop before it hits the restaurant or shore.

    o   What kind of anchor should be used, and how much scope will the anchor need?
    o   Will the anchor be dropped off the stem or bow? There might need to be two protocols,
        one for a loss of control (LOC) event before the 180° tum and another for a (LOC) after
        the tum.
    o   Will the seabed be free of debris that might keep the anchor from biting into the mud?

                                                 3

                                                                                              2- 813
                                        Page 918 of 1541




    o   Is there anything on the underside of the ferry (e.g. rudder. skeg, propellor) that the
        anchor line could foul?
    o   Will additional crew be needed to deploy the anchor quickly?
    o   When the anchor line comes tight, is there potential for injury to people near it, on the
        ferry or the docking float?                                                                     P84-9

The approach of the ferry to the dock and the dropping of the anchor would need carefully
thought-out protocols, which ferry personnel would need to be well-trained to execute rapidly if
a loss of control event occurs.

In my opinion, the dock should be positioned in a less exposed site, for example inside the
                                                                                                        P84-10
Marina or in a purpose-designed facility on the Golden Gate Fields shoreline.

This is a matter that should be carefully considered in the ferry project EIR.

Letter P84
Commenter:         Gordon Stout
Date:              April 28, 2026

Response to Comment P84-1
This comment does not pertain to the proposed project or the adequacy, significance conclusions, or
mitigation in the Draft EIR. Nevertheless, this comment has been included in the project record
considered by City decision makers. No further response is required.

Response to Comment P84-2
Refer to Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, for discussion regarding vessel
maneuverability, propulsion redundancy, loss-of-control scenarios, emergency response procedures,
marine safety features, regulatory oversight, and the conclusions presented under Impact TRA-3 in Draft
EIR Section 3.12, Transportation (pages 3.12-23 through 3.12-24). The Topical Response also includes
clarifying revisions to the Draft EIR in response to comments received regarding ferry vessel control,
docking safety, loss-of-propulsion scenarios, and emergency response procedures and a design
adjustment that has been made to the proposed project to include fender piles and donut fenders within
the project site in the water area to provide an additional passive safety measure by helping to absorb or
deflect vessel movement in the unlikely event of a loss of control during approach or docking. For
additional discussion related to electric ferry vessel assumptions, electric propulsion systems, vessel
procurement, and the environmental analysis of electric ferry operations and supporting infrastructure,
refer to Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry.
The City acknowledges the commenter's observations regarding a representative electric ferry system
and suggestion that failure analyses should be conducted or vessel systems. However, the City notes that
the diagram included in the comment depicts a vessel configuration operated by a separate ferry
operator and does not represent the final vessel design proposed for the Berkeley Water Transportation
Pier Ferry Project. As discussed in Section 2.2.10, Topical Response: Electric Ferry, the specific ferry
vessel model has not yet been procured or finalized. Accordingly, the Draft EIR does not rely on the
design, battery architecture, or operational characteristics of any particular third-party vessel. Rather, the
environmental analysis is based on the project description and operational assumptions evaluated in
Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description (refer to Section 2.7, Operational Details, pages 2-30 through 2-33).
Future vessel designs would be required to comply with applicable U.S. Coast Guard requirements, vessel
certification standards, WETA operational requirements, and all other applicable maritime safety
regulations. Therefore, statements regarding the configuration, reliability, or failure characteristics of a
specific third-party vessel design do not demonstrate a deficiency in the environmental analysis
presented in the Draft EIR.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR, including Impact TRA-3 in
Section 3.12, Transportation, remain valid as written. No further revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment P84-3
Refer to Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, for discussion of ferry vessel
safety systems, emergency response procedures, crew training requirements, vessel redundancy, and
regulatory oversight. As discussed therein, ferry vessels would be operated by trained and licensed
personnel in accordance with applicable U.S. Coast Guard requirements and WETA operational
procedures.
The City acknowledges the commenter's recommendations regarding emergency preparedness and
training. Specific training curricula, simulator use, drill frequency, and operating procedures are matters



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                       2- 815
