City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                     Response to Comments

determined by the ferry operator and applicable maritime regulatory authorities. These operational
considerations do not constitute physical environmental impacts requiring analysis under CEQA.
The comment does not identify a deficiency in the environmental impact analysis presented in the Draft
EIR. Therefore, no revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P84-4
As described in Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation, WETA would monitor weather conditions and make
operational decisions regarding ferry service based on passenger and crew safety considerations (see
Impact TRA-3, pages 3.12-24 and 3.12-24). However, the availability of alternative transportation for
passengers during weather-related service disruptions is an operational and customer service matter
rather than a physical environmental impact subject to analysis under CEQA.
Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15064, 15360, and 15382, CEQA focuses on physical changes to
the environment and the resulting environmental effects of a project. Potential inconvenience to
passengers, including delays, cancellations, or the need to make alternative travel arrangements during
weather-related service disruptions, would constitute a social or operational effect and would not, in
itself, result in a physical impact on the environment requiring analysis in an EIR.
The comment does not identify a deficiency in the environmental analysis presented in the Draft EIR.
Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or mitigation measures are necessary in response to
this comment.

Response to Comment P84-5
Refer to Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, which discusses vessel
maneuverability, docking operations, emergency response procedures, propulsion and control system
redundancy, regulatory oversight, and transportation hazard analysis under Impact TRA-3 in Draft EIR
Section 3.12, Transportation (pages 3.12-23 through 3.12-24). The Topical Response also includes
clarifying revisions to the Draft EIR in response to comments received regarding ferry vessel control,
docking safety, loss-of-propulsion scenarios, and emergency response procedures. As discussed therein,
ferry operations were evaluated with consideration of navigation conditions, vessel maneuvering
requirements, and potential vessel emergency scenarios.
The Draft EIR concludes that operation of the proposed ferry service would not substantially increase
transportation hazards. While the City acknowledges the commenter's concern that ferry vessels differ
from recreational or charter vessels and that the consequences of a loss-of-control event could be more
substantial, the comment does not provide substantial evidence demonstrating that the analysis,
methodology, or significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR are inadequate.
Accordingly, the analysis and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR, as supplemented and
clarified in Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, remain valid, and no further
revisions to the EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P84-6
Refer to Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, for discussion regarding ferry
vessel maneuverability, loss-of-propulsion scenarios, vessel redundancy, emergency response
procedures, U.S. Coast Guard oversight, and transportation safety analysis under Impact TRA-3 in Draft
EIR Section 3.12, Transportation (pages 3.12-23 through 3.12-24). As discussed therein, the Draft EIR
concludes that ferry operations would not substantially increase transportation hazards.
The analysis and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further
revisions to the EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Draft EIR, as revised and clarified in Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, remain
valid, and no further revisions to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Dear Ms. McNulty:

As a Berkeley resident and waterfront user since 1972, I have an interest in
the ferry project as it might impact my access to recreational opportunities
such as walking, visiting restaurants, and sailing, all of which I have enjoyed
over the years. I may also use the ferry as I have in the past when service
from Berkeley was available. My usual transportation option to the waterfront
is my car, as that is the most convenient for a person my age (83) and                                                  P85-1
abilities. In the past I have served as a parks commissioner and Sierra Club
officer, so I am familiar with many of the marina issues besides my own
interests. I have read the DEIR with both personal and community concerns
in mind.

The EIR must analyze ferry terminals parking and include a parking
management plan as an enforceable mitigation measure                                                                    P85-2


The DEIR reiterates that parking is not an environmental impact under CEQA
but that VMTs (vehicle miles traveled) are an impact because VMTs produce
emissions and greenhouse gases. But parking and VMTs are intricately                                                    P85-3
connected. The more parking, the more trips from home to the parking space.
The less parking, the greater the need for alternative strategies to arrive at
one’s destination. None of these contingencies are adequately explored in the
DEIR to demonstrate that:



                                                                                                            2- 819
                                   Page 924 of 1541



“Because the project would result in no impact related to VMT and would in                  P85-3
fact reduce regional VMT, the project would not contribute to a cumulative
impact related to VMT.” (3.12.25)

If the parking is adequate to meet the demand of ferry riders, the DEIR
provides no data that shows the drivers would otherwise choose to drive
across the bridge to San Francisco, the most frequent route. They could
alternately have chosen BART or a cross-Bay bus as transportation options                   P85-4
that would get them to work on time. There are three BART stations to the
north of University Avenue: Richmond, El Cerrito, and North Berkeley and
several cross-Bay bus routes with frequent service.

If parking is inadequate for ferry riders, they would likely choose public transit
over driving if they wish to avoid driving across the bridge and paying for
parking in San Francisco. The EIR relies on assumptions of reduced VMT
                                                                                            P85-5
rather than quantitative analysis. This approach ignores the potential for this
new ferry route to divert passengers from BART, AC Transit, and other ferry
operations. Attracting passengers from BART by lowering fares could be
used by Bay Ferry to increase ridership, which does not decrease VMT.

If parking is inadequate for ferry use, how can displacement of parking
intended for recreational uses, including visits to McLaughlin State Park, and              P85-6
for a future visits to a restaurant at the now closed H’s. Lordship’s be
prevented? Who will enforce the rules and pay for enforcement? How

Dear Ms. McNulty:

As a Berkeley resident and waterfront user since 1972, I have an interest in
the ferry project as it might impact my access to recreational opportunities
such as walking, visiting restaurants, and sailing, all of which I have enjoyed
over the years. I may also use the ferry as I have in the past when service
from Berkeley was available. My usual transportation option to the waterfront
is my car, as that is the most convenient for a person my age (83) and
abilities. In the past I have served as a parks commissioner and Sierra Club
officer, so I am familiar with many of the marina issues besides my own
interests. I have read the DEIR with both personal and community concerns
in mind.

The EIR must analyze ferry terminals parking and include a parking
management plan as an enforceable mitigation measure

The DEIR reiterates that parking is not an environmental impact under CEQA
but that VMTs (vehicle miles traveled) are an impact because VMTs produce          P85-14
emissions and greenhouse gases. But parking and VMTs are intricately
connected. The more parking, the more trips from home to the parking space.
The less parking, the greater the need for alternative strategies to arrive at
one’s destination. None of these contingencies are adequately explored in the
DEIR to demonstrate that:

“Because the project would result in no impact related to VMT and would in
fact reduce regional VMT, the project would not contribute to a cumulative
impact related to VMT.” (3.12.25)

If the parking is adequate to meet the demand of ferry riders, the DEIR
provides no data that shows the drivers would otherwise choose to drive

                                                                          2- 823
                                   Page 928 of 1541



across the bridge to San Francisco, the most frequent route. They could
alternately have chosen BART or a cross-Bay bus as transportation options
that would get them to work on time. There are three BART stations to the
north of University Avenue: Richmond, El Cerrito, and North Berkeley and
several cross-Bay bus routes with frequent service.

If parking is inadequate for ferry riders, they would likely choose public transit
over driving if they wish to avoid driving across the bridge and paying for
parking in San Francisco. The EIR relies on assumptions of reduced VMT
rather than quantitative analysis. This approach ignores the potential for this
new ferry route to divert passengers from BART, AC Transit, and other ferry
operations. Attracting passengers from BART by lowering fares could be
used by Bay Ferry to increase ridership, which does not decrease VMT.

If parking is inadequate for ferry use, how can displacement of parking
intended for recreational uses, including visits to McLaughlin State Park, and
for a future visits to a restaurant at the now closed H’s. Lordship’s be
prevented? Who will enforce the rules and pay for enforcement? How
practical are such enforcement strategies given that they would be in effect
most days all day and therefore require constant surveillance? If the EIR
relies on a parking management program both to protect recreational uses
and assure that the project reduces VMT, that program must be presented as
an enforceable mitigation measure.

Response to Comment P85-2
Parking supply is not considered an impact under CEQA; therefore, a mitigation measure to include a
parking management plan would not be required, and would not be an appropriate CEQA mitigation
measure. Nonetheless, separate to the CEQA process, the City has prepared a Parking and TDM Plan. 61
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a detailed discussion related to how parking is
addressed in the Draft EIR, and how the City plans to address parking, as a matter of policy.

Response to Comment P85-3
The Draft EIR does consider the relationship between parking and VMT. Section 3.12, Transportation
(page 3.12-21) states in part: “The project is overall resulting in a reduction in VMT, and potential VMT
increases due to searching for parking are expected to be nominal given the availability of parking (see
Appendix F). For these reasons there would be no secondary impacts on VMT due to scarcity of parking.”
For additional information about the lack of secondary impacts on VMT from parking, refer to Section
2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking.

Response to Comment P85-4
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for a discussion of parking adequacy.
Refer to Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, for a discussion related to the data and methodology
used to analyze VMT impacts. The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures
presented within the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further response or revisions to the EIR are
required.

Response to Comment P85-5
Refer to Section 2.2.27, Topical Response: VMT, for a discussion related to transit-to-transit mode shifts.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented within the Draft EIR remain
valid as written. No further response or revisions to the EIR are required.

Response to Comment P85-6
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, which clarifies the role of parking as it relates to CEQA
analysis and clarifies the analysis of secondary impacts related to parking. No displacement of parking at
McLaughlin State Park or at future 199 Seawall restaurant has been identified.
The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P85-10
The cumulative conditions analyzed in the EIR reflect projected growth over the approximately 15-year
planning horizon, including population and development associated with recently completed housing
projects, planned developments, the Corridors Zoning Program, the San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan, and
other future land uses identified by the City. The Year 15 travel demand forecasts were developed using
the travel demand model that was updated to support the City of Berkeley Housing Element. That model
incorporates planned development projects, including planning initiatives that were underway and
identified potential housing opportunity sites at the time the model was prepared.
While these planning initiatives are not individually identified in the EIR, they are reflected in the land use
assumptions incorporated into the travel demand model. Accordingly, the Year 15 forecasts are
consistent with the growth assumptions developed as part of the Housing Element update and account
for the anticipated development associated with those planning efforts.
The analysis and significance conclusion presented in the Draft EIR remains valid as written. No further
revisions to the EIR are necessary.

Response to Comment P85-11
The Transportation Impact Assessment (TIA) Memorandum (Appendix F) discusses the University
Avenue Overcrossing Project in the context of existing and future traffic operations at the intersection of
University Avenue and Frontage Road. As described therein, the University Avenue Overcrossing Project
includes a preferred alternative that would convert the intersection of University Avenue and Frontage
Road to a roundabout. The TIA Memorandum notes that the intersection currently experiences queuing
associated with an existing deficiency and states that the proposed roundabout would be expected to



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                           2-827
                                                    Page 932 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                                       Response to Comments

reduce queuing and improve operational and safety conditions at the intersection. However, the TIA
Memorandum also notes that implementation of the Overcrossing Project is uncertain because it
requires coordination with Caltrans and is not expected to be completed prior to the opening year of the
proposed ferry project (Appendix F, pages 8 and 9).
The University Avenue Overcrossing Project is a separate project from the proposed Berkeley Water
Transportation Pier Ferry Project and is not part of the project description analyzed in this Draft EIR.
Accordingly, specific decisions regarding the design, funding, schedule, construction, and implementation
of the Overcrossing Project are outside the scope of this environmental review and would be addressed
through the planning, design, permitting, and environmental review processes applicable to that project.
With respect to bicycle and pedestrian facilities, the proposed project includes improvements intended to
enhance multimodal access to the ferry terminal and Berkeley Waterfront, including a two-way cycle track
along University Avenue, Bay Trail improvements, enhanced bicycle facilities, and improved pedestrian
access (see Appendix F, pages 3 and 4; Draft EIR Chapter 2, Project Description, Section 2.5). These
improvements were developed to function under existing and reasonably foreseeable future
transportation conditions. The City will continue to coordinate with Caltrans and other affected agencies,
as appropriate, during project implementation and as separate transportation projects advance. Any
future connections between facilities located within different jurisdictions would be addressed through
the applicable interagency coordination and permitting processes.
The comment does not identify a deficiency in the environmental analysis presented in the Draft EIR.
Therefore, no changes to the Draft EIR conclusions or mitigation measures are necessary in response to
this comment.

Response to Comment P86-1
These statements provide introductory context and a general statement without supporting arguments,
data, or analysis. As such, they do not present specific information regarding the adequacy of the
analysis, significance conclusions, or mitigation measures in the Draft EIR. Therefore, a substantive
response cannot be provided. No changes are warranted to the Draft EIR analysis, conclusions, or
mitigation measures. No further response is required.

Response to Comment P86-2
Refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access, which
clarifies that the project would not result in any changes to the accessibility of the 199 Seawall Drive
launch point for watersports during low tide conditions.
The analysis and significance conclusion presented under Impact REC-1 in Section 3.11, Recreation,
remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P86-3
Draft EIR Section 3.12, Transportation, evaluates navigation safety and concludes that ferry operations
would comply with U.S. Coast Guard requirements and include standard safety measures to avoid
conflicts with other users (Impact TRA-3, pages 3.12-23 through 3.12-24). Operational compatibility with
water-based recreation is similarly addressed in Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, which explains that
ferry vessels would not interfere with water-based recreation (Impact REC-1, pages 3.11-16 through 3.11-
20).
Refer to Section 2.2.14, Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, regarding safety of ferry vessels.
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in Section 3.11, Recreation,
and related sections of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further revisions are required.

Response to Comment P86-4
Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, explicitly identifies water-based recreational uses, including sailing,
kayaking, swimming, and wind sports occurring in the Berkeley Marina and adjacent waters (see
Section 3.11.2, pages 3.11-1 through 3.11-7) and evaluates impacts to these uses consistent with CEQA
Guidelines Appendix G thresholds of significance (see Section 3.11.4, pages 3.11-14 through 3.11-24).
For discussion of the analysis of water-based recreational impacts, refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical
Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access, and Section 2.2.19, Topical Response:
Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational Activities).
The analysis, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented in Section 3.11, Recreation,
and related sections of the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No further revisions are required.

Response to Comment P86-5
Refer to Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access, which
clarifies that the project would not result in any changes to the accessibility of the 199 Seawall Drive
launch point for watersports during low tide conditions.
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, regarding the analysis of parking and of circulation.

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                      Response to Comments

The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written. No
revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P86-6
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, and Section 2.2.21, Topical Response: Potential
Impacts on Existing Recreational Water Access. The Parking and TDM Plan analyzes parking demand
based on observed usage patterns at the Berkeley Waterfront and WETA ridership projections and
demonstrates that the Waterfront will have sufficient spaces to accommodate all users.
Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, evaluates recreational access and use of existing recreational
facilities, including whether project-related changes could result in physical restrictions on recreational
access or the physical deterioration of recreational facilities. The Draft EIR concludes that recreational
access would be maintained and that impacts related to increased use of existing recreational facilities
would be less than significant (see Impact REC-1). Sections 3.2, Air Quality, 3.10, Noise, and 3.12,
Transportation, of the Draft EIR also evaluate potential secondary physical environmental effects
associated with project-related parking conditions and conclude that no significant parking-related
environmental impacts would occur. The analyses and significance conclusions remain valid as written.
No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P86-7
The Draft EIR does not rely on an assumption that water-based recreation is absent west of the South
Sailing Basin. Rather, Section 3.11, Recreation, identifies the Berkeley Waterfront and adjacent Bay waters
as supporting a range of water-based recreational activities, including windsurfing, sailing, paddling, and
swimming (see Section 3.11.2, Environmental Setting, pages 3.11-1 through 3.11-7). These activities are
described in connection with established use areas such as the South Sailing Basin as well as
surrounding Bay waters. Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis (pages 3.11-16 through 3.11-20), evaluates
whether the project would result in a physical restriction of access to recreational resources or create
incompatibilities with these uses and concludes that recreational opportunities would be maintained
(Impact REC-1). The project does not preclude water-based recreation in areas west of the South Sailing
Basin, and such uses would continue to occur consistent with existing navigation practices and
regulatory requirements. Refer to Section 2.2.19, Topical Response: Ordinance (Prohibited Recreational
Activities), regarding permitted uses throughout the waterfront.
With respect to safety concerns, the Draft EIR evaluates navigation, maneuverability, and operational
safety in Section 3.12, Transportation (Impact TRA-3). As described therein, ferry vessels would operate
within designated approach and berthing areas and would comply with applicable maritime navigation
rules, safety standards, and operational procedures, which are intended to ensure compatibility with other
water users. The analysis concludes that operation of ferry vessels would not increase transportation
safety hazards. Potential effects related to vessel movement, wave conditions, and user interaction are
further addressed through project design, engineering, and operational controls. Refer to Section 2.2.14,
Topical Response: Loss of Ferry Vessel Control, which explains that potential vessel maneuverability risks,
including low-probability loss-of-control scenarios, are addressed through vessel design, redundant
propulsion systems, crew training, regulatory oversight, and additional passive safety features. That
response also revises Section 3.12 of the Draft EIR to explicitly incorporate by reference the 2003 WETA
EIR, which provides a program-level framework for ferry navigation safety, including established
procedures and mitigation measures to minimize navigation conflicts.
Regarding the comment’s concern that removal of the pier could change patterns of recreational use,
refer to Section 2.2.29, Topical Response: Wind.
Accordingly, the Draft EIR adequately evaluates existing water-based recreational uses, navigation safety,
and potential interactions between ferry operations and recreational users, and demonstrates that the
project would not introduce unsafe conditions or preclude continued recreational use of the Bay.

The site is zoned Unclassified (U), and proposed uses are subject to discretionary review and approval by
the City. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.9.2, Environmental Setting (page 3.9-2), and Section 3.9.3,

Permit from the City. The Draft EIR explains that the establishment of a public ferry use is subject to the
City's discretionary review process, through which the City evaluates compatibility with surrounding uses
and applicable land use regulations. Accordingly, whether the project is an appropriate use at this
location is governed through the City's adopted land use designations, zoning regulations, and Use Permit
process.

Berkeley General Plan, Berkeley Marina Master Plan, BCDC Bay Plan, and other applicable land use
regulations under Impact LU-2 in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning. The analysis concludes that the
project would be consistent with applicable land use plans and policies and would not physically divide
an established community. The project would also continue to provide water access and recreational
opportunities through restoration of public access to the Berkeley Pier, construction of a new public pier
and breakwater, shoreline access improvements, the Bay Trail Extension, and other public amenities.

                                                                                                    P87-23

The current proposal for nearly 400,000 cubic yards of new dredging at the Berkeley site–nearly

Change Circumstances: Underwater Radiated Noise of proposed EV Vessels

        "Underwater Radiated Noise (URN) from shipping has grown signiﬁcantly over the past
        few decades due to increases in both the size and number of commercial vessels. In the
        past, URN has primarily been a concern for naval vessels... However, as the detrimental
        impacts on marine life become clearer, there is a need to understand and reduce the
        noise produced by commercial and recrea.onal vessels as well.... As well as large
        commercial vessels, the role of smaller vessels and ferries is being increasingly                        P87-28
        scru.nized, with studies ﬁnding that the noise from smaller recrea.onal vessels and
        ferries can dominate the soundscape in shallow coastal waters."2 (emphasis added)

        "Ship underwater noise aﬀects marine life and can cause both behavioral and
        physiological eﬀects depending on the noise level and frequency distribu2on."3
        (emphasis added)

It is well established that marine animals rely on their ability to use sound underwater to
communicate, ﬁnd food, navigate and more. Both volume and frequency range of underwater
noise maj ers. Diﬀerent marine species use diﬀerent frequency ranges to survive. It is therefore

Electric (EV) and diesel ferry vessels diﬀer in their underwater acousc signa tures. Diesel vessels
generate underwater noise that is primarily low-frequency. This low-frequency noise can
overlap with the same frequency band large marine mammals, like whales, use to communicate
and perform essenal lif e funcons. EV vessels, on the other hand, don't generate low-                                        P87-35
frequency noise but can introduce &/or emphasize higher-frequencies, introducing a kind of
"whine" or other sounds further up the spectrum which can overlap with communicaon of
some marine animals, like porpoises and dolphin. Thus, changing from diesel to EV ferries may
facilitate whale communicaons but in terfere with dolphins and porpoises.

resources immediately adjacent to and "in the vicinity" of the project are missing, even though

impacts of the project on Biological Resources in the vicinity, is deﬁcient and should be
expanded.

Procedure: Bifurca5on and piecemealing

CEQA Guidelines Sec#on 15378(a) deﬁnes a Project as "the whole of an ac.on, which has a
poten.al for resul.ng in either a direct physical change in the environment or a reasonably
foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment..." By deﬁning a project as the "whole
of an acon, " the law ensures that agencies cannot overlook the cumulav e impacts of a large
undertaking by breaking it into smaller, seemingly insigniﬁcant pieces.

The City of Berkeley bifurcated the Waterfront Speciﬁc Plan (WSP)11 and Pier/Ferry Planning
projects early-on in the planning processes. This segmentaon is pr oblemac as the Pier/F erry            P87-61
project lies geographically within the overall waterfront, the focus of the WSP. While the WSP
and Pier/Ferry are two separate projects run by the same Lead Agency, the City of Berkeley,
separang the analy sis of the environmental impacts of the two projects into two disnct
phases will make the immediate impacts of each Project look smaller. The reduced geographic
footprint of the Pier/Ferry scope represents piecemealing.

While the dEIR defends the bifurcaon – stang tha t the WSP and Pier/Ferry are separate
projects (pg. 3-11) and that the dEIR will consider Cumulav e Impacts of the pending WSP –
when it comes to real-world impacts, the bifurcaon of the W SP and Pier/Ferry violate sCEQA's
requirement that the "whole of the acon" be r eviewed.

SUMMARY

To adhere to CEQA Secon 15378( a), the evaluaon of the Pier/Ferry Project EIR should be
delayed unl the W aterfront Speciﬁc Plan (WSP) eﬀort is complete. Only then is it appropriate            P87-62
for the EIR to be undertaken, covering the enr e waterfront area, to ensure that cumulav e
impacts for all waterfront development are accurately evaluated and disclosed to the public.

lifecycles. It penetrates the upper layers of soil and water to disrupt microbial acvity . It disrupts
plants' seasonal rhythms. It interferes with marine animal movements, disrupng phot otaxis in

S. Sailing Basin). Under CEQA this intermi ent light polluon c onstut es a signiﬁcant impact on

Response to Comment P87-9
As described in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO‑1 (pages 52 to 54), the analysis evaluates
potential impacts to gray whales and other marine mammals based on current environmental conditions,
including increased whale presence in the Bay in recent years. The Draft EIR does not rely on 2003
assumptions regarding whale rarity or population trends. Instead, the analysis considers the existing
Central Bay transit corridor, which includes substantial commercial, recreational, and ferry vessel
operational levels, and evaluates the project’s incremental contribution to vessel‑strike risk. See Section
2.2.1, Topical Response: 2003 WETA EIR Applicability, for a discussion of Draft EIR references to the 2003
WETA EIR. No changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P87-10
As described in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 under Impact BIO‑1 (pages 52 to 54), the analysis evaluates
potential impacts to gray whales based on current environmental conditions, including increased whale
observations in the Bay in recent years. The Draft EIR acknowledges that vessel strikes are a known
source of mortality for gray whales and evaluates the project’s incremental contribution to this risk in the
context of the existing Central Bay baseline, which includes substantial commercial, recreational, and
ferry vessel operational levels. In addition, see Response to Comment O7-13 for a discussion regarding
potential whale strike. No changes to the Draft EIR are necessary in response to this comment.

Response to Comment P87-11
As described in Draft EIR Section 3.3.4 (Impact BIO‑1, pages 52 to 54), the analysis acknowledges that
vessel strikes are a known source of mortality for gray whales and evaluates the project’s incremental
contribution to this risk in the context of the existing Central Bay baseline, which includes substantial
commercial, recreational, and ferry vessel operational levels. The Draft EIR evaluates current whale
presence in the Bay and does not rely on assumptions from the 2003 WETA EIR regarding whale rarity or
population trends. In addition, see Section 2.2.28, Topical Response: Whale Strike, and Response to
Comment O7-13 for a discussion regarding potential whale strike. No changes to the Draft EIR are
necessary in response to this comment.

Regarding the geographic scope for biological resources, CEQA does not require analysis of biological

within which project-related impacts could reasonably occur. The Draft EIR evaluates biological resources
within the project site and surrounding areas where direct or indirect effects could occur and includes
consideration of adjacent habitats and species that could potentially use the project vicinity. As
discussed in Responses to Comments P87-55, P87-57, and P87-58, the City concludes that the
geographic scope of the biological resources analysis is appropriate and sufficient to disclose the
project's potential environmental effects.

Letter P88
Commenter:         Gordon Stout
Date:              April 28, 2026

Response to Comment P88-1
Refer to Section 2.2.24, Topical Response: Seawall Drive/View Access, and Section 2.2.20, Topical
Response: Parking. As discussed therein, the Draft EIR evaluates the proposed project's shoreline access
improvements, view opportunities, and parking configurations. The commenter's preference regarding
retention of existing view-oriented parking spaces constitutes a project design recommendation that has
been included in the project record considered by City decision makers. The comment does not identify a
deficiency in the Draft EIR analysis, significance conclusions, or mitigation measures. No revisions to the
Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment P88-2
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, and Section 2.2.6, Topical Response: CEQA
Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users. The Draft EIR's parking analysis is based on parking utilization data
and supporting technical studies prepared for the project. As discussed therein, the Draft EIR uses the
physical conditions existing at the time the Notice of Preparation was published as the CEQA baseline;
therefore, historical parking conditions depicted in the commenter’s aerial imagery do not represent the
baseline against which project impacts are analyzed and do not alter the conclusions of the Draft EIR.
The Draft EIR evaluates potential secondary physical environmental effects associated with project-
related parking conditions and concludes that no significant parking-related environmental impacts
would occur. The comment does not provide evidence demonstrating that the analyses or significance
conclusions presented in the Draft EIR are incorrect. The analyses and significance conclusions remain
valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                     Response to Comments


Verbal Comment TR1.1
Commenter:         Paul Kamen
Date:              March 16, 2026

Response to Comment TR1.1-1
These statements provide context for the commenter’s perspective. This comment does not pertain to
the adequacy, significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR. No further response is required.

Response to Comment TR1.1-2
The project design, including the proposed breakwater and the amount of fill and dredging required for
the project, has been developed by qualified coastal engineering professionals based on site-specific
studies, technical analyses, and engineering modeling prepared for the project. The design and
supporting analyses are documented in the Coastal Study prepared by COWI, which evaluated wave
conditions, sediment transport, operational requirements, and breakwater design criteria for the proposed
ferry terminal. The comment does not provide evidence, engineering analyses, or other factual
information demonstrating that the quantities of fill, dredging, or breakwater construction requirements
described in the Draft EIR are underestimated.
With respect to the comment’s concern regarding the cost of the breakwater, refer to Section 2.2.22,
Topical Response: Project Cost/Financial Feasibility, for a discussion related to economic considerations.
No further response is required.

Response to Comment TR1.1-3
Refer to Section 2.2.29, Topical Response: Wind, which discusses the engineering studies, wind and wave
modeling, and design assumptions used to evaluate the proposed ferry facilities. As discussed therein,
the ferry terminal, breakwater, gangway, and associated marine infrastructure were designed based on
site-specific engineering analyses and are subject to detailed design review by qualified engineers and
review by applicable permitting and regulatory agencies.
The comment expresses concern with the adequacy of the wind data and engineering assumptions used
during project planning; however, the comment does not provide technical analyses demonstrating that
the wind and wave studies relied upon for project design are inaccurate or that the proposed facilities
would fail to perform under the design conditions evaluated for the project.
To the extent the comment concerns the engineering design, feasibility, or operational performance of the
ferry facilities, those issues are engineering and design considerations rather than environmental impacts
addressed under CEQA. The Draft EIR evaluates the physical environmental effects of constructing and
operating the proposed project and relies on the project design and supporting technical studies prepared
for the project.
The analyses, significance conclusions, and mitigation measures presented throughout the Draft EIR
remain valid as written. No revisions are required.

Response to Comment TR1.1-4
Refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for a discussion of the data used to
design the project. Based on the data, modeling, and design gathered and prepared by the City’s licensed
professional coastal engineers, updates to the design are not needed, and updated analysis on the
amount of fill and dredging is not required. Pages 5-9 through 5-10 of the Draft EIR state the following:
“The exact length of the breakwater under this Alternative would depend on future engineering to identify
the shortened length that would still maintain the necessary safe harbor conditions for ferry vessels to


Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                     2- 963
                                            Page 1068 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                       Response to Comments

dock next to the proposed pier.” Any reductions in the breakwater would maintain necessary safe harbor
conditions. The comment does not identify a specific deficiency in the analysis presented. No revisions to
the Draft EIR are required.

Response to Comment TR1.1-5
Refer to Section 2.2.25, Topical Response: Siltation/Wave Climate, for a discussion of the data used to
design the project. Based on the data, modeling, and design gathered and prepared by the City’s licensed
professional coastal engineers, updates to the design are not needed, and updated analysis on the
amount of fill and dredging is not required. The comment does not identify a specific deficiency in the
analysis presented. No revisions to the Draft EIR are required.
Refer to Section 2.2.22, Topical Response: Project Cost/Financial Feasibility, for a discussion related to
economic considerations.

Response to Comment TR1.1-6
Refer to Section 2.2.12, Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative, for a discussion related to
why the City rejected the In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative from further evaluation.
To the extent the comment's reference to a more "economical" alternative reflects concerns regarding
project costs or funding, refer to Section 2.2.22, Topical Response: Project Cost/Financial Feasibility.
The comment's preference for an in-marina ferry terminal location is noted and has been included in the
project record considered by decision-makers. The comment expresses an opinion regarding project
location and does not identify a deficiency in the Draft EIR's environmental analysis. The analysis and
conclusions presented in Chapter 5, Alternatives, remain valid as written. No revisions to the Draft EIR are
required in response to this comment.

Verbal Comment TR1.2
Commenter:         Gordon Stout
Date:              March 16, 2026

Response to Comment TR1.2-1
These statements provide background information. This comment does not pertain to the adequacy,
significance conclusions, or mitigation in the Draft EIR. No further response is required.

Response to Comment TR1.2-2
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, for discussion regarding parking demand and
adequacy. The Draft EIR evaluates whether project-related parking conditions would result in secondary
physical environmental impacts and concludes that recreational access would be maintained. The
Parking and TDM Plan analyzes parking demand based on observed usage patterns at the Berkeley
Waterfront and WETA ridership projections and demonstrates that the Waterfront will have sufficient
spaces to accommodate all users. The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR
remain valid as written.

Response to Comment TR1.2-3
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, which discusses parking supply and adequacy and
Response to Comment TR1.2-2. The Draft EIR contains sufficient information to evaluate potential
secondary environmental effects associated with parking and access consistent with CEQA
requirements. The analyses and significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as
written. No revisions are required.

Response to Comment TR1.2-4
Refer to Section 2.2.20, Topical Response: Parking, and Response to Comment TR1.2-2. The analyses and
significance conclusions presented in the Draft EIR remain valid as written.
The commenter’s opposition to the project is noted and has been included in the project record
considered by City decision makers. However, the comment does not provide evidence demonstrating
that the proposed parking management strategies would result in a secondary physical environmental
impact or otherwise invalidate the analyses presented in the Draft EIR. Accordingly, no further response
or revision to the Draft EIR is required.

conceptual project documents, those references do not alter the project description evaluated in the Draft
EIR or demonstrate a deficiency in the environmental analysis. The Draft EIR evaluates the proposed

impacts associated with parking and access under CEQA.

Response to Comment TR1.13-7
The CEQA significance thresholds for energy consumption do not have requirement for comparing
efficiencies from one form of transit to another. The project as proposed is not anticipating replacing
existing forms of transit but rather including an additional option to remove passenger vehicles from the
roadways. The current bus and BART operations would continue with or without the project, and the
implementation of the project would not require or result in a change in trips of these alternate modes of
transit. Therefore, the energy consumption from buses and BART would continue consistent with what
they are consuming today. Therefore, the analysis of the project in isolation of an energy efficiency
comparison with other forms of transit is accurate. Further, Draft EIR Alternatives (Section 5.9) discussed
alternative projects such as increasing Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) capacity and improving access to
BART, both of which were alternatives that were considered but rejected as they did not meet the project
objective of provision of all-electric ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco. The analysis in the
Draft EIR accurately analyzes energy consumption with respect to CEQA and Bay Area Air District
methodologies and thresholds (see methodology approach discussion on Draft EIR page3.6-30 and
specific thresholds of significance on Draft EIR page 3.6-33). Therefore, additional analysis is not

vehicle travel (refer to Draft EIR Section 2.3).

Response to Comment TR1.15-2
The Draft EIR evaluates the environmental impacts of the proposed project on recreation, transportation,
biological resources, noise, and other CEQA Guidelines Appendix G resource areas throughout Chapter 3,
Environmental Impact Analysis. As discussed in Draft EIR Section 3.11, Recreation, the project would result
in a net increase in recreational facilities and opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront, including a
restored public-access pier, public-access breakwater, Bay Trail Extension, cycle track, public plaza, and
related amenities (see Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis, Impact REC-1).
Additionally, Draft EIR Chapter 5, Alternatives, evaluates alternatives and compares their ability to meet
the project's objectives while reducing environmental impacts. As discussed in Section 5.5, No Project
Alternative, the No Project Alternative would not provide ferry service, public access improvements, or
recreational enhancements because the existing pier would remain closed and continue to deteriorate.
The Draft EIR further concludes that the No Project Alternative would generally result in greater impacts
related to air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, land use and planning, and transportation because it
would not provide the transportation and environmental benefits associated with the proposed ferry
service. Section 5.10, Environmentally Superior Alternative, also concludes that Alternatives 2 through 4
would provide public access and recreational benefits, but to a lesser extent than the proposed project.
Accordingly, the Draft EIR specifically evaluates whether the project's objectives can be achieved through
alternatives with reduced facilities or through the No Project Alternative and concludes that those
alternatives either would not meet the project's basic objectives or would do so to a lesser extent than the
proposed project.
To the extent the comment is suggesting a restored pier without ferry service, please refer to Response to
Comment O10-215. As discussed therein, the City considered a "No Ferry Service with New Pier
Alternative" but did not carry it forward for detailed analysis because it would not meet one of the
project's two basic objectives: providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero-emission ferry service
between Berkeley and San Francisco.
The comment does not identify a deficiency in the Draft EIR's environmental analysis or alternatives
analysis, but instead questions whether ferry service is necessary to achieve the project's objectives. The
Draft EIR evaluates that question through its analysis of the No Project Alternative, the reduced-feature
action alternatives, and alternatives considered but rejected, and concludes that the proposed project
best achieves the project's objectives while providing greater public access and recreational benefits and
transportation-related environmental benefits than the alternatives considered. Therefore, the analysis

Response to Comment TR1.15-4

refer to Section 2.2.6, Topical Response: CEQA Baseline/Baseline Recreation Users regarding construction
and operation impacts on the entire marina community, including liveaboard residents. The City of
Berkeley maintains standards relating to pedestrian access during construction projects, which would
require safe and accessible paths of travel for pedestrians throughout the construction period. Prior to
the beginning of construction, the contractor will be required to implement the traffic control plan.
Adopted standards require that recreational and vehicular access be maintained during construction to
the maximum extent feasible. Accordingly, construction traffic control plans would maintain, to the
maximum extent feasible: (1) vehicular and recreational access to the South Cove area; (2) vehicular
access along University Avenue to Seawall Drive; and (3) access to the Bay Trail and adjacent
recreational areas. Pedestrian access along Seawall Drive and the shoreline would be maintained except
when actual construction of the Bay Trail was occurring, and pedestrian detours would be provided during
those periods.
With regard to operations, the Draft EIR for the proposed project evaluates project-specific and proximate
environmental effects associated with ferry operations at the Berkeley Waterfront using representative
operational assumptions (see Chapter 2, Section 2.7). These analyses focus on nearshore and localized
conditions, including terminal approach and docking, vessel presence within the project viewshed, and
project-related contributions to vessel traffic in the immediate vicinity. As described in Section 3.3,
Biological Resources, and 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, the Draft EIR concludes that operational
impacts associated with ferries, including vessel traffic, underwater noise, wake, and water quality effects
would be less than significant or less than significant with mitigation (see Sections 3.3.4 and 3.3.5).

remain valid as written. No revisions are required. The City will continue public outreach and engagement
efforts as the project progresses through implementation.

Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                       2- 990
                                            Page 1095 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project                                      Response to Comments

Section 2.2.9, Topical Response: Cumulative Impacts, cumulative projects were identified based on
publicly available information and evaluated according to the geographic scope and impact pathways
applicable to each environmental resource topic. The Draft EIR does not include every project occurring
within the City of Berkeley; rather, it includes projects that are reasonably foreseeable and that could
combine with the proposed project to contribute to a particular cumulative environmental effect.
The San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan area is located inland and outside of the Berkeley Waterfront and
project vicinity. The comment has not identified a specific project within the San Pablo Avenue Specific
Plan area that would combine with the proposed project to result in a cumulative environmental impact.
Moreover, because cumulative impacts are evaluated separately for each resource area based on the
relevant geographic scope of potential impacts, inland development occurring along the San Pablo
Avenue corridor would generally not combine with the proposed project's waterfront-related impacts
involving resources such as recreation, biological resources, hydrology and water quality, waterfront
access, or shoreline conditions. Accordingly, the City determined that the San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan
did not constitute a cumulative project requiring inclusion in Draft EIR Table 3-1. For additional discussion
regarding the cumulative impact assessment methodology, including the criteria used to identify and
evaluate cumulative projects, refer to Section 2.2.9, Topical Response: Cumulative Impacts.
With respect to the comment’s preference for recreational improvements in lieu of ferry service, the Draft
EIR recognizes the importance of recreational resources and evaluates both existing conditions and
project-related changes in detail. As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, the proposed project
includes substantial recreational enhancements, including a new publicly accessible pier, public plaza,
Bay Trail improvements, bicycle and pedestrian facilities, and related amenities designed to improve
public access to the waterfront (see Draft EIR Section 2.5.2). The environmental effects of these
improvements are fully analyzed in the Draft EIR.
As discussed in Section 3.11, Recreation, the City currently maintains a high ratio of parkland and open
space relative to population (34.5 acres per 1,000 residents, see Draft EIR page 3.11-1), and even with
projected population growth, the City’s park acreage per resident would remain well above established
City targets. As analyzed under Impact REC-1, assuming an estimated population of 141,000 residents by
2040, the citywide parkland to persons ratio would be 31.6 acres per 1,000 residents, approximately
eighteen times the established City target of at least 2 acres of parkland per 1,000 residents (see Draft
EIR page 3.11-19).
The proposed project does not present a binary choice between recreation and transit improvements.
Rather, it is designed to achieve multiple, complementary objectives, including expanding recreational
opportunities at the waterfront while also providing new zero-emission ferry service and improving
multimodal access (see Draft EIR Section 2.3, Project Objectives). As such, the project would both
enhance recreational resources and contribute to regional transportation goals, consistent with the City’s
broader planning objectives.
Accordingly, the Draft EIR adequately evaluates cumulative impacts and recreational effects consistent
with CEQA, and no revisions to the analysis are required in response to this comment.

presented in Sections 3.11, Recreation, and 3.12, Transportation, remain valid as written. No revisions to
the Draft EIR are required.

characteristics of the Berkeley Waterfront. Sections 3.3 (Biological Resources), 3.8 (Hydrology and Water

wake, and water-based recreation using project-specific data and technical analysis. Refer to Section

disturbance.

characteristics, and are not determinative of impacts at the project site. The Draft EIR relies on
site-specific analysis rather than comparison to unrelated facilities.

provide substantial evidence demonstrating that similar impacts would occur under the project
conditions analyzed. Accordingly, the analyses and significance conclusions presented in Sections 3.3,
3.8, and 3.11 of the Draft EIR remain valid as written, and no further revisions to the Draft EIR are required.

Transportation Pier Ferry Project. These revisions are minor modifications and clarifications to the

3.1         Changes in Response to Comments
Executive Summary

Areas of Known Controversy
Draft EIR Page ES-3:
    During the EIR scoping process, members of the public identified concerns related to the potential for
    the proposed project to affect parking availability for recreationalists, continued recreational access
    to the Berkeley Waterfront, potential impacts on biological resources including whales and other
    marine species, and the project’s consistency with broader waterfront planning efforts. Chapter 3,
    Environmental Impact Analysis (see Secondary Impacts subsection) identifies the approach for
    addressing parking impacts under CEQA for the proposed project and describes the relationship
    between the proposed project and other waterfront planning efforts (see Relationship with Draft
    Waterfront Specific Plan subsection). In addition, each environmental resource section within Chapter
    3 includes an EIR Scoping Comments Consideration subsection that identifies resource-specific
    concerns raised during scoping and explains how those issues are addressed in the environmental
    analysis. Public responses to the Notice of Preparation of a Draft EIR as well as public input received
    at the EIR scoping meeting held by the City are summarized in Chapter 1, Introduction.

                                                                    Burrowing Owl
                                                                    Prior to project construction, a qualified biologist will conduct a habitat assessment to determine if potential habitat for burrowing owl is present in or near the project site. If
                                                                    potential habitat is present in or within 500 feet of the project site, a qualified biologist will conduct a pre-construction survey of the project site (plus a 500-foot buffer as access
                                                                    allows) for the presence of burrowing owl. The survey will be conducted no more than 14 days prior to ground disturbing activities and will conform to CDFW guidelines for
                                                                    burrowing owl Take Avoidance Surveys as described in Appendix D of the 2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation.100 A report of pre-construction survey efforts and
                                                                    results will be submitted to the City within 30 days of completion of the survey. The report will include the dates, times, weather conditions, and personnel involved in the survey.
                                                                    Depending on survey results, the report will also include observations of burrowing owl or potential burrows, and the location and habitat description of the observations. If
                                                                    burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign (i.e., tracks or pellets) are not observed in the project site, no additional measures related to impact avoidance and minimization of the
                                                                    absent species are recommended. If burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign are observed within the project site, CDFW will be notified and the following measures will be
                                                                    implemented:
                                                                    • A qualified biological monitor will be present during landside construction on the project site to document burrowing owl observations, burrow statuses, and require that
                                                                       construction activities do not negatively affect burrowing owl. The duration and frequency of monitoring will be determined at the discretion of the qualified biologist and a
                                                                       monitoring report detailing monitoring results will be submitted to the City within 30 days of the completion of project activities or breeding season (February 1 to August 31), if
                                                                       applicable.
                                                                    • The biological monitor will visually inspect any pipes, debris piles, culverts, or similar structures for burrowing owl before the material is moved, buried, or capped. Open holes
                                                                       and trenches within the project site will be inspected at the beginning and end of each landside construction workday and immediately prior to backfilling. At the end of each
                                                                       such workday, trenches and holes will be ramped so that any animals that may have become trapped in the trench or hole can climb out. The ramp may be constructed of dirt
                                                                       fill or wood planking or other suitable material at an angle no greater than 30-45 degrees. If a burrowing owl is trapped in a trench or hole, work will stop and the qualified
                                                                       biologist will be notified immediately. The burrowing owl will be allowed to escape unimpeded.
                                                                    • If active burrows are observed on the project site, a non-disturbance buffer will be established restricting all ground-disturbing activities from occurring within the buffer and a
                                                                       qualified biological monitor will be present at the initiation of project activities. The buffer will be established by a qualified biologist and range from 330 ft. to 1,500 ft.
                                                                       depending on project activity, line of sight, and local topography during the breeding season. During the non-breeding season (September 1 to January 31), the buffer will range
                                                                       from 165 ft. to 330 ft. The buffer will be demarcated using brightly colored flagging and may only be reduced at the discretion of a qualified biologist based on the factors listed
                                                                       above and potential use of sound and visual barriers (i.e., hay bales). Removal of the buffer will only occur if a qualified biologist determines burrowing owl are not present in
                                                                       the vicinity and any potential burrows are inactive.

                                                   BIO-1(d): Conduct Pile Driving Impact Avoidance to Fish and Marine Mammals Prior to and During Construction. In-water work, including pile driving and dredging, shall be
                                                   limited to the window of June 1 through November 30. The soft-start, ramp-up, exclusion-zone and sound attenuation procedures described below apply to pile-driving and pile-
                                                   extraction activities. A “soft-start” technique will be used to allow fish and marine mammals to vacate the area before the pile driver reaches full power. For vibratory hammers,
                                                   the contractor will initiate the driving for 15 seconds at reduced energy, followed by a 1-minute waiting period when there has been downtime of 30 minutes or more. This
                                                   procedure shall be repeated two additional times before continuous driving is started. This procedure would also apply to vibratory pile extraction. For impact driving, an initial set
                                                   of three strikes would be made by the hammer at 40 percent energy, followed by a 1-minute waiting period, then two subsequent three-strike sets before initiating continuous
                                                   driving. Pile-driving activity shall not begin at any location if any marine mammal is observed within the applicable safe-zone distance for its hearing group, as defined for the
                                                   specific pile-driving method (e.g., pile diameter, vibratory or impact installation, and number of piles installed per day). Safe-zone distances shall follow the most current
                                                   NMFS-approved guidance and the Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan prepared pursuant to Mitigation Measure BIO-1(E). In all cases, a minimum exclusion distance of no less than
                                                   10 meters shall be maintained around the pile-driving location. If a marine mammal moves within the safe zone after pile driving has begun, the contractor shall implement the
                                                   appropriate delay or shutdown as described in Mitigation Measure BIO-1(E). A sound curtain, or bubble curtain, shall be employed during impact pile driving to break up sound
                                                   waves, as feasible. The sound curtain would consist of a perforated hose laid in a circle to release air bubbles around the pile and diesel impact hammer. Jetting methods using
                                                   pressurized water and/or wood cushion block methods shall also be employed as feasible to minimize impacts.
                                                   If the intensity of the pile-driving activity needs to be increased or a marine mammal is within the safe zone buffer for the activity, pile-driving shall be “ramped-up”, which is a slow
                                                   increase in the intensity of pile-driving. At the start of pile-driving for each pile at all locations, the pile shall be struck once with the hammer and the second pile strike delayed
                                                   long enough to permit adequate time for any marine mammals within the safe zone to leave the area prior to the start of sustained pile-driving activities.
                                                   This measure, including the technique and the size of the safe zone, may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory agencies.
                                                   BIO-1(e): Prepare Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan Prior to Construction and Implement Recommendations During Construction
                                                   Prior to construction, the City shall prepare a Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan (MMMP) to avoid and minimize potential adverse impacts on marine mammals during pile driving
                                                   and tug operations. The MMMP shall implement general guidelines set forth in the MMPA and incorporate the hydroacoustic modeling results developed for the project to define
                                                   site-specific protection zones and avoid exposure of marine mammals to underwater sound levels exceeding the most up to date Level A (injury) thresholds identified by NOAA
                                                   Fisheries. The MMMP shall include the following:
                                                   • Protection and Monitoring Zones: Using the hydroacoustic modeling results, the MMMP shall define shutdown and disturbance zones for each marine mammal hearing group.
                                                      These zones will be tailored to the pile type, size, and driving method and will correspond to the Level A and Level B effect distances developed for the project. The plan will
                                                      describe how these protection zones will be verified and monitored in the field, integrating them with the soft-start and observation procedures described in Mitigation Measure
                                                      BIO-1(d).

    The new pier and breakwater would have safety railings, public amenities (fish cleaning station,
    seating, shade canopy, and security gates). In addition, at the entrance to the pier, the City is
    proposing a gate that would remain open to the public, except in cases where public safety requires
    closure, such as during a tsunami evacuation, high wind advisory, or other emergency situations. The
    proposed pier would be a maximum of 1,080 feet in length and would have a width of 22 feet. The
    reinforced concrete deck comprising the pier would be an approximately 2-foot-thick slab. Piles for
    the pier are discussed in Section 2.6.1 2.7.2 below.
    The proposed new breakwater would create a safe harbor from the predominant southwesterly wind
    and waves for ferry vessel charging and boarding on the north side of the new pier. The breakwater
    would also offer recreational pedestrian access. The proposed breakwater would be approximately
    400 feet in length and would have a width of 15 feet. The reinforced concrete deck comprising the
    breakwater would be an approximately 2-foot-thick slab. Piles for the breakwater are discussed in
    Section 2.6.1 2.7.2 below.

Draft EIR Page 2-8:
    The project would include a Universal Charging Float or UCF featuring a 1.351 MWh Echandia battery
    weighing approximately 47,554 pounds. The UCF has not yet been designed and is not included in
    this rendering. UCF dimensions may differ from what is shown in this rendering; however, the
    environmental analysis in this EIR assumes a conservative maximum design envelope that
    encompasses potential variations in size, equipment, and operation.

Draft EIR Page 2-10:
    In accordance with standards as set by the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE), the proposed
    pier would comply with ASCE Risk Category IV requirements and base design loads. The project
    design takes into account projected sea level rise incorporates sea level rise adaptation
    considerations through the design of the pier, breakwater, ferry infrastructure, and related facilities.7
    Design elevations and structural elements were developed to account for projected increases in
    surface water levels and coastal flood conditions over the life of the project, while floating ferry
    facilities and gangway connections have been designed to accommodate a range of future tidal and
    water surface elevations. Refer to Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, for an evaluation of the
    project with respect to future flooding and sea level rise. The City prepared a Coastal Study, including
    a project-specific sea level rise risk assessment, consistent with applicable BCDC permit
    requirements.8

      Dredged materials and demolition debris would all be transported via barge that have a capacity of
      between 3,000 and 6,000 cubic yards. The location for disposal of dredged materials would depend
      on the sampling results of the dredged materials, as well as permitting requirements. However, based
      on the recently completed Berkeley Marina Dredging Project of 2024 to 2025, it is expected that
      disposal would occur at Montezuma Wetland Restoration Project (Beneficial Reuse), Alcatraz
      Disposal Site, or another disposal site in the San Francisco Bay. The dredging described above
      represents one-time, project-specific dredging required to establish navigable depths for ferry
      operations. This dredging would be conducted on behalf of the City of Berkeley and/or WETA, subject
      to all applicable permits and approvals from the United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE),
      Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB), San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development
      Commission (BCDC), and the Dredged Material Management Office (DMMO). Although dredging
      would occur within the alignment of an existing USACE-designated federal navigation channel, this
      portion of the channel has not been maintained by USACE in recent decades and is not currently

    included in an active federal maintenance dredging program. Accordingly, dredging at this location
    would constitute new work dredging, and the proposed project does not assume that USACE would
    conduct or be responsible for this initial dredging.
    Sediment transport modeling prepared for the project estimates that maintenance dredging, if
    required, would occur infrequently. Based on modeled sedimentation rates, maintenance dredging
    within the approach channel may not be needed for approximately 10 to 15 years, while maintenance
    dredging within berth pockets may not be needed for approximately 22 to 33 years, depending on
    operational depth requirements.23 Because the timing, extent, volume, methods, and regulatory
    requirements associated with any future maintenance dredging are presently unknown, no
    maintenance dredging program is proposed as part of the project at this time. Any future
    maintenance dredging activities would be evaluated and permitted, as required, based on the
    circumstances existing at that time.

Sub-Section 2.7.1, Operational Scenario and Ridership23
Draft EIR Page 2-30:
    A conceptual plan for ferry service has been provided in the 2022 San Francisco Bay Area Water
    Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, Version 1.0.24 This
    is a living document and updates to the Business Plan and contemplated ferry service will be
    captured described in future updates. The following ferry operation is proposed in the current
    Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, Version 1.0:
    • WETA would operate two 250-passenger electric zero-emission vessels on the weekday route
      between Berkeley and San Francisco.
    • Weekend service would operate a single 250-passenger vessel to Larkspur and a single 250-
      passenger vessel to San Francisco.
    • At least three round-trip services would be completed during peak hours for the Berkeley/San
      Francisco weekday service, pursuant to WETA Board-adopted standards.
    • The Berkeley-San Francisco service would travel 6.7 miles between the Berkeley Ferry Terminal and
      the San Francisco Ferry Terminal. The total one-way travel time would be 25 minutes, door-to-door.
      Weekday peak-direction headways25 would be approximately 35 minutes. Weekend headways
      would be 70 to 110 minutes, depending on the time of day.
    • The Berkeley-Larkspur service would travel 11.8 miles between the terminal at the Berkeley Marina
      and the Larkspur Ferry Terminal. The one-way travel time would be 35 minutes, door-to-door.
      Weekend headways would be 90 to 150 minutes, depending on the time of day.
    • Special event service may operate between Berkeley and San Francisco or Mission Bay (e.g., for
      events at the Chase Center or Oracle Park or future events at the Berkeley Marina), as well as
      between Larkspur and Berkeley.

Sub-Section 3.1.3, Regulatory Framework
Draft EIR Page 3.1-16:
    San Francisco Bay Plan
    The San Francisco Bay Plan8 developed by the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development
    Commission (BCDC) aims to maintain and enhance the Bay as a body of water that affords scenic
    enjoyment. Key aesthetics objectives in the form of findings and policies applicable to the proposed
    project include the following:
    …
   • Transportation Policies
     0 Policy 4. Transportation projects on the Bay shoreline and bridges over the Bay or certain

       waterways should include pedestrian and bicycle paths that will either be a part of the Bay Trail or
       connect the Bay Trail with other regional and community trails. Transportation projects should be
       designed to maintain and enhance visual and physical access to the Bay and along the Bay
       shoreline.

    Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces9
    The BCDC Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces (BCDC 2005) provides guidelines
    for shoreline design. Guidelines related to visual resources are listed below.
    • Taking advantage of existing site characteristics and opportunities, such as fishing, viewing,
      picnicking, swimming or boating.
    • Locating buildings, structures, parking lots and landscaping of new shoreline projects such that
      they enhance and dramatize views of the Bay and the shoreline from public thoroughfares and
      other public spaces.
    • Organizing shoreline development to allow Bay views and access between buildings. • In hilly areas,
      designing and locating shoreline buildings to allow for upland views down to the Bay and to Bay
      access areas.
    • In hilly areas, employing split-level roads to increase viewing and landscaping potential.
    • Designing towers, bridges or other structures as landmarks that suggest the location of the
      waterfront, even when the Bay itself is not visible.
    • Providing visual interest and architectural variety in massing and height to new buildings along the
      shoreline.



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                         3-15
                                             Page 1118 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

       • Using building footprints to create a diversity of public spaces along the Bay.
       • Articulating shoreline building facades with human-scale elements.
       • Using forms, materials, colors and textures that are compatible with the Bay and adjacent
         development.
       • Locating service areas, such as garbage facilities and loading docks, away from the shoreline or
         screen them with suitable fencing or landscaping.
       • Utilizing the shoreline for Bay-related land uses as much as possible; uses that do not complement
         the Bay should be set back from and not impact the shoreline.
       • Orienting the development to Bay views and providing physical connections to the Bay at every
         opportunity.
       • Orienting public access areas and improvements to take advantage of views of opposite shores,
         landmarks (such as islands and bridges) and adjacent maritime activities such as boat launching,
         gas docks, ferry landings or other marine-related uses.
       • Utilizing the shoreline for Bay-related uses. Uses that do not orient to the Bay should be set well
         back from the Bay and be sited, designed and managed so as to not impact the shoreline.
       • Provide buffers between roadways and public access areas, such as planting, low berms or
         roadside parking, and maintain views to the Bay.
       • Provide parking for shoreline access areas where appropriate, but keep parking areas reasonably
         sized, away from the Bay and adequately screened.
       • Provide small bayside parking areas or pull-offs for limited in-car Bay viewing, where compatible
         with existing roads and adjacent uses.
       • Provide elevated places for viewing the Bay.
       • Use site furnishings, such as benches, trash containers and lighting, to provide visual cues that the
         shoreline space is available for public use.
       • Use lighting to extend the hours of shoreline use.
       • Locate night lighting away from sensitive habitat areas.
       • Provide enough lighting to create a sense of safety, but designing to control intensity, glare, and
         spillover.
