Sub-Section 3.1.4, Impacts Analysis
Draft EIR Page 3.1-30:
       As shown in Figure 3.1-4 and Figure 3.1-5, the proposed ferry infrastructure would introduce a series
       of linear horizontal and vertical features and planes which would be visually consistent with the
       proposed pier infrastructure, but would be contrasted against the surrounding water in the Bay. These
       features would be most visually prominent on the north side of the proposed pier; when viewed from
       the south (Figure 3.1-5), views of the proposed ferry infrastructure would be interrupted and partially
       obscured by the sequence of evenly-spaced pier pilings. When viewed from a distance (Figure 3.1-6
       and Figure 3.1-8), the proposed ferry infrastructure would not present as a prominent visual feature,
       and would not exceed the height of the proposed pier infrastructure in a manner that would result in
       the degradation of surrounding views. Individual ferry vessel(s) would also be similar in size, and




3-16
                                          Page 1119 of 1541

                                                                                                          Errata



    perform similar functions, to those already present in the vicinity; and thus, would integrate with
    existing boat traffic.
    As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, ferry operations are evaluated using a representative
    weekday and weekend service scenario that reflects the maximum reasonably foreseeable level of
    service for purposes of environmental review (refer to Section 2.7, pages 2-30 through 2-33). While
    specific schedules, frequencies, and operational details may vary over time, the analysis evaluates
    vessel presence and activity within the viewshed based on these planning-level assumptions.
    While the visual character of the proposed ferry infrastructure would introduce new materials and
    massing, and additional vessels would be intermittently present in the viewshed, these components
    would be consistent with visual character of the surrounding infrastructure and development.
    Impacts would be less than significant.

Draft EIR Page 3.1-32:
    As shown in Figure 3.1-7, the existing shoreline is characterized by natural elements; specifically, the
    mature tree canopy provides a soft, variable tree line which largely dominates the view as it contrasts
    against the sky. The proposed solar panels over the parking area present a distinct, solid horizontal
    line against the sky that is generally only visible from KVP 4; all other viewpoints discussed herein
    lack prominent views of the proposed solar panels due to their location and angle of view. Distant
    structures and development across the Bay are vaguely visible through the series of vertical lines
    created by the solar support columns. The solar shade structures introduce new linear elements and
    repetitive architectural forms, replacing previously organic shapes and softened skyline with
    geometric forms and engineered materials. The proposed redevelopment of this area introduces
    more distinct built elements that would contrast with the existing naturalized features. While the
    proposed project would result in visual changes to this area, the proposed updates to the Seawall
    Drive parking lot would be compatible with existing uses, would enhance the site’s functionality while
    incorporating clean energy solutions, and would be designed and implemented in adherence to the
    BCDC Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces10 and the City’s goals, policies, and
    development review criteria related to the maintenance and enhancement of visual character, while
    also aligning with the City’s renewable energy goals. For these reasons, impacts would be less than
    significant.

    The BCDC Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces (BCDC 2005) provides guidelines

    • Using lighting to extend the hours of shoreline use;
    • Locating night lighting away from sensitive habitat areas; and
    • Providing enough lighting to create a sense of safety, but designing to control intensity, glare, and
      spillover.

    • Wayfinding signage lighting along University Avenue, Seawall Drive, and the proposed Bay Trail

       • Lighting at the Seawall Drive parking lot
       • Lighting on the new pier, breakwater, gangways, and floats

       Down-cast LED lights would be placed approximately every 50-feet along the Pier and Breakwater on
       16-foot tall poles. The pier canopy structure would be fitted with LED linear downlights attached to
       the roof and wall sconces attached to the columns. Stainless steel guardrails on the pier would
       contain LED handrail point lighting aimed at the deck, which would also to be used for emergency
       egress lighting. A solar-powered marine signal light would be installed on the float. Emergency LED
       path of egress lighting would also be installed on the central inverter. The proposed project lighting is
       required to support safe nighttime use of University Avenue, Seawall Drive, the proposed Bay Trail
       Extension, Seawall Drive parking lot, and pier by providing adequate visibility for pedestrian
       circulation, wayfinding, vehicle maneuvering, and hazard avoidance during hours of darkness, as
       required by the BCDC. Furthermore, lighting All project light fixtures would be photocell-controlled
       area lighting in compliance with Illuminating Engineering Society (IES) and DarkSky recommendation
       to minimize glare, reduce light trespass, and avoid light pollution. With utilization of DarkSky
       approved light fixtures, operational impacts related to new sources of light would be less than
       significant.
       Vehicular traffic from the proposed project would result in an increase in mobile light sources (i.e.,
       vehicle headlights) in the project vicinity. The existing visual setting is characterized by developed
       land uses, established roadway infrastructure, and ongoing vehicular activity that already introduces
       intermittent headlight illumination and associated glare during nighttime hours; thus, the baseline
       environment includes regular exposure to such light sources. As described in Section 3.12,
       Transportation, and Appendix F, the Project is estimated to generate 1,127 daily vehicle trips; however,
       it is anticipated that most of these trips are not new trips, and were originally headed to San
       Francisco by driving across the Bay Bridge. Project-generated traffic would incrementally increase the
       number of vehicles on nearby roadways, increasing the frequency of headlight visibility within the
       viewshed. However, this increase would be minor and dispersed, occurring within existing roadway
       corridors and parking areas already defined by vehicular movement and associated lighting. Vehicle
       headlights are inherently transient, directional, and mobile, producing short-duration illumination
       rather than static or concentrated light sources. Accordingly, the project would not substantially
       increase ambient nighttime illumination or introduce new patterns of light spill or glare beyond
       existing conditions. This impact would be less than significant.
       It is not anticipated that significant operational daytime glare would occur from proposed project
       structures (e.g. pier, breakwater, ferry infrastructure), given the lack of reflective materials in the
       proposed facility. While the surface of water is reflective, this would not be a change from existing
       conditions and, thus, would not introduce new sources of daytime glare. Potential glare resulting from
       Bay water would appear similar in character to existing, surrounding Bay water at the project site.
       Therefore, operational glare impacts related to new sources of glare would be less than significant.
       Discussion of project impacts to biological resources associated with proposed project lighting is
       included in Section 3.3, Biological Resources.

Section 3.3, Biological Resources

Draft EIR Page 3.3-7:
    The California Essential Habitat Connectivity Project, commissioned by the California Department of
    Transportation (Caltrans) and CDFW, identifies “Natural Landscape Blocks” which support native
    biodiversity and the “Essential Connectivity Areas” which link them.35
    The Pacific Flyway is the westernmost of North America’s four major migratory corridors. Each year
    millions of birds travel the Pacific Flyway between northern breeding areas and southern wintering
    grounds, relying on a chain of coastal and inland stopovers for feeding and rest. This migration
    corridor extends from Alaska through western North America to Central and South America, and is
    used by waterfowl, shorebirds, raptors, and passerines. The San Francisco Bay is one of the most
    important stopovers along the Pacific Flyway, as the largest estuary on the West Coast.
    PROJECT SITE
    Most of the project site is developed and urbanized and does not provide for wildlife movement
    corridors. The project site is not located within an Essential Connectivity Area or Natural Landscape
    Block.36 However, the project site is located within Baylands adjacent to marine foraging habitat, and
    trees within the project site may provide roosting habitat for migratory birds. The old pier and pilings
    also provide roosting and migration staging habitat for migratory waterfowl, seabirds, and shorebirds.

    Burrowing Owl
    Burrowing owl occupy open, dry habitats such as grasslands, coastal dunes, salt marsh edges, and
    sparsely vegetated disturbed sites that support abundant small mammal and insect prey. The
    species relies on a mix of invertebrates and small vertebrates for foraging, with peak activity at dawn
    and dusk. Nesting and roosting typically occur in underground burrows—often those excavated by
    ground squirrels, pocket gophers, or other fossorial mammals—or in artificial burrows and cavities
    with loose soil for excavation, while nonbreeding individuals favor undisturbed, low-vegetation areas
    for shelter and foraging.
    Although one occurrence has been documented within five miles of the project site and burrowing
    owls are known to overwinter at Cesar Chavez Park (“Farmworkers Park”), the project site itself does
    not provide the habitat conditions required for overwintering. The site lacks open, low-stature annual
    grassland and protected foraging areas with sufficient insect prey, which are essential for sustaining
    overwintering individuals.
    Adjacent areas, including fragmented grasslands in Shorebird Park and along University Avenue,
    contain limited open space but do not provide suitable overwintering habitat. While some ground



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                        3-23
                                              Page 1126 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

       squirrel burrows are present, these grassland areas are routinely mowed for park use and subject to
       heavy recreational use and frequent human disturbance, which reduces prey availability and limits
       habitat suitability. In addition, the grassland areas along University Avenue are narrow and linear, lack
       refuge from disturbance due to regular trail use, recreation, and the presence of dogs, and are
       exposed to numerous tall perching structures that support hawks and other avian predators.
       A migrating or displaced individual could briefly land on the project site or within nearby areas during
       movement; therefore, this species has a low potential to occur.

       Crotch’s Bumble Bee
       Crotch’s bumble bee occupies open, dry habitats such as coastal scrub, grasslands, chaparral
       margins, and sparsely vegetated alluvial terraces that support abundant spring and early summer
       blooming plants. The species relies on diverse nectar and pollen resources. Nesting typically occurs
       in abandoned rodent burrows or concealed upland cavities with sufficient thatch or loose soil, while
       overwintering queens select undisturbed, well drained areas.
       Crotch’s bumble bee has only one known occurrence recorded within five miles of the project site.
       Suitable habitat on the project site is of low quality because most terrestrial areas of the project site
       are paved or landscaped with sparse floral resources for foraging. Although small mammal burrows
       on the project site may provide suitable nesting habitat and floral resources for foraging occur
       adjacent to the site, the highly developed character of the project site and associated anthropogenic
       disturbance reduce the availability and connectivity of habitat needed to support the species.
       Therefore, there is low potential for this species to occur within the project site.

Draft EIR Page 3.3-19:
       Least Tern
       California least tern is a small tern with a distinctive black-capped head and is federally endangered,
       State endangered, and a State fully protected species. This species nests along the California coast
       and breeds colonially on bare or sparsely vegetated areas.62 The California least tern nests during
       summer from Baja California north to the San Francisco Bay. Least terns are migratory and spend
       winter months in coastal areas of Mexico and Central America. Least terns forage primarily on
       silversides (e.g., topsmelt), northern anchovies, Pacific herring, and surfperches.63 This species nests
       in colonies on bare or sparsely vegetated flat substrates, including beaches, alkali flats, or paved
       areas.
       California least terns have a low potential to forage over open water within and adjacent to the
       project site. This species has no potential to nest within the project site despite the presence of bare
       or sparsely vegetated areas due to the heavy recreational use and disturbed nature of the project site.

    Chinook Salmon - Central Valley Spring-Run ESU
    The Chinook salmon - Central Valley spring-run ESU is federally threatened. Chinook salmon is an
    anadromous fish spending most of its life in coastal waters. This population of chinook salmon
    spawns in the Sacramento River and its tributaries. Juveniles are reared in the San Joaquin Delta and
    migrate to the ocean between December, January, and February, and adult immigration through the
    delta and into the lower Sacramento River occurs from late January to early February.67 Therefore,
    there is a moderate potential for individuals to migrate, forage, and transit within the project site.

    Chinook Salmon – Central Valley fall/late-fall-run ESU
    The Chinook salmon - Central Valley fall/late-fall-run ESU includes both fall-run and late-fall-run
    Chinook salmon; however, only the fall-run is a CDFW SSC. Chinook salmon are anadromous,
    spending the majority of their life cycle in marine waters before returning to freshwater systems to
    spawn. Fall-run Chinook salmon migrate upstream through the San Joaquin Delta from July through
    December and spawn from early October through late December, with the timing of runs varying by
    stream.68 Late fall-run Chinook salmon migrate through the San Joaquin Delta from mid-October
    through December and spawn from January through mid-April. Following emergence, most juvenile
    fall-run and late-fall-run Chinook salmon rear in freshwater for approximately one to seven months
    before emigrating to the ocean, while a smaller proportion remain in freshwater and migrate as
    yearlings. Among the Central Valley Chinook salmon populations, the fall-run is the most abundant
    and exhibits a life history strategy characterized by a relatively short freshwater residence period. The
    fall-run population emigrates to the ocean during the spring, prior to the onset of elevated summer



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                        3-25
                                             Page 1128 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

       water temperatures, allowing juveniles to utilize lower-elevation reaches of Central Valley rivers
       during outmigration. This life history strategy, combined with the population's relative abundance, has
       resulted in fall-run Chinook salmon being the primary stock propagated at the five major Central
       Valley hatcheries.69 Based on the species' migration ecology, habitat use, and the location of the
       project site within a potential migratory corridor, there is moderate potential for Central Valley fall-
       run/late-fall-run Chinook salmon to occur within the project site and vicinity during migration or
       dispersal periods. Individuals may use aquatic habitats within or adjacent to the project site for
       passage and transient foraging; however, the project site does not provide suitable spawning or long-
       term rearing habitat.

Sub-Section 3.3.3, Regulatory Framework

Draft EIR Page 3.3-32:
       The SWRCB and RWQCBs have not currently established regulations for field determinations of
       waters of the State except for wetlands. In many cases, the RWQCBs interpret the limits of waters of
       the State to be bounded by the OHWM unless isolated conditions or ephemeral waters are present.
       However, in the absence of statewide guidance, each RWQCB may interpret jurisdictional boundaries
       within their region, and the SWRCB has encouraged applicants to confirm jurisdictional limits with
       their RWQCB before submitting applications. As determined by the RWQCB, waters of the State may
       include riparian areas or other locations outside the OHWM, leading to a larger jurisdictional area over
       a given water body compared to USACE. The San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board has
       indicated that along creeks and rivers, they would assert jurisdiction up to at least the top of bank and
       along the Bay shoreline, and they consider that areas of the bank below the epochal high tide line to
       be regulated waters of the State. For the purposes of this EIR, the one-year extreme high tide line was
       used to delineate the extent of jurisdictional waters, in line with USACE guidance, and assumed to
       encompass both waters of the U.S. and waters of the State. Further coordination with the SFRWQCB
       will be conducted during the permitting process.

Draft EIR Page 3.3-52:
    While the electric ferry vessels would introduce a new noise source, they would generate significantly
    less noise, especially at lower frequency sounds, than traditional diesel engines. Underwater noise
    measurements made of various hybrid electric and conventional ferry vessels indicate that a ship
    retrofitted with electric motors, generators, and batteries (Tellus) radiated less underwater noise than
    a ship with a conventional diesel propulsion system (Neptunus). A report from 2024 prepared by
    Silent@Sea notes the following: "according to our measurements, Tellus radiates less underwater
    noise than Neptunus, with up to 10 dB [difference].” A 10dB difference is a halving of noise, as if a
    wall or barrier has been put in place. The report states: “This is an indication that retrofitting ships
    with modern hybrid propulsion is a potential way to reduce their noise radiation.”94 Additionally, recent
    research evaluating underwater noise generated by electric vessels indicates that while certain
    electric vessel configurations may generate high-frequency tonal noise associated with electric
    propulsion components, underwater noise characteristics vary substantially depending on vessel
    design, propulsion architecture, and motor installation. In particular, Smith et al. (2026) found that
    electric vessels remained quieter than a comparable conventionally powered vessel across the full
    range of operating speeds evaluated and found that such tonal noise can be reduced through
    engineering measures including optimization of motor controller switching frequencies and
    electromagnetic interference filtering.95 Similarly, Gaggero et al. (2024) found that although electric
    vessels may generate high-frequency tonal noise, propulsion architecture and motor placement are
    important factors influencing underwater noise generation.96 Accordingly, following publication of the
    Draft EIR, WETA has advanced the design-build contract for the proposed electric ferry vessels to
    incorporate features consistent with those identified in the recent literature, including propulsion
    motors mounted inboard in enclosed Propulsion Rooms with water-cooled, resilient-mounted
    configurations, acoustic insulation and sound-damping coatings on propulsion equipment spaces,
    and third-party acoustic measurement and verification during construction. These design features
    would minimize the potential for the proposed electric ferry vessels to generate underwater noise
    that could adversely affect marine mammals. Therefore, in-water noise impacts on marine mammals
    due to operation of ferry vessels would be less than significant.

       MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(C): CONDUCT BURROWING OWL AND NESTING BIRD SURVEY AND AVOIDANCE
       PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION

       Burrowing Owl
       Prior to project construction, a qualified biologist will conduct a habitat assessment to determine if
       potential habitat for burrowing owl is present in or near the project site. If potential habitat is present
       in or within 500 feet of the project site, a qualified biologist will conduct a pre-construction survey of
       the project site (plus a 500-foot buffer as access allows) for the presence of burrowing owl. The
       survey will be conducted no more than 14 days prior to ground disturbing activities and will conform
       to CDFW guidelines for burrowing owl Take Avoidance Surveys as described in Appendix D of the
       2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation.100 A report of pre-construction survey efforts
       and results will be submitted to the City within 30 days of completion of the survey. The report will
       include the dates, times, weather conditions, and personnel involved in the survey. Depending on
       survey results, the report will also include observations of burrowing owl or potential burrows, and the
       location and habitat description of the observations. If burrowing owl, active burrows, or their sign
       (i.e., tracks or pellets) are not observed in the project site, no additional measures related to impact
       avoidance and minimization of the absent species are recommended. If burrowing owl, active
       burrows, or their sign are observed within the project site, CDFW will be notified and the following
       measures will be implemented:
       • A qualified biological monitor will be present during landside construction on the project site to
         document burrowing owl observations, burrow statuses, and require that construction activities do
         not negatively affect burrowing owl. The duration and frequency of monitoring will be determined at
         the discretion of the qualified biologist and a monitoring report detailing monitoring results will be
         submitted to the City within 30 days of the completion of project activities or breeding season
         (February 1 to August 31), if applicable.
       • The biological monitor will visually inspect any pipes, debris piles, culverts, or similar structures for
         burrowing owl before the material is moved, buried, or capped. Open holes and trenches within the
         project site will be inspected at the beginning and end of each landside construction workday and
         immediately prior to backfilling. At the end of each such workday, trenches and holes will be
         ramped so that any animals that may have become trapped in the trench or hole can climb out. The
         ramp may be constructed of dirt fill or wood planking or other suitable material at an angle no
         greater than 30-45 degrees. If a burrowing owl is trapped in a trench or hole, work will stop and the
         qualified biologist will be notified immediately. The burrowing owl will be allowed to escape
         unimpeded.
       • If active burrows are observed on the project site, a non-disturbance buffer will be established
         restricting all ground-disturbing activities from occurring within the buffer and a qualified biological
         monitor will be present at the initiation of project activities. The buffer will be established by a
         qualified biologist and range from 330 ft. to 1,500 ft. depending on project activity, line of sight, and
         local topography during the breeding season. During the non-breeding season (September 1 to
         January 31), the buffer will range from 165 ft. to 330 ft. The buffer will be demarcated using brightly
         colored flagging and may only be reduced at the discretion of a qualified biologist based on the
         factors listed above and potential use of sound and visual barriers (i.e., hay bales). Removal of the



3-30
                                              Page 1133 of 1541

                                                                                                           Errata



         buffer will only occur if a qualified biologist determines burrowing owl are not present in the vicinity
         and any potential burrows are inactive.
       • If active burrow avoidance is infeasible during the non-breeding season or during the breeding
         season, where resident owls have not yet begun egg laying or incubation, or where the juveniles are
         foraging independently and capable of independent survival, the City in coordination with a
         qualified biologist will consult with CDFW to prepare, authorize, and implement a passive relocation
         program consistent with Appendix E of the 2012 CDFW Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation.
       • A habitat mitigation plan will be developed in coordination with the City and CDFW for loss of active
         burrowing owl burrow sites if implementation of a passive relocation plan is necessary and/or
         burrowing owl are documented to nest on site or within 500 feet of the project site. This would be
         based upon the portion of the project site that overlaps with the primary foraging area around the
         burrow site (approximately 500-foot buffer) to be replaced at a minimum 1:1 ratio.

       Nesting Birds
       Project construction activities, including but not limited to vegetation removal and ground
       disturbance that result in noise or disturbance affecting potential nesting bird habitat, should
       commence outside of the nesting season (February 1 through September 15), if feasible. If
       construction begins outside the nesting season, a nesting bird survey is not required.
       If ground disturbing project activities begin within the nesting season (February 1 through August 31
       September 15), then no more than seven days prior to the initiation of project activities, a nesting bird
       pre-construction survey shall be conducted by a City-approved qualified biologist within the
       disturbance footprint, plus a 300-foot buffer for passerines and a 1,000-foot buffer for raptors. During
       construction within the nesting season, an additional focused survey shall be conducted prior to tree
       removal to identify active nests with the subject tree(s). If no active nests are observed, no further
       action would be required. Ground-disturbing project activities that are initiated outside of the nesting
       season may continue into the nesting season without requiring new nesting bird surveys.
       Pre-construction nesting bird surveys shall be conducted by a qualified biologist during the time of
       day when birds are most active and should be of sufficient duration to reliably conclude presence or
       absence of nesting birds on the project site and within the designated buffer. A report of the nesting
       bird surveys results shall be submitted to the City for review and approval prior to clearance for
       mobilizing equipment. If nests are found, their locations shall be flagged (if possible) and recorded
       with the use of a GPS unit. Avoidance buffers shall be established around active nests. Depending
       upon the species, suitable minimum buffers may be 50 feet for non-raptor species and 300 feet for
       raptor species, or as determined by the qualified biologist in consultation with CDFW based on
       species sensitivity, construction activities, and other factors.
       If active nests are present, all project work shall be conducted outside the established avoidance
       buffer zone from the nest until it is no longer active. No staging of large equipment shall occur within
       the avoidance buffer until the qualified biologist confirms that breeding/nesting is complete and all
       the young have fledged. If buffer zones are determined to be infeasible, a City-approved qualified
       biological monitor shall be on site to monitor project activities within the avoidance buffer zones to
       ensure active nests and nesting birds are not impacted. Nesting bird surveys are not required for
       project activities that occur between September 16 and January 31. A report of all survey results and
       any proposed avoidance buffers shall be submitted to the City for review and approval.
       This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
       agencies.

       MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(E): PREPARE MARINE MAMMAL MONITORING PLAN PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION
       AND IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS DURING CONSTRUCTION

       Prior to construction, the City shall prepare a Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan (MMMP) to avoid and
       minimize potential adverse impacts on marine mammals during pile driving and tug operations. The
       MMMP shall implement general guidelines set forth in the MMPA and incorporate the hydroacoustic
       modeling results developed for the project to define site-specific protection zones and avoid
       exposure of marine mammals to underwater sound levels exceeding the most up to date Level A
       (injury) thresholds identified by NOAA Fisheries. The MMMP shall include the following:
       • Protection and Monitoring Zones: Using the hydroacoustic modeling results, the MMMP shall
         define shutdown and disturbance zones for each marine mammal hearing group. These zones will
         be tailored to the pile type, size, and driving method and will correspond to the Level A and Level B
         effect distances developed for the project. The plan will describe how these protection zones will
         be verified and monitored in the field, integrating them with the soft-start and observation
         procedures described in Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d).
       • Vessel Operation Protocols: The MMMP shall include vessel-operation measures consistent with
         the MMPA. Construction vessels under power shall remain at least 300 feet from whales and 150
         feet from dolphins, porpoises, seals, and sea lions. When marine mammals are encountered,
         vessel operators shall reduce speed to no-wake, shift to neutral, and allow the animals to pass
         safely before resuming operations.
       • On-Site Monitoring and Response: A qualified biologist shall be present on site, either observing
         from the pier or aboard a vessel, during all pile-driving and tug operations. The biologist shall
         document all marine-mammal observations, note behavioral responses, and immediately alert
         project personnel if a whale enters the modeled harassment distance or comes within 300 feet, or
         if any other marine mammal enters the modeled harassment distance or comes within 150 feet,
         whichever is greater. Upon such an observation, the contractor shall implement the appropriate
         delay or shutdown procedures identified in the MMMP.
       • Adaptive Management and Coordination: The MMMP shall outline communication and reporting
         protocols, including stop-work notification procedures and coordination with NMFS Protected
         Species Division. Results from daily monitoring will be used to assess the effectiveness of the
         protection zones and adjust them, if needed, in consultation with NMFS.
       • Nighttime Pile Driving: Nighttime pile driving shall be limited to situations where safety concerns
         or significant schedule delays require that pile driving started during daytime hours extend beyond
         typical work hours. For instances where nighttime pile driving is required, the MMMP shall include
         non-visual monitoring protocols, such as passive acoustic monitoring, thermal/infrared cameras,
         and night-vision optics, as well as larger nighttime exclusion/shutdown zones, extended soft-start
         procedures, and the most effective feasible hydroacoustic attenuation.

       This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
       agencies.

    TERRESTRIAL
    Operation of the project would include vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians using University Avenue,
    Seawall Drive, and parking lots. These uses of the project site would be consistent with existing
    recreation and commercial uses. No new barriers or disturbances to terrestrial wildlife movement are
    proposed. Roosting birds and birds staging during migration may be temporarily displaced by
    removal of portions of the existing pier deck and pilings; however, the old wooden pilings at the west
    end where the majority of roosting birds occur would remain in place. Additionally, there are other
    roosting sites available in the project vicinity and wider bay, including a platform that was specifically
    constructed for cormorants on the new eastern span of the Bay Bridge. Therefore, there would be no
    operational impact related to terrestrial wildlife movement.

    MARINE
    Operation of ferry vessels would occur at the water surface level, with some incremental increase in
    ferry boat noise and lighting within the project area vicinity. The project proposes to operate two ferry
    vessels with regular service to San Francisco and weekend service to Larkspur, which are both is an
    active shipping ports with existing recreational and ferryboat use. Therefore, the project would
    represent an incremental increase in existing boat trips on the Bay.
    Temporary disturbance from ferry operations would be localized and intermittent, affecting only a
    small portion of the broad open-water foraging and roosting areas used by migratory and wintering
    birds in San Francisco Bay. The project’s operational corridor represents a minor fraction of the
    available bay habitat, and similar foraging and roosting sites occur immediately north and south of
    the corridor. Because displacement events would be shorter and birds can move to adjacent habitat
    with comparable resources, the loss of usable foraging or roosting area is expected to be temporary
    and minimal.

    In addition, the shoreline around the project site ferry approach area is made of armored rip rap,
    rather than exposed native soils or unconsolidated shoreline sediments.; therefore, there is no soil
    that could be eroded. As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, a localized section of shoreline
    along the eastern side of the Seawall Peninsula is currently experiencing deterioration of existing
    shoreline protection and exposure of underlying fill material. The proposed project would repair and
    stabilize this already-armored shoreline segment through in-kind replacement and reinforcement of
    existing shoreline protection features. Because the proposed shoreline repair would restore and
    maintain an existing hardened shoreline condition, rather than introduce new armoring into a
    previously natural shoreline, the project would not substantially alter shoreline geomorphology, wave
    reflection patterns, or erosion processes relative to existing conditions. Although shoreline armoring
    can influence localized erosion patterns in adjacent unarmored areas, the shoreline areas
    immediately adjacent to the proposed repair are similarly developed and protected with existing
    shoreline stabilization features. Therefore, the proposed shoreline repair would not substantially
    increase erosion rates in nearby shoreline areas beyond existing conditions. Finally, the ferry vessels
    approaching the project site would reduce speed to 8 knots or less when approaching the Berkeley
    pier boarding float, which would further minimize wake-related shoreline effects.68 For these reasons,
    operational impacts on erosion or loss of topsoil would be less than significant.

       While the discussion presented herein primarily references the City of Berkeley Mean Lower-Low

       The Berkeley Waterfront experiences mixed semidiurnal tides, with water levels ranging from
       approximately +6.8 feet mean lower-low water (MLLW) during average higher-high tide conditions to
       about +10.3 8.4 feet MLLW under 100-year extreme tide events during Highest Astronomical Tide
       (HAT) conditions. Extreme Water Level conditions may reach approximately +10.3 feet MLLW during
       severe storm and coastal flooding events. The design still water level, which accounts for
       astronomical tides, storm surge, and projected sea level rise through 2075, is estimated at +11.9 feet
       MLLW.

Draft EIR Page 3.8-11:
       A portion of the project site is located in a special flood hazard area. As shown on Figure 3.8-3,
       Central San Francisco Bay within the project site is mapped as “Zone VE” of the 100-year floodplain,
       which are coastal areas with a 1 percent or greater chance of flooding in any single year and an
       additional hazard associated with storm waves. Zone VE areas have a 26 percent chance of flooding
       over a 30-year period.29 As also shown on Figure 3.8-3, portions of the shoreline and surrounding
       areas adjacent to the project site are mapped as FEMA Zone AE, which identifies areas subject to
       inundation from the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event where Base Flood Elevations (BFEs) have
       been established. While the proposed waterside project components are primarily associated with
       the Zone VE flood hazard area, nearby shoreline areas include both Zone AE and Zone X flood hazard
       designations. FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Maps identify BFEs for the mapped Zone VE and Zone AE
       areas adjacent to the project site. The BFE for Zone VE ranges from approximately 12 to 13 feet and
       the BFE for adjacent Zone AE areas is approximately 10 feet. These BFEs represent the estimated
       water surface elevation associated with the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event and are used for
       floodplain management and project design purposes. Further offshore, the San Francisco Bay is
       designated as open water, which is not considered a special flood hazard area.30

    Construction activities within surface waters have the greatest potential to affect water quality in the
    San Francisco Bay. Impacts to the San Francisco Bay would be primarily due to construction-related



Final Environmental Impact Report                                                                        3-37
                                             Page 1140 of 1541

City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

       dredging, demolition of the existing pier, and construction of a new pier. In-water construction
       activities, such as dredging, existing pile removal and new pile installation, and pier deck demolition
       and construction, as well as any associated sediment disturbance, have the potential to directly
       affect San Francisco Bay water quality. Some of the existing pier piles, if wooden, could contain
       hazardous materials, such as creosote, that could be released during demolition and removal
       activities. Consistent with standard practice, existing wooden piles would be evaluated for the
       presence of wood preservatives and managed in accordance with applicable requirements, including
       requirements related to Treated Wood Waste, if applicable, as discussed further in Section 3.7,
       Hazards and Hazardous Materials. Dredging of debris, removal of existing pier infrastructure, and pier
       installation could resuspend bottom sediments, increasing turbidity in the immediate project vicinity.
       Elevated turbidity can reduce light penetration, affecting photosynthetic organisms and potentially
       adversely affecting water quality. Sediment resuspension may also release adsorbed contaminants
       such as metals, hydrocarbons, or legacy pollutants into the water column, where they can be
       transported by currents and dispersed to adjacent areas.

Draft EIR Page 3.8-30:
       Dredging activities have the potential to temporarily degrade water quality by resuspending bottom
       sediments into the water column. As described previously, in 2025, sediment sampling and analysis
       was conducted within five dredge units in the project vicinity and sediment samples were found to
       contain metals, organochlorine pesticides, polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, PCBs, and
       dioxins/furans. Although contaminants were present, the concentrations of such contaminants
       indicate that sediments are not likely to pose significant hazards if managed according to reuse site
       requirements.
       Any increase in suspended sediment concentrations resulting from dredging activities would be
       temporary and limited to the construction period. Suspended sediments generated during dredging
       would be expected to settle following completion of the work, and standard construction best
       management practices would be implemented to minimize sediment dispersion beyond the
       immediate work area. The sediment transport assessment indicates that the highest sedimentation
       rates would occur within the dredged navigation channel as natural sediment transport processes
       gradually infill dredged areas over time.48 Given the localized nature of dredging activities and the
       expected settling of suspended sediments near the dredged area, the project is not expected to result
       in a measurable increase in sediment deposition within the South Sailing Basin or a reduction in
       access beyond existing tidal limitations.

Draft EIR Page 3.8-40:
    The Universal Charging Float battery systems would be housed in smoke-tight, watertight
    compartments with real-time monitoring, automated shutoff systems, and multiple redundant fire
    suppression systems, substantially reducing the potential for pollutant release in the event of
    inundation. Additionally, as depicted in Figure 3.8-3, portions of the project site are located within
    FEMA-designated 500-year floodplains. However, the proposed ferry terminal includes infrastructure
    intended to remain structurally resilient during extreme coastal flood events. As described in Section
    3.12, Transportation, WETA and its contracted operator proactively monitor weather forecasts and
    U.S. Coast Guard advisories. In the event of an approaching storm, senior staff coordinate with vessel
    crews to evaluate the safety of continuing ferry service on affected routes. Although ferry operations
    may be temporarily suspended during severe storm conditions such as a 500-year flood event due to
    navigational safety concerns, the pier, breakwater, piles, and associated structural elements have
    been designed to accommodate water levels and wave forces associated with extreme flood events,
    as the project’s coastal engineering analyses considered future sea level rise and coastal flooding
    conditions over the life of the project. Therefore, any operational interruption associated with extreme
    storm or flooding events would be temporary and would not be expected to result in a substantial
    long-term loss of emergency transportation or evacuation capabilities, nor would any operational
    interruption indicate structural failure of the proposed facilities.

Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning

Sub-Section 3.9.2, Environmental Setting
Draft EIR Page 3.9-2:
    The project site has a Berkeley General Plan land use designation of Waterfront/Marina.1 The General
    Plan describes the Waterfront/Marina as areas intended to maintain and preserve areas of Berkeley
    adjacent to the Bay for open space, recreational uses, waterfront-related commercial and visitor
    services, boating, and water transit facilities. The project site has a zoning designation of
    Unclassified (U). Development within Unclassified areas requires a Use Permit in compliance with
    Berkeley Municipal Code Section 23.208.020, which governs Use Permits in Unclassified zones. The
    project site is subject to the Berkeley Marina Use Permit (Permit No. 5567), issued in 1965, which
    authorizes existing uses and permits implementation of the Marina Master Plan. This permit governs
    current uses at the Berkeley Waterfront and establishes a framework for future improvements. The

       Portions of the project site are located within the jurisdiction of the San Francisco Bay Conservation
       and Development Commission (BCDC), pursuant to the McAteer-Petris Act. The City will coordinate
       with BCDC staff, as appropriate, during permitting to confirm jurisdictional boundaries and applicable
       regulatory requirements.

Sub-Section 3.9.3, Regulatory Framework
Draft EIR Page 3.9-4:
       In compliance with the McAteer-Petris Act, BCDC prepared the first San Francisco Bay Plan in 1968
       which was transmitted to the California Legislature and the Governor in 1969. BCDC amends the Bay
       Plan over time to address regional needs. The San Francisco Bay Plan includes policies to guide
       future uses of the Bay and the shoreline. The Plan aims to protect the Bay from unnecessary filling,
       promote public access, and ensure sustainable development. It designates priority use areas for
       water-oriented activities, such as ports and recreational facilities, and establishes environmental
       safeguards to preserve the Bay's natural resources. The Plan also includes specific policies for
       shoreline protection, habitat restoration, and climate resilience, ensuring that land use and planning
       decisions support ecological health and community needs. Pertinent policies are identified and
       addressed in detail under Impact LU-2 within this EIR section.
       Although BCDC laws and policies have a regional focus and are therefore included within the
       Regional and Local Regulations subsection of Section 3.9.3, Regulatory Framework, BCDC’s governing
       legislation, the McAteer-Petris Act, has the status of State law and is effectively comprised of State
       regulations subject to approval by the California Office of Administrative Law.

Sub-Section 3.9.4, Impacts Analysis
Draft EIR Page 3.9-12:
       Given the project location within 100 feet of the San Francisco Bay shoreline, the BCDC San Francisco
       Bay Plan would be applicable in terms of land use planning. BCDC will determine whether the
       proposed project is consistent with the McAteer-Petris Act and Bay Plan policies. Such
       determinations are made by BCDC on a case-by-case basis when considering permit applications. As
       part of this process, BCDC will conduct an independent review of the project’s consistency with its
       governing laws and policies and may impose conditions or require project modifications to ensure
       compliance. To the extent that consistency with these laws and policies is subject to CEQA review,
       Tthe City’s evaluation of project consistency with applicable BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan policies is

Draft EIR Page 3.10-30:
       Noise from Operation of Ferry Vessels
       Ferry vessels would operate at the north end of the pier, as close as approximately 400 feet from the
       nearest sensitive receptor (i.e., the Skates on the Bay Restaurant located to the northeast). At this
       distance, operation of the ferry vessels would generate noise levels up to 52 dBA at the Skates on the
       Bay Restaurant, which would not exceed the City’s daytime or nighttime exterior noise limits of 65


3-52
                                          Page 1155 of 1541

                                                                                                      Errata



    and 60 dBA, respectively, at commercial land uses. Additionally, ferry vessels would operate
    approximately 430 feet from the nearest portion of the proposed Bay Trail corridor and approximately
    550 feet from Shorebird Park. At these distances, operation of ferry vessels would generate noise
    levels up to 51 and 49 dBA at the Bay Trail corridor and Shorebird Park, respectively, which would not
    exceed the City’s daytime exterior noise limit of 55 dBA for low-density single-family residential uses,
    which is the threshold also used for outdoor recreation spaces due to a similar level of noise
    sensitivity. Note that noise levels would continue to decrease as distance from the ferry terminal
    increases, therefore noise levels at all other parks located farther away (e.g., César E. Chávez Park,
    Horseshoe Park, Marina Mall, and Adventure Playground) would also not exceed the City’s applicable
    daytime exterior noise limit. Therefore, operational noise impacts associated with the ferry vessels
    would be less than significant. For the noise impact associated with operation of ferry vessels as it
    relates to potential impacts related to biological resources discussion, see Impact BIO-1 in Section
    3.3, Biological Resources.

Section 3.11, Recreation

Sub-Section 3.11.2, Environmental Setting
Draft EIR Page 3.11-1:
    Open space is a broad term for undeveloped land that provides public access, while a park is a
    specific type of open space that is developed for recreation and leisure activities. Parks can include
    playgrounds, sports fields, and paved paths, whereas open spaces can be more natural and less
    developed areas like forests, farms, or grasslands. Both open space and parks can be publicly owned
    and operated by a city, a regional jurisdiction, the State, or the federal government. A recreational
    facility is a specific, human-made structure or area designed for a particular recreational activity and
    can include elements such as parks and picnic sites, pathways and trails, boating docks, community
    and nature center buildings, sports courts and swimming pools, among other elements. For purposes
    of the EIR analysis presented in Section 3.11.4, Impacts Analysis, recreational resources include both
    land-based facilities, such as parks, trails, and open space areas, as well as water-based areas used
    for recreation, such as marina basins, lagoons, and San Francisco Bay Waters. Figures depicting park
    and recreation resources may include water features to represent the full extent of recreational use
    areas rather than solely land acreage.

Draft EIR Page 3.11-5:

    Berkeley Marina Basin
    The Berkeley Waterfront is an approximately 125-acre area west of I-80 in the City of Berkeley. The
    Berkeley Marina Basin refers to a subset of the Berkeley Waterfront north of the project site that
    includes the main boat harbor with approximately 1,000 recreational boat slips (Figure 3.11-2). In
    1937, Berkeley built the original yacht harbor (i.e., the Marina Basin) in the Waterfront area. In the
    1960s, the City participated in regional planning efforts to develop an East Bay Shoreline for
    recreation and public access. During this period, the City decided to re-develop the existing yacht
    harbor of 1937 into the modern Berkeley Marina Basin that exists today.11 The predominant activity at
    the Berkeley Marina Basin Main Harbor involves the operation of boat slips for up to 1,000
    recreational sailboats, as well as other activities such as dinner cruises, commercial charter boats for
    sightseeing and fishing, sailing lessons and dragon boat canoe racing. The Marina is a designated
    San Francisco Bay Water Trail site.12

       South Sailing Basin
       The South Sailing Basin, located immediately south and southeast of project site is identified as a
       Water/Recreational use in the Marina Master Plan (see Figure 3.11-2).16 The South Sailing Basin is a
       designated San Francisco Bay Water Trail site.17 Three public docks, located south of University
       Avenue and south of the sailing club facilities, and south of the project site provide public access to
       the water for small boats (sail, windsurf, wing, kayak, canoe, paddleboard, etc.) and swimming. The
       Cal Sailing Club and the Cal Adventures Center utilize the public access docks for sailing and other
       water recreation activities in the South Sailing Basin.

       San Francisco Bay
       The San Francisco Bay is a tidal estuary that provides a variety of natural resource and open space
       opportunities (see Figure 3.11-2). According to the BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, the San Francisco
       Bay is the most important open space in the Bay region, and it provides a variety of unique
       recreational opportunities. Primary recreation activities occurring throughout the San Francisco Bay
       include sailing, kayaking, paddle-boarding, swimming, windsurfing, kitesurfing, canoeing and dragon
       boat canoeing. Additional recreation activities on the Bay include wildlife viewing, fishing and boating
       via public ferry, private and charter boats. These water-based recreational activities often involve
       specialized equipment and access points to the shoreline and marina facilities, and are an integral
       component of the recreational setting at the Berkeley Waterfront.

Draft EIR Page 3.11-7:
       Open water swimming is a recognized recreational activity within the Berkeley Waterfront, including
       use of marina coves and shoreline areas. While the Draft EIR does not quantify user volumes, these
       activities are considered part of the existing recreational baseline in evaluating potential impacts to
       recreational access and facilities. Windsurfers, wingers, swimmers, paddleboarders, and kayakers
       launch from the South Sailing docks or Shorebird Beach for access throughout the South Sailing Cove
       and beyond. An un-improved rocky shoreline at the southernmost point of the 199 Seawall peninsula
       is used by some swimmers and windsurfers/wingers, primarily when low tides make launching from
       the South Cove undesirable due to shallow water and exposed mudflats. According to Berkeley
       Municipal Code Section 6.20.180, Prohibited activities, swimming, bathing, windsurfing, and wading is
       prohibited within the City jurisdictional waters except for the South Sailing Basin (including the
       Shorebird Park Beach and the sailing docks), and no personal watercraft of any kind may be operated
       within 1,500 feet of the Berkeley Pier.

Sub-Section 3.11.3, Regulatory Framework
Draft EIR Page 3.11-8:

       McAteer-Petris Act
       The McAteer-Petris Act, enacted in 1965, established the San Francisco Bay Conservation and
       Development Commission (BCDC) to address public concerns about the future of San Francisco Bay.
       The Act empowers BCDC to regulate development and fill within the Bay, requiring that changes
       promote public access and recreational opportunities. This provision mandates comprehensive


3-54
                                          Page 1157 of 1541

                                                                                                       Errata



    planning through the San Francisco Bay Plan, which includes requirements for parks and recreational
    areas to enhance public enjoyment of the Bay. Additionally, the Act empowers BCDC to issue and
    deny permits for projects within its jurisdiction, balancing development projects with environmental
    preservation and public access. In addition, Chapter 7 of the McAteer-Petris Act describes the San
    Francisco Bay Area Water Trail, a non- linear, recreational trail of launching and landing sites for non-
    motorized small boaters that circumnavigates the San Francisco Bay. The South Sailing Basin and
    Marina are designated San Francisco Bay Water Trail sites.

    BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan
    The San Francisco Bay Plan, developed by BCDC, serves as a comprehensive framework for
    managing the Bay and its shoreline. The Plan emphasizes the importance of preserving and
    enhancing public access to the Bay, including the development of parks, marinas, beaches, and
    fishing piers. It aims to balance environmental preservation with recreational opportunities, ensuring
    that the Bay remains a valuable natural asset for both current and future generations. The Plan
    establishes policies and identifies priority use areas to guide development within BCDC’s jurisdiction,
    including the “Waterfront Park, Beach” designation, which applies to portions of the project site. By
    guiding development and conservation efforts, the Plan supports the creation of recreational spaces
    that contribute to the overall quality of life in the Bay Area. Although BCDC laws and policies have a
    regional focus and are therefore included within the Regional and Local Regulations subsection of
    Section 3.11.3, Regulatory Framework, BCDC’s governing legislation, the McAteer-Petris Act, has the
    status of State law and is effectively comprised of State regulations subject to approval by the
    California Office of Administrative Law. The BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan includes the following

       Construction activities associated with the proposed project would be phased and managed to
       maintain recreational access to the Berkeley Waterfront to the maximum extent feasible. During
       construction, temporary access constraints may occur in localized areas used for staging or active
       work. However, the City would implement access management practices, including maintaining
       access where feasible, providing temporary detours around active work areas, and installing
       temporary signage and wayfinding to direct recreational users to available areas of the waterfront,
       consistent with the City’s construction permitting requirements and traffic control standards.

Draft EIR Page 3.11-17:
       While construction of the proposed project may temporarily influence recreational users to seek
       alternative park facilities, the Berkeley Waterfront area spans approximately 100 acres with multiple
       access points at other locations that would not be affected by construction staging. In addition,
       although access routes may be temporarily modified, construction staging and sequencing would be
       organized, to the maximum extent feasible, to minimize disruption to public access, while maintaining
       safe construction operations. Therefore, project construction would not preclude recreation at the
       Waterfront to such an extent that recreational facilities would physically deteriorate or new
       recreational facilities would be needed.

Draft EIR Page 3.11-18:
       For construction occurring in the water, swimming, bathing, wading, and wind surfing, sailing, and
       kayaking are prohibited at the existing and new pier areas, pursuant to Berkeley Municipal Code
       Section 6.20.180(A), Prohibited activities. Although Berkeley Municipal Code Section 6.20.180(B) also
       prohibits the use of jet skis and other motorized watercrafts in this vicinity, sailboats, kayaks,
       paddleboards, and other non-motorized recreational watercraft may continue to use waters in the pier
       area. Boats already navigate around the existing pier and other vessels in the Bay and Marina, and
       they would similarly be able to navigate around in-water construction activities. Boats entering or
       exiting the Marina would also be able to maneuver around the work area, as construction would be
       staged to maintain adequate space for vessel passage. Therefore, water-work would not directly
       impact water-based recreation. Therefore, pProject construction also would not substantially
       increase the use of existing park and recreational reactional facilities, including access to the San
       Francisco Bay for recreational use, such that there would be substantial physical deterioration of
       existing parks and recreational facilities and result in need for new or physically altered park facilities.

Draft EIR Page 3.11-19 and 3.11-20:
       Operation of the ferry vessels would not interfere with recreational uses of the Berkeley Waterfront
       area. While the project would introduce ferry vessel operations within the approach channel and
       berthing area, these activities would be limited to defined navigation corridors. Recreational sailing
       areas in the Marina and adjacent waters would remain available. Proposed ferry vessels would travel
       and dock in Bay waters north of the pier, in an area where swimming, bathing, wading, and
       windsurfing/sailing is are prohibited by the Berkeley Municipal Code Section 6.20.180(A), Prohibited
       activities. These restrictions represent existing municipal regulations applicable to localized areas of
       the Marina and are part of the existing baseline conditions; the proposed project would not modify or
       expand the geographic extent of these regulated areas. However, other types of recreational boats
       are permitted to use this area. Sailboats, kayaks, paddleboards, and other non-motorized personal
       watercraft are not prohibited by either Section 6.20.180(A) or Section 6.20.180(B) and may continue
       to use the area accordingly. At present, permitted recreational boats already navigate around the
       existing pier and other vessels using the Bay and Marina, and they would similarly be able to navigate
       around the proposed ferry infrastructure and ferry vessels. Boats entering or exiting the Marina would
       continue to be able to maneuver around ferry infrastructure similar to how they currently navigate the
       area, as ferry infrastructure would maintain adequate space for the passage and docking of permitted
       recreational boats. Ferry operations would comply with speed restrictions and navigation protocols,
       resulting in wake conditions consistent with existing vessel traffic. Recreational users, including



3-56
                                             Page 1159 of 1541

                                                                                                        Errata



    swimmers and non-motorized watercraft users, are not typically present within the proposed ferry
    terminal location, north of the Pier, due to the existing traffic of sailboats and charter boats entering
    and exiting the Marina. Ferry boats would be regulated near the ferry terminal and be restricted to a
    travel speed maximum of 8 knots.29 More specifically, at 0.33 nautical miles, or approximately 2,000
    feet from the terminal, ferry boats would begin to slow speed to reduce the effects of the vessel’s
    wake. At 0.25 nautical miles, or approximately 1,500 feet from the terminal, the vessels would be
    brought to neutral for transferring and qualifying controls at the wing station for docking.30
    Consistent with existing WETA practices, ferry operations would be subject to U.S. Coast Guard
    navigation and safety requirements and would incorporate standard operational protocols, including
    defined approach routes, speed controls, and coordination with marina traffic, to ensure safe
    coexistence with recreational water users (refer to Section 3.12, Transportation). In addition to
    compliance with speed restrictions and navigation protocols, recreational users, including swimmers
    and non-motorized watercraft users, are not typically present within the proposed ferry terminal
    location north of the Pier due to the existing traffic of sailboats and charter boats entering and exiting
    the Marina. There are no designated launch points within the immediate vicinity of the ferry terminal.
    Ferry operations would occur within areas already characterized by vessel activity and would not
    affect primary recreational launch areas located elsewhere within the Berkeley Waterfront. Therefore,
    the associated ferry wake would not be noticeable within the context of the Berkeley Waterfront area
    and existing sailboat, motorized boats, and other recreational craft use. Recreation in the South
    Sailing Basin would not be impacted by operation of the proposed project, given the ferry boats would
    not traverse that area.
    Operation of the ferry would not hinder existing and new physical access to recreational resources on
    the project site or adjacent areas. The project would not restrict shoreline areas used for water-based
    recreation within the South Sailing Basin, and existing access points to these areas would be
    maintained.
    While certain access points, circulation patterns, and parking configurations within the project vicinity
    would be modified, overall access to recreational resources would be maintained and enhanced. The
    proposed new pier and breakwater, Bay Trail Extension, and green space next to the Bay Trail
    Extension would be publicly accessible and access to such project-related recreational uses would
    not be hindered by ferry operation or riders commuting to and from the Berkeley Waterfront area to
    utilize ferry services. Furthermore, the proposed project would include amenities such as fish
    cleaning stations, seating, and public restrooms, which would enhance the experience of people
    visiting the pier and breakwater for recreation.

Chapter 5, Alternatives

Sub-Section 5.5.1, Alternative 1: No Project Alternative Description
Draft EIR Page 5-4:
       Under the No Project Alternative, none of the improvements associated with the project and the
       current uses would remain. Below is a summary of the No Project Alternative.
       • The pier, breakwater, and associated infrastructure for the ferry vessels would not be installed, and
         the pier would continue to deteriorate and remain closed to the public.
       • No new ferry service from Berkeley would be established and vehicle trips across the Bay would
         continue at their current rate.
       • No new public plaza would be installed.
       • None of the improvements along University Avenue or Seawall Drive would be installed, including
         no new cycle track, no upgraded bus facilities, and no Bay Trail Extension. Vehicles, buses,
         pedestrians, and bicyclists would continue to use the existing facilities.
       • The Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain in its current condition.
       • None of the construction associated with the project would occur.
       • Reasonably foreseeable projects, as identified in Table 3-1 would continue to be implemented.

Sub-Section 5.5.2, Alternative 1: No Project Alternative Impact Analysis
Draft EIR Page 5-8:

       Transportation
       Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure, public
       plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
       deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged, and vehicle trips
       across the Bay would continue at their current rate. At the project site, trips to the site for recreation
       would continue. In addition, if future development occurs at the Berkeley Waterfront, including but not
       limited to the development of a new restaurant at 199 Seawall Drive, local VMT would increase.
       Regionally, VMT would increase over time with projected regional growth, University Avenue would
       not undergo any safety improvements, and emergency evacuation capabilities would remain
       constrained. Alternative 1 transportation impacts would be less than significant.
       The proposed project’s impact related to transportation would be less than significant (see Section
       3.12, Transportation). Alternative 1 would have a greater impact related to transportation compared to
       the proposed project due to the lack of improvements on University Avenue that would improve
       circulation and pedestrian safety, the lack of zero-emission transportation infrastructure that would
       decrease VMT, and the lack of emergency evacuation capability improvements that the proposed
       project would provide.

Sub-Section 5.5.9, Alternatives Considered but Rejected
Draft EIR Page 5-27:
    Smaller scale ferry service. Under this potential alternative, smaller ferry vessels or a reduced ferry
    vessel schedule would be used. A smaller ferry or reduced ferry vessel schedule would still result in
    additional ferry vessels and would not reduce a significant environmental impact. Regarding
    biological resources, in general, fish and marine mammals potentially near the Berkeley waterfront
    are adapted to the high activity level of an active marina and would avoid ferry boats as they now
    avoid commercial and recreational boaters. An alternative that would introduce a smaller scale ferry
    service would still have the same potential impact. Therefore, this alternative would not reduce any
    environmental impacts. Similarly, the use of smaller vessels or smaller scale ferry service would also
    not avoid or substantially lessen significant environmental impacts associated with dredging.
    Regardless of vessel size or the schedule of ferry vessels, ferry operations would still require in-water
    improvements and construction activities within the San Francisco Bay to provide safe vessel access
    and passenger boarding facilities and therefore, although a smaller vessel could potentially reduce
    dredging requirements, there is no assurance that dredging would be avoided altogether. In addition,
    to the extent that a smaller scale ferry service or smaller ferry vessel could operate from within the
    Berkeley Marina using an existing berth or marina facilities, such an alternative would present similar
    operational and feasibility concerns as the Berkeley Marina Basin alternative (refer to Section 2.2.12,
    Topical Response: In-Marina Ferry Terminal Alternative, of the Final EIR). Similar to the Berkeley Marina
    Basin alternative, a smaller scale ferry service or smaller ferry vessel would result in operational
    inefficiencies and decreased reliability, as ferry operations within the marina would be subject to
    maneuvering constraints, increased docking and departure times, and potential conflicts with
    slipholders. Furthermore, a substantially smaller ferry service or smaller ferry vessel would not fully
    meet the project’s basic objective of providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero-emission
    public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco, as a smaller vessel or substantially reduced
    service schedule would lessen the project’s capacity to improve regional connectivity and reduce
    single-occupancy vehicle trips. Because this alternative would not reduce significant environmental
    impacts and would not meet the project’s basic objective of providing efficient ferry service, this
    alternative has been considered but rejected.

Sub-Section 2.5.1, Waterside (Sub-Section Proposed Ferry Vessel Infrastructure)
Draft EIR Page 2-10:
       The proposed ferry vessel infrastructure would include up to two 120-foot-long and 10-foot-wide
       gangways9 that would bring passengers from the pier to the two proposed boarding floats10, which
       would measure approximately 135 feet in length and 42 feet in width. Each float would include 4 to 6
       steel guide piles to moor the floats in place. In addition, there would be a total of 6 donut fenders (2
       at the end of each float and 2 near the breakwater), each of which would be 6-feet in diameter and
       would require a 3-foot pile. Since publication of the Draft EIR, the project design has been refined to
       include additional fender piles11 and donut fenders12 (steel protection piles, 36-inches in diameter)
       located adjacent to the ferry berthing area and around portions of the breakwater and turning basin.
       These protection piles would function as passive marine safety features and would supplement the
       guide piles and donut fender system associated with the proposed ferry facilities. The protection
       piles are intended to provide additional protection for waterside infrastructure during vessel approach
       and docking operations, including in the unlikely event of a vessel loss-of-control incident (see
       Section 3.12, Transportation).
       9.
         Gangway is defined as a raised platform or walkway that provides a passage. For the proposed
       project, the gangway would provide passage from the pier to the float.
       10.
             Floats are defined as structures buoyant in water.
         Fender piles are marine protective structures designed to absorb or deflect vessel impact and help
       11.

       prevent contact with adjacent facilities.
       12.
          Donut fenders are circular energy-absorbing devices installed around piles or other marine
       structures to cushion vessel contact and reduce the transfer of impact forces during docking
       maneuvers or other low-speed vessel movements.

Sub-Section 2.6.1, Construction Activities and Equipment (Sub-Section Piles)
Draft EIR Page 2-27:
       The landside retaining wall would be a mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) with a pre-case concrete
       panel face. Following the completion of the shoreline retaining wall and landside concrete abutment,
       the new pier would be constructed from the shoreline heading westward likely using a combination of
       a floating crane barge and shore-based cranes operating from the progressive extension of the newly
       constructed concrete abutment and pier. The 1,080-foot pier would be constructed using 24-inch
       octagonal precast concrete piles (24-inch concrete piles). Two 24-inch concrete piles would be
       installed approximately every 25 feet using a combination of jetting and impact pile driving. At the
       landside interface approximately 2 steel piles will be driven through the existing rock dike using a
       crane and a combination of vibratory and impact hammers. The construction of the pier would
       progress westward to include construction of the landing floats using 24-inch concrete vertical piles
       and eventually construction of loading ramps, and adjacent donut fender piles and fender piles using
       36-inch steel pipe piles as support guide piles. The 36-inch steel pipe piles anchoring the UCFs and
       donut fenders would be installed using a combination of vibratory and impact pile driving hammers.
       To complete the project and to help protect the ferry boarding areas and reduce wave energy, a
       concrete sheet pile breakwater perpendicular to the new pier would be constructed using 24-inch
       concrete batter piles and interlocking 48-inch x 14-inch prestressed concrete sheet piles (sheet piles)
       using a combination of jetting and impact pile driving hammers for the 24-inch concrete batter piles
       and sheet piles. Four 12-inch Precast Prestressed Concrete Marker Piles would be installed along the
       dredged channel to identify the limits of the dredged channel. Table 2-1 provides a summary of the
       kinds of piles and the number of piles that are proposed.

Draft EIR page 2-28:
    Dredging is the process of removing sediment from the bottom of waterbodies to make waterways
    deeper for boats. The following specifications represent the maximum extent of potential dredging;
    however, further design may decrease the proposed dredging footprint and/or volume. Nonetheless,
    for the purposes of environmental analysis, this Environmental Impact Report uses these
    conservative assumptions.
    As part of the proposed project, dredging would be conducted north of the closed pier. Dredging
    would be needed along the existing 100-foot wide United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)-
    designated federal navigation channel that parallels the closed pier and which future ferry vessels
    would use to travel to and from the pier. Refer to Figure 2-2 for the location of dredging. The dredging
    footprint represents a maximum envelope wherein dredging would occur and not all the areas shown
    in Figure 2-2 would be dredged. Rather, the exact location of the dredging channel will be refined as
    the project advances in its design. As needed, the final design plans will identify areas where buoys
    will be employed to identify the limits of dredging or anchoring, or to avoid sensitive areas outside of
    the dredging footprint. In addition, dredging would be needed for the turning basin, which would allow
    for ferry vessels to turn and dock at the two ferry boarding floats. Dredging would be done to a
    maximum depth of minus 12.51 feet City of Berkeley mean lower low water (MLLW)22, which is equal
    to -12 feet National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) MLLW. A maximum total of
    400,000 cubic yards of dredged materials would be generated and would require disposal.
    22.
          The 12.51 feet measurement uses City of Berkeley Datum.
